What a stellar remake of an already amazing game! I first picked up Spelunky Classic a year or two after it came out, and found myself thoroughly addicted for months. I was hesitant to pick up this version since I had already seen everything Classic had to offer, but Spelunky HD did not let me down. The new areas, enemies and items breathed new life into an old classic and the gameplay tweaks made it a much more polished experience.
Pros:
* Detailed new graphics brimming with personality.
* A jazzy, memorable new soundtrack. Miles better than the old one.
* Loads of new content. The game is about 50% bigger than the original.
* Achievements, which let veteran players push their skills to the limit.
* Dog kissing parlors.
Cons:
* The more organic physics take some getting used to.
* Missing some features Classic had, like some Kali rewards and a playable Tunnel Man.
* The new enemies and obstacles made an already-insane game even more difficult.
Overall, I'd highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed Spelunky Classic. And if you haven't played Spelunky Classic yet, give it a shot before you try this game out to see if it's for you.

I had fun with this game; I think any fan of South Park would like it.  A few caveats though:
1- The game is pretty short, especially for an RPG with a $60 price tag.  That being said, after 20 hours of the game, it had sort of run its course. The last few hours, I felt pretty impatient to get the game over with.
2- The novelty of the South Park setting wears off a little bit from the Stick of Truth.  Maybe there is more the developers could have done to fix that.  The expanded roster of allies is a plus, though.
3- Character growth and development is usually an important part of an RPG, but this game is pretty lackluster in that regard. You don't make many decisions for your character and none of the decisions really have any feeling of permeancy to them.
In short, the $59.99 price tag is really way too high for the game you end up getting; and there is a good chance that the DLC won't be worth the purchase price either.   I certainly would recommend not buying the DLC because I didn't finish the game feeling like I really wanted more.

It's a nice game, but it gets a bit boring if you don't play with a big group of friends.
Anyway, I still recommend it.
(Tip: buy it when in discount)

Coming hot off the heels of finally giving Burnout Paradise a go, I was eager for some more silly arcade racing goodness. Post Apocalyptic Mayhem has been collecting dust for quite a while and it looked (from the screenshots) that it would fit the bill perfectly.
I really adore the over-the-top and entirely impractical vehicles of destruction; my personal favorite was immediately the school bus. I jumped immediately into the first course and, within 30 seconds, was really disappointed. The game performs lovely, and visually it may not be able to compete with the likes of Mad Max but it’s nothing to complain about. Had this been any other genre, I would say the handling was abysmal; however, the floaty and silly vehicle physics fit right in with the style. Here’s the problem: it is SO SLOW. And I don’t mean that driving a 4 ton school bus outfitted with steel plate armor was a bit sluggish. On the contrary, I flew past everyone else on the track with very little effort. The problem is that there is literally no sense of speed. If I had to guess the approximate top speed I reached, I would say roughly 50-60 MPH with the rocket boost held down. There was zero thrill to navigating the course. What disheartens me more is that the problem couldn’t be solved with a simple edit of the vehicle data files because the levels are clearly not designed for any faster speed.
I loved the weapons and the vehicular combat. When I slowed down enough to engage the other drivers I had a blast flipping them over my head and peppering them with napalm cluster mines, but everything was just so slow and unenthusiastic. The excitement of any exchange of blows was immediately sapped away by the dull driving experience. I do not believe PAM is a bad game by any stretch of the imagination, but it’s not a game I would suggest a friend to pick up. I would be really excited to see a more aggressive and faster sequel because I think they have a decent foundation to work with here.

Post Apocalyptic Mayhem has more strategy than your average vehicle combat racing game and that's where it shines. The goal here is to get the most kills while on a closed circuit track rather than winning a race. A simple make it to the finish line would be too easy. Since you want the most kills, if you're in first place you had best slow down and let the others catch up to you so you can wreck them. However, then you risk them overtaking you and the person in front always has the advantage when only one weapon is designed for a forward attack.
Each of the game's twelve vehicles has their own set of three weapons. The front attack is usually something that shoots forward, the side attack sprays out mines of some sort and the back attack drops something. These weapons all do something slightly different. The childhood dreams school bus has a cow catcher that will throw a vehicle, the alchemist RV has an ooze gun. The logger has side saw blades, while another vehicle has mines that will throw you into reverse. The side and back attacks are temporary and disappear after a moment. When you use them a rear view camera appears so you can see if anyone hits them for your own fiendish glee. When you kill someone a notice pops up on the screen.
You can have all three of your weapons ready by driving through colored barrels. Blue is the side weapon, yellow is the front, red is the rear. Black barrels give you a random charge. Having three weapons at once makes you dangerous. In fact everyone here is dangerous. You need to watch your opponents for a red, blue or yellow glow on on each respective area. Well if there's a glow on their front you'll never see it coming. There is full camera control, but the problem is you need to rotate the camera to face behind you rather than a quick look behind you. Another shame is no indicator to warn you that someone is on your six.
To get into the lead position you have a nitro boost and a lot of it. If you run out, you can find more in green barrels, but otherwise it refills after a brief moment. This boost is more than a slow thrust, so there's no logic to using it. When you get a small amount of it, use it.
Your vehicle has health, so getting hit with a falling log or running over ice spikes still gives you a chance of surviving. If you die, wreck or even respawn, you lose all of your charged weapons and keep what's left of your used nitro. So Post Apocalyptic Mayhem has good strategy rather than quick and crazy car combat.
The courses are designed to make use of this combat with several sections that break up a map into narrow stalls, larger areas and bottlenecks. Kills are almost guaranteed without quick thinking to play defensive and let others through a narrow corridor or nitro ahead and leave barrels or fire for the others to run through. There are several different paths with each track so you always have a chance of finding a safe path to get ahead.
There's an arcade mode that lets you play one track at a time, but I much prefer the apocalyptic challenge which has you playing all eight tracks back to back with a score after each one and a final score at the conclusion. This mode makes it feel like a deeper game even if its limited. The game does offer multiplayer online with ranked matches, but four years after a budget title's release means the game is inevitably dead for multiplayer. I would have enjoyed it, because medium felt easy and the hard difficulty while it was still fun, it was difficult to exceed second to last place.
The vehicles all have character and there's a wide variety each with their own stats for acceleration handling and mayhem.  You have nine unlocked from the start and can select between a pair of dune buggies, a little car with a unicorn head that has a giant twisting drill, another small nuclear themed car and a few others. You'll need to purchase DLC with the ice cream truck, 1950s squad car and classic tow truck. On sale, I'd go for it. I'd advise against smaller vehicles, because a smaller body size means its tougher to hit the barrels to get weapon charges.
If you think there's a balance to smaller vehicles having less body to hit with weapons, you'd be wrong, because the weapons really scatter out making them tough to avoid without stopping. The mines themselves are tiny and blinking, so they're tough to even see.
The game plays like a lot of other racers with a chase cam and I feel like the game was really designed with a 360 controller in mind. Everything is color coated to the controller, even the barrels. Its true arcade style racing with throttle controls of forward and reverse. There is a hard brake, even if I never had to brake. Slowing down to let opponents catch up just meant I had to let off the forward.
Now that I've discussed the good, let's turn to the bad. The weight of each vehicle is so light it felt like driving a balloon with tires. Its difficult to stay grounded even in a logging rig, a school bus or an RV. There are a lot of jumps and ramps, but I'm talking about in general you can be driving on the walls. Coming down from a high jump can bounce you back up. Its ridiculous and it took me thirty minutes before I stopped laughing at the game and had some fun with it. You can also boost through the air, because your boost is a rocket rather than strict nitrous.
As for the graphics and art direction, it just looks faded and worn. I feel like I could enjoy the game more if the colors were bolder and it was more than a dusty covered look to them. I would say a dusty brown, but one of the eight courses feels little more than a happy winter wonderland of a previous course where rather than having brown sand blowing in the breeze its a snow dusting.
Another interesting thing is how much the demo or trailer plays in game if you wait too long in the menu. I enjoy when games have demos or trailers and it seems to be what's missing from games now, but it plays a little too often.
There's a lot working against the game despite all its positives. Its still far from a good game, but it was entertaining once I stopped laughing at it and found the strategy involved. In a sequel I would love more levels, more modes and a different, more vibrant art direction. I think a lot of people will hate it for how simplistic the weapons are with side, front and back coupled with the fact each vehicle's weapons are different and there are better vehicles.
If you find it on sale, take a risk.

After reading a rather terribly negative review on Rock paper Shotgun about this series of games, I felt obliged, after just recently having finished it, to write a review. Deponia is a colourful, not too long adventure game set on a planet full of trash. The setting, in my opinion, was vivid and interesting and highlighted at parts a social political sense of class division, which was not so much explored in the first game yet, but is promising for the other games afterwards.
Rufus is not your typical hero main character. In fact he is not very likeable at all. His humour is insulting at best, he is scruffy, goofy, not so intelligent, selfish and mostly mean. But that, to me, made the game perfectly charming. Whilst I feel as though the main character deserves every bit of bad luck coming to him, it was amusing to watch him. I agreed more with the irritated characters around him than with him personally, but it was refreshing to see that sort of character and reflect on his actions as handled through the player.
I personally find stories with dislikeable characters far more interesting than the typical likeable ones, and Daedalic has a talent for having unusual main characters take the spotlight. That being said, deponia is one of these games that should not be taken as offensive or as too seriously. The game's humour, in my percetion, relies on the meanness and dislikability of the main character, and if one is easily offended or insists on politically correct representation of everything, this game may not be the best option for them.
Anyone however who doesn't need to overthink such things and can enjoy a little ruder humour might very well enjoy the deponia series with a few nice puzzles, charmingly frustrated characters and colourful settings. Maybe not Daedalic's best piece of work in my opinion, but definitly worth a play.

I played many top down shooters before, but none are this satisfying. All the things you could possible want from a top down shooter is present in the game; you can pump up your stats by leveling and there are shops at the end of each level to buy new guns. The only downfall is that it’s terribly short; most should be able to beat this game with relative ease in around 2 hours. Not a must buy, but if it’s on sale for a dollar, you would be doing a disservice to yourself by not buying and playing it.

I purchased Train Simulator around six weeks ago, so now I'm pretty familiar with the ins and outs of the game and I feel like I can write a meaningful review. First thing to say is that, although I like trains and I like simulation games, this was the first train simulator I'd bought, and tbh the it was only the fact that it was on sale that made me consider it.
I've had some fun with it. The game play itself is basically about sticking to timetables, avoiding speeding, thinking ahead to upcoming signals and stopping in time at the stations etc. So although it has a fairly steep learning curve when you first start playing, once you've played it for a few weeks it's pretty easy to master and there's not really much of a challenge after that initial learning phase.
The graphics are good, in my opinion, and are the best thing about the game. Other than that, I'm not so sure I'll be playing this very frequently. It gets kind of monotonous and there are only a limited number of 'career challenges' with each route. There is also a 'Free drive' functionality, but that really isn't enough for me - I need a task to complete.
But the biggest drawback to this game is that you have to purchase new routes, and they don't come cheap - not at all! Typically a new route will set you back about 20 euros and it might have about 10 or 12 challenges (and some routes, amazingly, come with hardly any challenges at all). So all in all, I've got quite mixed feelings about this. It has potential, but either there should be more routes free with the base game or the routes should be cheaper and have more challenges. Although I've enjoyed playing, I was also left feeling a little ripped off when I found out that you have to keep shelling out for new routes.

Cons.

Overall, it's a great game and is going in the right direction.

2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

The reviews I read before playing this made me apprehensive... they made it sound kind of sentimental. The problem there is many of those reviewers don't realise this is a true faery tale. True in the sense that this is what a faery tale is meant to be, not some Disney-fied crap that makes kids feel special, but a bleak and beautiful story that is meant to educate some core life lessons to push kids to GROW UP, while also reminding adults that life can be a balance between the bleak and beautiful.

I can see myself replaying this for the story and general experience a few more times, and a few years down the line too.

Oh Tekken, one of the iconic cornerstones of fighting games that have been around since the '90s, and now it's finally on PC. This review aims to go a bit in-depth within the different design choices and fun element the 7th installment (other than the Tag series) has to offer. Though finally, Steam users can experience the gleeful combat that is Tekken on their PC, the game isn't really without its design flaws and faults.
1) Visuals and Design:
- It looks great, and it runs great, especially on a mid-tier PC. It's playable on an Nvidia 840M, a dated video card all the way from 2011. If you're questioning whether you're able to run it, chances are 85% you can, unless you still run XP or have an i3. The game is broken down individually among Story Mode, Arcade Mode, Treasure Battle, and Online Battle. Story Mode is quite lengthy with the cutscenes, and is of average quality. Arcade Mode is your classic stage brawler, beating up foes until you reach the final boss. Not much as changed. Treasure Battle has you beating up an endless chain of enemies at your own leisure, with every victory dropping certain customization items and clothes for any character in the game. Online mode can be quite fun, yet jerky at times. A few moments, I ran into some frame dips while fighting online, and there were definitely moments in which the game froze. The team at Bandai Namco is making some efforts to try to polish the online mode even more. There's no form you need to fill out before you get into a battle, there's no hard tutorial you need to pass, there's no red tape; you simply pick a mode, pick a character, pick a stage, and go. No fumbling around anywhere; every design framework is catered to be as easy and simplistic as possible.
However, there are an ample number of characters the player cannot play as. Devil Kazuya (with the exception of Story Mode) and Devil Kazumi are both unplayable characters, yet are necessary to advance the plot. While this design choice can be understood to some extent, it reduces the overall customizability of the game, just being able to play a character who is clearly out of grasp. There are a number of characters, yet it doesn't feel quite "complete" already unlocking every single one of them from the start.
It gets an 8.5/10.
2) Interface and menus:
- The game's interface is quite clean and sleek compared to older titles. Nothing is too cluttered when it comes to opening menus and adjusting options. However, assigning buttons to play with a keyboard can be daunting at times, which is why this game is garnered toward controller users as its main priority. Gamepad users are also welcome to plug in their devices, while keyboard users may have some buggy issues with ghosting (being unable to press a combination of three or four keys at a time). The menus are flashy in itself, perfectly harmonizing with the tone of the rest of the game. Not to mention the customizable health bar, which only involves putting custom borders around it. It's a good design choice, something to add a bit more individuality to the feel of Tekken 7; it looks exactly what it defines: Tekken 6 + 1.
However, the issue with Tekken 7 lies within the loading screens in between gameplay. I hate having to do treasure battle only to be interrupted with a 15-30 second long dark loading screen. It slows the paces of battles and the flow of overall gameplay. While the game requires much processing power, it's a shame that there are still long loading screens, even on the console version.
Overall, it gets an 8/10.
3) Gameplay:
- Tekken's overall feel and look of its fighting mechanics has been nothing short of amazing since its inception. Movements flow quite well, similar to that of Tekken Tag 2 and Tekken 6; the animations are largely unchanged, unless you're looking at minor tweaks and buffs to certain fighting scenarios that may happen 5% of the time. The flow of every match during battle is quite nice with responsive keys, combo inputs, and rage tactics.
While the rage tactics seem to be a controversial topic, I find it to be quite a refreshing look on Tekken's fighting system. Though it delves away from the classic Tekken experience, new things are often encouraged, though a toggle option to switch rage arts from on to off would be better to keep things fresh and customizable. Whether you enjoy learning characters through the combo system, or frantically mashing buttons to knock your enemy out, Tekken 7's got both down as great.
The camera zooms in when both fighters are attacking at once, providing a reasonable outlook for your response time when you launch counter attacks, giving you the opportunity to win a close fight. You get to watch your victories and failures as they happen in slow-motion for better analysis.
The moves haven't changed compared to Tekken 6, with many of the tactics largely taken from the same game. However, to ensure that Tekken 7 wasn't a copy-paste game from that of 6, new characters with unique movesets were also introduced to keep the game fresh. Though it doesn't offer much variety besides the moves given to the player based on the character they play, There is still variety for those ambitious enough to learn the game's combo and juggle systems.
If you're aiming to kill some time, it's nice to hop on casually and beat up a few opponents. You're playing a fighting game and a beat-em-up! There's nothing more fun than skillfully pummeling supermodels with aggression, and that is exactly what Tekken 7 for the PC offers!
It gets a 9/10.
4) Content:
- Is Tekken 7 ripe with content? Yes and no. The initial Story Mode can be beaten in roughly 4-5 hours, 6-7 if you are watching the cutscenes from start to finish. Treasure mode is endless. Arcade isn't mandatory, though for achievements? Most likely. All of the content still revolves around fighting however, as there isn't a current gamemode other than a 1v1 brawl with another character. There's little variety.
Most of the content comes with the perk of unlocking custom options for your intended character in the customization feature. You must rely on treasure battles that drop random loot in order to earn a specific piece of clothing for your character. While it gives the player incentive to play the treasure battle, the overall feel of grinding for a piece of clothing for a character is a big negative due to its repetitiveness. Then again, players aren't really meant to be playing Tekken 7 for 10 hours at a time.
With the Season Pass coming in at $25, the amount of content that it unlocks at the start is quite minimal. It gives you access to 2 characters in the upcoming future, as well as gold outfits for your characters. Not the content I was expecting at all. I would definitely recommend getting it on sale. If you're paying more than $10, you're getting ripped off. Regardless, even with the amount of things the Season Pass offers, you'll still be doing the same thing: fighting characters on and off with the same system.
Content for this game deserves a 7/10 at its current state.
5) Overall:
- Do I recommend the game? Yes.
- Should I buy it now? Yes.
- Should I buy the Season Pass? Right now, no. Wait for a sale.
Tekken 7 gets an 8.1/10.

The rare times you can actually connect to the servers in the first place, make it past character select without the game dropping, make it past the character intros, make it past the "fight" announcement without it dropping - the connection will almost assuredly be so poor that the best you can do is spam combos on downed opponents with the knowledge that if they block when they get up you'll be safe because they can't punish because of the delay, or if they hit a button your combo will hit them, knock them down, and then you repeat the process.

Brought to you by Daedalic Entertainment, Deponia is the first installment of a point and click trilogy. Amidst the top reviews on Steam right now, I will start this review out by saying that this game is NOT for those who do not enjoy stupid humor along the lines of Futurama, and/or those who cannot appreciate a challenging point and click title; or for those who do not understand that guides exist, for those of us who still enjoy point and clicks... but ultimately suck at them (yep, that last one is me!).
To this day, I have never been let down by Daedalic, and fortunately Deponia is no exception to the rule. The game is an outstanding throwback to old cartoon point and clicks from the late 90's and early 00's, with its intentional frame skipping animations, bright and colorful scenery, and vibrantly detailed character personalities. The whole thing screams "childhood" for those of us who grew up in the era of Windows 95 and 98, and perhaps that nostalgia is what we really cling to with this title. However, that isn't to say that the entire experience isn't enjoyable; Deponia is simply the first entry of a trilogy, and while the story isn't exactly riveting, it does a good job of setting up for the remaining two entries.
Players will take on the role of Rufus, a lovable idiot who really does have the best of intentions, but fails constantly to properly execute any plans that he may have. He honestly reminds me of Fry from Futurama, with his quirky dumbness and heart of gold that is led astray by him succumbing to whatever he desires; for instance, a lollipop over the better grade brain implant needed for his girlfriend. Rufus lives on the planet of Deponia, in the town of Kovaq, which is nothing but a junk heap from horizon to horizon. Rufus desperately wishes to escape the landfill, to the planet above Deponia called Elysium, and the game starts off with him on his first attempt to get there. Along the way, gamers are introduced to a hefty range of entities, including an Elysium woman named Goal; whom Rufus of course sees as his way to escape Deponia. Most of the other personalities within the game have just as much depth as Rufus and Goal, although some of them fall to the wayside as well.
Aesthetically, Deponia is an incredibly stunning game; from the many vibrantly colored scenes, to the well animated cutscenes. Every scene that the player will visit has a radically different appearance, and it's easy to get sucked into the junkyard that surrounds you. Not only are the visuals pleasing, but the soundtrack is one that you will not grow tired of quickly. Speaking of the soundtrack, between chapters there is a hobo who sings amusing songs; it really is one of the highlights to the game, so much so that it carried on throughout the franchise. It really is the absurd, stupid humor of the Deponia franchise that has caused it to become so popular over the years, and the singing hobo is just one great example of it.
The actual gameplay of Deponia is tough, and it has caused many people to give up on finishing the game. It's really one of those "take a wild guess" at what to do next point and clicks, but luckily in this advanced age of the internet and technology, many guides are available to assist when you inevitably get stuck. For those who don't believe in guides, you will have many hours of figuring out some complex conundrums ahead of you. For those of us who take the easy way out, you will pretty well solve everything in around 6-7 hours. For an extra added difficulty, once you complete the game once, you are able to playthrough again under the Druggeljug setting if you so wish; where every single word in the game is replaced with Druggeljug... this includes items, scenes, cutscenes, dialogue, and dialogue options.
Even though Deponia has a somewhat lackluster ending, it's important to remember that this entry is the first within the trilogy, and it is simply here to set up the remainder of the story. Despite its complexity, it's an incredibly immersive and wonderfully executed point and click title in both story and gameplay. The characters are memorable, the setting is unique, the humor is scattered in all the right spots, and Daedalic will have you hungering for more by the end of the game. Like I said at the beginning of the review, if stupid humor and complex problem solving are not your things, you're better off finding a different franchise to invest in. For the rest of us, there is the Deponia series, and it's one that I highly recommend.

Video format for people who prefer it:
Written first Impressions (6 hours pre-release):
Wasted: A Post-Apocalyptic Pub Crawler is a FPS rogue-like with several issues holding it back from being a great game. Instead it's just a good one that can be very frustrating for a lot of wrong reasons.
Like in many rogue-likes, dying plays a major role here. In many other rogue-likes, when you die you lose just about everything and have to start over from scratch. However, you are able to keep unlocks, achievements and other rewards to give the player a sense of progressing even after dying countless times. One of the reasons rogue-likes get away with not making players go nuts after they lose everything (usually) is because of their short length and RNG loot system. Games like FTL and The Bingings of Isaac can be completed in about an hour and even quicker if you get a good streak of rewards. Of course you can still lose everything but easy come, easy go. Wasted tries a different approach. Sure, you lose everything when you die but you can run across these courier boxes (once unlocked through a random encounter with an NPC) whereby you can store items to be picked up later even after you die. The game is designed differently than other rogue-likes. Instead of being able to complete the game in an hour, the game has deep progression in that you have multiple dungeons to explore with multiple levels as well as towns with NPCs that give you quests in those areas. The game also has a buyback system. Unfortunately, this might be currently bugged as it has never worked for me but how it should work is whenever you die you are able to buyback some or all the items you lost from the vendors who also give you back your stuff you deposited. It's a cool system that utilizes your in-game currency. Again, it never seemed to work for me which is a major issue. Especially if I am in a long stretch of dungeon with some rare items and I can't find a courier box and I get killed before I do. The game also tries to be more predictable than most rogue-likes. Rooms often repeat themselves but you can expect where one room will begin and where it will end (or won't). Wasted is trying to be more of an adventure game than a rogue-like and it does so surprisingly well when all the stars align (which is most of the time).
Visually, the game doesn't look good. It runs decent but there are a lot of low-res assets, especially the textures. Music is okay if not a bit repetitive only changing after several floors or in a different area. Voice acting and dialogue is pretty cheesy and the humor is crude. The game seems to take heavy inspiration from Fallout and Borderlands in its artistic department and even some of the dialogue down to the actual color and font of the text. It thankfully doesn't take itself seriously but it won't get a lot of laughs although I did chuckle every now and then though.
The game-play is strong with this one but it does have its issues like I previously mentioned. One of the biggest problems aside from the buyback system is how you are encouraged to complete a level as quickly as possible but the game is designed for a slower pace. Let me explain, this game has a lot of traps. Now what's cool about the traps and the enemies themselves is how you can pit them against each other. You can have suicide bombers hit a bear trap, get stuck, and blow up the dudes behind them. You can also open up a room full of infected ghoul-like creatures to attack and blow up on enemy raiders. There's a lot of variety and fun to be had and unlike most rogue-likes: Not everyone is teamed up to kill you. But there is one problem with this: By having no brightness and no FOV (field of view) options to speak of, the game is incredibly hard to navigate through sometimes. Especially with the map that you cannot pop out and view in full (restricted to mini-map view only). This is all on a timer for each level. You need to get to the end of the dungeon (or close to the end) to find a beer bottle to drink and get buffs which can also teleport you out of the dungeon and back to your home, keeping all your stuff. If you don't get to the next floor before this invisible timer expires, the game sends a machine-gun toting death-bot at you. Now I understand that this gives tension. You need to sneak through the game but also do it quickly enough to avoid this death-bot. The problem is the darkness makes it almost impossible to see half the traps in the game. The lightning isn't great and it feels like you are fumbling through the dark at times. The death-bot also highlights another issue with the game: Knock-back. So in the game you have some weird physics. You can almost moon jump and sometimes I have been shot into a ceiling (never stuck permanently though) but that can be annoying. What's really annoying is getting shot by this death-bot and getting pushed all the way to a wall because of the gunfire knock-back and getting spun around all while frantically using health items (of which there are a timer on to use so that adds even more time to exploring an are) and you're only paying attention to half the stuff on the screen at a time because your vision is splattered with blood and you can't pause to open the map so you end up losing AT LEAST 1/3 of your life within seconds. If you are on low health and you reach a dead-end with a death-bot behind you. You are boned. The biggest issues in this game can be fixed with a day one patch (most likely) but the balancing for how it handles difficulty needs some more time.
I think Wasted is a great game buried under problems that make it a good or just above average game with a lot of frustrating elements. It's definitely ambitious and I want to see more from the developer (free content updates would be rad). If they can patch the buyback then it's worth a pick-up if you at all a fan of the genre. I consider myself a casual fan and I sunk nearly 6 hours into the game already.
Thanks for reading.

You are (randomized character name) and you are one of the drunkards who drinks booze for buffs and perks throughout his adventure for more booze in the underground coolers (vaults)
Pro’s
+Original radio music
+Unique loveable characters
+Wide variety of weapons and customizations
+Fast gunplay, gameplay and replay value
+Randomized dungeons (coolers)
+Permanent perks and separate short term dungeon buffs
+Humorous dialogue: The dialogue stays somewhat close to home with Fallout with a sort of hilarious, twisted and bizarre, but relatable sense of humor (While not to dark) having silly, but strangely loveable characters.
My personal favorite so far being Val Killmore the total bro dude

Neutrals
Art style: The art style I personally find visually pleasing, but most likely will vary player to player
Semi-permadeath (you keep missions you were doing and can buy back special one of a kind items you lost your previous life but besides that, RIP items that you didn’t store safely at your house)
The S.O.B Purifier: High level enemy that follows you with a minigun when you take
AGES in levels, I personally don’t mind it and I think it changes up the gameplay, but others have complained about it on the discussions before.
RNG Flasks: Let me explain, there are 2 kinds of drinks in the game, Flasks and Beers. When you drink a beer you get a hangover (a permanent perk) that carry’s over with you for the rest of the game (In some cases you can remove it) downing a beer to avoid death to make it back out of the cooler is a cool and safe strat to do if you’re about to die, even if you get a negative hangover (IE: +10% Melee damage taken from enemies) The beers are cool in my opinion, but the flasks, THE FLASKS….
The flasks either carry positive, neutral, or negative buffs; but always seems to work against you in the end, either screwing you over, or giving you some lucky god tier runs. I’ve had to drink beers and get hangovers that are barely beneficial or just debuffs. I’ll type out a couple of examples of them
+Hairy feet: +3 Sneak
+Unbearable: Bear traps only deal 50% damage
+Trappin’: Bear traps no longer stun you
+Heavy Knuckles: +3 Hit
♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Bricks: A brick spawns on enemy corpses per kill
-Big Feet: -5 Sneak
-Soft Knuckles: -5 Hit
-Half life: Max hp halved Nice science joke btw
See the trend here? It’s like this for all of the characters buffs you gain from the flasks, the positive buffs are WAY outweighed by the negative buffs, while the positives give +3 to a stat the negatives give -5 to a stat; not to mention some of the positive buffs are BEARly beneficial

Con’s
-Unfair Randomized dungeon rooms: Sometimes the game will give you rooms with locked doors, some of the time you opening them can get you killed by some really silly ways. (My favorite so far has been dying by opening a locked door, being welcomed to a shotgun trap that triggers, blasting me in the face along with mutant freak men that open fire on me with assault rifles ending in my death)
-Enemy’s bullets and projectiles have WAY to much knockback
-Bad voice acting/quality: Most of the voice over’s are spot on and really deliver perfectly, but some characters voice over’s seem somewhat low quality (Not god awful, but enough to notice and be irritating)
-Frames Per Second: This only happens to me on the outside hub areas (where you don't fight at) but is still annoying none the less, while not too bad it still makes my FPS go from 80 FPS in cooler to 35-50 Outside.
I got this game 4 days before the launch and time I am writing this at (6/7/2016) from the Humble Monthly subscription (12$) after originally only subscribing to get Rocket League from the group of games, WASTED has been my favorite from the group, and I’ve honestly had a blast playing this rage inducing masterpiece, and wish there were other games like it out there. Everything about it seems planed out and works together well enough to support its ridiculousness and silly story that you actually find yourself slowly interested in it. So far this is my favorite game of 2016.

Well as I type this there is are no user reviews so I may as well be the first.
What we have here is a cartoonish rogue-like RPG FPS that doesn't take itself seriously and gets most of its inspiration from Fallout. The game is actually much more challenging than it appears from the marketing above and the the tutorial makes it seem easier than it really is as well.     Basically most of the game is dungeon crawling  in search of radioactive booze you cannot leave the dungeon until you find and drink one and each comes with permanent effects whether positive or negative.
The game play is simple to understand but quite the challenge.   Every enemy from  radiated dogs,  raiders,  zombies,  robot, and a power armored enemy  that comes to kill you if you take too long (more on that in a bit)  are all basically suicidal they have no concern for their lives and will rush at you  some of the humans even strap bombs on themselves and do massive damage.    There are also some oddities with the AI  for example the raiders will fight the dogs and zombies when encountered but they won't begin the battle until you've come very close.  Meaning they are peacefully sitting in rooms with each other until you get close.   If I had to guess why, I bet it has to do with the developer not wanting the AI on the entire floor to be processed all at once to ease the user's CPU use for very low end PC gamers.
So as you explore the dungeons or "Coolers" as the game calls them enemies aren't the only hazard sentry guns, radioactive goo,  land mines, bear traps are all around so you can't carelessly run through.   Loot is also gained in this  armor, weapons, consumables  the usual they typically have amusing names and descriptions  however the user's inventory is very limited until you find accessories that add spaces.   This can become a burden because everything takes up one space even ammo  so really each ranged weapon really requires 2 spaces for the weapon itself and the ammo.  Naturally you will want to wear armor  so  chest, legs, head is yet 3 more used up.  See the issue when you only start with 10 inventory spaces?    How you personally feel about item management is likely going to play a role in how much you enjoy this game.
Now here is the largest make or break  factor to the enjoyment of this game.  There is overpowered and extremely hard to beat in the early game enemy that comes after you if you remain on a floor for too long.    By "too long" I mean really not long at all you don't get much time to explore before it arrives and hunts you down.   This can be frustrating as you may not be anywhere near the exit and haven't even found the exit to the next floor yet and that thing is more than likely going to catch up to you.   If you like the idea of having to rush your butt off in dungeons you'll like this, if you're the type who loves to explore and are a completionist this is the biggest issue you will face with the game.
Lastly I think its worth noting that your first character you can name and adjust their looks (extremely limited) if you die you have deal a randomly generated character that follows.  It's not a big deal but something that caught me off guard.
Anyhow I enjoyed my time with it thus far and will continue to play it .  The game is quite fun and I recommend giving it a try.  I hope you found this review of it helpful.

The newest patch resolved some of the issue of the SOB power armored enemy.  He doesn't have the drastic knockback effect that he once had making him easier to survive if he begins to hit you.

And it must be noted that this game actually disappeared for quite some time from Steam Store only to quietly reappear at a later date. The reason for this seems simply to be because the developers disassociated themselves from the Meridian 4 group for a period of time. Even during the absence of this game on the store page, the PAM community was still playing it, with their friends quite frequently.
You will also notice that this game has what seems quite an absurd meta critic review score 44/100 when you compare it to the large amount of positive reviews from the gamers themselves. One of the biggest complaints to the game is that it has relatively few levels 7 all up and a handful of cars 12 only which some are quite decent.
The game is best described as a Mad Max version of Mario Kart. The objective is to not only be the fastest around the track, but also the one who has the most kills. Hence it is possible to win the game even coming in third place or something as long as those in first and second place do not have more kills than you.
To help you get the kills each car is fitted with a wide arrange of novelty weapons which only activate by running over the corresponding colored barrels on the race track. Each car has a weapon that shoots from the side of the car, shoots behind the car and shoots in front of the car, there is also a turbo boost you can pick up. Each directional weapon is color coded to a corresponding barrel color. While this may sound complicated you will pick up the idea within the first lap.
The cars handle really well and the map courses are quite eye pleasing and somewhat versatile when it comes to terrain. When the game suggests mayhem it aint kidding. On the harder difficulties you will spend most of your time bouncing around the screen by all the explosions thanks to your enemies. The game caters single player, multiplayer and campaign.
It must also be noted that there is a large amount of achievements that are dedicated to the multiplayer aspects of this game, the frustrating thing is that there are few that play the multiplayer online, unless they are playing with friends. So if your an achievement hunter you may wish to seriously think about buying the multiple pack of this game so that you can play it with your friends. This game is definitely fun and really quite decent, having said that I would still recommend that you wait for it to go on a sale.
Since the game was developed back in 2011, hopefully steel mokeys will one day stop scrathing and sniffing their behinds and give us more levels and dlc to please the players. There is serious potential here, but alas still only peanuts of material given.

Oh Tekken, one of the iconic cornerstones of fighting games that have been around since the '90s, and now it's finally on PC. This review aims to go a bit in-depth within the different design choices and fun element the 7th installment (other than the Tag series) has to offer. Though finally, Steam users can experience the gleeful combat that is Tekken on their PC, the game isn't really without its design flaws and faults.
1) Visuals and Design:
- It looks great, and it runs great, especially on a mid-tier PC. It's playable on an Nvidia 840M, a dated video card all the way from 2011. If you're questioning whether you're able to run it, chances are 85% you can, unless you still run XP or have an i3. The game is broken down individually among Story Mode, Arcade Mode, Treasure Battle, and Online Battle. Story Mode is quite lengthy with the cutscenes, and is of average quality. Arcade Mode is your classic stage brawler, beating up foes until you reach the final boss. Not much as changed. Treasure Battle has you beating up an endless chain of enemies at your own leisure, with every victory dropping certain customization items and clothes for any character in the game. Online mode can be quite fun, yet jerky at times. A few moments, I ran into some frame dips while fighting online, and there were definitely moments in which the game froze. The team at Bandai Namco is making some efforts to try to polish the online mode even more. There's no form you need to fill out before you get into a battle, there's no hard tutorial you need to pass, there's no red tape; you simply pick a mode, pick a character, pick a stage, and go. No fumbling around anywhere; every design framework is catered to be as easy and simplistic as possible.
However, there are an ample number of characters the player cannot play as. Devil Kazuya (with the exception of Story Mode) and Devil Kazumi are both unplayable characters, yet are necessary to advance the plot. While this design choice can be understood to some extent, it reduces the overall customizability of the game, just being able to play a character who is clearly out of grasp. There are a number of characters, yet it doesn't feel quite "complete" already unlocking every single one of them from the start.
It gets an 8.5/10.
2) Interface and menus:
- The game's interface is quite clean and sleek compared to older titles. Nothing is too cluttered when it comes to opening menus and adjusting options. However, assigning buttons to play with a keyboard can be daunting at times, which is why this game is garnered toward controller users as its main priority. Gamepad users are also welcome to plug in their devices, while keyboard users may have some buggy issues with ghosting (being unable to press a combination of three or four keys at a time). The menus are flashy in itself, perfectly harmonizing with the tone of the rest of the game. Not to mention the customizable health bar, which only involves putting custom borders around it. It's a good design choice, something to add a bit more individuality to the feel of Tekken 7; it looks exactly what it defines: Tekken 6 + 1.
However, the issue with Tekken 7 lies within the loading screens in between gameplay. I hate having to do treasure battle only to be interrupted with a 15-30 second long dark loading screen. It slows the paces of battles and the flow of overall gameplay. While the game requires much processing power, it's a shame that there are still long loading screens, even on the console version.
Overall, it gets an 8/10.
3) Gameplay:
- Tekken's overall feel and look of its fighting mechanics has been nothing short of amazing since its inception. Movements flow quite well, similar to that of Tekken Tag 2 and Tekken 6; the animations are largely unchanged, unless you're looking at minor tweaks and buffs to certain fighting scenarios that may happen 5% of the time. The flow of every match during battle is quite nice with responsive keys, combo inputs, and rage tactics.
While the rage tactics seem to be a controversial topic, I find it to be quite a refreshing look on Tekken's fighting system. Though it delves away from the classic Tekken experience, new things are often encouraged, though a toggle option to switch rage arts from on to off would be better to keep things fresh and customizable. Whether you enjoy learning characters through the combo system, or frantically mashing buttons to knock your enemy out, Tekken 7's got both down as great.
The camera zooms in when both fighters are attacking at once, providing a reasonable outlook for your response time when you launch counter attacks, giving you the opportunity to win a close fight. You get to watch your victories and failures as they happen in slow-motion for better analysis.
The moves haven't changed compared to Tekken 6, with many of the tactics largely taken from the same game. However, to ensure that Tekken 7 wasn't a copy-paste game from that of 6, new characters with unique movesets were also introduced to keep the game fresh. Though it doesn't offer much variety besides the moves given to the player based on the character they play, There is still variety for those ambitious enough to learn the game's combo and juggle systems.
If you're aiming to kill some time, it's nice to hop on casually and beat up a few opponents. You're playing a fighting game and a beat-em-up! There's nothing more fun than skillfully pummeling supermodels with aggression, and that is exactly what Tekken 7 for the PC offers!
It gets a 9/10.
4) Content:
- Is Tekken 7 ripe with content? Yes and no. The initial Story Mode can be beaten in roughly 4-5 hours, 6-7 if you are watching the cutscenes from start to finish. Treasure mode is endless. Arcade isn't mandatory, though for achievements? Most likely. All of the content still revolves around fighting however, as there isn't a current gamemode other than a 1v1 brawl with another character. There's little variety.
Most of the content comes with the perk of unlocking custom options for your intended character in the customization feature. You must rely on treasure battles that drop random loot in order to earn a specific piece of clothing for your character. While it gives the player incentive to play the treasure battle, the overall feel of grinding for a piece of clothing for a character is a big negative due to its repetitiveness. Then again, players aren't really meant to be playing Tekken 7 for 10 hours at a time.
With the Season Pass coming in at $25, the amount of content that it unlocks at the start is quite minimal. It gives you access to 2 characters in the upcoming future, as well as gold outfits for your characters. Not the content I was expecting at all. I would definitely recommend getting it on sale. If you're paying more than $10, you're getting ripped off. Regardless, even with the amount of things the Season Pass offers, you'll still be doing the same thing: fighting characters on and off with the same system.
Content for this game deserves a 7/10 at its current state.
5) Overall:
- Do I recommend the game? Yes.
- Should I buy it now? Yes.
- Should I buy the Season Pass? Right now, no. Wait for a sale.
Tekken 7 gets an 8.1/10.

Okay first off, let me just say that this game is fun and all, but it runs like hell. I'm not sure what the underlying problems are, but the game is just broken. I've read that this is all on AMD, but I've also heard some very stories so I'm not sure what to believe when it comes to this. At the moment though, I'm experiencing severe framerate drops (I'm talking dipping down to about 4 FPS at times, even in the character selection menus), random crashes, and some graphical glitches that make one map, Dead Woods, I believe it is called, completely unplayable. It's a real shame because from what I am able to play of this game, it's incredible.
Let's get to the actual review of the game:
Pros:
+ Fun, fast-paced fighting game
+ MK
+ Great story (IMO)
+ Easy to learn, challenging to master
+ Tons of unlockable items within the game (not DLC)
+ Interactive environments
+ Fun game modes
+ More tower options (living towers, klassic towers, endless towers, etc.)
+ Looks great when you aren't experiencing FPS drops or framerate issues
+ Faction Wars and related game modes
+ King of the Hill game mode
Cons:
- Framerate is VERY unstable
- All cut scenes including story, fatalities, and x-rays are locked at 30 FPS
- Random crashes EVERYWHERE
- DLC model is a joke
- Not too much content, you'll feel like you've done everything within 10 hours
- Online connectivity is still terrible, even after multiple updates
Bottom line:
This game is fun to play, but it will leave you frustrated if you're playing for hours and then experience a random crash or even multiple crashes within the same hour. Gameplay is smooth and addicting and will have you itching to rip out more spines when you're not playing the game. If it wasn't for the issues, I would give it a higher rating, but since it runs like complete garbage, here we are. In it's current state, don't spend the money if you don't have it. If the game goes on sale, pick it up, but I wouldn't bother with it otherwise unless you're a diehard MK fan. If they were to fix everything, however, pick it up as soon as you could. I've had a lot of fun with it and have put more than 25 hours in since I picked it up less than 6 days ago.
5.5/10  -         because of the issues described above
8/10     -         if they were to be fixed and then I'll be able to recommend this game

This is an extremely solid game.
Pros:
Battles feel natural and the game itself feels quite realistic.
Map reflects actual terrain for battles.
Dynamic RPG elements: Reputation, politics, and backstory are key factors.
Pick up NPC guides to assist with your conquest, making your warband stronger than if you were to try to lead solo.
Build enterprises and own castles/cities to collect wealth which will sustain your hungry army.
Work your way from nothing to become a King. Maybe even rule the entire map.
The game doesn't lead you by the hand which causes progression to feel natural and challenging.
Hell, you don't even need to be in a warband- you can be a trader for the whole game if you wish.
Cons:
For those people who're videophiles, the graphics aren't great.
The AI isn't the greatest.
The map travel can be frustrating, especially if you need to get some cattle for a quest. Why can't I rope those damn cattle?! $%#@%#$
The Arena is a joke. If you want to fight just go through tournaments.
TLDR Conclusion:
This game is incredibly authentic to its title. Its as if Sid Meier's Civilization were slowed down to a fixed era, sped up, and zoomed into an individual badass life. Politics and who you help become incredibly important. Battles and resources are meaningful. There just isn't much variation on what you can do. I wish I could go up to a castle with a prisoner and ask for a reward or exchange- nope.

Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is a game that needs to be recognized for being able to do very much with very little. From the control scheme to the storyline, Brothers does an excellent job of showing how immersion and innovation can make all the difference in making a memorable narrative.

The control scheme for Brothers is intuitive, yet unique. Each brother is controlled independently by the two thumbsticks and triggers – a concept that is simple in theory, but throughout the entire game I would have moments where the hemispheres of my brain wanted to battle and I would need to reset the brothers’ position on screen to sort things out (I typically tried to keep the older brother on the left, younger on the right to coincide with the thumbsticks). The controls are largely a part of the experience with this game, as the brothers need to use teamwork to solve puzzles, both in tandem and acting independently from each other. Also, each brother is capable of completing tasks that the other cannot, such as reaching a high ledge or fitting between narrow bars. While this could have very easily become a muddled mess, the puzzles never try to become too clever, and it’s very simple to make forward progress. The handful of deaths that I did experience were only because I wasn’t quick enough to ascertain the situation from a glance, but these instances only required a second try to keep going.

The story is at its roots a simple fetch quest, but it’s all about the journey, not the destination. The fantasy world of Brothers gives you a glimpse into a world that is rich and living. The developers seemed to take pride in this, because scattered throughout the game are benches that you can have the brothers sit in for a moment so the camera can pan and give you a better view of the world around you. There’s no achievement for doing so, but I still sat in every bench to observe where I was, where I came from, and where I needed to go. It also doesn’t hurt that the game is very beautiful - you see painted landscapes that extend far into the distance and you have the knowledge that you will eventually visit these places on your journey.

Furthermore, the characters speak in gibberish, so you mainly receive story beats from gestures and expressions, yet nothing is lost on the player. There are moments of extreme sadness in this game, probably more-so than upbeat segments, which grounds the game in a reality in a way that I could possibly relate to Game of Thrones – these are flawed creatures, and not every princess is saved from the castle to live happily ever after.

In all, Brothers is a very satisfying game. Although not very long, I was able to place high value in the time invested, and I’m glad that I had the experience of playing it. Recommended for all.

It is a game in which you constantly make big and important decisions that can determine whether you live or die. A game for people who love tight game design, replayability and fair difficulty.

Do you like dying a lot?  Do you like going through caves?  Have you fallen at any point in your life?  If you answered yes to any of these questions, then Spleunky may be right for you.  Please consult your doctor before trying Spelunky.  If you suffer from any suicidal thoughts or actions from playing Spelunky, please quit immediately.

Tekken 7 is a perfect example of how a fighting game should be.  It is easy to pick up, and difficult to master.  Game feels very optimized. I am able to run on highest settings at a consistent 60fps.  My rig is ~ 4 years old, so I'm very impressed by this.
As usual, Tekken soundtrack is great - and the roster is full with a wide variety of characters.  If you do not like how they look; there is a deep customization mode so you can really make them look how you want.
My only complaints are:
1) there is not a "combo trial" mode like in Street Fighter 4 and 5.  I'd bet that Namco adds this in.
2) there is no cross-platform play, like how in Street Fighter 5 PC can play against PS4.  This will limit the community a little.
If you're looking for a fun fighter for casual, or hardcore play - this is going to be very hard to beat on Steam.

You drive around, you pick up colored barrels to give you weapons (blue (X)=side weapon, yellow (Y)=front weapon, red (B)=back weapon, green (A)=nitrous). You fire the weapons at the opponents and get kills. Basically, most kills wins. And thats how it's fun: it's a 'racing' game where you attack the other racers (like all the other ones out there, only not as well put together).
Graphics, music, sfx, original weapon designs for the different vehicles are all good. A decent number of tracks, though some are similar in appearance (wasteland, airplane graveyard, cold war beach). And the tracks are fairly open, with wide/multiple lanes/paths (which is necessary or it would litterally be a cluster*#*ck).
Ok, but here are the problems:
You can only hold one of each type of weapon (so you can't stock up) and your attacks only last for so long (even if you're laying mines or ice crystals or what have you,) they'll eventually just disappear, so it does no good to be in first place if you're too far ahead of all the other racers.
Physics are
too arcady. The cars weigh anywhere between a balloon and a foam football (with wings). You hit a slope/ditch in the track and you're up in the air for over second, and probably tipped to the side, too. Which means when you finally come down, you'll have to wait for your car to slowly roll onto its wheels. And if you hit a bump just right and launch yourself almost vertical, then you'll be stuck spinning/floating in the air for several seconds while all the other racers pass you by. I also managed to hit an oil slick while I was flying
it. It spun my car out and I had to wait 5 seconds for my car to absorb enough damage to die, then watch it blow up, then wait for a respawn. It's that Mario Kart agony of getting hit with a shell on the last half of the last lap, only it happens in this game over, and over, and OVER! But that's ok because laps don't matter.
This brings me to one of the biggest problems: It's not actually a racing game! In fact if you're first, you'll more than likely loose (because you didn't get enough kills). As far as I can tell, Kills and laps are both worth the about the same. (I think damage you deal counts for some of your points, too.) So this game went from racing game to just driving in a circle shooting at the other racers. The circuits are so long, if you're actually racing, you can probably manage finishing 2 to 3 laps in the time limit. But then you'll miss out on getting around 5 kills a lap, so you loose!
If you like a game that has you playing with ping pong balls physically, has a LOT of ups and downs, a game where coming first is bad, then buy this and go play with kitty.

I quite anticipated this game since the first one came as a nice surprise but could'nt get around the feeling that Ubisoft would ♥♥♥♥ it up somehow.
In short, what I feel I played is a much shorter, wonkier and less funny version of Stick of Truth.
I finished the game in approx. 12 hours (most sidequests included), and went to the end just for the sake of finding a redeeming factor whatsoever to those long hours of going from point A to point B, resolving bland enigmas and suffering a hit and miss comic factor.
If you're interested in the South Park universe and haven't played Stick of Truth, play it instead of its sequel, the latter being more focused on newer seasons of the show, thus reducing the overall appeal and comic factor enclosed in it in my opinion.
The new battle system, though renewing a stale and sometimes abusive one from the first game, is much more bland.
The choice of classes is not as endearing and bold (in the meantime, what beats playing a Jew class ?) as what you could think from the get-go.
The buddy system is horribly repetitive, uninspired and heavy to use (you've got to repeat and repeat and repeat the same wonky scan and then wait even more from the cutscene of your buddy to resolve before completing the action).
The story is far from great in my opinion, the ending feeling rushed (one can even sense the game trying to buy time by negating you the right to fast-travel at some point, dragging you from point A to point B without any real motive) but more than ever, the sidequest really feel like fillers, unlike some of the great sub-plots you could experience in Stick of Truth.
That's a shame really, a lot of sub-plots could have been better developped and it feels (unlike the first game) that the town of South Park is empty.
More than being upset, I feel disappointed by this sequel; a lot of the South Park universe could have been better used and developped than it is right now in this state of the game.

There is no doubt in my mind--Zombie Shooter is the absolute pinnacle of modern PC gaming.  Drawing deep from the well of both classic English literature and Germany philosophy  (Heideggerian-Existential theories and Kierkegaardian paranoia colliding with Titus Andronicus-esque drama and bloodshed, anyone?) But calling it a PC Game is doing this game a disservice--Zombie Shooter is far more than a game.  It is an experience comparable and competitive with the greatest of cinematic (Citizen Kane, step out of the way) and sonic (Tchakivosky and Wagner look simply elementary compared to the rhythm of this game) experiences.  We could dwell on art direction or sound design, but that would only prove to be eclipsing the most important trait of Zombie Shooter:  story.  Never before have I felt so interwoven with a protagonist.  In fact, I am at this moment uncertain if I am actually writing this review, or if my life is contained within this game.  100 / 100.

I'm rewriting this after beating the game.
This game is a masterpiece. That South Park immersion from the first game has been stepped up and the 60+ FPS over the 30 from the previous title is very welcome. Your asshоle is more powerful than before and I found myself glued to the screen for hours at a time, appreciating the attention to detail not only in the world, but also the characters. The humour is on point, as you would expect, and while playing the first game felt like
an episode of the show, this game takes it to another level. It's a very worthy successor.
I want to emphasise the amount of detail put into this game. Every possible combination of allies, enemies, attacks, situations and environments will trigger unique dialogue lines from the enemies, allies and passers-by. There are countless references to the show mixed in with these. The world is rich in detail and every nook that you couldn't explore in The Stick of Truth is now open to you, and more. I got lost really just wandering around looking at everything.
The gameplay is refreshing and fun; getting ambushed isn't as frustrating as it was in SoT. That said, even playing on Mastermind difficulty isn't particularly hard, the only times you'll lose a combat is on specific bosses, but even then it only takes one or two losses to find the right ally and powers configuration.
It's ridiculous that all the reviews on Steam are people saying that the game is good, but then they mark it as not recommended because of Ubisoft. I understand that that's your opinion, but seriously? The rest are just people complaining about bugs, but I never experienced any of what they're talking about. My experience was completely smooth. The game was a joy to play.
TL;DR -
- Great visuals
- Great humour
- Extreme detail
- Refreshing, fun gameplay
- Lots of exploring possibilities and inside jokes and references
- Hilarious,
South Park story
- 20-40 hours to complete the story, depending on your pace
- The price*
- Bugs**
- Uplay/Day One DLC***
* Yes it's expensive but anyone who likes the show should definitely get this game.
** As mentioned above, I didn't encounter a single bug in the nearly 40 hours that were my first playthrough. I don't even want to mention this as a con, but it's apparently all over Steam.
*** Annoying, I agree. Ubi up to their usual shιt, but little implications in the frame of the game as a whole
To conclude: buy this! Even I was skeptical when I discovered that Ubisoft was doing this one but I wouldn't say I'm disappointed about a single aspect of this game.
South Park lends itself so well to a video game and they pulled out all stops. One of the best games I've played all year.

There are people who very heavily complain about stories and games. They say "if I wanted stories, I'd go watch a movie". Other people just feel that games without a story are unengaging and arid. To both groups I recommend
. Both will gain a new perspective.
Rarely a game manages to deliver such rich, emotional and well-developed storytelling. As a lifelong gamer, voracious reader and a professional that understands the power of drama, I can tell you that this game has it all. Every single element shows the maximum attention to detail, storywise.
Careful planning and masterful presentation are noticeable at every single moment. Only a master storyteller, playwright or writer can achieve this. Music, setting, colors, sounds, environment, level design, camera angles, zooming, pacing, "dialogue" and a hint of mystery here and there make this game a superb and very enjoyable experience.
The world is rich and interesting and the characters are empathic and show more personality in 3 hours' worth of playing than most others from famous lengthy franchises or dull modern novels/movies. In a time and age of predictable endings, cookie-cutter stories, boring conventional scripting, forced and faked emotional stimuli and lame plot twists,
brings a breath of fresh air.
Yes, the game is quite short for today's gaming standards. Bear in mind though that the narrative is excellent and the duration is perfect. Think theater or cinema: more than 3 hours would be just too much. This is more akin to that than to Call of Duty, Minecraft or Super Mario.
The controls at first are awkward but soon you'll get used to them. A gamepad is strongly recommended, and there's a reason for that.
I am quite sure that you've never played a game like this. Bought it on sale; after finishing I would have gladly paid twice the regular price. The developers deserve it. It is that good. Maybe not a game for everyone, but definitely one worth playing.
Unconditionally recommended.

Not all in one sitting - this game deserves to be "sipped" like fine wine, and the beautiful environments explored - but I think I may have missed out on some of the game's impact by taking too long.
Highly, highly, highly recommended.

Spelunky is a hard sell.
Dark Souls is a hard sell, but I can say with authority that the game rewards you for being patient and skillful.  Spelunky is... you know how carnival amusements and claw machines are literally programmed to make sure you don't win?  Like f'rinstance, the claw only closes one in every 1,000 plays?  Spelunky feels a lot like that.  You play, hoping the levels give you what you need to win - knowing that, FAR more often than not, you are going to die in a few minutes/seconds.
You know the game is going to pull cheap moves on you - like giving you the jet pack, the shotgun, all the tools you need to find the secrets of the game... and then springing a dark level full of giant spiders and spikes.  This game is brimming with one-hit kills.  This game is overflowing with cheap deaths.  This game is absolutely teeming with a litany of gurgling curses, choked-out between spittle-spraying clenched teeth uttered by the players over the last few years; getting rocked by the spikes after a monkey jumped on their back, bounced(unconscious) into a caveman who threw them 40 feet in some kind of Rube Goldbergian, assisted-suicide Kevorkian machine tends to breed a depth of crude language that we spent eons evolving *out* of - I have learned swear words I did not know were in my own vocabulary.  The whip is too slow, you can hurt yourself by tossing a rock 2 feet into the air and having it crush your skull, and arrow traps haunt my nightmares.
So why do I play?
VENGEANCE.  I play this game out of the pure engine of hatred that it has built within me, solely to crush the dungeons and see those smarmy shopkeepers blasted by their own shotguns.
10/10, would hate self again.

I don't like Point&Click games - at least that's what I thought Deponia blew my mind.
The character you play, Rufus, is a constant thief, tries out everything no matter how much harm it does and generally is an egocentric who doesn't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about other people's feelings... Which, actually is the incarnation of how you automatically act when playing an Point&Click adventure.
I love Deponia for this kind of subtle, intelligent humor. I love Rufus. And I love Daedalic for developing another sequel, Deponia: Doomsday. The adventure isn't over yet! Hurray!

Deponia is a point-and-click adventure game reminiscent of the Lucasarts classics. It tells the story of eternal screwup and egomaniac Rufus and his efforts to escape the garbage-filled planet he lives on to reach a floating city, Elysium.
All in all, the game is well paced, funny, and the right mix of challenging and logical. There was no singular moment where I was just baffled over an answer, though the game does offer large enviroments that can sometimes be overwhelming.
If you are a fan of the genre, this game (and it's sequels) should definitely be in your collection, but it certainly won't be worth it to those who are not.

So i'm going to keep this review simple and short as I want to play more tekken after this. THIS REVIEW IS PURELY BASED ON THE MULTIPLAYER THE SINGLEPLAYER AND OTHER FEATURES THAT DO NOT PERTAIN TO THE STORY. So basically this is a spoiler-free review.
There are six areas we will be discussing about today that makes up the bulk of the content and the majority of that 35gb download.
-Offline is what I first went to when I first booted up Tekken 7. There are 4 modes within offline, each pretty cool. The first is your typical arcade mode. This mode is a standard in all tekken fighting games and while this mode only consists of five matches per run, they present an enjoyable experience towards the end of them. The second mode is called the treasure run. Similar to arcade where you just fight a bunch of enemies this is where you get your loot for costumes and mostly cosmetic stuff (However some items actually do something in the game when equipped). Next is VS and practice which is pretty self-explanatory.
-This mode is awesome. The servers are perfect. I have never gotten any bugs or glitches with the servers. The netcode is responsive and satisfactory. The opponents are friendly and challenging. You have ranked and regular matches. However the new tournament mode seems really cool. Unfortunately I haven’t been able to get in one because they haven’t really been active.
-The customization in this game is AMAZING. Now, what makes this game’s cosmetics different from any other games cosmetics? Simple, they are not just purely cosmetic items. They have various effects on the game. Not in a stats way, but a cool after effect. For example some guy had a halo item on his character. When he was KO'd body rose like he was going up to heaven. Just little things that are really cool and add life and variety with every character.
-Lets get this out of the way by saying this is the most pumped up fighting game I have ever played. The music is strong and gets you up from your chair and shaking your controller. It changes with the arena and the fight and is flexible and really compliments the game's vision of the combat.
-This game is the best looking tekken game by far! I mean holy crap! From the particle effects to the textures of the characters to the details of the settings this game is a work of art. You will spend hours just staring at the art and characters on your free time. Whats even better is that it all runs super smoothly. I mean i am getting 60fps during the game at all time. The loading screens can make me drop to 30 frames but I don't mind it one bit.
-Okay down to the wire what is this game capable of? Is it as good as the other modern day fighting games? Can it take the title? Is it possible GAME OF THE YEAR? Hahaha okay let's settle down there. While this game is amazing at other aspects it is not a game of the year yet. The fighting is super fun and simple. The buttons are not complex and just like tekken's beforehand this one is a pick up and play. Juggling is fun and the combos are only to be used strategically. The maps are really interactive and expansive. The combat is fun and all about pacing. If you attack to early they can counter you. If you attack to late you might be pushed back to the corner then you are really screwed. The rage arts (X-rays for MK players out there), are cool and should be used with caution.
Overall this game is worth the 50 bucks. There is much to unlock. The costumes, the movies from past tekken's, the story,and the gameplay! I highly recommend getting this game because I promise you won’t regret it.
9/10

I know I haven't logged that many hours with this game, but currently I'm having a lot of fun with it. I've always been the person that was never satisfied with vanilla mincraft and was constantly trying to turn it into a sandbox fantasy rpg-esque game with mods. I feel like this game fills that void! It's decently optimized for my computer, it's fun to play with a friend, biomes are small islands so I don't have to worry about a chunk cache, and it has the fantasy rpg element I was searching for without the need to install 20+ mods. Like I said, I haven't logged that many hours so....I haven't come across any problems like "depletion of resources" on islands, but I mean, I assume, there's very easy workarounds for that. Make sure to replant everything you harvest, also if you need ores, and you don't see them respawning, create a new world to farm them. (I'm pretty sure you can transport resources/items from one world to another).
Currently I believe the game has about 60+ hours of content to explore, I say that in a sense of you shouldn't speed run a game like this. Explore the islands, gather materials, build farms, ect. This isn't the type of game that you wanna rush through as fast as possible, if you zerg you're gonna get bored...and then you'll have wasted money.
