Hmm, that´s a hard one...
I have more hours on this game than steam lists, I was playing a "not so legal" version if you get my drift.
A little background, I started playing MS Train Simulator back when I was a kid.
I took me years to find out that there´s an editor, it too me until my adolescence to fully understand it.
But I was hooked, I loved beeing able to have my own little model trains in digital form.
Was always a sucker for trains, I guess.
As Trainz was never really my thing and MSTS was getting rather old I was looking for a new TS that suited me.
Than I stumbled on this game, modern, rather well put together with a lot of useful tools and gadgets to have your own experience.
So let´s start with the actual train driving.
Even though it still lacks the full immersion in my opinion the simulation is outstanding when it comes to physics and the "feel" of trains while you operate them.
It´s addicting, fullfilling and especially expert line models are really worth every cent and really give you a realistic experience.
The HUD takes a while to get used to, and the learning curve is rather steep when it comes to the actual controls of a locomotive or Multiple units.
So read the instruction manuals or you´ll get stuck not know what PzB/LzB/Sifa means, and you don´t wan´t that if you accidentally switch your train operation mode to expert mode ;-)
Every good model needs time to get used to and learn to properly function in your hands, just like you need some time to understand every function of your car.
So that´s a total plus of this game, the actual experience when it chooses to work is exceptional.
Which takes us to the downsides of complexity and the mass of content available.
The game is a bug fest, I find myself saving my longer drives ever so often because you never know when the game will decide to crash on you.
Next is the editor, my gosh is it a pain in the butt seriously. IF you have the illusion that you can actually create your own world in this game forget it.
It will suck the life out of you!
Learning to operate it is absolutely necessary for you to actually use the thing, this doesn´t save you from random crashes and the AI´s ability to do ANYTHING but what you tell them to do.
You need to treat your traffic trains like a complete imbecile, they will constantly change their paths if you don´t set waypoints for basically everything.
Big European trainstations become a real pain to manage, you´ll spend more time in the editor trying to figure out timing and routes of your trains, than driving them only to find out that in the actual simulation they completely change their behaviour and suddenly derail?!
And by the way you can´t copy the routes of your trains from one train to another one.
Even MSTS had this feature, jeesus!
So let´s say you create your own scenario on the RSSLO Südbahn, it´s 110 Km in length.
Takes a commuter train about 1:45h to get through....
The amount of traffic you need to manage for such a big track is immense, good thing the AI behaves like a ISIS guy on a rampage maken your live absolute hell.
So you´ll end up creating traffic train after traffic train, until you get to the point where TS2017 suddenly decides to stop working.
Trains start to have "uknown errors", can´t find routes anymore or just stop in the middle of the track for no apparent reason to have a nap or something?!
Getting a custom scenario to work is like having a baby 9 months of pain for something that will eventually try everything to make you life miserable :-P
So yeah buy it, if you´re a masochist^^
Here´s hoping that the developers actually adress some of these issues, most of them are the same since TS2013 which kinda tells me there won´t be any change soon.

Train Simulator, like any core simulator, has it's ups and downs. That being said, as a base simulator to support additional DLC, it suits the needs of even the most avid simulator fan. Much like Flight Simulator X, and the subsequent releases from other developers (Lockheed, and Dovetail), the simulator on it's own leaves some aspects to be desired. That being said, the more rigid aspects of simulation are more than made up for from developers such as Victory Works, Just Trains, Meshtools, and Smokebox (the latter being possibly the best developer on the platform).
The core simulation is fine for those looking for an introductory simulation on trains, and probably is best in class considering the adaptability, ease of use, train and route coverage, etc. As you advance in your understanding of the mechanics of locomotives, you'll eventually graduate to the various DLC addons. As such, the simulator serves it's purpose and ranges from the most basic almost arcade-esque simulation, to high end simulation. Considering how many hours and the enjoyment I've gotten from this platform, I just can't not recommend it for anyone looking to simulate locomotives.

Finally purchased and played through this game after hearing rave reviews from sources I trust.  A simple game really, two brothers going on an epic quest to save their father.  No combat, minor puzzles, and most of the game isn't even sensitive to timing/controls.  Those pieces that are are exceptionally forgiving.  Gameplay isn't what makes it great, and realistically not even the visuals, even though they are stunning.  The story is key here.  No dialog, no text, just a few voiced nonsense words in a language that's never translated.  It conveys emotion, and that's all it needed to do.  Most of why this game was something special for me is going to be in a spoiler section at the end, but I'll go ahead and break down the rest.
So a quick breakdown:
So basically the controls were a touch frustrating.  I don't do that well with dual stick and keeping things straight as I just don't spend much time with a gamepad in my hand.  That said, gamepad really is the way to play.  Thankfully the gameplay was forgiving enough that I could get past it.
Top notch.  Visuals were stunning.  Don't pass up the park benches.  Sit down, take a minute or two and just enjoy the awesome vistas they put together.  The artists deserve incredible credit for what they did.
It's a really simple game with a few puzzles to keep the journey interesting.  They serve to give you a sense of each brother's personality and to give you some challenge so you're not just walking through.  Nothing special, but servicable for what they needed it to do.  The game is short, but I'd actually say if it wasn't it just wouldn't work.
Here's the heart of it.  The story is also a simple one, and one that has been told before.  The difference here is in the telling.  They've told in a way only a video game could do.  It's impressive, and because of that they've earned every bit of praise this game will ever receive.  The rest of my thoughts on the story are in the spoiler below.
So final thoughts.  It's an understatement to say I recommend it.  I may not call it one of the best games I've played, because if the gameplay is all that was there I wouldn't have enjoyed it.  Brothers is almost feels more like something you have experienced than as a game.  That said, it's well worth a few bucks and a few hours of your time.

This was the game that made me a believer in the procedural generation school, and it has perhaps the most robust such algorithm I've seen in games. Combined with deep mechanics that affect each other in complex, unpredictable ways (traps are triggered by and affect any moving object, for instance; some enemies cause explosions that trigger hilarious (and tragic!) chain reactions) and a gigantic repertoire of very unique items and enemies, no two runs are alike. Hundreds of plays later, it still feels as fresh as the first time. You'll start collecting all sorts of interesting emergent tales the more you play, such as that one time you took too long but still managed to reach the exit chased by an invincible one hit kill ghost across half the level, or the time you had only one rope and a bomb left, but still managed to climb out of a snake pit by doing something wacky.
It's a hard as nails platformer; in fact after some 30 hours and hundreds of tries (including the free version), I have yet to reach the end. The theme is what you'd expect to find in a (good) Indiana Jones game. While the commercial version is an upgrade in basically every aspect in relation to the free one, the latter will give you a very good idea whether you'll enjoy the former or not. If you have any doubts, give that one a try.

Easily the best Mortal Kombat ever. Furthermore, it can hold it's own against Capcom's majors like Street Fighter and MvC. MKX is a solid and deep fighting game that takes the foundation laid by MK9 and brings it to a more advanced level.

Despite the horrendous launch, Mortal Kombat X is a great game. Those who take a glance at the User Review Summary at the top should keep in mind that MKX was deeply in the red day 1, due to the fact that no one could play.
That said, now that the cluster♥♥♥♥ of a launch has been fixed, the game plays extremely well with a few hiccups that I hope get fixed in patches. The gameplay is an overall improvement from MK9, with the combos flowing much smoother and better, and the overall gameplay being much faster. They removed ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t bosses that don't get staggered from uppercuts like mini-boss Goro or Shao Kahn, and instead have the AI get kicked up a notch for those fights. Overall, there's more kontent than MK9, despite the exclusion of Tag-Team Kombat. With ladders of various kinds, and hourly-updated new ladders available if you have a net connection, it's a good time-sink.
The Multiplayer suffers from a bit of lag, which is compensated as input lag on your end. While awkward, I'd prefer this over people just teleporting everywhere. As of writing, I know they're attempting to address this issue, but we'll see how well that goes. That said, the lag is still an improvement off of MK9's horrendous latency issues.
All-in-all, MKX is a great game, that's a little battle-scarred by the launch and a few technical issues. I give this 9 Johnny Cage Autographs out of 10.

.........BUT: Don't celebrate too much - 'cause if you just fell in love being "home" at the Cordon or the Garbage again - well, enjoy, because you most likely won't get there a second time. The story line is just too linear to find any sense in travelling back.

I'll start off by saying I really enjoyed this game and I played it on the highest difficulty setting, "Mastermind", and my review is based around that experience and will mostly explain what negatives I found from it. If you have/have not played the first game and want to pick this one up, I would encourage you to watch some playthrough first if you're on the fence. I repeat these are all the negatives of the game.
The combat system is different now and felt a bit basic. They removed world objects that could be used during combat that you could hit with a skill and have it fall on your enemies, like the first game. After the first 4 hours of fights I felt very drained and almost wishing there was a "flee" option. I don't want to spoil anything with too much information but it's incredibly repetative. If I could give the mission style a perfect explenation, I'd say EVERY mission felt like the first mission you'd receive in World of Warcraft. You know the one. "Go kill 6 boar and bring me their tusks." Although the whole game does have every bit of political wit, controversy, and comedy you'd expect out of South Park, I can't help but feel like this is where the missions fell short.
Something else that sort of left me feeling a bit bored and frustrated was the length of the game compared to the first one. I know that's silly to complain about because we all want more content, right? Well this kind of felt like the latest Transformers movie, if you've seen it. It just kind of continues to drag on when you think it's over and the hype is dying but you've invested so much in it already, so you keep going. As I've said, every quest felt like a WoW intro. one unlocks the next and then the next... But you can't do the next one because you have to go do one by another person who has another that is linked to another person. I played the game on Mastermind difficulty which is supposed to be the hardest setting but all I found was that it made the battles much more lengthly and there wasn't an achievement for beating the game on it. My advice is to play on easy or normal because all Mastermind did was lengthen the combat. Your enemies will heal each other more often and your bosses have a lot more health. I was stubborn and kept playing on Mastermind and I felt like it posed too little of a challenge as far as strategy and only made me more frustrated to spend 30 minutes on a boss fight that ended up giving me scrap metal and an artifact that is way below my current one.
Lastly, I found myself fidgiting around in my seat the longer I played. You fight one enemy. He calls a boss. You fight the boss but the boss calls another boss who then calls 4 more minions. Those minions die and then the first boss comes back to life. The whole game kind of carried this playthrough. You think you're done with a part of the story but then something else goes wrong. You fix that and something else goes wrong. There was a LOT of "beating around the bush" and "wandering off track". My advice is to save before and after big fights. You can't rely on autosave checkpoints.
I don't want to sound like I'm being negative. I highly recommend this game but I'd also like to point out in this review what I felt was wrong with it. There are a TON of side missions and there are a ton of collectibles including gear and player mods. This review is based on almost 50 hours of gameplay and I completed everything in game except a side mission that requires a lot of ingame currency that I refuse to farm for. You'll find out when you get to it. I try to play a game for 100% completion and this one has me fidgiting and trying to convince myself to just finish the content.

I have never played minecraft, apart from briefly years ago during alpha/beta so I cannot really compare nor do I like too really.

Graphics:
“Cutesy” non offensive, children can murder monsters without crying or getting upset. Just watch any video, not much more to say.

Character classes:
Somewhat limited, melee is really underwhelming, almost pointless, choose a warrior and just use a bow was for me much better than swords etc. Have not tried mage.
Levels go up to 30 currently, this game is less about levelling though and there is virtually no customisation options for levelling up, just more health/stats etc with “perks” every five or ten levels.
This are could do with a little more fleshing out but it is minor as it is not that kind of game where levelling up is paramount.

Monster variety
Pretty good, different “Biomes” have different monsters including night time harder monsters, bosses are somewhat easy although I struggled on the last boss a lot, currently 3 major bosses, again for me this game is not about a massive challenge against uber bosses instead they are gate keepers to further regions.

Biomes/Regions
Around five or six different types of regions currently, the worlds are relatively small but there are a lot of them (44 out of 47 for me IIRC) I do not find the small worlds an issue personally

Crafting
So many different options of crafting, if you are a mage I think you will need to rely on mining/crafting a fair bit more than melee/ranged but have not tested this. Quite a few different types of tools weapons and armour can be created.
There are many types of blocks to create homes/buildings etc but the higher level blocks need a considerable amount of mining to create large dwellings

Farming
This is one area I really hope gets fleshed out, there are loads of seeds to forage and plant but honestly there is at the moment little point in doing so as I comfortably “completed” the game so far with almost zero need for farming, the potential for this side of the game could be great though and plants/tress seem to grow in real time.

Endgame
This is what interests me, I am level 27, comfortable enough to go anywhere and defeat anything without too much difficulty leaving me free to now play the way I intended to play, I love building homes and farms and crafting the land around me, this aspect of the game is almost limitless in that respect although interior decoration cannot be “used” by your avatar and again currently is somewhat limited

Currently I cannot recommend this game. It's a fun game, but twice now it has deleted my character. Not going to waste time building a third. You know what they say "Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, shame on me. Fool me a third time, clearly I am a complete idiot". Maybe I will check it out in a year or so, probably not.

Dead Rising 2: OTR is an alright game IMO with a good concept, solid voice acting, and decently aged graphics.
However, it desperately needs:
- a proper settings menu. Every PC Steam game needs a ♥♥♥♥ing settings menu for god's sake. It's clearly a console port, but that doesn't mean you can skimp on almost any graphics settings, FoV, or even basic V-Sync settings. Near unacceptable for me. The fact that you can't access settings or even adjust controls until 5 minutes in is annoying. That leads me to another thing:
- a proper controls menu or even a way to see PC controls. You can't modify any controls on this PC version. That's also unacceptable. But what's worse is that you can't even see what they are in the first place. What the hell? This is some of the worst porting I've seen done, simply because of these two issues. It is playable, but we shouldn't have to ask for features that are literally in every other regular PC game. Even console ports don't neglect a controls or graphics menu. Jeez.
- to eliminate the few seconds between applying clothes and picking up weapons/food. It's horrible to lose health when I'm in a shop because I want to try some clothes or actually enjoy the customization aspect of the game. It really just makes me mad how many details were glossed over when Capcom made this game. So many issues, and if it's this much of a hassle to put on clothes and experience new things, maybe I just won't bother playing.
- a sprint button. The flow of this game is awkward without it. I'm basically walking through the zombie apocalypse, desperately trying to outmaneuver these horribly scripted AI, that are basically walking scripted cutscenes. It sucks that this great game has so many problems, but this is easily the biggest one. It's much easier to be grappled, floored, and killed when you can't run or maneuver properly. Very subpar of them to not polish this feature from the first game.
- an unlimited time mode. I wasn't aware of the time constraints in this game, although I had played DR1 before. This mistake led me to lose about a half hour and $60,000 of Casino Golf money becuase I didn't get stupid Zombrex in time. I mean c'mon, I don't care about getting cured or taking it seriously. I need to be able to sit around as long as I want, try out all the stores and items, and kill as much♥♥♥♥♥♥as I want. That's the point of a sandbox, at least to me.
- a more precise combat system. The melee swings with an axe, bat, or hammer are so mediocre, for example. When I'm with survivors, I can't save them most of the time because I'll just swing and hit them while trying to save them. On a game with a fragile time system and weak as hell survivors that you have to save, it's a necessity that the controls be tight. Dead Rising as an entire series suffers from a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor combat system with wonky animations and terrible detection. To add to that:
- better AI combat collision. Many times a zombie's swing will collide with me and nothing happens, and many times a zombie can take me down without actually striking my character model. This is faulty and bizarre. Sometimes I have been floored and killed by a random zombie, just because I didn't mash the correct key fast enough, and the original attack was unblockable. That leads me to another point:
- a way to escape a zombie's grasp without "wiggling" the mouse. It's an extremely frustrating and annoying thing to have to feverishly swing your mouse on the desk just because the glitchy AI caught you in their Quick Time Event. A game series as famous as Dead Rising should not have simple enemy AI collision issues, and QTEs are outdated. They become very annoying if I have to see them every minute or so. ***This is quite a long review but it’s an honest one so please read it all the way through*** Being an avid train enthusiast I would definitely recommend this game to any person who loves trains as much as I do. Living in the Uk and loving all the trains we have here I obviously buy the Uk trains in game. The locos in the game have extremely accurate sounds and do sound very close to the real life locos they’re modelled off, although there are little discrepancies (this is purely based off of me hearing the trains myself and I personally think the sounds used are very good) I’m sure this would be the same for trains from other countries but I cannot comment on that as I have never heard or used foreign trains in real life or the game.The routes are also quite detailed and are close to how the look if you were to actually visit them in real life. The scenarios are one of the best things to do in this game if you’re looking to challenge yourself and want to somewhat experience what it would be like to actually drive a train on the main line, these scenarios aren’t perfect but all of the main aspects are included such as the how you can sit in the trains cabin and drive the train using the actual controls that you would have in real life, and how the lines have all the working signals etc. There is also a free roam choice where you can choose a starting destination and where you want to drive to, you can then freely drive a train of your choice along the route, nice for if you want to just listen to different locos or just want to mess around. However, the game does have drawbacks and I won’t dispute that fact. The DLC’s are costly for anyone who doesn’t just want to stick to the standard routes and locos that you get for purchasing the game. I personally don’t mind paying the money for these DLS’s (I know that some people don’t agree with the DLC prices and that is totally your opinion which you are entitled to) as I want to expand on the amount of different locos I have, the amount of scenarios I have to complete and the amounts of things I can learn how to do in the game. I also understand that it does take a lot of time, effort and input for Dovetail to develop all the different DLC packs, and also the money to get licenses to use the designs of trains and other things like that. You have to look at the situation from both points of view to understand why Dovetail do charge for the DLC. If you’re looking to play this game and you’re on a budget then I’d suggest to save up an amount of money and wait for a sale, you can get anywhere from 20 to 80% off some of the DLC’s which would allow you to maybe buy more than one pack for how much you would’ve payed for one originally. Another thing would be that you do need somewhat of a decent computer to run this game without frame rate issues. I have an EVGA GeForce GTX 960 SSC and an Intel i5 4960k which for me run the game well with an occasional lag spike, I’m sure for other people who have the same specs (or near to) would also have no problems running the game above 60 fps with the occasional lag spike which is bearable when playing. Other than this I don’t really having anything else to say about the game, I personally enjoy the game and will continue to play it. I hope that anyone reading my review will find it helpful as I wanted to make it honest for you if you’re trying to decide whether to buy the game or not, I hope it helps! If you have any other questions about the game send me a message and I’ll be happy to help answer them for you!

Sniper Elite is a third-person shooter franchise that has found success so far with two main titles, and two spin-off Nazi Zombie Army games; at least, at the time of Sniper Elite III's release. Up until now, the games have been set in Germany during the tail end of World War II, although Sniper Elite III has set out to change that direction slightly by taking the player to Africa during the early 1940's. Certainly, the same location and era can only be done for so long, and publisher/developer Rebellion know that and have attempted to revitalize the series before it wears out its welcome in Nazi Germany.
First off, if you are running any variation of Windows 8 or 10, you are not going to have a good time. I myself am running Windows 10 x64, and needless to say I did not have a good time. When I say that Sniper Elite III crashes a lot, that's an understatement; everything from the .exe crashing, to Runtime errors, to the game freezing up, to weird FPS drops before the game just gives up. There is no rhyme or reason for occurrence of these crashes, they're seemingly random, and Rebellion have done nothing but shrug and offer multiple band-aid "solutions" that do not work. Great "solutions" such as verify the integrity of the game cache, disable your firewall and anti-virus, and run the .exe in compatibility mode for Windows 7, none of which worked for me.
Needless to say, my entire experience with this game has been marred with considerable frustration. Of the 5 hours I've spent with the title, I've managed to not even get halfway through the game due to the aforementioned issues. It's not even that the whopping 8 missions (the least amount in any Sniper Elite game, by the way) are long, in fact I finished the first one in under 20 minutes, it's that every time the game crashes, you have to start back from whatever checkpoint you might have been lucky enough to grab; either that or remember to save every 2-5 minutes.
Plethora of bugs and crashes aside, you once again control our good friend and American OSS Lieutenant Karl Fairburne, this time on his journey through the Battle of Gazala during 1942. The skilled sniper has been sent to assassinate General Franz Vahlen and recover intel on his secret project. Overall, the story is very skeletal and lacks any real substance, with a large chunk of the meat having been shamelessly saved for a three part DLC add-on. The same lacklusterness can be said for the soundtrack, which feels like nothing more than a rehash of what was included in V2.
The levels this time around are much larger than those presented in V2, and are on par with how big they were in the original Sniper Elite if the game was translated into modern gaming. With plenty of main and optional objectives, along with a multitude of collectibles and locations to discover, there are enough reasons that any player would want to explore each map to its full potential. Despite the adequate size of each map, there's very little that will make one feel as though they're in Africa, as opposed to any random desert location. The graphics haven't really been upgraded or changed much since Sniper Elite III's predecessor, although the character models don't look quite as clay-like.
Rebellion have brought back the visibility meter in Sniper Elite III, something that was missing from V2, and as well they have added close-encounter knife stealth kills. Along with these implementations is also a leveling system, one that any gained experience points from either online or offline events contribute to. The higher your level, the more items that you unlock for your loadouts; of which, you can have four at any given time, and they can be selected from at the beginning of any single player mission. As well, this time around you have the option of playing through the campaign in co-op mode with a friend.
Before wrapping things up, let's talk about the difficulty of the game and the inconsistent AI. Thankfully, Rebellion have brought back the harder difficulty that the debut Sniper Elite was so well known for; they've even added a fourth difficulty option known as Realistic. Of course, the ballistics are still in play for any mode above Cadet (easy), which is another staple feature of the series. Realistic mode is incredibly unforgiving, and truly only for the most hardened of sniper simulation enthusiasts as there is zero help for showing where to aim, or how to calculate wind resistance and gravity. However, the enemy AI is notoriously inconsistent; even though you can now finally sneak up behind a foe to stealth kill them while crouching, if you're underground and walking upright an enemy on the very top floor can and will hear you.
Even though the idea of sticking with a 1940's era and moving the location of the story from Germany to Africa is a brave one, it just hasn't worked in favor of Sniper Elite III. Overall, the game is excruciatingly dull, we still haven't been given any sort of backstory on Karl, there's nothing but a few exotic trees to indicate that we are in Africa, the AI is overly sensitive, online is completely dead, and the title crashes so much that it's not worth putting up with the frustration to continue playing. Sadly, Rebellion have really dropped the ball on this one, and the fact that they've only offered band-aids to atone for Sniper Elite III not working properly on any OS newer than Windows 7 is simply atrocious. Either get this one on console, or don't bother at all. Hopefully the next installment brings us something more flavorful that will actually work on newer operating systems.

I love stories. I love escapism and temporarily living in another world. It's why I love video games; their ability to transport you elsewhere to any world, any time, any place. And as technology advances, the immersion of it all becomes better and better every day. Brothers: A tale of Two Sons is a beautiful piece of storytelling, probably the most emotional 90 minutes I've ever spent playing a video game.
I first noticed Brothers months ago; it was another one of those games that I got as part of a bundle. At the time it was marked as "Requires a controller" (even though it's only on PC), so I pretty much ignored it and got on with life. However, since I bought an XBox wired 360 controller for my PC a couple of weeks ago, I've been making a list of all the games in my Steam library that had full controller support and started working my way through them. Brothers was at the top of the pile, so here's my view on the playthrough!
First thing's first - it is technically possible to play this game with a keyboard, but I would highly recommend buying a wired XBox 360 controller if you don't have one; it's worth it for this game alone. The clue is in the title - you play as two brothers, and this is their story. The mechanic that makes this game unique across all games I've played is that you control both of these brothers (Naiee & Naia) at the same time independently using different sides of the controller. The left joystick controls Naia, the right joystick controls Naiee - and the left and right triggers are their context-sensitive action buttons. That's it - simple and effective. It takes a little while to get used to controlling two characters at the same time, but it's very effective and made me wonder why it hasn't been done before.
I was immediately intrigued by Brothers when I noticed it had a
. That's damn high for any game, in fact it's high enough to earn it a place in the top 100 Metacritic PC games
. At less than 2 hours playtime, it had a lot to squeeze into those two hours to warrant a score that high.
The game starts with the younger brother Naiee paying his respects at his mother's grave, whom you see drown in the opening cutscene, Naiee unable to save her. The two boys' father is sick, and the doctor tells them that the only way to save him is to collect water from the tree of life which, conveniently, is located on the top of a mountain far far away. One of the great things about this game is that although it's all about the storytelling, it doesn't actually use words. You need to see this to understand it fully, but in essence the characters communicate with each other in a similar fashion to how the Sims do - they use noises that sound like words, which have emotion behind them, but aren't actually real words. This helps to focus on the characters themselves and how they're feeling. It actually works pretty well.
So off we go on an epic adventure to find some medicine for our sick father. The trail is long and the journey treacherous, but thankfully it's also damn pretty to look at and I found myself taking screenshots pretty much every five minutes. It's built on the Unreal Engine so the game is optimised, smooth and gorgeous.
I found myself smiling for about the first half hour as I got to grips with controlling the two boys, how the mechanics worked and solving the charming puzzles. The first few puzzles in the game I exclaimed "Ah! Clever!" as I started to realise the potential of the dual-control mechanism. It teaches you how the boys have to work together to solve problems, and they're both suited to different tasks. Naiee might not be able to reach a ledge by himself, but if Naia kneels down underneath and gives him a leg up, Naiee can climb up then throw a rope down.
They really explore the possibilities of controlling two characters. Some sections involve a brother jumping off a cart to open doors for the other to go through, controlling both brothers to lift a long pillar through a corridor (much like trying to get furniture out of a living room, working in tandem), or getting one brother to pull a lever while the other goes and turns a handle. One of my favourite sections early on was in a field with a guard dog. Each brother distracted the dog to run after them while the other jumped across to the next hay bale, then shouted for the dog to come after them, working together to reach the other side. It's difficult to talk about the originality of the puzzles too much without spoiling it for you - half the fun was realising how you could get round a problem by getting the brothers to work together. The focus is always on teamwork, and how important the two boys are to each other.
I'm not going to spoil any of the story for you; the journey is the core of this game. Having smiled pretty much all the way through the first half, I nearly cried at the end an hour later. Brothers has some harsh truths buried in there; life is not always easy.
The music does it's job pretty well; it's a lovely background soundtrack, and I noticed at several points that the music had stopped entirely and I was just enjoying being in the world. At key points though, the music really does it's job and helps deepen the immersion in the world Starbreeze Studios has created.
The character development has plenty of depth, even though they never speak a word of English to each other. You learn by playing through the brothers' eyes how important their family is to them, how far they're willing to go to help their father, and this is pivotal to the storyline. I also found myself getting rather attached to a little griffin I rescued.
I can't recommend this one highly enough. You'll probably complete it within two hours, but it was easily one of the most enjoyable two hours I've ever spent inside a virtual world. I was blown away at the end of the game; it's a powerful story with strong truths about life and the journey we take. If you enjoy video games as a medium for storytelling, or just want to experience some unique gameplay in the sea of bland copycat titles in the world at the moment, pick this one up.

I just wanted to say here that this game is great for younger kids, from the aesthetic, to the difficulty. Enemies are cute as well as block design. For kids this world size is ideal. If as a parent you've ever played a large open-world game with a kid you know they generally run circles in a relatively small area anyway,lol.
Yes, it's not infinite generated worlds. Yes, it's largely quite easy. It is really fun though, and having many randomly generated, but finite worlds is actually pretty refreshing since you can see it all and move on to the next area. Each area has a few places to explore and some things to do. There is a decent variety of biomes and enemies, as well as enjoyable crafting and gear system.
The combat will throw you off if you are an adult playing this that's used to action games, but for a little kid the lock on and ability to focus on dodging/item use instead is great. My son is 8 and in his 2 hours of play time has come to say it's his favorite game in my list.
Don't let expectations ruin for you what is actually a very enjoyable game. I know even as an adult I'm going to be running through at least a portion of this game after the young fella goes to bed at night.
Cheers!

This is South Park: Vanilla.  So many games and movies recently are being made to be geared towards younger audiences, thus expanding the accesible audience and increasing profits.  This is no different.  Fractured but Whole perfectly describes the integrity of the product being sold here.  Buggy but (technically) complete.
I knew immediately that I would be refunding this game after encountering the disappointingly simple and awkward character customization at the beginning.  I remember a "Create-your-own South Park character" internet flash game 10 years ago with better options.

I'll start off by saying I really enjoyed this game and I played it on the highest difficulty setting, "Mastermind", and my review is based around that experience and will mostly explain what negatives I found from it. If you have/have not played the first game and want to pick this one up, I would encourage you to watch some playthrough first if you're on the fence. I repeat these are all the negatives of the game.
The combat system is different now and felt a bit basic. They removed world objects that could be used during combat that you could hit with a skill and have it fall on your enemies, like the first game. After the first 4 hours of fights I felt very drained and almost wishing there was a "flee" option. I don't want to spoil anything with too much information but it's incredibly repetative. If I could give the mission style a perfect explenation, I'd say EVERY mission felt like the first mission you'd receive in World of Warcraft. You know the one. "Go kill 6 boar and bring me their tusks." Although the whole game does have every bit of political wit, controversy, and comedy you'd expect out of South Park, I can't help but feel like this is where the missions fell short.
Something else that sort of left me feeling a bit bored and frustrated was the length of the game compared to the first one. I know that's silly to complain about because we all want more content, right? Well this kind of felt like the latest Transformers movie, if you've seen it. It just kind of continues to drag on when you think it's over and the hype is dying but you've invested so much in it already, so you keep going. As I've said, every quest felt like a WoW intro. one unlocks the next and then the next... But you can't do the next one because you have to go do one by another person who has another that is linked to another person. I played the game on Mastermind difficulty which is supposed to be the hardest setting but all I found was that it made the battles much more lengthly and there wasn't an achievement for beating the game on it. My advice is to play on easy or normal because all Mastermind did was lengthen the combat. Your enemies will heal each other more often and your bosses have a lot more health. I was stubborn and kept playing on Mastermind and I felt like it posed too little of a challenge as far as strategy and only made me more frustrated to spend 30 minutes on a boss fight that ended up giving me scrap metal and an artifact that is way below my current one.
Lastly, I found myself fidgiting around in my seat the longer I played. You fight one enemy. He calls a boss. You fight the boss but the boss calls another boss who then calls 4 more minions. Those minions die and then the first boss comes back to life. The whole game kind of carried this playthrough. You think you're done with a part of the story but then something else goes wrong. You fix that and something else goes wrong. There was a LOT of "beating around the bush" and "wandering off track". My advice is to save before and after big fights. You can't rely on autosave checkpoints.
I don't want to sound like I'm being negative. I highly recommend this game but I'd also like to point out in this review what I felt was wrong with it. There are a TON of side missions and there are a ton of collectibles including gear and player mods. This review is based on almost 50 hours of gameplay and I completed everything in game except a side mission that requires a lot of ingame currency that I refuse to farm for. You'll find out when you get to it. I try to play a game for 100% completion and this one has me fidgiting and trying to convince myself to just finish the content.

Dead Rising 2: Off the Record may be one of my favourite games of all time.
You play as Frank West, a washed up middle aged wrestler who's making a comeback. You're trapped in a place named Fortune City, a Vegas inspired, zombie infested city. The world is made up of about 3 casinos with differnet themes, a few shopping malls, a theme park and an outdoor area. Inside each of these smaller areas that make up Fortune City are various side activities, quests and themed areas...within themed areas. There's clothes store where you can find formal and wacky attire, food stores with different food depending on the type of restaurant it is (high end, western themed, etc.) and the world design is one of my favourite parts of this game.
I played this game as a coop game, as it has a Coop campaign that becomes unlockable once you complete the prologue, and I feel like it was ten times as fun having a friend join me along the way. When a friend dies, they enter a state where they aren't dead, but will slowly deplete in secondary health, while being immobile and unable to do anything until you revive them by giving them food.
The campaign isn't that long, about 15 hours, but I enjoyed every minute of it. There are plenty of sides missions and each mission has a limited time frame in which it has to be completed. The side missions were as wacky and sometimes serious as the environment. I never felt bored of any of the missions it provided, even if some of them involved doing the same activity, but in a different area. I never felt like the game was short however.
The game is super colourful and I feel like that's reflected in the environment, the story, side quests, the colour palette and the clothing you can wear. The soundtrack is also super fun and parts of it are memorable, even if every track is basically just a one minute jingle where the middle is dragged out.
The only real issue I had with the game was that it was frustrating once or twice, the weapons broke too fast, and because of the variety of weapons I found in the game world there was really no reason to craft stuff. These are however minor knocks to a very amazing game.
Due to how much I enjoyed this game, I ended up playing Dead Rising 3 as well.
If I had to give Dead Rising 2: Off the record a number, I'd say 8/10.

This would be one of the better Early Access games on Steam, if it were Early Access.  However, the devs somehow seem to think this game is "complete".  It's not.  The mechanics are there, but there's no real game yet.  No goal.  The cars really aren't balanced that well, the game mechanics could use a bit of fine tuning (it's really easy to just chain red barrels with a car that has a great rear attack).  This game is a good start, but it's not polished enough for me to recommend it.

Post Apocalyptic Mayhem is a car combat game set in — you guessed it— a post-apocalyptic world. Players take control of one of 9 oddball vehicles (12, if you fork over for the DLC, Chaos Pack) and battle it out over 7 sufficiently desolate tracks.
The player has four powers available to them: a forward attack to ram their foes, an attack from left and right to side-swipe opponents, a rear attack to lay traps for unsuspecting pursuers, and a depleting boost power to catch up to the competition. The objective of single-player is simple— kill the most opponents to win the race. Doing so requires driving over color-coordinated barrels to power attacks, and then unleashing them on enemies. Combat is fairly satisfying, particularly when accomplishing a revenge kill, or when a kill notification pops up from the traps left in a vehicle's wake.
Both keyboard and controller are supported; indeed, PAM seems to have been built around the use of a controller, such that I wouldn't be surprised if I were told that this was an XBLA port. In fact, not much effort seems to have been placed into the keyboard control scheme, as the vibrant 360 button colors representing powered attacks on the HUD, a perfectly suitable UI indicator if using a controller, remain largely unaltered for their keyboard counterparts.  A minor quibble, to be sure, and notable only for the impression it gives.
There are only two modes to choose from, though it could be argued that there's really only one: regular kill-based races in Arcade mode, and the marathon version, Apocalyptic Challenge mode.  This means you better really enjoy the handful of tracks and the base game, because Apocalyptic Challenge is simply Arcade Mode with no pause between maps.  Therefore, don't expect a mode devoted to racing, no matter how fun or obvious that might seem, as it's only present in the multiplayer.
Speaking of which: there are only seven tracks, as previously stated, one of which is a festive reskin of the first. Admittedly, each is stylized appropriately to fit their given theme, and are varied enough (save the reskin) not to be repetitive between maps.  The cars fair a little better, with nine/twelve vehicles to choose from, each with different stats and unique abilities.
There's no narrative element to the game, unless one counts the blurbs for each of the racers. I'm not expecting some grand, magnum opus, mind. However, the side effect to no explanation for the surprisingly controlled, accommodating chaos is that the racers don't come to life at all. In fact, one wouldn't be remiss for thinking that PAM was a hardcore alternate reality of Cars™, as the player never actually
the person behind the wheel. A step in the right direction would have been to model the racers of each of the automobiles, even if only as a flat image by the vehicles. Another, would have been to provide a motivation, a “carrot-on-a-stick,” for why these racers have chosen to participate, instead of taking their insanity out on the vulnerable remaining post-apocalyptic population.
Achievement hounds will find no satisfaction here without a little help from their friends; a fair amount of them revolve around the game's multiplayer, which is a veritable ghost track. One such award also  requires interaction with someone not on your friends list; a problem for the aforementioned reason. This is another negative to level in the game's direction, as the achievements and the lack of modes give the impression that multiplayer was meant to be an integral part of the game experience. A solution for this would have been to allow for completely bot-ed multiplayer when the prospects had all dried up, maybe with unique AI to differentiate them from Arcade mode. Perhaps that would be defeating the purpose, but I would argue the same for a multiplayer mode that has no players. Another, perhaps more practical solution, would have been to focus on the multiplayer or single-player to provide a solid experience from one or the other, rather than a middling/minimal experience from both.
The sound design is decent, if not memorable. The music is a standard, instrumental rock affair, including a rocked out version of Jingle Bells on the “Winter Wasteland” track. Sound effects, such as the winding of the engines and blasts from weapons fire, don't seem out of place.
The graphics are average; they're not going to break even a modestly equipped rig, but they're not blindingly awful, either.   The themes of individual tracks are represented well enough. Each of the vehicle's attacks have interesting visual effects unique to them, as well. Glowing spots on vehicles indicate if an opponent has an attack powered up or not— a nice, practical touch . The explosions can be satisfying, but they often obstruct the player's vision, obscuring the view of any potential traps laid out, and rendering damage and obstacle avoidance to hit-or-miss.
Ultimately, I don't recommend this game.  It's a combat racing game on a budget, and it shows in the lukewarm delivery of the single-player and multiplayer modes, and hand-me-down, controller-based UI.  That's not to say it doesn't have its merits; I'm not well-versed in Steam's car combat offerings, but I'll guess that there aren't many available at PAM's on-sale price point, so if you're itching for a vehicular action game and need a quick fix, this could be your thing.  And if you were already planning to play this with friends, I could see you easily getting your money's worth with the multiplayer, provided you didn't expect to have any fun with it when your friends aren't available.

I remember having played the demo of this game so long ago and I thought to myself then, "Man, this game is awesome! Why didn't I think of this before?!"
Well, after having aquired this one once more as the full version this time around, I can still safely say that the game still holds up rather well. The graphics look very nice, the controls are rather simple, the music sets the tone of what it is that you're going again and everything in between just works. Despite there are some times where it can get a little frustrating and trust me, there will be times when you will encounter quite a lot of them, if you LET them, of course.
The game doesn't really have a story mode per se, but it makes up for it with a little campaign mode that runs about an hour or so, pitting you against five other racers that are all out for each other's blood, where the only way to win is if you've completed more laps than they did and got more kills then they do, instead of traditional racers where only first, second or third gets you the win. The weapon systems for each individual vehicle is tied to specific buttons, where you have a front, side and rear weapon. Each has their own characteristic, their own style and has their own method of doling out punishment. You can only use these once before you have to grab a color coded barrel that ties to the weapon in particular. Red ones for the rear, blue for the side and yellow for the front. Green ones are for your speed boost, which comes in handy when you're trying to catch up with pack, but over time, you come to figure out that there's really no need for it, unless if it's a long run. There's also black barrels, which gives you something at random. It's more or less a crapshoot, but it comes through in the clinch.
There's really not much I can say about the cars, since they're pretty much exactly what you would expect.
But of course, I will have to agree with some detractors that the game doesn't offer much in terms of vareity and that it wears out its welcome fairly quickly. Multiplayer does in fact have a limited shelf life and this is something I can agree with, but even then, whether you're playing with random people, with friends or even by yourself, you'll still have a great time,
Overall, this game gets a positive recommendation from me.

This game is absolute perfection for a fighting fan. The gameplay is an evolved version of Tekken 4, 5, 6 and Tag Team Tournament 2, and even features from Dark Ressurection and Revolution. This is a very, very, VERY long review because I actually believe this game deserves attention and an active community. No memes this time, boys.
IMPORTANT: I use an Xbox Elite Controller and a USB connector to play the game, I have no Idea how it plays with a keyboard, nor how it performs with wireless devices. If you want to play this as accurate as possible, get a cable and a controller.
The core gameplay works seamlessly well with the ragdoll and hitbox physics of the Unreal Engine. And I strongly believe no other fighting game using this engine achieved this level of accuracy. The new addition here is the Rage Arts, which can be easy to activate but tricky to land. They are a last resort move, specially because you need to have low health for it, and messing it up will leave you open for a final blow. Also note that if your enemy survives the attack, they will have their own chance to land a Rage Art on you.
Those new to the series need to know: The game keys are divided in Left and Right Arms, and Left and Right Legs. you will need to master each character to understand their own attacks, if they are High, Medium or Low, then if they are Strong or Weak. Mapping extra buttons for certain combinations is a must, and I recommend getting rid of the two original assist inputs since you won't use them even in story mode.
Arcade mode is relatively short, but the ending battles are well made, even more if you play as one of the Mishimas. Where you will dunk hours of gameplay is the treasure mode, and you will understand what I mean by that when I reach the customization. Versus is well, versus, you pick a fighter, play against a cpu that you chose or against a friend, nothing new here. Practice is evolved and allows you to actively customize all the conditions you want, including simulating connection lag, life gauge, special gaige and rage gauge. I recommend also activating "input display" so you can see what you pressed. Use the move list to see demos of the movements to check if you are doing the right thing.
The Mishima Saga story mode is akin to Mortal Kombat, in a sense that it has segments that are very unique and fun, for instance, some fights start as a third person shooter and you quickly switch to the core gameplay, kinda like a fully interactive cutscene. I have to thank the UE4 engine for that possibility, and it's really interesting. The side stories portion offer a more focused type of Arcade mode from previous Tekken games, where you have unique interactions between rivals that don't happen normally and introduce a canon resolution to the fighter's path in the franchise.
The character customization is back and it is amazing, though I kinda miss creating hairstyles like Dark Ressurection offered, where you would pick a base hair and modify each side, this time they offer basic hairstyles that are mostly short cuts that remind me of Dante and Raiden from DMC and MGR. Where the customization shines is in the Unique outfits and pieces for each character, which offer hidden skins and modify Rage Arts depending on the character. There are many common tier outfits but they range mostly from team shirts and jackets (without shirts underneath, it seems a bit odd to wear a leather jacket without one). Personally I think they are saving their more creative pieces for the free and premium DLCs, but since the unique skins are all in the game already, I am going to spend a few hours trying to unlock them.
Now the ultimate quest is giving certain props to each character, specially Yoshimistsu and his multiple swords. Some less rare props even offer alternate versions of attacks, including guns, drinks, melee weapons, but I have to see how that will apply to a competitive/online scenario. Auras and hit effects are perfect as always, and there is a particular hit effect that I love for it's comical reasons, I won't spoil this one.
So how do you unlock skins and outfits? There are two ways, either you get Credits by playing the game and use them to  buy outfits, that can cost up to 1,5M if they are unique full body pieces, or you unlock pieces by playing the treasure mode, where after each match you get at least one chest with a piece you haven't unlocked. Some fights hold costumes that are unique for each fighter, these are called Heist Matches. A good thing about the treasure mode is that you don't have to buy what you unlock, and you even get credits to buy the remaining pieces. Micro-transactions AREN'T present, and you get 30k credits for every offline match. Also, you have 10 slots for each character, so chances are you might want to do 5 outfits and do one recolor for each.
Player customization offer new gauges and titles for your profile, some are unlocked by credits, other by specific actions, such as reaching certain proficiency ranks with some charcters.
At the time of this review the Online is very stable, with minimal lag. I advise getting confortable with the characters you are going to use in offline modes first, and get a custom skin just to show off.
Oh yeah, speaking of DLC: Tekken characters like Eliza WILL be free for everyone, but Crossover characters will be premium. The season pass comes with extra modes, stages and outfits for all characters, so for the price they are asking I can recommend it aswell.
IN CONLUSION: Tekken 7 is a "Fated Evolution" of the genre. It is a series that never went back in it's mechanics and embraced new tech for its ultimate goal: be competitive and be accurate. This game gets a legit 10/10 on my regard, a must have for ANY PC player. Let's hope soon we will also get the Soul Callibur VI we deserve.

Apart from the banning of OpenIV, Rockstar clearly encourages griefing in their lobbies, makes it harder to play alone, and does everything they can to coerce people into buying in-game money with real money.
1. Almost everything fun in Online save for guns and the low-end vehicles is hideously expensive, from $3 million sports cars, to $3.5 million bikes, to $6 million yachts, etc. To even get into the new Gun Running update, you need to buy a bunker for between $1.1 million and $3.5 million depending on location. And to customize any of the multi-million dollar vehicles from the update AT ALL, you need to blow another $2 million on a special mobile operations center vehicle (why can't you just get a paintjob at the usual garage?).
2. Making money is stupid slow. Your daily objectives pay out $25k a day. Missions take upwards of 10 minutes and reward less than $10k on average. Exporting a car at the docks if you manage to find a wanted one pays MAX $8k. Really, anything apart from heists and CEO work is pocket change. Heists are a little better, but require four people to do and can get old fast since there's only four (plus a fifth, two-player intro heist). And only one of THOSE pays enough to be worth farming. CEO work can only be done in a public lobby and still only pays a maximum of maybe $300k an hour if you're really good, which still means 6-12 hours of work for most single purchases. Plus it's tedious work.
3. Public lobbies are grief-fests. If there's another player near you, there's about an 80% chance that they're hostile and will use a powerful weapon like homing rockets or a nigh-indestructible car to kill you over and over again. They'll also go after your CEO work shipments/cars and destroy them, meaning no money for you whatsoever and a meager payment to them as a reward, since starting CEO work also pings everyone else's map and specifically tells them to destroy the shipment for a reward. Did I mention that you can ONLY do CEO work in public lobbies? And they keep patching methods to join empty public lobbies.
4. Online modders are rampant, either griefing every player in the lobby by spawning vehicles or explosions on them constantly, or giving them large amounts of experience and money (which usually results in all of your money being taken away, modded or not), and it's not unheard of to be banned for receiving the money against your will. The only updates they push are either new content (which is expensive and grief-friendly) or fixes to exploits. They never fix bugs, they never improve or balance existing content.
So in short, they make everything outrageously expensive, make the only viable money-making methods highly griefable (in fact, the game tells other players to grief you), and make it harder to play alone. It's plainly obvious to anyone that they're doing this to encourage players to pay up for their shark cards.
In general, I do not recommend the multiplayer portion of this game unless you have a few friends to play in private lobbies and do missions/heists with, and to try and brute-force your way through CEO work with. But if you have friends and manage to make some money somehow, it can be some of the most fun you've ever had.

I would say that this game has a lot of potential with a few patches.  It has the allure of South Park, as with the Stick of Truth.  There's a ton of fun easter eggs as well.
However, it is extremely buggy.  Aside from the loading screens taking way too long, you're often not sure if your game just crashed or if the game is taking too long to process.  I'm not going to continue playing until the developers fix the game because it feels like there's more time spent on loading screens than gameplay.

This game does everything you want from a sequel. It keeps all the South Park animation style and humor you've come to expect from the original, while greatly expanding the combat system. It has a good length of content, and while a bit pricey at 60 bucks, if you don't want to pay that just wait til it goes down to 40 or 30.
My one complaint is that the block system from the first game, which demanded attention and skill, and the timing of attacks from the first game, which were important, have been watered down. This is balanced by the much higher levels of strategy that comes with movement being added, so you not only have to worry about what attack to do when, but also which character is where, and how to move and coordinated the enemy. This gives the game depth and keeps it fresh.
I see a lot of complaints saying the gameplay gets stale. I don't get this. You're offered new classes and options frequently to mix things up and try new skills, much more than the first. In addition to the added complexity of movement into the system keeps the fights fresh and interesting.
If you're worried about bugs or the price tag, I get it. Wait a few months, pick it up on the December sale. It's still a great game, and a worthy successor to the original.

What made Stick of Truth good? Despite its mechanics-lite approach it was a fun ride as it went there; from 8 bit Canada to alien anal probing. It had those moments that you loved as a fan and explored a lot of South Park. Fractured But Whole has been a long time coming but it just doesn't feel complete. I am going to break down this review into three parts: mechanics, story and other.
Stick of Truth had a very basic turn based system. The RPG mechanics didn't really matter or change much. It had fart power interactions to move around levels or find collectibles.
Fractured But Whole uses a tile based system. Your powers can have certain status effects (knockback, shock, charm etc) and effect certain squares. Essentially you want to position yourself and other members on your team to effectively use their powers. Unfortunately despite being given other abilities to try the combat grows monotonous.  Some of the boss battles however force you to think more tactically to avoid their attacks and to defeat them. The best part of the combat is these boss battles.
To augment your powers you just attach artifact slots which you unlock as you level up. Despite some artifacts providing different bonuses to certain areas it is often just better to attach those that increase your might. The system is very basic.
The second mechanic is 'puzzle' solving. Unfortunately it can't really be called 'puzzle' solving. You unlock certain buddies who enable you to interact with the environment to find collectibles. These interactions also appear in missions but are so obvious and easy it doesn't really add much.
The third 'mechanic' is crafting. Unfortunately it can't really be called 'crafting'. Three types of items can be made: artifacts, costumes and consumables. Unfortunately there are barely any of them. The system is so pointless you wonder why they didn't just let you find items out in the world. There are very little ingredients that go into construction and you find yourself with an overabundance of items.
Remember the anal probing section that was literally censored in certain regions? Well in comparison this game feels rather tame... The story does a nice whip round. There are a couple mini games that could cause offense to some but it just doesn't feel as if it is pushing the boat out.
There are a few great story sections but others just feel like they are rehashing episodes more so than doing something different. There are a series of missions filling out your character sheet that just aren't really missions. They are just meant to be little gags but it is a case of been there done this.
I remember a great bit in Stick of Truth that absolutely encapsulates why I love the story.
Unfortunately Fracture But Whole doesn't have these laugh out moments, or at least, has them in short supply.
I experienced a lot of bugs and performance issues. Walking down a ladder caused a glitch where I couldn't move. Some buddy interactions causes similar glitches. Starting the game went to a black window if it wasn't put into windowed mode. Some bosses froze and some froze after I had beaten them (especially annoying on some difficult bosses). I had several moments where it was my turn in combat and the game just seemed to stop.
I don't normally mention price as that is up for individual consumers but it does seem steep. The original game only had rather basic and unecessary comestic DLC. Infact Matt and Trey seemed rather unwilling to have DLC with Trey Parker saying “♥♥♥♥ that”
Now we are left with a season pass. I can only speculate that edgier content or good missions might be in this.
The DRM is again up for individuals. I don't find it that intrusive but others might. People have also accused the game of having microtransctions but the things they appear to be talking about are a few costumes available in Uplay that you can get just by playing the game.

So, coming back to Sniper Elite 3 after a break, I decided it was time to update my review of the game. My previous review was mostly negative, harping on problems I had with the AI and the difficulty.
Then I played Authentic mode.
I was wrong. I failed to understand how my perspective on the game was flawed. To put it simply, playing this game on anything other than Authentic mode does the game an injustice. Clearly, the developer balanced the game around Authentic, and then dumbed everything down for the lower difficulty levels.
My major complaint before was how inconsistent the AI was when reacting to threats. Why do some AI not see me when I'm standing almost directly in front of them, and then at other times they spot me a quarter of a mile away? Why can they not find me when I'm clearly firing a sniper rifle next to their ear, and other times they can hear me through 3 concrete walls?
As far as I can tell, it's due to the way the game nerfs their ability to react. On the lower difficulties, they still retain some of their faculties from Authentic, but lack certain common sense elements that would make them believable. This creates a jarring inconsistency on the lower difficulties, where you aren't sure what the AI can and can't do. You're basically playing a shoot-em arcade game with a half-crippled AI.
Sniper Elite 3 is at its best when it's an open world, serious, cautious, thoughtful sniping game. The highest difficulty forces you to relearn how you approach the game. It's no longer a run and gun, but a puzzle game. You look at each soldier as a piece you need to remove to get to your objective. At a certain point, half way through Authentic, everything became routine, and I found myself plowing through the levels with relative ease. It wasn't that the game became easy, it's that I became a better player. What felt like a disjointed mess on the lower difficulties, felt like a complete game on Authentic.
So, if you haven't tried Authentic, give it a few goes. Really settle in for the long game. Spend a few minutes scoping out each soldier, and figuring out who the weakest link in the pack is. You might find it to be much more satisfying than playing on Marksman or Sniper Elite.
As a carryover from my previous review, the multiplayer is still phenomenal as always. There is a handful of people still playing, though expect to get your butt handed to you pretty regularly. It's also great for LAN parties.
Oh, one last thing I realized. As I was playing through on Authentic, I suddenly had the thought.
"This is literally what a 3D First-person Commandos game would be like..."

This game is absolute perfection for a fighting fan. The gameplay is an evolved version of Tekken 4, 5, 6 and Tag Team Tournament 2, and even features from Dark Ressurection and Revolution. This is a very, very, VERY long review because I actually believe this game deserves attention and an active community. No memes this time, boys.
IMPORTANT: I use an Xbox Elite Controller and a USB connector to play the game, I have no Idea how it plays with a keyboard, nor how it performs with wireless devices. If you want to play this as accurate as possible, get a cable and a controller.
The core gameplay works seamlessly well with the ragdoll and hitbox physics of the Unreal Engine. And I strongly believe no other fighting game using this engine achieved this level of accuracy. The new addition here is the Rage Arts, which can be easy to activate but tricky to land. They are a last resort move, specially because you need to have low health for it, and messing it up will leave you open for a final blow. Also note that if your enemy survives the attack, they will have their own chance to land a Rage Art on you.
Those new to the series need to know: The game keys are divided in Left and Right Arms, and Left and Right Legs. you will need to master each character to understand their own attacks, if they are High, Medium or Low, then if they are Strong or Weak. Mapping extra buttons for certain combinations is a must, and I recommend getting rid of the two original assist inputs since you won't use them even in story mode.
Arcade mode is relatively short, but the ending battles are well made, even more if you play as one of the Mishimas. Where you will dunk hours of gameplay is the treasure mode, and you will understand what I mean by that when I reach the customization. Versus is well, versus, you pick a fighter, play against a cpu that you chose or against a friend, nothing new here. Practice is evolved and allows you to actively customize all the conditions you want, including simulating connection lag, life gauge, special gaige and rage gauge. I recommend also activating "input display" so you can see what you pressed. Use the move list to see demos of the movements to check if you are doing the right thing.
The Mishima Saga story mode is akin to Mortal Kombat, in a sense that it has segments that are very unique and fun, for instance, some fights start as a third person shooter and you quickly switch to the core gameplay, kinda like a fully interactive cutscene. I have to thank the UE4 engine for that possibility, and it's really interesting. The side stories portion offer a more focused type of Arcade mode from previous Tekken games, where you have unique interactions between rivals that don't happen normally and introduce a canon resolution to the fighter's path in the franchise.
The character customization is back and it is amazing, though I kinda miss creating hairstyles like Dark Ressurection offered, where you would pick a base hair and modify each side, this time they offer basic hairstyles that are mostly short cuts that remind me of Dante and Raiden from DMC and MGR. Where the customization shines is in the Unique outfits and pieces for each character, which offer hidden skins and modify Rage Arts depending on the character. There are many common tier outfits but they range mostly from team shirts and jackets (without shirts underneath, it seems a bit odd to wear a leather jacket without one). Personally I think they are saving their more creative pieces for the free and premium DLCs, but since the unique skins are all in the game already, I am going to spend a few hours trying to unlock them.
Now the ultimate quest is giving certain props to each character, specially Yoshimistsu and his multiple swords. Some less rare props even offer alternate versions of attacks, including guns, drinks, melee weapons, but I have to see how that will apply to a competitive/online scenario. Auras and hit effects are perfect as always, and there is a particular hit effect that I love for it's comical reasons, I won't spoil this one.
So how do you unlock skins and outfits? There are two ways, either you get Credits by playing the game and use them to  buy outfits, that can cost up to 1,5M if they are unique full body pieces, or you unlock pieces by playing the treasure mode, where after each match you get at least one chest with a piece you haven't unlocked. Some fights hold costumes that are unique for each fighter, these are called Heist Matches. A good thing about the treasure mode is that you don't have to buy what you unlock, and you even get credits to buy the remaining pieces. Micro-transactions AREN'T present, and you get 30k credits for every offline match. Also, you have 10 slots for each character, so chances are you might want to do 5 outfits and do one recolor for each.
Player customization offer new gauges and titles for your profile, some are unlocked by credits, other by specific actions, such as reaching certain proficiency ranks with some charcters.
At the time of this review the Online is very stable, with minimal lag. I advise getting confortable with the characters you are going to use in offline modes first, and get a custom skin just to show off.
Oh yeah, speaking of DLC: Tekken characters like Eliza WILL be free for everyone, but Crossover characters will be premium. The season pass comes with extra modes, stages and outfits for all characters, so for the price they are asking I can recommend it aswell.
IN CONLUSION: Tekken 7 is a "Fated Evolution" of the genre. It is a series that never went back in it's mechanics and embraced new tech for its ultimate goal: be competitive and be accurate. This game gets a legit 10/10 on my regard, a must have for ANY PC player. Let's hope soon we will also get the Soul Callibur VI we deserve.

I am a long-time Tekken fan and I can assure you this game is Tekken perfected.
Pros:
-It has the best graphics in the series yet (especially on PC) all thanks to the Unreal 4 engine.
-All the mechanics are familiar and polished. The gameplay in this Tekken is the most balanced out of the other Tekkens.
-The PC version is absolutely fantastic. This is due to the fact that the games was built on PC, and then ported to consoles. On a side note, more games should be done like this.
-The online play is absolutely phenomenal provided that you have a decent internet connection.
-Competitive Tekken is growing and this is great for people who love competitive gaming.
-Offline versus battle is easier than ever because of this game's PHENOMENAL controller support. My friends and I have two sticks and two pads, and switching between controllers is an absolute breeze.
Cons:
-There is a distinct lack of singleplayer content for casual players. The story mode is short, the character episodes are also short, and the offline modes are lacking.
-Customization is also lacking in variety. There isn't much flavor you can add to your character. Although, more may be added in future updates (or worse, DLCs)
-The lack of a decent tutorial also punishes beginners.
-The story mode is pretty underwhelming. If you love the Mishimas, then the story mode is perfect for you. If you love everyone else, then you'll be disappointed.
-No Jukebox on PC. :(
To conclude, this is the best Tekken in terms of gameplay, mechanics, and graphics. If you are a long-time fan and/or a competitive player, Tekken 7 will satisfy your Tekken needs both offline and online multiplayer.
If you are a casual player who bought the game just for the story, then this game may not be for you. Tekken 7 lacks singleplayer content to keep you satisfied.
Lastly, if you are a new player looking to get into Tekken, then hold on. Tekken 7, a game with a steep learning curve, lacks a tutorial to even the basics. My advice? Look up Avoid the Puddle, TheMainMan, Level Up Your Game, etc. The examples given are youtubers with amazing guides to help you get started.
It's a great game, and I highly recommend it!
