I certainly recommend this game to anybody who enjoys sniping, hunting  Nazis, epic shots, stealth, and hunting Nazis.
Pros:
Excellent cinematic gunshots, bullet mechanics seem on point (so to speak), and I found missions to have their unique feel to them and I often thought of Medal of Honor games and their objectives (they felt like they had a point, weren't for a flashy, over the top storyline). I can appreciate the feel of WWII and tasks that one such badass may need to do represented by a video game. I can absolutely appreciate the customizable loadouts, being able to play as I want. I am a big M1 Garand fan and it isn't required for me to switch to another gun loadout; if I want to use another one I can. I feel very badass when being stealthy and using game mechanics to mask gunshots, strategically take out enemies, and improvise distractions and misdirect enemies if needed. The storyline did feel interesting to me. The level design I thought was beauitful in both scenery and providing challenging terrain to setup a variety of ways to go after enemies (or maybe you sneaky-sneak right past them).
Cons:
Sometimes weird things have happened, albeit rarely, just like in any game. ANY, game. LIke bugs or "hiccups." I am not a fan of "collectibles" in many cases, it can feel immersion-breaking, so I often feel seeing missing long shot opportunities or other items was like a taunt that I wasn't as cool as I had felt playing the missions. Granted that does invite me to find those long shots, etc. but I would prefer to have that feel a bit more natural and not like an odd grade report. But that is simply my opinion, because that collection of info (long shots, cards, etc.) is actually a pretty interesting way of exploring maps and it does actually have a purpose. I happen to prefer less worry about collecting, more hunting. In addition, modifying the weapons can feel confusing at times. Such as a modifier bar going up or down to indicate change, but being unsure if that was a good or bad change to begin with. Once you play around with it you can start to clear up the confusion. But as far as being clear from the get-go, it is a hit or miss, which is definitely not a good feeling for a sniper (hint: you want to feel confident it is definitely a hit). Not including DLC bits, I feel like I would have liked more levels for campaign. Missions tend to have good meaty time to them, but I do wonder about having more to the overall campaign.
Overall:
If a player loves sniping, enjoys the hunt, and has the patience of a hunter, I think you will very much appreciate and enjoy this game. In just about any game with ranged combat, I love to assume the role of a sniper, and when I want to get a fix punishing Nazis in World War 2, I like to play this game.
If you want to run around and shoot-em-up, don't like to "let the shot come to you" or ou otherwise want to be running, screaming through a battlefield, you may in fact dislike this game, although if you are careful enough you could possibly play that way (but it could easily turn to disaster).

It however becomes unfair when they drop on you from off screen, where you have no chance of knowing they are there. But those are only minor annoyances compared to the shop keepers. Heroes and Generals is a WWII shooter, based around capturing key positions on the battlefield to push the enemy forces back.
In Heroes and Generals, you start off as a basic Infantry soldier. You have 3 factions with one of these soldiers in each. The goal is to advance through the ranks, unlocking new weapons and vehicles until you reach the rank of General. As you level up, you may branch off into different positions, such as a tank crewman or a pilot.
Pros:
-Rank system
-Multiple weapon and vehicle choices
-Large open-world battles
-Multiple gamemodes
Cons:
-When you advance into a different branch (a pilot, recon, ect), you must buy all weapons and gear for that branch. Nothing carries over
-Mostly a grind fest. You have to play many battles to get any sort of money, which all goes into weapon and vehicle maintenance. You will have very little spending money
-If you want anything, you have to devote a lot of time into battles, or you have to pay for expensive Gold Packs
Overall:
I rate this game 3/10. It has a great idea to it, but the devs are very greedy. The game forces you to spend hours on battles for money, which all goes into keeping your gear fixed and refilled. Very expensive Gold Packs will have you spending a lot of money for in-game money that will barely get you anything. The battles are long, sometimes taking an hour or two (Yes, I have played hour long battles), along with a penalty for leaving mid match. If you dont have good internet, you will get no where in battle. This game is a grind fest in all. In all honesty, this is a very top notch free game, but in the end, you will still have to pay money to get anywhere.

“South Park: The Fractured But Whole” takes reign of power from its predecessor “South Park: The Stick of Truth“ by putting you into the same small Colorado town but into different shoes  - now you are the superhero and dammit you’ve got to beat Freedom Pals and bring glory to the Coon and Friends’ Movie Franchise!
“The Fractured But Whole” improves many aspects of the game:
- Combat is completely redone. Instead of only quick time events which determine whether you succeed or fail, now there is a grid with multiple friends and foes each having 4 different Superhero attacks. Each attack has different range allowing to you to focus on one enemy at a time inflicting more heavy damage or targeting/manipulating group of enemies using weaker attacks. This combat requires strategic thinking. So it’s a miss or hit for everyone individually. For me it was definitely a hit. (Quick time events are present, but they only affect additional damage)
- Instead of choosing one class in the beginning of the game and sticking with it, you can now have multiple classes (available as the story progresses) and you can change your class/es and the loadout of powers associated with them.
- Not only base damage of specific attack type (brawn, brains) and health can be upgraded using enhancers, but you can also focus on boosting special effects like critical strike, health recovery and knockback combo.
- For character personalization the whole screen is used where the avatar you create is bigger and better.
- Character’s powers like teleportation and shrinking used in “The Stick of Truth” are replaced by powers of your buddies. It pads the time needed for activation it by just a bit, but shows cool mini cutscene.
However, there are also things that “The Fractured But Whole” does worse:
- Tutorials and specific events you need to do are forced on you, especially very early in the game. It is frustrating as most of this stuff is very simple and self-explanatory, but you cannot skip it. In some instances the game will simply not progress forward if you don’t do exactly what you are told to.
- Although I very enjoyed the setup for the story, it sadly didn’t deliver the top notch experience.
- There are times during combat, when the grid is wider than the screen with some enemies being at the ends of that grid. The issue is that you cannot scroll the grid left or right to see the further enemies by using keyboard or mouse. The only ways are to move and hope that they will be revealed to you or wait for them.
- You cannot upgrade your Superhero powers with enhancers to do additional fire or freeze damage, like it was with weapons and armour enhancers in “The Stick of Truth”.  This is a shame, as it would put the combat onto another level and make it more satisfying.
- Quests, Map, Costumes and other pages cannot be accessed via hotkeys. Wouldn’t be a big issue if this wasn’t done in the previous title as well.
- In this game simple crafting is introduced. Each item requires certain crafting level; however progression here is painfully slow in the first half of the game and ridiculously fast in the second.
- Character progression allows you to have more slots for the enhancers. Unfortunately, this progression is also painfully slow. It is somewhat compensated by the amount of enhancers found across the town, but that’s not quite it.
Some quests are great with that true South Park feel, were jokes are right in the target. Others, unfortunately, are just dull and boring.
I had a blast with new combat system and Superhero powers and the game wasn’t short of truly awesome fights.
However, the biggest let downs are the villain and the writing, which overall felt more like watching last couple of seasons of the TV Series – too soft and nowhere near as funny as it used to be.
It feels like a big step forward and a couple steps backwards.

is one of the more interesting free to play games I've played so far combining the extreme sports of downhill skiing and snowboarding and open world gameplay. We've had such marvelous games like SSX and Skate that have had open world elements in them but SNOW takes the whole open world aspect a step forward.
In the core SNOW is just like another game you would expect ftom the genre. You go fast, you do and combo different kind of tricks and compete in offline challenges or go on a multiplayer session and play at the same time with other players. There are your usual time trial missions which require for you to go through checkpoints and reach the goal in some particular time, score attacks, downhill skiing missions which are the same as time trials just without checkpoints but with an open road for you to ride and last but not least there are mssions where you have to do certain kind of tricks in certain spots. Nothing out of the usual but that's what I was expecting when I got in to SNOW.
The open world aspect of SNOW is executed quite... interestingly though. You have different kind of levels, or mountains and parks, to play in and while most of them are quite small the mountains are huge and have the whole area open for you to explore. Which, listen carefully, is encouraged and almost madatory for you to advance in the game. Exploring the areas might award you experience, which awards you more challenges and rewards, or new spawn points and challenges inside the level. This quite neat idea since SNOW doesn't really hold your hand on the exploration part. This unfortunately is one of the main problems of the game too.
SNOW still has quite some problems. It still is in Early Access however so we can only hope for the developers to fix some of the issues. But let's get to the point. Like I said SNOW doesn't hold your hand. And in fact it doesn't really even explain itself well enough. SNOW is an open world game but pretty much the only thing that gives it away is the Steam Store page and the occasional loading screen tips that courage you to explore for new rewards. So if you miss these signs you really have no clue how to unlock some of the stuff. And that's a pretty big problem. SNOW isn't really a newbie friendly game and it took me quite some time to realize how to unlock some of the unlockables but now that I got it figured out I can safely say I am enjoying the open world in SNOW so far. However the lack of unstructions isn't the only problem. Another one comes from the extremely glitchy and wonky controls and physics. Especially on snowboard. Sometimes the physics make you fall down from the slightest of bumps and sometimes you'll just bounce of the rocks like nothing happened. Hopefully this will get fixed someday.
But at its current state SNOW is a fine game despite its problems. It is fun, it is innovative in its on genre and it is free to play. There's really no reason to pass the game if you can run it.

You and your brother are on a perilous journey to find medicine for your dying father.  Along the way you must control each brother simultaneously or individually depending on what obstacles you come across.  The entire game consists of traversing incredibly unique environments and any dangers you may encounter.  Atmospherically, it's beautiful.  Loved the scenery throughout the game and I will give the developers credit where credit is the due especially in regards to its art style.  It's easy on the eyes and the colors are blended in wonderfully.  It's also important to note that the characters do not speak English in this game and there are no subtitles, obviously.  They speak a made-up language and the purpose of this is to help draw the player more into the game.  If you can catch this game for $5 or less definitely pick it up.  It's a fun experience.
CONS
-Really short (between 4-6 hours) but I guess that's to be expected?
-Controls can be frustrating at first, particularly at the boat part where you have to paddle.  That could have been ironed out a little more.  Other than that they are flawless.

The story is remarkably well developed given that there isn't any understandable dialog (any communication is gestures and intonations in a made up language). Relying on the situation and subtler details to convey love, loss, urgency etc draws you in that much more effectively. Start to finish gameplay is quite short, about 3.5 hrs depending on how much you like to stop and look at the scenery.
I thorougly enjoyed my playthrough, but there is nothing there to draw you back for another journey. Consider the shortness, lack of replayability, but very satisfying visuals and story to decide what value you might place on the game. At typical sale prices I think it is definitely well worth it.

The PC version is much superior than its console counterparts. The PC version renders full 1080p and 4k (if you have a really good video card like GTX1060) while the PS4/XB1 renders only 900p (tradeoff for buttery smooth 60 fps).
Gameplay-wise, It's still the same Tekken you have known ever since the first one with new mechanics like Rage Arts (when low on health, think Street Fighter V super moves), Rage Drive (when low on health too), and Power Crush.
Akuma's moves, mechanics (Super Bar 2 and Focus Attack), and combos are imported from Street Fighter IV with new Tekken moves. Very good transitioning from 2d to 3d thanks to Capcom and Namco.
Pros:
+ If you're a Tekken fan, this is a really good buy.
+ For newcomers, I recommend this because it's one of the most successful and smooth fighting game ever released on Steam. The practice mode is very good in this game. It will improve your skills.
+ The graphics is very good for this fighting game (it runs in Unreal Engine 4).
+ It's cheaper than its console counterparts and the only Tekken title released in PC after so long (22 years maybe).
+ The story mode and the transition from cutscene to gameplay is smooth.
+ You can view cinematic videos from previous entries (from Tekken 1 to Tekken 7, Tekken Tag Tournament 1 and 2, and Tekken Revolution).
Cons
+ Arcade Mode is very short (5 stages).
+ The graphics customization setting is not that detailed.
+ No VR mode in this release (PS4 only).
+ Only Two modes for Offline Single Player (Arcade Mode and Treasure Mode)
9/10 Because of this release in PC, we can now play Tekken everywhere if you have a gaming laptop. :)

This game is great. When you can get a match.
It's good. Basically. It's still true that nothing is Killer Instinct, but match-hindering lag has been rare for me, so far. My connection speed is high, though--200 mbps. So, all I can say is that, if Killer Instinct is perfect, then Tekken is less than perfect. I also see more consistency with the newest version of MKX than I do with T7.
The exception to this rule is tournament mode. Conceptually, it's the coolest feature I've seen added to a fighter in a long time. Some rando (maybe even you!) creates a tournament. Others join. You have a tournament. Losers spectate matches that happen after theirs. You can type in chat with your keyboard. You get fight coins based on how well you finish, and then you spend those fight coins on cosmetics for your characters. Delicious.
But, tournament mode sometimes fails for no stated reason. Suddenly, you're all just sitting in the lobby, and the game won't initiate any matches. So, all you can do is drop out. The game also offers no visual indication that a match is in progress. So, when it breaks, you don't know until you've waited too long and you ask in chat "Uh, is anybody fighting right now?"
Even though match quality is generally high, finding a match can sometimes take way too long. You're waiting in the queue, then Tekken pairs you with somebody, you accept and are immediately given a "could not connect" type of error. This could mean one of two things: Tekken's ability to connect two players is pretty bad, or lots of Tekken players dodge matches for some reason. The only info a player gets at this point are opponent name, opponent character, opponent rank and connection quality. There are no patterns to any of those when a match is declined, so it's hard to say which of those possibilities is the most real. In either case, it makes for a bad experience and it hurts the game's quality, IMO.
It has a story mode. And Akuma's presence makes sense. Tekken treats Akuma with extreme care, as well. He's a legitimately scary person, easily the kind of power the Mishimas should fear. The "fathers and sons hate each other eternally" message is also delivered really effectively. Even though I don't like the rushed manner by which the story was told, I did finish it with a sinking feeling in my stomach over the Mishima family's relationships.
However, the story itself is mostly only cool on paper. It plays out in very disjointed fashion, seemingly skipping a whole bunch of important scenes as it progresses through the Cliff's Notes. You learn about the Mishimas, and especially about Heihachi and why he seems like such an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Everyone else is relegated to side episodes. These episodes are one-match affairs that end with a familiar Tekken-style cutscene. It's essentially the reason we play arcade mode without all the fights that don't matter.
Voice acting is extremely boring, throughout. The narrator, especially, is aggressively boring. His tone almost never shifts. He demonstrates no emotion, even when he's lamenting the deaths of his entire family. And there's no story-grounded reason for that. The rest of the cast are your standard examples of bad Japanese voice acting. Men sound constipated, like they're trying to blow a tractor trailer out their♥♥♥♥♥ Women sound like they're having consensual sex but are surprised that it kind of hurts.
It's Tekken. If you've played other Tekkens, you have played Tekken 7.
But, now you have rage drives and rage arts. Rage arts are your super moves. Your ultimate combos. They're just a lot less hype. Usually, your character just hits the other a bunch of times after a freeze frame. If the match ends on one, you get another freeze frame and the screen turns black and white. It's alright, but every other game with an analogous mechanic does it way more hype-style than Tekken 7 does. And rage drives are armored moves that set you up for bigger combos.
What I don't like about Tekken, mechanically, is its chosen high-damage mechanic. In Street Fighter you have target combos. In KI you have the combo mind game. Guilty Gear has its wakeup mind games. In Tekken, as it goes with Netherrealm's games, you get big damage by juggling. Juggling, in my opinion, is the most boring way to get big damage in fighters. You open the guy up one time, then you execute the series of inputs you spent 30 minutes in the lab memorizing, and you're guaranteed the big damage you always get. ~50% of a life bar. For free. Just because muscle memory after 30 minutes of practice. Meanwhile, your opponent makes a sandwich.
All of my favorites are here: Yoshimitsu, Brian, Dragunov, Jack, Nina, Xiaoyu and Hwoarang. In my opinion, they fixed Craig Marduk by turning him into Gigas. Instead of a big hairy generic guy, he's a brutish slam master from hell. He punches really hard, you guys, and it feels so good when it happens.
However, Anna, Christie and Lei are missing. Some folks online are really upset about that. Especially about Lei. I'm kind of upset about Lei, too. Anna and Christie were reskins. Lei was unique. That's pretty sad. Maybe the free DLC that's coming will solve that.
Oh. Also, Akuma is awesome. He plays like a Tekken character with fireballs, tatsus and shoryus. It's as weird and interesting as it sounds.
Taking a page out of the universal game dev handbook, Tekken 7 lets you grind for your gear. You get gear or fight coins for doing almost everything, but there's also a dedicated PvE mode called "Treaure Fights" to make the grind faster. You just play against CPUs until you lose. After every fight, you get a prize. Prizes get better as your win streak grows. Every now and then, you have a "special fight" that gives you a rare item as a prize.
I'm not sure if duplicates are a thing in this game. Technically, you don't earn duplicate items. However, I've noticed that the drop rate of coins has increased the longer I play this game. That might be the game auto-converting a duplicate into currency for me.
You can't go wrong with this game. Lots of fun. Online functions pretty well (but not perfectly). And tournament mode should now be in all fighting games.

I'm not a train fan to begin with, but I found myself enjoying playing Train Simulator. Driving trains feels like what I would imagine it feeling like in the real world and there certainly is enough routes and locomotives to choose from. Most of them come in form of DLC and are relatively expensive. But if you aim to actually master the game, you'll be driving same route over and over again (just like in real life) anyway, so you don't need to purchase all of them, just the ones that you find interesting. This definitely isn't one of those games where you want to splurge and buy each and every DLC unless you have lots of disposable income.
Graphicswise the game isn't particularly flashy, but good enough. There's some performance problems on my computer and I had to turn down graphics quite a bit. Sounds are ok, if you like train sounds of course.
Every route I have purchased comes with a pdf manual explaining a bit of background of the route and how signaling works on that particular route. Same pdf also explains how to correctly operate the locomotives included in the route. Some of the routes are really beautiful, like the Semmeringbahn set high on (and in) the mountains.

Train fans will love this. There are a few glitches to be aware of though. "AI" traffic does derail occasionally thus ending the scenario being played. That's irritating. The basic game gets you started with supplied trains, routes and activities. There are all kinds of extra trains and routes that can be purchased. Wait for the sales that will be announced. The savings are substantial and considering what some of these extras cost, it is essential. Routes and reskins are plentiful for free via the "workshop" section. Most are good. There are a few that really should not have been released. One problem with these scenario offerings is that there is a lot of particular trains, rolling stock and other routes you need to have in your system ( purchased, in other words ) in order for them to run properly. That can add up to a lot of money out. Still, I have plenty of items loaded in and spend many hours driving these trains. A lot of people will get bored with it all very quickly. Not enough shoot 'em up action, fireworks, crashes, etc. The clear target market here is the train fan. Many in number and mighty in strength. Yes, the vanguard of tomorrows cosmopolitans. Recommend this - you bet ! ! !

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Clear Sky is an open world post-apocalyptic game that followed up the beloved Shadow of Chernobyl as it's official prequel. It is the underwhelming game of the trilogy, given it's rushed release date, bland and uninteresting story, incomplete implemented gameplay elements, pacing, and several game-breaking bugs. Which is not to say that Clear Sky has no qualities to it. It is most likely the best-looking S.T.A.L.K.E.R. installment, by a long shot - although it was much more demanding. The story of Clear Sky revolves around Merc, a character who is forced to chase Shadow of Chernobyl's protagonist - Strelok, and the scientific faction that saved and hired him for the job - Clear Sky. The game takes you through some of the iconic locations of Shadow of Chernobyl (alas, slightly changed given it happened at different point of time - and highly underwhelming parts of the journey), as well as few new locations, which have some great landmarks to them (there was a lot of potential in the Swamps, new Red Forest, and Limansk). The problem with most of these locations is that many of them are traversed rather too quickly to impact on player's feel of the place like Shadow of Chernobyl or Call of Pripyat does. The 'prequel' SoC locations that the player travels are much less interesting than in Shadow of Chernobyl, and the game doesn't really give the player much to discover or to do in all those locations except to keep hunting Strelok. The faction wars mechanic is uninteresting, buggy and too inconclusive to be player's main focus. The ending of the story does tie to Shadow of Chernobyl's beginning in a satisfactory way, but it reveals absolutely nothing about the world of the Zone and its secrets.
Not everything is black. S.T.A.L.K.E.R. has the best community you could wish for, so there are many mods being made for Clear Sky with great devotion and care to give the game a chance to be a solid S.T.A.L.K.E.R. game although it's without a doubt the weakest one in the trilogy. Playing the game through Arsenal Overhaul+Sky Reclamation Project+AtmosFear is actually a very enjoyable experience for a fan of the franchise, with all major bugs removed and added graphic quality and weapons arsenal.

Epic in every sense, a true fantasy adventure.
Not only is the concept amazing, telling a story about brotherhood in both plot and mechanics, this game delivers on every level. The art direction hits home its fantasy roots, and the score is wonderful, enhancing every moment. However, perhaps the most impressive is the cinematography. Yes, cutscene cinematics are great, but Brothers is one of the first games I've played where the in-game cinematography is more nuanced than a pre-rendered camera. The third person perspective does a fantastic job of highlighting objectives and story details, while providing a fantastic frame of the gorgeous set pieces, all without obstructing gameplay in the slightest. I could go on and on about the details, but the best way to see it is just to play for yourself. The player camera is expressive yet functional, and few games can claim such.
If I was to get critical, the only drawback is the gameplay. The mechanics are solid, ingenious really, and I was impressed with just how much of the world I could interact with (even if such interaction weren't always meaningful). However, it is simplistic. A couple of puzzles made me smile out of sheer ingenuity, but most, if not all, can be solved without much thought. If anything, I'd say that the greatest puzzle lies in the controls itself, as controlling two characters simultaneously on a single gamepad is quite the mental obstacle, and the game highlights this throughout. Still, there were a few moments where I wish the designers had pushed mastery of the controls further, as you can stumble your way through every chapter without much problem. However, providing such a challenge could possibly distract from the experience itself, so it's hard to fault the creators for going with accessibility over difficulty.
The bottom line is this; if you want a great story where gameplay enhances the user's experience, play this game. Brothers is a great glimpse into the possibilities games present in the narrative arts.

Rarely does a game come a long which can take you through emotional highs and lows. Rarer still is a game which blends those emotional experiences so seemlessly with the gameplay mechanics instead of shoving it down your throat in lengthy cutscenes. Brothers is a shining example of a successful blend of story and mechanics. The game's puzzles are well designed and feel satisfying to solve, almost always making use of the 'one player coop' asymmetry between the characters in unique and celver ways to progress through the game. Brother's Environments are extremely varied from grand mountain vistas to muted yet intricate caves. It feels like a world teeming with interesting fables and legend, yet the game insists on leaving lore and backstory to your imagination. This means the pacing feels pretty impecible throughout.
Now, the game's characters don't speak a word of any particular language. Pretty much all of the communication between characters is done via body language. This perhaps sounds a little pretentious - but it works SO much better this way. Never did I feel like I didn't understand what a character was trying to communicate. Admittedly it was jarring at first, but after a half hour you'll start to see why this method of communication works in harmony with the game.
I won't spoil what makes up this game's 'emotional' qualities. - and I know you want to punch me in the face for saying "emotional qualities". Just know that Brothers isn't just a sad game. Quite the opposite, it makes you feel a range of emotions. This game is funny, charming, thoughtful and touching. For me personally it's had a greater emotional impact in its 4 hour length than any film, book or indeed game I've ever played. All that whilst not saying a single word of English. Do yourself a favour, lock yourself away for a few hours, play this game from start to finish and immerse yourself in the story.
As a final note - I would recommend playing this game with a gamepad. Wait! Don't through your pitchforks yet! The game still plays on a keyboard - though this game feels like it's built for a controller in mind. I would argue that keyboard control would detract from experience, and I'm pretty damn ardent about mah keyboard n' mouse.

This game is great. When you can get a match.
It's good. Basically. It's still true that nothing is Killer Instinct, but match-hindering lag has been rare for me, so far. My connection speed is high, though--200 mbps. So, all I can say is that, if Killer Instinct is perfect, then Tekken is less than perfect. I also see more consistency with the newest version of MKX than I do with T7.
The exception to this rule is tournament mode. Conceptually, it's the coolest feature I've seen added to a fighter in a long time. Some rando (maybe even you!) creates a tournament. Others join. You have a tournament. Losers spectate matches that happen after theirs. You can type in chat with your keyboard. You get fight coins based on how well you finish, and then you spend those fight coins on cosmetics for your characters. Delicious.
But, tournament mode sometimes fails for no stated reason. Suddenly, you're all just sitting in the lobby, and the game won't initiate any matches. So, all you can do is drop out. The game also offers no visual indication that a match is in progress. So, when it breaks, you don't know until you've waited too long and you ask in chat "Uh, is anybody fighting right now?"
Even though match quality is generally high, finding a match can sometimes take way too long. You're waiting in the queue, then Tekken pairs you with somebody, you accept and are immediately given a "could not connect" type of error. This could mean one of two things: Tekken's ability to connect two players is pretty bad, or lots of Tekken players dodge matches for some reason. The only info a player gets at this point are opponent name, opponent character, opponent rank and connection quality. There are no patterns to any of those when a match is declined, so it's hard to say which of those possibilities is the most real. In either case, it makes for a bad experience and it hurts the game's quality, IMO.
It has a story mode. And Akuma's presence makes sense. Tekken treats Akuma with extreme care, as well. He's a legitimately scary person, easily the kind of power the Mishimas should fear. The "fathers and sons hate each other eternally" message is also delivered really effectively. Even though I don't like the rushed manner by which the story was told, I did finish it with a sinking feeling in my stomach over the Mishima family's relationships.
However, the story itself is mostly only cool on paper. It plays out in very disjointed fashion, seemingly skipping a whole bunch of important scenes as it progresses through the Cliff's Notes. You learn about the Mishimas, and especially about Heihachi and why he seems like such an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Everyone else is relegated to side episodes. These episodes are one-match affairs that end with a familiar Tekken-style cutscene. It's essentially the reason we play arcade mode without all the fights that don't matter.
Voice acting is extremely boring, throughout. The narrator, especially, is aggressively boring. His tone almost never shifts. He demonstrates no emotion, even when he's lamenting the deaths of his entire family. And there's no story-grounded reason for that. The rest of the cast are your standard examples of bad Japanese voice acting. Men sound constipated, like they're trying to blow a tractor trailer out their♥♥♥♥♥ Women sound like they're having consensual sex but are surprised that it kind of hurts.
It's Tekken. If you've played other Tekkens, you have played Tekken 7.
But, now you have rage drives and rage arts. Rage arts are your super moves. Your ultimate combos. They're just a lot less hype. Usually, your character just hits the other a bunch of times after a freeze frame. If the match ends on one, you get another freeze frame and the screen turns black and white. It's alright, but every other game with an analogous mechanic does it way more hype-style than Tekken 7 does. And rage drives are armored moves that set you up for bigger combos.
What I don't like about Tekken, mechanically, is its chosen high-damage mechanic. In Street Fighter you have target combos. In KI you have the combo mind game. Guilty Gear has its wakeup mind games. In Tekken, as it goes with Netherrealm's games, you get big damage by juggling. Juggling, in my opinion, is the most boring way to get big damage in fighters. You open the guy up one time, then you execute the series of inputs you spent 30 minutes in the lab memorizing, and you're guaranteed the big damage you always get. ~50% of a life bar. For free. Just because muscle memory after 30 minutes of practice. Meanwhile, your opponent makes a sandwich.
All of my favorites are here: Yoshimitsu, Brian, Dragunov, Jack, Nina, Xiaoyu and Hwoarang. In my opinion, they fixed Craig Marduk by turning him into Gigas. Instead of a big hairy generic guy, he's a brutish slam master from hell. He punches really hard, you guys, and it feels so good when it happens.
However, Anna, Christie and Lei are missing. Some folks online are really upset about that. Especially about Lei. I'm kind of upset about Lei, too. Anna and Christie were reskins. Lei was unique. That's pretty sad. Maybe the free DLC that's coming will solve that.
Oh. Also, Akuma is awesome. He plays like a Tekken character with fireballs, tatsus and shoryus. It's as weird and interesting as it sounds.
Taking a page out of the universal game dev handbook, Tekken 7 lets you grind for your gear. You get gear or fight coins for doing almost everything, but there's also a dedicated PvE mode called "Treaure Fights" to make the grind faster. You just play against CPUs until you lose. After every fight, you get a prize. Prizes get better as your win streak grows. Every now and then, you have a "special fight" that gives you a rare item as a prize.
I'm not sure if duplicates are a thing in this game. Technically, you don't earn duplicate items. However, I've noticed that the drop rate of coins has increased the longer I play this game. That might be the game auto-converting a duplicate into currency for me.
You can't go wrong with this game. Lots of fun. Online functions pretty well (but not perfectly). And tournament mode should now be in all fighting games.

I'm running GTX 1080, i7 6700k, 16gb DDR4 ram and on my first run I was getting 5-10 FPS.
Was also unable to use controller. Many have reported similar issues with this game.
After doing research installed "Flawless Widescreen" which has specific plugin for DR2:OTR. This fixed all issues immediately, including controller support. I reccomend that you make sure this program is accessible if you use multiple monitors and otherwise be aware of potential performance issues. Now for the actual review
This game is a reimagining of DR2, which is already a good game. The main difference is a new protagonist, Frank West, who also brings with him a new main storyline more in the vein of the first game, and a variety of new/changed encounters and bossfights. Engine imrpovements are good, more zombies on screen and the additional content really finishes up the experience.
For those who havent played DR2 or any other DR game, DR2:OTR is vaguely action-RPG mostly about time management. You are put in a mall (leisure resort thing with casinos, theme park, etc) and there are many zombies, and you must survive. You can use most objects of scenery as weapons, although most are fairly ineffective. There are a variety of wacky and fun items but they tend to be least effective as weapons as a trade off for being gruesome or silly. Items can be combined into better weapons, but again the entertaining ones (rocket powered wheelchair) tend to be barely effective in terms of gameplay. Things like Knifegloves or Fire-axe-Sledgehammer will be your go-to. Weapons degrade over time which encourages you to seek out good weaponry or be forced to use impromptu scenery in a pinch.
The game is on a time limit, and while you can just survive till it runs out, you'll be given a variety of calls and objectives to go rescue survivors and uncover the conspiracy behind the game. This is the funnest part of the game; getting 2-3 calls on opposite ends of the mall and then dashing between them with survivors in tow to try and get everything done before the calls (and the game) times out. There is a degree of inventory management too, as the best weapons can be hard to produce, and healing items and magazines which provide buffs will take up precious space for weapons.
Bossfights are varied and challenging, and show up in just the right numbers to prevent the game from getting boring. Bosses have patterns that must be learned and also vulnerabilities, some of which require getting creative (flamethrower boss can be easily beaten by water which stops his guns, or by cooking oil that sets him alight, or marbles that make him fall over, etc). Bosses also have interesting, if gimmicky characters to them too which can be entertaining or terrifiying.
Dead Rising does not take itself overly seriously. Although there are a lot of nasty events, it tends to be weaved with a dark humour throughout most of them. There are some genuinely disturbing scenes (Randy, for instance) but even those tend to be with some sort of wacky scenario.
Controls are generally tight but sometimes can be a bit awkward. Unlockable moves have difficult commands on controller (LT, RT, B held for 3 seconds while unequipped) and there is only one attack button (press for standard move, hold for strong attack) which can lead to missed inputs. Attacks tend to auto target enemies too which can lead to missed attacks or accidentally attacking survivors. First person aiming for throwing and ranged weapons can be difficult to use also.
Zombies are slow and shambling; no special infected or anything. They are very basic and after a while barely threatening, but the theme of the game is how Frank develops to become a master of improvised zombie fighting, so if anything that is actually really appropriate. Frank will level up from kills, and by taking photographs of zombies, psychopaths and survivors, and by also just completing missions and such. This unlocks new abilites, moves, inventory slots and health slots.
Also Online Co-op, although i havent had the oppurtunity to play with a friend recently. It worked very well when the game first came out btu I've heard reports of bad connectivity post-steamworks integration. No promises.
Overall, Dead Rising 2 and Off the Record are games close to my heart. They are not like any other game series I can think of, with a very unique gameplay formula that makes them hard to define as a particular genre: action-RPG is a very vague title, I will admit. It is absolutely an RPG and it's easy to put many hours into it, trying to come up with new weapon combos or optimise your times from one area to another. Despite the performance issues (which I have shown how to resolve) the game is fantastic and I can see myself replaying it once or twice in the coming weeks, and then probably some more way off into the future.
You will like DR2:OTR if :
you like hectic gameplay against the clock
you like rpg-based gameplay
you enjoy wiping out tons of zombies
you fancy trying out lots of wacky weapon combos
you want a game you can (and will probably have to) replay at least once or twice

“South Park: The Fractured But Whole” takes reign of power from its predecessor “South Park: The Stick of Truth“ by putting you into the same small Colorado town but into different shoes  - now you are the superhero and dammit you’ve got to beat Freedom Pals and bring glory to the Coon and Friends’ Movie Franchise!
“The Fractured But Whole” improves many aspects of the game:
- Combat is completely redone. Instead of only quick time events which determine whether you succeed or fail, now there is a grid with multiple friends and foes each having 4 different Superhero attacks. Each attack has different range allowing to you to focus on one enemy at a time inflicting more heavy damage or targeting/manipulating group of enemies using weaker attacks. This combat requires strategic thinking. So it’s a miss or hit for everyone individually. For me it was definitely a hit. (Quick time events are present, but they only affect additional damage)
- Instead of choosing one class in the beginning of the game and sticking with it, you can now have multiple classes (available as the story progresses) and you can change your class/es and the loadout of powers associated with them.
- Not only base damage of specific attack type (brawn, brains) and health can be upgraded using enhancers, but you can also focus on boosting special effects like critical strike, health recovery and knockback combo.
- For character personalization the whole screen is used where the avatar you create is bigger and better.
- Character’s powers like teleportation and shrinking used in “The Stick of Truth” are replaced by powers of your buddies. It pads the time needed for activation it by just a bit, but shows cool mini cutscene.
However, there are also things that “The Fractured But Whole” does worse:
- Tutorials and specific events you need to do are forced on you, especially very early in the game. It is frustrating as most of this stuff is very simple and self-explanatory, but you cannot skip it. In some instances the game will simply not progress forward if you don’t do exactly what you are told to.
- Although I very enjoyed the setup for the story, it sadly didn’t deliver the top notch experience.
- There are times during combat, when the grid is wider than the screen with some enemies being at the ends of that grid. The issue is that you cannot scroll the grid left or right to see the further enemies by using keyboard or mouse. The only ways are to move and hope that they will be revealed to you or wait for them.
- You cannot upgrade your Superhero powers with enhancers to do additional fire or freeze damage, like it was with weapons and armour enhancers in “The Stick of Truth”.  This is a shame, as it would put the combat onto another level and make it more satisfying.
- Quests, Map, Costumes and other pages cannot be accessed via hotkeys. Wouldn’t be a big issue if this wasn’t done in the previous title as well.
- In this game simple crafting is introduced. Each item requires certain crafting level; however progression here is painfully slow in the first half of the game and ridiculously fast in the second.

I could write a long, rambling essay but I think that'd be pointless. Let's be concise.
Positives:
1) Base simulation engine is solid and smooth under most conditions.
2) Allows great scope for varied scenarios.
3) Some excellent DLC.
Negatives:
1) Scenario editor returns nonsense errors (e.g.: Line blocked by train which has been deleted; "Unknown error").
2) Unclear or absent instructions.
3) Defective pathfinding AI.
4) Defective dispatching AI.
5) Defective base physics modelling for wheelslip, steam production/consumption rates, injector operation.
6) Low-detail graphics for background features.
7) Frequent signalling bugs (e.g. signals displaying permanent Danger aspect when line ahead clear).
8) Frequent collisions due to defective pathfinding AI.
9) Frequent scenario initialisation errors due to defective dispatching AI.
10) Numerous startup crashes with unusuable .dmp file output (han't found a .dmp reader that actually reads these things so far) (since v59.2a, may be corrected).
11) Accurately-modelled vehicles etc. only available by DLC.
12) Defective modelling of structures (e.g. rain passing through solid roofs).
13) Unindicated pathing restrictions (i.e. unidirectional line not marked as such; passenger/freight-only line not marked as such).
In summary: A basically decent game that has been released in a state best described as half-finished, and which you will have to fight tooth and nail to make work properly. When it does work properly, particularly when using some of the more advanced DLC, it's excellent. Much of the time, however, it's a shoddy, bug-ridden excuse for a game which milks its customers by ensuring the content they actually want is only available via DLC, bugs be damned.
Average, could be so much better, but believe this is restricted by the game engine. Some parts of DLC are amazing, some are meh

-----------Original review-----------
At the time of this writing the game has still some serious technical issues, therefore I suggest to wait for these to be fixed.
Many people are complaining about optimiziation issues, stuttering and online reliability, though most of the issues at launch seems to be resolved. It seems to me that it's very much hit or miss whether you will encounter these problems or not.
But how's the game itself? ...Superb! Mortal Kombat X is MK 9 on steroids.
The idea behind the game is to see a new generation of fighters rise, with the classic combatants now older and ready to pass the torch to the new ones. The roster includes 24 characters plus Goro and another four as dlc, each of them come in three different variations that will change the combat apprach.
The new characters are decent overall, but not without a few complaints on my part.
- D'VORAH and FERRA/TORR are by far the best ones, they're original in both design and gameplay
- CASSIE CAGE is the daughter of Sonya Blade and Johnny Cage and of course she's a mix of those two characters, she plays very nicely but it somehow feels redundant to have her AND her parents in the roster (I would've kept Cassie and dropped Sonya and Johnny)
- JAQUI BRIGGS is Jax's daughter, again there's a little redundancy here, but at least she plays a little differently than Jax
- TAKEDA is Kenshi's son and Scorpion's apprentice, good design and moveset very different from those two, but overall the character is missing some personality of its own
- KUNG JIN might be the most uninteresting of the bunch, cousin of Kung Lao but completely different combat style and original design, yet it didn't strike me at all as a suitable MK character
- ERRON BLACK, uninspired design and boring moveset, yet it fits in the MK world better than Kung Jin or Takeda
- KOTAL KAHN is a little difficult to use but very satisfying to master
It's great to see MK departing from the usual roster made up by different color shades of ninjas, but I can't help but think that I'd be happier without some of the uninteresting new characters in favour of some of the older ones, like Rain, Sindel, Smoke, Nightwolf, Fujin, Borai Cho and Baraka that only make an appearance in Story mode but you cannot actually play (unless you use mods or if they will ever be added officially).
Besides these complaints, the game is fantastic. Combat system is precise as ever, tons of play modes for offline and online players alike and many unlockables to collect. Theres so much content in this game that'll make it worth your money.

Portal knights is a game where you venture world to world, holdling down left click.
Whilst this game sure does look nice, it sure is boring! don't get me wrong, the start of the game is fun. Like the quest thing was nice, but it went on vacation after world 1. The enemies looked cool, until i saw the same one in about 7 different worlds. The dungeons were cool, until they just... stopped? I'm not exactly sure why, but after a certain amount of levels, i saw no more buildings, or dungeons. Just islands with enemies and materials on them. The combat was fun, until i realised the enemies just walk in a straight line towards you, deciding if they should attack or stare at the butterfly going by, and also realising you can just nerdpole up a little for most of the enemies and they will just stand there, regretting their life decisions as you hack into them with your weapon of choice. The worlds are apparently randomly generated, yet the youtuber that influenced me to buy this game seemed to have all the same islands as i did. Not to mention the worlds are extremely tiny. you can walk from one end to the other in most worlds in roughly 30 seconds to a minute.
I really want to enjoy playing this, but i can't in the current state. All there is to do is hold left click. Like yeah you hold left click on different things but it's still just holding left click to do EVERYTHING.
There's no excitement, or suspense. When i die, i respawn with all of my items, and just a little bit of reduced health that quickly gets fixed by popping some berries.
There's no reason for me to build a base since you get a free one you can just teleport to whenever you want.
There's no point in having classes since you can use any class-specific weapon no matter what you pick. You're an archer? Sure have that battleaxe, and high level spell. Why not?
I feel like mining is a chore, since you have to get so many ore for one ingot, and even though 4 gold ingots doesn't seem like a lot for a chestpiece, you have to get 14 gold per ingot. and then the coal. and the ore veins are hard to find if you don't turn off scatter, and they're TINY. you get like 5 ores in one group if you're lucky. so have fun HUNTING down materials. It will take you the best part of an hour trying to get enough for half an armour set.
The only reason to fight is to get portal shards. That's it. Well, if you want to stock up on health pots, go to the mushroom islands and kill the green hollow knights. They drop strong health potions for some reason.
I think i've complained enough. Here are some things i think would make the game a tad more interesting.
>A better loot system.
When i open chests and kill monsters, i don't want to expect to get the same few blocks, mana potions, and god damn palm tree leaves. Maybe make a randomised gear drop system? So i could kill a boss, and get something worth the fight, like a new weapon/armor piece with random stats (tied in with the level of course). Heck, you could even bring in a rarity system to make it that more desirable. This boss might drop that weapon/armor piece that has a cool skin, and a higher chance of getting good stats? yeah, i'll fight it a few times and try to get that item.
>A redesigned crafting system or more worthwhile mining.
This is purely to make mining a little more worthwhile. The requirements and time consumption are to high for the little payout you get from mining. Needing 14 gold ore for one ingot is ridiculous. Please either lower the cost, or make actual caves, and tunnels for me to explore and get resources that way. I know there are tunnels in the game already, but they are more or less dungeons. The only places i see abundances of resources are UNDER THE MAP. I had to jump off a world to confirm a suspicion i had. I though i saw at least 20 nodes in an unreachable spot, so i kill myself to find out, and yep. There was at least 20 gold nodes in an unreachable part of the map.
>Exciting combat.
You know something's worng when all you have to do to win a fight is to hold left click, then s, then left click again until the enemy falls to the ground. There is no need to dodge for the majority of the enemies. Maybe have a dark souls style dodge system? something to keep me on my toes? Like all you really need to do is speed up the enemies a bit and have them attack more often, maybe add a few extra attacks to each monster. Like those turtles that beyblade around at you are excellent. They really pose a threat and keep me on the move. do more things like that.
>Class specific skills, weapons, abilities, etc.
At the current moment you can use anything from any class whenever you want. Why? What is the point of having classes if they can all do whatever they feel like? Make players put some thought into picking a class. Wanna play mage? well you get this and this, and only you can cast spells. you're strong in this area, but you're weak in that area so make sure to take this into consideration before you pick that class! can this be a thing that goes through our minds when we pick a class?
>Actually randomly generate the maps and increase the map size.
Saying this because it is ADVERTISED that the worlds are randomly generated when they aren't.
They all start to feel the same after a while. I want to enter a portal wondering what's on the other side.
>Fully implement the questing system from world 1 in every world.
I don't  care if the quests are randomly picked, but it would bring me much more play value if i had things to do when i enter a new world. I would be happy to kill this many monsters to get that much xp and maybe an item or two. I'd be perfectly fine with mining this area's specific gem or ore if i were to get some xp and a few items.
I have somewhat enjoyed my time on portal knights, but if you read this whole review and are still asking "should i buy this game?" my answer is no. Unless you have friends to play with and maybe set yourself some goals,♥♥♥♥♥♥around, and all that stuff friends do in games, then buy it. But if you're like me, the only person out of my entire friend group to own the game, do not buy it. you will get bored very quickly. Maybe wait until a few new updates come out, see what's new, something to make the game a little more interesting and fun. But as of now, i can't reccomend this game.
Thank you for reading. I hope my words may have influenced your decision to buy this game or not.

And then, it got removed! i just wanted help and my post gets removed! I honestly would not be surprised if this review gets removed too. Yes. I recommend Portal Knights, however it doesn't take two brain cells to praise a game. I will focus on the problems I have with the game. I honestly believe reviews should focus on such things in the first place.
Cheesing through the game is easy to do. Some mistake this as the game being 'too easy'. (Similar to having your mom or dad play a game for you in the 80's and saying you beat it.) I will not go into any details other than the fact that the Monster AI is really easy to outwit. I spend most of my time playing 'by the rules' but still abuse the cheesing factor from time to time.
Gender selection seems pointless. (Note the keyword 'seems'.) Choosing female gives the same options as selecting a male character. That is to say... you can choose female and have a beard. Yar! Right now 'gender' has no other purpose than to make you feel better.
Right now, stats go up automatically when you hit the level up button. Developers have said that this is going to change in the future. This is only a concern because of the wording used on the character stat page. (Which says you can place your stats despite the fact that currently you cannot.)
Sometimes monsters fall through the environment when killed or trying to reach you.
Items can glitch and use a knotted rope icon. Normally closing and re-opening the container fixes it.
Combat is simple. You cannot move while in mid swing/cast/draw. (Neither can monsters.) This is aggravating if you are used to games that do allow movement while engaged in non-magical actions. (Especially using a bow.) Important to note that while in combat you will not swing yourself of the edge of the map. But you do automatically move towards your target.
I am mixed about the target system. It is easy to use/understand but can be a hassle sometimes to break combat just to target a monster next to the one you were focusing on. (Not always necessary, but once in a while tab simply refuses to move to the monster next door.)
The islands are small. Yes you can explore each island's ('world' hence forth) surface within a few minutes at most. There are caverns and chambers, but they can be a pain in the but to locate. I've jumped off the edge a few times just to see if I could find anything below the worlds.
Death carries no weight. This could be good. But is easily abused. Falling off an island or being overwhelmed with enemies has no penalty save for going back to the world's warp and being low on health. (If you are deep in a cavern, this might be quite annoying actually.) The lack of a penalty is why I feel this game is very casual friendly. Even if the monsters like to swarm me like ants to a sugar spill.
Why then am I recommending the game? It is enjoyable in my opinion. For people who enjoy games such as Starbound, Terraria, and Mindcraft it is worth the money and hopefully worth the investment. (We need to remember it is an early access game.) I don't suggest it because of the graphics, music, or general mechanics. It is simply a nice game to casually sit and play at the very least.
If you are looking for a game with an in-depth story, that holds your hand step by step to tell you where to go an what to do... You'll enjoy it for about 10 minutes. After the tutorial (if it takes you that long) you'll find yourself bored after cheesing it to 'see the ending' or simply bored of the story-less grind to get to the next world or crafting tier.

Game is extremely boring and lacks a story. It leads you along, but you have to make up your own dialogues and story as you go. The controls lead to fingers/thumbs because you're constantly holding down triggers and rotating joysticks. After only 2 hours of gameplay I had already beat the entire game, which may be the best part about the game(the fact that it didn't drag on and on). There are some really nice aesthetic aspects of the game, but the lack of a true story makes the visuals not as immersive.

Brothers is an isometric quasi-platform game with a lot of storytelling. The emphasis of the game is the storytelling and the visual art, which is stunning even on a low-end PC. The sounds are very interesting, although some of the songs get repetitive by the end. There are some puzzles which take a little thought, but nothing too difficult. Overall the game is quite easy, although engaging for the most part.
As a kind of interactive storybook, this game is a great success. Even though there is no dialogue (the characters speak in gibberish) there is a lot of drama in the story. The scenery is extremely well done, and there are a lot of extra touches to give the brothers personality.
As a game there are hits and misses. The dual-character-control idea is quite clever, and there are some cool things that you can do with this scheme. The potential of this concept is not fully realized, some of the same kinds of puzzles appear multiple times. There are a lot of puzzles, but most only take a minute or so of contemplation to see the answer. This is good for keeping the story moving, but it made the game somewhat easy and short.
If you are into a game that is a kind of work of art, and is cleverly designed, this is the game for you. If you are looking for a hard-core challenge, this game may disappoint you.

People that have played Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons usually fall into two groups. The first group of people looked at the
reviews that this game received, tried it, then found it stupendously overhyped and underwhelming. Then, there’s the other group, who found the game to be
. I am glad to say that I belong to the latter party.The late great film critic Roger Ebert once said that videogames can never be art, a controversial statement at best and blatantly offensive and wrong at worst. With that said, we’re going to have to forgive Mr. Ebert, because a)He was great at what he did, and b) He never got the chance to experience
You play as two brothers who are sent off on a journey to find a cure for their father’s ailment. You, as the player, are tasked to guide the two brothers through multiple trials and tribulations throughout a variety of beautiful and mystifying locations. Along the way, you will encounter numerous characters, many of which are heavily inspired from classic fairytales and fantasy mythology. There is so much more to talk about here, but once again, this is something you really need to experience yourself. You really will get more out of this game if you go in
blind.
It’s worth noting that the game is completely
. No, I don’t mean that the game merely lacks voice acting. I mean that there is essentially no actual dialogue – voice or text, in the game at all. Sort of. The characters technically do talk, but in a fantasy language without translation. Instead, the story and interactions are told through beautifully-animated gestures and changes in tone and inflections. Despite this, there is never any ambiguity about what’s happening on-screen, and somehow, the game manages to weave a heartfelt story that, at times, can truly invoke a heavy feeling in the chest.
is a story-driven adventure/puzzle game with a novel control scheme. Each brother is mapped to a single stick on the controller. The left and right stick/shoulder buttons control the older and younger brother, respectively. It’s a unique control scheme for sure, in the sense that this game
like a co-op game for two players, but is actually a single player game, intended to be played on the same controller. The challenge in the game is largely dependent on the player’s ability to co-ordinate both characters at once. The ambidextrous be warned – this game will probably offer you very little challenge.
It’s worth pointing out at this point that contrary to what the text in the orange box says on the store page on Steam, a
. The game will work fine using a keyboard, and you’ll be more than able to progress to the end of the game without a controller. With that said, a controller is
for this game.
For the combat-oriented players – sorry, but this game is completely combat-free. Instead, the game largely involves puzzles comprised of environmental interactions and exploration. Each brother has their own perks. The older, taller and stronger brother is able to reach heights, boost the younger brother, push levers and swim, whilst the younger brother can fit into smaller spaces. Unfortunately, delving into more of the interactions between the two brothers would spoil the game for you.
The game is never overly challenging or frustrating. OOT Water Temple this is not. Puzzles are, for the most part, fairly straightforward, but are often challenging enough to invoke a sense of satisfaction when you do overcome them.  Death can and likely will occur, but checkpoints are frequent, sparing you from repeating the same segments repeatedly.
One of my only gripes, gameplay-wise, was the repetition of some of the puzzles. Using the big brother to boost the little brother up to a ledge got very old very quickly. With that said, even the puzzles that are solved the same way are often presented in a different setting, with a different outcome, which helps to keep them fresh.
My only other "criticism" is that this game is short and lacks any compelling reason to go back to it after you’re finished. This is, unfortunately, a consequence of any game that is primarily
.  The game
support achievements, but these involve optional, easily-missed activities in the game, and are neither challenging or particularly satisfying to obtain.
This game is
. Not the realistic kind of beautiful that we’d expect from AAA games such as … The Watch Dogs E3 trailer, but
. You would not want to play this game and have it look like anything other than what it looks like. The world that
takes place in is strikingly magnificent. The town you begin your journey in is vibrant and colourful, whilst later settings are often appropriately darker and harsher. The shadowing and lighting in this game also look tremendous.
The most impressive aspect of the graphics however, is the incredible work that was done to illustrate the enormous
of the game. No matter where you are, there is always a lot going on in the background, making you feel incredibly small and insignificant in the grand scheme of things – something that will be very familiar to those that have played the God of War series, or the critically acclaimed Shadow of the Colossus. Moving to new locations was often breathtaking, although each individual is area is so gorgeous on its own that it's hard to move on.
This, of course, was no accident. The game was clearly deliberately
to immerse you in the environment, and allows you to interact with almost everything, despite the fact that this is completely optional and you are not awarded with anything other than the short animation that accompanies your action. In other words, the game doesn’t force you, or even encourage you (from a gameplay perspective) to sit on a bench in town and really take in the gorgeous scenery, but you, the player, will want to anyway.
The music and sounds also complement the game perfectly, and contribute immensely to the emotional impact of the game. I’ve honestly listened to the music numerous times since finishing the game, and all the emotions I experienced from the game just come rushing back. I honestly can’t fault a single thing about the audio in this game, as I feel that it perfectly complements both the emotions and the atmosphere that are conveyed.
In case it wasn’t obvious, I loved
. There is very little about the game that I can fault. With that said, I’ll admit it’s not for everybody. The game is very narrative-driven and requires a heavy emotional investment – something that not every gamer is prepared to, capable, or willing to do. It’s worth noting that this game could very well have been another To The Moon, or Gone Home – games which I personally loved, and are very story/emotionally-driven, but lack any real gameplay, closely flirting with the definition of what a “Game” truly is. No one played either of those two games and said “Wow, that was fun”, because plain and simple, the
in those two games are complete garbage.
, however, manages to capture the same kind of narrative and emotion (and arguably exceeds them both) without compromising on the gameplay. There is no doubt in anyone’s mind that this is, in fact, a game. That is the true magic of
.

South Park The Fractured But Whole is a game made up of boring references, a frustrating storyline that I stopped caring about at one point, a nice combat system and there are some bugs/crashes.
The story is really bland and there were hardly any interesting points. This is because the entire game is a journey that you as the player go on to discover who you are in the world of South Park. The first thing you'll learn is that everything revolves around you. Every character believes you to be the reason for or answer to their problems. As you go on this journey you find a lot of content but that almost none of it is funny or wild like the show, and if it is it doesn't lasts long. If that wasn't bad enough, the moment
shows up the plot slows down and becomes repetitive. In addition, perhaps I'm too tired right now to remember, but I don't seem to recall the $100 reward being claimed for the cat. Being that the entire mission is
to be about getting the money it irriates me that such a thing is not resolved.
You are forced on your quests to "solve puzzles". These puzzles generally consist of: You scan the area and see the very obvious way to disable something. You then move into place and wait for the animation of an ally arriving and hear one of two lines you hear every time you do that puzzle. All of these moments just felt like a grind because there was no actual question of what to do, or what could happen if you did something. Clearly no one gave cared much about the level design.
The combat in this game was the only thing I really enjoyed. I unknowingly played on the 'Token Black' experience which is play a black character on the hardest difficulty. I have no idea if the color of your skin actually affects anything in the game. Most enemies can defeat your heroes in two hits some can defeat them in one. Throughout the game I found team composition and the tactical positioning of my heroes to be important, and were a few battles with enviromental influence.
Starting up the game for the first time I was greeted with a black screen. I could already feel disapointment seeping through my veins. I experienced a game crash
, and several animation loops when I used my fart rewind power. After a couple times I simply stopped using that particular power.
In conclusion the game was fun and tactical in combat but sucked in all other regards and it should be purchased for 1/4th the price.

I would recommend this game for fans of South Park. What I wouldn't do is say that it's perfect.
As many have pointed there is a requirement to join UPlay, something made clear in advance, but there is no paywall or necessary DLC. You get the whole story. As for community rewards and pay to win, simply playing the game will unlock them all.
Pros
-Very funny, with many call backs to the show's history while expanding on old jokes in outrageous ways. (The main reason to play the game)
-Boss fights, very often, include special mechanics favoring different hero combinations keeping combat from becoming too repetitive.There is no "Perfect team".
-Good variety of character abilities allows the New Kid to be slotted into any role and played how you want to play them.
-Excellent voice acting, music, sound effects. Clearly made by people who take this sort of thing seriously.
-The game looks how South Park should. Everything is rendered beautifully on the highest quality construction paper money can buy.
Cons
-Game suffers from infrequent minor audio, achievement and loading bugs. For example, you will complete the "yaoi master" title before finding all pieces in game. While none of these are game breaking, they can easily be discovered by a 100% playthough and should never have made it into the final game.
-Quest design doesn't properly communicate all requirements to unlock the next part. For example, some parts don't unlock until you reach a higher hero rank or enough time passes but this is never communicated.
-Overall story is very linear. There isn't even a branching path to allow you to side with one group against the other as there was in Stick of Truth. A single playthrough is all you need to see everything. (Minor voice lines reacting to your character's identity are present but there is no effect on the story.)
-Poor UI design. Everything takes much longer to navigate than it should.
Overall, this game feels 95% finished. Given the ten month delay in releasing it, I find it frustrating that there are so many minor mistakes and poor design choices. Regardless, this is still a fun game to play, good story, good combat, looks great, good customization and is South Park through and through.

A fun little game that goes back to the basics of "getting the high score".  Your character's task is to collect as many crates as possible while dodging the waves of enemies that spawn (usually from the top of the screen); the amount of crates you collect is your score. The only catch is that the enemies that reach the bottom will fall into the fire pit and respawn at the top, but will be moving faster. Make sure not to neglect shooting the enemies.
After some time, you will unlock new characters, new weapons, and two new stages. The characters are simply cosmetic, but the weapons (such as the disc gun) provide new strengths and weaknesses for you to deal with. The disc gun is a great example, as it can kill small enemies in one hit, large enemies in two, and kill yourself if you get hit by it (as most weapons don't damage you in any way). The stages simply change the strategy of what you do; for example, the third stage has a corner that you can stand in safely, but has two fire pits at the bottom for enemies to fall in instead of one.
The only problems with the game is that it doesn't like to close out properly (which means Steam won't close) and that it likes to crash frequently (not on my computer, though). Also, it is a bit on the short side (lasting around 10 hours of gameplay to unlock everything).
I highly recommend this game to those that enjoy old school games. Considering it is free, there isn't much to lose.

Imagine 2011's MK reboot in a greatly refined form, and you get MK X. You have to accept the fact that it plays how it does (a bit clunky) - that's Mortal Kombat for you. It's a game that's more accessible to newbies than Street Fighter, but it has enough depth for those looking for their competitive streak. There's a smoother transition now between animations - characters don't look as herky jerky anymore. There are also small touches that show the amount of care put into this game, like Erron's twitchy fingers. The fighting also gets the same smoother treatment. Linking combos to special moves feels less detached now. It still can't compete with the fluidity of Street Fighter, but here you would be more inclined to discover the combos yourself without looking at the move list. I love how they made those dialled-in combos short. It eliminates the memorization-heavy problems that plagued the series since they were introduced in MK3. And finally - they've created a final boss that is not cheap as hell. Bravo. If you've played MK9, you'll immediately feel right at home here. These refinements would be noticeable to you but you'll adapt in a few minutes.
It's great that online is not limited to VS battles. There's something for everyone in here. Don't want to get your a-s-s handed to you by more experienced players? Hang out by the Towers or try to fulfill your Faction goals. Heck, there's even the excellent tile-based, FPS RPG-like Krypt too (and, lest we forget  to mention, the copious amount of unlockables). Else, if you're the competitive type, there's always the various VS modes. I haven't gone into an online match yet as I have also been plagued by the game's launch woes. Just see my warning at the end of this review. And as before, Story mode is excellent. I wish it had less family drama and more of the big picture stuff though.
Graphical fidelity is sublime. Beads of sweat, skin pores, cloth textures are all seen crystal clear. There also is a  way, way better display of damage. Unlike the previous MK, which had what I would say are set orders of damage textures, this one has me looking very closely at my screen to see if it would repeat any blood or damage textures. Zero repeats so far. Either they have much more sets of textures, or the damage modelling is done in real time. Either way, it rocks.
Sound effects are bone-crunchingly impactful, while music is just adequate. Everything is wrapped up in a more elegant and minimalistic interface. I absolutely love how they frame the the end of each round. And the art direction, top notch.  It's safe to say that no one will make palette swap jokes this time around, but to replace them would be the next-generation bloodline of some of the human characters (i.e cassie plays like her daddy, johnny). They actually are the ones who are more generic in design, but they're still nice to look at (i owe that to great detail rendering).
As a fighting game fan, this will be another game that I will play for months to come.
CAVEAT EMPTOR: As of now, the game still has bugs that need to be ironed out. I run a rig with an i5-3470 that I overclock at 3.8 ghz, 8GB of RAM, and an AMD R9 290 GPU. The most glaring glitch is that from the Dead Woods stage - it's currently a pixelated, artifact-y mess after the recent 15GB update.
All things considered, if you loved MK9, this is a no brainer. If you want to get into figthing games, this would be a great starting point. It's a complete package that has something for everyone, already content packed even in single player mode.
