While Torchlight II does fall into the same genre as that of Diablo, it has so much charm and unrelentlessly polished gameplay that the comparisons between the two are only at face value.
Torchlight II is one of the handful of games that I start playing and have a very hard time stopping, the only reason that I don't have more hours is because I need to stop myself from starting it up and losing myself.
But on to the review itself, the visuals first off are nothing special, but on high settings they only really serve to compliment the world and the uniqueness of each playable class.
Outlander, Berserker, Engineer and Mage all play differently and have their own specialized gear and play styles. Each skill tree had a group of abilites, and finding a play style may take multiple playthroughs, as it is basically impossible to have every ability at your disposal, considering the amount of time you would be required to put in. This is kind of akin to games such as World of Warcraft, where you can't have everything, but where WoW has the option to spend some money and respec, Torchlight will only allow you to undo the last three skill points spent, which means that the first  thing you want to do is download the mod where you can fully respec from the Steam Workshop, I myself have an Outlander with 7 wasted skill points as I traded the dual pistols with a pistol and a sword. Which brings up another shining point about this game, the flexibility of combat and character development. Along with the skill trees, with each having helpful abilites and passive skills, you can outfit your character with a wide array of gear, you can also instantly switch between two loadouts of weapons, so you could have a mage with a spear for long range, and instantly switch to dual wield swords for close quarters.
The game itself doesn't have much of an engaging storyline, what keeps you going is the quest for better gear, completing quests, getting filthy rich and spending it all on enchantments for armor you may end up replacing in 20 minutes, it all works and melds perfectly together. And also each area is generated randomly, which means every playthrough may have certain quests start in different places, new areas open up, while some places are static and do not change much, the hub areas do, which are large enough to be packed with content and enemies to defeat, but not so big that traversing them feels like a chore.
Bosses in this game are also pretty difficult, even with my Outlander, which in my opinion is an overpowered class, some bosses require multiple attempts in order to defeat them. But when you die you are given 3 options, to respawn back in town and not lose a thing, to respawn at the entrance to the area and lose a minimum amount of gold, or to respawn exactly where you are and lose a lot of cash. Thankfully as you do multiple playthroughs through New Game Plus, you can get a huge amount of teleport scrolls, which open up a portal wherever you are standing, and while only one can be active at any given time, they can be a great help to prepare for dungeons that you know will be difficult. And to top it all off, once you start a New Game Plus, new content is added to the experience of the late game, I found a Minecraft dungeon, complete with Creepers and a Golden Sword with surprisingly high stats.
All in all, this game is fantastic, it is worth the ridiculously low cost. Buy it

Deponia takes place on a futuristic world comprised up of almost entirely junk.  You play as Rufus, an egotistical jerk who has absolutely little understanding of how his actions effect those around him.  He's very much a scoundrel, and I can understand why some people don't warm up to him.  He has a particularly quirky sense of humor that really grows on you if you give it a chance, and as the story progresses its clear he's not such a bad guy, even if he is a tad selfish.
Living with his Ex, who just barely tolerates him, he dreams daily of combining the right sort of spare parts and combustible chemicals to finally achieve his lifelong fantasy of leaving the garbage heap behind and living with the rich and elite in a floating city above the clouds, appropriately named Elysium.
Due to his efforts he encounters a beautiful redhead from Elysium named Goal, and through her he sees his chance to make it off Deponia.
Of course the story ends on a cliffhanger, but that's because it just the first part of three.  :)

A cartoon looking point and click adventure game that allows you to take control of Rufus, a dimwit jerk who uses everyone around him without care.
The story starts off slow and begins to pick up a little bit as you reach the middle of the game, but I still found it lacking even 5 hours in. You play as Rufus, a selfish and slightly empty minded tinkerer who wishes only to leave the junkyard he calls home. Well, the planet he lives on is a junkyard.
Did you know if you double click a location you don't have to walk to it? I didn't, you should probably do the tutorial.
I found the characters hard to like and the protagonist even harder to enjoy. He acts like a childish pig and makes for really cringe dialogue when talking to his ex girlfriend. I also found that there was too much highlight on the protagonist, making you fall out of the story every time he opens his mouth.
The puzzles follow little logic, often being very hard to follow and require the use of a walkthrough if you don't want to go insane. I've found many other reviews complain about this problem too, and it really put me off.
I found trying to finish this game was a chore.
It does have neat steampunk graphics that are fun to look at, and silly humour that will give you a little giggle here and there. The music is also pretty decent for an indie game.
Save often, as this game bugs out every so often ending you not being to move or just plain out interact with items.
I got it on sale, and I would recommend avoiding the full price as the game is too short (around 8-10 hours for first playthrough) and has little replayability.

Do you love point and click adventure games? Play it. Otherwise, it depends.
Deponia is the first in a trilogy of point and click adventure games. However, it distinguishes itself from the rest by giving a great presentation and interesting story. The graphics are awesome with what look like hand drawn models, backgrounds, and animations. The game supports modern resolutions (oh thank god) and it sounds and looks very good. It's the best presentation that I've seen in a P&C game.
The plot of the game is interesting. The lore of the society is intriguing and it's funny how it passes off class and income differences as a mere side note. The main character is annoying but the goal is commendable and he is relatable. The side characters are funny and I wish I could have spent more time with them.
HOWEVER, the game commits the major Adventure game problem of inventory ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. The puzzles in the game require an insane amount of "pick everything up and combine it with everything else from a room you visited 20 minutes ago so don't forget to pick up anything or you'll have to backtrack." At one point in the game, you want to get some out out of a house so you need to combine a hook from somewhere with balloons with helium from a doctor's office to release from the basement. Then you go and pour water in his basement using a drill that you stole from a doctors office 10 minutes ago. What the ♥♥♥♥? The logic is absurd and I followed a guide. I know that you aren't supposed to play it like that but I wanted more of the story rather than the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t inventory puzzles.
There are several things the game does to make up for it. Double clicking makes you teleport to the next area which is very helpful when you backtrack 100 times because of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t inventory puzzles. There are certain mini puzzles which you can skip because it didn't explain what the switches do and you're expected to find that out via trial and error. ♥♥♥♥ that noise.
Overall, good for a adventure game lover but good if you want the story but for others. Maybe I'll look at the other two but I'm not rushing for it.

The epitome of all that is holy and extreme. More extreme than Tony Hawk's DOWNHILL JAM! Just the other day I played it only to call it the best game in the universe, but to my amazement I figured out everyone doesn't know about it so I took that statement back. But after a night out with the boys at McDonald's, we saw the unthinkable, a kid was playing SNOW!!!!! What madness, that was the event that sold the idea of this being a great game and the template needed for awful games such as EA's FIFA and Madden.

For a free game, I would highly recommend a download. SNOW is an awesome open world skiing or snowboarding. The gameplay is pretty good and the maps can sometimes seem endless going down the mountain. The game has a very organized and easy to use interface to make everything available to you. In short, the game is engaging and is very well thought out to deliver the essentials of being on a mountain.
The
in SNOW is pretty good (especially for a free game). Some manoeuvres can seem a little block-ey, but for the most part the game delivers a solid playing experience for casual and avid mountain gliders (recent 2017 updates have addressed some of the block-ey-ness). Players controls are quite standard and include everything you would expect from a game of this type. Players can speed up, jump, do tricks and grind when the opportunity is present. The different amount of game modes is absolutely appreciated and are very easy to start (even if you are in the middle of the mountain)! Players can compete with themselves or go against other players (which is an awesome feature)! Different game modes include free play, single events, half pipes and the long jump event off the big ramp (I'm sure there is a specific name for that). I think for a free game, you definitely get a solid introductory package and the leveling system seems quite fair.
The
are pretty good, but at times can seem a little "empty". There are cabins, trees, and the skis make marks in the snow, however the environment still feels like it can be a little busier (2017 update - objects are getting more detail and the environment is becoming quite the scene). The game is early access so I am hoping for a little improvement in this domain.
are basic at the moment. I believe a little more work could be put into this to better the playing experience. All basic sounds are there, but if a guy bails on a rail slide, I'd like to hear the bailing and ping noise from hitting the railing!
Overall, a pretty good start to an early access game. The user interface is really friendly and very neatly kept. I like how this game is developping and especially love the price (free)! I would say give it a shot! A note to the devs : I would try to make the grind aspect a little more involved with the player and the controller. Make it feel like we're in total control (when the situation is right)!

Fails to live up to its potential. While it has good visuals, great music and some interesting concepts here and there, the overall experience is fatally sabotaged by three problems:
1. Some of the puzzles are much too contrived and hardly make any sense even with a walkthrough. Making puzzles that are broadly accessible, and yet not facile, is, granted, an art. Whoever designed these puzzles has a tin ear.
2. The game keeps making in-game excuses for why there are no people anywhere for you to interact with, and all that's left are notes and documents. Unfortunately, because the playtime is too long and there are no hazards to distract you, the suspension of disbelief gradually breaks down and it becomes impossible not to see this for what it is: an overused trope, a gimmick all too present in modern games where the devs wanted to avoid the expense of hiring artists capable of drawing and animating humans. It feels cheap and tiresome.
3. Without providing too many spoilers, I can tell you that the game plainly cheats you of a satisfying conclusion and practically nullifies all the investment you put into the characters for all those hours. This is another instance of writers going overboard with "clever tricks" that only fellow writers will appreciate, and forgetting about the fundamental rules of how the consumer related to the characters.

Horror adventures tend to have you investigating some horror like a ghost, not casting you as an investigating ghost. Goetia bucks that trend in a big way by giving you control of a plucky little ball of protoplasm in search of answers. They won’t come easily though, and in fact turning them up may be too great a challenge for many players. A lot of this is down to how the puzzles are designed, clever though they may be, making a pretty steep barrier to entry to an otherwise casual and creepy game. Still, the other elements work well enough to make this little ghost tale one worth seeing.
You’re dead, that much should be evident from the dreary grave you start in and the incorporeal form that follows your mouse cursor along. Your ethereal charge was a young girl before her demise, and your adventures together are mainly concerned with why she hasn’t passed on to the great beyond. Her family features heavily in this mystery, and as you explore their manor and its surroundings you begin to uncover a plot of diabolical portend. I won’t go into any more detail than that because some of the encounters are fine surprises, but there’s plenty of supernatural machinations to delve into here.
This setup is perfect for the point-and-click genre, since your ghostly friend always hovers around your mouse. You can move freely around the screen this way, unimpeded by walls or structures, and fly on to the next area simply by clicking on the edge of your view. The cursor also changes to indicate something interactable, and those points of interest can be inspected, used, or possessed as is appropriate. Those first two options should be self-explanatory but possession is the important one here, because it’s how you’re going to solve many of the puzzles in the game. As a ghost your little ladyfriend is limited in how she can affect the world, but possessing items allows her to fly around as that item and place or use it wherever it is needed.
You can only possess one item at a time, of course, and they stay where you leave them. This makes inventory management in the absence of an inventory a key aspect of the game, one that contributes largely to the steep difficulty. You might come across a wooden horse you can possess and have no idea what to do with it, and then find a note an hour later about a wooden horse and not remember where you left it. Most items are used in the immediate vicinity but not all of them, and the ones that need to be taken elsewhere can really throw you for a loop. Figuring out where items need to be used also figures heavily into what ending you get, making the best ending a steep challenge to reach.
That’s only half of the puzzles, mind you. The other half are more conventional code-cracking, lock-picking, button-pressing adventure game puzzles. There’s plenty of creativity and variety to find in them, everything from locating the correct key on a key board (a wall-mounted board of keys, not the thing on your computer) from reading notes to typing out an audio code in a text parser. You’re also going to contend with more esoteric puzzles like figuring out a sequence of gravestones from poetry or reaching a purely arbitrary weight on a scale, and it’s here that the precipitous difficulty rises up once more. I’m no point-and-click pro, I resort to walkthroughs on plenty of titles, but Goetia reached a point where I had absolutely no clue how to proceed, and even after consulting a walkthrough felt unprepared to follow through.
What’s crazy is that the puzzles aren’t bad, they’re really that hard. They’re not illogical like cat hair mustaches or brutal like throwing a shoe at a cat so you don’t die an hour later. Goetia’s puzzles are just extremely puzzling, fully expecting you to pore over every note and process every potential connection between clues. The solutions make sense when I look them up, but at the same time I have a hard time imagining how I would have sussed them out myself. To be fair the game really tries to help you along, with your ghost girlie often musing out clues when she find something important and your journal listing similar suggestions at each milestone. But you’re still going to have to be paying attention and thinking outside the box, because some of these puzzles punch right through the box into seemingly non-Euclidean space.
I’m not even sure the difficulty is a shame or not, because like I said it’s not at all unfair. It’s a very challenging game, and it fits with the excellent atmosphere of ancient secrets and ghostly intrigue. Waking up dead and alone decades after you lived would be a challenging situation for anyone, and answers would not come easily. They certainly don’t come easily here but they’re worth chasing down, presented in detailed, moody graphics with some delightfully reserved sound design. Goetia is a gem of an adventure game but it’s edges are sharp enough to cut, and you’ll need to be even sharper to even reach the end of it.

Spelunky is a hard (but fair) rogue-like platformer where you objective is to steal all the gold you can Indiana Jones style.  It's mechanics are very simple and easy to get into, but is unforgiving enough that it took me the first month just to get out of the first set of rooms.  The problems that I have with this game are mostly in its execution.  Because it's a randomly generated map (like every other platoformer and their dog) the difficulty can vary all over the place.  Often the game will spawn enemies, traps and/or bricks right in front of the shopkeeper, meaning that I either can't enter, it'll send the guy after me regardless of what I do, or both.  The hit detection is a little bit off, as well.  It can be really trial-and-error at times as to whether or not my whip will hit an enemy or just menace the area slightly in front of it.  All that said, though, it is a very solidly designed game and well worth your time and money.

Summary: Easy to learn, graphically fantastic, terrible online experience.
Update 2: Over a month since my initial purchase on release. It's rare that a day goes by without steam trying to download between 500mb & 10gb of patches for this game. What it's patching I have no idea & I am certainly beyond caring. What a terrible release.
Update: Since the latest 15gig patch I can confirm that the online now runs at 60fps.
However, I have had repeated trouble connecting online matches with wait times over 2 minutes & have repeatedly seen King Of The Hill matches drop mid-fight. Leaderboards are still not reporting correctly & search parameters to find good connections are still non existant.
-----
Mortal Kombat X is a great looking game & compared to other titles in the fighting game genre, relatively easy to learn with forgiving controls & few mechanical systems to learn.
While MKX doesn't have as strong a story as MK9, due to the extensive cinematic presentation, the story mode is far better presented than most other games of this genre. However, short of farming the game's inbuilt unlockable currency 'koins' to acquire additional costumes & concept art you probably wouldn't want to play it through more than the once. Completion of the story mode will average you around 5 hours max.
As with all fighting games, the meat of the product is with the competitive VS mode.
Locally as with the story mode detailed above, it runs at 60 FPS, looks amazing on max settings & as such the only lag for your input depends on your monitor or television's refresh setting & your system itself. Online is a whole different story & ultimately where the game (in its present state) suffers a real 'fatality'.
As with MK9 before it & the PC release of both SFIV & KoF, the netcode is spotty at best, outright broken at its worst.
The frame rate drops down to a locked 30fps for online matches, making all the combos & control inputs you learn locally in practice & story mode, completely worthless. Added to that an omni-present lag both in the character select menus & the combat itself & finally an inability to be able to search by parameters for ideal connections & you have an unenjoyable mess of a product. It's also worth pointing out that at the present time, even if you do can connect (or find) a ranked match, that the leaderboards for this mode are also completely broken.
If you plan to take this game seriously at a FGC competitive level, you'd be best served getting the PS4 version as it's undoubtedly what will be used by organisers at tournaments anyway! Reports also state that the net-code on that system is comparatively problem free as it was developed in house by Netherrealm themselves, unlike this outsourced, seemingly second class PC version.
Negatives aside regarding the online, If you just want to see where Mortal Kombat has come in the last 20+ years, there's a large variation of single player endurance & challenge modes & a trouble free experience of playing friends locally. Showing off all the outrageously gruesome fatalaties is likely to provide half an hour of entertainment during a game night at the least.
It stands to reason, that when the most important component of a fighting game is in such a sorry & broken state, that I can't recommened the product.
The developer has fully dropped support for this game on PC. Don't give them your money.

Some poeple might wonder what the benefeits of driving the trains are. Why are we even driving trains? What is a train? Does anyone even ride these trains? How are the little baby trains made? It is a little bit annoying figuring out that you don't get paid at all for driving the trains, and the healthcare and dental care benefeits for train drivers are kind of terrible, but I still get off of my flame adorned spoilered train at the end of the day with an immense feeling of satisfaction. After all, I had better, or else the boss will drag me behind the train like he did to Jerry. Poor Jerry. We miss Jerry. I stole Jerry's wife. All of these things are just parts of the job. Sometimes as I lie in bed, I can still feel my leg and my arm, even my fingers. The body I've lost, the comrades I've lost...won't stop hurting, it's like they're all still there. I wonder to myself, "Why am I still here?" First Impression:
This game was the single-most frustrating racing-shooter game I have ever played. I can give you the nutshell:
The Ugly:
INVISIBLE WALLS. And if they aren't invisible, the existing walls sure as heck have longer edges than what appears.
TRAMPOLINE physics. No such thing? Might as well be. You launch yourself in the air with seemlessly "almost" zero gravity that you will more than likely fall of the track, lose all your pickups (which are not random and almost useless sometimes) OR bounce off the invisible walls, only to be facing the reverse direction which takes longer to spin yourself around and continue forward than it does to just push the "reset" button to have the game reset your position on the track (which is hella far away).
POOR CONTROLS
I'd rather play outside in the snow naked right now. Sure it sounds fun in theory, but then come inside the house after all itchy and frostibitten. Then try pooping with a chapped butt. P.s. it seemed like every time i landed from "air time" that the car would immediately turn a hard left or hard right upon landing. So don't take large jumps, there's no reward for it other than the feeling of flight (but it's a racing game).
The Sadness:
I was a fan of Re-volt, Toy Commander, Mario Karts (most of them), Rock n Roll racing, Death Race, Road Kill Rally (you bet!), Micro Machines racing (amazing!) and EVEN the long forgotten 360 game that was made by SEGA "Full Auto" (which failed to present a sequel on the 360 but continued on PS3).
This game would have been way better off choosing to either have a balanced mechanic for fighting WHILE racing OR just a Twisted Metal/Interstate clone. There is no point to the racing. It had potential at some point. I feel like the developers gave up or something. Maybe one of them quit? It happens. People are scumbags in the coding world (they all have egos).
The Good:
Being that this game was free, I still don't care for it. I just got it for the steam cards (sorry devs, but it's true). I just... I don't know. The menu looked okay, but WHY IN GOD'S NAME DID IT START ME IN THE LOWEST RESOLUTION POSSIBLE (240p)?
What else... I don't know. The sound was used from stock sounds and borrowed from other games. I don't know if you can copyright every game sound in existence.. but that's not a good thing either.
OH here is another good thing, when and I mean WHEN you fall way far behind the goon cars, you have a crazy amount of turbo to help you catch up (it relieved some stress), but the poor controls only ended up making it my worse enemy.
Metascore is totaly misleading.The game isn"t top quality but it sure is a lot of fun specialy if you play with friends.

Post Apocalyptic Mayhem is a fun, arcade-type racing game where the goal is to destroy as many opponents as possible with a variety of weapon pick-ups. There are no laps and your position in the race does not matter, there is only a countdown timer that signifies the end of the match. Unfortunately, that simple description is where the fun ends.
The game is broken. Some vehicles are obviously better than the others and the ones that are lacking in certain areas are not awarded any compensation in the remaining aspects as you would come to expect. A vehicle that is extremely slow generally does not gain a weapon that can be used over distance, rather requiring you to home in on your enemy before launching an assault from the front, side, or rear. Vehicles faster than you can manage to "hoard" all of the pick-ups, leaving you with the frustrating realisation that you are crippled and unequal.
Fast vehicles have the advantage, even if they have horrible steering. Certain faster vehicles in particular have weapons that create an area-of-effect that can wipe out every opponent in a single attack. Unless you like the challenge it is simply unwise to select a vehicle that is slow and cumbersome.
In my short experience I've come to understand that the online matchmaking system and netcode is completely broken. There is no way to cancel a connecting session, you are simply forced to sit and stare at what might be a match being made or what might turn out to be a failed connection. Once you've successfully joined a game you might find yourself stuck in starting position, like stone, as you watch other opponents speed off only to look to the side and see another half-dozen opponents frozen in the same position as you. There is nothing you can do, the only course of action here is to force-close the game by using the task manager or through Alt+F4.
I've also now discovered that if you check someone's "gamercard" while you're waiting for the match to start you will not be able to close the Steam overlay as it will continue opening the person's Steam profile over and over again. The only way to successfully stop this is to wait for the match to begin and close the overlay or simply force the game to close through the task manager, as the overlay prevents Alt+F4 from working most of the time. This is a massive oversight on behalf of the developer and who knows if bugs such as these will ever be fixed.

For those who have played or grown up on point and click puzzle adventure games, you would find this game fits in nicely into that mold. While still suffering from some old problems. Starts out strong with solid puzzles which can be solved with knowledge gain within the game but then ends on relying on music themed puzzles too often.
Quick Pros and Cons;
+ Power-up mechanics aids in solving puzzles without relying on hint button
+ Captivating story telling
+ Ability to show all click-able items
- Object Management doesn't exist, allowing trash objects pile up
- Information Management doesn't exist, allowing pile up of information on solved puzzles
- Relies on Musical Knowledge, forcing people to have to look up musical information that isn't provided in game
Some interesting things they do is offer power-ups which comes in the form of optional puzzles to solve. These power-ups either open up more puzzles or make other ones easier to solve. This is a nice touch away from games where they either have a hint button, or have the protangontist passively pointing out something as a hint.
Most of the puzzles are piecing together clues provided inside the game. While there are a handful of music puzzles which requires the player to be musically inclined. That is knowing how to read sheet music, knowing musical notes, knowing how to play the piano, and knowing how to transcibe music into sheet music. One of the worst feelings is having to look up the solution to a puzzle solely because there isn't enough information given in the game.
Can't go into details without spoiling it. All I can say is there are a handful of difficult puzzles in the game which turns the table on how the player perceives other puzzles in the game, for better or worst. Normally, puzzle games slowly sets up the rules of the game for you. But when it's abruptly broken, it leads the player to believe the broken rule now persist for proceeding puzzles.
Some quality of life issues they have and haven't addressed. One of the best things to have for a point and click adventure is a clear way to see what the player can interact on, without having to wave their mouse all over the screen. In this game, they allow you to highlight all objects with a press a button. However, they haven't gotten rid of disabling or destroying items that aren't used for puzzles any longer.
If you already like puzzle adventure games, you're probably are used to the issues I've pointed out. However, if you're new to the genre, this one might be not a friendly starting point with all the rough edges around it.

Things that I liked:
- Good looking game, nice art.
- Great music.
- Interesting story, keeps me wanting to see more although it's unfinished...
- Most puzzles are fair, not too hard but also not easy.
Things that annoyed me:

- The story is unfinished, the ending was really disappointing. And not just for the story, but also because it was rushed and anticlimactic, even the setting was depressing and dull. I already knew there are like 5 or 6 other games, but I thought at least the first one would have a satisfactory ending.

There is dialogue.  A lot of it.  And while you can skip over it, kind of, it's not as easy to skip as in come other games.
The main character walks slowly.  Seriously slowly.  I assume that was meant to be part of his laid-back character but, again, by the end of the game, it gets to be annoying.  There are cuts to different places that you can use but still, he needs to walk some places.  Slowly.
I had a few technical issues. The Inventory link would disappear at random intervals and a couple times the program shut down, with no explanation as to why.  A reload always fixed it though.
Ultimately, the game was fun and I enjoyed it, which is why I recommend it.  The story was engaging as well, so I'll definitely play the sequels.  All in all a nice, relaxing couple of hours.

Spelunky is a hard (but fair) rogue-like platformer where you objective is to steal all the gold you can Indiana Jones style.  It's mechanics are very simple and easy to get into, but is unforgiving enough that it took me the first month just to get out of the first set of rooms.  The problems that I have with this game are mostly in its execution.  Because it's a randomly generated map (like every other platoformer and their dog) the difficulty can vary all over the place.  Often the game will spawn enemies, traps and/or bricks right in front of the shopkeeper, meaning that I either can't enter, it'll send the guy after me regardless of what I do, or both.  The hit detection is a little bit off, as well.  It can be really trial-and-error at times as to whether or not my whip will hit an enemy or just menace the area slightly in front of it.  All that said, though, it is a very solidly designed game and well worth your time and money.

People that have played Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons usually fall into two groups. The first group of people looked at the
reviews that this game received, tried it, then found it stupendously overhyped and underwhelming. Then, there’s the other group, who found the game to be
. I am glad to say that I belong to the latter party.The late great film critic Roger Ebert once said that videogames can never be art, a controversial statement at best and blatantly offensive and wrong at worst. With that said, we’re going to have to forgive Mr. Ebert, because a)He was great at what he did, and b) He never got the chance to experience
You play as two brothers who are sent off on a journey to find a cure for their father’s ailment. You, as the player, are tasked to guide the two brothers through multiple trials and tribulations throughout a variety of beautiful and mystifying locations. Along the way, you will encounter numerous characters, many of which are heavily inspired from classic fairytales and fantasy mythology. There is so much more to talk about here, but once again, this is something you really need to experience yourself. You really will get more out of this game if you go in
blind.
It’s worth noting that the game is completely
. No, I don’t mean that the game merely lacks voice acting. I mean that there is essentially no actual dialogue – voice or text, in the game at all. Sort of. The characters technically do talk, but in a fantasy language without translation. Instead, the story and interactions are told through beautifully-animated gestures and changes in tone and inflections. Despite this, there is never any ambiguity about what’s happening on-screen, and somehow, the game manages to weave a heartfelt story that, at times, can truly invoke a heavy feeling in the chest.
is a story-driven adventure/puzzle game with a novel control scheme. Each brother is mapped to a single stick on the controller. The left and right stick/shoulder buttons control the older and younger brother, respectively. It’s a unique control scheme for sure, in the sense that this game
like a co-op game for two players, but is actually a single player game, intended to be played on the same controller. The challenge in the game is largely dependent on the player’s ability to co-ordinate both characters at once. The ambidextrous be warned – this game will probably offer you very little challenge.
It’s worth pointing out at this point that contrary to what the text in the orange box says on the store page on Steam, a
. The game will work fine using a keyboard, and you’ll be more than able to progress to the end of the game without a controller. With that said, a controller is
for this game.
For the combat-oriented players – sorry, but this game is completely combat-free. Instead, the game largely involves puzzles comprised of environmental interactions and exploration. Each brother has their own perks. The older, taller and stronger brother is able to reach heights, boost the younger brother, push levers and swim, whilst the younger brother can fit into smaller spaces. Unfortunately, delving into more of the interactions between the two brothers would spoil the game for you.
The game is never overly challenging or frustrating. OOT Water Temple this is not. Puzzles are, for the most part, fairly straightforward, but are often challenging enough to invoke a sense of satisfaction when you do overcome them.  Death can and likely will occur, but checkpoints are frequent, sparing you from repeating the same segments repeatedly.
One of my only gripes, gameplay-wise, was the repetition of some of the puzzles. Using the big brother to boost the little brother up to a ledge got very old very quickly. With that said, even the puzzles that are solved the same way are often presented in a different setting, with a different outcome, which helps to keep them fresh.
My only other "criticism" is that this game is short and lacks any compelling reason to go back to it after you’re finished. This is, unfortunately, a consequence of any game that is primarily
.  The game
support achievements, but these involve optional, easily-missed activities in the game, and are neither challenging or particularly satisfying to obtain.
This game is
. Not the realistic kind of beautiful that we’d expect from AAA games such as … The Watch Dogs E3 trailer, but
. You would not want to play this game and have it look like anything other than what it looks like. The world that
takes place in is strikingly magnificent. The town you begin your journey in is vibrant and colourful, whilst later settings are often appropriately darker and harsher. The shadowing and lighting in this game also look tremendous.
The most impressive aspect of the graphics however, is the incredible work that was done to illustrate the enormous
of the game. No matter where you are, there is always a lot going on in the background, making you feel incredibly small and insignificant in the grand scheme of things – something that will be very familiar to those that have played the God of War series, or the critically acclaimed Shadow of the Colossus. Moving to new locations was often breathtaking, although each individual is area is so gorgeous on its own that it's hard to move on.
This, of course, was no accident. The game was clearly deliberately
to immerse you in the environment, and allows you to interact with almost everything, despite the fact that this is completely optional and you are not awarded with anything other than the short animation that accompanies your action. In other words, the game doesn’t force you, or even encourage you (from a gameplay perspective) to sit on a bench in town and really take in the gorgeous scenery, but you, the player, will want to anyway.
The music and sounds also complement the game perfectly, and contribute immensely to the emotional impact of the game. I’ve honestly listened to the music numerous times since finishing the game, and all the emotions I experienced from the game just come rushing back. I honestly can’t fault a single thing about the audio in this game, as I feel that it perfectly complements both the emotions and the atmosphere that are conveyed.
In case it wasn’t obvious, I loved
. There is very little about the game that I can fault. With that said, I’ll admit it’s not for everybody. The game is very narrative-driven and requires a heavy emotional investment – something that not every gamer is prepared to, capable, or willing to do. It’s worth noting that this game could very well have been another To The Moon, or Gone Home – games which I personally loved, and are very story/emotionally-driven, but lack any real gameplay, closely flirting with the definition of what a “Game” truly is. No one played either of those two games and said “Wow, that was fun”, because plain and simple, the
in those two games are complete garbage.
, however, manages to capture the same kind of narrative and emotion (and arguably exceeds them both) without compromising on the gameplay. There is no doubt in anyone’s mind that this is, in fact, a game. That is the true magic of
.

Josef Fares and Starbreeze studios made a simple, yet beautiful and enchanting game about two brothers journey to find a cure for their ill father, before he dies.
The two brothers journey takes the player through various folklore-inspired landscapes that are both visually appealing and some times even scary.

I picked up this game after seeing someone play the first 15 minutes or so, because it looked like a pretty interesting game. I anticipated I would enjoy it, but that it wouldn't be one of those games that I never forget. I was dead wrong.
Unlike most memorable games, Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons will not be remembered for incredible gameplay. In fact, the gameplay isn't all that great. The fairly unique mechanic of controlling 2 different characters is cool, but the 'cool factor' wears off, and the puzzles are all fairly straight forward, and mildy repetitive. The game is not difficult to complete - most gamers will be able to finish it is 2-3 hours no problem. However, what makes this game so memorable is the storytelling. The story of these two boys is deeply emotional, and something everyone can relate to. While playing the game, it is easy to become completely immersed in the characters, and this is used a great effect throughout the game to make you feel terror, sadness, love, and more.
Another brilliant part of this game is the artwork. Throughout the game there are benches that the player can sit on. If you do, the camera will align to a view of the current scene. Each of these feel like a beautifully crafted piece of artwork, and effectively reflects the mood of the current chapter of the game.
The creators of the game made a great choice when they told the story through a fantasy lens. While many of the settings and characters are highly unrealistic, their motives, actions, and feelings could not seem more real. Sitting back and reflecting on the game after playing it was just as interesting for me as playing the game. Drawing the parallels between the game and real life is fascinating.
There are two particular moments that stand out as the best moments in the game for me. However, I do not want to spoil any of these moments for those who haven't yet played the game. If you have not played the game, please skip to the next paragraph, as these spoilers could ruin the effect he game has on you while you play. The first moment is when you bury your brother. The game doesn't just force you to watch your brother die, it forces you to bury him. It is an incredibly emotional experience, and one that I will never forget. The second moment is when you, the little brother, walk through the water by yourself. Throughout the game, we have seen the little brother's fear of water, and being forced to walk through it, in this moment of total vulnerability from losing your brother, is a powerful struggle. These two moment are definitely not fun moments, but they are (good examples of) what make this game so memorable.
I highly, highly recommend this game for anyone who enjoys being immersed in a game, and enjoys powerful storytelling. If all you are looking for is fun gameplay, this is probably not the game for you.

After the release of the game, after I eventually got my game working, and all the players finally figured out that this "Kombat Pack" people were talking about was a season's pass, I felt a little tempted to buy it. 30 dollars for all the DLC (even the DLC that was out a few weeks after launch) seemed like a steal, so I eventually bought the Kombat Pack. I quickly noticed that I got a DLC or two, and maybe five dollars extra DLC a few updates later. There was a good amount of paid DLC being released, typically costumes, that I had no access to. Trust me, I researched my purchase before buying, but Netherrealm gave us no information. I feel bad for people who bought Kombat Pack 2, because they got fooled twice. Netherrealm legitimately sold an incomplete game and then began milking their customers for DLC money once they realized that nobody was buying their game, presumably after hearing about the initial 19 GB patch that didn't do anything but erase everyone's saves.
I hate very few companies, because I feel like it's a thing a lot of people do because they're petty or trying to be edgy. No, I hate Netherrealm because they did the shadiest♥♥♥♥♥♥by launching this game and they never even acknowledged it.

I've played the whole Deponia Series and, put simply:
Deponia (1) is good, but a bit short and easy.
Chaos on Deponia (2) is better, takes longer.
Goodbye Deponia (3) is a lot better than both.
The writing is awesome, the dude(s) behind it is(are) brilliant. I can't remember the last time I actualy read every single line of a game, if I ever did. Every single line of 3 games, in this case. Once you get familiar with Rufus, you laugh your whole way through... he is one of the best heroes ever... characters... anti-heroes... imaginary world threats... whatever.
I hate to admit it but I had to read a walkthrough once in Chaos on Deponia and once in Goodbye Deponia because there's one particular situation in each of them that requires unusual solutions, which is great and in my opinion should be all over adventure games... but I couldn't figure them out, and now I hate myself. (Maybe if they ocurred more often we'd be ready for it... I tend to assume the game bugged... but, sadly, no, it didn't)
Other than the dying/permanently screwing up your game that was possible in old Sierra games (although it is possible in one point), I think everything you can hope for in an adventure game is here, specially in Goodbye Deponia. A bit of Day of the Tentacle, some Full-Throttle's-end-like parts, and...
THE MINIGAMES! I almost forgot about them... mini-games, puzzles, call it what you will. Lots of them throughout the series, very creative, very interesting. Daedalic team was really inspired-- those guys are good and they sure put a lot of effort into this stuff.
Another thing is that instead of things declining by the end of the game (series), which I feel happening quite often these days, in the Deponia it ramps up nicely.
It is hard to compare against adventure games' golden age classics such as Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis, Monkey Island 1-2 and Day of the Tentacle-- which in my idealized childhood memory are unbeatable-- but, from the adventure games I've played in the last 15-20 years or so, I'd say the Deponia Series is the best.
Each game has several achievements that, if you want, you will have to go after on purpose. I left several behind, having no idea whatsoever of how to get/how did I miss them but they are there, and you can fry your brain further if you dare chase them all.
Damn... now that I think of it, along with the achievements I probably also missed some good lines...
Last and least, there's a con, which you may not see as one: you can hold the spacebar down to show all interactive spots on the screen. I hate that, it feels like cheating... and it's right there, so easy to use that I end up doing so.
Put shortly, if you like adventure games, I say definitely get this one (these three).

Spelunky… What is that? Spelunking, we’ve all heard of it but what does it mean? According to
it is the act of exploring a cave. That is also the essentials of this wonderful, cozy and addicting game. It’s hard to exactly pinpoint what it is about this game that makes it so awesome and enjoyable to just sit down and play. However with the use of this review I will try and trot down the aspects that I am enjoying the most in this game.
The game does not really have a story. Except for maybe the intro sequence that shows the player’s character going into the cave with, judging from the intro’s text,  some kind of amnesia. That’s it for the story basically. Looking at the character’s clothes, you are an explorer (an Indiana Jones-inspired one! OMG!). Your mission is to explore a cave (A CAVE?!?! OOOOMG!!). The game offers a tutorial in the beginning which I recommend going through (not actually sure if you can skip it) where the player finds a manual from a previous explorer who presumably perished in the cave’s vast depths. The tutorial describes the basic game mechanics of the game and nothing more than that. So on to doing the tutorial’s job and explaining the game mechanics!
THE CAVE!
The basic mechanics of the game are as simple as they are genius. Everyone could pick up the controller and know exactly what to do. Think Super Mario Bros. kind of. You can jump, whip stuff with your whip, climb ledges, duck, walk and run fast. As you might’ve realized, the game is about exploring the cave. You start from point A and shall make your way to point B and try to pick up treasure on the way to earn cash so that you can buy nice tools and stuff when (if) you reach a store. There are different environments in the game and you start in the Mines. Each environment consist of 4 different levels. So you start at Mines 1-1 and when you reach the exit you get to Mines 1-2 and so on. You have a time limit for every level because after ~2½ minutes a large ghost will appear that’ll kill you instantly if he comes in contact with the player. Eventually you’ll reach new environments and find various things to explore, if you manage to stay alive. If you die, you die. You start from the beginning again and the twist is that the cave is ever-changing (read randomly generated levels). So when you die you don’t get to explore that cave anymore! I really don’t want to spoil more of the exploring because there are so many things to encounter and interact with, I think you’ll be happier to find them by yourself. The random generated levels makes every exploring run unique because of all these different things you can interact with. As said though, these wondrous things should be left for you to explore by yourself!
However this doesn’t sound so revolutionary, it doesn’t sound super interesting, we’ve had random-generated levels since Diablo! This is probably what you’re thinking right now. The randomized levels are the key for this game, this is simply because the game is super hard. You’ll die so many times you’ll not even think it’s funny. You will die within seconds. That’s the thing though, playing this game the first few times I just thought it was boring and bad because of the “super hard” difficulty. It’s just another platformer for masochistic gamers! I was wrong, so wrong. The thing is that it’s not the game that’s hard, it’s just you who suck. The game is super fair, if you’re not careful you will die. The learning curve is very steep the first few tries you do. However when you realize that the game is just hard because you’re stupid and when you for the first time manage to survive for >2 minutes you feel so damn totally awesome you’ll probably try and run for presidency next year.
Death has never been so close… and so frequent!
That’s one of the charms with this game, you learn the game and as you learn it you get better, much better. You can feel the difference. When you get better you also get to explore further into the cave and when you thought you’d seen it all, you enter a new area and your mind will be blown yet again of the vastness of the game. When you die, you’re left with a hunger. A hunger to explore, to dodge that stupid jumping spider next time that blocked the exit and reach that next area, whatever that would have been. You will play again, and again, and again, and again, AND AGAIN! It’s almost too easy to become addicted…
Another aspect which I really like is that it’s so easily accessible. You start the game and with one click you’re in the game. I’m playing with a XBox-controller so I just spam ‘X’ when the game logo appears which lets me skip all the menus and just start exploring. I’m also a bit busy with studies atm so I usually don’t have the possibility to have long game sessions. Spelunky is the perfect solution. Whenever I’m struggling with some lab report or stuck in some programming exercise, Spelunky lets me pick up the controller and do a fast run, a quick fix for my gaming addiction. I haven’t played super much but I’ve started to get a somewhat good feeling for the game, my runs usually last around 8 minutes. So when I’ve done a run I can jump back to whatever I was doing before. A quick, satisfying break. There’s also the Daily Challenge which you get to play once a day where you go as far as you can and then you’re ranked based on how long you survived and how much treasure you gathered. I rarely find a game I can just pick up and play for 15 minutes and actually feel I got something from it. It’s nice and casual in that way, very few manage to deliver such an experience.
Why you should buy this game? If you like challenging games, exploring and very well made platformers I’m not recommending you to buy the game, I’M ORDERING YOU TO BUY THE GAME!  I really don’t have much more to say except for buy the game, it’s THAT good. I think everyone can get something out of it and enjoy a quick 15-minute-exploring-run, it’s really rewarding when you start to understand the game and overcoming the challenges of staying alive.
For myself I will abandon this review now and venture down that addicting, mesmerizing, punishing and absolutely wonderful cave yet again.. See you on the ranking lists!

When I first downloaded Super Crate Box, i thougt that i might spend some time playing it and eventually get bored.
Well... Since i played this game for over a hundred hours now an so far didn't get bored, I think it's time for giving a little review.
The principle of the game is fairly simple: At the top of on of the three levels spawn monsters that run to the bottom. Whenn they reach the fire at the bottom, they respawn at the top, but now they are red and run faster. You have jump around these guys and collect crates in which there are weapons you need to kill the monsters.
The first few hours this will be very, very addicting and fun. Then, after some time, you'll get to a point at which you might think you have reached the skillcap of the game. Then the fun begins. You find little tricks that help you dodge the monsters or kill them more efficiently and make it possible to get a better highscore.
The only real point of criticism is that there is not that much of content. There are 15 Weapons nad three different levels to play in. The diversity of gameplay experience really comes by the player finding new ways to deal with the benefits and drawbacks of the different weapons and getting better at dodging the monsters. If that's enough for you, theres not much I would critizise about Super Crate Box.
Basically this game starts as an addictive arcade game that transforms into a min-maxing-driven and very fun game. However, you should only play this game if you like other jump'n'runs like Super Meat Boy and are resistant to any frustration.
Personally, I love this game and I am very happy to give it a 9/10 rating.

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is an adventure puzzle game set in a fantasy world centered around (gasp) two brothers trying to save their father. It requires a controller to play as you control both brothers simultaneously using a thumb stick and the trigger to control movement and action for each brother. It's an interesting and different idea; one your brain and hands will need to work out eventually to complete the game. While the puzzles aren't very hard to figure out, sometimes the hardest part is just getting your hands to do what you want them to do. Thankfully, Starbreeze was kind and made it impossible to fall off unintended cliffs making traversing small walkways and balance beams a non-frustrating obstacle.
The game world is beautiful. It is a very pleasant wash of soft colors that is very pleasing to the eye. The developer knows they crafted a fantastic fantasy word as they've strewn benches throughout the adventure for you to sit and admire the vista they created for you. Many times I was blown away by the size and scope of the environments, truly breathtaking. The human character models are a bit weird though and their animations can be clunky at times, but it's not enough to take away from the overall aesthetic.
As you can see this game has a lot going for it and, not surprisingly, this game has overwhelmingly positive reviews.  In this review, I'd like to express a dissenting opinion on the game. Please do not mark the review as unhelpful simply because you disagree.
One of the first things you will notice is the game has no written dialogue. None. The characters in the game speak a Sims like language and there are no subtitles. The game has a language setting but that effects only the menus. Because of this, we know barely anything about the characters or the world they inhabit, which is a shame. Many times throughout the journey, you will come upon impressive locales that must have a great story behind them, but you'll never know. There's no journal to give you backstory, there's no writing at all, only a rare pictogram. The entire quest for the brothers is based around a picture of a tree on a scroll given to them by a doctor (or priest?) of questionable skill. Is the tree magic or a medicine? While traversing the landscape I came across many trees that I thought looked similar to the picture but since the characters did not react to it, I had to figure the princess was in another castle. Throughout the game I found myself wondering, who was that person, what's that animal's/non-human's story, what is this place, what happened here and so on but never really received any answer. The lack of anything to give you any insight into the world you're supposed to be getting emotionally attached to prevented me from investing in it. It felt lacking in depth.
The same applies to the brothers; because there is no true dialogue, we never get a very good feel for their personalities, who they really are. We get one brief flashback each showing them interacting with a parent, but that is not enough to tell us who they are. The majority of the reviews I read before playing the game said the game was very emotional, but after playing the game, I cannot say the same. I never felt an attachment to the characters due to their lack of depth. There are scenes of them speaking to one another in their sim-language and the player must try to figure out what they are saying, but why bother? Why not have them simply gesture at each other. It just feels like during production someone said they should talk about blank here, but they didn't have anyone who can write believable dialogue, so they just faked it. The entire story feels like an outline: Find tree to save dad; the player can make up the rest.
People say the ending was emotional, but again, having never invested in the characters at all, it felt hollow and got rather boring. The end started to mimic The Lord of the Rings: Return of the King in that the end seemed to never come. Fade to black at a logical stopping point, wait there's more? Okay, got through that, fade to black. Still more? I completed the game in under 3 hours and the last 15-20 minutes of it, I wanted it to end. I know I'm in the minority here, but that's how I felt about it.
In the end, I found the story incredibly lacking, the characters shallow, and the game itself more like an interactive artwork than an actual game. I didn't hate the game but I didn't love it either, and I think that is the problem. You really have to love it, invest in it, to really get a lot out of it. I was unable to do so and left feeling conflicted. I know I
like this, but I didn't.
I don't recommend the game as a game I enjoyed personally, but I do recommend people pick it up when on sale and form their own opinion. 5/10

A spoiler-free, in-depth review of Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons.
It's a bit weird that a pc game can only be played with a controller, but playing this with a keyboard/mouse would not do it justice. You play as two brothers, both controlled by one joystick and one button on the controller. This makes the gameplay unique and opens a whole new world of puzzles. It takes a little bit of getting used to, but learning these controls turned out fun for me.
Brothers is a very atmospheric game, and the story will be remembered by most who played it since it is a very touching and unique one for a videogame. The storytelling is by far its strongest point but the effort put into the environment is also very visible. During this adventure there is always something interesting to see, but sometimes you have to look for it very closely. Little (often humorous) interactions with the environment are plenty, emphasizing the different characters of big and little brother. Details in the background can easily be overlooked but they give the game character if you find the patience to look for them, which is, in essence, why some people do not like this game.
To really enjoy Brothers, you need to take your time, be patient and think about the characters. The pace of the story is relatively slow, and if you do not try and look for the awesome details and sights you might find yourself bored and rush though the game without enjoying what the creators intended you to see. A little bit of exploration will often lead to a nice achievement and a funny or beautiful moment. The music does not live up to the story or environment, but does its job nonetheless.
The puzzles are fun, not too hard and often focus on the different qualities of both brothers. After four hours you are pretty much through the game but a second playthrough to reach all achievements is never off the table, even for the non-completionists among us.
If you are able to take your time and go through this story somewhat patiently, it is a wonderful and memorable experience. A Tale of Two Sons is worth the price, and a very unique addition to your steam collection whether you had the ending spoiled for you or not.

So as of right now, I can not recommend people pick this game up.  Ultimately this comes down to simply being an unstable experience on PC, if they can sort out the crashing to desktop and you need your newest MK fix, then maybe it's worth looking into.
As far as the game is concerned, as a Mortal Kombat experience, this is a perfectly acceptable game.  Little by little NetherRealm Studios is build a more and more fluid fighting engine.  There is still that MK stiffness and awkwardness to the animation which is as much trademark to the series as it is anything else.  The single player modes are adequate.  The story mode is a good 3-4 hours but is in no way the best story mode in any fighting game to date.  The most lavishly produced maybe, but far from the best, Persona 4 Arena for example while lacking the production values had a far more fulfilling story mode.  I'm not sure character variations are going to add much to the game long term, except wishing you could have a character who simply had all the moves you would like to use in one version.  A better training mode would be much appreciated as well as the character variations make figuring out which character you'd like to learn that much more daunting a challenge.  Regarding unlocks, there is plenty to unlock in the Krypt, though I do wish you knew what you were unlocking without some sort of guide so you could focus on unlocking the finishers/concept art/etc that you wanted as opposed to hoping you got something you cared about and then going back to the koin grind.  It's a solid if ultimately still second tier fighting game.
My main issue currently is with the frequency with which the game crashes to the desktop.  Each night I have played, I experience 2 to 3 crashes to desktop (roughly 1 crash per hour) which just makes my desire to get back into the game decrease with each one.  I have plenty of games in the backlog that won't boot me out multiple times per play session.  Fortunately, I have not yet had some of the performance issues that others are experiencing, this is not to say my experience has been perfect either.  In-fight, before and after patch, things run pretty smoothly regardless of stage.  However, the pre-fight intros, fatalities etc all suffer frequent pauses of varying lengths.  It is on the whole a very unpolished port and the underlying game while serviceable isn't quite good enough to overcome the issues with the port.  Unfortunately, the PC market remains a bit light in the realm of fighting games which makes it all the more disappointing this (and DoA5LR for that matter) is at best a mediocre PC port.

****2nd EDIT****
Now I have a lot more time on this game... I feel I am much better positioned to give feedback.
1. The combo system is rubbish. Unless you want to do no damage, you are forced to use certain moves to capitalise on damage, making the combo system very boring.
2. There has never been such a large gap between the imbalance between characters ever! (Some characters have incredibly easy, very damaging combos. (Here's to you Bryan/Leo/dragunov etc)
3. Due to the combo system and the level layouts, this game has literally become a slamfest. 1 combo will get your opponent against a wall, and with a little patience and awareness of your character moves, you can be almost guaranteed victory (and repeated perfects) as there is no way to escape these situations.
4. The hit boxes are beyond ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. They clearly use an explosive hitbox system (once you press a button your hitboxes rapidly expand), I understand the use for this system, but visually, it looks sloppy, and makes zero sense. (just watch some slow mos on YT, you will see low kicks hitting (missing rather) an opponent from 50% extra distance away just because they jabbed.) This makes for loads of in-game ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t (even when you are on the winning side of it, it makes you feel bad for the other guy). Also, not sure if it is intentional, but there are certain moves that are made to NOT hit when they visibly and clearly should! making many combos/ possibilities go to waste.
5. The online, for me, has never been that bad, but since they have taken away your ability to not see which characters people have picked, its been a nightmare of people spamming the same characters, making it incredibly tedious. I can see why they have done this, but considering its a problem to do with character balancing, there is good reason to avoid certain people.
6. I want more levels with no walls. Sick of the slam fest, win or lose. Tekken was founded on the principle of having no walls. The Tekken guys have ♥♥♥♥ed up here big time.

Sniper Elite 3 was worth the money when I initially purchased it at near-full price, and now that it's being routinely offered on Steam Sales, it's definitely worth picking up.
First off, one important thing to keep in mind: this is NOT a simulation game.  It's far too arcadey, with regenerating health, ridiculously short-ranged, inaccurate handguns and SMGS, and most importantly how drastically the bullets are affected by wind, bullet drop, and have unusually short maximum ranges.  You'll only get a handful of opportunities hit a target past 250+ meters, and you'll need to compensate quite a bit to make that shot happen.  Yet the game clearly loves sniper rifles and makes every effort to have you use them constantly, because they're the most accurate, powerful and well-rounded of the guns.  Oh, and how you're also allowed to defeat armored vehicles if you can find their weakspots, often gas caps, crew members, or ammunition storage.
Unlike it's predessor, Sniper Elite 3 is much more open-ended.  While the first couple of missions are rather linear, beyond that the game begins to open up and allow you to approach objectives however you please.  Stealh is still a major gameplay mechanic, since the enemy is accurate and will quickly swarm and gun you down if you're discovered, but not to the point where it's mandatory. They're easily distracted, easily dispatched when alone, and have limited numbers. And even better, they got rid of the incredibly irritating design of the snipers from the previous game and made them behave more fairly and realistically. (seriously, their previous iteration could instantly spot you ANYWHERE AT ANY DISTANCE, even when not directly looking at you, and were extremely accurate; not fun at all to fight).
It has a multiplayer mode too, and it is pretty fun, albeit average.  It follows the typical FPS formula with Free For All, Team Deathmatch, Capture the Flag, etc, along with leveling up and unlocking guns and equipment.  But given the brutal competition faced these days by other FPS multiplayer juggernauts I doubt this will be neither a selling feature or something to get you addicted.
TL;DR?  If Metal Gear Solid V: Ground Zeroes focused entirely upon lethal options and sniping and was set during WWII, you'd have something pretty close to Sniper Elite III.

There are a lot of good things too, like the Uranus Zone, a couple of awesome new psychopaths that make this game really worth it, and the return of the Camera feature from the first game.

-gameplay and content:
The atmosphere is awesome and incredible.
however KI is sometimes dumb and sometimes frankly unfair (enemy grenades fly far and very precisely, hitting you an any angle as long as you are within the ridiculous range. oh and by the way, you cannot throw as far as the enemy nor with such precision). some characters also like to run at each other forever due to collision and pathfinding issues and sometimes they get stuck at doors etc. they also like to block you due to the same reasons.
weapon-safezones: at the HQ of every faction and important person you can not draw your weapon. this takes a lot from the freedom feeling the game normally creates. Supposedly it is to protect the important characters but I say there is no need for it. First, linearity sux anyway and you should have the freedom to mess up the story as you want (there should be alternative solutions anyway). Second, coincidentally at these locations are some stashes which must be broken open for items, so you just don't get them. Third, if you happen to wage war with this faction, it sometimes still blocks your weapon, which means you cannot defend yourself. I say no to this kindergarten.
the faction war is beside the main quest the only other chain of connected quests. it is advised not to join a faction too early in order not to lose access to some characters, traders and quests. The fight also continues after you completely destroy the enemy as the reinforcements will steadily (and a bit too frequently imo) reconquer their base.
after entering limansk you will not be able to go back to explore so save before it. such a shame for a rich open world full of secrets.
speaking of secrets: the scavanging and explorative aspect of the game are very interesting but are undermined by the fact that the hidden stashes (except normal stashes) are empty as long as you didn't recover any information about them from an enemy corpse or a broker. thus venturing into dangerous places sometimes has no rewards whatsoever for you if you didn't unlock them.
the number of quests, both unique and repeatable are far too low for such a rich universe.
just as the number of unique characters or dialogues.
unfortunately the number of artifacts is fixed and no new appear.
dungeons: basically there is only one dungeon in the game which is really underwhelming.
_______________________________________________________
-engine: somewhat clumsy and clunky when it comes to object collision. if you have bad luck some items will fall in places where you just cannot pick them... I also enjoyed climbing things like a tree in order to get a secret... NOT. it is also very unhandy that every other person in the game is considered a solid unmovable object for you which can however push you by just walking on you, thus characters sometimes block entrances to buildings etc
-graphics: still not bad. surely it's not crysis or something, but still enjoyable.
-main story: unfortunately you have no alternative endings and no way to change the main story. the finale is also somewhat unspectacular and boring. the "boss fight" is nothing innovative/not enjoyable.
-afterplay: once again you have no ability to discover the world after the main story ends, such a shame for such an open world game. also after entering limansk there is no going back.
-bugs: no significant bugs were detected. once the game crashed and the last save file became corrupted, so frequent saving with several alternating files is advised.

So as of right now, I can not recommend people pick this game up.  Ultimately this comes down to simply being an unstable experience on PC, if they can sort out the crashing to desktop and you need your newest MK fix, then maybe it's worth looking into.
As far as the game is concerned, as a Mortal Kombat experience, this is a perfectly acceptable game.  Little by little NetherRealm Studios is build a more and more fluid fighting engine.  There is still that MK stiffness and awkwardness to the animation which is as much trademark to the series as it is anything else.  The single player modes are adequate.  The story mode is a good 3-4 hours but is in no way the best story mode in any fighting game to date.  The most lavishly produced maybe, but far from the best, Persona 4 Arena for example while lacking the production values had a far more fulfilling story mode.  I'm not sure character variations are going to add much to the game long term, except wishing you could have a character who simply had all the moves you would like to use in one version.  A better training mode would be much appreciated as well as the character variations make figuring out which character you'd like to learn that much more daunting a challenge.  Regarding unlocks, there is plenty to unlock in the Krypt, though I do wish you knew what you were unlocking without some sort of guide so you could focus on unlocking the finishers/concept art/etc that you wanted as opposed to hoping you got something you cared about and then going back to the koin grind.  It's a solid if ultimately still second tier fighting game.
My main issue currently is with the frequency with which the game crashes to the desktop.  Each night I have played, I experience 2 to 3 crashes to desktop (roughly 1 crash per hour) which just makes my desire to get back into the game decrease with each one.  I have plenty of games in the backlog that won't boot me out multiple times per play session.  Fortunately, I have not yet had some of the performance issues that others are experiencing, this is not to say my experience has been perfect either.  In-fight, before and after patch, things run pretty smoothly regardless of stage.  However, the pre-fight intros, fatalities etc all suffer frequent pauses of varying lengths.  It is on the whole a very unpolished port and the underlying game while serviceable isn't quite good enough to overcome the issues with the port.  Unfortunately, the PC market remains a bit light in the realm of fighting games which makes it all the more disappointing this (and DoA5LR for that matter) is at best a mediocre PC port.

Is it the South Park that we used to know and love? No, not at all. Gone are the DGAF Days of Matt & Trey and now the show and this game have embraced the newer writers fully. PC Principal not long ago would have been funny for being PC, but now it is an attack on White Frat Boys and little more. The PC aspects are actually thoroughly embraced throughout the game. The more SJW your actions (Which let's be frank, you really don't get any choices in this "RPG"), the better the outcome.
Let's speak a little about this being called an RPG. The first one didn't really deserve the title either, so that isn't new, but it seems to be worse this time around. The game has as much depth as a 20 page Choose Your Own Adventure book, yet maintains a $60 price tag reminiscent of much deeper AAA titles like Dragon Age 3, Fallout (any of them), etc.
The jokes just aren't really funny this time around, and that is where The Stick of Truth has it beaten in spades: that game was hilarious. This one is a 8 hour fart joke with endless fan service. I'll admit the Mitch Conner portions had me laughing, and Classi wasn't bad either, but that's about it. The satire that South Park was famous for is mostly gone for heavy handed BLM and SJW Themes like "All police are so racist they are feeding blacks to demons".
The technical issues are fairly well known by anyone looking into getting this: black screens for 4k players, crashes for a few, and complete character hang ups that require you to restart the game to move forward. They aren't really that bad for a major release, to be fair.
Overall, I give the game a 5/10. It just wasn't very funny, and when you pair that with the utter lack of depth and the $60 price tag, the game just doesn't deserve accolades or recommendations.

Judging superficially, I should love this game. The art design is good, the sound design and voice acting is fine. Overall it's competently implemented and predictable from the perspective of a mid-age mouse-centric adventure, like say Monkey Island 3. But there are a couple of problems.
The easy one is the mechanics. I've been spoiled by more recent adventures like Broken Age that provide sensible shortcuts for getting around, such as running or warping across screens. None of those are present here, which means watching the protagonist Rufus amble infuriatingly slowly across the map. And you'll be doing a lot of that, because the puzzles are often of the logic-free, "lateral-thinking", try-everything-with-everything-else variety that have thankfully become less fashionable these days. The walking in particular annoyed me more than other older games I've been playing such as Broken Sword. How did they manage to be worse than adventure games from almost twenty years ago? Not sure. In any case, dealing with these irritations to push through the game would be easier if it weren't for the second problem, which is the writing.
It tries so hard! But the jokes are either flat or just mean. I recognize the jokes, I just don't really feel like laughing at them. None of the characters are really likeable, the protagonist least of all, so I don't at all feel invested in seeing the story through. As a result, I've done my few hours of play and have given up.
Sorry, Deponia. Close, but not good enough. Perhaps the later games are better, but I'm not willing to play through this one to find out.
