I absolutely love this game. I never got into the whole Minecraft thing partly because of the aesthetics and partly because crafting has never been one of my favorite things. PK resolves both of these issues: the aesthetics are great, the world is beautiful, and the characters are adorable (in an improved Lego-universe-esque kind of way). Unlike Creativerse, which is a similar concept, the monsters and other critters you encounter in PK aren't ridiculous looking - they look like mosters and critters should - kind of intimidating and scary, but in a way that wouldn't make a 5 year old run away in terror. Craftng is also simple and straightforward - read the recipe, find the ingredients, then use the proper piece of equipment (workbench, forge, anvil, or altar), and boom, there ya go. Getting to the next tier of stuff requires upgrading your workbench etc, which requires materials on higher level worlds. Then the upgrades give you new recipes for higher tier weapons, armor, spells, potions, etc., which in turn require new ingredients from higher level worlds. That whole dynamic makes it almost like one of the good Civ games - you want to play just a little longer to find the portal and discover the next world, or harvest enough X so that you can finally craft that whoziwhats that you've been waiting for. The whole game feels very lovingly constructed and nicely polished for an early release.
The only downside so far is that sometimes the portals which connect the worlds are located in really obscure and hard to find locations. No, I'm not talking about the deepest levels of a dungeon that you only know exists because you can see it and access it through a grate in the floor. I'm talking about places that you can find only by jumping off the edge of the world and dying multiple times and trying to spot the entrance to a cavern way down at the bottom of the world, and then you have to try to find a way to dig down and locate it. If the portals are close enough to the surface, apparently you can hear them, but when they're that far down, at least I can't. That whole thing can be a bit frustrating.
Portal Knights is like if Minecraft, Lego Worlds, and Cube World had a baby, and it got the best features of all the parents. Chances are, if you like one or more of the above, you'll really like Portal Knights, so give some love to a great indie studio and drop the $15 on it. If the additional content they're promising is as good as this early release, it will be awesome.

This review will update over time with how I feel with the game. This is just my first impressions after 6 hours of game play.
tl;dr: Its early access and its not a bad game so far, just needs a lot of tweaking in certain areas. It has a lot of potiential otherwise. Its similar to Minecraft but its got some features Minecraft doesn't have.
So, I recommend this game somewhat. I didn't get to try the newest update yet so take that into consideration when reading this.
From its presentation, you'll probably assume this is another game that copies Minecraft. You have the right to feel that way because thats how I felt looking at the trailer. However, I paid the 15 dollars to give it a solid try and I don't regret it honestly. It feels different from Minecraft. And there's a few reasons for that.
So, for my first nitpick, The first person camera needs work since you can't see your own character at all. They should at least move your weapon lower on the screen to where you can't see the handle of your sword just floating in space like you are using the force to use it. Its a nitpick and not a deal breaker. You'll probably spend a majority of the time in 3rd person mode like I do since its way better for open field walking and combat. However, there's another mechanic of the game where you will be using the first person mode of this game.
And that mechanic is mining. Yes, this game, just like Minecraft, has mining. Its more bare bones and not incredible deep from what I saw so far.
However, the combat is pretty good actually, though basic. You can dodge, swing a sword or axe around (my style), use magic (never done it), use a bow and arrow, or jump off a cliff leading to nothingness trying to look like a bad♥♥♥♥♥ Its good, basic, but good.
Reason there's nothingness is because the game's story is where someone separated the world into little floating islands and the only way to access said islands is through portals you have to create. Instead of heading to the Nether, you are accessing more of the world. You'll get portal shards from fighting enemies and you use them to craft portal cubes. Its usually 2 shards per portal cube. Yes crafting is in this game and its different from Minecraft. That'll be for later.
(They fixed these problems in the newest update 0.5.0)
My main reasoning for only sorta recommending this game is because the islands are way, way, way, way too small. You can get bored very fast spending a half hour on one island at a time. Its so damn small and they need to be bigger. You can climb a big hill and see the whole island easily. It doesn't require much draw distance to see it all. Oh and there's RPG elements to this game so each island is focused on a specific level. They won't restrict you and make you stay on a island the same level as you but its just a recommendation.
The main difference of this game from Minecraft is the combat and the RPG elements. Now, the RPG element in this game....its underwhelming. Big time. You don't quite feel you are dramatically improving and it can take a while to go from one level to the next after level 5. This needs to get tweeked because its so unsatisfying to grind for hours only to get a slight bump in strength, endurance, or magic (you get the choice to improve on whichever one at least). There are perks but only on certain levels and I haven't seen any after level 2 or 3. Relating to this, there's three classes. Person who uses melee weapons, person who uses magic, or person who uses ranged weapons (they have names, but I don't exactly remember them). This affects how you level up and how you craft since you can craft armor and weapons.
The crafting, yes there's crafting and its surprisingly deep crafting too. You have to use different types of work stations to craft different things. An anvil will help you craft items made out of metals and stuff. A forge can make those materials you mined into ignots. A Workstation does most of the crafting, its for building lighter armor, building materials for houses, fences, misc items, etc... And the difference here from Minecraft here is that if you want to craft more stuff, you have upgrade these work stations using materials you've gathered. Its fairly basic upgrading it but it makes it feel different from Minecraft's crafting which is basic compared to this. Still both are pretty heavy in this department.
I haven't gotten to fight a boss battle yet, I heard they exist but I haven't encountered one yet.
If you're waiting for Dragon Quest Builders to be localized to the West like I am, sure, give this game a try. Just don't expect to have deep exploration. There is occaisional small dungeons to go through but they are really small for the most part. Not to mention there's been no friendly NPC's that I've encountered yet which makes the game feel quite empty. Now, there could be some and I just hadn't seen them yet, but as far as I can tell so far, none found.
I will update this when I see some significant changes or features that I've yet to explore.

Dead Rising 2: Off The Record is a hard game to judge.  Dead Rising 2 was a good game, the problem with Dead Rising 2 is that it's the same game.  By that I don't mean "Oh they reused the assets" or "They used the same map".  Both of those are acceptable.  No Dead Rising 2: Off the Record, literally did a character swap and changed less than a third of the story.
To be honest, this should not have been it's own game.  This is almost DLC masquerading as a full release.  There is some other changes (a few more survivors, a few changes to survivors, I think a few new psychopaths)  but if you've played Dead Rising 2 right before this game, this is going to be like a second playthrough of Dead Rising.
As for the story, there's really two major changes that I noticed.  Instead of Chuck being blamed for releasing zombies, another person is blamed.  (A character that appears in the original game).  And the ending.  The final boss, (literally the final scene) is different, with a significantly change to the ending.
There is one new (and rather large) area that is added to the game, that is a nice addition, but it's just that, an addition, not a whole new world.
Other than that, the game, majority of psychopathes and majority of the mall is the same.  You're seeing similar people doing similar things, and fighting similar enemies.
So there's really three ways to look at it.
If you played Dead Rising 1 and want to play Dead Rising 2, I would recommend Off The Record, over Dead Rising 2.
If you played Dead Rising 2, you likely will not want to play Off The Record.
If you played Dead Rising 2 but the whole time thought "I want to play as Frank West" Then Dead Rising 2 Off the Record is for you.
It's not a BAD game, it's fully functional, vastly improves on Dead Rising 2 (You don't have to stand still to talk to Otis, who is not in this version, you get a really functional ear piece as well).  The achievements are better as well, the game works well, and you don't have to constantly return to the hideout to give Zombrex to Katie (what an awful gameplay element that was).
If you don't have Dead Rising 2, this is the better version.  If you do... I find it hard to recommend this version as you already have a working game.  It's not a bad, and I can't not recommend Dead Rising 2: Off the Record because it does nothing wrong.  But it is quite a bit of a cash grab for Capcom, and honestly they could have told an all new story.  A shame, because this is a rather fun series.
Still I had a blast replaying Dead Rising 2 as I played it when it first came out, and for that.  Off the Record delivered exactly what it promised.  A retelling of Dead Rising 2 with a new main character.

First review ever.
Game itself? Amazing game. But this port to PC is just beyond horrific and the launch of this game was beyond terrible. Don't get me wrong. I would buy this game a thousand times over...for consoles that is.
First off, the port to PC...Even with grand specs, my computer can not run it without some hiccups. The best I can do is run it on 800x600 resolution with low quality, which gives me a steady fps. The x-rays are 30 fps, which i don't mind. What I do mind is suddenly when you do an x-ray, you notice that visual drop in fps.
Now, the launch of this game on April 14...I was one of the ones that pre-ordered the game in hopes of it being a superior port to its predecessor (MK9). I pre-loaded the ~3 GB "game" and it asked me to download 29 DLC packages/patches. I looked at their explanation and it said you can play the game as it downloads, but do the developers not know that you can't download while in a game on steam? Of course they do. My guess is that, really the developers were not ready for a full release of the PC port on April 14.
Slyly disguising an incomplete port in the form of DLC patches, they managed to sneak in the fact that DLC patches #5 and #9 were oddly missing from the full package on release day. And of course major features were missing such as story mode, faction mode, and general online play on release day. Furthermore is the fact that on April 18, a 15 GB "Patch" was uploaded. A 15 GB "patch"? You might as well call that half of the game. I rest my case that this game was never ready on release day and was never meant to be released before it was ready. Even with the 15 GB patch, there are features missing. The netcode is still horrible. People lag out of online matches, especially King of the Hill.

I understand turning this into a PC port is a quick buck, and hell you got my money. Even for the DLC, you got my money. But none of the DLC characters are actually available yet... The MK games are notorious for  bad PC ports. I mean, just look at the reviews for the MK series on steam. Just bad ports all over the place. This game is another shoddily coded Mortal Kombat game and has let me down. High Voltage, I understand you're work-for-hire developers, but just stop hustling PC gamers if you're going to do a shoddy job of a port.

One of the most complex, innovative puzzle adventures of the last decade. In a genre which has largely given way to hackneyed point and click, hidden object and inventory combination puzzles, Goetia takes a step sideways and harks back to an era that did not play dumb to its audience. While frustrating at times due to some issues in puzzle design, Goetia should be on every puzzle adventure enthusiast's wishlist.
The graphics and gameplay are simple but atmospheric and engaging. The audio is rudimentary, but is underpinned by a haunting soundtrack that adds depth to the mystery of Blackwood Manor. Particularly innovative is the use of object possession by the protagonist (Abigail, a spirit). The player must switch between playing as incorporeal Abigail, to functioning in the world as a physical object - each option changing the possibilities and physics of the game.
The puzzles are satisfying complex. However, the game most likely suffers from a lack of playtesting. Many of the puzzles are practically unsolvable without brute force (or using one of the available walkthroughs). This is normally not the result of poorly designed puzzles (though in some cases the answers are too sensitive or bugged), but more often due to extremely vague hints and misleading coincidences. If the developers were to address some of the ambiguity surrounding certain puzzles, the game would run smoothly and without undue frustration for the player.
The mystery of Blackwood Manor is certainly engaging. Set against a backdrop of World War II, the player is able to explore several extensive locations in order to piece together the whereabouts of Abigail's missing family. While the number of screens could easily overwhelm the player, the game comes with a helpful map (which flashes with Abigail's current location - a helpful retroactively added feature). The player is able to use this map to teleport to certain locations, removing the frustration of clicking through a large number of screens to investigate something new. However, objects are not able to be teleported.
The number of screens and objects is seemingly enormous, removing the temptation to try each object with each hotspot (though you may feel tempted if stuck). Unfortunately, the objects are easily misplaced, and the game has no way of tracking them. With objects as small as pens and screwdrivers and no way of knowing which will be important down the track, this can quickly become a frustrating time sink. No walkthrough can save you here.
Cut-scenes are seamlessly integrated into the game, momentarily losing control of Abigail in the presence of Goetia demons or other figures. The Goetia invocation itself adds another layer of realism and history to the game, using sigils and real demonology to underpin the puzzles. This itself lends a certain believability to the presence of the puzzles in the first place, and the neurotic privacy with which the Blackwoods guard their secrets.
While decked out with a sophisticated and intriguing storyline, the resolution and final twist is somewhat of a let-down. The final scene happens in a rush, and the pay-off is not really foreshadowed satisfyingly by the lead up. Though heavy with emotion and themes of human folly, players may find themselves unable to sympathise with the plight of Abigail as the narrative comes to an abrupt close.

First, this game wasn't terrible. It was slightly above average, but most reviews liked it a lot, so I wanted to warn people that it might not be for them.
I was completely disengaged from the story emotionally by the game's poor characterization of the brothers and their world. They're about to go on an extremely perilous journey, but they never show any insight or emotion into it beyond what is immediately happening to them. The disconnect between the different environments jarred me too. You have sunny human villages and warring giants, blood cults, and ruined castles existing in the same world, but no part mentions or reacts to the other. It just took me out of it to see this fantastical, extremely dangerous world, but to see people act like everything was normal and fine.
Finally, there were too many invisible walls and travel decisions that made me wonder how in the world the brothers would get back home. The entire journey was just too obviously on rails at every moment for me to be invested. This carried over into the puzzles, several of which were too particular by far in the brothers' mechanics, especially with the one with the gear. Avoiding spoilers, if you can safely traverse the gear challenges with no partner, why does the game demand each stand on opposite sides to make the mechanic work? Constant issues like these pulled me out of immersion.
Outstanding visuals though.
P.S. Massive thumbs down for the inability to help the girl score a basket and for having an achievement to dump her ball down the well. That's just cold.

TLDR: If you like trains, buy it. Don't buy all the DLC, ignore reviews that say you have to.
This simulator seems to be something that people love to bash on, because of the headline DLC price figure when you go to "Add all DLC to Cart". While it's true that there are a great deal of issues with this simulator, it's not as bad as people make out. By all accounts, the core game engine can do a pretty good job of simulating trains. It's just while in the DLC that's available, there are quite a few good ones, but there are also some pretty bad ones as well. It's worth noting that not every DLC is made by Dovetail Games, there are plenty of third-party add-on developers that produce Steam DLC for TS. About the DLC, you aren't supposed to buy everything. In fact, due to licensing issues with some American DLC, unless you live in the US, you CAN'T buy everything.
The best way to enjoy this game is to find what you like, and just enjoy it. Don't try and collect everything, this isn't Pokémon. If you are interested in British trains, buy British DLC. If American Freight is more your thing, go for those. If you're not interested in the UK, US or Europe? Possibly the cheapest tastes out there then. There's something for everyone, to a certain extent. Despite TSW, there's still content under development and will be for many years yet.
Treat this game like a train-set in real life. Would you buy every Hornby or Bachmann model ever made? Of course not.
Performance-wise, the game suffers from using a DX9-based game engine that's pretty much 10 years old at this point. You will hit performance issues on some complex routes (for example South London Network being one of the worst offenders). Don't try and chase the magic 60fps number at 12k resolution, it isn't going to happen. Read reviews of each and every DLC you buy. Don't buy anything full price. Everything goes on sale fairly quickly. Be prepared to read manuals for add-ons, there are some complex ones out there, as well as some very simple DLC. Do your research.
A tip - any route DLC that says Train Simulator 201x is not required to play this game has a bug where the reviews never show up. In these cases, search on YouTube to see what the route is like. An example of this is West Somerset Railway, which is an excellent route, that also performs very well on my rather modest PC, always being 50+ fps pretty much maxed out.
My PC specifications for reference: AMD A10-6800k, GTX 750 Ti, 12GB RAM, with TS on an SSD.
PS: Goes without saying, but don't just buy this to play half an hour, write a negative review saying "hurr durr DLC iz $5000", and then refund it. It helps no-one, and drowns out the more informative reviews.

I've spent a lot of time playing games in my life: a shameful amount. For the past two years or so I've been in a rut with games, feeling like everything I'm playing is 90% the same when jumping between games, and it has been. Portal Knights was not an exception. While it may have a few things going for it, and maybe there's depth hidding somewhere beneath the surface, overall I felt bored with it very soon after I started, and even after persisting and pushing further in, the feeling stayed with me the entire time, so I decided to close it and come write this review instead.
I'm just going to start with what I'd personally like to see in any review; the combat and the character building aspects, since depth in those are so commonly lacking in games, and that really hurts me. In Portal Knights, once you attack an enemy you enter "combat mode" where the game locks on and automatically directs your attacks towards the enemy, allowing you to dodge their already clumsy attacks and button mash your way to victory. All of the enemies I encountered on the first and second islands had one attack each, and long gaps inbetween. The first enemy you're likely to encounter when you start will be a generic blob enemy, and guess what it does; it leaps at you, and while as a blob I suppose it can't ever do much else, this exact same enemy with this exact same mechanic is present in the early levels of inumerable other games, and at this point its inclusion as a serious enemy is just laziness. On the second island there were mostly three enemies, turtles-men, orcs, and flame knights. The turtle man did a shell spin, then sat there eating damage for around three full seconds, the orc threw a clumsy melee attack, and did the same, and the flame knights-get this- carried a big sword, wore armor, and shot fireballs at you exclusively. They could've had a slow flame slash attack that hit a pretty good sized AoE in front of the flame knight, but they took the generic fireball spell that doesn't even make sense thematically. Maybe the enemies are less crappy and make more sense later, but honestly, having to play through levels of horrible generic enemies before you get to anything decent is already a red flag for me.
Now let's move on to the character building aspect of the game. Essentially, you choose one of three classes that changes up the passives on your talent tree, only one to two are truly unique tops; the rest are generic passives that appear on all of the class trees, some have different icons or tweaked effects to suit your class better but it's the exact same scheme every time. i.e. At level two every class gets a passive that raises their primary attribute by 30%, at level 5 every class gets to choose between faster mining or enhanced durability for mining, at level 10 is a unique passive that suits your class, and from there the rest are generic. Stats automatically raise when you click the button so there's no fun there.
Overall, the combat and character building are complete crap. It's a baby step up from Minecraft combat and that's about it.
Next up is the building; it follows the same course as Minecraft where you can craft some things by hand, and then you need a crafting station to get further. Unlike Minecraft however you start with a house that's mostly built for you and pretty much no reason to explore since everything you want is right there. I went into the old mine, and it featured around five stone blocks. That was it. I tried digging down, and found it was 90% dirt, and very shortly after I found the bottom of the island which drops into the unknown. From there I want and explored the stone structure near the starting point, which is a dungeon with a single enemy, and then a chest after; I stole a lot of the blocks, and doors, and lighting, giving me pretty much everything I needed for free. Rebuilding the starting house took about 10 seconds, and I was set to move on. Since there was nothing else to really do, I put together the portal and went on through. I came out in a desert biome that was also composed of 90% dirt. With cactuses everywhere and one or two unique plants that were cloned all over the biome. Honestly, by this point I felt no drive to continue playing. I took no joy in the combat, or the character building, or the new environments, or the quests that try and subtlely railroad you along, not that they need to since each zone is exhausted fairly quickly and moving foward is your only relief.
Overall, the character creation wasn't too bad actually. They have a variety of haircuts, and color option, and minor changes to your character's expression, but nothing too great. Your character looks like he came out of a Lego set, and the two voices I had to choose from sounded the same. The environments and effects were actually pretty good, not stunning or charming, but they certainly weren't bad in my opinion. The environments feel more poorly put together than they do low quality.
I would have to give it a 5. It's playable, and somebody might have fun with it, but overall, I feel like it's a huge waste of potential, and definitely not worth $15. I understand it's a WiP, but what they have so far is just bad; it feels like they just slapped together a playable game without taking time to make sure that it's also enjoyable. If it shapes up I'll update this post but I don't think it was worth the purchase as it stands.

From there you just hold the attack button and dodge. No skill required, certainly no challenge involved. The leveling system is incredibly simple. Not in a good  way. First off, let me say this is an absolutely stunning game with so much entertainment value. The price is absolutely worth it. I'm currently trying to encourage all my friends to get this. This game is great thus far. However, there is much room for improvement at the same time. I think with the right development this game could contest minecraft and terraria.
SUGGESTIONS:
Classes and Perks:
I'm a huge fan of games where you can play with your friends and everyone has a specific role. As it stands right now, there is much variety for classes yet. The three basic classes are a good foundation, but for this game to truly take advantage of players having roles, you should add subclasses to each of the classes.
ie
Mage:
-Battle Mage
-Support Mage
Ranger:
-Sniper
-Infantry
Warrior:
-Brute
-Assassin
Those are just a handful that i could think of, but i'm sure you guys could think up more. And their should be crafting that caters to each of the sub classes. Which leads me to my next suggestion.
Looting/Crafting:
The crafting system itself is near perfect. I LOVE how you have to upgrade your stations in order to achieve the ability to craft better gear. There should however be a lot more to choose from for every level. (also having a crafting level would be a fun addition) Not only should their be more variety withen the crafting, there should be more variety with random npc drops. I personally would find more pleasure in traveling to different biomes to grind if there was a chance of a particular monster having a 3% chance to drop a certain weapon, or armor, or item that in turn could be crafted into a very rare item. Bosses and uncommon monsters should naturally drop better loot. I gain so much more incentive to put hours into a game when i can finally get an item that none of my friends have. and there should be 100's of legendary items like that. Games like these are best when you can show off. The crafting for the most part is okay, but i think a complete overhaul of the loot/drop system is in order. ( i think a lot of inspiration should be drawn from terraria for this specific area of the game.
Stealth/NPC pathing:
First off, a stealth system would breath more life into the world. Sneaking through dungeons, Hiding from enemies while recovering health. Right now there is zero stealth and approaching mobs feels so direct and boring. Being able to sneak up for additional damage would be amazing, and could allow for you to add classes such as the assassin and sniper.
Companions/Mounts:
Considering the maps are pretty easy to get around on foot, the idea of having a mount is a merely for entertainment over functionality one. Unless there were flying mounts that could fly to floating islands. And Companions are an excellent addition to ANY game. Perhaps make companions or mounts a extremely rare drop.
Random Events:
Every biome should be subject to several rare random events. The thought of a random mini boss or waves of monsters breaking into your base would add a little spice to staying in one place for a while.
Ethetics/Materials:
Add way more furniture and a variety of color in wood and stone blocks.
Water blocks... that should be absolutely mandatory in any game like this. Even add an oasis to desert maps. The main reason i want water blocks is for ethetics at my base. I'd like the option to build a classy fountain in my town square. Furthermore, it could be used to make the farming process a bit more complex. Also, in the current game farming isn't that useful. I think adding a hunger bar would make so much since for farming. i mean you can't really have one without the other. It would also add more challenge which this game desperatly needs.
Difficulty:
I appreciate this game for what it is, but it's incredibly easy. I would love to see this game include a revival system for downed allies. Currently there are just no repurcussions to dying other than losing a little health which is so easy to get back. Or at the minimum a respawn timer. This entire game is just low risk high reward. I need a deterant to jumping off a high cliff to reach an edge in a canyon. I should think twice about most my decisions.Perhaps losing a little experience upon death would be a good system as well. Also, level zones should be more relevant.
Mage spell revamp:
This is my most passionate area of the game that i'd like to see improvement in. As it currently is spells have A LOT of power, but they all cooldown at once. What i desperately suggest is, nerf all the spells and make them cooldown individually, so you can chain spells together. I should be able to buff myself then immediately use an lightning attack. And what would balance this change would be the mana consumption. The mage class just doesn't feel like it utilizes the spells enough.
And............... An in game chat system. I don't believe i have to explain why a multiplayer game needs this.
Overall, this game is spectacular and i love it for how it is, but i know with adding new features you could increase the replay value by so much.

Following the standard point-and-click RPG in implementation but altogether wacky and challenging in practice, Deponia in its craziness makes for a fun game. Sometimes, the characters hint at what you’re supposed to be doing next - and other times, you really just have to try the crazy things that the game would think is funny (and then be surprised that it worked).
I wasn’t a fan of Rufus, personally, but I can’t diss the story or the character in the slightest; while not particularly exemplary, it was still wonderfully crafted and enjoyable to experience. How the characters develop changes your view from being exasperated with them into being appreciative of them, and in general you can find something to like about everyone.
In terms of Achievements, I think Deponia did it right. The bulk of the Achievements are for progressing the story and completing the Minigames, but there are some that are easily doable if you thought to look for it; you don’t have to do them to continue the game, but reward you fiddling around with the objects (which is a good touch!), mostly to humorous effect.
The thing that makes Deponia tedious is the final achievement, “Droggeljug”. I have no clue as to the etymology or reasoning behind the term, but what it represents to me is a gruelling challenge and a reason to mute voiceovers. Basically, replay the game with everything - dialogue, mini games, items, voiceovers, cutscenes - replaced with “Droggeljug”.  Fortunately, it’s optional, and more of a fun option for replaying the game (another good touch), but unfortunately there have been people reporting problems regarding the achievement not popping up.
Thankfully, I managed to get it after a good long (tiring) rerun with the setting.
On a parting note, if you like point-and-click RPGs, Deponia is a very good game to pick up, especially with how it’s a trilogy!

Alright, I have about 400 hours or so roughly at the time of this review. This should add some credibility to my point of view of this game.
- Alright, some people might like or hate this combat system but I enjoy how smooth it is (at points). You deal damage based on your skills, your speed, as well your proficiencies affecting your weapons. Lords actually feel like tough enemies, as well as more end-tier troops, while peasants are sliced through like butter. I'll talk more on some aspects of the system in other parts.
- You can RP as some bandit lord roaming around raiding caravans, villages, and all that. Or some prissy daughter of a lord from a far away land who wants to become Queen at some point. But you're not a normal prissy daughter, you are fine with getting down in the dirt to slit some throats. The game sets you up to be whatever playstyle you want. Some pro xXMLGXx archer on horseback that does 360s with his horse mid air. Or a big tough guy with a two-hander that demolishes the Swadian Knights even. The skills sets you up on what you need to grab that is important for you and your party. Either you focus on yourself first while grabbing a few party skills, or what have you. You can delegate certain roles for your companions. This makes you think on what you want to do.
- A feature added in Warband over the original. You can create your own kingdom than be classified as "rebels" as be screwed over by multiple factions at once. This lets you do diplomacy with other factions when needed, and a bunch of other stuff. I hadn't finished a game fully with my own kingdom, but I played on mods where I managed to start a kingdom and gotten a run down on how the system works. Keep your lords happy, you have a stable kingdom. Take lands that you know you can take, otherwise wait til they are weakened are you're stronger than they are.
- This game has quite a bit of mods. It ranges from Warhammer Fantasy to a player's own fantasy world all the way up to Star Wars. They can add their own lore, scripts, a bunch of new weapons and armors and etc. The first mod I played was Floris Evolved. Pretty much vanilla Warband in terms of lore and location but with a lot of new features, units, and all sorts of goodies. Warband maybe not the best in modability but it has the ability to be modded for whatever you want it to.
- I found marriage to be an eh thing. Like it is great as a female since you pretty much technically get a second army that can rebel with you when you finally defect. Or just another army to help you out to take over castles, and towns. As a male it helps out with Right to Rule (what you need as a ruler)...pretty much it. Ladies don't do much at all in vanilla Warband and most mods for it. This is my opinion as well, but I wish you could marry your companions that you grown attached to than just some random lady (or lord) you want to bone just to get some 3 measly points.
- I don't play multiplayer that much so I'm placing it in the neutral zone for now. I played vanilla M&B multiple for a little bit, but it pretty much goes as such: kill, earn gold, buy slightly better gear, die and lose gold, try to do objective, die to guy who mastered the combat system, repeat. The only time I do play multiplayer is on the Full Invasion 2 Mod. And since they recently made the Invasion mode formal, I tried it to find it kinda meh. So I don't really care for multiplayer but It would be nice to see co-op at some point in Bannerlord.
- One of the early money makers and farm for renown in the game. Just save, bet all you can, and try to win the tournament for a butt ton of money early on. However I just don't like the vanilla tournament system that much at all. The arenas are different with each city, but the loadouts are sometimes atrocious to the point of having me rage because I am pitted in an unfair matchup against a named NPC who could insta-kill me with one good swing. I mostly played mods that have the arena system based from the Floris mod where you can customize the tournament in terms of what loadout you want based off a point system. As well as setting up what weapons people will use and how many people you will fight. You wont earn a lot of money from this system but it helps out if you favor a certain weapon and playstyle than the one you would get from random. I am hoping that they will change the tournament system in Bannerlord in some way where you can choose the loadouts and that is really it. Or some sort of change. But I can do vanilla style as it is.
- Well technically there isn't really much a story to this game as it is a sandbox medieval world that you make your own. But so far there is just little snipits that they give you that isn't much. You get a "story" from companions who tell you their story on why they are in the tavern and what happened to them. And whenever you pass by a certain castle or town they give a backstory on that place. Even one of the companions refuses to go into the town because
there. It is fine that the game doesn't have a story, but I would like to learn more about the history of Calradia and a bunch of there stuff than the snipits. Also your backstory doesn't really play a major part of the game than just adjusts your stats. Prophesy of Pendor adds in events based off of your backstory to the game, such as assassins from the island you're from and etc.
- So far the graphics is an iffy subject. People hate it, while some thing it is fine as it is. I think it is fine as it is. But the game came out in 2007 originally, so the graphics are dated. But there is games that came out in 2007 that looks much better than Mount & Blade out there. So far I dont have a huge issue with it, since the game runs pretty good on my computer with many guys on the battlefield (depending on the mod) so I don't have a major issue with it there. Not really great, but the main point is gameplay.
- Holy hell these are one of the worst part of combat I have ever encountered. Either it is a single ladder siege, or it is a siege tower siege. I find the siege tower one to be worst. Pretty much to sum the siege combat is just a funnel that gets clogged up with beefy men and women in plate armor trying to get up a single chokepoint getting shot at by archers, crossbowmen, throwing axemen, and javelineers. It takes forever to make progress up onto the wall whenever there is a decent garrison inside, or just a garrison in general (unless it is just really weak). The AI falls off the ladder, they push you off the ladder, they get stuck on the tower, get stuck in the tower, etc. Thank god Bannerlord fixed this issue by adding multiple siege points as well as other siege equipment. Plus you can now sally out than the AI randomly sallying out if you either starved them out (takes forever btw) or seems like you have less odds of winning in the siege battle.
- So far one of the most useless features in my opinion that I noticed in combat. People might disagree with me on this, which is fine, but I tried using kicking in combat just to find it not effective at all. Kicking leaves me vulnerable to damage in tournaments or in dire situations. Plus when I do manage to hit, it doesn't seem to do much at all.
- There is good quests, and then there is the bad. The good is when you get quests for the first time to collect taxes or what have you. The bad being getting the same quest over again and the damn bandit quests. The looter quest is impossible to finish, same with the troublesome bandits if your pathfinding isn't good enough to catch them. Lords can kill the bandits before you get to them and you fail the quest.
Overall: 9/10

Stalker clear sky… A standalone addon to the Stalker game, which was very interesting from the side of new or fixed gameplay procedures and features, most noticeable from which are clan wars and system of weapon and gear upgrades. Also the feature with emissions where you in the middle of normal exploring all of sudden have to run fast to any shelter or die under not-so-clear-sky of the Zone. And new system of loot hunting, where you need special detector to find the Zone relics… And many other little things, most of them were invented and even implemented by the original game community.
Being a hard fan, obsessed with the Stalker immerse world, I was able to made it through all Clear Sky quite fast, when it was just released. And I even felt the need to protect that title from blasphemous critics, who’s just not getting the point… But then I started the game for the second time, to really enjoy all its secrets and tight spots. And now I was puzzled with so many development decisions. Why they done it like this? Really, there should be some other way, there is no any logical base for this move. And that turn. And that was unnecessarily too… Now I feel only a shame for the developers, who ruined such interesting setting with totally unreasonable game plot. And, the worst thing is what all the bad stuff comes at player right away, just from the start! The first level in Swamps, after open wastes, forests and industrial compounds of the first game we need to follow the narrow passages... That's even worse than playing the second Crysis game right after the first one! A way worse. And after you manage through Swamps, the gameplot rushes you to go right on the army's outpost, with the outrageous machinegun (if you never played the game, just watch some vid's about "Clear sky military machinegun" on the youtube, there will be plenty). And if you managed to run out of that setup, you'll come into the Main Clear Sky Feature - the Clan Wars questline. Things finally starting to get interesting after Cordon... right until the moment you realise that all those clan wars are broken beyond repair. The major tip in the community about that quest line - don't do that!
I can say the same about the whole Clear Sky in general. Unless you're a hardboiled Stalker veteran and going to download (or create) some mods for Clear Sky - don't even bother to start it, just get the Call of Pripyat instead, for much better experience.
Me, I prefer the first STALKER game the most, even without mods. Even vanilla Shadow of Chernobyl gives you the biggest amount of adventure, and diversity of gaming experience. Both Clear Sky and Call of Pripyat are just two (of many) mods with the hope to improve some gameplay aspects. And Clear Sky is a lost hope. It done some good, but as a standalone game - it's a very frustrating experience, not worth of your time. Mark 5/10.

I love to get sassy and cheeky, but the fact that this game felt like it had a chance just sort of makes me sad.
"But it's early access!"  True, true.  But unless the developers are purely invested in art and animation and didn't consider game balance at all yet, unless they don't think that most of this game's craft/gather/fight balance is where it should be, it has no future.
First and foremost my experience was a bit painful at the start for 2 reasons:  The characters look like Lego's met anime.  And every character sounds like a 10 year old.  It just gives this feeling like you're playing a free to play Iphone app store game meant to sucker an easy parents money.  I tried my best to shake that feeling, but it's just such a similar and overused style of animation in that industry that I couldn't entirely get rid of it.
The game had me a bit excited at first once I saw that it was a very similar Z targeting system to The Legend of Zelda OOT, but soon it became more annoying than helpful with the jump being replaced by a roll and finding yourself at strange camera angles due to random generation.
The enemies at least had differences unlike most games these days.  Some would spawn little ones, some would teleport, some were harder to hit by chance, some shot tricky bouncing projectiles...and then there were the Eye bats.
Those need some work.  I played as a Knight and in order to fight bats you have to jump, attack once, leave combat, and do it again.  Once you're in combat mode with them they are almost impossible to hit and the electric ones get guarenteed hitscan strikes on you.
The game lacks balance and progression at the moment of any kind, I could go through a large list but the 2 most obvious examples are how suddenly, when you get to Iron teir, it takes twice as much ore and coal from before to make bars, it takes 8 silk per silk cloth, 4 silk cloth per armour peice...and we found 24 on one island total...for 2 players.  The chest upgrade for iron only incrased the half inventory sized chests by 4 slots and is not worth 16 iron ore (2 bars) at all.  You would be far better off using some copper ore you no longer have ANY use for for another 12 slot chest.
The developers need to hire someone with a sense of game balance or this game will only be enjoyed by kids who just love playing "a game".  It will never be anything special unless it is tuned properly and more than that, they need more traits, many more interesting items (most armour and traits are literally just stat modifiers and add no new mechanics),
I'll keep my eye on this game, but in the future I see from the experience I've gathered and analyzed, this game will be nothing special at all.  Just a big art display and fun for a 8 year old to lose his childhood in.

Some good content in this game that is well intended and planned, however the game is so buggy, to my machine, that most of it is completely unusable after some hours of playing the game. In the last few hours that I attempted to play the game on even my huge PC running Windows 10, on a very fast 3500GHz Intel i7 Processor with 8GB of RAM, the game crashed right on startup, making the game completely impossible to play.
Since I did not have much time to review the product before the game suddenly started crashing, losing much of my progress, the product itself was very hard to accurately judge due to these crashes. The artwork however, is quite nice and enjoyable, especially in the Academy templates, which came to me after fiddling around with it. Train Simulator also shows very realistic simulation of train physics and kinematics, which is what this simulator is built for. The junctions look excellent and reflect the true nature of railway junctions in the real world, and the gameplay experience, when not littered with bugs, is simply fantastic!
But the reason why I say "not recommended" is due to how glitchy it is. I'm always tempted to autosave at least every minute due to how frequently the game crashes. And then the moment I go onto settings to change it, however, the game does exactly what it wants to do, blow up. Recently, I had no hope playing the game, but only to write a review on what I found in only 38 hours (as of writing this) when it crashed and glitched right in front of me every time the game booted up. Even if it doesn't explode in front of my screen, Train Simulator still proves to contain many poorly designed features, especially in the route editor, such as inconsistent latitudes and difficulty in forming railway junctions in the game.

You start out knowing only this: You are clearly dead, and the family mansion and the surrounding area are abandoned. Everything is broken, dead, or decaying. How long has it been? What happened? Where is everyone? As it should be in any good adventure game, the story sucks you right in. Finding answers only leads to more questions at first, and you slowly begin to unravel the tragic tale of a town ravaged by war and a family that unknowingly brought on its own demise.
A quick search on Wikipedia told me this: Goetia is a practice that includes the invocation of angels or of demons. And indeed, you quickly discover that these people have seen more than their fair share of supernatural beings.This is a pretty standard premise, and most horror fans will have seen it many times. However, it is so superbly done in this game that you won't mind. By the end of the story, I had no questions left at all. Everything made perfect sense. That's a rare and impressive feat.
A great example of this is your character's amnesia. Amnesia is a condition we see all too often in games, and in many cases, there is no real reason, besides the developer not knowing how to explain things properly. That is not the case here. You don't find out until very late in the game, but you have amnesia for a very good, logical reason. And when you find out, many pieces of the puzzle fall into place. The many letters and journals you find throughout your journey are similarly well-written. You really get to know all the people who once lived here, because their journals and notes all show distinctly different personalities. For point-and-click games, the writing is arguably the most important part, and it was done very well here.

May I present: Rufus. Our protagonist (technically true) and hero (not true even after three servings of cactus juice).
He lives in Deponia. He hates Deponia. Deponia hates him.
Now that you know the inter-relational dynamics of the situation, let me tell you something more about Rufus.
He has flaws.
And by that I mean he is a glib-tongued, self-absorbed, egotistical megalomaniac with inclinations for projects from the 'mad scientist' category. He might also be an arsonist. And he steals. Like, a lot. For example, if you have a firefly-powered miner's hat on you and Rufus is in the vicinity, chances are you don't really have it. Maybe you never even had it to start with? You just thought you had it?
See...?
Normally I try my best to avoid surrounding myself or even being associated with those kinds of people. But there's just something in him, you know? Not his brains, he has proven more than once that he is a little slow on the uptake, if you catch my drift.
I have no idea how he does it but he makes me a worse person with each and every meeting we have. I admit, he got me so hooked that I took the bait (*hint*hint*), line and sinker and started playing Chaos on Deponia immediately after finishing this one.
Rufus! Oh, the fun we've had! The only downside to it all is that I am afraid my moral compass isn't pointing north as much as it used to.

This game doesn't deserve all of the bad reviews it's getting, although I can see why people are mad about this game.
The game itself is actually really good, in fact this game is better than Stick of Truth in almost every aspect of gameplay. I love the new combat system, which adds a new demention of stratagy to the game. The comedy is on point, and it fees like you are actually playing an episode of South Park. The much talked about skin color/ difficulty system, and gender choosing is pretty great and adds South Park's classic brand of social comentary. The plot is good, although it is reminiscent of Stick of Truth's plot.
Overall, this would of been a great sequal to Stick of Truth, if it wasn't for Ubisoft's BS.
I personally am not an Ubisoft hater, and like a lot of their games, even though they do tend to be greedy. I have also never had problems with DRM or Uplay (both of which are included in this game).
However, Ubisoft has done this game a huge disservice by tainting it with their BS:
- Payed DLC was released with the game on day 1 that contained content that should of been included with the base
game
- The game was released with lots of glitches, some of which forced me to reload saves in order to get passed. These
glitches weren't compleatly game breaking, but they should of been ironed out before release, and make the game feel
unfinished. In addition, there were some things that didn't even seem to be glitches, but just unfinished in general, like
some NPC's mouths not moveing when they talk
- There was an unobtainable "test" achievement at release, although it is removed now, further suggesting this game is
still unfinished
- I played the game on my 2 year old gaming laptop, well within the required specs, and still experienced lag at medium
graphics settings, constanty at 12 - 18 fps, and sometimes below 10 when it got bad
That being said, I still really like this game, and do intend to finish it.
If this game ran perfectly and didn't have DLC, I'd rate it 9/10, but since this is not so, I will give this game
7/10 - A great game, that was released before it was finished
Edit: I forgot to mention, $60 is way too much for this game, I still recomend this game, but maybe wait till it is on sale

Stick of Truth: Developed by Obsidian (Fallout New Vegas, KOTOR, Pillars of Eternity, Wasteland)
Fractured But Whole: Ubisoft SAN FRANCISCO (Rocksmith 1 & 2)
Yeah, it should have been quite obvious that this was never to reach the height of the original and that it would be of much lesser quality-- put short this game is quite similar to Mass Effect Andromeda, though at that a little bit more polished.

Pros;
- Gameplay.
The gameplay is actually pretty solid. Good mechanics including a turn-based party system, classes, puzzles and special abilities.
- Combat.
The new combat system is an improvement. Although I did enjoy the one from Stick of Truth it was admittedly simplistic. In this game you have to actually think about your next move against the tough enemies. I say this as someone who went through "The Token Experience".
- Side quests.
A couple of side quests. Not many but its a step in the right direction. Perhaps afew too many "collect this" quests.
Cons;
- Originality.
Every joke, without exception, is a reference to something that happened in an episode with very little original material. We spent three times the amount of money it would cost to get Seasons 11 - 15 (I looked it up) and yet we got new content equal to about half an episode. Probably less.
- Humor.
You remember that hilarious part in The Stick of Truth where you're dodging your Dads balls while fighting Underpants Gnomes? How about the alien abudction where we got probed by aliens? Or the old school Canadian part where we caught  "dire aids"? Nazi Zombies anyone? Remember how much we laughed? Stick of Truth was full of moments like that. There is not a single moment that comes close to being as funny in this game. Why?
- Story.
You might think story isn't a strong point of South Park anyway but I disagree. Random humor doesn't mean theres no narrative. Stick of Truth had a pretty awesome narrative with a pretty satisfying conclusion and it did it while making us laugh. Not only did this game not come as close to being funny but what the $%@! was with that story? Seriously? Was *anyone* satisfied with that ending or that last fight? I'm not going to spoil it but the "big bad" is revealed maybe about half-way through the game and wow. It is both dissapointing and predictable.
- Replayability.
There is none. Even if there was you would have to scrap your character and start fresh because once again new game plus was not implimented despite high demand for it.
Conclusion;
Look, I'm not going to tell you what you should or shouldn't be satisfied with but heres the facts; Trey and Matt didn't bother applying one tenth of the effort they do with their episodes. Thats a comment on the writing, not the gameplay. Gameplay is decent but thats thanks to the people who developed it and who actually bought this for gameplay? If they did they're going to be dissapointed, its definitely not worth the price.
What people wanted was basically a decent game combined with a super long, super funny South Park episode turned up to eleven. Instead they got peddled a bunch of "memberberries" for the price of, and I cannot emphasize this enough, several seasons of South Park. Look it up.

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons.
After completing the game, I am really having a bad time calling it a game. I would call it a 3D story or graphical adventure other than anything else. It is story telling at its finest - something that you would likley see in some artsy an meaninful anime movie such as Spirited Away (in fact, after the initial couple of minutes of gameplay it is easy to imagine "Full Metal Alchimist" Edward and Alphonse Elric running around doing the same stuff).
However, it poses no challanges whatsoever. The puzzles are easy, it is fairly clear to understand what you have to do instantly, and the boss fights arent really boss fights. In the end, you are not playing a game... you are just guiding the characters through the story.
So here are the summary of strengths and weaknessses
+ nice artwork and scenes
+ nice and simple soundtrack
+ game with a message
+ simple and responsive control
+ can be played as a single player or 2 players in the same keyboard, similar to any "good old games"
- not really a game
- not much fun to play either (interesting concepts but a bit boring gameplay - but again, it isnt really a game)
- too short (or perhaps that is a plus, because if it was a 20 hour game it would probably be boring as hell)
- a bit pricey for what you get.
Conclusion:
As a game I wouldnt recommend it.
As a story telling experience and curiosity for something fresh and different - then thumbs up.
If you want it and dont mind waiting  , get it with 75% discount or greater discount (I have seen it in discount in every single steam sale, so it shouldnt be hard if you dont mind waiting) , otherwise you may feel cheated. Then again... we are paying over 8£ (over 10€) to watcha movie in a theater, so perhaps paying full prize isnt that bad.
I think that the creators/producers have made an excelent work with Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons, as I am sure that the game is a pure reflex of what they wanted to convey.
(I have seen too many "YES" for this game. I am going to give it a "NO". I have liked it, but people should be warned what they are really getting, and I feel that there are too many people over inflating the game...
.... and I cant stress this enough, this isnt really a game in my point of view).

I have overlooked "Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons" when it first released over a year ago. I guess it seemed to me like this is just a puzzle game with two-character gimmick to differentiate it, and pretty much nothing else. And while that may be partially true, it is also so much more that I actually regret not getting it earlier. It was only the demo on my XBox 360 (which I got only this year, pretty much after it's generation ended, but that is another story) that convinced me of this game's value.
As stated above, superficially this game is a fairly simple puzzle solving affair. You control two brothers at the same time, with left and right analog sticks of your controller, and you can make them perform contextually chosen action by pressing and holding the corresponding trigger. Sounds primitive, yes, but the developers managed to hide a surprising amount of depth within that simple mechanic. Most situations in the game require splitting attention and cooperation of both brothers, and many of them also force you to think ahead, plan and synchronise actions of our both protagonists. "Brothers..." surprised me multiple times about just how much can you do with one button per character.
There is no tutorial, objective indicators or on-screen prompts (sans about three explaining simply what the buttons do) and absolutely no dialogue nor written text throughout the entire game, and yet I never missed them once. In fact this adds to the game, omitting the additional layer of artificial detachment. You have to observe the world around you, learn how it works and use those rules to your own advantage. This is actually a hallmark of excellence in game design and something unique in modern times.
"Brothers..." tells a beautiful and multi-layered story, but does so without a single word. The characters all speak pure gibberish, but through intonation, facial expressions and body language they often express what would normally take pages of written text. Most of the story is told through interaction and gameplay itself, and I was shocked how effective the game is at dealing with extremally difficult subjects at times. I won't spoil it for anyone by giving examples though, because the greatest part of it is discovery.
Finally - the game's presentation is absolutely stunning. It is not only thanks to beautifully crafted High Fantasy world and incredible musical score complementing the visuals, but also because of how it all flows together. As the journey to save their father takes Naiee and Naia further and further away from home, they find themselves travelling through more dangerous and inhospitable areas of very different design, yet the transitions are always smooth and subtle. "Brothers..." is a prime example of a game that does not need any latest graphical bells & whistles to deliver fantastic presentation, and never needs to segment itself to show us all it has prepared for our protagonists.
Overall - this is a fantastic experience, but not everybody will enjoy it. It's brief (around 2,5 hours), simple gameplay-wise and not very challenging, but it surely excels in being a story-driven affair, though very different from "cinematic experiences" that most companies are trying to sell us nowadays. Controls may seem unwieldy at first, and playing with a keyboard can be detrimental to the overall experience, but once you get used to it there is pretty much nothing else "wrong" with "Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons". If you're after storytelling, don't hesitate.

Snow is one of the greatest psychological horror games on not only Steam, but the market as a whole in recent times. Snow is the story of a man, a man who we can assume committed horrible atrocities in his time and was sent to his own personal hell. This hell consists of mountains, barren cities, your characters dopplegangers, and most importantly snow. The cities show signs of civilization but no one else besides the player character ever appears suggesting that the game takes place in a post apocalyptic setting. The hills take hours to scale and don't give much of a reward for reaching the top, which foreshadows the end of the game where your character becomes fed up with the snow tries to escape by scaling the mountains, only to trip and fall into the void for all of eternity. Truly a masterpiece worth paying $5 in micro-transactions for the snow mobile.

Intro:
I feel that the main goal of Bossa Studios for the original game, was to get a quick laugh from the audience and maybe make some money off of it, I feel the same for this version. Ask anybody that owns it about why they bought the game and they will most likley say "Because it looked funny". I think the only reason you would buy this game is due to the fact that it looked freaking hillarious to see a scalpel jammed into some poor man's eye. I mean, who really want's to buy this for the pure challenge of preforming sugery on a patient? I would assume you want to buy this as an escape from the daily life, to the inner realms of video games where everything that happens is supposed to be a fun experience, and I think it does this fairly well.
Gameplay:
I think that the gameplay is pretty hard, and the fact that it is hard is just the point of the game. The devs as gamers thought about the most annoying things you could implement, and afterward implemented them. I think that the devs never expected this to be a really good game that people played and speedran just due to the fact that it was only intended as a quick laugh and nothing more. When it comes to the Pros and the Cons of the game I don't like adressing them just due to the fact that as previously stated, the cons were intended for the end product long before the release of the game. I can't judge the gameplay of this as it really depends on your sense of humor and expectations of what a game should be.
Conclusion:
Since this game was mainly to make a funny statement about something, I don't feel like you should even consider playing it like a real video game, but to play it as a form of comedy that you may come back to after a hard day of work. To actually play it as a fully fledged video game is just foolhardy, and if you want a FAIR challenging experience, I wouldn't really recommend it in any way shape or form. 100%ing this thing was really pointless in the whole scheme of things, and in all honesty it ruined the experience of ever playing a game like it again. I think if it's on sale (which it usally is) go for it, there is no crime in laughing at a fake man's misery, or doing psychologically questionable things to his organs, however, I urge you to never ever play it like a real game, but to only ever play it as a silly satire on the "Simulation" genre of today...
Side Note:
If I could give this a "Mixed" or "So-So" review I would use that instead, but alas I am stuck with the current steam system of reviewing something.

123 hours and 493 deaths later, I have finally conquered this beast.
Don't be fooled by the seemingly simple gameplay. On the inside, this is a very complex game.
In the beginning, you gleefully frolic through a beautiful system of caves hoarding every piece of shining gold or gleaming jewel in sight. "This is great!" you think to yourself as you open a chest full of rubies and emeralds. You start to whistle a tune as you delve deeper into the caverns. Then you see a golden idol. Excitedly, you grab it. The caves start to shake as a giant boulder comes tumbling toward you at high speeds. With a lucky jump, you survive the huge ball of death. A few seconds later, a spider comes out of nowhere and knocks you down a pit, where you're met with an angry old shopkeeper who is maniacally running, jumping, and firing his shotgun. You're struck with a bullet and sent over a ledge. As you slam into the ground, an arrow is launched from an inconveniently placed trap directly into your face. As you might imagine, you're now dead. Adding insult to injury, your lifeless corpse is flung directly into a pit of spikes.
This experience leaves you speechless. As you recover from this ordeal, you think to yourself "That wasn't fair." Little do you know, the whole thing was entirely your fault. You had failed to thoroughly scan your surroundings before grabbing that cursed piece of gold. Turns out, the boulder had obliterated an altar, causing a swarm of angry spiders to begin making their way to you. After this, the boulder rolled down a hole and smashed into the wall of a weapon shop, sending the shopkeeper into a violent frenzy. This is when one of the provoked spiders jumps onto your unsuspecting head and sends you to your doom.
Nearly everything in this game can lead to your death.
There are many lessons to learn in this game. With every run, you increase in knowledge and skill. Eventually you make your way out of the caves, and you're in a foreign place filled with all kinds of new things that want to kill you. That blue frog looks kinda cute, right? WRONG. That "cute" blue frog HATES YOU. It will stop at nothing to murder you.
With every death and every success, you suddenly have a bunch of new questions. "What is that fleshy thing sticking out of the wall?" "What happens if I blow this up?" "Can I safely traverse this terrain?" "Why does that gravestone say 'Ash' on it?" You must find the answer to these questions. There is a great feeling of satisfaction and confidence every time you discover something new.
Overall, Spelunky is an amazing game. It will not fail to entertain, and will keep you coming back for more. There is plenty to discover, with lots of secrets and surprises. It's very unforgiving, and you will have to be vigilent and persistent if you want to conquer it. The extremely challenging achievements assure you that there is always another goal to reach.
Go ahead, give it a try. You'll be pleasantly surprised.

It is the most strange, misterious and difficult game from Square Enix that I have played so far. It has 16 achievements. These achievements only appear when the player quits the game. It took me sometime to get used to the dynamic of the game. I've only finished it after the third time after starting it. Graphically it's amazing, especially the attention to details and small objects in the scenery. Sometimes the scenery is upsidedown. The soul of Abigail Blackwood comes from the grave. Her soul goes to the Blackwood Manor, the family Manor. Her soul gains powers along the game like the power of vision, the power of strength, the power of seeing through cracks on the walls, the power of possessing objects, like a feather or a screwdriver. Abigail has to banish several demons , having each one a specific colour; blue,green, yellow, red and purple, so that she can get access to more divisions on the Manor. There are several codes and puzzles, musical puzzles and the clues are scattered through the manor, especially on books. Besides de Blackwood Manor her soul can go to Eldwitch Forest, Oakmarsh, Fields of Stone and Silver Labyrinth. Abigail's soul has to find four objects that belonged to Annie's four sons. When she finds them (in pairs) they go automatically to the Nexus. After that she can go to a secret passage to confront Malphas, a demon that is a bird for the last time. Her soul can go through paintings and holes in the walls. The player can have access to the journal (key J) and the Codex (Key C), to see and read all documents in the game. The sound has an important role in the game. The creators advise the use of headphones. I think that is important that a player plays different kinds of games. Buy this game and be prepared to live a new experience, like I did.

I love this kind of game.  I bought it based mostly on the positive reviews.  It is a simple "point and click" with a twist. You play as the spirit of a dead girl and can move thru walls...at least as long as they're not blocked by sigils or if you've possessed somethig that then makes you somewhat solid.
The story is quite in depth and involved and spread out over several chapters. There is a Codex or ist of things you have looked at or taken which helps you solve some of the many puzzles. There is a journal that automatically tracks your progress and gives you some idea of what to do next without really giving anything away and also lets you know when you have completed a level. There's also a map that you can use as you progress to quickly get from spot to spot, otherwise there can be a lot of floating from screen to screen to screen, etc.  The graphics are very ncie and the music is simple and soothing. A few of the "effects" are a little cheesy, but does not distract from the story or the game. During the game you gather or read many documents so that you do have a reasonble idea of the story line.
I only have one complaint. It has to do with some of the puzzles.  I've been playing these kinds of games since the original Myst came out so I'm really comfortable with making deductive leaps or conenctions to solve most puzzles. It's not that I never reach for the walkthru, but it's rare. In at least a couple of instances, I knew "what" to do, but not how to do it. I reread the information that I had and carefully looked at the environment, but in the end I had to go get a hint. After reading the hint, I was left thinking "hmm OK, that sort of makes sense, but I guess I don't know why I would have assumed that was the way to solve the puzzle". It's like the developer was thinking one way, but didn't, at least from my perspective, put forth anything that would have taken me down that same path.
This is an extension of my original  review. I have finally finished the game. Unfortunately I had to use the walkthru several times in the end to solve some of the more obtuse puzzles. I will once again reitrate that I think the puzzles are one of this games best points and one of its worst. For example, I used a hint to solve the barrel organ puizzle.  Once I knew the secret of it, it was plain that I just hadn't invested enough time into the puzzle and it was one that I should have been able to solve on my own.  But a couple of others (sorry no spoilers) just weren't evident to me that the item that gave the solution went with that puzzle or that the solution didn't seem to make logical sense - in other words, I'm not sure I would have ever figured it out..
While I doubt that I'll do a replay of the game,  over all I thintk it's a great game and would recomemnd it.

My all time favourite game series finally comes to PC. Mwah.
The single player is quite packed with content contrary to popular belief. I personally only play for Treasure Battle and it is worth every penny even if you don't play online. I personally think its better than Ghost Battle.
Online is great too, works, great netcode and much more simple to play than 6/Tag 2 so it has a lower skill ceiling.
So yeah, if you love story and AI fights it is certainly worth it. If you love playing against people online it is an instant buy.

Preface: This review doesn't cover online play.  I might add that later.  It's been a long time since I visited the Tekken universe because I mainly play games on PC. Combos are expanded, newer mechanics like Rage give you a chance to come back in a match, and characters are customizeable with cosmetics to a large extent.  The controls are pretty clean and responsive using an XBox 360 controller and there is just generally more content than the Tekken releases I loved from the past.  And it's not restricted to playing on a console!

Deponia is a point and click adventure puzzle game about a man named Rufus who lives on a "Planet" entirely covered in garbage. (I say Planet with quotations simply because the characters state it's on a planet different form a city called Elysium, located high in the sky, presumably in orbit, even if that doesn't work at all). It's set in the future of our time so you could say it fits into Sci-Fi aswell.
Either way, Rufus wants to get to Elysium and he's... well he's rather mad, but he has the brains to get out of any situation, including the situation where he's on Deponia, a place he hates more than anybody else.
The game takes... well about as long as it's taken to beat it, but unfortunately like all games in the same genre, once you play it, it takes basically 30 minutes tops to beat it again, knowing all the information, even if that's good for a few laughs.
When you play this game, in order to beat some part you REALLY gotta think with conventional logic or even like a smart person and I sometimes fail at that, requiring a walkthrough to figure out what to do with some things.
The game has alot of tongue-in-cheek humor bits, and even some normal bits of humor. The art style is very nice with great animations, although unfortunately the lip-syncing is sometimes a bit off, like in the start of the game, it's not too big of a deal.
The music is also great but if you get stuck, turn it off or you'll hear it again and again. There's not really too much music, variation for music would've helped somewhat. The game has cats at one point and they're miserably adorable.
The puzzles are challenging, but ofcourse it's the main reason as to why it takes 30-40 minutes to beat it given all the puzzle answers are given to you.
The story is very engaging though, it's easily the best part of this game. I love Rufus' character, the other characters are just as great, all of them very well voiced and even to say the least, they are even interesting people... when looking at main character such as Gizmo, Rufus, Wenzel, etc.
I personally loved playing this game start to finished and even after all this time, I still have the puzzles all memorized to heart... mostly.
Droggeljug mode is a special mode that makes it extremely difficult if you don't remember dialogue options, or even know how to skip things as literally every word of text and even dialogue is replaced with the word Droggeljug. Just one of them for text, however this would've been nice for dialogue too as it doesn't follow the same thing, causing Droggeljug mode to be deeply irritating. It could be changed by simply having one word per dialogue option instead of it being word for word replacement.
Altogether, the game gets an 8/10. It's great fun, has a splendid atmoshpere, world and story, and the characters are nice too.
It would score a 10/10 but Droggeljug mode being really annoying as the word that characters say have no variation, it's just one sound clip looped over and over per character, it detracts from it a fair amount in addition to the fact that many items used on something results in the exact same reaction from Rufus in contexts that don't really make any sense for it, and also if the music had some variation, as it will eventually lose it's value as you get stuck (if you're like me, you WILL get stuck at least once) and hear it for many loops of it.
