I am trying hard to like this game, but there's a dozen little annoyances that keep it held back from being a reccomendation to anyone except Dead Rising fans.  I hate to say this game is garbage, but I've been screaming at the monitor for all its gameplay flaws after 10+ hours.
1.  The Survivor AI is terrible and they're a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to manage.  It's every nightmare you always think of with Escort Missions.  Almost half the characters you find can't use a gun, 1/8 of all of them can't use melee and take up an inventory slot for you to carry them.  You get surrounded by zombies way too easily even if you give them a gun.  Don't even try if you have a group of survivors because they'll just shoot through and even kill other survivors.  (The Leadership Buff didn't help either.)  If they get grabbed, it stops the entire pace of you running through the constant thick crowd of zombies and you have to rescue them.  If you didn't notice them getting grabbed, hit the restart checkpoint option becaues they'll definitely die with how fast their health goes down.  (You WILL hit Restart Checkpoint A LOT.)
2.  You take damage too easily from the bosses.  You will constantly try to find or keep health items during any boss fight because they can take off half your life bar in seconds.  You will have to constantly pick at them because several can regen their health.  And ♥♥♥♥ those Militia Hunters in the central plaza.  Rapid firing sniper rifle ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who you WILL have to lame it out with eather going for rapid melee or peek shooting from behind the air vents.  Seriously, as soon as you see their introductory cutscene (they're the group of sterotypical rednecks with Berrett Jacksons), go to the Dead Rising Wikia entry on Hunters for their Locations.  You will have to take them out immediately since you go through the central plaza all the time and survivors will be shot too.  Each bullet takes off 1/4 survivor health and you can't stop them.
Then I got to the sheriff after them who could shoot guns out of my hands.  This gimmick boss♥♥♥♥♥♥is super frustrating and is the one time I'd recommend to anybody of finding a way to cheat to get infinite health JUST for the bosses.  You really do have to find a way to lame it out or read the Wikia on tactics to beat them.  Their AI is pretty exploitable at times, but the cheap gimmicks make them frustrating.
3.  It's increidbly hard to enjoy the environment or exploring because of the constant time sensitive objectives.  I'd recommend Sanbox mode first just to memorize the locations, finding the secret caches of good weapons, and read how to unlock the shortcuts.  There is a gunshop on the right side of the map called High Noon Something.
4.  The zombies should have thinned out.  I know it's part of the game franchise, but the zombie hordes are THICK.  You will have a tough time just trying to avoid getting swiped or grabbed because they're everywhere, unavoidable, and using weapons slows you down, making you even more of a target.  Try getting any powerful rapid fire and AOE weapons like the Rocket Launcher, the parasol blower combo, or Queens.  Don't use normal melee weapons for anything except as a last resort.
5.  There seems to be a lot of engine optimization failures and it's inherent in the series.  There's a lot of fade in as you move from one area to the next things faze out of existence all the time.  It's either because of the team that designed this series isn't experienced enough to optimize well, or it's just part of the sub par PC port.  (The same problem is within DR3 as well.)  The framerate doesn't♥♥♥♥♥♥itself hard like it does in DR3, but it can be noticable in thick areas.  I haven't had that problem since I have a powerful PC, but there are other problems like lack of a Windowed mode.  The blanking of both my PC monitors for 5 seconds going into and out of DR2 along with the lag and potential crashing is the reason why I always support PC games having a Windowed mode.  This is inexcusable.
For the positives, what can I say, it's a Dead Rising game and a spin-off title that takes place in the same universe as the normal DR2, except this one has Frank West as the main protagonist.  Surprisingly, there are people who still play in co-op in this game, but I haven't been able to join or receive someone.  I'm not sure if it's the probelm with Games For Windows Live API or something, but it's a little screwy.  This is really one of those games that needs a difficulty setting because I feel like I'm playing on Hard Mode the entire time and it's kicking my♥♥♥♥♥  I'm not sure how long I can play this, but I'm not coming back after this.

Stick of Truth: Developed by Obsidian (Fallout New Vegas, KOTOR, Pillars of Eternity, Wasteland)
Fractured But Whole: Ubisoft SAN FRANCISCO (Rocksmith 1 & 2)
Yeah, it should have been quite obvious that this was never to reach the height of the original and that it would be of much lesser quality-- put short this game is quite similar to Mass Effect Andromeda, though at that a little bit more polished.

Pros;
- Gameplay.
The gameplay is actually pretty solid. Good mechanics including a turn-based party system, classes, puzzles and special abilities.
- Combat.
The new combat system is an improvement. Although I did enjoy the one from Stick of Truth it was admittedly simplistic. In this game you have to actually think about your next move against the tough enemies. I say this as someone who went through "The Token Experience".
- Side quests.
A couple of side quests. Not many but its a step in the right direction. Perhaps afew too many "collect this" quests.
Cons;
- Originality.
Every joke, without exception, is a reference to something that happened in an episode with very little original material. We spent three times the amount of money it would cost to get Seasons 11 - 15 (I looked it up) and yet we got new content equal to about half an episode. Probably less.
- Humor.
You remember that hilarious part in The Stick of Truth where you're dodging your Dads balls while fighting Underpants Gnomes? How about the alien abudction where we got probed by aliens? Or the old school Canadian part where we caught  "dire aids"? Nazi Zombies anyone? Remember how much we laughed? Stick of Truth was full of moments like that. There is not a single moment that comes close to being as funny in this game. Why?
- Story.
You might think story isn't a strong point of South Park anyway but I disagree. Random humor doesn't mean theres no narrative. Stick of Truth had a pretty awesome narrative with a pretty satisfying conclusion and it did it while making us laugh. Not only did this game not come as close to being funny but what the $%@! was with that story? Seriously? Was *anyone* satisfied with that ending or that last fight? I'm not going to spoil it but the "big bad" is revealed maybe about half-way through the game and wow. It is both dissapointing and predictable.
- Replayability.
There is none. Even if there was you would have to scrap your character and start fresh because once again new game plus was not implimented despite high demand for it.
Conclusion;
Look, I'm not going to tell you what you should or shouldn't be satisfied with but heres the facts; Trey and Matt didn't bother applying one tenth of the effort they do with their episodes. Thats a comment on the writing, not the gameplay. Gameplay is decent but thats thanks to the people who developed it and who actually bought this for gameplay? If they did they're going to be dissapointed, its definitely not worth the price.
What people wanted was basically a decent game combined with a super long, super funny South Park episode turned up to eleven. Instead they got peddled a bunch of "memberberries" for the price of, and I cannot emphasize this enough, several seasons of South Park. Look it up.

South Park: The Fractured But Whole is not a terrible game by any stretch of the imagination. But for a full 60$ game I really expected more. I absolutely loved the previous game, The Stick of Truth, and naturally had high hopes for the sequel.
However, TFBW just fails to deliver. It absolutely has the South Park feel to it, with tons of humor and references. The problem is that the game just can't coast by on that alone and the rest of the game is just... boring. The story isn't particularly interesting and you never felt there was anything at stake, something to drive you along. In the 20 or so hours it took me to play through the game I felt I spent most of my time fighting trash, searching for collectibles and doing fetch quests. Only at the very end do you see anything in the way of stakes and it all ends with one of the worst final battles I've ever seen and an incredibly anti-climactic ending.
There are also other issues I have with this game, the price being one of them. At 60$ I expect more content than I received. The game is very short, even with all the side content included. And the inclusion of a very expensive season pass and day one DLC doesn't help either. And of course the cherry on top is the fact that you have to use UPlay whether you want to or not. Ubisoft... no one likes your stupid client. Stop pushing it.
And there are some technical issues as well. I didn't have the black screen problem others have had, but I did have to play through the entire game with a very annoying grey bar at the top and bottom of the screen because my monitor uses a non-standard resolution. Oddly enough, The Stick of Truth did not have this problem so I don't see why this game should have it. The game is also very resource intensive, excessively so compared to the Stick of Truth.
And finally the game feels very much like a console port, this is glaringly obvious with the in game phone menus and the control scheme, particulary when trying to do the toilet challenges.
In the end I suppose the game is worth a play if you loved the previous game, just wait for a steam sale, it isn't worth the full asking price. But all things considered, if you haven't played the previous game I would suggest skipping this and picking up The Stick of Truth instead. It's just a better game in every way.
Final rating: 6.5/10

The story mode in this game is one of the best in GTA history, with fun gameplay and lots of memorable moments. The triple protagonist design brings a lot to the table, allowing everyone to play the game a bit differently. My only complaint about the campaign is that you seem to be thrown around to random areas without any sense of organization, and the map itself is full of empty space, especially Blaine County. It just feels like a bunch of wasted opportunities. It's a shame they didn't follow GTA San Andreas's design of having the player move in a circle around the map, but that's just a small thing.
And then, there's Online.
Online is, well, pretty bad right now. First and foremost, the Online mode uses a Peer-to-Peer system, meaning that when you are on a server, your ip adress is THERE. If someone wanted to, they could very easily doxx you and steal your personal information. Secondly, it is filled to the brim with greifers, and Rockstar seems to be grooming them into destructive money pits with pricey, completely unbalanced weaponized vehicles. Then there's the hackers, who can either flood your account with millions of dollars, or clear a server with a push of a button. Either one is bad news for the game, because the former leaves players with no drive to continue playing, and the latter makes the game completely unplayable. And the worst part of all is that GTA Online is the only part of the game that Rockstar is supporting at the moment. Single player DLC has been completely cancelled to make room for Online, which really sucks. Each update leaves singleplayer more and more dated and buggy, and soon it might not even load correctly. To have your product in such a state, it's just poor management. If you're planning on playing GTA Online, bring a friend. Unless you're one of those sadistic♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥dry humping their opressor, think twice before buying this game for full price.
TL;DR: Great single player, cancerous online mode. Developers piling new content on top of abandoned old content. Only play online if you have a friend.

I still owe this game a review, so I think it's time to write one.
PAM is a vehicular combat arcade, and that word combination describes it quite neatly. Your primary goal is to destroy your opponents by means of weapons installed on your post-apocalyptic car. I shall underline it again, because it's not immediately clear from media files and game description: this is NOT a race. It does not matter if you come first or last: the winner is the player who killed more enemies (and got more points, consequently).
All cars and weapons are available from the very beginning, there's no profile development and no campaign mode. Some of the most dangerous cars are locked, though; you will need to buy the DLC to open access to them. You will be able to make an informed decision, because the AI always has access to all cars - there'll be the chance for you to fight against DLC cars, watch their weapons in action, and decide whether you need them or not.
Any car has three weapons: front, side, and rear. They are more or less balanced, but different: each one is useful in its own certain situation, so there's no universal solution fitting for any track. When you start the fight, you don't have any weapon available; you need to activate them by picking barrels distributed throughout the track, and after you have used a certain weapon once, it is deactivated again, until the next barrel. Tracks are very peculiar, both in terms of scenery and of layout. A bit of physics is included, but it's not very realistic (so far as it's an arcade).
Don't expect too much of a game where ice cream refrigerators kill others by giant ice cream balls falling from their rear door, and small pink cars with ponies on their hood flood the road with dozens of teddy bears filled with explosives. Just have fun and enjoy the mayhem and chaos you wreak along with other horrible, rusty, freaky cars that had somehow survived the unknown apocalypse.
Good for a laugh, good racing compet game. 8/10

shes actually a passenger engine, I care not that the real thing is a shunter and rarely if ever operated passenger trains.. or that they only do 28mph flat out on a good day with the wind behind it..

if you find something you love in DLC - Then buy it and enjoy it

J94 saddle tank and a battery locomotive on a mining route - I love it!.. the kind of thing you wouldnt find in a packaged game out of the box because its NOT Popular enough.. yet to me this means the world -

Tekken 7 is not an accessable fighting game. First and foremost, it's very baised against pick up and play. It emphasizes extensive knowledge of your character and learning the moves of nearly the entire cast. The odds are stacked and new players will often be destroyed by even the easiest CPU.
So why am I, as someone who is coming into tekken with this game, giving it a thumbs up with all this negativity? Because what it lacks in accessability, it makes up for in a flawless combat system that has an insane ammount of depth, turning the game from something where mashing a single button is a combo, blockstring and a frametrap as other fighting games are, to a mental battleground of pokes, spacing, and hard reads. In my 10ish hours of playing one character, I've managed to learn enough that I can at least manage to defeat the computer semi-consistantly, and the feeling of reward from doing so (and the actual cosmetic rewards!) is incredible.
Filled with single-player content such as Arcade and Treasure battle along with the main story, it looks beautiful and runs smoothly even on ultra graphics settings, and brings with it a very solid netcode for multiplayer, Tekken 7 is the premiere fighting game of 2017 bar none.

I thought this game was pretty bloody amazing in honesty. The story is rather 'take what you want' with only the bare bones given to you outright. The majority of it is in the notes, books, mysteries and solutions you uncover. The sound is subtle and matches the atmosphere for the game. So to sum that all up, it's visually and audibly pleasing with a well executed story.
Puzzle wise, the difficulty can vary from "was that even a puzzle!?" at the start to "why am I bald now? Why's my hair is clumps on the floor!?" later on, especially the musical puzzles! I consider myself to have quite a good ear, what with being a pianist and guitarist, but some of the music puzzles took me far too long to respect myself for. I'd say there's one, possibly two puzzles that are insanely difficult to work out without A) a guide or B) Re-reading all of the notes you've collected from the whole game to make sure you've not forgotten one tiny little detail. After going with B for a while, I settled with A and have no regrets as it instantly made me realise I'd seen the answer staring me in the face already.
Throughout the game, you'll unlock new areas, which in turn lead to new powers, and provide solutions to puzzles you previously were unable to complete, so, in a simpler way, you'll find yourself backtracking sometimes (but there's a teleport to certain rooms/areas). The powers all added to the game and they were provided at a quick enough pace that nothing felt stagnanted by the time I came to the conclusion of my playthroughs.
As a side note: The developers have been exceeding helpful with resolving issues (both with the game and with general answers on the forums) and as such, I feel that supporting them is worthwhile. Value for money wise: From my playtime you can see, I effectively spent less than £1 an hour and all that time I enjoyed the game so I wholeheartedly recommend this game.

while i still haven't completed portal knights and am only about halfway through all the worlds you can portal to, i'm in love with this game. it reminds me of creativerse but with a dark souls inspired combat system. being able to set any of the worlds i've discovered as my new home world is a nice touch. i haven't explored any of the multiplayer aspects yet, so i can't comment much on them except to say that i was excited by the idea of running through this game with a party of friends. my main character is a level 15 or 16 mage and i like the variety the game provides in terms of customizations. i assumed since i picked a mage that i wouldn't be able to wield the archer's bows or the warrior's melee weapons, but i totally could. i can even pick whatever kind of armor to wear that i want. if i want to be a mage blasting spells while shooting a bow and wearing heavy damage resistant armor, i can and i really really like that.
as for the crafting aspects of the game, most things need to be built at a workbench for most blocks and tools, or at an altar for your magic spells, armor, and weapons. there's also a furnace for smelting ingots out of ores and an anvil for making nonmagical weapons and armor. all of the crafting stations can be upgraded and by upgrading them, you learn new recipes for crafting more, bigger, and better stuff.
all of the enemies and the magic weapons/spells in the game belong to one of 4 elements. i'm not sure what they're called ingame, but it's your basic lightning, nature (earth), fire, and water elements-complete with weaknesses and resistances. in order to make elemental weapons and gear, you'll need to mine or kill enemies for special gems/crystals. the crafting costs get higher and higher for the better items/gear, but since armor doesn't appear to degrade and weapons/tools can all be repaired, you'll never have to make more than one of each. my favorite part of the game is the dowsing rod you can make that helps you find gems and ores across the various worlds.
in all, it's a great game-even more so for being in early access for a little less than a month. it's great to look at, fun to play, there's a ton to do and i imagine they'll add even more as it goes along. this doesn't feel like an early access game. it feels like it's already completed and i can't wait to see what else gets added

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Cat on a Diet is a casual level-by-level puzzle game that plays like a cross between the Incredible Machine and Angry Birds.
The goal of each level is to manoeuvre the obese cat of the title, Dr. Meow, into a cookie jar (or other appropriate container). But you can't directly control the lazy feline; instead you exert your influence on the various platforms and devices in the level in order to allow the world physics to drop, bounce, and roll our squishy hero towards his tasty goal.
Although only just released on Steam, the game has been available on mobile platforms for a couple of years.
Graphics - Graphics are big and colourful, with a consistent cartoony style. Colouring is mostly a bit washed out, with grainy-looking textures, giving each level the feel of a movie set or similar: an effect that I can only assume was deliberate, as it works to good effect.
Each of the four areas includes a short, partly animated introductory comic, but these are really just a short distraction from the game proper. Dr. Meow is suitably plump and he squishes, flattens, and bends in amusing and satisfying ways when contacting the various parts of each level.
There are other nice touches, too, like cute animated appearances of little creatures in the background, and Dr. Meow getting bored and going to sleep -- complete with an endless stream of Zs floating away from his head -- when you leave the game alone for too long. The game also includes a large number of costumes for Dr. Meow hidden throughout the game. These don't seem to have any in-game effects, but some are quite cute or funny, and they're a nice graphical addition to the game. There are also a lot of them; I count 80 in the game's wardrobe section.
Graphics options are almost non-existent, and simply come down to this: "Will that be full screen or window, madam?"
Sound - Sound is pretty minimal. There's a forgettable, but mostly unannoying music track, and basic, but suitable sound effects. Dr. Meow is strangely quiet throughout the game, thereby missing a potential opportunity for some nice cat sound effects.
Gameplay - The game consists of four areas in Dr. Meow's house, each with (I believe) 24 levels.
Each level begins with Dr. Meow seated somewhere away from his cookie-container goal, and three muffins positioned in mostly inconvenient positions around the level. Your job is to use as few swipes of the mouse as possible to cut items in the level (e.g. ropes, or wooden beams), activate simple devices, or otherwise manipulate the level's obstacles in such a way that the world physics move Dr. Meow to his desired cookies, preferably collecting all three muffins on the way. Later levels include movers and dangerous devices that can harm Dr. Meow, making your task far more difficult.
Up to three stars are awarded upon completion of a level: one for completion of the level itself, one for collecting all three muffins, and one for using no more than the stated maximum mouse swipes (or 'cuts') for that level. Completing a level with three stars awards you one of three special bonus powers: a muffin magnet, which draws nearby muffins towards you; a soap bubble, which encases Dr. Meow and allows you to move him about by clicking on or near the bubble; and a shield, which protects Dr. Meow from any dangers present on the level. Once you've collected one of these powers it can be used on any level by clicking its icon.
There's also a collection of bonus levels that are unlocked by collecting the stars. I've only played the first nine of these so far, and these have all involved moving a bubble-encased Dr. Meow around the level by clicking, trying to collect three muffins before the time runs out. These are a nice distraction for a few minutes if you get stuck on one of the normal levels.
Pros:
+ Simple and easy to get into
+ Cute and colourful graphics, with some nice added touches to add interest
+ Steam Achievements to help keep you motivated
+ Trading Cards
Cons:
- It gets repetitive fairly quickly, especially in the early levels when there's not much going on, and when you keep retrying a level to get that cut just right
If you like casual puzzle games then Cat on a Diet should keep you busy for a while, especially if you're also a Steam Achievement hunter.

Stalker has been considered by many a post-apocalyptic first person shooter game. But it isn't, your in a Cordon zone of the Chernobyl area that has been abandon since April of 1986 due to NPP4 catastrophic failure rendering the environment hazardous to live in. Yes, the place dose exists for real, all locations are based on real locations in the real zone. Life is still going on everyday for the people out side of the zone. The Stalker game series is inspired off the book "Roadside Picnic", which is a short science fiction novel written by Arkady and Boris Strugatsky in 1971. More information on this book is available on a wiki, and the book is also available in English now.  The game is a open world exploration as well as mission directive, Remember that.
Clear Sky has its bugs elements but I like the game and has been fun, I been in the zone here since the first release of the dvd of the 1.0 version.  Here your in the Cordon off Zone in which has become a prison. You can get in, but you can't get out.
There is trading with traders, and different factions that may or may not care for you. Many dangerous anomalies to contend with, and artifact to collect and sell for money. Have to watch out for the areas that are radioactive still. One of the things to remember is question everyone and trust no one. Being skeptical with a gut feeling at times is better than a fire fight, When in this game it is important.
The annoying draw back in this game is the bug issues, for some reason even a updated version of the game on steam has not cleared bug issues that rolled over from the 1.0 of the game. For this game, mainly if you plan to use a mod, you really need to have at lest 4gigs of ram for the best results. It works on win7 64 bit, but there has been complaints pending Operating systems causing issues with the game. You may want to check in the forums. Due to the buggy issues I normally would not recommend the game, but Others had been able to play the default game and complete it. And the stalker community out of many I have seen is the most helpful there. It seems every stalker dose what they can to help you. And a good community like that is a nice thing to have.  Makes it hard not to recommend the game.

When you see the 44 metascore you might think this game is broken, but if you actually read the reviews you'll find out that the reviewers always complain about the same 3 issues:
1st, they were too dumb to notice that this game is NOT a simulator, it's a mayhem arcade (a kind of 3D Rock 'n' Roll Racing). So, complains about the "unrealistic physics" are just stupidity. It's like complaining that Mario Kart is not realistic!
2nd, the game is too short. Now, it is true that there are too few tracks and too few cars, but the game actually runs very well with no bugs at all and it is actually fun for some fast destruction racing with friends.
And 3rd, the graphics are not top quality. But in my opinion, they are good enough. (Actually, I just can't understand why people give so much importance to graphics on games. Fabulous graphics may impress you at first, but after some minutes you get used to it and your entertainment will actually rely much more on other aspects, not on the graphics, unless it's so bad that it hampers gameplay, which is rare and definitely not the case here)
Though there are better titles out there, it's 44 metascore is simply absurd. This is not the first time I see a totally misleading metascore. I can't trust it anymore after this one.

Sorry. I'm bleeding. I should stop now). The idea was good, but it's burried somewhere in between the lipstick-smeared graphics, ear-bleeding noise, fatally boring gameplay and all the blood that's coming out of my arm.

But still have to get used to some classic abbilities, that they have different combinations now. Example - Scorpion's (my favourite character) spear. Instead of back back  X (if you're using XBox controller), it's back forward X now.
That's all :D
And about microtransactions. No one forces you to buy DLCs. They'll not affect gameplay itself. I'm not agains microtransactions that will not affect game. Look at CS:GO and Dota 2 (also my favourite games). No one is crying about microtransactions is them.

I was just expecting a short, slightly creepy puzzle game that I could walk away from, but instead discovered that Goetia has compelling storyteling and engaging detective work. I've lost sleep following up on 'just one more clue'. The world and its mysteries are detailed and revealed at just the right pace. There is a reasonable degree of sleuthing and satisfying sense of accomplishment for the effort put into exploring this world.
Goetia is a beautifully crafted mystery: the graphics, the music and the story are all a delightful exploration of Victorian suspense, tragedy and quiet horror.

I like it.  Bought it for the Steam Summer Sale.  It's a point and click game with some good atmosphere, and solid controls.  Example: You do NOT have to randomly click on every blinking thing on the screen to figure out what's interactive, you can just hold CTRL and see what can be played with.
The puzzles have some Guide Dang It! moments (See tvtropes if you don't know what I'm talking about) reminiscent of Monkey Island and that ilk.  They're rare though, and they make sense in hindsight (unlike some of Monkey Island's...).  If I had a complaint it's where you can and can't walk through walls as your ghostly self, and that makes for some confusion when you're possessing an object as to where you can actually take it.

Goetia provided well in its promised setting and mood. The story was interesting and the music added a lot to the gameplay. The visuals were pleasing too, with a lot of detail given to all of the rooms. The ending didn't dissappoint either and I would love to know more about the story and characters, so no complaints there
The puzzles however, I often found hard and tedious. There were some very strange leaps of logic and some puzzles required power ups that were very tricky to find. I usually play these games without a walkthrough because I enjoy figuring it out myself even if it takes hours, but for this game I ended up finding a walkthrough simply because I couldn't cope with it anymore. A couple of puzzles I still don't understand even with the walkthrough. A more detailed map would have been a good help, because near the end of the game I started to lose my bearings of where I had left a lot of objects behind in this game and which routes I could use to transport them to the other locations.
Storywise and for visuals/mood this game gets all the points, gameplay wise I would have prefered more logical puzzles or at least better hints as for what to use where.

I love puzzle games. I finished and enjoyed masterpieces like Riven, Witness or Talos principle. I grabbed this game in heartbeat seeing great reviews everywhere. What a dissapoitment!
I warn all puzzle game lovers! Goetia is NOT a puzzle game. It's more story-telling / exploration game. If you encounter something which looks like puzzle it's usually just garbage put together without any logic. I've had enough after solving constellation "puzzle".
The game contains beautiful graphics and great sound effects and music.
I would recommend this game to people who like mysterious stories, ghosts and like to explore areas designed by real artists with great attention to detail.

Tekken 7 is not an accessable fighting game. First and foremost, it's very baised against pick up and play. It emphasizes extensive knowledge of your character and learning the moves of nearly the entire cast. The odds are stacked and new players will often be destroyed by even the easiest CPU.
So why am I, as someone who is coming into tekken with this game, giving it a thumbs up with all this negativity? Because what it lacks in accessability, it makes up for in a flawless combat system that has an insane ammount of depth, turning the game from something where mashing a single button is a combo, blockstring and a frametrap as other fighting games are, to a mental battleground of pokes, spacing, and hard reads. In my 10ish hours of playing one character, I've managed to learn enough that I can at least manage to defeat the computer semi-consistantly, and the feeling of reward from doing so (and the actual cosmetic rewards!) is incredible.
Filled with single-player content such as Arcade and Treasure battle along with the main story, it looks beautiful and runs smoothly even on ultra graphics settings, and brings with it a very solid netcode for multiplayer, Tekken 7 is the premiere fighting game of 2017 bar none.

Let me start off by addressing that even though I'm recomending this EA game it does not mean I think you should purchase it in the state it is in now unless just to show support for the project. I have not played hours of the game ,because it did not need that kind of time investment to get an idea of what shape it currently is in. Now with that out of the way  I'll put down some pros & cons.
Pros
+ Combat system is fun ,and is clearly akin to that of 3d Zelda games which given the graphical style of the game fits perfectly.
+ Classes though not need are a nice add on to this style of game ,by which I mean the whole Minecraft trend.
+ Crafting is easy to access ,and doesn't require any guides to makes items as the recipes are listed in the crafting  stations.
+The leveling system was a nice touch that when completely flushed out will add something more to the game ,and helps give a better blend of RPG & Voxel games.
Cons
- The maps are extremely small to the point that you can travel one end to the other in seconds.
- Though it doesn't make or break the game everything being blocky could hurt the game when compared to other voxel games moving away from it.
-As mentioned in the pros the leveling system needs to be worked on ,but I'm sure it will be (or at least can be since it's still an EA game).
- Game will need more things to craft in the long run which includes armors/weapons.
- Not being able to be on different maps while in multiplayer needs to be addressed as well
In conclusion the game does show great promise if you're looking for a fantasy based voxel game ,but being Early Access ,and  only recently coming  out on steam  time will tell if it gets the treatment it needs.

This game is phenomanal, both with a lot of content and a lot of new mechanics that make the game engaging. Although the story could have used more balance, since you spend a lot more time with Coon & Friends than with Freedom Pals (which was a downer since you don't get to use Mysterion as much). The strategy mechanics are a wonderful addition and make gameplay more thoughtful, and the freedom to change your classes additionally means you can vary your gameplay whenever you please. There's a lot more puzzle-solving too, which makes for extra fun if you're into that sort of thing. Also you will have a more comprehensive conversation about gender in this game than you will in most people in your life, which is pretty damn impressive at how well the game approached that almost tertiary detail of character construction.
My biggest problem right now is that the game NEEDS A PATCH because there is a GLITCHED STORY MISSION that will HALT YOUR PROGRESSION. If you get the Shady Acres combat glitch, there's basically no sure-fire way to debug it yourself (I've tried re-verifying my cache, uninstalling the game, restarting the computer, doing other missions first, the whole shebang to no avail). I can't give a full summary of my opinions on the game because I literally cannot initiate a story mission!!!! I've gotten to the point I can't complete any more side missions because I'm either blocked temporarily due to the point in the story or because I'm just under-levelled. That is literally the only problem with the game right now and, well, it's a pretty damn big one because I cannot complete the game despite having spent nearly 30 hours in it already!
TL;DR The game is definitely worth the price and will give you a lot of wonderful content, but Ubisoft needs to get it together and patch their game so they don't ruin some of the best material they've produced over the past five years. I shouldn't need to start my hardest difficulty playthrough just in hopes I can actually finish the game in that file. That's like super lame.

An adventure game that looks like a LucasArts one but, at least in terms of the puzzles, occasionally feels like a Sierra one.
The story is pretty simple: A loser wants to escape his garbage dump of a home, and leave for someplace better.  The captions have some spelling errors, the voice acting occasionally falls flat, and the puzzles both halt the game's pacing, and sometimes serve to frustrate the player. Not many times, mind you, but there are a few that will make you ask, "Really?"
So, why do I like the game? Well, I love adventure games, and Deponia is a nice throwback to the 90s halcyon days. Even the lead character, Rufus, feels like Guybrush Threepwood (Monkey Island). Actually, he feels more like a mix of Futurama's Fry and Bender, if that makes any sense.
Of course, Deponia fans know what Rufus is really like: Herpes. Or, should I say, "a cooler version of herpes."
The trilogy goes on sale fairly often, so I'd say wait for a deal and scoop up all three. Happy gaming!

As somebody who owns and has played both Dead Rising 2 and Dead Rising 2: Off the Record, I will be comparing it to Dead Rising 2
Pros:
More Combo weapons
Taking Pictures
New Bosses
Sandbox Mode
Frank West's humour
Concept art gallery
Cons:
New Bosses: As much as I like the replacement for the Leon Bell fight (not saying who his replacement is), the new final boss is worse in all aspects. It feels like one big gimmick, and since all of the buildup for Dead Rising 2's twist boss is unchanged, the new boss just comes off as forced. Whereas the other new boss is just lame and annoying with bland music.
More bugs, ranging from helpful (infinite paddlesaw) to irritating (Weapons clipping through the floor) to even horrendous (getting stuck on things)
Online is worse
No graphics options
Removal of Terror is Reality (far from a dealbreaker imo)
Overall, I prefer Dead Rising 2, but Off the Record from pure content is a better game. I prefer 2's storytelling, though Off the Record does have it's moments of great narrative (working Brandon into the main story was cool). If you just want story and some fun get 2, but if you want more ways to kill zombies and more time to kill zombies(or just even if you enjoyed 2) I recommend Off the Record.

Still one of my favorite childhood games and series. Dead Rising 2 Off The Record takes a what if story viewpoint of number 2. For most of the game the storyline is pretty similiar to number 2 just with Frank of course like I mentioned along with small little changes. There is now a really enjoyable sandbox mode where you can run around Fortune City and do whatever you want along with killing all the pyschopaths as well. Everything else is still the same basically like co-op mode and what not but there are a few new psychopaths and survivors in Off The Record along with Uranus Zone the newest add on to Fortune City. Overall this game is a hell lot of fun especially with a friend me personally went through the storyline with my girlfriend who never played Dead Rising so it was quite the adventure. Personally I think it's worth the $20 hell I would pay even more for it but if you are a cheap type of person I'd wait till it goes on sale.

Wow!  What an elegant game!  Thoughtful (sometimes very difficult) puzzles and set in an intricately drawn world.  It's the best game-playing I've had in a long time.
On the plus side, the story is tantalizing.  As you find objects, clues, story lines, you just get pulled more and more into the game.  The story does not have much interaction with other characters but that, in a way, is preferable.  It lets you work at your own speed and explore the many facets of the scenes while you piece together the bits of knowledge and things you uncover.  You never know what item may be helpful so you really get a chance to thoroughly inspect the fantastically rendered artwork of the game.
For me, it had some negatives, too.  It's a dark story in a dark setting.  I'm not a person drawn to death/dying/dark/sad games as I don’t think death should be fodder for entertainment.  No, I’m not a squeaky-clean member of the pep squad who wants all sunshine and rainbows.  It’s just that when I play a game, I want to escape to a better or more interesting place than where I am now.  The game setting is definitely interesting so I did enjoy the playing of the game.  I just kept hoping that there would be some sort of retribution, vindication, or salvation for the character(s) I came to care for.
Overall, I am glad I played the game because it is beautifully rendered and thoughtful game play.  I may have to play something a bit lighter now to perk up my mood but I do recommend it for gamers who like to solve puzzling games and mysteries.

While definitely flawed and lacking in some areas, Goetia is a very competent point and click adventure with a terrific atmosphere and a well-designed puzzle difficulty curve. Full review here:

I was drawn to Goetia by its atmosphere, and it didn't take long for the game to make me want more. The puzzles are rather difficult, but in my opinion mostly fair. There were only a few that I felt were too vague or hard to solve, and a few extra that were more tedious than difficult, but they did nothing to hamper what is otherwise a great game - especially if the idea of racking your brain for lengths at a time to solve a puzzle appeals to you.
The writing in the game was also very captivating and always left me wanting to learn more as I progressed. So even if the difficulty isn't for you, I feel many people would still get a great experience if they used a walkthrough for the tougher puzzles and focused more on the story.
The game is definitely worth giving a try.

- Nothing is included in the base game. If you want to do anything, it will cost you. And at this point, it will cost you more than the game.

If you want a train simulator program, you have two better options:
1- Go to eBay and pick up a copy of Microsoft Train Simulator.
2- Try out Open Rails. (It's open source, so you can try it for free)
Both of those options have active communities which will give you hours of _free_ content.

The long wait is finally over. How is Tekken 7 for PC?
Pros:
+ runs, looks and plays fine
+ netcode is smooth even on longer distances
+ menus have an elegant and modern look
+ lots of characters
+ full remapping for both controller and keyboard
+ you can add pizza and pineapple to your character*
Cons:
- no tutorials
- no combo trials
- extremely long loading and syncing times before each match
- no rematch function makes loading even more tedious
- story mode is short and disappointing
- arcade is only 5 battles
- incoming game mode (Tekken Bowl) is DLC exclusive
- player lobby menus are a little weird and unintuitive
- some menu bugs and crashes
- you can add pizza and pineapple to your character*
There is an overall unpleasant feeling that the game has been rushed out to avoid delaying the release once again OR to milk people with some extra DLC. Offline content is kinda barebones and the game won't teach you anything about how to play it, so if you're gonna jump online without any knowledge about 3D fighters you'll probably get destroyed.
If however you like playing 3D fighters against other people and you're okay with having to search all the tech on the net this game is definitely for you. It's fun and relatively easy to pick up.
* BUT NOT AT THE SAME TIME
Runs flawlessly. It's a must buy people!!

I'm glad I bought this on PC as I've been able to get 1440p/60 working perfectly.
Specs:
i7 5930k 3.5ghz
980ti Hybrid
16gb 2100Mhz DDR4
Monitor: Predator XB217HU (for Gsync)
Controller: I've been using the Hori RAP4 Tekken 7 Edition fight stick with no issues in the Xbox 360 mode. I'm not sure why the Xbox One setting isn't working, but this could be something I haven't installed. Lovely fight stick if you're on the fence about it.
Tekken 7 on the PC is simply amazing, especially considering I want to review it on "day one" (6/2). I've had the game for 24 hours and to me, it's worth the hype this title has been getting. Online is the biggest draw for this game, but I've been very pleased with the offline (albeit short-lived) content. The story mode is quite short, at only a little over 2 hours for the main saga. The following character episodes are only one, maybe two fights. I am looking forward to the Season Pass content to bring some new game modes.
My biggest disappointment isn't really anything this game does, it's what it no longer does. The biggest change I don't like is the Arcade mode. I really liked the previous Tekken games where characters had several battles in Arcade, and a small plot arc, with a sub-boss mid run (e.g. Stage 4) and at the end, the final boss. Now, Arcade runthroughs are only a handful of battles, with the sub and final bosses at the end. I wish the older format was there, merging the Story - Character episodes into a longer, more substantial Arcade playthrough.
Despite this, Treasure Battle and Practice mode are LOTS of fun. Even if you're not big into online like I am, this title is still absolutely worth checking out, even if you only have a keyboard to use. Highly recommended.

For 15 bucks, it's not a bad game. It's very small though. The islands aren't nearly big enough for my liking. There are 44 islands broken up into individual stages which is fine but the islands are all too similar structurally. Towards the end of the game, they're broken up a bit more but still fairly solid. There are 3 islands dedicated to boss fights which is cool but the boss fights themselves weren't especially interesting. Just your normal boss battle fodder.
The combat gets repetitive after a while. I can only speak of the mage class as that is all I've played. They tried to break it up between a few different playstyles but ultimately, you're just mashing the same few buttons and/or holding left click until everything is dead. You get your main attack and then you can craft some spells but those are ultimately useless except the healing spell. You end up doing more damage with your wand/staff if you match it with the weakness of whatever you're fighting.
The gathering/crafting mechanics are solid though could use a bit of work still. An example would be after you've moved on from your first set or two of armor, you'll no longer need the materials used to craft those for the next sets however mobs all the way to the end of the game drop materials used to craft the lowest set of armors for no reason other than to fill your inventory. Each new set should require materials from previous sets to make the gardening mechanic actually worth while. Mining is great and works well here as you have to be mindful of the danger of falling off the island if you dig too deep. I would however, like to see the multitude of tools go away. Just have a pickaxe only and maybe the drill. There's no reason to have that many tools for such a small game.
The building aspect is something I didn't really get into because I just didn't really appreciate the small nature of the islands and the fact that I couldn't keep mobs away from me and my build. I tried to build but ultimately just stopped as I got annoyed that mobs would still spawn in and around my home. It's nice that it's there but there was no real benefit to having it in my opinion.
For what it costs, it's not a terrible game but it definitely has a ways to go before I'd ultimately recommend it to anyone.

tl:dr The gameplay is enjoyable when it actually works. However, this game is plagued with bugs and glitches which inhibit my ability to have fun playing.
The gameplay is really fun, and I enjoy the story. However, these successes are severely overshadowed by the bugs and glitches I have received while playing this game. Among them are the following:
- Started the game with a black screen. This is a common issue that is easily corrected by pressing Alt-Enter. However, a common issue such as this taking place before the game even begins is wholly inexcusable. It would appear that little-to-no playtesting was conducted.
- Throughout the game, I would encounter a bug during which I would be unable to move. I could spin around and perform any other action, however my character would remain fixed in place. Sometimes, the game would resolve itself after 10-30s of me hammering away at my keyboard in frustration. Other times, I would have to completely restart the game.
- I would also encounter bugs during in-game cutscenes. Most freqently, everything would stop in a cutscene. The game wouldn't freeze, but rather all characters in the scene would have some idle animation for 30-60s during which the scene would not continue. Additionally, NPCs would sometimes teleport to another part of the screen during the scenes, and they would remain there even after I resumed control of my character.
- Loading times are horrendous, even when installed on an SSD.

Deponia is a great point-and-click adventure game with really well-implemented puzzle mechanics. Not to mention that the following results of your actions in the game are, more often than not, hilarious as hell (or at least I find wreaking havoc, destroying things and ruining people's day pretty damn comedic). But if not for the puzzles or comedy, I at least found the story very compelling (made me sat through the whole game in one day).
Definitely would recommend this game, or even the whole trilogy, to anyone who wants a giggle or those who simply enjoy good puzzles and good story.

Now, Part 2 of the revisions. To recap after the 1st stalker game revision....this is based on the vanilla experience.
Ah, the prequel. Also, the game that the stalker community thought was forgettable. Me? I personally LOVED this game. Sure, it's missing a few things....namely hunger, and an all-around creepiness with some of the environments. But to counter, this game introduced some features that proved to be worthwhile; for instance, the weapon and armor upgrades and repair. Do the weapons and armor still degrade? Yes, but now you can enhance them with more armor plates, flex the durability, and even add protection against anomalies. It's needed because if you ask me, this is the hardest of the 3 stalker games. Just as is with the first game, once you get to a certain point, there's no turning back. So, be prepared for ANY situation again.
The story revolves around Scar, a mercenary that inserts himself into the faction war. Various factions are battling for territory in the zone in a race to reach the center. When a group of stalkers reaches the center, the zone changes and becomes more unstable, making the territory more valuable.
Gameplay is relatively the same with a few changes. First, the artifacts aren't just there for the taking this time. You need a detector to find the artifacts, which involves getting into the thick of the anomaly. The weakest detectors won't spot the best artifacts, so you need a top notch one to make up for the weaker ones shortcomings. This game also manages to feel less like a sandbox, only because as you progress through the story you are able to uncover more of the map. In other words, you're actually blocked from progressing far into the zone until you progress through the story. Once you get so far, then it's open for you to explore all over. Numerous players weren't fond of this because of the open nature of the 1st game, but i think it worked well here because it made for better pacing. You couldn't get the best weapon in the game very early, giving you a major advantage. Even the armor suits were paced better, as an exoskeleton suit COULD be given to you about half way through, but required some work on your part in joining the faction wars for Duty or Freedom. Better pacing equals more fun if you ask me. The stalker way is the hard way.
Artifacts were not so abundant here, as each map in the zone contained a few anomalies, which hold artifacts. With less artifacts comes less money, which means upgrading or repairing was a little tricky because you had to draw the line between keeping an artifact or trading it in for a valuable upgrade. Less money also equals more fun. Stalker games are supposed to be challenging and this adds another layer of challenge. Of course, once you get so far and have your armor or weapons upgraded, then you can save some money for future use.
The AI has some improvements, but still has its pros and cons. The faction wars can be a bit buggy sometimes, as the AI isn't entirely supportive. You may find yourself doing alot of the work, and while this game is difficult as it is, i personally don't mind doing most of the work. It's a shooter.....you shoot things. The more the merrier.
Most of the maps are reused from Shadow of Chernobyl, with the addition of a few new ones. The swamps and red forest are the highlights, creating a fresh change from gloomy landscapes to lush vegetation. Also, some of the reoccurring maps have been slightly altered to appear more lifelike. Remember, this takes place before the events of SoC.
All in all, i think this game gets a bad rap. What it is missing from other stalker games it makes up for by introducing some iconic stalker features, like the upgrades. Again, mods are a-plenty here, but do yourself a favor and play vanilla first...on MASTER difficulty. It's brutal again, and the difficulty spike is worse this time around in the end, so be even more prepared. While it still may not be every stalker fan's cup of tea, it's still part of the stalker lore that every fan should check out. It's my personal favorite of the 3 games, mostly for the reasons of the pacing and balance. Difficult as hell, borderline rage-inducing in the end, but still worthwhile. Crowning achievement completing this on master. Good luck stalker.

Personally I do enjoy this game and while this game certainly does have its ups and downs, I am not here to praise or criticize this game. I am here to offer a phenomenal 4 Cheese Ravioli recipe!
Here are the ingredients you will need!
Ravioli Dough: 2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 pinch salt, 1 teaspoon olive oil, 2 eggs, 1 1/2 tablespoons water.
Ravioli Filling: 1 (8 ounce) container ricotta cheese, 1 (4 ounce) package cream cheese, softened, 1/2 cup shredded mozzarella cheese, 1/2 cup provolone cheese, shredded, 1 egg, 1 1/2 teaspoons dried parsley.
Pesto-Alfredo Cream Sauce: 2 tablespoons olive oil, 2 cloves garlic, crushed, 3 tablespoons prepared basil pesto sauce, 2 cups heavy cream, 1/4 cup grated Parmesan cheese, 1 (24 ounce) jar marinara sauce.
1. Mound the flour and salt together on a work surface and form a well. Beat the teaspoon of olive oil, 2 eggs, and water in a bowl. Pour half the egg mixture into the well. Begin mixing the egg with the flour with one hand; use your other hand to keep the flour mound steady. Add the remaining egg mixture and knead to form a dough.
2. Knead the dough until smooth, 8 to 10 minutes; add more flour if the dough is too sticky. Form the dough into a ball and wrap tightly with plastic. Refrigerate for 1 hour.
3. While the dough is resting, prepare the ravioli filling. Combine the ricotta cheese, cream cheese, mozzarella cheese, provolone cheese, egg, and parsley and mix well. Set the filling aside.
4. Heat 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a skillet over medium heat. Add the crushed garlic and pesto sauce and cook for one minute. Pour in the heavy cream, raise the heat to high, and bring the sauce to a boil. Reduce the heat and simmer for 5 minutes. Add the Parmesan cheese and stir until the cheese melts. Remove the pan from the heat and keep warm.
5. Meanwhile, in a separate saucepan, warm the marinara sauce over medium-low heat.
6. Preheat an oven to 375 degrees F (190 degrees C). Beat the egg with the tablespoon of water to make the egg wash.
7. Roll out the pasta dough into thin sheets no thicker than a nickel. To assemble the ravioli, brush the egg wash over a sheet of pasta. Drop the filling mixture on the dough by teaspoonfuls about one inch apart. Cover the filling with the top sheet of pasta, pressing out the air from around each portion of filling. Press firmly around the filling to seal. Cut into individual ravioli with a knife or pizza cutter. Seal the edges.
8. Fill a large pot with lightly salted water and bring to a rolling boil over high heat. Stir in the ravioli, and return to a boil. Cook uncovered, stirring occasionally, until the ravioli float to the top and the filling is hot, 4 to 8 minutes. Drain well.
9. Grease a baking sheet. Place the cooked ravioli on the sheet pan and bake in the preheated oven until brown, about 4 minutes.
10. To serve the ravioli, divide them among four warmed serving bowls. Drizzle the marinara sauce over the ravioli and then top with the cream sauce.

This is a really fun game. Play this is you are angry or mad at someone and just pretend that Bob is that person. I may not suggest this for stress relief though. Because it really is stressful to save Bob's Life. Soundtrack is awesome and controls are hard, but it is intended to be that way.
Here's my gameplay of it.

Tons of letters and words below. If you enjoy long reviews with some comedic relief, read on. If you don't like long reviews but want a laugh somewhere..still read on. If you just wanna dislike my review because you hate reading, I could care less.
Let's just take a moment to remember all the fallen Bobs whom have died for Nigel to be a true doctor. Finished? Okay good, because right now we're going to search Bob's brain for several reasons why this is a good game.
Strap into your scrubs, trainee, because you're about to take over. Our best doctor has been taken out in a tragic gunfight and so you're in his shoes. Fix this patient, Nigel Burke, you're our only hope. I present to you, Surgeon Simulator.
Now last time I checked this is the only Surgeon Simulator out there game wise on Steam, but don't let the name fool you. Not only do you have to carefully remove a certain patient's body parts in several areas and in several different locations, but you have to control a one-handed doctor whom seems to have no idea where the sharp part of the tomahawk the hosptial has lent you into the patient's skull. Nigel seems to have this inability to control his fingers without your assistance.
As many of the reviews say, this is another QWOP game, but that's where they are wrong. This game is easier because if you lodge your hand in between the patients rib cage, you don't die from having somehow recieved a brain tumor. You have to use certain keys like QWOP, but you're in much more control than it's believed to. Some may find this easier than others of course, as this game does take a bit of mastery to actually complete. For example you may be extracting Bob's heart and you won't know where to cut the arteries connecting to it, seeing as you can't rip it out, so you swing your mighty scalpel until you cut whatever and pop goes the heart but at a cost of a ton of the patient's blood.
The game is rather frustrating when you can't find the things you are looking for, but that just makes it all the more fun. Can't find your bonesaw anywhere? No problem, let's use the electric pizza cutter to cut open his ribcage and slice through the veins. No hammer to whallop the skull? Alright, let's use the axe and hopefully split his skull while hoping to cut the brain stem.
There are a ton of fun things this game has to offer and many different ways to improvise your surgeries. It kills time while giving you a laugh as your buddy controlling the mouse throws the spare heart against the wall like a wet paper towel.
9.7/10. Watch Rage Quit on it, it's what will want you playing with friends.

I am really enjoying this game.  I have over 10 hours playing.  At first I wasn't sure if I was going to like the POV because it was a sidescroller and I had just finished playing a 360 degree view game.  But I got used to it quickly and really like how the character floats and zips through rooms and countryside.
The puzzles are great and none to easy.  At times I found myself quitting the game so I had time to think through the clues and figure out my next steps.  At first, you are limited to a few locations, but after you solve some puzzles more locales open up.  I like that as I become claustrophobic when games have just a few locations to explore.  The character has no inventory but can use items by possessing them.  This works because the items are normally used fairly close to their original location.
There is a journal that keeps track of clues and a codex that records all the various texts you encounter.  Both are useful to remind you or give the information t to solve a puzzle.  It takes a while (or for me it did), to figure out the family relationship of the various characters that have left notes and clues.  In fact, I think I am still figuring that out because I am hung up on one puzzle that uses that information.
I've run across two problems of a technical nature.  One is resolved and that is related to getting one of my possessed items into a place I couldn't get it out of.  I found some tech help and got that fixed.  The other is that I have some background problems in that the scenes are broken up and I have a black tunnel across the screen.  Frankly, I didn't realize it was a problem as I thought it was an artistic device for certain locations to show I was in a different realm.  So far it hasn't been a problem and it is not at all locations. EDIT:  Background problems resolved.  Had to reload some files and it cleared up the issue.  Yay!
I highly recommend this game to anyone that wants to think and work out answers to puzzles.  If you want HOGs or easy linear games, this is not the game for you.  If you want to use reason, logic and think about a game even when you are not playing....this is the game for you.  Go get it!

An intelligent combination of exploration and point and click adventure. The strong atmopshere of all locations is enhanced by the stunning detail of the beautiful artstyle.

I loved this game. I'm a sucker for 'old style' point and click having started gaming with the Myst series, and this was amoung the best I've tried since then. I'm an impatient gamer generally, but found myself more than happy to take my time with this, absorbing the atmosphere, exploring the beautifully drawn settings and solving the many puzzles which ranged from fairly straightforward to  fienndishly tricky. In general, the puzzles are very satisfying to solve, although not always obvious - it often didn't dawn on me until later in the game that things were part of the puzzles - but that's not necessarily a bad thing. It certainly makes you think (and I admit to resorting to the walkthrough towards the end).
I had no problems running the game; no bugs while I used it.
There is a lot to read, and notes will likely help although most everything you need is stored for you in your journal and in the codex, and there's no voice acting (which might be considered a plus compared with some games) but that fits with the story and feel of the game.
So - if you like point and click, relish a challenge, and don't mind putting in the effort, this is an absorbing, atmospheric and satisfying way to spend a fair few hours. I'm only sorry the journey is over!

Tekken 7 on the PC is simply amazing, especially considering I want to review it on "day one" (6/2). I've had the game for 24 hours and to me, it's worth the hype this title has been getting. Online is the biggest draw for this game, but I've been very pleased with the offline (albeit short-lived) content. The story mode is quite short, at only a little over 2 hours for the main saga. The following character episodes are only one, maybe two fights. I am looking forward to the Season Pass content to bring some new game modes.
My biggest disappointment isn't really anything this game does, it's what it no longer does. The biggest change I don't like is the Arcade mode. I really liked the previous Tekken games where characters had several battles in Arcade, and a small plot arc, with a sub-boss mid run (e.g. Stage 4) and at the end, the final boss. Now, Arcade runthroughs are only a handful of battles, with the sub and final bosses at the end. I wish the older format was there, merging the Story - Character episodes into a longer, more substantial Arcade playthrough.
Despite this, Treasure Battle and Practice mode are LOTS of fun. Even if you're not big into online like I am, this title is still absolutely worth checking out, even if you only have a keyboard to use. Highly recommended.

-About the Gameplay itself-
It's Tekken. To be honest, if you've been following the series for some time like I do, not much has changed. Tekken is not about crazy shifts from one game to the other. It's more like small increments and changes. The game does look much better than Tag 2 and also way more accessible. For beginners, it's not as hard to escape ground mixups anymore and some new characters like Katarina are very easy to pick up and play but also efficient and flashy.
It still has a steep learning curve and not much in the way of a tutorial, but I'll get to that later.
Rage arts (this game's "Supers") are a much better "comeback mechanic" than previous ones like rage damage increase from T6, because you actually have to use the mechanic well in order to earn your comeback instead of just playing normally and causing more damage for free just because you're about to lose.
There's a "Slow Motion" mechanic that kicks off in the middle of battle dynamically when one of the players is about to lose, both players attack at the same time and it's not clear which one will land the hit. It's very hype inducing.
There's also a cool quality of life mechanic that lets you pick a side when playing online and guarantee that you'll start the match on your preferred side (Left or Right). If the opponent picks the same side, the game is shown mirrored to him on his screen, so both players get to play on their preferred side.
All in all, the game looks very balanced and fun to play. Lots of different characters, but no clones whatsover, tons of unique moves to each of them, good combo potential without being too overwhelming, and some characters have very unique traits that are completely new to the series like Akuma and Eliza with their projectiles and meters.
-About the Game Modes-
For offline play, you get Story Mode, Arcade Mode, Practice, Treasure Battle and Versus.
For online, there are Ranked Matches, Player Matches and a Tournament Mode. You can also practice your combos against a dummy while you wait for the game to find a match.
There's also a Gallery and Character Customization.
Story Mode is where most of the work seems to have been spent when it comes to offline play. It's very cinematic, and it has lots of memorable moments. It also teaches you some of the game fundamentals, making up for the lack of a proper Tutorial mode. It's pretty basic in that regard though.
Practice has a loooot of options. It's probably a much better tool for learning than Story Mode's tutorial sections. Going over your main character's entire movelist and sample combos, trying to execute everything perfectly in Practice mode will already help you a lot as a player. After that you can pick other characters and test their movelists against you, trying to learn what you can punish or not.
Customization is very similar to Tekken Tag Tournament 2. Lots of options when compared to most fighting games, but it's actually a step down from previous entries in the series.
Treasure Mode is a fun little endless grind mode where you unlock customization items and gain in-game currency, which you can use to further unlock customization items. For the fashion inclined players, that's where you're gonna spend most of your time. You actually rank up your offline rank while doing so, which is a nice bonus.
Online seems decent enough. You can rematch against the same player once. Not a lot of disconnects. Had some instances where the game would stop to sync here and there, but it was probably my internet. Not a lot of lag during the match itself, outside of the syncing issues I had.
-About the PC Release Specific Stuff-
Perfect PC version. Not one of the common problems that multiplatform and japanese games usually have are present in here. The game is light, well-optimized and very beautiful. Lots of graphic settings and input options. Controllers are recognized automatically (both DirectInput and XInput). You can use Xbox 360 controllers, PS3, PS4, Arcade Sticks and generic controllers as well out of the box. Keyboard inputs also work really well, and it's actually pretty easy to play on keyboard as most stick motions are actually pretty easy to execute and the game has lots of attacks that use multiple buttons simultaneously, which is actually a bit easier to do on Keyboard and/or Arcade Stick than on Gamepad.
When it comes to the Graphics Settings, I highly recommend setting post-processing to either "low" or "medium". Higher settings add a Film Grain effect and Chromatic Aberration, which makes the characters veeeery blurry during the fights. It's a matter of taste really, but it kills the definition you get from higher resolution. Maybe it hides some imperfections on lower resolution, not sure how intense it is performance-wise. Just be sure to test both below medium and above medium and see which one you like the most.
-Conclusion-
It's an excellent fighting game, from a excellent franchise, finally making its way to PC. And it did so brilliantly since day one without major problems. It's the best version of the game when compared to the console versions, and with the added focus (albeit slight) in acessibility, it's the best possible entry point for someone who never played Tekken and wants to start now. Highly recommend it.

+++ It definitely feels like a good old Tekken, but this time with some great graphics, stable framerate, direct controls and a lot of combo possibilities. +++
The PC port is actually very good. You have a lot of graphic options to play with and if those options are not enough you can still go into the  config.ini an change some of the effects to your desire. Imagine getting rid on your PS4 of the annoying blurr effects, some film grain, etc. But you can't therefore the PC version is the first pick. Also when you fancy stable framerates.
It plays very well out of the box with the XBOX controller or with your favourite arcade stick. Gameplay is fast. That's what I like most about Tekken. No a too longpause between combos, or between matches. You have the feeling the moment you push a button you are actually going for something. Sure it might be difficult in the beginning to remember all those button configurations, but you get into it after a short time and you will win your first online matches.
Online multiplayer works pretty good out of the box. You can even change the quality of the connection in ordre to have more choice of possible challengers. I mean how cool is this to finally an out of the box option like this without having to change some config files, etc. in this regard. Excellent job on this.
Since I played every major fight game in the last 2 - 3 years, I have to say I am most convinced by Tekken 7. I like MKX, but Tekken 7 is doing the better job when it comes to a functional package. I always liked Street Fighter V, but Tekken 7 is just faster, more direct and the combo system not limited to a handful of special moves. Yeah and Killer Instinct, let's say Killer Instinct has always been my favourite game since SNES times and good old Ultra 64 platines in the Arcade, what a shame they made some free2play MS game out of it. What I need now is Soul Calibour. Since this is my alltime-favourite from Dreamcast times.
Long story short. I recommend Tekken 7. The game had a great start and I see it will build definitely a great fanbase on PC which won't bleed out so fast.

By no means is The Fractured But Whole a perfect game, but I believe it took what Stick of Truth did wrong and changed it. There are many things wrong with the game, but almost all of them are the fault of Ubisoft.
There are many things to like about the game. Stick of Truth is included free with purchase for those who never played it. It was a smart move to include it as some things in The Fractured But Whole rely heavily on your knowledge of Stick of Truth. Another thing to really like is the enhanced and improved combat system. There's far more pressue now, as instead of just attacking, you have to plan out every move to make sure it won't be your last. And finally, I think the most important change is the story. This game relies heavily on it's story, where as Stick of Truth was more focused on gameplay. The story gets WAY heavier in The Fractured But Whole, which I welcome with open arms.
However, with positives there are negatives. It seems The Fractured But Whole has the disease known as Ubisoft. This means that the game suffers from big bugs and glitches from time to time. During my playthrough, I had 3 crashes, (one of which from a standard enemy attack) a few visual bugs and audio cutting out from time to time. The bugs in this game are on a whole other level than Stick of Truth's cutscene glitches, and it just makes me feel like the game wasn't tested properly. Perhaps a frw more months in development would pump all these issues out. And of course, the biggest issue of all... U-Play and DRM. I don't understand Ubisoft to be honest. I paid for the game through Steam, I should be allowed to play it JUST THROUGH STEAM like Stick of Truth. But alas, Ubisoft decided to shove U-Play down everyone's throats and I'm not a fan of it. I don't have an issue with U-Play itself, but the intergration did not need to be there. Same with DRM, except I do have an issue with that.
HOWEVER, if you can look past all of the bugs, glitches and terrible Ubisoft choices, you're looking at one of the best games this year. It's humor is amazing and keeps very inline with South Park, the characters are as loveable as ever, the missions are fun and creative and it's just a great experience overall. I would recommend this game for any fan of South Park and anyone who enjoyed Stick of Truth!
P.S: Play this game with a controller for the love of god. The keyboard controls are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

In the end i want to say i loved this game a lot. It has unusual love story. I recommend this game, even to those who are not fan of such games. But you should try something different, as different is sometimes cool!

Note: This review is concerning the singleplayer component of the game.
Grand Theft Auto V is a barely interactive linear action game. It is not a sandbox game by any stretch of the word, and nor is it a good game in general. Yes, it is humorous, the graphics are amazing, the production values are high, and the world is nice, but all of that does not equal an engaging experience. Other than the dialogue and the scenery, I couldn't find much else to enjoy in this game.
I'll get the story out of the way first. While the campaign does have its moments—via humor and social commentary—overall, it fails to tell an interesting story, or at least a sensical one. It's ridiculous and over the top. With the exception of Michael, the protagonists are badly written: they lack motivation and aren't relatable. The trio lacks chemistry with one another, and you often wonder why they are doing the things they're doing. It also doesn't feel like they are in control of their story but rather just pawns in it.
The core gameplay in GTA V comes down to driving, shooting, and flying. Coming from GTA IV, you'll notice that all of the above was dumbed down to a laughable level. Driving a car and riding a bike now require way less skill and caution: cars take tons of damage before their performance suffers to any significant degree and, with both cars and bikes, you'll rarely lose control at any speed. Likewise, shooting is now also extremely forgiving and, again, requires almost no skill mostly due to the lack of recoil and recovering health but also thanks to the huge arsenal of weapons you're able to carry and the practically infinite ammo capacity. To make matters worse, all three player characters have superpowers which turn the game's mechanics into an even bigger joke.
GTA V's campaign delivers gameplay through extremely linear missions. The vast majority of them consist of three main elements: driving from A to B, cover-based shooting, and chasing or escaping enemies in various vehicles. Of course, none of the missions challenge you or require you to use your brain. You have a built-in step-by-step walkthrough text instructing you at all times, characters yelling instructions at you every 10 seconds (even if they're your subordinates story-wise), waypoints and GPS routes, and finally, a mothеr♥♥♥♥♥ing skip button. Furthermore, any deviation from the tightly-arranged path results in a "mission failed" screen. The same screen appears if you happen to die, and of course, it respawns you pretty much where you died. Not only does the game not punish you for failure, it actually heals you to full health and offers to skip the section.
To summarize, GTA V fails at fulfilling the basic requirements I have for a game. It expects nothing from the player, so the player won't feel like he achieved anything. It doesn't demand tactics, good driving, navigational skills, or any sort of situational awareness. The text at the bottom just blatantly tells you what to do. You can watch TV and eat popcorn while playing this game on mute and still finish it. You cannot defend it by saying it's a "sandbox." It is absolutely not a sandbox; blowing up cars and playing horde mode with the police is not a sandbox. And to me, It's a great shame that they utterly failed to put the pretty world they have created to good use.
