Note: This review is concerning the singleplayer component of the game.
Grand Theft Auto V is a barely interactive linear action game. It is not a sandbox game by any stretch of the word, and nor is it a good game in general. Yes, it is humorous, the graphics are amazing, the production values are high, and the world is nice, but all of that does not equal an engaging experience. Other than the dialogue and the scenery, I couldn't find much else to enjoy in this game.
I'll get the story out of the way first. While the campaign does have its moments—via humor and social commentary—overall, it fails to tell an interesting story, or at least a sensical one. It's ridiculous and over the top. With the exception of Michael, the protagonists are badly written: they lack motivation and aren't relatable. The trio lacks chemistry with one another, and you often wonder why they are doing the things they're doing. It also doesn't feel like they are in control of their story but rather just pawns in it.
The core gameplay in GTA V comes down to driving, shooting, and flying. Coming from GTA IV, you'll notice that all of the above was dumbed down to a laughable level. Driving a car and riding a bike now require way less skill and caution: cars take tons of damage before their performance suffers to any significant degree and, with both cars and bikes, you'll rarely lose control at any speed. Likewise, shooting is now also extremely forgiving and, again, requires almost no skill mostly due to the lack of recoil and recovering health but also thanks to the huge arsenal of weapons you're able to carry and the practically infinite ammo capacity. To make matters worse, all three player characters have superpowers which turn the game's mechanics into an even bigger joke.
GTA V's campaign delivers gameplay through extremely linear missions. The vast majority of them consist of three main elements: driving from A to B, cover-based shooting, and chasing or escaping enemies in various vehicles. Of course, none of the missions challenge you or require you to use your brain. You have a built-in step-by-step walkthrough text instructing you at all times, characters yelling instructions at you every 10 seconds (even if they're your subordinates story-wise), waypoints and GPS routes, and finally, a mothеr♥♥♥♥♥ing skip button. Furthermore, any deviation from the tightly-arranged path results in a "mission failed" screen. The same screen appears if you happen to die, and of course, it respawns you pretty much where you died. Not only does the game not punish you for failure, it actually heals you to full health and offers to skip the section.
To summarize, GTA V fails at fulfilling the basic requirements I have for a game. It expects nothing from the player, so the player won't feel like he achieved anything. It doesn't demand tactics, good driving, navigational skills, or any sort of situational awareness. The text at the bottom just blatantly tells you what to do. You can watch TV and eat popcorn while playing this game on mute and still finish it. You cannot defend it by saying it's a "sandbox." It is absolutely not a sandbox; blowing up cars and playing horde mode with the police is not a sandbox. And to me, It's a great shame that they utterly failed to put the pretty world they have created to good use.

Goetia is the first offering from Sushee Games, a French indie studio. It draws you in from the first moment as the ghost of Abigail Blackwood awakens to confusion.
The music and mystery keep you pulled in as you find puzzles, and while I'm only about an hour and a half in, the puzzles seem to be fairly well designed.
While puzzle and point-and-click games aren't everyone's cup of tea I do suggest giving it a shot if you like mysteries. I don't think you'll be disappointed at all.

I'm really enjoying Goetia. There is a lot of reading involved and there are some strange turns of phrase occasionally. This might be due to the developer being French, perhaps it was translated into English. Some scenes contain many visual elements you can get a description of and I have seen instances where the order you view them in might have flowed more smoothly. So far the story is interesting, thought a bit terrifying. There is some question as to what happened to the children of your older sister and I am certain that will be central to the final story.
At the beginning you are somewhat restricted in which parts of the manor you can visit, but it opens up in the first two hours of play. I like the way additional parts of the manor have to be unlocked.
The game runs well. I can maintain 1080p at 60fps. The background audio gets a bit monotonous. In the end it is probably better to have the ambient sounds than music, but the game tells you at the beginning that sound is important. So far there has been only a single sound which was important to hear, and your character responds to it in text anyway.
I can recommend the game if you enjoy point-and-click adventures and are not put off my reading a lot of text. For those who prefer full voice acting I suggest you look elsewhere, or watch someone else play it.

Before playing this game, I happened upon a Let's Play video that one of my favorite Youtubers had done. Granted, he was mostly just derping around to check out the game rather than dig into the meat of it, but it prompted me to buy it.
I was in love with the art, music, and overall concept before the game even truly started. What an amazing world these lovely developers created!
That being said, the gameplay is rather straightforward - You play as the ghost of a young woman named 'Abigail'. The setting is around the late 1930's to early 1940's. You spend your time in the game doing puzzles to piece together an understanding of what has happened to young Abigail, and her family. As a ghost, you can 'float' through walls, and posess objects to further your quest.
I will say one last thing before you decide to buy this game - make sure you pay the @#$% attention. Some of these puzzles are not for the feint of heart and require reading and understanding the notes and things that you find in the game. Abigail will also give you clues here and there in her journal, and hints as she 'speaks' to you about an area. Read everything, touch everything - more than once if you have to. One blessing in-game - all areas have their own puzzles. So you're not forced to carry objects from one area to another. One room to another, sure, but not to other areas.
Everything leads back to the Blackwood manor...Will you discover the secrets that it holds?
10/10 would pull my hair out doing puzzles again.

He's covered wars y'know? Frank West is back, and he is fatter and more out of shape than ever! This game takes the prestine gameplay of Dead Rising 2, and spices it up with a bit of Frank West. In this game, you play in an alternate "what if" version of Dead Rising 2, where you play as everyones favorite fighting (ex-)photojournalist Frank West. It depicts Frank after the Willimette mall incident, having become overweight and bankrupt, due to the overexposure to the limelight. He is participating in the Terror Is Reality zombie killing game show, in order to net some cash, and get himself back on the map. Unfortunately, there seems to be trouble brewing in the bowels of Fortune City, as Frank finds himself in the middle of another Zombie outbreak. It is up to you, as Frank, to find the truth, and save as many survivors as you can. The gameplay is identical to that of Dead Rising 2, with a few improvements to animation, as well as more missions, bosses, and ways to kill. There is nothing but praise I can give to this game, try it out for yourself, you won't regret it. Dead Rising 2: Off The Record gets an 8.5/10. This game lost a point due to a few side missions that glitched for me, making them unplayable.

This was the question I asked myself and researched about before purchasing this title.  In short, Off The Record is essentially the original Dead Rising 2 with more content, so if you've yet to play the original Dead Rising 2, or simply wish to enjoy the somewhat altered storyline and additional features, choose this title over the original.

I might be a little bias on this title as I absolutely love George A. I have nearly 500 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews - Game 11
Arma - Gold Edition
Purchase Date: 1/16/2014
I ended up getting a bunch of the Arma games as part of a Humble Bundle.  I only really heard of Arma because of the DayZ mod that everyone talks about.   Normally this isn't the kind of game I would be looking to buy, but I appreciate that the Humble Bundle gives me a good excuse to try out some games I'd otherwise ignore.
The first thing I did when I started the game was go right to the graphics options.  Since Arma has been out for awhile, it looks a little dated, but this also means that I can crank up all of the graphics options to make it look as nice as possible.  Arma gives plenty of options to tweak, much as you'd expect from a modern game.
Since I had no idea how to play or what I was doing, I made sure to start with the tutorial.  Arma provides a series of tutorial missions, starting with a basic obstacle course to run through.  It gave me the option to do a run through first without being timed, which I'm glad it did as it took me a little bit to get used to the controls.
I had an issue with the default mouse controls.  By default Arma is configured to have this huge 'floating' area on the mouse.  This floating area defines how far you can move the mouse before the camera moves.  So it's kind of a sensitivity thing, but for me it just made the controls feel super laggy.  Luckily the options menu let me turn this all the way down.  I can't imagine why someone would want it configured otherwise.
Once I had the controls nailed down, I finished the obstacle course, with the drill sargeant barking at me as I went.  Next up was a shooting range, so I could have a chance to get used to all of the weapons.  The game offers various lanes, each with a different weapon.  The game gives certifications on each weapon, based on how well you can shoot.  First I trailed with a rifle, then a sub-machine gun, followed by a pistol.  I ended up doing pretty well with these, but then I bombed with the grenade launcher.  The last lane contained a sniper rifle.
The next tutorial introduced me to my squad, and consisted of me giving my squad various commands.  I found this part of the tutorial rather cumbersome.  I get that this is a simulator so it's supposed to be in-depth and give a lot of options.  But it also seems a lot harder to get things done than it should be.  I hit a key to toggle my whole squad, but it wasn't really obvious to me when all of my squad was selected.  I wish it had been a little easier to know which squad members were selected and which ones weren't.
The squad menu has an impressive list of options.  I can do things like order my squad into a particular formation, or move the squad members to a waypoint.  This took some getting used to; in particular I had a hard time getting my squad to enter a vehicle I had targetted.
I should mention that the game is fully voiced, which sounds nice, but I wasn't the biggest fan of the implementation.  Some of the voicing was fine, like in the earlier tutorial where the drill sargeant was bossing me around.  But I didn't like the squad voicing as much.  A lot of the dialog is stitched together dynamically, where words were recorded one at a time, and then spliced into sentences.  When played back like this, it just doesn't sound natural, and it's kind of jarring.
Once I got the basics of squad combat down, the next tutorial put me in a tank.  This ended up being pretty fun as I rode around and fired at various targets with different weapons on the tank.  Again I struggled with the controls, and remembering which key is supposed to switch weapons.  I liked how the game simulates the different positions in the tank, as I went between driving, gunning, and commanding.
I mentioned above about the dialog being stitched together.  This got really old when I was trying to command the tank to move back to the base.  I had a hard time telling which direction the tank was facing, so I kept hitting keys to rotate the tank.  Every time I hit a key, the game would bark that command to the driver.  I kept hitting keys in fairly rapid succession, and the game kept barking commands like I was directing some kind of demented Simon Says game.
Once I parked the tank, the final tutorial mission I took part in was flying a helicopter.  The mission starts out with the helicopter pilot telling me to get in and fly, and he'll join me as a co-pilot.  So I hopped in the helicopter and started up the engine, and the game proceeds to explain the controls.  So I take the helicopter up slowly as directed.  Then the co-pilot starts yelling at me because I left him behind.  Oops!  It was kind of hilarious because on one hand, the game is happily telling me how to fly, and on the other hand my co-pilot is screaming at me from the ground.  I tried to land the helicopter so I could let the co-pilot board but instead I ended up killing the co-pilot with the helicopter blades approximately .5 seconds before I crashed the helicopter and died.
I ended up restarting the mission so I could get a proper start.  This time with my co-pilot in the copter, I took off and started flying around.  It didn't take me long to realize that I am pretty terrible at this.  I was doing okay until the game wanted me to hover, which I couldn't do at all.  I finally ended up skipping that step in the mission, and next the game had me go to pick up some soliders.  Instead I ended up crashing the helicopter.  Predictably I died.
At this point I was over my hour, and I didn't get to check out the final tutorial, which would have taken the helicopter into combat.  It's probably just as well I didn't try that one, given my meager piloting skills.
So I'm left deciding whether to give this game a thumbs up or thumbs down.  I'm going to be reviewing Arma II next, so I'll be curious to see how it differs from this one. I'm really pretty torn here because this was really a mixed bag of things I liked and things I didn't.  I can see where this game would be fun, and I know I barely scratched the surface of what the game has to offer.  But I also have to be honest with myself and realize that I don't see myself bothering to come back to this game.  So based on this I'm going to have to go with the thumbs down.

Everyone, hail the new Diablo 2!!
Tochlight 2 is the sequel to (You guessed it), Torchlight. It takes everything the first game did wrong (Or not quite good), starting for the lack of Multiplayer, and fixes it, improves it, and makes it right. For torchlight 2 the developers did really listen to the communitty and did their homework: Gameplay, mechanics, upgrades... everything is fixed, polished and balanced. The multiplayer, although with some connection problems here and there, tends to work great and is really well implemented into the game (both loot wise, as each player gets its own loot so no more fighting over the coins and mod wise, as you can easily connect with other players who has the same mods) and, as expected, not only really fun to play, but the main reason to get the game.
But, this is it. It's a polished but already known formula. If you are a veteran in this kind of games, you will feel at home in the world of Torchlight 2, but maybe you will feel it is "too home": There's nothing you have already seen in other diablo like game, nothing original in its approach, even each of the acts style is similar to the Diablo 2 acts (desert-jungle-hell/volcano anyone?): It's a genuine jewel, but a jewel we all have seen in a lot of places before.
A huge extra point is the communitty behind this game. Mods like synergies have added TONS of new places to kill monsters, TONS of new monsters to be killed, TONS of new weapons to kill with and TONS of armor to avoid getting killed. Although the vanilla game is short in its main campaing (remember: the fun is in the second time you finish the game), with the mod support the Torchlight world expands beyond any other Diablo like game.
Torchlight 2 is a great game many of us have already played. If you are looking for the next step in the Diablo formula, you are not looking in the right place (maybe the workshop has some hints already), but if you are looking for a step in an already stablished place, a consistent, fun and balanced Diablo clone, Torchlight is the best option you have right now.

By no means is The Fractured But Whole a perfect game, but I believe it took what Stick of Truth did wrong and changed it. There are many things wrong with the game, but almost all of them are the fault of Ubisoft.
There are many things to like about the game. Stick of Truth is included free with purchase for those who never played it. It was a smart move to include it as some things in The Fractured But Whole rely heavily on your knowledge of Stick of Truth. Another thing to really like is the enhanced and improved combat system. There's far more pressue now, as instead of just attacking, you have to plan out every move to make sure it won't be your last. And finally, I think the most important change is the story. This game relies heavily on it's story, where as Stick of Truth was more focused on gameplay. The story gets WAY heavier in The Fractured But Whole, which I welcome with open arms.
However, with positives there are negatives. It seems The Fractured But Whole has the disease known as Ubisoft. This means that the game suffers from big bugs and glitches from time to time. During my playthrough, I had 3 crashes, (one of which from a standard enemy attack) a few visual bugs and audio cutting out from time to time. The bugs in this game are on a whole other level than Stick of Truth's cutscene glitches, and it just makes me feel like the game wasn't tested properly. Perhaps a frw more months in development would pump all these issues out. And of course, the biggest issue of all... U-Play and DRM. I don't understand Ubisoft to be honest. I paid for the game through Steam, I should be allowed to play it JUST THROUGH STEAM like Stick of Truth. But alas, Ubisoft decided to shove U-Play down everyone's throats and I'm not a fan of it. I don't have an issue with U-Play itself, but the intergration did not need to be there. Same with DRM, except I do have an issue with that.
HOWEVER, if you can look past all of the bugs, glitches and terrible Ubisoft choices, you're looking at one of the best games this year. It's humor is amazing and keeps very inline with South Park, the characters are as loveable as ever, the missions are fun and creative and it's just a great experience overall. I would recommend this game for any fan of South Park and anyone who enjoyed Stick of Truth!
P.S: Play this game with a controller for the love of god. The keyboard controls are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

In terms of replay value, Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is not a good buy. It's only got one main storyline with a few sub-objectives, and once that's over, that's it.
However, in terms of overall worth, it is by far worth the buy at any reasonable price.
The narrative of the game follows two brothers (no duh) traveling to a great tree in a far away land in order to save their sick father. While it starts off alright, with the player (namely myself) thinking "Why exactly am I playing this game?" That feeling actually remains for the next hour or so. However, as the story progresses and one sees more of the characters and who they are, the story gradually becomes gripping and emotional; while it is a short game (roughly 3 hours), it holds themes and motifs that are easily worthy of high quality movies, and it takes the player on a proper emotional rollercoaster that leaves him or her thinking about it afterward.
The gameplay is kind of intuitive--controlling two separate characters with your analog sticks (controller only, I don't know how the keyboard works) is unique and compelling for a bit, but it wouldn't last long. Luckily, as I said before, this game is short and therefore its gameplay remains fresh throughout the first playthrough, which is a valuable component to any game. It even consistently switches things up and introduces variations of its few mechanics so that by the end of it, the player doesn't feel bored or underwhelmed.
Along with the side quests and absolutely beautiful world design, this game is a must-buy. I can't recommend it enough if you have a couple of hours to spend.

Dead Rising 2: Off the Record is a stand-alone expansion to Dead Rising 2. It is essentially a response to fans of the series who loved the second game but weren't big fans of the protagonist Chuck Greene and wanted a return of Frank West.
In Off the Record you play as Frank West, the protagonist of the original Dead Rising. There are a lot of notable differences the two characters have compared to each other. Frank is a lovable charismatic scoundrel who largely looks out for his own self interest above all else. His animations are also different given how he's much pudgier. You go through mostly the same story and missions as the original, just with Frank instead of Chuck. Frank being the protagonist greatly improves the quality of the story to this game, and it feels like a more natural continuation of the original Dead Rising.
The biggest differences between Off the Record and 2 is in the sidequests. The photography minigame from the original returns, alongside a very much improved endless mode. The endless mode is the biggest reason to pick this game up since Dead Rising 2 lacked it. It allows the player to explore Fortune City with no time limit and additional challenges. The user interface is also much improved.
If you are a fan of the original Dead Rising 2 I guarantee you'll love Off the Record even more. It's exactly what fans of the series originally wanted and delivers in almost every way. I would even recommend it over the original release due to how similar the two experiences are to each other.
One last thing to note is that Capcom graciously patched Games For Windows Live out of both this game and the original Dead Rising 2. So I would greatly recommend the Steam release for it is now the definitive version of the game.

Spelunky is one of my favourite games. The constituent parts are simple - it's a platformer with strong rogue-like elements. That is, permadeath with random levels, and as hard as nails.
A good complete playthrough will take about 20 minutes, but you'll spend tens of hours perfecting your skills to get to the stage where you can actually beat the game.
The controls are perfect, the mechanics extremely well tuned, and the game never feels unfair. Every situation is navigable, every death preventable, it just depends upon your skills. And deaths are hilarious - they're usually something really stupid you've done.
I once saw a streamer (Anthony Burch of HAWP fame) daze himself from falling and ended up accidentally sacrificing himself on an altar, killing himself instantly. Right near the end of the game.
My favourite part of this game is just how much the randomness affects the game strategy and gameplay in general. Random levels often feel bland and uninspired, but Spelunky manages to make the randomness really matter. You have to make meaningful decisions and hedge your bets. I could use a bomb, but, I've only got 3 left and might need to use a couple later on..
Anyway, this is the cream of the crop as far as platformer roguelikes go. There are none better, that I've played.

A truly atmospheric puzzle adventure. I have not ever been into this kind of games, but this one is unique enough to try it out. The graphics (or rather, photography) and the enviroments are amazing, with a gloomy, lonely feel. The puzzles are very well crafted, they have introduced me to code systems that makes Silent Hill 3's puzzle hard mode seem easy in comparison.
I cheated a little at the end asking for help, but trust me that you that it feels extremely rewarding to do it for yourself. Also, one of the best aspects for the game is to do everything at your own pace, because once you advance 2 hours in the game, the map expands a lot, giving access to 4 additional stages and more sectors of the mansion, which you can all explore with little to no barriers...this is a thing that many lineal adventure games should be learning from : allow the player to explore freely.

It was a pleasure to visit the old manor and the other places around.
I might have had a hard time with some puzzles but the community was always there to help me, or put me in the right direction and explain the big picture to find the smaller details myself.
I do not regret backing it and I would recommend it to all the point and clicks lovers, people who love beautifully designed indie games and everyone who's in for 20h of scratching your head and fixating over the faintest hint.

I bought this expecting a minecraft clone and I was half right, even though it is in its infancy this game has a lot of potential as Im hoping the developers keep on working with it as these days a lot of MC clones seem to be rushed out for only to empty a few pockets then fall by the wayside.
My experience with the game so far has led me to a few niggles,
The CRAFTING:
Limited at present with a few dozen recipes but with future updates I'm sure it will become as extensive and as intensive as MC, maybe not building reactors with redstone intensive but hopefully a more entertaining craft recipe list. There are certainly more weapons than MC and most with additional bonuses to crit rates and damage.
The MOBS:
There are a few different the further you go on but mostly the same on various maps, but they look better than standards MC (without mods or graphics packs), but never the less they do suffer from some glitches such as getting stuck behind doors with you out of their reach, but not so the other way round as ytou can hit them but they cant hit you, one for the kiting and dropping them off in a pit fans, as they cant jump or climb apparently plus they simply stare at you as you slowly erode their health as they can't reach you, I almost pity them but I want their loot so I dont.
The BOSSES:
Only 3 so far but if your not ready they'll still kill you plus theres the added danger of falling off the platform if your not aware of where your stepping, frustrating when the boss is about to die after 10 minutes of dodging his attacks onlyfor you to fall of the edge of the platform. Plus the way to defeat them is pretty obvious once you know.
The WORLDS:
At times some are very dark and the torches you can carry only light a some area, even if you pop a couple of them on the ground they only lights a slightly larger area, plus when you mine the blocks either pop out of existance or sometimes delay disappearing and it can be a bit offputting when mining. Plus resources are scarce but at least the DEV's have thought of a way to find them with the diving rod.
But other than that a good game to look forward to, so please DEV'S keep at it.

Best World war game in terms of historic weapon-accuracy, fun and active gameplay and beautiful landscapes. Because of its midsized, non-mainstream playerbase, the game allows players to work together as teams and communicate much more technically and effectively than other games of the genre - with a very, very low rate of trolling, abuse and overall stupidity. Another brilliant point about this game is the wider focus on what the Second World War's warfare actually involved, using capture points and bases and allocating certain soldiers to different roles in the battlefield. The game cleverly isn't just about fighting and killing, but also strategy, protection and communication.
Although the game does need improvement in areas (matchmaking, spawning at the beginning of battles, queue times, squad leaders and members issues) - this game has a ton of potential. Its unique style of campaign, along with its "olde-worlde" atmosphere and graphics create an accurate, addictive (healthy/unhealthy sometimes :D ) game with a helpful and knowledgable community of players and developers.

A tale of two sons traveling through the world to find a cure for their dying father.
There'll be happy moments, there'll be bully moments, there'll be scary moments, there'll be gross moments, there's betrayal, there's parting, there's sadness... All the joys and sorrows of traveling, in one tight package.
The gameplay is unique: You are controlling two boys at the same time with one controller. Each analog, back and trigger button for each son. While you're puzzling over trying to control both of them at the same time, the game throws puzzles at you that are made, obviously, specifically for this control scheme. While this may sound tough, worry not young gamerawan, you'll do just fine.
The story is also uniquely told. Instead of talking you get incomprehensible words and lots of body language. The story is also very fairytale-like, what with the world filled with all kinds of mythical creatures, such as trolls (both kind), giants and griffins. You'll be traveling from the bright and comfy countryside to gloomy caves, breath-taking mountains, gigantic castles, and more. All of this is emphasized by the amazing graphics.
The only thing this game falls literally short on is its length. I wasn't lying when I said "tight package" - It took me 3 hours to clear this game once. I'm not surprised if you think this doesn't deserve the full price, but please think of grabbing this when it's on sale.

*Brothers* is both one of the shortest and best games I have played.
There are a few flaws. There are no natural stopping points in the game, so despite the short length the game seems to drag at a few points.  The unconventional controls make gameplay more fatiguing that it normally would be, although I don't consider that a failing.  The world is filled with a hodgepodge of fantasy elements and NPC's that are beautifully done, but don't seem to go together.  The setting is vaguely Iron-Age Indo-European, yet there are huge libraries of books, NPC's with glasses who look like homeless college professors, steampunk machines, and armies of giants.
The art style and mood is consistent and very appealing, but the lack of connection between all the writers' ideas make the setting more disorienting and less immersive than it could be.
The characterization of the two brothers is the best part of the game.  The only other modern media I've seen that portrays fraternal love with such sensitivity is Fullmetal Alchemist.
My criticisms don't diminish my opinion that this is an excellent game, and shows tremendous potential.  I hope to see more from these writers and their studio.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky
It has been a while since I last played it, but after noticing some updates for some mods I used to play and the lack of a review, I decided to write this.
Anyway... What can I say? An aweful lot, but I'm going to keep it short. This review will touch on two aspects of the game; modded and unmodded.
I'm recommending this game because of mods. The S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series is among the most moddable game series out there. Despite this game being the weakest in the series, mods can quickly turn it into one of the strongest, if not
strongest. I've put more hours into this than I have into say, Shadow of Chernobyl or even Call of Pripyat (though between Misery and the recent release of Call of Chernobyl for CoP, my CoP playtime is catching up.
Why? Simple really. A single mod called 'The Faction War' or TFW for short. It takes a wonderful mechanic brought into the series (but removed for some reason in CoP) and turns it into something more. What might this feature be? Faction wars, of course.
Join one of the many factions and fight for supremacy, or go alone in the zone and fend for yourself against mutants, bandits or any factions you decide you don't like. It turns the game into an RTS of a sort, with reasonably large scale firefights - or, if you want to, quiet night-time operations.
The game is good without mods, but it is arguably the weakest in the series. It has an number of bugs which can be fixed through the use of mods and community patches. Other mods serve to enhance the story and gameplay, so by now you're getting the picture. You can play through the game fine, but you'll end up turning to mods to enhance, fix or even overhaul the game.
I'll go into more detail another time, so for now this'll have to do.

Don't even consider PAM for single-player alone unless you really want MarioKart (any of them), but can't get it. I won't say that PAM isn't fun, but I will say it's not worth the money spent.

Satisfaction and progression. Those are the key words in my opinion. I don't get the same kind of satisfaction playing this as with, say, Binding of Isaac: Rebirth and Rogue Legacy. The moment you start Binding of Isaac, you get satisfaction when RNG is with you, or when you clear the game when RNG clearly wasn't with you. You get more interesting items by playing it, you progress in a sense. With Rogue Legacy, it's the same thing. When you die, you get to spend the money you got from that run to make your child fare better in the next run. Your defeated bosses stay defeated. You feel you're actually progressing trough the game.
With Spelunky, I don't feel any satisfaction or progression while playing it. Also, I'm not really the fan of the art style of the game.

Spleunky is a dungeon crawler with rougelike elements. Each level is randomly generated, giving you a new experience every time you play. The game uses marioesque type leveling system, for example you start off in the mines. Each area has 4 levels, 1-1, 1-2, 1-3, and 1-4. Your goal of each level is to reach the cave to the next level. On your way you must collect as much gold and equipment on your way. There are a ton of traps and monsters to try and kill you. You may take as long as you like to scope throughout the level to find as much gold as possible, just use your rope and bombs wisely. Be aware, you have all the time you need, but can you survive the time? After a certain amount of time a huge ghost appears with the text saying "A chill runs up your spine..." This ghost will chase you down in an attempt to kill you. So yeah this is pretty much the entire game played out through multiple areas until you reach the end. But it does not feel repetitve in any way, each area presents you with a new mechanic and enemies that give you new things to learn. Giving you new dangers to adapt to and make your way through. You also have a journal to keep track of what items and enemies you encounter.  Also, the music is probably my favorite part of this game. It combines a feel of adventure with mystery. It fits the tone of the game really well, and there is differnet music for differnet parts of the game. I have one nitpick if you want to call it that with the game that I will go over right now. This game is VERY unforgiving, and i don't mean that in a bad way. I enjoy difficulty in games, like i said i don't think i would call this a "nitpick" i consider more of a draw to the game. Traps and monsters can do anywhere from 1 heart to death. This game makes you think about going through a level, and has you at the edge of your seat when you're low on hearts, and you just entered the ice caves. I highly recommend this game to anyone that wants a game to kill half their day. 10/10

But this is for anyone who wonders if it's worth paying for the HD version when the original version is still free: Absolutely (too). The graphics are gorgeous. There's a book with Monsters, Places, Traps and Items that lists your statistics. There are new monsters, new traps, new weapons, the dark levels have new mechanics that are making it both more challenging and more interesting. And there are new levels too which I am far from getting to yet. I have died 120 times so far and are yet to make it to the Final Boss.
This is for anyone who thinks the game will be too hard: You will likely be better than me, but you won't beat it right away either. That's not the point. Have the tunnel man build you tunnels and do some practice. Get to know the game before you even attempt to reach the end. You'll enjoy every minute of it.

Oh god, I wish I could stop myself for writing game reviews at less then 10 hours, however, on TEKKEN 7, you can see what game offers to you in less then 10 hours.
Before a long post, I want to say the fact that I've bought this about 40$ (with Season Pass, not just base-game) and still not regret it. It's a cool price for damned country like Turkey.
Also want to mention that I've played almost every installment to the series including non-canon and crossover ones. I'm not to new to the series and I've played lots and lots of online matches in both of TEKKEN 6 and TEKKEN TAG TOURNAMENT 2.
Now, I want to compare few things from TEKKEN 6 (which is 2 games before this in series) and want to talk about them. First of all, TEKKEN 6 has more content. Yeah, you can't even versus to CPU in vs. mode in 7. There is no Survival, no Team Battle, no Beat Em' Up game mode like Scenario Campaign (or Tekken Force in 3 and 4). You can play Story: The Mishima Saga which is can be completed in less then 3 hours, play some Arcade which is not have both epilogue and prologue, farm some items in Treasure (Which is just Ghost Battle without the ability of select who you want to fight), watch some cutscenes from all previous Tekken games including non-canon ones and that's all. You can play Online mode afterwards if you fan of it.
Customization. I didn't asked for healthbar ones, but i must admit they are kinda cool. However, it seems like this game suffering from Character Customization. Yeah we have lots of items but without funny/meme ones, which is I completely hate (Seriously, why the ♥♥♥♥ I want to have Jenga blocks on my ♥♥♥♥ing head?) and the ones that shared with every character, there is almost nothing left. Instead of these "humor"-d ones, I want to see outfits like CLAMP. Also why the heck I can't change my hair color if I put some Head accessories? Oh god, I missed TEKKEN 6 already.
Characters. Where is Lei, where is Anna, where is Julia?! GOD THESE CHARACTERS WAS LIKE ALMOST ALL IN OTHER TEKKEN GAMES! I don't even mention about other ones.. Don't get me wrong, character roster should be evolved, I know but some characters have been barebones to the series, and missing them is kinda bad.
Yeah, I think i've mentioned everything that I want to compare. Now, lets talk about what did this game correct, shall we?
Graphics. They make this game even more A E S T H E T I C. It keeps it graphic-style and evolved it. Not best graphics i've ever seen, but it's enough for our generation.
Optimization is beyond good. It's exactly perfect. I've never-ever seen game drops on 59FPS, even on Ultra with my RX 580. We need more games like this. With more content ofcourse. Oh, also, game runs too light, it's one of the things I want to mention. It not makes both GPU and CPU takes too much load.
Gameplay is still keeps it Tekken vibe even without bounds and with special Power Crushers, Rage Art and Drives. I still trying to adapt in to new mechanics. Slowmotion is a cool feature that makes who connect attack first. Power Crushers are hyperarmour which is will negate your damage animation during startup frames. All of these new mechanics seems familiar from TEKKEN REVOLUTION, which is IMHO, they make that FTP game to test community of TEKKEN about special arts.
I must admit i love indivisual Arcade endings more, however, unlike almost all of other Tekken games, this game explains story very well. Also, i like plot twist about Mishimas, but man, don't forget Tekken 3, Mishimas did evil things back in the day.
Biggest addition, you can select your starting angle! Everyone can be on their favorite side, thanks to newest system of TEKKEN. It's never had be done in other fighting games. It'll make both players placed in left if they want to with some camera magic.
Not gonna lie, this game has good Tekken OST, and probably have taken my first place right above of TEKKEN 5. Especially with I AM HERE. Also stage ost's are good too. Sorry 5 ;__;
Well, that's probably everything that I want to state what they did good in this game. I wish fighting games have more content these days. It's not first, we know this situation from SFV. Before my last words, I want to talk about console/pc differences. This game have less content on PC then PS4 version, which is cool feature like Jukebox and classic costumes.
Even with more content I still would bet my money on PC release. Consoles has input frame delays and lower resolutions unlike PC, people say PC has bad network code, but I still not occured something bad in online. Technical issues matters.
I don't know why this game takes 60GB place. It's not have contents like old TEKKEN games. Remember TEKKEN 5? It was on DVD and has both TEKKEN 1, 2, 3 in of it. And it has unique Arcade epilogue and prologues, Survival and Team Mode, more characters and a uber cool game mode named Devil Within. Still these bad things doesn't changes up my mind. I wished I could tag this review with "Mixed Thoughts" but I can't.
With the price I've payed, I'll go with Recommend. After all, instead of halfy release of Street Fighter V, this game has more than 20 characters, a proper story mode, more customization, even I don't like those and I like to mention about instead of the touch of Street Fighter X Tekken, Akuma is feel like a Street Fighter character that ported in to Tekken. And they promised about more characters, gamemodes and stuff. With and without season pass. So I'll go with recommend it with my price, which is now costs more than it, thanks to our game distributor. Oh, also please add the ability of checking latest players from Steam's Player section in Overlay. Please.

Goods:  The story, combat, world.
The Story:  If you watch the show, you will know The Coon trilogy.  ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is back, and he joins the gang in their fight to find Scabbles, a cat that has gone missing and has a reward for $100.  The story is everything a South Park fan loves, gross out humor, funny storylines, and overall what the South Park kids go through when they're having their adventures.
Combat.  In the first game its like a Pokemon style of game-playing. Now its more like Fire Emblem.  you choose where your character goes and where to attack.  This adds more variety to the combat letting you figure out who to attack first and which attacks to use.  They also added a bar where you can do a super attack on the enemies, and this is just for you, every character in your party can do a super attack.  Honestly I love the new combat, its fun and challenging at points.
World:  To be honest, it feels like an exact clone to Stick of Truths world, but they have added a few more places which is nice.  There's nothing else to say, if you know the Stick of Truth map you will know this map pretty well.
Bads: Framerate and crashes.
Ok here comes my problems with the game.  If you see the most reviews going up on here you will see people complaining about crashes and framerate issues.  Personally I haven't ran into framerate issues a lot, but I have ran into a few crashes/resets.  First will be even before you start playing.  Sometimes you will have the title screen come up, sometimes it will be a black screen.  The only way around this is to alt+tab out of there and then close your game.  Its annoying, but you will get used to it.  Second is loading times.  I notice that everytime I either fast travel/or load into a fight, my computer takes a little bit to load up the fight/enviorment.  Not awful, but it gets annoying, wspcially when you lose the fight and you have to go to your last checkpoint.  This last one is why I can't play the game anymore.  This will be a Spoiler so if you dont want to be spoiled, just stop reading now.   On day two you will have to go keep a prescription for Classi.  When you cut through an alley, you will have to face Raisin waitresses.  I fought them once and lost, but when I tried to load up the fight again, my game crashes.  This is why I wrote the review, because of this bug.
Last thoughts:  I really do love this game, its a great sequel, but in my opinion, wait a little bit before buying it, wait until the make a patch fixing the bugs.  Honestly if you love Stick of Truth, you will love this game, but just proceed with caution.  I am giving it a like because the hours I was able to play this was fun and addicting, but its comes with an astericks, because of the bugs.

I read the reviews before purchasing this game.

DRM/Uplay
I did not encounter any issues with either the DRM or uPlay.
I downloaded the game, clicked play, and the game performed all of the Uplay setup with only a single click from me.
(Note, I did already have a Uplay account for a previous game)
Since installing I have had 0 errors launching or playing the game.
Performance:
I have seen reviews of people having performance issues.
I have not encountered any stuttering, but that may be because my PC specs are very high.
The game runs at 60fps at all times
Specs:
1080ti OC
64GB DDR4 2400
Intell 7700k
Sandisk Ultra II SSD's running in RAID 5
There is one quirk I noticed. There appears to be a ghosting effect on the objects in game when moving.
There will be a bright shadow left behind objects.
Gameplay:
Let me preface this by saying I thoroughly enjoyed The Stick of Truth.
This sequel is no different
The redesigned combat system more closely resembles a tactics game than a typical turn based RPG
I am really enjoying the combinations of classes that are available.
The crafting system doesn't really seem necesary, as I rarely need to use items (Even on the Mastermind difficulty), though that is completely anecdotal.
The character customization is perfect for what I want, I was a little saddened that there was very little in the Stick of Truth.
Overall:
Since the DRM and UPlay were non invasive and didn't cause me any frustration I would definitely recommend this game.
The purpose of DRM is to protect the works of the company, and if possible do it in a way that has little to no impact to legitimate purchasers.
I feel that the DRM for this game does not detract at all from my experience.

It has all the things that made Dead Rising great put into this Off the Record. Along with tweaks to animations, combat, and AI from the first. However, I do think this one lacks the charm and feel that the first one had.
The atmosphere just isn't on par. The boss fights lack the unique characterization from DR1, the music seems to not have the same flair either; some tracks just come off generic sometimes. The combat retained the same kind of problems that one had, and getting stuck in a stun animation from a boss never felt more annoying; and the damage limiter that they implemented to how much bosses can get hurt from constant player attack is not a great thing either. Only about three bosses made me feel invested and not frustrated; and this was at higher player levels too.
I can't help the feeling that anything interesting about this game is just a carry over from the first; but there are some meaningful additions that feel like natural and fit into the whole game. Don't get me wrong, I think this is a great game and I had a lot of fun. It's still Dead Rising at heart, and still a unique and great experience; there is just something missing, but that's just me.
Sadly this one isn't canon to the story, but rather a "what if" unlike the original Dead Rising 2. However that shouldn't push you away from it. If you ignore the canon, just think of it as a more direct sequel to DR1.

I got this game for 99 cents. For that price, I would definitely recommend it. At a much higher price, I wouldn't. But I don't want to base my recommendation on price, and since I wouldn't play the sequels even for free, I'm gonna go with "not recommended".
If you like humorous 2D point-and-click adventures, Deponia might be for you. It combines a fresh setting with "industry"-standard storytelling and mechanics. I liked the artwork a lot and the protagonist, Rufus, is quite enjoyable.
There are a lot of things I didn't like, however. First off, it aims for the classics, but the writing is not remotely as good (with a some exceptions). A few times the humour is so forced that I couldn't help but feel remote shame, as in "did they really think anyone would find this funny?"
Most of the quests and puzzles are straight-forward. But some of the puzzles are just aggravating. We've all been there, trying anything with everything in the inventory, to no avail. Or clicking different levers to see the desired effect. But some stuff in Deponia is just completely non-sensical and drove me mad. I admit I had to look into a walkthrough a few times, and mentally flipped the finger towards the developers a few times once I'd found out how something was supposed to work.
From a technical perspective, there are 2 things I found wildly inappropriate for a 2012 title, especially if it's published at (almost) full price: #1, the animations. You will see a lot of generic "empty hand movements" when you do stuff with things. I found this particularly disappointing given how much love went into the artwork otherwise. #2, lots of interactions will just yield the same line over and over again. For instance, when you are trying one specific item in your inventory with every other item, you'll hear the same crappy joke over and over again. Very tiring.
Overall, I would say Deponia shows lots of promise, but some aspects are just disappointing and frustrating.

So, the game is regularly on sale for 0,99€, which is a STEAL don't get me wrong. I suppose that's how most are going to be picking this up.
But this game did not inspire me to play the rest of the series. Didn't enjoy it enough.
The game is a classic point'n-click, with all the hallmarks of the genre. The humour, collecting things, rubbing things together to make new things, list-based dialogue trees and "quirky" characters. So If you have nostalgia for these sort of games, you may enjoy it more. But I grew up in a different era, and while I enjoyed some of the monkey island games for their kickass music, this game doesn't quite have the same sort of charm. It also brings along the thing that ruined my enjoyment of the game: the adventure game logic. I played this game with a guide open in another window, and I have some shame for that, but I spent maybe two hours of play time stuck on various puzzles, and that just isn't my idea of a good time. One unintuitive puzzle would be an anomily, but more than three is more like poor design.
The Visual are, well, lopsided. from the stills and the promotional art, you might thing that the game looks pretty good. in action though, the animation is really basic, with a minimum number of frames used to convey movement, and a limited number of facial expressions. Voice acting is also decent overall, with few standout performances for better or for worse.
And the story.... well, the writing has some pretty good moments, but on the whole it still often fails to entertain. I will still give the game credit for the writing of Rufus, the MC. A lot of games try to go for a "scoundrel" type of main character, who's somehow a rebel who doesn't play by the rules, but also has a heart of gold, but here they bring the contradiction in that type of hero to it's logical conclusion: Because he acts like typical adventure game character, the other charcters see Rufus as a useless, kleptomaniac, harebrained and unpleasant person, while he sees himself as "too good" to live among them. I would say his defining character moment is when he has an arguement with his ex-girlfriend (who still houses and feeds him) to get the key to her first aid kit, from which he takes some tranquilizer which he uses to  come back, drug her and steal her stuff. Having Rufus be a real ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is what's important for him to have any real character developement.
As for the side characters, some get laughs, and some get groans, and some are simple plot devices. Unfortunately, the latter category includes the series female lead, Goal (seriously?) who is the cornerstone of the plot for the whole game, yet doesn't say anything meaningful to make you invested in her.
All in all, Deponia is only recommended to the fans of this particular genre, and especially hard puzzles. For the uninitiated, the game can be frustrating.

An amazing fighter with both returning characters, and new characters abound!
This game is the 2nd game in the reboot series of Mortal Kombat, being a direct sequel to Mortal Kombat 9.
The game takes place 22 years after the ending of Mortal Kombat 9, and many of the old fighters have had children who have become realm-class fighters over the years as well.
Because of this time shift a breath of fresh air has gone over Mortal Kombat.
New fighters such as Cassie Cage, Takeda, Ferra/Torr, and others have really brought some new blood to the fights, while still feeling eerily reminiscent of the past games. This allows you to pick them up and know what you're doing, but not feel like it's a clone of an old character.
Now onto the gameplay.
The game plays VERY similar to Mortal Kombat 9, but replaces many of the annoyances many had with it.
They removed MANY unblockable moves, in mk9 if you lined up your unblockables right you easily could destroy anyone.
They added variations. The BIGGEST feature in my mind. The fact that each character has 3  "playstyles" means you can play a character that in a standard fighter is ALWAYS a grappler as a zoner, or you could play a zoner as a rush down. These variations add- well.. VARIATION!
The graphics: Though minor for most people who play fighting games, the graphics are VERY appealing. Incredibly realistic look to everything makes love and cringe at the same time as you rip your enemies in 2, all at a nice 60 fps.
SIDE NOTE: X-rays, fatalities, and menu's are displayed at 30fps, this WILL cause some minor jitter at times that could bother you.
Netcode: The game has an ALRIGHT netcode, if you played Mortal Kombat 9, you'll see it as an improvement for sure. If you play a game like Skullgirls with GGPO or Street Fighter IV, you may be dissapointed though as some matches WIll be unplayable.
So over all I feel this game if FANTASTIC of a fighter, and can't wait to see how the competitive scene evolves around it!

If you're looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if you're looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R Clear Sky is a Prequel to the original S.T.A.L.K.E.R Shadow of Chernobyl. Released in 2008, It tells an alternate timeline story of "The Zone", which is the highly contaminated and radioactive area surrounding the Chernobyl Nuclear Plant and neighboring areas, after a second explosion occurs at the plant. S.T.A.L.K.E.R's are scavengers who traverse the Zone in search of Artifacts, as Guides, Mercenaries, and for research related operations. In this prequel, which is recommended prior to playing S.T.A.L.K.E.R Shadow of Chernobyl, you play as a S.T.A.L.K.E.R known as Scar, who is injured by an unknown energy emission, while escorting scientists through the zone. Somehow Scar survives and finds himself at Clear Sky, a research colony trying to understand what is happening to the Zone. From here you begin your journey into the Zone, to unlock it's mysteries, as well as to save Clear Sky from the dangers at their gates.
S.T.A.L.K.E.R Clear Sky, came after S.T.A.L.K.E.R Shadow of Chernobyl, so it plays much the same way. You have a set amount of inventory space, an array of weaponry to loot or purchase, armor to help keep you alive, as well as medpac's, bandages, grenades and more. Mods exist for the S.T.A.L.K.E.R games, which are extremely popular such as The Stalker Complete set, Misery, and the Oblivion Mod, all of which, change the game mechanics and overhaul the games graphics. S.T.A.L.K.E.R has been a decent Horror FPS series, and spawned another sequel following the events of Shadow of Chernobyl called, S.T.A.L.K.E.R Call of Pripyat.
If you like games such as Fear, Resident Evil, Silent Hill, you should enjoy S.T.A.L.K.E.R Clear Sky. Again, it is the second game in the series, but is meant to be a prequel to S.T.A.L.K.E.R Shadow of Chernobyl, so I recomment playing Clear Sky first.

Taken together, Analogue: A Hate Story and Hate Plus might represent the creative apex of the visual novel: both are multilayered, meditative, and stridently political, with a shared emphasis on anthropological research and dialogue-based waifu seduction. I was gobsmacked by these games. I mean... come on. Cosplay, chocolate cake, and hours of in-depth archival research—what more could you possibly want from a game?
I liked this game, although I still prefer the original.
The game that made people bake an actual IRL cake and go through all five stages of grief. Killer song in the end too.

I think Analogue: A Hate Story is one of the best visual novels around. Hate Plus is pretty good too, but it falls short in a couple key areas.
One weakness is the character of *Hyun-ae, who is cute and funny and all, but moreso than in Analogue doesn't really feel like she has much purpose except to make fun of visual novel heroines (hence the cake achievement and all). Since she is one of the three possible routes for the game, that ends up being a pretty big problem. She just doesn't contribute all that much except being a vehicle for the author to poke fun at the player; she doesn't have anything to do with the story this time around and the game's format doesn't really allow for her to develop a rapport with the player character, so there's not much room for character development.
The biggest problem with Hate Plus is the plot. The idea is that the player character explores a new set of logs recovered from the Mugunghwa which purportedly explain how the spaceship's inhabitants went from being an authoritarian but somewhat egalitarian society to the neo-feudal dystopia we got to know and love in the first game, with one or both of the A.I.'s reading over their shoulder as you go. There's more of a linear narrative there, but the most important characters, especially Old *Mute and the villains, aren't fleshed out enough to carry it. The story ends up feeling incomplete and unsatisfying, especially when your A.I. pals are portrayed as profoundly affected by it. There end up being quite a few plot holes and unanswered questions. It's fairly unsatisfying.
Spoilers: I also thought the endings were a little strange. The one that feels the most satisfying is the jokey harem ending which seems like it's not supposed to be taken seriously, but is the only one that really gives *Hyun-ae and *Mute some closure and a sense of moving on. *Hyun-ae's story is difficult to take very seriously because of all the fourth wall breaking (though it's not so bad if you're not trying to romance her). *Mute's story comes to an abrupt end; it's sad but there's not much closure. From a meta perspective I suppose the idea is, "Hey, not everything gets wrapped up in a neat little package in real life!" I'm not sure that idea justifies a weak resolution to the character arc.
At any rate, Hate Plus is very good in all the ways that Analogue was, but in the areas where it tries to be more ambitious it falls short. I still think it's great anyway.

You should really just look up the log files online somewhere.First of all, this was not a full second game. It’s really an epilogue to Analogue: A Hate Story, and the internet tells me it was originally just going to be DLC, which makes sense because it’s not a full game in any sense. Presumably it was split off and called a sequel for dollar-related reasons.
It’s also just not as good as Analogue for some pretty irritating reasons. First of all, you can only read 18 log files every 12 real-time hours. The result is that the game can only be played over the course of three days, and if you want each route it’s nine days, which the achievements smugly inform us is “the way it’s supposed to be played.” This is a gimmicky way of disguising the lack of actual content, and it’s infuriating. There’s not more than 3 hours of gameplay here, and when I sit down on a Saturday to dedicate a couple hours to a game, that’s the time I have. I’m not going to go through the process of blocking out time of my life on weekdays just because this game is an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I’m also not going to play through all three routes, because I have better things to do with my life (I do, okay?). I loaded up my “harem ending” save from Analogue because I figured having Mute and Hyun-ae together would get my the most content for the least annoyance.
Which brings us to the second major issue, which is that Mute is completely insufferable. The game has lost all of its subtlety with her, and I have no idea why, because the insidiousness of the sexism in the last game was part of its impact. Here, Mute screams WOMEN ARE SO STUPID GOD every five freaking seconds, and no, it’s not social commentary, it’s just normal sexism and it’s both frustrating and annoying. To make it worse, she steamrolls Hyun-ae’s opinions at every opportunity, which makes sense for their characters, but is a nightmare to read and means the reader doesn’t get a voice in what’s going on.
Speaking of Hyun-ae, she is as flightly and not-a-person-who-went-through-trauma as last time, and the game is still framing a serious story with “LOL anime cliches! We so cray-cray! hehehe lylas” and I still don’t like it. The frame story has even less substance than last time, since there’s no mystery like with Hyun-ae’s identity, and it’s just annoying and not what I came for. And then at the end she decides she’s in love with Mute and apparently doesn’t care that Mute’s not into it, and basically starts sexually harassing her and it’s really weird.
All of that said, if you played and enjoyed Analogue, it’s definitely worth at least reading through the bonus log files here, because they’re very well-written and the way the story, which details the fall of the previous society and the rise of the one the Pale Bride existed in, was great. But save yourself the pain, and just look the logs up online. Trudging through the time caps and Mute’s awfulness is not worth it.

Sniper Elite 3 is one of those games that reward patience, careful planning and precise execution. With its ballistical mechanics and (mostly) realistic bullet physics, it's probably the best sniping simulator out there on the market right now.
Gameplay:
It's more refined, polished when compared to V2. Stealth system finally makes sense and is viable in every mission. Rock throwing is pretty wooden tho, as it usually alerts every single guard in the area, rendering it useless. There are also quite a few innovations, such as: jumping over abyss, climbing on rocks. These contribute towards a more open-world feel, providing you with multiple possible approaches to your final destination.
Gunplay:
It's amazing. I cannot stress enough how great it is to learn the game's ballistics and learn to snipe without holding down "E" button. It feels way more challenging and at the same time you WILL feel absolutely bad♥♥♥♥♥after every single succesful headshot (or whatever body part you like). My personal favorite is Russian Mosin-Nagant because of its high bullet velocity, thus requiring less compensation over long distances. And it looks gorgeous!
Graphics:
Screenshots don't lie. This game looks good and it also runs perfectly. 60 FPS with zero (or minor) glitches. Day levels are bright, sunny with some jaw-dropping vistas, while night cycles are starry, silent with sharp shadows.
I would recommend to pick this up if you enjoy WW2 theme or sniping in general. You can finish SE non-stealthy, however you will harness not even a half of what it has to offer. Friendly recommendation: be stealthy, roleplay as an elite sniper operating behind enemy lines.

Brothers left me speechless. Let first say to anyone looking for a short review, "Buy this game. It is 100% worth any money you will spend on it." I would also like to take a humble moment to confess that this game made me cry. Yes, I cried.
Now that the confession is out of the way, this game is a work of art. The story telling in this game is so fulfilling that the fact that story includes no dialogue only adds to the art form.
The player is greeted in the beginning with horrifying story of a boy not able to save his mother from drowning and having to deal with emotional stress as a young child. The story continues by giving the two brothers the task of curing their sick father. The story itself is an adventure in emotion and storytelling. The brothers venture off into an unknown world coming across all sorts of different people and creatures, both needing help and helping the brothers along the way. A wonderful part of the story is the side stories that you stumble upon that have nothing to do with main plot. It’s a rich element of character to an already impressive story.
For the second part of this review, let’s talk about the controls. The game is designed to use an Xbox style of controller utilizing the analog sticks to individually control each brother. Interaction with the environment is as simple as pressing the triggers, one for each brother. It is a lesson in coordination that for this guy was occasionally challenging. If the brothers swapped sides on the screen from the layout of the control sticks, it confused my thumbs. But I would not give up the uniqueness of these controls.
This may have been a short game (approx. 4-5 hours) but the story and cinematography outshined anything. A truly unique game and must play.
A very beautiful game which has a lovely emotional story and all controlled in a very unique way that tests how ambidextrous you are. A must buy.

So, the game is regularly on sale for 0,99€, which is a STEAL don't get me wrong. I suppose that's how most are going to be picking this up.
But this game did not inspire me to play the rest of the series. Didn't enjoy it enough.
The game is a classic point'n-click, with all the hallmarks of the genre. The humour, collecting things, rubbing things together to make new things, list-based dialogue trees and "quirky" characters. So If you have nostalgia for these sort of games, you may enjoy it more. But I grew up in a different era, and while I enjoyed some of the monkey island games for their kickass music, this game doesn't quite have the same sort of charm. It also brings along the thing that ruined my enjoyment of the game: the adventure game logic. I played this game with a guide open in another window, and I have some shame for that, but I spent maybe two hours of play time stuck on various puzzles, and that just isn't my idea of a good time. One unintuitive puzzle would be an anomily, but more than three is more like poor design.
The Visual are, well, lopsided. from the stills and the promotional art, you might thing that the game looks pretty good. in action though, the animation is really basic, with a minimum number of frames used to convey movement, and a limited number of facial expressions. Voice acting is also decent overall, with few standout performances for better or for worse.
And the story.... well, the writing has some pretty good moments, but on the whole it still often fails to entertain. I will still give the game credit for the writing of Rufus, the MC. A lot of games try to go for a "scoundrel" type of main character, who's somehow a rebel who doesn't play by the rules, but also has a heart of gold, but here they bring the contradiction in that type of hero to it's logical conclusion: Because he acts like typical adventure game character, the other charcters see Rufus as a useless, kleptomaniac, harebrained and unpleasant person, while he sees himself as "too good" to live among them. I would say his defining character moment is when he has an arguement with his ex-girlfriend (who still houses and feeds him) to get the key to her first aid kit, from which he takes some tranquilizer which he uses to  come back, drug her and steal her stuff. Having Rufus be a real ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is what's important for him to have any real character developement.
As for the side characters, some get laughs, and some get groans, and some are simple plot devices. Unfortunately, the latter category includes the series female lead, Goal (seriously?) who is the cornerstone of the plot for the whole game, yet doesn't say anything meaningful to make you invested in her.
All in all, Deponia is only recommended to the fans of this particular genre, and especially hard puzzles. For the uninitiated, the game can be frustrating.

It is very good in some ways and not so great in others. I do recommend it, but it could have been a cult classic with a bit more polishing and thought.
The artwork is very good. The voice acting is good. The general presentation of the game is good. Sometimes the animations are a bit off - the generic animations of Rufus rarely match the actions he is supposedly doing, but I consider that a very minor gripe and customizing all those animations would take a lot of time.
The main problem is the puzzles as many solutions are downright bizarre. It isn't even really the solutions that are the problem. It is the lack of hints. You have to spot and figure most of it all out manually. Whereas in Monkey Island, Guybrush might say a hint when trying to do something that is blocked, the only hinting in Deponia is buried in long dialogs and usually not for the whackiest puzzles.
Some items/objects are almost impossible to spot without a helping hand (not provided by the game, I might add).
Also the walking around is time consuming. The town centre can take a considerable amount of time to navigate, and sometimes it is a bit clunky to move between areas of a scene that aren't on the same level.
Sadly, only the absolutely determined (those prepared to try every item combination and pixel hunt every scene) will complete this without a guide.

If I were going to be as fair with this review as this game was with me, it would be a one-sided argument of anger and frustration, lined with bits of compliments. However, I'm going to give this game something it never gave me: A ten second head start and a bandage when I really needed it,
So for starters, let's be genuinely honest here; This is the most unique shooter experience I've ever dealt with. For starters, I've never played a game in which you fight armies of angry Russians armed with Iron Curtain weapons and even a few westernized weapons while I only have weapons with effective equivalence of Airsoft guns. Furthermore, every single person in the Zone is a better pitcher than anyone on any baseball team on earth. I mean, I have never been hit in the forehead with a grenade quite so often as I have been in in this game. I could cower behind a wall and say a prayer that I don't die and get hit with a grenade(Not the explosion, it literally bounces off my character) from half the combat platform away. Fast-Travel does exist, but it is quite literally the least convenient source of mobility since holding L2 to walk forward on a Playstation system.
I believe I've made enough statements on how bad it may be there, but there are in fact positives. I am basing this review off my own personal experience, so certain aspects which may be good or bad for me may not be experienced by you personally.
Now the start of the game is interesting enough, so long as you have a well enough understanding of the map and controls and how to utilize your PDA and the Artifact tracker. Seeing as I did not have a great understanding of these things, I went into the swamps and got half way to the second area of the game without completing the first two missions. So be warned, follow the yellow arrow and monitor the grey arrow as well. Now to the good aspects for real
Pros:
+Vast area to explore; The Swamps are interesting to explore but only so long as you can avoid the anomalies.
+Many different weapons and upgrades available
+Random encounters with Mutants make this a horror experience as much as a shooter
+Upgrades have weight to them, just as they have consequences
+Buildings offer a lot of atmosphere
Cons:
-Fast Travel can be the most expensive habit in the game
-Most buildings have the most amazing atmosphere, but are too often empty of much worth exploring
-Invisibility also means transparent/not able to be touched physically by weapons
-T is for Tedium!
-The ending sequence of the game is literally the best reason to Rage Quit
-Game Breaking Bugs(Example: If you retrieve your gear before you go into Duty territory and talk to the commander, the option to talk to anyone is lost and the game can no longer be continued)
-Pistols do not have iron sights but assault rifles do(Contrast to the older game, Shadow of Chernobyl)
-Dude from Freedom Faction MAY TRY to sell you drugs
Overall, it's not a great game. It's not a good game. It's barely within the respective zone for being an Okay game. I gave this game a legitimate try. I gave it serveral tries. As a matter of fact, on the last sequence of the game, I gave about sixty-four tries. However, if I were to count only the amount of times I restarted the campaign, it would be six. Three of those were due to glitches, three were due to Laptop changes and difficulty adjustments.
My Final Rating for this game is
A Red First-Aid Kit/10

+ Many locations and characters from Shadow of Chernobyl make a reappearance in this title
+ Equipment and weight limitations do much to force the optimization of one's gear, and make one choose what to discard and what to keep; this leaves the player feeling both challenged and rewarded as they acclimate to the concept
+ Artifacts add slight RPG-like stat combinations; these are more challenging to use than in the previous installment, though many will enjoy the increase in challenge
+ Very, very strong sense of atmosphere pervading throughout
+ Boasts a large and active modding community (many mods do well to address some of the game's various pitfalls)
+ Ambient sounds are absolutely fantastic, and keep the player consistently unsettled
+ Manner of interaction with various game-world NPCs is largely determined by the player's actions throughout the adventure; can join and help differing factions, netting different rewards (friendly factions will even show up occasionally if you're in a firefight, and they will aid you)
+ The game's world and atmosphere complements an intriguing plot; the story, itself, rewards inquisitiveness
+ Absolute plethora of side-missions
+ The game's environments are vast and very detailed; visuals, too, are crisp and the lighting mechanics excellent
+ Fast travel is included (for a fee, unfortunately)
+ Finding artifacts, as compared to the game's predecessor, is a new and unique challenge
- Lip syncronization is absolutely atrocious
- Hunger and thirst has been removed; some may view this as a positive, but as this series tends to attract the purists in the RPG community, most would likely see this as a negative
- Bullet mechanics can often be questionable in behavior
- Crouching, much like in the first installment, is laughable; one's character lowers by perhaps an inch, and it offers virtually no protection in any given situation

Here are the facts, not opinions. The game takes a little while to get used to. The sway on the weapons model a real life person's sway which means that players used to games that have little or no sway might have a trouble adjusting. The game is relatively balanced with the three current factions focused on their types of weapons. The key bindings are the same as most other games. Grinding takes a big part of this game, meaning that you will not spend 5 hours and automatically have  an STG-44,m1/m2,or AVS-36.(opinion time). This game was desgined so that as you played, you would become more skilled, know the terrain better, know how to outsmart opponents, and know what to do. Having a better weapon won't make you a better player instantly. Tough guys with their MG42s can be easily taken down by well placed shots from any starter rifle, if you use cunning, you can defeat any opponent, no matter what weapon they have. I believe that people take this game for granted and call it broken, biased, and unfair because they don't use strategy, or try to outsmart the other team. I see this constantly when I join a game. One man holding off 6-10 people in a major capture point because they all rush through the front door and get mowed down. Not just by automatic fire either. A lone sniper held off the entire advancing team until we got up to his position and secured it. These are some facts and opinions. Give the game a try.
