This game is great, but I might be biased because I'm too good.

-Single Player Experience
Compared to something like Guilty Gear or Injustice, there is not much going on here for offline/single-player focused players. There is story mode, arcade, treasure mode, local VS, and practice mode.
The story is disappointing unless you're really invested in seeing the "final" showdown between Heihachi and Kazuya. Otherwise there isn't much dramatic buildup and the narrator is poorly done. I played on normal and found myself dying on most every stage. I attribute most of that to me being new to Tekken for the most part (haven't played since 4) but some sequences, especially towards the end, were insanely difficult. I know fighting games are known for BS boss fights but this was way over the top. It also took me about ~2 hours to beat. In addition to the main story there are a couple of character specific episodes to enjoy. I haven't played these yet but I miss the "traditional" Tekken story experience.
Arcade is just back-to-back fights until you reach a boss. No story but is a fun way to practice.
Treasure mode is like an endless arcade where each fight gets you a piece of customization. Customization is way more miss than hit for me. A lot of the accessories seem like joke items and the clothes that are decent make the character models look horrible.
Local VS is limited to just that. You can't go in here and fight computers - you have to use one of the other modes.
There is NO TUTORIAL in this game. Story has segments where they "teach" you some stuff but they don't exactly cover everything. Thankfully the practice room has every you'd need. You can scroll down the movelists, select a combo to remain on the screen, and practice it away. I'd love to have seen a Street Fighter styled Trials option but this satisfies that condition pretty well.
If you have no plans on playing online, I'd give this game a pass. Story sucks and the customization options aren't incentive enough to grind treasure mode.
-Multiplayer/Online
Good connections get good games. I have run into issues where I get "failed to connect" over and over but Bamco says they're working on it. Considering it's the first day or so, I'll give them a pass for now. It would have been nice to have more filter options when searching for lobbies or the ability to go best 2/3 in ranked. But it is overall a solid experience.

Rated T for Tekken.
I originally was a Tekken 3 player then I didn't play until TTT2. TTT2 is amazing and I hoped that this game would hold up to it as it's the only Tekken on Steam.
So far I really like the feel of it. The fighting feels close to most other Tekkens, but the Rage attacks are new to me and I'm not sure if I like them or not.
There is a grainy look if you set it to Ultra everything. I had to drop the Post Processing to medium as it was really distracting not having the game perfectly clear during a fighting game.
Performance-wise, I have no issues at all. It runs as smooth as butter. When you play online, make sure that you connection with your opponent is a four or five bar otherwise it will be an awful experience with major slow downs. My first match was like this and I was worried that the online was broken, but it isn't. That was the only time I ever had any slow downs.
The gripe that comes in second is that they didn't use the announcer voice from Tag 2 and I can't edit my anouncer. I would love to have him say "PERFECT" over the new announcer as he just doesn't sound enthused about it while the previous felt like he jumped out of his chair to announce your victory.
The extra money that I spent to get the season pass and such doesn't seem like a whole lot at the moment, but I know a lot of the extra stuff is supposed to be in the future.
I havent found a way to talk to other players during battle. Only time that I have been able to communicate with anyone is in tournament lobbies.
For some reason the menus are odd. Warm up is on top of match list in the lobby but after a match it is the opposite. Why? Game Updated - This is no longer an issue. Thanks Devs. I'm not sure what else the update fixed, but I will keep looking.
Now I just need to practice again so I don't get whooped in online.  Oh and the practice mode in 7 and TTT2, if you haven't played them, are some of the best practice modes I have seen in a fighting game.  Rather than just displaying a combo, you are able to watch a preview of it to know if you are doing it correctly. Plus you can easily glide through the moves that you want to practice without going to the pause menu. The Back/Share/Select button plus R1/R2/LB/RB will change it to the next or previous move. They do not include all of the major juggles that you will see if you play online but I believe there is a few for each character.
Story mode is okay, I like that you get to play as all of the characters during it, but everything just happens too fast. Trying to read the captions and watch the action at the same time is a bit rough.
And for arcade mode.... Where are the endings? What fighting game doesn't give you a proper ending during arcade mode. What is that all about? I expected to see different endings for everyone but I played through arcade once and there was about a 4 second scene at the end of the final battle then it went straight to credits. This is my main gripe about the game. Please go back and add these in. I didn't feel rewarded at all at the end. I know they have purchasable, through game money, endings and videos from all of the Tekken games, but I wouldn't think that they would make you pay for the current game. It looks like all that you would unlock for the Tekken 7 extras is just the story mode videos that you will see anyways if you just play the story. I played it for maybe 30-45 minutes and I am already half way through. Edit: I believe they changed out the arcade endings for character chapters in story mode. It's not part of the main story, but you can get their stories that way. I haven't actually played the character stories yet but I assume they will be connected to the main story in some way.
But contradicting the previous statement. They give you all of the story from all of the previous games, so if you are new to the series or missed a game or more, you can find out what happened. You just have to unlock them with in game currency.
If you like Tekken, go ahead and get it. If you've never played, watch gameplay videos first and then decide now or later. It's fun and it is fairly easy to pick up and start playing, but if you are new and you want to switch characters every match, you are going to whiff every other attack.

I am not a fan of point-and-click games, but Deponia makes it just a an easy stress-free medium by being a point-and-click release. You hardly seem to notice that after you play the game for a while, because the flow of it is that smooth. The story itself isn't anything mind blowing, but it is captivating to make you go back until you find out what the future holds for Rufus. As for Rufus himself, there were times when I would get just downright annoyed by how much of an egocentric egomaniac he truly was, but he had me back on his side with his goofy humor. The rest of Deponia's inhabitants have their undoubtful charm, Lottie in particular. The cut-scenes are hilarious at times, the whole "science" and "philosophy" in game are completely absurd (along with their love counsel) and thus gut-busting. The graphics themselves are pleasant to the eye, even though most of them depict what essentially is a junkyard. They add to the absurdity of the game. In general, great game if you just want to relax and laugh a lot, without playing games that all give you the same feel of over-chewed gum. In terms of being a point-and-click game it convinced me to look more into these, maybe I'll find more of such gems.

Quick version:
If you played MK9 and liked it, you will like this game.
If you played MK9 and hated it, you’re better off not buying it.
Long version:
Story modes back and follows the same format as before, you get to play as a whole bunch of the characters (id say about a dozen) and it does a good job of giving you a feel for the game. Storys ok, its not gonna win any awards or anything but it gets the job done and is interesting enough that I wanted to see how it turned out. The characters are fairly varied personality wise and there are some well choreographed fight scenes throughout the story. The pre-fight banter is pretty cool too, although that’s usually reserved for versus matches as the story mode is doing its own thing. If you’re creative you can even create your own drama as you force a girl to shoot her own mother in the jaw and take a selfie of the result or make a guy fight his girlfriend’s father in a battle to the death which ends with the dad puking his own guts out.
Visually this game is a looker. Im kind of amazed they put this much effort into the graphics, to be honest, even on my aging rig it still looked very good.
Gameplay-wise its more or less like MK9, except for a couple new things they added in like a stamina bar and brutalities. Characters also have 3 “stances” or whatever they’re called and they can make a big difference on how they play. They put a lot of effort into some other stuff though, like the Krypt, which plays out like and old school first person rpg in which you unlock extra content like skins and concept art. They also added the faction system, which is still too early to get a proper feel for but basically lets you chose between 5 groups and throws some challenges your way. Towers are back and now encompass the arcade mode too (classic tower or something to that effect) and offer you some nifty challenges, with living towers changing every so often.

Sniper Elite III is a third-person tactical shooter stealth video game developed by Rebellion Developments and published by 505 Games. The game is a prequel to its 2012 predecessor Sniper Elite V2, and is the third installment in the Sniper Elite series.
Sniper Elite III is set around three years prior to the events of V2, following the exploits of Office of Strategic Services officer Karl Fairburne as he participates in the North African conflict during World War II, in which he learns of a secret wonder weapon programmed by the Nazi forces.
The game retains and builds on the mechanics of Sniper Elite V2. Players go through large battlefield maps based on the North African conflict.
The sniper rifle is the player's primary weapon, though additional weapons, including submachine guns and pistols, silenced or not depending on the situation, are available. In addition to hand grenades, the player can deploy tripwire booby traps, land mines and dynamite. Binoculars can be used to tag enemies, displaying their position and movements. The player-character must hold their breath to properly line up the shot. A red icon appears in the scope, marking the projected point of impact. There are weapon parts spread out all over the game, found when looting dead enemies, allowing players to customize their weapons in the predeployment menu; the menu also allows equipment loadouts.
Stealth mechanics have been reworked. An eye icon squints or opens to denote the player's level of detection by the enemy. Enemy soldiers will also have a circle meter over their heads to indicate alert status. Players are also forced to relocate periodically to prevent detection with a white ghost image to mark their last known position and the enemy will search a wider area. As in the previous game, loud sounds may be used to mask sniper shots.
A points system is instituted for actions such as stealth close-combat or sniper kills, with the points accumulating towards promotion to higher ranks. Players can go around the map to collect special reward items such as collectors' cards and unlock sniper nests. Journal pages also provide further backstory into the events of the game.
V2's X-Ray kill cam system is retained as well. Where the previous game only shows the body's internal structure at point of impact, the new game expands to visualize the rest of the cardiovascular, skeletal, and muscular systems. The player can still target vehicles, but now has a chance to shoot the engines and disable the vehicle.
Multiplayer in Sniper Elite III consists of 5 modes of competitive gameplay; Team deathmatch, Deathmatch, Distance King, No Cross and Capture the flag. There is a large selection of maps to play on with large open environments.

It is one of those games you have a lot of fun while playing, but the further you go the more you start to recognize its flaws and you end up playing it through just once for the lolz.
The sniping mechanisms and the ballistics are really well done and the graphics are more than decent. The X-ray vision is also really awesome and makes you feel the impact of your shots.
The AI,however, is REALLY dumb, which was seriously annoying after some time. If you walk upright 100 meters away from an enemy, he will magically hear you and come looking to your exact spot. If you kill a guy standing directly besides another guy with a silenced pistol or masking your shot, the other guy will just go "Huh? Thats not good" Skyrim style and go on with his life.
Everything but your sniper rifle has the accuracy of taking a leak with morning wood. Using a secondary weapon (SMGs) or a pistol from a distance greater than point blank results in VERY frustrating firefights, enemies however hit you with automatic fire from 300 meters away. This makes you choose from only 2 options: Either you go in all sneaky-beaky like, or you find yourself a nice sniper spot and take everyone out from there. The option of engaging in mid range, sustained firefights is pretty much left out, unless you want to try your luck at hitting something with your secondary weapon. This really takes away the feeling that you can play your style out.
All in all, the game is really fun, until the obvious flaws start to become more and more apparent. Then it is just about those satisfying long range headshots and finally finishing the game with an ending that was pretty much "meh".

The only word to describe this game is: beautiful. The art direction, soundtrack, color patterns, interaction with the world, controls... everything is beautiful. To be honest, this was my very first sandbox style game (Nevarr really been into minecraft, always preferred RPGs and such). At surface value, I wasn't sure what to make of this game. My brotharr suggested it to me and so I decided to give it a try. I have to say, I have not regretted it yet.
For such an inexpensive game still in testing, it is a work of art to say the least. I adore the graphics and outfits ranging from shining knight armor to viking attire to devious rogue's garbs (even pirate outfits, which for me REALLY makes a game worth sticking with haha), this game really is outstanding in the visuals department.
The gameplay is pretty straightforward and simple and I really appreciate that. It's often burdensome to deal with games where you have to take everything seriously and try yarr hardest at all times. This game is mindnumbing and easy to fall into. It's beyond entertaining being able to landscape and mold your own world and fight the monsters that inhabit them. I've created so much already and have only scratched the surface of creativity.
There arr a few minor things about the game that urked me, but nothing too serious to dissuade me from spending all my time in it.
-Combat. As I've said, it's really simple and I love it, but if it could be expanded on even a little bit (skills, difficult mobs, etc.) I think it'd really make a difference.
-Gear. Yes I do love me some fashion, but after reaching end game I was hoping to see some miraculous new ensambles, but instead was left wanting with the same outfits as previous levels only altered color wise. I would love to see more diversity there.
-Mining/farming. The only issue I have with the main aspect of the game is that often times when trying to target a brick, if you have anything directly behind you in your camera focus, you'll eitharr hit that object or just hit nothing at all. I'd like to see that fixed..
All in all, if yarr looking for a great game to come home to after a long day and just unwind and forget the world, this game is absolutely perfect. <3

A Brilliant 3D Cartoony RPG, Fantasy, Magic, Action Adventure Randomly Generated World game in which you can play as one of the three typical Medieval RPG Fantasy classes, Warrior, Ranger and Mage. Fortunately you can use weapons and abilities of other classes allowing for fun creativity, however the class effects your focus combat style.
One thing to note is this game is sandbox, so you can do the standard dungeon crawling, monster battling or you can be a village builder, explore all the worlds, or even start a little garden to grow things.
This game is very fun and pretty, it's timeless cartoony graphics give it a beautiful yet ageless look and it's gameplay allows for alot of fun. Worlds are different from the universe you make and spawn in, each world brings in new biomes, resources, enemies and structures with over 50 worlds to explore. The Combat is very exciting, when entering in battle while in 3rd person mode goes into this cinematic camera mode in which allows you to dodge and dash around your enemy as you attack them. 1st person mode makes it a standard first person hack and slash.
The classes are really fun to play as, a great thing is that weapons and items aren't class restricted however if they are not your ideal class they won't be as strong as they can. Warriors do the standard epic sword swinging, shouting and brute force, Rangers do the standard bows/crossbows from a distance or up on top of structures as they pick off their enemies one by one, using agility to their advantage, and Mages do the standard Wand attacks, spells and potions in which Mages can have a large array of epic spells like lightning, fireballs, healing etc.
A great thing about this game is that you can jump to new universes to start in new generated worlds again and keep leveling up your character and getting new resources so it easily has endless fun. Co-op Multiplayer is intergrated into this game so that you can play by yourself, with a friend or on a public universe if you wish in which you can do what you can but with your friends/posse and become efficent monster battlers, structure builders, explorers etc.

Having bought this game in 2012 I'm obviously a fan of the genre. I stopped playing after a year as I couldn't afford the DLC. I rekindled an interest again in 2014 and found the game was still there, updated and ready to continue where I'd left off. Free updates every year are great, although new improved features and options are a thing of the past it would seem. Any updates are merely cosmetic, blink and you'd miss them.
The DLC is still over-priced so like many others I only buy during sales. The game is the leader of its genre, it has no natural competitor. This manifests in the game developers only having to try 'so hard' to bring new DLC or indeed to fix existing problems and issues. 9 times out of 10 they don't even bother, so with Dovetail it's a like it or lump it scenario. If there was a competitor prices would come down and issues would be fixed. Such is life.
Personally I love the editor and making my own routes. Making your own scenery and trains is possible, but there is a chronic shortage of clear information out there to do it properly. Those that have learnt the skill guard their knowledge. Whilst the user community is good overall, you get a few know-it-alls who will rivet count you to death. Bug repairs are available, Dovetail leave the tidying up for other people to do for free.
I would recommend this game if you love trains. I would recommend this game if you love to create content. Just wait for the sales and understand that not all DLC is equal. There are some real stinkers out there, always check out reviews if you can on YouTube and the like. Beware the train sim Twitch channel, it really is only just a long advertisement played on a high-end Chillblast computer. It won't look the same on your set-up.

This game is a sequel to Analogue: A Hate Story.  I strongly recommend playing that first as the events in this game would not make much sense otherwise.
Much like its predecessor, Hate Plus has you reading through logs to find out what happened in the past.  If you liked Analogue, you’ll like this.  This time you explore the events before the year zero and find out how the ship’s society changed to a traditional one with strict gender roles.  However, due to story reasons, you are limited on how many files you can read per day.  After reading around a third of the files, you are forced to wait 12 hours before continuing.  This can be cheated by adjusting the system clock, but it is something to be forewarned about.  My biggest issue with this game is the slow scroll speed in the logs.  Since the game has to load your AI companion’s reactions, it limits how fast you can scroll.  Also, one of the achievements is not achievable in any way, so you’ll never have 100% completion.  Despite these issues, I still recommend this game.

If all you want to know is if Spelunky is worth it then YES it very much is. If you want to know more, read on.
Spelunky is a roguelike at heart at every time you die you start over. It's randomly generated each time like, say Minecraft and this fact makes it very replayable. I've spent more hours in this game than i care to admit (I've played plenty offline too so 71.4 hours doesn't cut it) and i love it to bits. You can do many things in Spelunky. Try speedrunning, steal a jetpack and fly around having fun, trying to reach the golden city (which I did recently. Get on my level! Sorry just really happy about that) or just trying to collect as many things as possible and beat the boss. One of the great things about this game is the fast playing style and jumping about. The control is fluid and responsive and this game will run on most toasters you have to hand. The artstyle is cute and fits well enough and the items are pretty cool. The enemy AI is pretty one note but that just means you'll eventually make an artform of dealing with them. It's fun to jump about on top of enemies and use crazy skills to get to higher positions by jumping off them. The whip does seem to lack a little "punch" though if you know what i mean. Most of the other weapons are nice and satisfying though (especially the shotgun). I love how dynamic the game is with experiences. You can lure enemies into traps, steal from a shopkeeper and become a wanted criminal, throw a stunned scorpion as a weapon etc. It all goes together very nicely to create a fun experience.
On to the gripes. While the different worlds are nice and creative and a welcome change of scenery there does seem to be lacking in the variety department overall and if you're not sold on trying samey levels until you reach mathematical perfection this game might not be for you. Also the  enemies are predictable if you've seen 'em a couple of times. The biggest problem I think is the occasional seemingly unfair death. And that is very true. The difficulty is quite high especially at the start and reaching a new place for the first time you'll get your♥♥♥♥♥♥handed to you and everything seems like a death trap (and most things usually are). It seems intemidating and it might not be for everyone.
But in the end the game is great and replayable and very much worth it (especially on sale). If you want a fun platform roguelike adventure with some nice ideas and a dynamic experience it doesn't get much better than Spelunky. Buy it and have fun.

I've spent hundreds of hours playing the Dead Rising series, and there are few games like it. Off the Record really has the most going for it. Dead Rising 2 fixed many issues that Dead Rising 1 had, and OtR polishes DR2 even further. It features all of DR2's famous weapons, plus the photography mechanic from DR1. Many dismiss photography as unnecessary to DR's gameplay, and I disagree. It's a comedic and gory game, and being able to take photos of the mayhem you cause and be rewarded for that turns that into a game mechanic. I can't count the times I wished I could have taken a photo of something unapologetically silly in vanilla DR2 and in DR3.
Co-op mode is a lot of fun. Use the Invite button on the friends list from the in-game menu to ensure you get the partner you want, as the Play Online option on the main menu seems to be only for joining random people's games. The host player will be Frank West as in the single-player mode, while the client is Chuck Greene from vanilla DR2. Chuck's unarmed special moves are functionally similar to, but different from, Frank's, but that the only real difference to learn. He has a camera like Frank too, of course, so both players can take photos of each other doing outrageous things. There is no voice chat, however, so be ready to use Skype or something if you don't want to have to communicate by jumping and running around in circles.
If you haven't played a Dead Rising before, are interested, but are unsure where to begin, I strongly recommend this one over any of the others, including DR3. Should you buy it if you already have DR2? I did, but only because I was buying the PC versions of the games I liked most on 360. For that I am glad it exists, but I wouldn't say there's a point to owning both if you wouldn't already have a reason to own two copies of the same game. It's a lot like when Pokémon comes out with the "third version" like Crystal that is both superior to, and essentially the same as, Gold and Silver.
One last thing, though: getting it to support controllers is a pain. It has to be a specific version of x360ce. 2.0.2.158 is the one that's working for me and my wired 360 controller, but it doesn't work with my friend's Xbone controller even though it recognizes it.

"Sniper Elite 3" is everything great about "2," but in much greater quantity and turned up to 11.
In its predecessor, you could get a tiny bit claustrophobic. Even though the levels were "open," you could still get the feeling that you were being herded from tactical arena to tactical arena.
With "3," you have much more room, and many more viable paths. This game is much more about what I would call the "total mission." The previous entry in the series was (almost) all about the weapon handling. It was a technical shooter with stealth elements - basically, a single-mechanic exercise. (A really good one.)
This offering, on the other hand, ups the ante by being a game that succeeds with being really good at two things: First, it's a really well built stealth infiltration game. Second, all the technical shooting elements are still there. This creates a much more expansive experience, where the world reacts to you in a way that feels natural and generally uncontrived, and where your imagination has free range to help you keep the enemies guessing.
(And, a big bit of kudos goes to the developers for creating, shall we say, "target rich" environments where you can still feel invested in every shot and relocation. Excellent work, that.)
Yes, there are a few little glitches. Every so often, I would get into a situation where the aim indicator showed my shot as being blocked, but I couldn't figure out why. Then, when prone in a sniper nest, the aim indicator would show a valid shot...but, no, actually, my rifle was clipping through geometry and the round was immediately deflected.
Another thing to be aware of is that "3" doesn't do as much hand-holding as other games. It's not completely opaque by any means, but you are expected to be able to figure out the basics on your own. If you're not familiar with some of "Sniper Elite's" conventions,  I image that you may be a bit bewildered at first.
Following along with the above, the loadouts and rifle customizations are a bit of a rough spot. They present a great number of options to you, but at the beginning of the game most of those choices are locked off. The exact requirements for each unlock are never made particularly clear, and as such, there was a scope customization that I wanted but was never able to get.
But those aren't major issues in the end.
I was looking forward to playing "Sniper Elite 3," and I was not disappointed in any way. It's a very, very worthy successor to "2," and I would call it a must play for fans of this kind of game.

Change 1; Gear:

Its been quite a while since I played Stick of Truth, so I'll just say that I'm reviewing this game as something standalone - I remember the basic story from SoT, but not much else.
This game isn't a terrible one, by any stretch of the imagination. But it does feel very shallow and a lot less fleshed out than I'd expect a game delayed so long to be.
Firstly, the story. It is a decidedly South-Park story. The game doesn't disappoint when it comes to references to the series it draws from. The main issue is that these references pad out the game and come with little depth or intrigue to them. Wanna see the whole "Gay Fish" joke again? Cool, here's a crappy flappy bird minigame and a handful of dialogue, now move on. Wanna meet Towlie? Cool, here's one fight, now never speak to him again. There are just so many of these moments that the game starts to feel disjointed, but not in an episodic sense. Every other thing is a passing reference that feels empty and like the writers were just given a quota of references to meet and started throwing them in there. There's a whole section of the game that is completely pointless outside of introducing the demonic Woodland Critters and Santa, and making them fight one another.
Fight mechanics-wise, the game plays out like a very limited grid-based strategy RPG. The fighting area is small and your characters cannot occupy the same space as another character, friend or enemy, or any stage hazards. It feels unessecarily slow, possibly because of things like being unable to skip the Ultimate attack cutscenes even if you've seen them twenty times already. Attacks all have a certain shape to the squares they can attack, with most being designed to attack along the horizontal plane. Vertically, your options are very limited - apparently characters can punch to their right or left easily, but if someone is standing directly in front of them its an impossibility.
There is a knockback feature in combat that works fairly well, allowing you some limited control over where the enemy is on the map. There is only one big battle I can remember that requires some good use of knockback in order to damage an otherwise undamageable boss. One gripe I have with boss fights in this game is that some of them seem to be the only place to use a certain power, period - for example, one late game boss prompts you to gain a new ability... which you never use in combat again.
There are some scavenger-type missions if you're into that sort of thing, and pre-fast-travel South Park feels a bit of a slog to explore (especially if you don't have all the buddy powers unlocked). But overall, the whole experience is over too soon. At 26-ish hours I've completed all but one scavenger hunt mission (which isn't worth booting the game back up for), with the incentive to replay the game being borderline non-existant (no new game+? C'mon guys).
Overall, this is a mediocre gimmick-filled reference-spewing 25-30 hour game with one of the worst actual endings (and final bosses) in my recent memory. But it is decidedly a South Park game, fitting the style of the series well even if it tries to cram in too many shallow references.
I'd recommend it once the price drops quite significantly.

All in all, while this game can be a lot of fun, it frustrated me more than it gave me game pleasure. So... Next!

This game taught me something.  Namely, you cannot have an utterly vile protagonist in an adventure game because that undermines my willingness to advance the plot.  Some of the things Rufus does (that you are absolutely required to do to advance the plot) are monstrous.  All the other characters in the game hate Rufus and by the end of the game I did too.  I guess I'm just not malevolent enough to laugh at Rufus's antics.
[Minor Spoiler Alert]
For Example, during the third act of the game, you find out that his love interest, the girl he's been dragging around like luggage the entire game has a hard drive in her head that contains her memories and personality.  You are told the reason she is catatonic and speaks in gibberish is because it's damaged but later learn it only has dust on it's contact points.  You are warned sternly that even minor scratches could leave her a vegi.  So what do you do? "Clean" it with a gross pool cleaner brush then use a steel brush to buff it before carving R Heart G in the contact point like it's a tree.  And that's after explicitly finding gentler methods and rejecting them as "girly".  I've never been so revolted.
So yeah, the writting spoiled the game for me.  I simply cannot abide being forced to do lothesome things to accomplish some random, short term goal.  It's sad too because the art was beautiful, the animation decent for the genre, the supporting characters were somewhat interesting, and the puzzles were... well they were all over the map for quality and tilted toward "mash together evertything you've ever laid hands on" but they were mostly fun.  Still this game had the humor of little boys who get off on kicking pets and spiking the punch bowl at a party with laxatives.  If that discribes you, dive in.  Otherwise run far away.

When I first played Analogue: A Hate Story, I was blown away by it. So much in fact, that I almost was afraid to try its sequel. It stayed in my Steam game list, unplayed, for a year.
When I finally replayed Analogue to get the other two endings, and then booted up Hate Plus, I felt like punching myself. Hate Plus is possibly even better than Analogue.
Although it is a bit more random with the order in which you discover plot points, it is exactly that discovery that feels much more engaging. Rather than trying to coax *Hyun-ae and *Mute into sharing more logs with you, you're decoding logs six at a time from a whole set of them (most of which are available right from the start), and therefore you read them together for the first time. While you scroll down you immediately see their reactions to twists and turns in the stories. But as you read more and more of the logs, slowly a story of treason and political intrigue starts to reveal itself, explaining how a small civilisation that was already in decline after 1600 years could undergo such drastic changes in a mere 300 more, and the role *Mute played in it.
Every now and then, the AI whose path you picked asks you for a short break, and you have some conversations with them. For *Hyun-ae, these are quite funny (such as the conditions for the famous cake achievement), but for *Mute they can get very emotional. The dual route combines the best aspects of both other routes.
I personally recommend to play the game with *Mute the first time, and *Hyun-ae the second time, saving the dual route for last. But I understand if you want to play the dual route second. So did I.
Analogue: A Hate Story was good, but in exploring the lead-up to the dystopia, Hate Plus excels in carving out a compelling sci-fi that is nevertheless told in very human voices.

Analogue : A Love Story was an interesting game, a visual novel that wasn't just focused on romance with a bunch of NPC. It had an interesting, original setting, and the goal of the game was to solve a mystery, rather than pursue a romance. Romance was there for people who wanted it, but it was definitely optional.
Unfortunately, its sequel, Hate Plus, deals with what happened far into the past. Thus, you know the setting, you know how it ends, and it's just a matter of reading about the details. There is not enough to capture the attention, you're stuck reading a bunch of stories which just do not have enough in them to keep your interest alive. Besides the main "story", most (all ?) of the other are related to love and relationships, which are fine subject, but I think they each lose their individual interest when all of them shares the same topic. The game actually asks you to pace yourself, forcing you to log off from time to time, but every time i did that, I was losing even more interest (at one point I forgot about the game for a week before logging back in).
So you know the ending before you start, and if you're not very interested by the stories, what is left ? The AI from the first game. They are with you, but you already know their personal story. So it now comes down to their reaction to what you're reading and your "relationship" with them. That's where the game becomes really creepy. That's where it goes back to the full romance system of most visual novels, the thing that Analogue had cleverly managed to avoid. Either you approve to what they say or ask, or the game makes you feels like a jerk.
I'm not sure if there is a middle road somewhere, but it's possible. I just can't be bothered to find out due to all the forced steps and pauses needed to do it. Especially when sometimes, there are conversations where none of the dialog choices are what you would actually want to say.
Another creepy part of the game is related specifically to Mute*. The way she react to what happened to the ship, as it was before her times, and thus she had different values. I know she is extremely conservative but having her disparaging every single story gets tiresome. Page after page about romances Mute disapproves of...Once again the clever writing of Analog has become way too black and white, because the context, of having to solve a mystery and getting away from the endangered ship, isn't there any more to balance things out.
So while I heartily recommend "Analogue : A True Story" to anyone playing games, my advice is to skip Hate Plus. Despite an improved UI, it has lost the good pacing and the balanced approach of the first game, replacing it with creepy AI, a weird fixation on maids and other visual novels tropes.

Wait, wrong game. Hate Plus isn't quite as excellent as Analogue, but it still spins  a gripping tale.
The biggest improvement is variety. A lot more characters and NPCs are in play, so there's more stories to shift focus between and lots more drama to follow.
This is also kind of the downside. Analogue was pretty much the story of the Pale Bride. Hate Plus is Mute's story, but it's also the story of everyone that gets pulled into the spiral with her. It's great as backstory, and the story is still as engrossing as ever, but Analogue had a more compelling hook, I think.
This is more like a doomed outcome from the start, while Analogue keeps you guessing all the way.
These are just minor gripes, though. It's still a very enjoyable VN, and(I can't stress this last bit enough), the realistic character art is PHENOMENAL.

The story was ironic to me. Here we have people ripping each other a part then all of a sudden we have a corny story line. It was luring at certain points, but it had me rushing to see the final scene. I felt they could have done a better job managing the story with the characters they have. Felt like it was eager to go from fight to fight instead of taking the player for magical carpet ride. Injustice felt like it had more depth to it. Komplete edition had it's mystique with the time fractures. This, just felt like we were here for the hype. This game follows Komplete edition's style of story telling but mimics Injustice in a few senses. Whether this is good or bad depends on you, the reader. To me, would have liked to seen some distinct differences between the two games. I did like how they portrayed the characters (Scorpion VS Hanzo Hasashi).
The game play no doubt seems to have stepped its game up. Although Deception combat and ability to manipulate scenery still remains my favorite feature of any MK, this one does feel fluid when fighting and streaking combos together  (couple of buttons, then do a special move, then throw the guy into the scenery or throw it at him). I liked the fact they did incorporate some scenery in the game play, but I would have liked to have seen more options of objects to throw. There were some, but after throwing one, the level can feel empty (besides the jumping ability in some levels). Throwing scenery is cool, and like injustice, switching up fight styles is fun, and yes the fighting is very fluid but it just seems to lack. Sort of feels something more could have been done but, something's missing.
The graphics are as good and sounds are fairly accurate. Would have been nice to seen more than bones in the spine cracking though when it came to x-rays.
Do I recommend this game? I do to hardcore MK fans, but I would suggest waiting for a sale. It's a good game, but it isn't great. ****MULTIPLAYER DOES NOT WORK AS IT SHOULD****

and the mouse doesn't work, it does however have a functional keyboard layout which is more challenging but makes it more fun in my opinion, you might find your hands playing twister on the keyboard and give yourself a high-five when you succeed, though it's kinda hard to fail. You control the elder brother with your left hand (WASD + Space to interact) and the younger brother with your left hand (arrow keys + R-Ctrl to interact).
, they're not very challenging at all though and you will mostly know what to do almost immediately/naturally but it actually adds to the charm of the game.
This is the most interesting part of the game in my opinion and I think the game could have done more by delving deeper into the world/myth, though I think much of it can be researched elsewhere. Its been quite a while since I played Stick of Truth, so I'll just say that I'm reviewing this game as something standalone - I remember the basic story from SoT, but not much else.
This game isn't a terrible one, by any stretch of the imagination. But it does feel very shallow and a lot less fleshed out than I'd expect a game delayed so long to be.
Firstly, the story. It is a decidedly South-Park story. The game doesn't disappoint when it comes to references to the series it draws from. The main issue is that these references pad out the game and come with little depth or intrigue to them. Wanna see the whole "Gay Fish" joke again? Cool, here's a crappy flappy bird minigame and a handful of dialogue, now move on. Wanna meet Towlie? Cool, here's one fight, now never speak to him again. There are just so many of these moments that the game starts to feel disjointed, but not in an episodic sense. Every other thing is a passing reference that feels empty and like the writers were just given a quota of references to meet and started throwing them in there. There's a whole section of the game that is completely pointless outside of introducing the demonic Woodland Critters and Santa, and making them fight one another.
Fight mechanics-wise, the game plays out like a very limited grid-based strategy RPG. The fighting area is small and your characters cannot occupy the same space as another character, friend or enemy, or any stage hazards. It feels unessecarily slow, possibly because of things like being unable to skip the Ultimate attack cutscenes even if you've seen them twenty times already. Attacks all have a certain shape to the squares they can attack, with most being designed to attack along the horizontal plane. Vertically, your options are very limited - apparently characters can punch to their right or left easily, but if someone is standing directly in front of them its an impossibility.
There is a knockback feature in combat that works fairly well, allowing you some limited control over where the enemy is on the map. There is only one big battle I can remember that requires some good use of knockback in order to damage an otherwise undamageable boss. One gripe I have with boss fights in this game is that some of them seem to be the only place to use a certain power, period - for example, one late game boss prompts you to gain a new ability... which you never use in combat again.
There are some scavenger-type missions if you're into that sort of thing, and pre-fast-travel South Park feels a bit of a slog to explore (especially if you don't have all the buddy powers unlocked). But overall, the whole experience is over too soon. At 26-ish hours I've completed all but one scavenger hunt mission (which isn't worth booting the game back up for), with the incentive to replay the game being borderline non-existant (no new game+? C'mon guys).
Overall, this is a mediocre gimmick-filled reference-spewing 25-30 hour game with one of the worst actual endings (and final bosses) in my recent memory. But it is decidedly a South Park game, fitting the style of the series well even if it tries to cram in too many shallow references.
I'd recommend it once the price drops quite significantly.

I wanted to like
– I really did, there's lots of great stuff here, but it all falls flat.
To me there are four things that make a great adventure game: A good story, clever puzzles, interesting characters, and an interesting world for those characters to inhabit.
Deponia gets one of those four right. The world of Deponia
interesting. This great junk planet is not only a bit unique, but it is also beautifully rendered. A junk planet full of scrappy, adaptable people should be a great setting for an adventure game, right? Well...right. But that game is not
. Lets take a look at those other three categories...
Story. Can't have a good adventure game without a good story. Unfortunately for
, it didn't ship with a great story. While it starts off well enough, the plot becomes a bit predictable and uninteresting. Some reviewers have even complained about an undercurrent of misogyny in the game. My take? I can certainly see what those reviewers are talking about, but I'm not going to go into that here. Lets just say that there are few women in the game. Of those women: one gets naked, one is unconcious for 90% of the game, and the other is a man. And the unconcious one? Getting her and winning her over is the goal of the game. Her name? Goal. Clever.
Puzzles. Some are good, but most fall into the "meh" or unintuitive category. Puzzles don't have to be unintuitive to be wacky or challenging. It's a cheat, and a poor one at that.
Characters...well...they're forgettable. That's not the worst crime though. The worst crime is that the main character - the one you should be made to empathize with (or at least get a good laugh out of) is actually irratating and unlikeable. Rufus, who is supposed to be a likeable slacker with a sharp wit and an inflated ego often comes off as posessing a grating personality with few likeable qualities. The puns? Bad...in a bad way. A few might be amusing, but the rest are either cringeworthy or fall flat.
My recommendation: Skip it or wait to pick it up in a bundle on the cheap - and only if you're desperate.

I have a mixed bag of games I enjoy, I play COD and BF, GTAO etc, as well as games like Farming Sims and this game. One thing about a lot of the bad reviews for this Train Sim game is those gamers are probably the ones who need a fast paced game like COD etc.
One telltale sign I see on the bad reviews is low hours in the game, 1.7’s and 3’s and 5’s. Why I think those gamers have given the game a bad review, is mostly because they haven't really played the game properly, or are those who want to rush it, (just watch a lot of YouTube videos to see that kind of thing).
In this game you cannot just rush up to a station and slam the brakes on! You will end up stopping a mile and a half beyond that station with the passengers complaining of whiplash!
Those complaining gamers are not really train-sim fans and not interested in learning to use the controls and don’t have the patience to sit there with nothing much else to do except sound the horn and hit a button or two every once in awhile. It's like asking an air pilot if he enjoyed the slow sea voyage.
This game ‘IS difficult’ to play and keep the train on schedule, I do my best, but often that’s not good enough for the game's unforgiving chastisements for speeding and being late, early or even missing a station or failing to stop at a light. There’s a handful of missions I just cannot get past..
The other bad reviews that I don’t understand are the ones that have hundreds of hours in the game, and they have still given it a bad review and claimed it’s a boring game, (yes there are some), Are they stupid? Why would you play a game for so long if it wasn’t interesting, challenging, entertaining and addictive, their very own - ‘hours-spent playing it’ - record proves it!
Train Sim is one of my Fav games, although STEAM claims I only have 86 hours on record on this account. - I play this on another STEAM account too, where I have over 300 hours invested.  That should speak volumes to you, if you are on the fence about buying this Sim.
If you are a real and true train sim fan - buy it, if you are not, and COD, BF or Rocket League is more your speed, then simply don’t buy it, you will be disappointed!
It's more than just a train sim, to me it's a hobby and a passion. I play a lot of train sim layout and building sims too, so this is a nice change to have the tracks all set out and waiting for you to drive. As well as scenery to see and challenges to complete.
Just be careful that it doesn’t become an addiction like it has with me, or it could end up costing you an arm and a leg in add-ons. That’s the only real drawback. They are always updating the game and bringing out new add-ons that I simply have to buy.
TIP: If this game really grabs you, it's going to be expensive! Take a look at all the add-ons!
I play this particular account across two PC’s so the STEAM Cloud comes in handy, although it doesn’t always update or sync when I want to play. I did lose quite a bit of progress upto the point where I noticed the STEAM cloud wasn’t always syncing properly. Now I just keep a written note.
TIP: If you do play across two or more PC’s, keep an A5 notebook if you can, - to keep track of all your games on STEAM so that you know what money / level / targets you already acquired..
Or else the STEAM cloud trolls you and you won’t even know it!

Surgeon Simulator, if I were to sum it up, is 20 minutes of hilarious insanity, followed by a few hours of frustration, mixed with the occasional, satisfying, successful procedures.
Surgeon Simulator is packed with hilarious moments of utter chaos and insanity, such as performing dental surgery with a hatchet, bonesaw, and pencil, or trying to figure out the hilariously awkward controls to perform simple tasks like picking up your phone, or putting a floppy disk in a computer. You have probably seen all that on You Tube.
But after about 20 minutes (varies from person to person), but the chaos gets old really quickly. And then comes the frustration.
You'll be trying to actually finish a surgery, only to be constantly pestered by your character's inability to perform simple tasks, such as picking up items, cramming his hand into tight places, putting more than 20 centimeters between his hand and the patient, inability to peek around his arm, and last but not least his spontanious fits of cerebral palsy.
Which is to say that sometimes your character will fail to pick up items despite his hand being straight on top of them when you flex the fingers, the reach of your arm is so short you cannot reach the farthest edges of the operating table, and in surgeries where the patient is upright, you can barely get your hand over your patient's head, making it nigh impossible to avoid smacking your patient in the face with whatever you're wielding. Besides that, your arm will almost constantly be blocking the view of either your tool or the organ you're trying to sever, and you will constantly drop things despite having a firm grip on them.
These arduous controls are what make the game fun for the first twenty minutes of intentional chaos and carnage, but are also what makes the rest of the game time horrible, and filled with unintentional chaos and carnage.
It does have plenty of good humor, though. I particullalartly liked the TF2 easter egg.
I have decided not to recommend it, but this is only because I would not recommend it at its normal price. I bought it during a sale, and that is probably the primary reason I am not overly disappointed with the game.
If you like chaos and mayhem and randomness, then you'll probably have a good time. If you like to get stuff done, then this is really, really not the game for you.

I've had this game for awhile now, forgot to make a review,
The game is great, challenging and full of adventure. Mods make it worth your time, and the battles when scaled higher are amazing. (Viking Conquest does this for you already up to 750)
Just a few pointers,
Battle size can be changed in your documents/warband/rgl.txt file, under battle size, should be at 1.0000 changing the single digit nearly doubles the actual size, very performance heavy. ex. 2.0000 will be 270 units instead of 150. Or 2.5000 will be 240 or so.
Turning AA and particle systems off, makes the Fps go up alot even on a super computer.
Now for Load Textures on Demand. If you have a modern day computer this should ALWAYS be off. Makes the game run way smoother on a medium to high end computers. Basically when it's off it loads everything before the battle so there's not as much lag. > (somewhat Longer loading periods between battles)
Now to do this on Modules that are from workshop/moddb/nexus etc. (Don't go to nexus). Moddb is prefered, You have to go into the individual Module.ini and add the following lines under the mod name. Without doing this you will recieve a crash as most modules don't have the following lines.
reduce_texture_loader_memory_usage = 1
use_texture_degration_cache = 0
use_scene_unloading = 1
If you have a newer GTX card you can use DSR in your Nvidia game lib to run the game at 4k upscale. Makes it look a little neater.
Hope this helps people, great game. Bannerlord will be even greater I'm sure.

TL;DR: Unless you are OK with a painful 300 hour grind or investing hundreds of dollars in a free to play game before you have enough stuff to compensate for the extremely punishing play that newbies have to endure, stay away.
=====
At the bottom of this window is the question: "Do you recommend this game?" and to me, that is the same question as, "Do you recommend the use of crack cocaine?". The short and not so sweet answer is NO!
Here's why:
Just like crack, once you start down the dangerous path of use of this game, you'll most likely get addicted. But doing something through addiction doesn't mean it's healthy, good, or even fun. Same goes with this game. Well OK, this game *IS* fun. Sometimes. But it is much more frustrating than fun, that is for sure. Look at other negative reviews, a lot say the same thing. There's a reason for that.
This is a free-to-play game, and is definitely *NOT* pay-to-win. That being said, the game will tempt you into putting paycheck after paycheck into it. I added how much you would need to just buy top hardware for each soldier, for one soldier per class, per faction: $5,000. That's right, U.S. Dollars, equivalent to about 4,000 euro.
It's not pay-to-win because, you will eventually discover that your starter weapon is pretty much the best all-around gun in the game, no matter which faction you choose. There are of course situationally better weapons (SMGs for short range, Bolt-Action for long range, etc.) There are tons of upgrades for each weapon and they make a huge difference.
But it's free, and if you try it, chances are you will find this game is pretty fun, and that with some better equipment, and the larger battles that await as you rank up, the game REALLY CAN get epic. And it can, rather it *COULD*. Except it will disappoint and frustrate you, but we will start with the good.
THE GOOD:
========
- Recreates the WW2 atmosphere with realistic weapons and vehicles
- 3 major factions, the USA, Germany and the USSR
- Minor factions are promised to be added
- The maps are big
- The war mode: thousands of players participate simultaneously in a huge campaign
- I can't emphasize this enough, the aforementioned War makes this game completely unique
- There are tons of unlocks
- Weapons and vehicles can be upgraded
- The skill ceiling is fairly high
- There can be 3-way battles
- Teamwork with friends or with a clan is a complete blast
- It runs decently and the FPS game very rarely crashes
THE BAD:
=======
- The game is designed to make you wait, run, die, wait again, run again, die again. So that you really really want to unlock that jeep, that bike, that whatever vehicle that will prevent that god-forsaken running insanity. -=FRUSTRATION=-
- The game is designed to make you want the equipment, the guns, the upgrades, and these cost credits. You must also unlock them first, and this requires XP. You get both of those by playing the game. Except of course, since you really really want those, you'll tend to focus on things that give you the most, sort of. So if a player wants to boost his recon unlocks, he needs to get long-range kills. That's why he's sitting miles from the action even though you need to capture that objective NOW and need every body on it. It's not in his plan, he needs long-range kills. Every class and every weapon has this sort of game-disrupting mechanic. -=FRUSTRATION=-
- The game trains players to play a single-player game ("Teammates? Nah, there's just ME, MYSELF AND I" type of attitude. And if you think it's bad in other games, wait until a teammate spawns the very last jeep of the game, drives away from spawn, leaving 8 teammates stranded who are all begging for a lift, and goes to crash himself against a tree, destroying the jeep and all hope of winning. This is one example from an endless list.) -=FRUSTRATION=-
- The game used to have bonuses for doing smart things. But no more. So, that objective that was just captured, there is pretty much no bonus at all for defending it, while there is massive XP & Credits for capturing the next. So? Nobody defends. They all rush on to the next, and if the team loses the previous? Well, we will cap it again! Yay, more XP & Cr! Except that's not winning, that's losing while making the most XP & Credits, which is exactly what the game trains the players to do. -=FRUSTRATION=-
- You are playing as a tanker? Good luck! Your "friendly" infantry will blatantly ignore the anti-tank dudes in the process of destroying your tank. They don't care that without tanks they will lose. XP & Cr for "ME ME ME ME ME", that's all that counts. -=FRUSTRATION=-
- The list of ways this game trains the players to commit the most destructive insanity is nearly endless. -=FRUSTRATION=-
CONCLUSION
=========
This is a game unlike any other, combining MMO, FPS and RTS elements. It has so many things going for it, too bad it has even more going against it.
The worst is, the developers could EASILY fix EVERY SINGLE THING that makes this game an exercise in extreme frustration.
Maybe its community acts with such extreme retardation because the game is free to play, and it attracts morons and other un-gifted people that could never hold a job or function in society in the first place. Or maybe it's the game design that encourages it and this er... more easily influenced segment of the population goes for it to the max. Either way, the community sucks to the max and beyond.
The frustration makes you throw money at the game so you can end up enjoying it, but sadly your teammates are all farming XP, Credits and ribbons, and not actually playing the battle like a battle should be played. So it doesn't matter that you have equipment, vehicles, weapons and all that. You won't win, the teammates are not interested in that.
As such, this game is like crack cocaine: it promises greatness, but that promise can never be realized, it only results in emptying your wallet and make you curse mankind.
If you have a large group of friends to team up with though, you can largely ignore the destructive, blatant, wanton stupidity and have a great time.

Personal review of: S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky
Mods: S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky Complete
Difficulty: Master
S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky is a sequel/prequel to the events prior to Shadow of Chernobyl. Taking place in 2011, where a second emission took place and created the Zone, a place filled with mutants, strange anomalies, and it's populated by STALKERS, basically scavengers/fighters/artifact seekers, you get the point. You play as Scar, a veteran STALKER chasing down Strelok when an emission hits and you are left incapacitated. You wake up at Clear Sky base, a swamp base where this faction is devoted to understanding the Zone and learning all it's secrets and uncovering the strange phenomens going on. After you finish a few tasks you are free to explore the Zone and side with whatever faction you want, explore and play the game. I won't say more than this since it took me 2,5 hours just to leave the Swamp areas (doing quests, exploring etc.), so the rest is up to you to find out. The game is built on the same X-Ray engine, with a few updated changes. Mainly the AI has been tweeked to fit the new faction war system, visuals have been upped, and many more changes have been implemented. As far as Stalker Clear Sky goes, almost all the weapons have been reused for this prequel, half of the areas too meaning you will revisit some familiar places while exploring new ones. Enemies, NPC's too, so you might find the actual content of this one a bit lacking. Onto more relevant changes, the HUD got reworked, being simplified, also the PDA got some new features, being able to track more easily your tasks, you can now see enemy/friendly factions on the radar, giving you a better understading of where they are being concentrated, etc. The hunger system has been removed, don't know why honestly, weapon upgrades are available, the way you collect/obtain artifacts has also been changed, to the point where you need to use an artifact detector to "see" them. This also implies you will have to walk into the middle of anomalies and hope you won't get killed before you collect them. Stalker Clear Sky has received some flak, being the "weakest" part of the trilogy, and I can see why. This game really kicks you in the balls, same as Shadow of Chernobyl, you start off really underpowered, with little to no ammo/supplies to push through the onslaught of enemies in the Swamp areas. Beware, playing this game and rushing the main storyline will result in a frustratingly hard game. I recommend taking your time and exploring, doing side-quests, parting with different factions as it will result in a much more relaxed experience. It's hard as ♥♥♥♥. There's no doubt about it. But why is it hard? All Stalker games are hard, there's no question about it, this is how these games were built, as an PC exclusive hardcore survival/rpg-ish experience, but S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky comes short in some areas. The thing is the atmosphere, lighting, texture quality is on par and beyond it's first game, but it falls flat in AI behaviour, there are less underground areas to explore (which were a highlight), side tasks include a lot of fetching and killing. These are the most basic things about it. Then we move into combat, wich remains largely unchanged except for one thing.
, I can't stres enough how annoying this addition is, not only will NPC's hit you 90% with them, they will also result in an instant death on higher difficutly levels, which is not very Stalker like. We all know how you can't really take cover in these games, being surrounded by anomalies, high radiation levels and NPC's throwing grenades makes the combat feel unfair at times. Also the fact that they still use the same weapons as you use, only with 100% accuracy and 0 bullet drop is just horse♥♥♥♥♥♥ Seriously. My main gripe with this game is the combat. It feels so random and so luck based that it's the single thing that really kills this game. Don't get me wrong, this is a massive game, with tons of stuf to do, but when it comes to combat (being an FPS game also) it sucks. It just ♥♥♥♥ing sucks. Bullets dance around hitboxes all the time, it feels like when you shoot in S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky you play roullete or you roll the dice. It all comes down to what the game wants to hit, not you. Fully upgraded weapons feel the same, so there's no excuse here. Secondly, the last part of the game (Once you reach Limansk) is just A grade bullcrap. This whole area is designed around enemies placed in hard to reach/predict areas, Monolith soldiers are so buffed, I died almost 50 times in the last part of the game alone. Seriously, a fully upgraded suit will only serve to protect you against 2-3 bullets maximum. There are also a lot of engine crashes here and plenty of bugs, so expect to be disappointed near the end of the game. And now, we have to move to the Chernobyl NPP area.
Once you reach Chernobly, this is where the game was at it's worst. First off, there are so many enemies at once, it's likely you will die 90% of the time without any chance of shooting back. Why? They never miss, they take 10-15 bullets to get killed. Also you're presured by the fac that you have to hit Strelok with a gun that isn't effective at all against all the Monolith soldiers being spawned  in this area. This last level is probably one of the worst I've ever played. No joke, hitscan enemies everywhere, almost 0 cover and little or no indication to what you're supposed to do or where Strelok is, I'm not asking for a ♥♥♥♥ing bullseye above his head, but seriously the minimap is useless here, and so are the teleporters, serving only to confuse the player. Want to know how♥♥♥♥♥♥this level is? It took me one hour to finish it, only because I died constantly and 70% of the time I was loading my last save game. When I did finish it, Strelok got stuck in an area off screen, seriously, he was outside Chernobyl and I was able to snipe him only to get the ending which only disappointed me. I played SoC and CoP and those game featured multiple endings, to my delight, here it's just the same 30 seconds cutscene, which I won't discuss for the sake of your own discovery. Anyways, let's cut the crap since this game is from 2008 and I've talked so much already nobody is going to bother reading this anyway, so here is a small list of what works and what doesn't in the 2nd Stalker instalment

Another solid fighting entry from Netherealms Studio.
Pro:
- Amazing graphic. All the moves are fantastically animated and looks cool. Charactor models are so detailed and amazing.
- Some very interesting new characters. Ferra/Torr is the coolest little girl in fighting games, ever.
- Old charactors grew up in age and have their children joining the fight. A tip of hat to those of us who grew up playing the series.
- Improved fighting mechanics over MK9. Fighting is more fluid. Pacing is fast and furious. Many cool special moves that increases the strategic depth of each charactors.
- Charactor variations add more depth.
- A lot of stage interactions. Each stage feels unique with's it's own atmosphere and lighting. Each location feels exotic. You can kill your opponent by throwing an old-lady bystander at him LOL.
- Amazing fatality, brutality, x-ray moves. As a real life osteopath and anatomist, I can say that the anatomical detail is very accurate. Totally brutal to behold.
Con:
- DLC galore! Day 1 DLC, paid unlock, paid easy fatality. Also there are many charactors you can face but cannot play (Rain, Baraka) hinting future cash grabs.
- Many people are experiencing frame rate issue, although I had no problem so far. I play it on R9 290x BTW. (Edit, new patch actually screwed up all AMD users. Now all of us have to roll back to older catalyst driver or suffer graphical glitch on one of the stages.)
- Many unexplained game freezing. Mostly in menus or when accessing online features.
- Story feels half-hazardly put together. Nowhere near the epic feel of MK9 or Injustice, but still league ahead of other fighting games.
- Only 13 stages with 3 more variations. Seriously? MK9 had 26.
- Netcode inconsistent. Waited 5 min on a Friday afternoon cannot find a simple player match? But other days were fine. Online match is often plagued with lag. Playable but annoying.
- Leaderboard is full of cheaters. Not cool.
Conclusion: A well made fighting game that is fast and furious. a few points taken off for technical flaws and questionable business model. 7/10. Recommended though...

A Tale of Two Sons is a very interesting game. You play as two brothers who must embark on a treacherous journey to save their ill father. Using a controller is a must. You control both brothers at a time, solving puzzles and evading enemies. When I played it, I was playing with my older brother (Im 17, he's 21) so I controlled the younger brother with my right hand on the controller, and he controlled the older brother. The storyline is very well thought out, with several plot twists. The fact that every character in the game does not speak english (they speak similar to the Sims) makes you really understand the emotions of the characters. However, do not let the screenshots fool you. This game is dark. VERY dark. It's quite disturbing at some points, and it seems out of place, but still develops the story. Like I said before, have some tissues, because the emotions in this game run deep, and I guarentee you will cry. My brother and I did.

J'ai eu Deponia dans un bundle pack, du coup, pour le prix que j'ai payé, je ne peux décemment pas dire que ce jeu est raté. Il reste sympathique à jouer, dans une ambiance de point&click steampunk. Il y a malheureusement quelques points qui méritent d'être soulevé pour être tout à fait honnête... Et vous aider dans votre choix.
Je le noterai 4/10. Pourquoi ?
- L'univers : c'est LE gros argument de ce jeu, car le reste n'est pas très original. On se retrouve catapulté dans la vie d'un loser dont le seul rêve est de quitter sa planète vers d'autres cieux plus cléments. Tout en dessin animé, Deponia propose un traitement graphique proche du cartoon, qui annonce d'emblée l'ambiance voulue : l'humour de situation. En cela, rien à dire, ça reste cohérent et bien réalisé. Malus notable à propos des personnages : le héros est un♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥égocentrique, le seul protagoniste féminin est dans les vapes et traitée comme un objet, et les autres personnages détestent tous le héros donc eh bien... A vous de vous en tirer avec ça.
- Les énigmes : ni trop dures, ni trop faciles. Certaines vous donneront du fil à retordre, même si l'ensemble est réalisable sans avoir besoin de réfléchir des jours durant. Le gros point noir reste l'évident manque d'ergonomie du jeu, ce qui le rend bien trop leeeeent. En effet, certaines énigmes vous demanderont des allers/retours entre les tableaux, et vu la vitesse de votre personnage... Cela pourra en frustrer plus d'un.
- L'arc narratif : convenu, bien que souvent rafraîchissant de par son traitement décalé. En gros : c'est fun, ça fait parfois sourire, mais l'histoire a tendance à sérieusement se dégrader en deuxième partie du jeu. C'est bien dommage... La fin arrive comme un cheveu sur la soupe : qui aurait voulu ça ?
- La musique et les bruitages : un point supplémentaire pour la première, aussitôt gâché par les seconds. Les chansons entre les actes sont originales, entraînantes et à propos, mais alors les bruitages, les bruitages, mon dieu...! Trop présents, trop forts, trop longs... Certains vous suivent durant tout votre déplacement, et couplé à la vitesse légendaire de votre personnage... Vous imaginez fort bien le tableau lorsque vous êtes dans l'obligation de traverser toute la map avec le bruit strident d'une sirène d'alarme. Juste POURQUOI.
En conclusion, c'est un jeu que je regrette d'avoir terminé. Non pas parce que le plaisir d'y jouer s'est fini, mais parce qu'après le début si prometteur, en arriver à cette fin... C'est presque criminel. Vraiment dommage. Une note peut-être nuançable si on envisage la trilogie.

Hate Plus is amazing. It's a deceptively simple visual novel follow up to the excellent Analogue: A Hate Story, but it's so much more than that. Where the first game succeeded by hitting a variety of visual novel tropes perfectly for an incredibly satisfying experience, this game succeeds by being the exact opposite. Hate Plus will defy your expectations at every turn and frustrate you beyond belief, in the best possible way. Import your saves from the previous game and struggle through another round of cute flirting mixed with traumatic ethical quandaries as you try to convince yourself you're getting a happy ending. Watch out for day 3!

Excellent follow-up to Analogue a Hate Story. Both of these games don't follow the traditional Visual Novel formula. Yes, you still interact with 2d beautiful, anime girls, but you are acting more as a historian than as an actual character in a story. The way that you go through text files and read the unfolding drama is fascinating and intriguing, and the writing does a good job of making absolutely everyone feel sympathetic, even the worst characters in the game. If you've never played a visual novel, give Analogue and it's sequel a chance.
P.S. The interface in this game is drastically better than the one in the original Analogue, especially since you can look up character names by clicking on them. But you won't understand this game AT ALL if you don't play Analogue first, so go do that. It only takes about 3 hours for each title, so it's not a huge time sink.

Huh.
Well, I'm not sure what to say about this game.
First of all, I found the beginning delightful.  I felt like I'd stumbled across a game where they did everything right.  Moving from area to area did not mean waiting for your character to amble on over, because 99.9999% of the time, they gave you an option to 'instant-travel' to the next screen.  Glorious.  Dialogue was skippable.  Double-glorious.  Cutscenes were quick, witty, and to the point.  Super glorious!  And the main character appeared to be one of those loveable jerks that you just can't help but love.  Unfortunately 'appeared to be' was kind of what it turned out to be.
I found that at about the point where Rufus is stumbling around the Lower Ascension Station, the game experienced a sudden drag.  Where on the first night I played far too long, the second night I found myself easily deciding to continue playing another time, and the third night I simply argued myself into finishing it for the sake of finishing it.  And unfortunately I have to pin this mostly on the main character.  Rufus turns out not to be a loveable jerk, but just a jerk.  A really selfish, thoughtless, egotistical jerk.  He spends about 90% of the game being that jerk, and then suddenly at the last moment does a 180 just in time for the game to end 'happily'.  Now, I did *like* how they managed to pull a last-minute win out of the bag, but unfortunately I felt like Rufus's character wasn't believable as a nice guy because he'd spent far too long in the game verbally abusing everybody, and treating Goal (oh, god, that name) like a realdoll.  From consistently lying to her about who he was to her, to referring to her as "his", to ♥♥♥♥ing around with her memory whenever he feels like it, to... well, it was just weirdly uncomfortable, especially as there's no real explanation for Goal.  What the hell is she?  WHY is she?  What is her purpose in the game?  Because she seems to have been Cletus' realdoll too, and the way the rest of the town treated her it felt like that was how they viewed her too, and that just made it WAY weirder as the game progressed.
My only other complaint is that the voices of the Orgonians were physically painful to listen to - every time they showed up I had to turn the volume down to half what it was, meaning I could barely hear the other characters.  Turn it up to hear the other characters once they'd gone, then bam, hearing blasted again when they show up again for another 3 lines.
This is one of those games where I really dislike the black-and-white "yes" or "no" choice you're given for rating the games on Steam.  Because I honestly even now can't really decide.  I think it did a lot of things right, but in the end the characters - a jerk and a realdoll - failed to hold up the story sufficiently to keep me interested in what happened to them.  Which is a shame, because that ending would have been a *lot* more affecting if I'd gotten as attached to the characters as the game clearly hoped I had by that point.  Therefore, I give it a reluctant "no" and hold out hopes that the company has or will take all the things it got right in this game and apply it to better in the future.

What makes Spelunky different from your average game?
The average game coaxes you gently. It gives you a gentle push in the right direction, like a father teaching a son how to ride a bike. It watches eagerly as you improve and master the game.
Spelunky pushes you onto the ground and beats you again and again with a club until you agree to its terms. Then, it watches as you try to survive and fail yet again. And it laughs.
But when you conquer the average game, you feel like you've done no more than a walk down a straight path.
When you conquer Spelunky, you feel like you've climbed the mountain.
