TL;DR: Unless you are OK with a painful 300 hour grind or investing hundreds of dollars in a free to play game before you have enough stuff to compensate for the extremely punishing play that newbies have to endure, stay away.
=====
At the bottom of this window is the question: "Do you recommend this game?" and to me, that is the same question as, "Do you recommend the use of crack cocaine?". The short and not so sweet answer is NO!
Here's why:
Just like crack, once you start down the dangerous path of use of this game, you'll most likely get addicted. But doing something through addiction doesn't mean it's healthy, good, or even fun. Same goes with this game. Well OK, this game *IS* fun. Sometimes. But it is much more frustrating than fun, that is for sure. Look at other negative reviews, a lot say the same thing. There's a reason for that.
This is a free-to-play game, and is definitely *NOT* pay-to-win. That being said, the game will tempt you into putting paycheck after paycheck into it. I added how much you would need to just buy top hardware for each soldier, for one soldier per class, per faction: $5,000. That's right, U.S. Dollars, equivalent to about 4,000 euro.
It's not pay-to-win because, you will eventually discover that your starter weapon is pretty much the best all-around gun in the game, no matter which faction you choose. There are of course situationally better weapons (SMGs for short range, Bolt-Action for long range, etc.) There are tons of upgrades for each weapon and they make a huge difference.
But it's free, and if you try it, chances are you will find this game is pretty fun, and that with some better equipment, and the larger battles that await as you rank up, the game REALLY CAN get epic. And it can, rather it *COULD*. Except it will disappoint and frustrate you, but we will start with the good.
THE GOOD:
========
- Recreates the WW2 atmosphere with realistic weapons and vehicles
- 3 major factions, the USA, Germany and the USSR
- Minor factions are promised to be added
- The maps are big
- The war mode: thousands of players participate simultaneously in a huge campaign
- I can't emphasize this enough, the aforementioned War makes this game completely unique
- There are tons of unlocks
- Weapons and vehicles can be upgraded
- The skill ceiling is fairly high
- There can be 3-way battles
- Teamwork with friends or with a clan is a complete blast
- It runs decently and the FPS game very rarely crashes
THE BAD:
=======
- The game is designed to make you wait, run, die, wait again, run again, die again. So that you really really want to unlock that jeep, that bike, that whatever vehicle that will prevent that god-forsaken running insanity. -=FRUSTRATION=-
- The game is designed to make you want the equipment, the guns, the upgrades, and these cost credits. You must also unlock them first, and this requires XP. You get both of those by playing the game. Except of course, since you really really want those, you'll tend to focus on things that give you the most, sort of. So if a player wants to boost his recon unlocks, he needs to get long-range kills. That's why he's sitting miles from the action even though you need to capture that objective NOW and need every body on it. It's not in his plan, he needs long-range kills. Every class and every weapon has this sort of game-disrupting mechanic. -=FRUSTRATION=-
- The game trains players to play a single-player game ("Teammates? Nah, there's just ME, MYSELF AND I" type of attitude. And if you think it's bad in other games, wait until a teammate spawns the very last jeep of the game, drives away from spawn, leaving 8 teammates stranded who are all begging for a lift, and goes to crash himself against a tree, destroying the jeep and all hope of winning. This is one example from an endless list.) -=FRUSTRATION=-
- The game used to have bonuses for doing smart things. But no more. So, that objective that was just captured, there is pretty much no bonus at all for defending it, while there is massive XP & Credits for capturing the next. So? Nobody defends. They all rush on to the next, and if the team loses the previous? Well, we will cap it again! Yay, more XP & Cr! Except that's not winning, that's losing while making the most XP & Credits, which is exactly what the game trains the players to do. -=FRUSTRATION=-
- You are playing as a tanker? Good luck! Your "friendly" infantry will blatantly ignore the anti-tank dudes in the process of destroying your tank. They don't care that without tanks they will lose. XP & Cr for "ME ME ME ME ME", that's all that counts. -=FRUSTRATION=-
- The list of ways this game trains the players to commit the most destructive insanity is nearly endless. -=FRUSTRATION=-
CONCLUSION
=========
This is a game unlike any other, combining MMO, FPS and RTS elements. It has so many things going for it, too bad it has even more going against it.
The worst is, the developers could EASILY fix EVERY SINGLE THING that makes this game an exercise in extreme frustration.
Maybe its community acts with such extreme retardation because the game is free to play, and it attracts morons and other un-gifted people that could never hold a job or function in society in the first place. Or maybe it's the game design that encourages it and this er... more easily influenced segment of the population goes for it to the max. Either way, the community sucks to the max and beyond.
The frustration makes you throw money at the game so you can end up enjoying it, but sadly your teammates are all farming XP, Credits and ribbons, and not actually playing the battle like a battle should be played. So it doesn't matter that you have equipment, vehicles, weapons and all that. You won't win, the teammates are not interested in that.
As such, this game is like crack cocaine: it promises greatness, but that promise can never be realized, it only results in emptying your wallet and make you curse mankind.
If you have a large group of friends to team up with though, you can largely ignore the destructive, blatant, wanton stupidity and have a great time.

Universally considered the "worst" STALKER game out of the three, it is not necessarily a bad game. In short, if you like any other STALKER game you should give this a playthrough.
This game lacks the bleakness and some of the atmosphere found mainly in Shadow of Chernobyl but also Call of Pripyat. The Zone is very populated by NPCs compared to other STALKER games which very much contributes to the fact that the environment feels less hostile. Compared to the 4 horror centric underground areas of SHoC, Clear Sky only has one that is less frightening compared to the SHoC counterparts. Compared to unmodded SHoC, Clear Sky is in many ways a bit more polished in terms of better animation quality, graphical effects and user interface. Clear Sky also introduces a much welcomed weapon upgrade/repair system that was absent from SHoC.
While I generally think that the first time you play a STALKER game it should be unmodded I would say that I make an exception for Clear Sky. Clear Sky unmodded has some issues that are flat out annoying and I would consider it bare minimum to install the Sky Reclamation Project (latest version as of 2015-06-30 is 1.0.4) to fix most of those issues. SRP is still pretty close to a vanilla experience and is provided mainly to fix various bugs.
I would also like to mention the following mods that doesn't impact gameplay but makes it look a bit better.
Atmosfear 1.3 - Improves weather effects, improves game atmosphere (This is also available for Call of Pripyat)
Absolute Nature/Structures - High resolution texture mods that makes things look a bit more crisp (This is also available for Shadow of Chernobyl and Call of Pripyat)

Let's get first things first: Sniper Elite 3 is not a realistic sniping game. It's a third person shooter with stealth elements. The plot is as follows: Nazis have secret weapon and America Man needs to destroy it.
Most of the marketing focuses around "celebrated rifle ballistics" which is really stretching the things on offer. The series is already over 10 years old and when it was new, this might have been true. What you have here is a sniping system that has many elements: Sights wobble, bullets drop and are effected by the wind. Also the player needs to hold breath to focus the shots. Wind is the only thing that is not also present in most of modern shooters so it's not that special. It takes a bit of skill and luck to hit enemies while timing shots with sounds of passing planes etc. It's a nice spice to the standard gameplay but with the level design and mission objectives that Sniper Elite has, it is in no way realistic.
While there are many elements to the sniping, some key things are missing. Most notable is penetration. Bullets won't pass even through wooden fences! Kills at 20 meters are much more common than they should be and a "long distance" kill is awarded at over some 170 meters. This doesn't feel realistic at all.
Maps are fairly large and kind of open. A single map might have 3 objectives, which are all in their own areas such as a depot or a village. In these areas it's possible to move about quite freely, but the areas are divided from each other by canyons and other tight corridors. So it's not open world but a series of open "arenas". Often the map design feels really forced and make no real-world sense. This also ensures that you'll never have more than about 300 meters of space from end to end. For a shooter it's ok, but for a sniping game it's not.
Sniper Elite 3 puts a lot of emphasis on sneaking and it is possible to sneak for really long parts of the levels, silently taking out guards, dragging bodies, luring with noise, setting traps etc. Usually things go badly at some point and after that it's just your regular shooter. Even on the hardest (custom) difficulty, the player can take a load of bullets with ease and the game doesn't punish for going guns blazing. No mission failures, no overwhelming enemies, nothing. Maybe some of the achievements are lost but that's it. This is by far the biggest weakness because there is no need to stay silent. It really doesn't matter if you get caught and some 30 infantry are alerted. It's too easy and also faster to kill them the loud way. Hardest difficulty on offer (authentic) removes saving and sounds like tedium the game. As it's hardly suitable for co-op, this review is based on custom difficulty with hardest AI and ballistic realism.
Enemy AI is seriously flawed in that they don't coordinate with eachother in any way. They will spot corpses and hear gunshots etc. but they work as individuals. Also they will forget strange sounds and such almost immediately and never raise a base-wide alarm. Relocation system is a key selling point in Sniper Elite 3 but it's kind of silly. If spotted a radius of 50 meters appears around the last known location of the player. Run out of that area and your relocation is instantly succesful and enemies no longer no where you are. If you for example get spotted in a bunker with a 50 meter long dead end corridor, just run to the other end and you are hidden again.
Most of the levels end in a showdown against a tank which of course appears without infantry support and must be destroyed with conveniently available mines or rocket launchers. This is always a mission objective and you can't sneak away from the area. In some missions the player takes spot in a sniper nest and covers someones exit. These kinds of missions usually end with over a 100 kills. And of course maps are littered with red barrels and canisters that explode from a single bullet. Sniper Elite 3 clearly is just a standard third person shooter.
As a standard shooter Sniper Elite 3 is actually ok. Main campaing can be played in co-op and it's forgettable but fun. In co-op the main campaign can be completed in less than 7 hours. Season pass adds some more, but overall the game is really short. It is possible to coordinate with a parther but its not necessary. There are unscriped moments where best action is to eliminate two guards with simultaneous shooting and setting those up feels great. Deponia is a great game. Maybe not quite as great as The Walking Dead or Sam & Max, but if you like adventure games and already worked over Tell Tale's catalog then Deponia is pretty great.
There are a few caveats though. Things that, if they rub you the wrong way might ruin your enjoyment.
1) Rufus is a dingbat. No, worse... he's a teenager. Stereotypical in his awful self centered laziness. It's well done, and great that he isn't generic angry dude #57, but he might give you flashbacks of your awful teenage self. Some people might not be able to handle that. (particularly teens themselves?)
2) You know the stereotypical video game plot. Save the princess. It's a little overdone... industry wide sexism, yada yada yada, I don't care. I care if it's good or not, and it is! ... mostly. What do I mean? Well... the princess is named Goal. Think about that for a moment. I don't care what your position on the topic is, if it's a hot button topic for you then having it pointed out every time her name comes up (and it's a lot) will be fairly distracting. You could use this as ammunition for ether camp. 'See? You can have well rounded characters with funny dialogue in such a cliched plot.' or 'See? This is everything that's wrong with games right here!'. But in ether case that will mean you're not really enjoying the game anymore.
Myself I enjoyed the subtext of the game. I found that it was making fun of the cliches and the standard hero archetype. But it's so blatant it's hard to say it isn't distracting, and as I said, if it's a hot button issue for you then you might get turned off. (And no, she's not really a princess).
3) If you're a Hardcore environmentalist ... well, Deponia is a trash world. And aside from Rufus's constant complaining that the world is trash, ... it's actually kinda cool. If you're seriously invested in environmentalism, having it depicted as 'people mine through the trash heaps and build stuff out of scraps, isn't that cool?!' might be a serious bummer.
4) Nagging girlfriend. Tonii ... though with good reason.
But if you aren't overly sensitive about any of those topics you'll find Deponia an enjoyable game. Heck, it even has a satisfying ending! (though you'll still probably want the next 2 games. Turning the ending into a 'No, wait, adventure isn't over yet!' is a small eyerolling moment in the next game, but I still think it's going to get a thumbs up too.)

I've always been a fan of point-and-click adventure games, and I'm happy to count this as one of the better examples of the genre.
Now, it's not perfect - however, some of my complaints are my own fault for skipping the tutorial.
Important tips to anyone starting off:
1) Double clicking on any 'arrow' location will warp Rufus to that location, which is great, since some of the maps are big, and Rufus doesn't run. (Figured out on my own ~1/2 of the way though the game)
2) Hitting space will highlight all interactive objects. (I never found this one out, and one of my complaints was going to be that some of the puzzles were a little pixel-hunter-esque.)
Generally, I found that the game was really superb for the first 2/3rds or so - the puzzles were just straightforward enough that you could figure out most of them through intuition or through the somewhat-subtle clues that characters would say when you tried the use the objects. I was able to make it through this entire section without having to hit the internet.
The final area, however, was definitely not as polished as the rest. Puzzles weren't nearly as clear, a lot more pixel-hunting (again, my own fault for not knowing about using space), and some of the solutions were much more "you have to know what drugs the creators were on when they thought this one up." I did have to hit the web a couple times for this part (stupid whale bait.)
The story was excellent throughout, and although the humor wasn't always up to Monkey Island standards, it was always enjoyable. Most of the voice work is good. Good cast of memorable characters.
I only ran into the most minor of errors - some graphical glitches where Rufus would, instead of walking to an object to interact with it, just reach out from where he was standing. No crashes or other problems.
Overall: A great purchase for any point-and-click adventure game lover.

First of all, this is a sequel. You have to walk through Analogue: A Hate Story and continue the save. Or at least play the Hate Story. While the previous game was about.. well, hate and traditional society, this is mostly about sex.
The previous game had lots of letters written somewhere after Year 300. Now you've found lots of letters before Year 0. Why did they reset the calendar? Turns out... well, politics. Now you have 3 realtime days to read all these letters.
Based on your previous save, you have up to two AIs. Hyun-ae is a girl who's extremely curious about sex. It doesn't help that you'll be reading light LGBT erotica here. She comments every single lewd phrasing. Mute is a girl who is extremely "conservative" and shy about sex, so she also comments each time you're reading something lightly romantic. And also turns out she has a rough past, so her route is much more interesting but that comes in play only on Day 3.
The VN is good-looking but the look won against the common sense. There are lots of clunky animations. Even with full animation off, you'll have to wait for each menu to fade in. Also you read each text with your AI pals - that's a nice touch, they react to the letters but they also are a big distraction.
There is also a gameplay aspect that opposes common sense. You play in real time. After you read the first 9 letters, you actually have to "power down" your ship, save and wait 12 realtime hours to continue the game. As a result, you can feel compelled to start two walkthroughs at the same time - that's totally okay but you'll crack open all the mysteries earlier and the game would become just MORE boring.
Hate Plus is packed with text and this prose is a lazy one. Every POV character (except two) is gay, bi or asexual. This can be strongly hinted at but mostly you just read it in plain text. The only straight characters write about sex problems and sex offenders. Also every POV character is a tragic one. This comes out the wrong way because the combination of messages "she suppressed her gay nature" and "she lived her miserable life to the end" tells something I don't think the author wanted to tell here. Also I don't reckon much about the future packed with lesbians.
The game is simply boring, especially Hyun-ae route. There is no big decision to make. You just sit for 3 days, read a lot of text, have some talk with your AI pal, you can bake a cake for her and that's that. It's a weak try to give the previous game some closure, nothing else.

The sequel to A Hate Story is still based on the same concept of the original. You’re an investigator who hacked into the Mugunghwa, a colony ship that lost contact with Earth a long time ago, and you managed to save an AI(s) from the doomed vessel. Like in the previous game, they can talk to you but you can’t talk to them due to an installation error/mcguffin. You do have a few more options in what you can say but they still boil down to: yes/no/maybe. This time around, the AI has more log files from the colony ship that you didn’t get to see in the previous game. These logs have clues into what caused the enactment of the oppressive society and then the eventual events that you read about in the previous title. So, it’s time to find out what happened. This time around, the AI will actively read the logs with you and provide colorful commentary every now and again. This is especially amusing if you rescued both Hyun-ae & Mute from a previous save game. So, read the logs and find out what happened.
This game seems easier to follow than the previous one. The game provides a photo (for most) and profile for characters to help you keep track of who’s who. Logs are still setup to be read at your own pace and in the order of your choosing. That said, the game makes sure that they’re relevant regardless of when you read them. There aren’t any notes on pronunciation (which I found to be helpful in the previous game) and the two family trees aren’t listed. Probably because it wasn’t the main focus of this story. Overall, the story is about the same as the previous game in terms of how densely it uses lore, name usage and politics. Which is a bit more than the average story. But this time, you have a more solid grounding of what’s going on with the characters. Even if you’re new to this series, you’ll be brought up to speed quickly enough.
There’s a real world aspect to this game that I haven’t seen before. The store page states that it will take three days in order to finish this game. The in-game reason is that your ship is running on emergency power and has to recharge after every document extraction. So, the game will have you wait 12 real world hours before it lets you continue to the next chapter. You get about 1-2 hours per chapter. I think this will be a love/hate mechanic with a lot of people. I like it because I treat these games as something to wind down to before I go sleep, so, it gives me the right moment to save and shutdown for the night. But on the other hand, you have to wait before you can complete the game and you can’t finish the game in one go. I’m sure if you meddled with your PC’s clock, you could do it one finish. But then, where’s the fun in that? Some will like this, other’s will see it as an unnecessary inconvenience. It’s up to you to decide which way you go.
Expected genre settings are here. Text speed, animations on or off and English/Korean language. Audio sliders for music and effects are available as well. Resolutions are still restricted to 1024x640 and 1024x600. I still think those are odd resolution choices but the game scales well so I can’t complain. The UI has gone through some UI changes but keeps much of the same setup the previous game had. However, there’s an odd flickering to the UI that happens once in a while which seems to be intentional. I don’t like it because it’s more distracting than immersive. Additionally, scrolling through logs has an odd, frequent pause while reading it, especially when you have two AIs with you while reading. This seems to be caused by the frequent changes in the facial expressions of the AIs and the game checking to see if it needs to display their comments or not. It’s not a big deal. Game is stable and bug free as far as I can tell.
It continues where you left off, allowing you to load the save from the previous game or start fresh, letting you set which AI you saved and what their attitude is towards you. Hyun-ae & Mute get even more time to develop their character and backstory, though more of the focus is on Mute and what happened to her. I really like that they get to actively participate in the reading of the logs rather than sit in the background and come out every now and again to give their two cents.
While the sequel doesn't get as dark as it’s predecessor, it still paints a disturbing story of culture change and betrayal. The mystery, the futuristic setting and serious dark tone are still well executed. Maintaining it’s sci-fi atmosphere with the music and futuristic UI glues all the pieces together for a great experience in the AVN genre. Hate Plus gets a recommendation from this Paladin.

My husband and I were looking for a new game to play together after getting a little bored of Minecraft. We came across this game and were really excited! For me personally, what really sold me on this game was that it was like Minecraft BUT had this awesome component of really working together as a team to defeat mobs and bosses, and explore new worlds. While you can play this alone, I find it much more fun with a partner where you can work together.
There are definitely parts of this game I don't care for too much and hope to see improved/changed. I understand this is an Early Access game, so naturally there will be aspects of the game that need improvement. Some things that bug me is that you can't split items in your inventory, you can't drop items (you must use a chest to transfer items between people), inventory seems to fill up too quickly, you have to travel to a different world with the people you are playing with (you cannot split), and finally, only one person can use a chest/anvil/workbench, etc at a time. I have heard some really promising things about this game, and I'm excited to be there every step of the way!
Overall, this is a pretty fun game, but does need some improvement. If you like Minecraft but wished it had more combat, this game is probably for you!

(Before reading this review, read my review of stalker shadow of Chernobyl)
(And just like before I played this game on the highest difficulty and WITHOUT MODS, and don’t start whining at me saying you need to use mods)
Clear sky is a prequel and near the end happens at the same time as shadow of Chernobyl. In clear sky you play as a mercenary called Scar who is able to survive emissions and ends up working with the faction Clear sky, whose goal is to stop Strelok from reaching the middle of the zone where it is believed something catastrophic with happen.
Clear sky does add a few new things into the game since now you can upgrade and repair weapons and armour, artefacts are much rarer and you need a detector to find them, you now have guides who can take you into different places, you can side with most factions, you now need slots for artefacts and you must have a minus radiation value artefact if you have a plus radiation one to counter it otherwise you will slowly die of radiation poisoning, and the hunger and thirst system was removed so food now just acts as health items and energy drinks are just to boost your stamina, but other than that this is very much the same as shadow of Chernobyl.
Clear sky also improves a few things that were in shadow of Chernobyl, the map and PDA have been improved, most of the weapons are a bit more accurate than the previous game but they still aren’t great, moving is no longer headache inducing, and thankfully loading quick saves won’t cause the enemies to go back to their starting positions which can be right next to or in front or behind you and you'll get killed instantly.
This is still a strangely compelling game but it still comes with problems from the previous game and it adds its own.
The gunfights aren’t anywhere near as to what they were in the previous game but it is still a little random on whether you’ll get shot or not and the damage output.
The amount of bandages and med kits used to stop you from bleeding out is random to the point where sometimes it will only take one bandage, but other times you can go through all of the bandages and med kits in your inventory.
The map is incorrect with the directions used to go to this one area that’s south east of the red forest, you’d think you’d have to go to the exit pointing south east but that takes you to Garbage, you actually have to go to the NORTH exit point to get to the area that is SOUTH EAST of the red forest.
The height difference between standing and crouching is two or three inches.
Enemies can now throw grenades, they can throw grenades from over 100 yards away and they explode a second after they land and this is really annoying when you are trying to kill a group of enemies only to have a few grenades land at your feet.
Your weapons jam far too often.
Just like shadow of Chernobyl getting this game all comes down to whether you think you can put up with these problems and I actually enjoyed this a bit more than shadow of Chernobyl to a certain extent.

Brother Wings developed by Brogames for the PC platform on: Jan 10, 2017. As of this writing, there is no score/user reviews on Metacritic
. A 'shoot em up' vertical game. This product is far, far away from giving consumer a 'bullet hell' type of gaming experience nor does it even come close in providing moments of 'madness'  'excitement' 'Thrill'
It's just a very 'tame' product with very little innovation in it's design. Sadly. but that doesn't warrant it as an awful/bad game. and no, its not a terrific game either.
What is it about?
Brother Wings (BW) is an action, top down view, shoot-em up air craft game. You basically need to survive the endless waves of enemy ships on your screen. You are given to play 2 characters; Marko and Guida. Who apparently are brothers - this coming from the product description. A brother with a long pink hair? hmmmm. Hmm indeed.
The Controls
Standard WSAD keyboard and mouse. Nothing fancy.
The Visuals & User Interface
It's simple, plain, clean and bright.
The UI is simple, it shows the important stuff
it overlaps/covers the battlefield on the left hand side of the screen - which I find it annoying. I can understand that without some fancy design to show your ship life information, it may look dull..but overlapping the battlefield is a no no. Especially for a game that requires your "agility/reflex" - you practically doomed people who strafe their ship to the left - unable to see incoming enemy ships/missiles in that region.
As of this writing, BW offers 2 game mode:
There is also a leaderboard but from my own experience, I am not sure whether it's working as intended.
As the product describes, you get to play either 2 of the brother characters with (very little) "different" looking ships. You are given 5 life and your goal is to survive@destory as many ships as you can possible can. Once you lose all your life, it's game over.
Throughout your battle, you can pick up health drops and ammo drops. health drops replenish your missing life while ammo drops upgrades your ship shooting ability. Your ship starts of with a single missile firing mode. You can upgrade it to a double missile firing mode and the final form is a barrage of 5 or 6 missiles. No more.
Enemy ships comes in at least 3 forms but they only have 2 roles; mobile fighters and immobile fighters.
mobile fighters = moving targets
immobile fighters = not moving targets
There are "Boss" fights too. Sometimes 2 boss ships at once. Talk about the mess.
Other than this, there's no story, no level progression, no ship upgrade abilities, no weapon upgrade abilities (just the 3 different mode of missiles)...I think I covered it all.
My Personal Thoughts
I am not sure how to approach BW. For me, this product is sitting on a flimsy fence and depending on how I word this writing, 1 little gush of air is all it takes to topple it into the shredder machine or into a bin for safe keeping.
It's a simple product with no bugs. It has a variety looking enemies but with only 2 roles (mobile & immobile) - this hampers the gaming experience. It's not exciting. There's no thrill. If I may reference a classic game: TwinBee - for example offers so much more excitement. Different form of enemies with different movements and theres a secondary fire mode for land enemies and the random drop "bell" loot that gives upgrade to your ship..makes the whole game so much better than what BW has to offer.  (minus the co-op experience of course)
2 brothers 2 ships but there's just so little difference between them. It's just aesthetic and both ship function the same way. Why not be a little bit brave@creative and design both ship to behave differently?
As I've mentioned in the above, theres no level progression. If you added in different levels/maps - you could offer your consumer with a different gaming experience; different map/different enemies/different boss. Here in BW, 1 map. 1 song. 3-4 standard enemies. Period.

Don't be fooled by the advertising and marketing.  This seems to be yet another game designed specifically for consoles and it shows.  As soon as I poked around trying to remap controls and that 360 controller image popped up I knew what I was in for.  To be fair, the controls aren't as horrible as say, Ghostbusters (barf), which had no mouse support to begin with whatsoever, but they aren't spectacular in the least.
It's not really a First Person Shooter at all.  It's a 3rd person action game, with "sniping" that behaves more like a little mini game rather than a real FPS.  For the most part, your view is over the shoulder 3rd person.  You sneak around, creeping up on guys ala Metal Gear and shiv your way into a vantage point.  The CQB combat doesn't really pack a punch.  The only comparison I have would be those old Manhunt games.  From being a couple hours in the game already seems to be boiled down to a formula.
You sneak up on an enemy, get in range, hit E, and watch the little mini-cutscene unfold of you taking him down.  You worm your way to a vantage point and "mark" all your targets by using the binoculars ala MGSV.  Then you use the environment to mask the sound of your shots and try to take down all the guys you marked without being spotted or heard.  I'm sure as the game goes on it will stack more modules on top of this basic formula, but I can already tell 87% of the game is going to be what I wrote right here.
As for the actual "sniping" (if you can call it that) this is where the console port monster really rears its head.  See, you don't just zoom in and fire the way you do in most FPS games.  It's a little mini game of sorts, where you aim through the scope, zoom in, and hold your breath.  Most of you reading this would already be arguing about the whole 360 noscope showmanship nonsense but it doesn't really work in this game.  The entire engine is built upon forcing you to zoom in and hold your breath.  Once you're zoomed in and holding your breath, time slows down and a little red reticle diamond appears.
I can't for the life of me figure out the dymanics behind this idiotic thing.  It would be one thing if the diamond appeared on what you're trying to hit, with another diamond showing where your sites are lined up.  Then you'd have to slowly line them up while time was slowed down and zoomed in.  This is not how it works.
Instead, there seems to be some sort of goofy console FPS style auto-aim garbage interfering with this.  The single red reticle shows where your shot is going to land, but the stupid thing jumps around on its own, latching onto enemies, but only some of the time.  I'm on a friggin' PC with a mouse and a keyboard, and I can't seem to find a way to turn this moronic auto-aim off.  It absolutely wrecks my shots half the time.  There doesn't even seem to be any windage or physics behind it.  A straight shot is always a straight shot.  The red diamond reticle seems to do all the "math" for you.  The videos showing off the cool bullet-time with the bodies flying apart are pretty neat, but they're just masking the underlying awful controls which appeal to the lowest common denominator, aka: console 360 noscope auto-aim pleb twelvies.
To recap, The game is:
1. Running around from node to node.
2. Entering the sniper mini game.
3. Fighting the stupid red diamond target in hopes that you can force it onto whatever you want to shoot.
4. Clicking the fire button.
5.  Rinse and repeat.
As for technical difficulties, the game keeps going to a black screen.  I can still hear the game sounds, and I can hit ESC and hear the cursor blipping as I move it over the menu items.  I haven't figured out why, even after trying multiple graphics settings.  The environments aren't large at all and it doesn't seem to be overly demanding on my system.  This arcade shooter lacks polish all around.  If you're absolutely bored get it when it's on sale, but don't expect much out of it.

That said, the gameplay is not without its flaws and bugs that may cause you to have to reload a checkpoint which are somewhat conservative in their distribution.
Beyond the gameplay, there lies a very emotional story that makes the overall experience unforgettable. There are moments where you will be taken back by the beauty of the fantasy setting, moments of happiness along with comedic relief, but there are also moments of overwhelming sadness and remorse.
Not a perfect game, but a unique one with an emotionally-engaging plot. It should be said that the game is also pretty short; I personally was able to finish it in three hours. So Spelunky, what a dumb name. But actually the game is great, addicting and kinda infuriating. It is a side scrolling randomly generated adventure game in which every playthrough is different, Everytime you play the game you want to go off but you just cant resist playing on for a bit longer. But there is one more gamemode, one that causes you to have hatred toward your friends, this demon is called, deathmatch mode. The most intense gamemode of the entire game, with small fast paced maps, play with up to four other people, with crates containing any of the items in the game, even if nobody is online you can play against bots, but it is very hard and the bots move at an amazing pace so watch out and have fun. Also there is a mod called Frozlunky which has many features but (arguably) the best of them all is the online feature. It is a great game and that is why it deserves the rating it has gotten.

The Fractured But Whole's a good game, but in many ways is not as good as Stick of Truth. The combat mechanics were not nearly as good as in the past game. There is not as much combat modification as the last game. The armor is purely cosmetic which means you can choose any armor you want without being penalized in combat. This makes you character's looks a lot more customizable, but there is not as many ways to change your combat style. The grid style combat is not as fun as the small/ heavy attack system. The dialouge writing is not as good as it was in Stick of Truth, but is a lot more dark/ edgy. It still has the great "new kid" feeling even after you already were a major character in the last game and South Park episode feeling.
Overall the game is still good, but even though it is not very important for the games story I would recommend playing the Stick of Truth first. But if you look at various cultures throughout history, there are actually many instances of relatively egalitarian societies slowly morphing into socially stratified class systems, often drastically reducing the quality of life for a large segment of the population. Compared to

Instead of the black-on-white look from before, it goes with a striking (if still largely monochromatic) color scheme, mostly using lighter text on dark tinted backgrounds. The character sprites have seen an expansion of their palette of poses and facial expressions, making them even more expressive. Long documents are no longer paginated, instead there is free-form scrolling. Texts are imbued with hyperlinks pointing you to "

The player freedom regarding the order in which the story is explored is so much bigger that it is almost impossible to overstate. If you felt artificially constrained by

I would argue that the pendulum may have swung too far into the "player freedom" direction, as it is easy to ruin any dramatic arc and feel completely lost by choosing the wrong files early on or skipping some important ones for too long.
Your companion A.I. choice has a significant influence on the delivery of the story. Since the events documented in

One interesting mechanic that bears mentioning if only for its controversy is the
. Since you are reading the files throughout your trip back to Earth, you are twice met with a mandatory break time of twelve real-world hours, to sleep and recharge the ship's batteries. From what I've seen, many people are understandably critical of this design choice. However, I personally believe that I benefitted from the extra time I had to let the details sink in. I also know myself well enough to say that I likely would have binge-played it if this mechanic had not been in place, and I would be remembering it with less clarity right now. I understand how it might feel weird to not be solely in charge of your game pace, but I would encourage you to simply go along with it.
With much of the game being rooted in plot exploration, there is little of the story that I would want to give away here. It is more or less like

Ok so this is my first S.T.A.L.K.E.R. game and I have to say I LOVE IT. I almost didn't get it however, because of video reviews on youtube. They were all pretty negative but I have to strongly disagree with them and say I'm super glad that I got it. Now here are two things that I have seen so far to be common negatives in reviews but I haven't seen in game:
- I have not been sniped with a pistol.
- I can easily avoid grenades. (I use easily lightly. I just mean they're not like tactical nukes)
I am, by the way, using no mods. Don't get me wrong though, this game is extremely difficult. Especially if you have no idea what your doing and die from radiation without noticing it and making the same mistake... again.. and again. But to me this makes this game beautiful. It's a harsh world that you just get thrown into. If you save a lot (and I mean A LOT), you should be fine and get a hang of the game pretty quickly without too much frustration.
Another thing I will address is that some people have a problem with the shooting mechanic. I have heard that it's really just rolling the dice. Now I know this sounds bad, I thought it did, but when I actually played, I realized it wasn't as bad as it was said to be. You are going to miss, but this just adds to the realism. And the AI aren't that bad either. The worst I've seen so far is a soldier still firing his gun after all the enemies were killed, which, by my standards, isn't anything incredibly bad. They are kinda tactical and are good to fight alongside.
Now, on the line of atmosphere. IT IS PHENOMENAL. Keep in mind I don't use any mods, so this game is just made this well! Speaking mostly from the swamps, the atmosphere is pretty engaging. From the AIs all moving around and communicating within a real time world to the footsteps you can hear in the bushes alongside the path (I'm not kidding. It's creepy), this atmosphere really plays out the situation well and keeps you engaged.
So if you take anything from this review, just know that your opinion is probably different from another review, so if you're even thinking about getting it.. get it. Trust me it's worth it. DARK SOULS + FALLOUT = S.T.A.L.K.E.R.

Brother Wings seems like it is the start of a game concept rather than the finished product. With its simple yet clean graphics and variety of soundtracks to listen to while ducking and dodging the enemy fire, you'll find yourself immersed, if only for a few moments, in this very basic shooter.
Take command of your starcraft (just like in Galaxian), shoot other ships (just like Galaxian), obtain powerups that shoot multiple rockets (just like Galaxian) and do your best not to die (this is actually the only major difference!). However, avoiding enemy fire seems more like a chore as the backgrounds assist the enemy rockets in blending into the back drop, where you'll find yourself dead before you've realized what happened.

I personally purchased this game. I reviewed it for my 99 Cent Gaming series.
Being a big lover of all things SHMUPs I couldn't wait to take this game on for my first impression series. I was really afraid I'd be unfair in my review due to this love but decided I would give it my best go. Somehow, I still came away from this highly disappointed.
For starters, Time Attack mode does not work as described. Selecting this mode did not show any timer and no indicator that you were nearing the required number of enemies to reset it. At first I thought Infinity Mode was selected by accident. It wasn't. To make sure I even played Time Attack mode without killing any enemies for a couple of minutes with no consequence.
Secondly, and this is only because I've dabbled in the program's tutorials myself concerning SHMUPs, the entire game feels like the developer took all the basics from GameMaker's tutorial on how to make this type of game (or perhaps completed it fully) and swapped in his own assets without giving anything a unique spin. Everything from the scrolling background to the random movements of enemies is straight out of the basic tutorial.
Now, while the first issue is more likely a bug that can be fixed pretty easily (the developer probably just needs to delete or modify a faulty event) and will probably be addressed in an update, it's really the second issue that drove my final verdict.
Many would take the easy route and say the game just isn't good because of the lack of variety and overall feel of a copy/paste job. While others see a bad game, I see a fellow SHMUP fan taking their (or his) love for the genre and showcasing what they've learned and apply it to their own game.
Looking at this objectively (and with my love for SHMUPs) the only thing that makes me not recommend this game is having a price at all.  As I've made it a goal to only do these first impression on the premise that games are bought out of pocket, the 99 cents spent on Brother Wings was 99 cents too many. If they had released this for free as a game maker showcase, or even released this build as a demo while continuing to work on adding their own unique spin to the overall package it would have been a no brainer to recommend this. In its current form, even if Time Attack worked, I cannot recommend this game. I would love to revisit this as updates are made and hope Brogames have some planned in the future.
Usually I have more to say in my video review but every point was hit here. Check out my play through if you want to see how I reached my verdict in moving picture form xD

Oh man...  OH MAN!  Tekken on PC.  This is how I die.  I'm going to have to apologize to my wife, because I'm not totally sure that she's the most important thing in my life anymore.  *skip down to get to the review or read along to watch me reminisce*
Let me break it down for you.  I started playing Tekken in the arcades back in 1995.  When Tekken 2 came out, I had a few friends who got into it so I got a bit competitive with them.  By the time Tekken 3 rolled around, I was in college and I practiced for literally thousands of hours.  I knew every character, every mixup, every counter there was to know.  At that time the FGC wasn't really a thing, finding competition was difficult to impossibe, and I lost interest in dedicating myself that entirely to competitive fighting games.  I moved on to other games after that, but Tekken always had a special place in my heart.
Recently I started seeing ads for Tekken 7 and it brought me back to that time that I poured my heart and soul into learning everything there was to know about a fighting game.  In recent years I've played some other games... MKX, Guilty Gear, SFV... but nothing grabbed me the way Tekken did so many years ago.  I never fealt that need to dedicate myself to absolutely destroying everyone who stepped in front of me.  Up until two days before Tekken 7's release, I thought that I'd let this one pass me by.  I'm so, so, SO very glad that I didn't.  Because Tekken 7 is amazing.
*start review*
Let's start by talking about performance.  It is fantastic.  Solid 60FPS (Yes, it's locked at 60 as are ALL fighting games.  It is for technical, competitive reasons.  Please accept this as fighting game gospel and move on), maxed settings, and it is GORGEOUS.  Load times are there, but they're acceptable.  I have played online VERY little but the games that I did play were smooth.  I've heard from others that it's a mixed bag, so hopefully this game is starting from a good place and will get better as is usually the case with fighting games online.  Netcode tweaks seem to always need to happen before the community is really happy.  Character customization is fun with some great options, and is much more varied than other fighting games where you just have a choice of a different outfit/color.
Gameplay is classic Tekken.  For those who have never played a Tekken game, I will summarize in saying that each character has a staggeringly long movelist, most if not all of which are situationally useful, and the core combo system is based mostly around juggles.  As I said, I haven't played the series much in the past 18 years since Tekken 3, but I was able to hop on Ling, Nina, Heihachi, and Kazuya and pick up more or less right where I left off, knocking some of the rust off not withstanding.  Two-decade old combos still work for the most part, and after watching some videos and going into practice mode I see that I'm going to have a lot of fun learning the new optimals.  I believe the Rage system is new in this game, and right now I'm not totally sure how I feel about it.  Catch-up mechanics in fighting games have never sat particularly well with me, but it's not completely game-breaking so it's really more of a taste thing.  I wish it was handled a little more like V-Gauge is in SFV because I think that's a well-handled mechanic, but again... more of a preference thing than anything.
Story mode is... fine.  I've heard some people say that Tekken has a great story, which I don't really understand because I've never thought any fighting game had a story that was more than an excuse to have a bunch of weirdos fight each other, but to each their own.  I've played through the first few chapters and so far have just been taking over the Mishimas and catching up on the story so far.  Personally, I've been spending most of my time in the treasure mode, unlocking cosmetics while I re-learn mechanics and try to practice new combos.  It's a pretty good, rewarding way to spend bot time practicing rather than just doing it in practice mode and getting nothing other than... well... practice out of it.
The most important thing to say is this game is fun with a ton of polish.  There are a ton of little details that make this game a blast to watch as well as play.  One of my favourites is when both players are low on health and throw an attack, the game does a slow-mo finish to show the last attack landing.  It doesn't affect gameplay at all (the slow-mo kicks in only after both moves have been thrown and a killing blow is going to land) but really adds a cinematic feel to the conclusion of a fight.
So now I have a problem, and that problem is I need to balance my obsession with Tekken with being an adult.  I don't want to be an adult.  I want to be a kid again with someone else paying for everything and all I want to do is sit around and play Tekken.  So everyone, tell my wife I love her and I'm sorry, but Eliza and Kazumi both look really cool and I need to go figure out what they're about...

So far MKX has been a blast...in single player mode. The game runs for me at 60fps almost flawlessly, except for the cutscenes/fatalities and whatnot (which run at 30), but I can live with that. It also looks great and plays smoothly.
What I cannot live with, in the online play.
Both Ranked and unranked matchmaking only work about 10% of the time, and even then it's with constant re-queueing. Rather strange, since I would have thought ranked 1 vs. 1 would be the games most popular online mode. Apparently there's just nobody out there I can be matched with?
I had much more success fighting opponents by joining one of the 'Rooms', this system seems to work much better. You can challenge people within the room, or accept challenges from other people. However, this is also where the real issues begin.
Right from the second I get to the character selection screen upon accepting a challenge, there's a considerably noticable amount of input-lag. So much so that every 5 seconds or so, it won't actually register my button press to scroll across to the next character. In games this is just down-right unplayable. For a game that relies on a trigger finger to block incoming combo's, and then counter within the thin time-frame the game allows, this is just game breaking.
Before you say it, it's not my connection. I'm on a 50mb down and 25mb up wired connection. Even the game displays the maximum amount of 'green bars' for me. However, latency for all opponents (at least with-in one of the games 'Rooms') is always stuck loading, and never actually visible. Perhaps this is lag compensation, I thought, but I couldn't help feeling that all my opponents were having absolutely no problem pulling off intricate combos and blocking all my attacks. I felt like this was only on my end. I've also read plenty of reviews that state that the Online mode is the best yet, and the netcode is far improved over MK 9. So obviously, just isn't effecting everyone.
From there on it gets worse. Huge lags during character selection screens, fatalities, brutalities, you name it. Occasionally my gpu will stop responding altogether, causing a CTD. I'm using the latest driver recently released for GTA V, and everything else works flawlessly with it.
Netherrealm really need to get their♥♥♥♥♥♥together and fix this. I might try rolling back drivers, but in all honestly I don't see why I should, since everything else on my system is working fine. I'm also skeptical that it would do anything, since the single player modes work great without any input lag or slowdown whatsoever.
I wouldn't recommend picking this up just yet, unless you're only interested in the single player mode. For me Online is where the fun and longevitiy of this game lies, and right now, it's about as fun as being on the receiving end of most of the games fatalities.

I've yet to play Portal Knights a lot (10 hours at this moment), but feel like writing a review of my experience so far anyway. >_<
I bought this because my brother recommended it to me, and mainly to play together with him. So far, we have played a bit in one of his worlds and I've played some in my own.
Having played games like Minecraft, Cube World and Trove a lot (and liked them, to a point), I felt that Portal Knights could be my kind of game. So far, I'm not disappointed. In PK, you first get the sense that you've been put into something like Minecraft, but with obvious RPG elements. You choose your class, so far there are the 3 basic ones (Warrior, Ranger, Mage), and then go on to customize your character (a bit limited at the moment, but as a new game, I didn't really expect that much yet) and choose a name. Pretty basic stuff for an RPG.
Then you choose a Universe(/World), from the 3 you can have at once (you can also have 5 different characters, which all share the same 3 universes), and enter it. The first "Island" is a tutorial to get you into the basics of controls, crafting, combat, exploring, etc. Again, basic stuff.
But then comes the thing that, in my opinion, makes Portal Knights sort of unique. In each universe, there is a certain number of Islands. These Islands were once a combined world, but as you get to know in the intro to the game, the world were broken into pieces. Those pieces are the "Islands", which you msust explore to find Portals leading to other islands.
Through fighting enemies, you get pieces of Portal Blocks that are used to make these portals work, and at times you might find yourself actually having to look around for a while to find the portal to begin with (I spent almost an hour on a Level 11 Island looking for the Portal to the next island, which was hidden in a dungeon BELOW the surface, so I had to dig some to find it...xD).
On each of these islands, you will find a different kind of scenery, from forests, jungles and plains/hills, to deserts, snowy mountains and mushroom-covered svamps. Every island has enemies, some which are unique to a certain kind of scenery and some that you can find on several different ones, and different resources that you have to collect to craft new items, weapons and armor to help defeating stronger enemies as you progress.
You also get to choose a "Home" Island in each universe, which you can easily travel back to from the map using a button there, that you can use as a base. I'm currently using the "Tutorial" (Lvl 1) Island, as the mobs there are easy to knock out, and they give some decent resources you need early-mid game. It is also one of the smaller islands, so I have some control on the enviroment and enemies spawning (well, once I find out how to stop them from spawning certain places...).
Also, at some point, you will be facing Bosses, which are, obviously, stronger, more dangerous enemies. These have their own islands (so you won't be meeting them randomly) and, at least in my opinion so far, gives some challenge when you have the "right" level and gear. And they're not just plain tank-and-spank either. You actually got to find a way to beat them without dying, even the first one (honestly not that hard once you find it out though :P)
Pros:
- Easy to learn
- Fun to play with others (as far as I know, there is a 6 Player Limit, but still fun)
- Great, cartoony art-style
- Enjoyable, not too intense background music
- Many different sceneries, enemies, etc.
- Crafting system
- Small, easily explored areas
- Easy resource farming
- Repeatable bosses
Cons:
- Maybe a bit too easy
- Not that much difference between classes, other than the main stats and a few level-up skills
- Small inventory space... (You'll find yourself traveling back and forth to your Home a LOT to clear out bag space)
All-in-all at the moment I feel it is a great, enjoyable game that I'd recommend to anyone liking sandbox RPGs like Minecraft and Cube World.
A solid 8/10 for now, as the lack in class differences drags it down in my opinion, but otherwise great :D

One of the best indie games ever made. Spelunky is randomly generated done right. The game is always a challenge, and at the start may seem repetitive or frustrating, but the more time you pour into this game, time this game deserves, the more you will notice the complexity and fascinating level of depth the game has.
Gameplay
The game might not be for everyone, in that victory is not guaranteed and a simple mistake may mean restarting from the first level of the game. You play as a spelunker and a boiled down summary of the aim of the game is to get to the next level by maneuvering from the top of the level to the exit at the bottom, all the while avoiding a multitude of enemies and traps. Each playable character (and there are a variety to choose from) is equipped with a whip to kill enemies or smash pots or deflect arrows. Really it serves as a multipurpose tool.
Graphics
Colourful, vibrant and beautiful 2D art that complements the game perfectly. Pretty explosion effects. It is a nice looking game.
Replayability
Conceivably infinite. Every level is different as they are all randomly generated. It is highly unlikely you will ever play the same level twice and if you did you would most likely not notice as you'd be too busy whipping bats and jumping spikes and enjoying avoiding death.
It took me 100 hours of co-op to beat the game with my brother and that was most fulfilling experience ever. And technically I haven't actually beaten the game yet as I only defeated one of the games bosses.
Highly recommend this game.

Plus, the fact that uPlay is being used for the game itself rather than Steam. uPlay and Ubisoft are always two things you just don't want to see on a game, Ubisoft always litter their games with bugs and uPlay is a♥♥♥♥♥♥application for running said games. Anyway, I played the game for roughly 1255 minutes and that was in ONE SITTING, I was completely addicted to the game and spent the entire day on it from 8am to 5am the next day. Enthralled would be a better word, as a huge South Park fan I might be a tad biased but I can wholeheartedly say that this game is a ton of fun.
Combat has been improved quite a bit, it's more strategic than previously and with a whole range of classes at your disposal, you'll have a lot of fun mixing and matching abilities, hitting opponents into each other and setting up your best attacks. That being said, some classes that were said to be released weren't actually in the game. I remember seeing "Netherborn" on the class list, but I think it was replaced with something else. With music you really just can't go wrong can you? It's South Park, the music captivates you and makes you nostalgic. You'll walk into stores and hear songs you have already heard from the show itself, you'll really believe you are in South Park with the music and general sounds in the game. Sounds are a huge part of a game, and I think they did pretty well with making it somewhat immersive and enjoyable to listen too. Battle soundtracks are pretty dope as well, making boss battles quite enjoyable.
Graphically the game is nice to look at, you can't expect the game to look like Crysis because it's South Park but it's beautifully well drawn and should I mention that the entire game is hand drawn from what I've heard? Huh, that's pretty impressive right? Makes you really appreciate it a lot more for what it is. I would try and cover graphics more, but there really isn't much to cover in terms of graphics. Most of the costumes make you look like a fanny, but that's just the humor of South Park. I did find some costumes that were pretty bad♥♥♥♥♥though, and I haven't found all of the costumes yet. Crafting is a blessing, thank the gods I don't need to continually buy health items or run back to town to nab a few bottles of antidote. You need to find the recipes first, but once you have them it just makes following the story a lot easier since you don't need to constantly restock provided you have the ingredients to make items. (Which you should If you loot pretty much everything.)
Let's talk about the story, the game is throughly well-written and I mean it's good enough to keep me playing it all day and only getting up to have a shower and grab something to eat. The way they have made the game this time round is different, you'll do a main story mission but then you won't have another mission to do which is confusing. However, another story mission will pop up in like 15 minutes or so, I don't know If this correlates with your power increasing via relics or If they are just timed to pop up at certain times. Regardless, I found this function fun because it meant that I could explore more and do side quests while waiting for the main story line to show itself. It gives you time to travel around the city getting loot, selfies and nabbing up them juicy side quests. I'm not going to spoil the story, so I won't say anything beyond that. Otherwise, I'll just get too involved in telling you what happens and ruin it.
Would I play this game again? Hell yeah, but not right now because I used up all my steam in that one playthrough. If you can get the game somewhere else though, then I would recommend it. (PS4, Xbox One etc) Ubisoft really does suck, but If not then just know that you can still enjoy the game regardless. You'll definitely encounter some bugs along the way though, have fun!

This review contains spoilers:
Story: When I was playing FbW I was constantly thinking, that you really notice, that Stick of Truth was done by Obsidian, a company that has experience with RPGs. I am not saying, that FbW was bad, no it is not a bad game, however I constantly felt like something was missing. I felt like the story was somehow less interesting than that of Stick of Truth. I somehow felt alot less connected to my companions, perhaps because it were just too many. The only companions I really felt connected to were Craig & Tweek. It was like the TV series translated into the game, because in the current South Park season the only episode I liked was the one with Craig and Tweek as well. So I would have preferred if the Story had been a little more character driven.
I enjoyed creating my character sheet, however I felt like it didn't really influence the game at all. Great now I can play as a female. But most of the time I was addressed as boy anyway, the only thing that changed were a few comments made while passing people and not in the games dialogue itself. The same was for all other choices, which didn't really make a difference either. That's where I wondered why they did implement it at all, when it doesn't really make a difference, not even in the ending.
Somehow the games humor was worse than Stick of Truth as well. I mean I don't have a problem with fart jokes, but it seemed at times like that was the only humor the game had. I mean everything your character can do as far as riddle solving goes has to do with farting, I prefered the Stick of Truth approach there.
And speaking of the ending. When I was later in the game I didn't really feel good anymore playing, because my character was constantly put down by everyone 'It is his fault'. And the worst part was when I had to kill one of my characters parents and didn't really have another choice and the character just does it, that went way too far.
Also at the actual last scenes I didn't feel like I got any closure on the game. Yay, we defeated Mitch Connor (who I didn't like as a plot element anyway), but what about the franchise plan. What will happen now, etc? I mean I was happy to see the ending at my characters home, but I would have liked to get closure with the other kids.
Bug: I had one bug that was nearly game breaking. When fighting Shub Niggurath I picked my companions and the fight wouldn't start with these companions, even on reload. So I had to pick different companions than I wanted, but oh well.
Controls: I played the game solely on keyboard, and the controls were horrible. Most of the time I didn't even know which keys to hit. That was particulary bad in the minigames, which is why I didn't even do the toilet minigame, but the problem was evident in other areas too. Like I switched the WASD controls with the Top, Left, Down, Right controls causing the prompts for the time farts to be complicated to read. Also using the phone I was always confused that Tab closed it and you went backwards with Esc. I also generally don't like those timed button hitting sequences most of the time anyway, oh well. If you play the game I suggest using a controller.
Fighting: Fighting was also a big annoyance. My character didn't really feel more powerful in later levels, quite the opposite, he did feel weaker, and I had set the fights to easy, then I want really easy fights. I don't have a problem with people enjoying harder fights, but that is why there are difficulty levels. I just want to concentrate on the story, not on how to fight right. Also I was annoyed you could barely hit the spot above or below your character except with aoe. Stick of Truth did fighting alot better.
Even with all that I somehow still enjoyed the hours I put into the game, because I'm a huge South Park fan. That is why I still suggest the game (since there is no star system on steam and you can only choose black or white) particulary to fans of the series.  If there were a percentage or star system I would rate it 70% or 3 of 5 stars.

NOT FOR ACHIEVEMENT HUNTERS.
Let me state this first and foremost: If you play the Steam Achievements metagame, where your goal is to 100% as many games in your library as possible, YOU WILL NEVER 100% THIS GAME.  There is one achievement on here that was added, but purposely not coded in, because plot/reasons. While I can appreciate the statement by the author, I feel this is an abuse of the Steam Achievements system.  So let this warning stand; if you want to get a Perfect game, you never ever will.  If you feel any sense of compulsion to complete things, then AVOID this game, because it will be a permanent itch you can never scratch.
That said, now I will get into the game review itself.
Hate Plus is the sequel to Analogue: A Hate Story.  In the previous game, you are investigating the downfall of a pre-FTL ship with the help of the ship's AI.  Over the course of the game, you -- the player -- can read about some tidbits about the ship's severely patriarchial culture (based on Korea's Joseon dynasty, 1392 to 1897 AD) and the culture shock one of the protagonists in the logs suffers when they awaken from a cryogenic sleep and are essentially thrown back in time (in a cultural sense).  The story that unfolded in the first game and the cultural influences and motivations the player can read about are pretty interesting!
Sadly, much of that seems to be lacking in Hate Plus.
In a sense, Hate Plus is a more of a "prequel" than a sequel, but the term can only be used loosely.  The log files you are investigating in Hate Plus take place before the events of Analogue.  And while it does fill in the gaps as to the "what happened" the previous game left open, it seems to lack the same kind of "why did this happen" punch that Analogue delivered.  The relevant political entries feel dry and perfunctory, and the relevant personal logs somehow lack personality.  As though it all culminates to say, "I do the things, because reasons!"  As a result, the experience feels more hollow.
Perhaps it's the method of delivery.  As in the previous game, you are given an artificial restriction on how much you can read.  However, unlike the first game, you have no restriction on which files you can read first, with the exception of one or more encrypted files that must be brute-forced (meaning the event always occurs at a specific point in the game, regardless of which of the other logs you've read).  This essentially means that all of the other logs cannot contain anything too important, lest the player read those ones first.  The result feels like so much incohesive, dry filler material than actual plot or story, even when selectively extracted by storyline and sorted/read by date.
Overall, I found myself unable to connect or empathize with any of the actors in this story as well as I was able to in Analogue.
I picked this up in a Humble Bundle, so at the very least I can feel some gratification that most of the money I spent went towards a charity. But if you don't have that option, have played Analogue, and are looking to solve the mystery of the Mugunghwa's cultural shift proposed in that game, well, you are better off pocketing your money.  This is one mystery better left unsolved.
Especially for the achievement hunters.

A sequel to Analogue: A Hate Story, this game digs into what led to the world depicted in the previous game into becoming a Neo-Confucianist nightmare. The gameplay is more or less the same, though a bit improved in a few areas so you spend more time reading the logs and less time poking the AI to ask them their opinions. In fact, they just interject with comments as you read the logs themselves, so you will get their reactions as you are both reading it at the same time. I've not finished the other routes yet, but the so-called "Harem" route where you have *Hyun-ae and *Mute together results in quite a few amusing moments (particularly from *Mute, who basically is the "straight man/tsukkomi" here).
While perhaps not as... no, nevermind. The story is still pretty dark and still can be a difficult one to get through, though the end of it honestly was fairly predictable. But if you liked the first game, then check this out too because it answers unresolved questions from the first game and has more crazy, raunchy, and depressing stuff for you to read. Woohoo!

TL;DR: I accept that this is a sequel worth playing/reading if you've finished Analogue, but while Analogue deserved much praise, this title deserves much criticism. I recommend the game on the premise that you have played and finished Analogue, because you should have no interest in it otherwise. The sexual content is way overplayed.
Mechanics spoilers ahoy, I mean, if you care about that.
The mechanics, interactions, and other minutae that made Analogue: A Hate Story one of the best visual novels are conspicuously absent, and instead replaced with infernal time-gating (thankfully, tied to the system clock) and lonely cake baking. Steam says I spent 5.3 hours to get through *Hyun-ae's path, and that's with me taking frequent breaks, including to make tea in lieu of checking my kitchen stocks since she apparently doesn't trust me to know what's in there (extremely immersion breaking to ask the player to go to the grocery store when they're supposed to be a solo starship pilot). AI character writing direction seems to have drifted away from what I would expect, at least for *Hyun-ae. I haven't yet decided if I will sit through probably the exact same writing to see *Mute's reactions.
Where the predecessor had many touch points with the active characters for most text entries that let you explore their feelings and personalities, this game sadly just has them looking over your shoulder, mumbling incomplete commentary about the text before you're able to read it. *Hyun-ae had few relevant things to say about most of the events covered, and I felt a lot of what she had to say was unseemly for her character. Compared to the skillful, asymetrical revelations made in Analogue that progressed your understanding of the events in a way that made you ask more questions despite easily figuring out the ultimate end, this game is effectively a linear text with enforced interruptions.
The discussion of sexuality in Analogue was masterfully revealed and, within context, tense, shocking, titilating, even dismaying and uncomfortable
. The sexual content of Hate Plus had no lead-up, and I felt it was quite gauche, bland, disinteresting, and way overdone. That's not to mention it was almost wholly unrelated to the main events and characters that shaped them (2 actual plot relevant characters and 1 implied side character involved with plot character of 10 total characters that be doin' it - 7 are "just there"). Given consideration of the supposed origin of the texts in the AI's code, I find the percentage of sexual and unrelated content pretty bizarre and unexplainable. I understand human preoccupation with sexuality as much as the next person, but I don't think I'm alone in feeling that sticking it onto (into?) everything kills the appeal. And I had to talk at length about it just now because it's just so much of the text that it can't go unaddressed.
Analogue touched on a lot of personal themes and had a tragic story that was difficult to swallow, a setting with mystery, and revelations that packed a punch and really made you feel a lot of different things. Hate Plus's story made sense, but didn't have any particular revelations, after all, we already know the aftermath, but
. I'll not fault it for being what it is, an explanation of what happened immediately leading up to widespread illiteracy and loss of records on the colony ship. But, to be frank, the pre-existing class system made it seem like it was not far off from that to begin with, and more could have been written about earlier events that cascaded up to that point. About how a somewhat 'modern' society could be sustained on the ship despite the decline of knowledge. More about the gradual loss of knowledge and technology, was it related to the fertility issues? Tying more side characters into the main plot instead of leaving them stranded.
I think the biggest take-away from Hate Plus is that I didn't really have any strong feelings for any of the characters introduced by the narratives. Maybe a couple, but not
feelings. I felt sad for Analogue's passing, and I felt awful having to decide which AI to save, a tense feeling sitting at the command line, wondering if I made the right choices before typing out 'download'. I did not feel much of anything for Hate Plus's passing. I wondered how a starship's engineers couldn't know the deleterous effects of gamma radiation, something every school-aged child knows, something discovered in the 1930's. I wondered how they could still have working computers with that kind of basic knowledge lost. Was this really where the downfall occurred? I guess the answer is no. That said, this could only really be a stepping stone, after all, the Chinese still use Chinese characters. Playing out the plot of Tree With Deep Roots in reverse wouldn't cause a modern society to collapse on its own, so I still feel like there's a lot missing.

The two exceptions were the two states of a mousetrap in the inventory. By the looks of it the image was read out wrong and thus skewed. In some cases the background panel for dialogue choices was missing.
The voice acting is superb and characters are portrayed with consistency thus contributing to mysterious, outlandish (in a good way) story.
I do despise the main character and the way you have to go along with his egotistical and destructive reflections, disregard and actions - there is one decision forced on the player much alike "Why use the door handle when you can break down the door?" However, that character is also consistent and driving the story. Also, he makes practically every other character pretty likeable - his ex even before she enters the screen. I do hope the final scenes are supposed to indicate a change of character, i.e. a future moderation and an emergence of care for others
I can't say much about the background music of the game since it quickly became unnerving enough for me to mute it and so I don't know whether it improved later on. However, the intermission songs are despite there shortness awesome - think Bard's Tale songs. And they really cracked me up in Drogglejug mode.
A few times some very loud sound pieces or music were played, e.g. when making "the discovery" coming back to the candy store. Also, Argus is too loud. I would have wished for those to be tuned down with the other volume settings.
I really liked the interface, e.g. how the mousewheel seamlessly brings in and out the inventory. I think it an ingenious idea to have a shortcut to the save/load menu from the inventory and I applaud the employment of F-keys.
The game logic is sound and puzzle threads are well graspable so that the player can follow the story without much stumbling.
I really liked Drogglejug mode. It took me forever to get the reference even though multiple related hints appear throughout the game, e.g. the globe.
Two more flaws:
1. Sometimes the subtitles glitched from English to German.
2. A major, almost off-putting, problem are the blocking black screens that happen when starting or quitting the game. With their three to five minute resolution time - all while catching any keyboard event, e.g. Alt+Tab, Ctrl+Alt+Del, Ctrl+Shift+Esc - I think a lot of people may have hard-reset their machines before realising the problem would resolve itself with time.
I had the luxury of having another machine on my desk that I could use to search for the problem thus not experiencing the minutes as pure waiting time, otherwise I would have restarted machine 1 after less than 2 minutes. And I refrained from quitting the game in order to write this review without delay. So it's waiting time for me next.
In case I didn't make it clear so far, I enjoyed Deponia :)
I was looking forward to playing it and wasn't disappointed. And after my 3.5 play-throughs I'm looking forward to the sequel: Chaos on Deponia.
