So far MKX has been a blast...in single player mode. The game runs for me at 60fps almost flawlessly, except for the cutscenes/fatalities and whatnot (which run at 30), but I can live with that. It also looks great and plays smoothly.
What I cannot live with, in the online play.
Both Ranked and unranked matchmaking only work about 10% of the time, and even then it's with constant re-queueing. Rather strange, since I would have thought ranked 1 vs. 1 would be the games most popular online mode. Apparently there's just nobody out there I can be matched with?
I had much more success fighting opponents by joining one of the 'Rooms', this system seems to work much better. You can challenge people within the room, or accept challenges from other people. However, this is also where the real issues begin.
Right from the second I get to the character selection screen upon accepting a challenge, there's a considerably noticable amount of input-lag. So much so that every 5 seconds or so, it won't actually register my button press to scroll across to the next character. In games this is just down-right unplayable. For a game that relies on a trigger finger to block incoming combo's, and then counter within the thin time-frame the game allows, this is just game breaking.
Before you say it, it's not my connection. I'm on a 50mb down and 25mb up wired connection. Even the game displays the maximum amount of 'green bars' for me. However, latency for all opponents (at least with-in one of the games 'Rooms') is always stuck loading, and never actually visible. Perhaps this is lag compensation, I thought, but I couldn't help feeling that all my opponents were having absolutely no problem pulling off intricate combos and blocking all my attacks. I felt like this was only on my end. I've also read plenty of reviews that state that the Online mode is the best yet, and the netcode is far improved over MK 9. So obviously, just isn't effecting everyone.
From there on it gets worse. Huge lags during character selection screens, fatalities, brutalities, you name it. Occasionally my gpu will stop responding altogether, causing a CTD. I'm using the latest driver recently released for GTA V, and everything else works flawlessly with it.
Netherrealm really need to get their♥♥♥♥♥♥together and fix this. I might try rolling back drivers, but in all honestly I don't see why I should, since everything else on my system is working fine. I'm also skeptical that it would do anything, since the single player modes work great without any input lag or slowdown whatsoever.
I wouldn't recommend picking this up just yet, unless you're only interested in the single player mode. For me Online is where the fun and longevitiy of this game lies, and right now, it's about as fun as being on the receiving end of most of the games fatalities.

The good:
-The art style and execution is well done.  It's like Fable or Overlord but with a bit more of an artist's eye applied to every environment.  Even the animations are usually very good.
-There are very few indications of what you have to do.  The game trusts you to figure it out, and the design is straightforward enough that even with almost no prompts, you'll know what to do and how to do it.
-The narrative is effective at tackling rough emotional topics with honesty and sincerity, and the relationship of the Brothers seems genuine and relatable.
The bad:
-It's rarely a game.  It's almost a shame to see all that great art in a game like this because it could've been used so much more in a game that took advantage of the assets fully.  The gameplay of Brothers consists primarily of "Go here".  Like an extremely watered down Prince of Persia, but without any of the guessing / decision-making about how and where to platform.  There are a few moments where there's an actual gameplay aspect to your interaction, and it's like a breath of fresh air.  In my opinion, that's really sad.
-I am extremely annoyed by the voice acting.  The characters in Brothers speak jibberish, and even the non-verbal voiceovers are done in a way that's really overreacted and cheesy.  I would rather them be perfectly silent.
-Stupid representation of females.  Every female in the game is based on an extremely overused, cliche trope about women, and as a couple of the major plot points depend upon those cliches, it left them feeling very hollow and stupid.
The neutral:
-You'll never quite get used to the control scheme.  It's not a big deal, and I appreciate how they used the controls as a contributor to the narrative.  But at the end of the day, it's hard to use, which can't be a positive thing.
Summary:
It's a really short game that's not very fun to play but pretty art.  If you wanna take an artful journey, go ahead.  If you want to play something that's fun, look for that somewhere else.

Oh man...  OH MAN!  Tekken on PC.  This is how I die.  I'm going to have to apologize to my wife, because I'm not totally sure that she's the most important thing in my life anymore.  *skip down to get to the review or read along to watch me reminisce*
Let me break it down for you.  I started playing Tekken in the arcades back in 1995.  When Tekken 2 came out, I had a few friends who got into it so I got a bit competitive with them.  By the time Tekken 3 rolled around, I was in college and I practiced for literally thousands of hours.  I knew every character, every mixup, every counter there was to know.  At that time the FGC wasn't really a thing, finding competition was difficult to impossibe, and I lost interest in dedicating myself that entirely to competitive fighting games.  I moved on to other games after that, but Tekken always had a special place in my heart.
Recently I started seeing ads for Tekken 7 and it brought me back to that time that I poured my heart and soul into learning everything there was to know about a fighting game.  In recent years I've played some other games... MKX, Guilty Gear, SFV... but nothing grabbed me the way Tekken did so many years ago.  I never fealt that need to dedicate myself to absolutely destroying everyone who stepped in front of me.  Up until two days before Tekken 7's release, I thought that I'd let this one pass me by.  I'm so, so, SO very glad that I didn't.  Because Tekken 7 is amazing.
*start review*
Let's start by talking about performance.  It is fantastic.  Solid 60FPS (Yes, it's locked at 60 as are ALL fighting games.  It is for technical, competitive reasons.  Please accept this as fighting game gospel and move on), maxed settings, and it is GORGEOUS.  Load times are there, but they're acceptable.  I have played online VERY little but the games that I did play were smooth.  I've heard from others that it's a mixed bag, so hopefully this game is starting from a good place and will get better as is usually the case with fighting games online.  Netcode tweaks seem to always need to happen before the community is really happy.  Character customization is fun with some great options, and is much more varied than other fighting games where you just have a choice of a different outfit/color.
Gameplay is classic Tekken.  For those who have never played a Tekken game, I will summarize in saying that each character has a staggeringly long movelist, most if not all of which are situationally useful, and the core combo system is based mostly around juggles.  As I said, I haven't played the series much in the past 18 years since Tekken 3, but I was able to hop on Ling, Nina, Heihachi, and Kazuya and pick up more or less right where I left off, knocking some of the rust off not withstanding.  Two-decade old combos still work for the most part, and after watching some videos and going into practice mode I see that I'm going to have a lot of fun learning the new optimals.  I believe the Rage system is new in this game, and right now I'm not totally sure how I feel about it.  Catch-up mechanics in fighting games have never sat particularly well with me, but it's not completely game-breaking so it's really more of a taste thing.  I wish it was handled a little more like V-Gauge is in SFV because I think that's a well-handled mechanic, but again... more of a preference thing than anything.
Story mode is... fine.  I've heard some people say that Tekken has a great story, which I don't really understand because I've never thought any fighting game had a story that was more than an excuse to have a bunch of weirdos fight each other, but to each their own.  I've played through the first few chapters and so far have just been taking over the Mishimas and catching up on the story so far.  Personally, I've been spending most of my time in the treasure mode, unlocking cosmetics while I re-learn mechanics and try to practice new combos.  It's a pretty good, rewarding way to spend bot time practicing rather than just doing it in practice mode and getting nothing other than... well... practice out of it.
The most important thing to say is this game is fun with a ton of polish.  There are a ton of little details that make this game a blast to watch as well as play.  One of my favourites is when both players are low on health and throw an attack, the game does a slow-mo finish to show the last attack landing.  It doesn't affect gameplay at all (the slow-mo kicks in only after both moves have been thrown and a killing blow is going to land) but really adds a cinematic feel to the conclusion of a fight.
So now I have a problem, and that problem is I need to balance my obsession with Tekken with being an adult.  I don't want to be an adult.  I want to be a kid again with someone else paying for everything and all I want to do is sit around and play Tekken.  So everyone, tell my wife I love her and I'm sorry, but Eliza and Kazumi both look really cool and I need to go figure out what they're about...

The game is freaking Tekken. Rage Arts are new and exciting, though their armor properties can get frustrating if you're not careful (like me.) Rage Drives are enhanced versions of a staple move of the character's arsenal that either become safe or get new juggle opportunities. Netcode is the best in a fighting game so far, save for something like Injustice 2. No rollback, no stuttering, no dropped inputs. The online lobbies work really smoothly, HOWEVER there is no best 2/3 in ranked match mode. If the match goes 1-1, you do not have the option to run a final match. Very silly. There's a certain charm is firing lasers from your eyes; launching fireworks from a lead pipe and slaughtering inordinate amounts of zombies while choosing whatever you want to wear. If you like the idea of a slightly overweight middle aged reporter wearing a summer dress and a mask reminiscent of a LEGO piece; you can do that!
The joys of the game come from how stupid the game is. Unlike almost every other zombie game which seeks to take itself seriously, Dead Rising recognises the humour that you can bring to a dark scenario. They don't bother with morbidity in this variation of the story and instead kick it to the curb in favour of juvenile humour. This game might try to tell you it has a "mature" age rating; but in actuality that would be like saying that alcohol can only be enjoyed by "mature" people. Once you're old enough to buy it, you aren't necessarily wise. The sense of humour is crude and trashy, which is part of the charm.
That being said, it isn't much of a game for kids either. There is a copious amount of blood, mutilation and things which some people would say are unsafe for children. But it isn't for "adults" either. This is one of those games which isn't overtly mature but isn't something you'd give to a five year old. It's stupid and immature; which is the charm of the series. Dead Rising 1 tried to be serious and was "okay." Dead Rising 2 tried to make you care about characters which honestly didn't work for anyone. Off The Record fixes that problem in the same way that Saints Row 2 did. It stops trying to make things serious and meaningful and just says "why don't we make it fun instead?"
Sandbox gives you the ability to just run around indefinitely and without consequence. You don't get forced to give a damn about giving Katie zombrex, you don't have to worry about survivors getting killed. Well, you kind of do but in a whole new way. You get to kill every survivor and you get paid for it. No more "oh damn I lost that survivor so now I have to load the last save." It becomes "sweet, I melted that survivors face off with my god damned laser eyes!"
And in my opinion, that's all the series has needed. It NEEDED that stupidity and to stop caring about being meaningful and serious. If I had to recommend this game for one thing, it'd be for getting rid of any seriousness to it. It became stupid and that took away the thing I found most boring in it. So my advice is that if you're sick of Dead Rising being serious, this is the game you buy. If you want a meaningful and sensible zombie game, then look again. There are plenty of games that try to do that.

Summary Review:
While certanly not graphically impressive, nor especially innovative, Mount and Blade: Warband presents an old game in a fun, exciting new way. While the gameplay is repetative, it is so much to play this game.
Mount and Blade: Warband sets you in the medival world of Calradia, populated by 6 kingdoms, each losely based off a real world culture. You can play as male or female, commoner or noble- and interestingly this affects things! While a male nobleman has a different game (especially at the start) than a female commoner.
Anyway, the main thing you do in this game is raise and fight in wars (although playing as a trader as possible). While picking the noble beginning naturally starts you already with some power, playing as a commoner means you have to claw your way up from the bottom of the barrel- and step on many others while doing so.
Eventually, you will become a vassal and granted the privilages that come with it. However, with power comes responability, and you will now be faced with managing a feif and paying respect to your king. You can no longer run off to another faction should yours become weak; you must go down with it, else risk being charged with treason, exiled, and forced back the bottom of the barrel in a brand new society.
From there, you can chose to run for Marshall- the commander of the military. Now, you are not responable for just your feif, but the defense of the entire kingdom.
If you become a marshall, your character is almost certanly very power, and you will likely have a few friends in court. Ever think King Ragnar was weak? Well, you can do something about it. You can stage a revolt against your leige, and try to take the crown for your own bloodline.
Breakdown:
Challange: 8/10
This game has a very good approach to challenge. Most games (Civ 5 for example) approach difficulty by giving the AI unfair advantages or disadvantages as difficulty is raised or lowered. While in M&B damage multipliers are used for difficulty, they are set by the player. You can also change how good the AI is.
Grinding: 3/10
There is quite a lot of grinding if you play normally, mostly to gain renown to raise your troop limit. However, this can be circumvented by not having an army- fighting on your own give a lot of renown, even against weaklings like Looters.
Questing: 5/10
Tends to be repetative. However, this isn't a questing game. The only times you'll be questing is to raise relations with a lord.
Graphics, Bugs, and Stability: 8/10
Graphically, M&B definitely shows its age. Its not pretty.
Stability wise, M&B runs at a solid 60fps and I haven't had any issues with crashing.
Bugs: No major bugs, just minor glitches (such as at the town of Yalen, because of its postioning on the map, armies appear to climb up a 90 degree cliff)
Controls: 10/10
No problems here
Story: N/A
While Viking Conquest adds a story, vanilla Warband has no real backstory. Overaching goal is set by you.

South Park: The Fractured but Whole is a direct sequel to Stick of Truth in terms of story, though playing Stick of Truth prior is not a necessity. You play as the New Kid on the block, undertaking a new adventure with Coon and Friends, Freedom Pals, and the rest of South Park to find a missing cat for that sweet, sweet reward money.
~Gameplay~
The bulk of the gameplay is split into two parts, freely walking around South Park and surrounding areas, talking to people, helping them with their problems like any good superhero, and taking selfies with them. There's a fast travel system in the form of nodes scattered across South Park, and plenty of collectibles scattered throughout the world to find for the compulsive explorer in us all.
The other half of the gameplay is the battle system, in which the New Kid and (up to) three friends engage in a turn based grid battle system. Not nearly complex enough to be called a tactical RPG, you could probably handle every battle in the game without learning what "Spunk" actually means, but it has number crunching and harder difficulties (No not the skin tone joke, actual easy/medium/hard for combat) if you're into that kind of thing. Dying is not a big deal, you just reload to before the fight/obstacle rather than last save, a blessing for someone like me who only saves when done playing for the day. You have 3 abilities and an ultimate, the New Kid can swap out his/her abilities and choose from 8 different classes, though only 3 of which are available at the start, and switch classes almost any time by returning to the Coon's base. You can equip artifacts increase your might (Think item level) and increase secondary stats like ultimate generation, status effect damage, etc, while your superhero DNA unlocked later on can change your core stats that affect the damage/healing/effect of a move relying on that statistic, encouraging interesting combinations as New Kid unlocks new classes.
~Graphics~
It looks like an episode of South Park. Only higher fidelity moments than that are dramatic stills, there's no 3D models or anything like that. There's no shaders that aren't present in the show, bloom knows it doesn't belong here in a cartoon.
In terms of performance, I have a toaster of a computer by today's standards (A8-7600 APU pretending to be a real processor with a 950 GTX) and had 60 fps across the board at 1920x1080, only dipping in Shi Tpa Town to about 40, not a big deal when you're just walking around town. If you're experiencing problems and your computer is made up of anything made in the last 5 years, update drivers and retry the redistributals with admin permissions.
~Sound~
Sounds good, no complaints. Has goofy songs sung by Cartman on intentionally sounding lo-fi radios in stores and such, as well as other songs referenced in the show. Same voice actors you know and love, even if you can count them all on one hand. On the flipside, I wouldn't call it great. No tune in the game really
to me, like how O Canada did in Stick of Truth, but I'm a metalhead and I don't expect that kind of music in a game like this, so that's just me.
~Story~
It's always hard to review a story without spoiling things. But I'll tl;dr first then give a few vague details
tl;dr) It's hilarious. If you enjoy South Park's brand of humour, with the occasional sprinkled in "serious moment", you'll enjoy what this game has to offer.
The story begins with the Coon sending the Coon and Friends out to search for a missing cat for $100 in reward money to get the Coon and Friends franchise off the ground, and into the realm of theatres and Netflix. A suitably accurate premise to an adventure undertaken by fourth graders. Over time though, you'll stumble upon an actual crime ring in South Park and discover the hidden secrets behind them all, and obtain actual superpowers with the help of Morgan Freeman. Of course, you can always take on some sidequests and talk to Mr. Mackey about life as a "Heterosexual Cisgender Girl", and are promptly harassed and assaulted by Rednecks who are conveniently bigotted against exactly whatever you are. It's a good time, if you've seen the show, you know what you're in for, it feels like a very long episode, which is far from a bad thing.
~Summary~
South Park: The Fractured but Whole is a game I had loads of fun playing, and will continue to do so. It may lack replay value, as in inherent in games that don't have some kind of arbitrary grindfest or infinitely randomly generated post-game, but it's an adventure well worth your time. I'll be doing a second playthrough in the future to try different classes and see how diverse the dialog gets if you pick more outlandish options when creating your character and describing yourself.

Possible spoilers in this review. I will try to keep it to low-key spoilers, but be warned regardless.
I'm not as impressed with this game as opposed to its predecessor. The original was a tragedy about how a regressed society can put their nail in their own coffin to seal their ultimate demise by being too rigid in their beliefs. The premise behind this game is in a similar vein; it shows how an advanced society based on future technology can regress down to pre-modern times.
The story itself is pretty good. The council of the Mugunghwa has a major problem threatening to revolutionize the government aboard the ship. A movement has been gaining steam and will hit a critical mass within a year and what the council needs is a bold plan to make this movement lose steam until it becomes a non-issue. *Mute, the security AI and one of the councillors aboard the ship, has a bold plan in mind. It sounds great in theory, but there's one problem with this:
The plan involves putting Councillor Ryu, Councillor of Captaincy, to the Chief Councillor seat.
Why is this a bad thing? Because Ryu is the man who, seven years later, will overthrow the government and create the regressed, patriarchal society that would eventually cause the downfall of the ship.
This isn't a major spoiler by any means. If you start on *Mute's route, she will make it known immediately that this is the man who became the first Emperor of the new society.  The main story is how this man slowly took over the government over seven long years in order to create the perfect society of his choosing.
The other main feature of this game over the predecessor is how much more emphasis it places on society outside of the primary plotline. It shows a famous actress who falls in love with a peasant girl, and eventually loses both her love and her career to the changing society. Another woman who slowly figures out why the shipwide birth rate is steadily decreasing despite everything else in her life doing its best to prevent it. A nobleman who falls in love with another man only to have his heart broken. Society and how it changes over these several years causes huge shifts in these people's lives, and the setting feels very fleshed out and deliberate as a result. This is an excellent way to use non-linear storytelling, and I have to commend Love for how this was done.
So why exactly did I give this a non-recommended rating?
It's simple. Outside of the logs themselves, the game is a huge step down. The AIs in the original story had very clear reasons for being there and their stories in of themselves were a big part of what made it so deep and enjoyable. The sequel... much less so. *Mute has an interesting storyline since she has no memory of anything that her former self had done in any of these logs, plus all the cultural things that don't fit what she thinks is right (having only experienced the post-government takeover) makes her a much more respectable character than she was in the original. Something happens that throws a wrench in this completely, however, and that ruins the suspence for me.
Hyun-Ae... I don't even know what happened. Her personality from the first game is intact and shines through, but that's all there is here. There's nothing that stands out about her that *Mute doesn't already have except for the fact that she takes her relationship with the protagonist investigator very seriously.
That by itself isn't negative, but it arises with one of my biggest pet peeves this game hits: forcing people to wait.
I personally hate this design choice and I don't feel it was the optimal one here. The primary draw is the story inside the log files, but the story outside of them is still a big part of what made the original game good. Love clearly tries to have the same effect in the sequel, but the forced waiting comes off to me as trying way too hard to force it. The mandatory 12 hour wait between log sessions (of which there are 3; I'm fully aware there is a skip button, but it's very clearly meant to be played without using it) arbitrarily breaks up the story. I'm not entirely sure what kind of emotional buttons its trying to press, which is worrying when annoyance is the primary emotion I was feeling. The other big issue is the very beginning of Day 3 in Hyun-Ae's route, where she forces you to wait several minutes using the subtext of expecting you to bake a cake. It's very clear what Love was going for by having this in the game, but it's extremely awkwardly placed (come on, I started day 3 to finish reading all the logs... I have to WAIT now?) and it feels like a shallow attempt to force Hyun-Ae's route to have some meat to it. It's not conducive to good characterization in my eyes and it ruins the flow of the story more than it already has.
I haven't played the harem route yet and I won't until I decide I want to go for the nine day achievement, so I will refrain from commenting on it here.
All in all, this is a good sequel if you want just to know the context as to why the Mugunghwa was so far in the past in the original. Otherwise, this isn't worth the money in my eyes.

I Tried To Like This Game, But It Wouldn't Let Me
I liked Analogue: A Hate Story much. It was interesting, it was fresh, it had memorable characters, it had some nice mechanics for its genre. So I bought this game too, a sort of prequel-sequel.
I'm sorry. I hate it already. Let me explain. It shall be my own hate story. Bear with me - for if you played this game, you are so, so used to emotional pain.
First, the plusses. You can continue with the ending unlocked in Hate Story. This is good. Either of the AIs or both (solitary route not supported). You get full interactions from the Harem route, and it is also good. Also, you get to know (step by step), what exactly happened before the events of Hate Story. This should be good, but in fact isn't.
And now to the crux of the matter. The negatives. Why I hate Hate+. Hate is such a strong word, maybe I am just emotionally exhausted. Playing this game feels like wading through filth. And the game won't let reach you any emotional catharsis, no. You have to suffer through it three consecutive real-time days, because the nasty bugger won't let you continue (except for outright cheating). Smart, eh? No, not so much.
Characters. Did I like them in Hate Story? Not that much (maybe because most of them were monsters, including AIs), but they were at least believable and played their roles well. Here, in Hate+. they are TRAGIC monsters. Even the worst villains were so emotionally crippled I wondered how they managed to breathe at all. Please. No more. It's like taking a super-concentrated dose of poison. I don't need my old depression back, thank you very much.
The narrative gets to the point that practically all light is gone, all hope lost, made more obnoxious by zero distance the leading AIs have towards reading the old logs. Yes, *Old Mute was *Mute's previous incarnation, but I dislike how one BIG event in the game was resolved (no spoilers). There should be a limit to self-wallowing.
This game is bleak to the point of ridiculousness, writing is worse than in Hate Story (*Old Mute and her chief officer are laughable characters, Mary Sue and her faithful sidekick played hammy to the max), not much of meaningful choices in comparison to Hate Story, even the mechanics are worse. LGBT love stories feel forced here - am I supposed to be thinking all the evil stems from unhappy lesbian love? That manipulative, cruel, nasty, controlling people are like that just because their One True Love was doomed because of the evil society? How stupid do you think I am? The artwork is inconsistent (stay anime or not, why stretch my suspension of disbelief even further?). The whole "mystery" is plain worse - *why* is sometimes not as important as *if* something happened.
If you liked *Mute or *Hyun-ae, don't play this game. Save them stress. Save yourself some stress.

Analogue was a pretty good visual novel, how does the sequel compare?
It's alright, yeah. It's just... sterile. Poorly presented overall. None of the characters really have any weight in the story, it's all reading about things that happened in the past that neither character was there to experience, so it doesn't matter much who you pick because the end result is about the same. Why couldn't we, maybe, have a story told from *Mute's perspective leading up to the event that caused Year 0? It would make it a lot more compelling than reading through a lot of logs with an AI companion making comments on stuff. Meh.
The story itself is alright, there's a lot of characters to keep track of and they all have names that are kind of hard to remember but there's a few characters than stand out as more important, so I guess it's fine. Nothing ever really gets resolved in the side-plots though. I mean there are implications given the nature of what comes next, but... ehh. The central story is pretty decent though, a lot of politics but not without a point, and the characters are pretty strong even without any direct interaction between them and the player.
The forced wait between days is also possibly for the better as I don't know if I could stomach just reading through logs for too long, I'd probably be waiting anyways. It's not a game for long sittings anyways, unlike Analogue which could easily and most likely would be completed in one sitting. But that had a variety of gameplay elements, reading over (shorter) logs, interacting with the console, interacting with the AI... that's the thing, there's not much to interact with here, compared to Analogue. I don't know why that's the case.
Overall I'm left just feeling very meh about this. It feels haphazardly thrown together because the author wanted to continue the story but didn't have any ideas for a game. I'd give it a slight recommendation if you've read Analogue already but otherwise there's no reason to get this one.

Oh where do I begin with Clear Sky? For some reason a lot of game journalists hated on this follow-up title, I'm not sure if they expected a more fully fledged sequel, but that doesn't make sense when you look at games like Crysis Warhead which, while improving on the original game in terms of playability, sort of trimmed up the narrative elements for I don't know brevity's sake I suppose. I mean look IGN gave it a full .9 game review units lower than Shadow of Chernobyl. I take that to mean that the game reviewer spent 9% less time playing it? That was a terrible joke.
I have started Clear Sky and yes I'm using the COMPLETE modpack that sort of patches the game up more or less, and yes it does seem less buggy than I remember from playing it a few years ago. It's also much more visually impressive; you've got to hand it to GSC they really do work hard on making the game both functionally a living-breathing world, but also a visually impressive and at times terrifying visual spectacle. The story throws you right into the world of "The Zone" much like its predecessor, but unlike its predecessor your character's motivations are much more established in the opening scenes. With the first game it's more of a mystery of your identity that you have to solve (despite the game not ever explicity stating that your identity is unknown to your character). Clear Sky puts you right in the muddy worn-out boots of a STALKER who, while escorting a group of scientists, gets inocculated and then rescued from an event that for some unknown reason, you survived. So there is a mystery of yourself that you have to navigate the world to solve, but it's much less dramatic and much more modest, but that modesty grants you an awesome amount of freedom in the game-world.
In Clear Sky, because you're not "The Marked One," your main questline doesn't feel so out of congruence with your doing side quests. For me it always felt weird to deviate from the main questline in Shadow because it felt out of character given the circumstance thrown upon "The marked one." The writing and acting from the NPCs reinforces this weird illusion that despite your in-game days of deviating from what should be an imminent threat, they resume helping as if nothing is wrong. I know there's a certain suspension of disbelief you have to engage it, but it's always nice to see developers navigate around these consequnces through the use of clever narrative devices. Clear Sky presents you with a traditional figure-out-the-game set of quests that do override the open world, but once you finish them (which takes less than two hours) you're free to roam and really do anything you want--including working with and eventually joining factions.
I'm done talking about this game for now because I want to play it. I'm not done beating it (again) and will finish my thoughts once I've dumped a few more hours into it.
Yes I think it's better than Shadow of Chernobyl.
ADDENDUM: Actually it is worse than Shadow of Chernobyl. I have decided this based on my last few hours playing and (sort of) beating the game. It just really loses a lot of steam, and the flaws inherent in the combat mechanics render the final quest line push nearly impossible to play.
For one thing, the faction war, while intriguing, is really funky. Sometimes your squads never show up to reinforce your position, making your faction's advance toward the enemy base totally stalled--meaning you can't actually beat this portion of the game. There really isn't any good incentive to do this anyway, but completionists will have their knickers in a twist upon realizing that sometimes the faction-war system just breaks. This is big problem with the game.
Combat mechanics are similar to SoC, but enemies will have no trouble noticing and then shooting your face from 100 yards off within a matter of like 3 seconds. It is too difficult, and also highly inconsistent with how the combat appears. Sometimes you'll crouch and hunch behind a piece of cover, completely obscuring your view of the enemy shooter, only to have him still shoot you through a tiny gap in the cover, or what I can only assume is a small visible portion of your head that they can see. This makes the game infuriating at times.
The ending is so thrown together and terrible, that I'm surprised I was able to complete it without totally cheating. I mean at one part you have to fight through like 25 Monolith stalkers by yourself, your squad leaving you behind for no apparent reason either. I just used the wish granter and spawned a few friendlies to make that encounter not totally terrible. It was still a challenge just not a stupid hard one.
It's cool chasing and fighting Strelok at the end, and the implications of the ending are spelled out in the original title. therefore the game lacks any alternate endings, as well as any real tangible consequences with respect to the faction-war. The narrative comes off as dry and very one-tracked, and you're just waiting for it to finish so you can install Call of Pripyat and have a good time.
The game's world is awesome though, and to its credit it does improve on quite a lot that SoC lacks. Finding anomalies is much more of a challenge, as you have to navigate dangerous obstacles produced by the anomaly, relying on your trusty bolt, scanner, and anti-rad drugs. Weapon customization is really worth it in this game, and decking out an AK that shoots super fast and has no recoil is always a good move.
Clear Sky is such a mixed bag, because there is so much wrong with it, despite it's solid roots in the fantastic original, and it's smart improvements on that formula. It's buggy and many of the level design and AI encounters feel really ♥♥♥♥y. If you're looking to get into stalker, I wouldn't feel bad telling you to just skip this one unless you're really curious. Call of Pripyat is just so much better, and feels like a polished complete title. This feels like a really elaborate mod for the original game that never quite made it to a stable release.

Short version: This is a good game, but if you don't have any of them, the Complete Journey is a much better investment. The games integrate well together, there are more achievements, and it's available on more platforms.
This is just a cut down version of my review for the Complete Journey.
By now you've probably heard some things about these games and about how the creators are the "German Lucasarts" [which seems a bit unfair given there isn't an American Lucasarts any more].
Well, I for one really enjoyed these games. There was a good balance between outright comedy and drama and the design and animation is top-notch, and it seems to be impossible to get stuck or killed.
The first game is not as good as the second and third though. I found Rufus to be a bit of a jerk and rather unlikeable, the backgrounds pretty though mostly static, and the puzzles largely illogical. Oh, and the game seemed to suffer from the same problem that Simon the Sorcerer did. It thinks it's funnier than it is.
The creators do seem to have made point-and-click adventures their "thing", and rather than Telltale who seem to have rounded all the corners off and made their games simpler for a new generation, Deponia is aimed squarely at people who enjoyed these games when they were in their heyday. That doesn't mean they're old-fashioned though. The control interface is reasonably straight forward, the games are gorgeous (did I mention that?), the voice acting is excellent and the music is..well, it's alright. You can switch it off if it gets on your nerves.
I'm not going to compare the game to Monkey Island. Just because it's a point-and-click game doesn't mean it has to be like a Lucasarts game. It's not as wacky as Cokel's Gobliiins series, nor is it as serious as The Dig. Perhaps it's more like Sam and Max, with the gleefully anti-social protagonist. Regardless, if you like point-and-click games and want something with a good storyline and hours of gameplay, it's difficult to go wrong with this.

TLDR; It's Tekken. On Steam. We have been waiting for this, and now it is here and it is glorious.
Tekken has had us mashing buttons and losing quarters by the handful in the arcades since 1994, and now the action has finally come to PC for the first time (also available on Xbox One and Ps4) with Tekken 7. While the Streetfighter x Tekken mashup did release on Steam back in 2012, it was met with terrible reviews and we are going to pretend it never happened (Thanks a lot, Capcom). I picked up a copy last night and got a chance to smash some faces and it is glorious.
The classic Tekken gameplay returns with only one major change, Rage Arts. The Rage Arts are special moves that each character gains as they take damage. Take enough damage and the fighter can unleash an extremely powerful attack to put the fight back on even ground or earn a KO. The attacks can be blocked or dodged, but when used with a combo attack they are oftentimes deadly. This adds a unique twist to the otherwise unchanged gameplay and can really change the tide of battle for a player. Both keyboard and gamepad work well with the game, because unlike Street Fighter and many other fighting games there isn’t any “rolling” required for moves so a player can smash away on their keyboard if they so choose. I stick with an XBox controller, however I foresee an arcade stick in my near future.
Tekken 7 brings a huge cast of characters to the table, including fan favorite Akuma from the Namco x Capcom and Streetfighter x Tekken games as well as Kazumi Mishima, Kazuya’s mother. The storyline is a little cheesy and strange as is normally the case with Tekken, but the cutscenes are gorgeous and the still-frame animations that drive the story forward are equally as beautiful. The storyline follows the Mishima family’s drama through flashbacks across the ages to the scary war-torn future in the campaign mode, and while the fighting takes a passenger seat to the cutscenes it is really satisfying to watch if you can get over the bad English dubs.
Online and arcade play give players a chance to earn cosmetic items ranging from badass to downright ridiculous (ever wanted to wear a giant pizza on your back? Me too), as well as “Fight Money” to purchase the items and decorate your player cards and health gauges.
There are several game modes: Campaign, Arcade, Treasure Battles (a survival mode earning you extra loot as you progress) as well as ranked and exhibition online play.

I love it, honestly. I have been a Tekken fan since the start of the series, and I have played every single Tekken game out there, been playing ever since I was a kid. It was a looooooong wait, but it's finally here. :)
Tekken is one of my favorite games of all times, I love the fights, I love the characters, I love it all!
So, I am just going to write down what I have seen and noticed during my playtime of Tekken 7, and
This game was the only reason for me why I needed a PS4! But now that it's on PC, I am beyond HAPPY! The optimization is brilliant, I don't have a high-end PC, I really only play on a low-end gaming rig (FX-6300 and RX 460) but I am still enjoying the game a lot, no lags, no massive drops, nothing. Though I only play at 1280x720p (Windowed) High Settings, I am very sure it's playable even on 1080p, but considering the rig I have, I might have to lower down the settings. But it's not a problem for me since I truly do not mind that.
Visually, this game looks beautiful, some might still not be completely satisfied unless they play on 4k/Ultra Settings, but honestly, I didn't expect anything more. The effects look amazing.
There are 38 playable characters in this game (including palette swaps, eg. Violet for Lee Chaolan), I believe. Lots of new characters, but some of the ones introduced in Tekken 6 are not available in this game (YET! :D) Hopefully, some of the main ones will be added in the future. (Some long-time Tekken fans might be disappointed to see that Armor King/Lei Wulong etc. are not available in Tekken 7)
There is a new mode called 'Treasure Battle', which gives you fight money and customization items as you progress. It might be Tekken 7's 'Ghost Battle' mode, one can say. I am going to wait for what the season pass brings us, and will update this part of the review accordingly.
The fighting mechanics are great, and well-balanced too. I need to play more of it to judge properly though. The new rage art system is awesome, looks badass. The power crush move is quite decent as well, it absorbs the damage coming from an incoming high or mid attack, yet it doesn't interrupt your power crush move. Useful against people who find themselves being cornered by rapid mid or high attacks, remember though, it's weak and ineffective against low attacks and throws. These additions might give you more opportunities to develop unique tactics suitable to your play style.
I am still playing the story, and I am really looking forward to finishing it, when I first started playing Tekken, I wasn't too interested in the story, but after Tekken 3 and 4, I really became quite interested in it. This one seems to focus a lot on the Mishima family, and the conclusion of the saga, so I am hoping to be entertained by it. :)
EDIT: I finished the story, it was nothing too special, honestly. If you have been a Tekken fan like me and know the story already, then there is hardly anything new you will find out. Maybe you will be more entertained if you are completely new to the series, it depends. So, the main story was just average. On the other hand, the super short character episodes are fun to read, watch and play. They are basically the replacement for character prologues/endings featured in previous Tekken games. (Where you needed to beat the Arcade Mode to unlock the ending of each character)
The online mode, well, to be honest, I don't expect ANY fighting game to do good with online multiplayer, but I was so surprised to actually find a quick online match on Day 1, and it was a decent one, no lags or anything. But you probably do need to have 3 or more bars to hope for a good, lag-less fight.
The soundtrack, in my opinion, it's really good. Some might not agree with me since it's more Electronic than your classic Tekken soundtrack that might suit your taste, but I believe things change throughout time, so I am not complaining. I still find it great. Too bad that the Tekken Jukebox mode is not available on PC and only exclusive to PS4, it contains the soundtracks of previous Tekken games which were also beautifully composed, I hope it won't stay exclusive to PS4 for too long. :)
It seems like there are tons of customization options, and a lot of stuff that needs to be unlocked, I think. I wasn't very much into customization in Tekken, but sometimes one just needs to look unique. :)
Hmm, I can't remember anything more right now, but like I stated earlier, I will update the review as I progress more. :D

Oh boy, Super Crate Box! Man, what is it with fast-paced, action games having the word "super" or other words that have a similar meaning like "mega", "fantastic" or something?
Super Crate Box is a 2D action platformer that involves you running around on an arena, beating up baddies, and collecting crates for random weapons and points. The main objective is to collect as much crates that you can to unlock characters, weapons, and arenas and to get a highscore.
At the start, you have a pistol. Yeah, it's pretty weak. But upon getting a crate, you throw away the little peashooter for another weapon, and you keep switching weapons every time you collect another crate. Crates spawn at random places around the arena one at a time. If you get a weapon you like, lucky you. If you get your most hated weapon, then tough bananas you get what you get so deal with it. Enemies spawn from the top of the arena, and there is a fire pit (or fire pits) at the bottom. If you fall into the pit, then you obviously die. But, if an enemy falls into it then it spawns back at the top enraged, as in it's movement speed increases dramatically along with it getting a furious reddish/purple-ish color to it. Also, one thing worth mentioning is that you die in one hit. Enemy touches you? DEAD. Fell in the fire? Dead. Overwhelmed by a horde? Dead. Fire again? Dead. Dead. Dead. Dead. Dead. Dead. DEAD... Yeah, the game also is challenging. One thing that Super Meat Boy has taught me is that if a game has the word "super" in the title then chances are it's hard, and Super Crate Box does not disappoint.
It's concept is simple, yet the game goes more in-depth than it looks. The main goal, like I said, is to get as much crates that you can in a run. But, if you focus mainly on collecting crates, the enemies will start to bundle up into a massive horde running around the arena and that will end your run in a matter of time. Also, if you focus mainly on killing enemies you won't get much crates and the enemies you kill do not count towards your score anyways (except for your statistics, which is mainly for showing off). Also, the randomness of the weapons really change up the situation, along with the random spawn of enemies. You can get a cool weapon and be able to take care of enemies very easily, but then after getting the next crate you get a weapon your either not comfortable with or it is just horrible for the current situation. Pair this up with the endless amounts of baddies, and *BOOM* very high tension.
With the randomness going about in the game, I will guarantee you that every run you do will never be exactly the same to another run. The game forces you to work with your undesirable weapons in the most uncomfortable situations from time to time. You, hopefully, will learn how to use different weapons in various situations, therefore, you come to understand how much of use those "horrible weapons" really can be. It also forces you to move around and get on-edge by sometimes spawning the crates in the worst of spots, i.e. in the center of a horde or at the top right under the enemy spawner. It's challenging at first, but with much practice you will triumph eventually (only if you have the patience).
So allow me to list all the things I find good and bad about the game, whether they are very minor details or game-breaking factors:
>Pros:
-Gameplay is always random. No two runs will ever be the same. (Could be a double-edged sword, though.)
-You, hopefully, learn from your mistakes and become better.
-You are forced to work with even your most-hated weapons to make you, perhaps, actually learn to use them.
-Unlockables, because what's some effort given without a reward?
-It's addicting and a good time waster, too.
-If you have friends who also play or are interested in playing, you can compete for high scores.
>Cons:
-Lack of key-binding. There are some people out there that complain that they don't like the controls. (Arrow keys to move, z/up to jump, x to shoot on keyboard) Doesn't matter for me but it may matter a bit to you.
-The randomness of the game can be unfair at times. Say you start your run and you're with the puny peashooter, the first crate spawns right under the enemy spawner, then a big enemy drops in right in front of your way (the big ones take a lot more hits than the little ones), and then after being forced to pull back while firing at the biggun' more enemies spawn after, force you to pull back further (and may I remind you that the peashooter is still being used at this point), and then after having took on a horde of the little ones with only a pistol another one of those bigguns' drop right in between you and the crate (the FIRST crate of the run). So, unless you've got pretty good reflexes and a super human finger for mashing the fire button, you'll inevitably lose the run. It's these times where I just curse the random nature of this game. The unfairness of this nature shines more brightly on the 2 harder modes.
-Lack of naming for characters and arenas. Now this is very much nitpicking on my part, but it would be a bit convenient to show the names of the characters in the statistics and the names of the arenas in the arena selection. For example, in a run you unlock "Billy". Alright you got Billy! Whooo! Then you go to the statistics to change character. Hmmm... Which one is Billy? A better example is for the arenas where your are trying to unlock new ones and it says "Score 10 points in the Rocket Silo" or something like that. Alright, which one's the Rocket Silo arena? Again, this might be exaggeration and it is very much nitpicking but this bugs me a bit when I think about it. Otherwise, I'd say this is very minor.
-Not too much diversity, though this will likely not matter to some people as opposed to others. There are only 3 arenas with different platforming structures. There are only 3 enemy types (the little runners, the big runners, and the little flying skulls). The characters are mainly for looks as they have no perks, but that doesn't matter too much to me. There are 13 weapons, but to some this may actually seem too little, as for me it doesn't matter too much either.  There are 3 different modes, however, to change up gameplay. Again, this is very much nitpicking, but for those of you who are gratified by diversity in games, this is one thing to consider.
-The game window, if not running on fullscreen, will always reposition itself to the center of the screen no matter where you put it whenever you start a run or go back to the main menu. Basically, there's really not too much of a point placing the window in your desired spot every time as every time you restart another run during gameplay the window will reposition itself to the center. This will most likely be very annoying to some, and it could be a bit of bad programming as the rest of the games that I run on windowed never do this, but this could also be considered nitpicking I guess.
Now with those aside, would I recommend this game? Yes. But I find that there is still some room for improvement, whether it is little or big. Otherwise, this game is fun and good for those of you who are obsessed with high scores, unlockables, and competition.

South Park: The Fractured but Whole is a direct sequel to Stick of Truth in terms of story, though playing Stick of Truth prior is not a necessity. You play as the New Kid on the block, undertaking a new adventure with Coon and Friends, Freedom Pals, and the rest of South Park to find a missing cat for that sweet, sweet reward money.
~Gameplay~
The bulk of the gameplay is split into two parts, freely walking around South Park and surrounding areas, talking to people, helping them with their problems like any good superhero, and taking selfies with them. There's a fast travel system in the form of nodes scattered across South Park, and plenty of collectibles scattered throughout the world to find for the compulsive explorer in us all.
The other half of the gameplay is the battle system, in which the New Kid and (up to) three friends engage in a turn based grid battle system. Not nearly complex enough to be called a tactical RPG, you could probably handle every battle in the game without learning what "Spunk" actually means, but it has number crunching and harder difficulties (No not the skin tone joke, actual easy/medium/hard for combat) if you're into that kind of thing. Dying is not a big deal, you just reload to before the fight/obstacle rather than last save, a blessing for someone like me who only saves when done playing for the day. You have 3 abilities and an ultimate, the New Kid can swap out his/her abilities and choose from 8 different classes, though only 3 of which are available at the start, and switch classes almost any time by returning to the Coon's base. You can equip artifacts increase your might (Think item level) and increase secondary stats like ultimate generation, status effect damage, etc, while your superhero DNA unlocked later on can change your core stats that affect the damage/healing/effect of a move relying on that statistic, encouraging interesting combinations as New Kid unlocks new classes.
~Graphics~
It looks like an episode of South Park. Only higher fidelity moments than that are dramatic stills, there's no 3D models or anything like that. There's no shaders that aren't present in the show, bloom knows it doesn't belong here in a cartoon.
In terms of performance, I have a toaster of a computer by today's standards (A8-7600 APU pretending to be a real processor with a 950 GTX) and had 60 fps across the board at 1920x1080, only dipping in Shi Tpa Town to about 40, not a big deal when you're just walking around town. If you're experiencing problems and your computer is made up of anything made in the last 5 years, update drivers and retry the redistributals with admin permissions.
~Sound~
Sounds good, no complaints. Has goofy songs sung by Cartman on intentionally sounding lo-fi radios in stores and such, as well as other songs referenced in the show. Same voice actors you know and love, even if you can count them all on one hand. On the flipside, I wouldn't call it great. No tune in the game really
to me, like how O Canada did in Stick of Truth, but I'm a metalhead and I don't expect that kind of music in a game like this, so that's just me.
~Story~
It's always hard to review a story without spoiling things. But I'll tl;dr first then give a few vague details
tl;dr) It's hilarious. If you enjoy South Park's brand of humour, with the occasional sprinkled in "serious moment", you'll enjoy what this game has to offer.
The story begins with the Coon sending the Coon and Friends out to search for a missing cat for $100 in reward money to get the Coon and Friends franchise off the ground, and into the realm of theatres and Netflix. A suitably accurate premise to an adventure undertaken by fourth graders. Over time though, you'll stumble upon an actual crime ring in South Park and discover the hidden secrets behind them all, and obtain actual superpowers with the help of Morgan Freeman. Of course, you can always take on some sidequests and talk to Mr. Mackey about life as a "Heterosexual Cisgender Girl", and are promptly harassed and assaulted by Rednecks who are conveniently bigotted against exactly whatever you are. It's a good time, if you've seen the show, you know what you're in for, it feels like a very long episode, which is far from a bad thing.
~Summary~
South Park: The Fractured but Whole is a game I had loads of fun playing, and will continue to do so. It may lack replay value, as in inherent in games that don't have some kind of arbitrary grindfest or infinitely randomly generated post-game, but it's an adventure well worth your time. I'll be doing a second playthrough in the future to try different classes and see how diverse the dialog gets if you pick more outlandish options when creating your character and describing yourself.

Stalker Clear Sky, like its predecessor Shadow of Chernobyl, is a post-apocalyptic survival-horror shooter taking place in the Zone of Exclusion around Chernobyl. Now, unlike its predecessor, Clear Sky has added certain new features that enhance the gameplay, such as the Factions War. In the game, multiple factions are vying for control of the Zone, and your character can join a group and help them secure the Zone, bringing in wealth, but also making new enemies, so choose wisely. Furthermore, the ability to repair and upgrade weapons and armor is now available to the player, allowing you to alter your equipment to best suit your play style. However, the story is quite frankly not as good as Shadow of Chernobyls, in my opinion. It lacks the intensity and depth that Shadow of Chernobyl has. I played this game with the Clear Sky Complete mod, which again fixes numerous bugs and noticeably improves graphics. All that in mind, this is a fantastic shooter, with several new features that set it apart from the original, although it doesn't quite measure up to the original in terms of atmosphere and story. Overall Score: 9.5/10

Sim, Clear Sky beira o 'ruim' e o 'não tão bom quanto o SoC mas bom'. O jogo começa bem, open world como o primeiro, te dando opções pra completar as missões, escolha de facções pra uma faction war q parece interessante. Depois começa a frustração. O jogo se afunila e fica linear como um Call of Duty, matando qualquer tipo de exploração e uma ♥♥♥♥♥da de situações scriptadas. O faction war não funciona: você limpa e captura pontos, mas seus aliados não ocupam o local, e qdo vc sai os inimigos simplesmente voltam. Você então desiste do Faction War e foca na story line. Mesmo na dificuldade Normal, os inimigos conseguem te acertar mesmo q você esteja sem 1% do corpo a mostra - atras de cobertura. Conseguem dar tiros certeiros q tiram metade da sua vida. Pra piorar, sua armadura tem durabilidade e a única forma de consertar é com NPCs, e custa caro e nem sempre você tem acesso a eles, principalmente da metade pra frente do jogo, qdo vira um rollerscoaster. A última fase então é um ♥♥♥♥ fest: tem "tempo limite", inimigos q teleportam na sua frente e atras de você, com screenshake atrapalhando sua mira, e você tendo q correr contra o tempo.

I've gotten through the first three missions and feel that I've played enough to be able to give a solid review of this. In full disclosure, I have not played any other Sniper Elite games.
Sniper Elite 3 is a single-player and multiplayer first-person shooter with incredible ballistics. You can even change how simple or realistic that you want them to be. The strategy that you use matters. For example, if you're too lazy to move the bodies of your victims, an enemy could see it and become alerted to your presence. You also have to relocate often if things don't go according to plan. Enemies are able to deduce where your shots are coming from if you're not careful.
Having said that, the enemies seem pretty stupid (at least at the difficulty on which I configured them). They hear your walking around (without crouching) but they can't hear your crawling around. What sense does that make? They also won't hear you stab somebody two metres behind them.
The game can be buggy sometimes. It is frustrating when the sniper won't fire. It's rare but it happens and you'll have to scoot over a few feet to get it to work. Or sometimes if you shoot for a perfect headshot, the bullet will completely miss despite the tactical assistant telling you that it will hit them. These are all minor issues that can be fixed and they shouldn't significantly affect your gameplay.
Speaking of gameplay, the game seems a bit repetitive. There's not too much depth to it. It's still very much enjoyable, but it's not a game that you'll want to binge play for an entire day.
If you're looking for a game with a good story, then you'll be disappointed. There's just enough story to make you feel like you're not just shooting arbitrary targets and that's it. The "cut scenes" are very elementary too.
I have a few somewhat serious complaints though. None of the secondary weapons are overly useful. There are times in which stealthily killing all of the enemies is impractical—it would take way too much time and effort. You will have face-to-face combat. But the secondary weapons are hardly useful in such situations unless you manage some headshots. Additionally, if a bullet can enter the skull, travel through the brain matter, and exit the skull, then it should at least be able to do something to the chest. I'd shoot somebody in the chest and after stumbling for a second, they'll run off like nothing happened. If you physically got shot in the chest by a sniper, then you would almost certainly completely lose blood circulation or have a punctured lung. In neither situation would you be capable of running. But the enemies are capable of this.
Though I enjoyed this game, I can't recommend paying full price for it. I don't feel that it's worth $49.99. $39.99 tops. Get it on sale and it will be money well-spent.
As for DLC, I haven't played the additional missions yet, but you should definitely get the DLC with the Type 99, which, in my opinion, is the best rifle in the game.
Lastly, use the rocks! The rocks are god and can get you out of tight situations or give you an advantageous opportunity.

This game is of enormous quality in almost every aspect. The poor user reviews are mainly due to the troublesome release, and the semi poor netcode(even though only SOME of us experience actual problems with massive lag).
Game is actually extremely well optimized, it will run on poor computers fairly well. The sound and graphic design is of the highest quality and there's ALOT to this game. Content wise it literally is very big and complicated. The constant faction battle between online players is also a very big plus and fun to participate in.
Pros:
+Good port, it's well optimized
+Very responsive controls, and much more keyboard friendly than any other fighting game out there
+Even though the graphics themselves aren't particularly amazing, the detail is
+Top notch voice acting
+Interesting characters of which some have actually in depth backgrounds
+Amazingly fun to play
+No gameplay glitches either graphically or collision wise(not as far as I've seen, or seen rants about)
+Enormous amount of content for your money
Cons:
-There're some very obvious balancing issues
-Pay to unluck more content
-Annoying ''exploring'' minigame which feels a bit like a DnD game. It is necessary to play this to unlock addition content, and it's really obnoxious in my opinion
-Memory leak, but will be fixed asap(some users experience the consequences)
-Some players experience tremendous lag in the online mode
-Ceilingheigh pricetag, but if you're into fighting games it's more than worth the money
-Some players experience poor preformance. Even though most do not. It's not AMD related at least, as I have no issues whatsoever
Recommended for sure. The quality of the game itself is undoubtebly fantastic. Issues like memory leaks, poor netcode and some players experiencing poor preformance might ruin all of it almost in it's entegrity however.

Summary Review:
While certanly not graphically impressive, nor especially innovative, Mount and Blade: Warband presents an old game in a fun, exciting new way. While the gameplay is repetative, it is so much to play this game.
Mount and Blade: Warband sets you in the medival world of Calradia, populated by 6 kingdoms, each losely based off a real world culture. You can play as male or female, commoner or noble- and interestingly this affects things! While a male nobleman has a different game (especially at the start) than a female commoner.
Anyway, the main thing you do in this game is raise and fight in wars (although playing as a trader as possible). While picking the noble beginning naturally starts you already with some power, playing as a commoner means you have to claw your way up from the bottom of the barrel- and step on many others while doing so.
Eventually, you will become a vassal and granted the privilages that come with it. However, with power comes responability, and you will now be faced with managing a feif and paying respect to your king. You can no longer run off to another faction should yours become weak; you must go down with it, else risk being charged with treason, exiled, and forced back the bottom of the barrel in a brand new society.
From there, you can chose to run for Marshall- the commander of the military. Now, you are not responable for just your feif, but the defense of the entire kingdom.
If you become a marshall, your character is almost certanly very power, and you will likely have a few friends in court. Ever think King Ragnar was weak? Well, you can do something about it. You can stage a revolt against your leige, and try to take the crown for your own bloodline.
Breakdown:
Challange: 8/10
This game has a very good approach to challenge. Most games (Civ 5 for example) approach difficulty by giving the AI unfair advantages or disadvantages as difficulty is raised or lowered. While in M&B damage multipliers are used for difficulty, they are set by the player. You can also change how good the AI is.
Grinding: 3/10
There is quite a lot of grinding if you play normally, mostly to gain renown to raise your troop limit. However, this can be circumvented by not having an army- fighting on your own give a lot of renown, even against weaklings like Looters.
Questing: 5/10
Tends to be repetative. However, this isn't a questing game. The only times you'll be questing is to raise relations with a lord.
Graphics, Bugs, and Stability: 8/10
Graphically, M&B definitely shows its age. Its not pretty.
Stability wise, M&B runs at a solid 60fps and I haven't had any issues with crashing.
Bugs: No major bugs, just minor glitches (such as at the town of Yalen, because of its postioning on the map, armies appear to climb up a 90 degree cliff)
Controls: 10/10
No problems here
Story: N/A
While Viking Conquest adds a story, vanilla Warband has no real backstory. Overaching goal is set by you.

Tekken 7 is no doubt the best 3D fighter around for PC. The launch was smooth as silk, even online and the game feels really polished (which is reasonable after all that time spent developing the game).
Tekken 7 FR truly feels like it was built for the fighting game community to thrive in. With slick online functionality and both interesting and balanced characters, even getting your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you is a joy.
The practice mode is extremely solid and is accompanied with a sea of smart details, like for example placing you in practice mode while you are waiting for online matches.
Finally I want to point out how well optimized the game is. My somewhat average gaming PC easily maxes out the (very pretty) graphics without ever dropping below 60 FPS. This is extra important when it comes to fighting games, since reaction times are key.
Fighting kino.

I don't do Steam reviews very often. But Tekken 7 here certainly deserves it. If you haven't picked up Tekken in a long time, or if you're a longtime Tekken fan. Then this entry's definitely worth getting. Especially if you're of the former, and contemplating on getting it? I'd definitely recommend do so. Tekken's always been about easy to pick up, and hard to master. This one's very much accessible. The PC port in particular is -very- well optimised, and that's a rarity in today's world when it comes to PC ports.
And the netcoding? A fantastic job. Hardly any issues with playing against other players in my region, and that says a -lot- during a Day One release. It tends to be the norm to see unpolished games hit the shelves.
If you're a Tekken fan, or a fan of the fighting genre. Please pick this up, and support good games, and ports to the PC. Who knows? If there's a Soul Calibur in the near future, then perhaps we'll get a PC port of that. Trust Namco to deliver a decent product of this calibre.
One thing I'll add, however. Do not pick it up solely for the single player. The content for that is rather lacklustered in comparison to previous titles.

Okay... so. This game, at its core, is a South Park episode. This inherently makes it really hard to mess up.
But there are a few issues I personally came across.
With a decent gaming laptop, it takes 5 to 15 minutes for the game to start up and get past the logos.
Time decreased when I went into task manager and made the game's process priority high.
Time decreased a bit more by playing in offline mode.
With a decent gaming laptop, I found lag about the same as 500 ping in an online game. Horrible.
The toilet minigames are IMPOSSIBLE on the higher difficulties because you can't time anything right.
Sure, most of this game works fine with 500 ping because there aren't many quick-times and nothing's real-time, but it's still really annoying.
Annoying like the PC controls. You learn to deal with it, but they're all pretty unintuitive.
With all that said and out of the way, I say the game is still enjoyable. All the new mechanics, from the crafting to the battle system, is fun. I like pretty much every concept in this game. I'll probably still play it through, issues and all.
Seeing as everybody seems to have separate issues, I hope that something is done about everything happening here. I'd love to enjoy the game to its fullest without having to use a thousand workarounds for all of its issues.

An interesting visual novel, something that I think really differentiates itself from the other 'moe-blob' VNs that you see in the Steam catalogue.
Pros:
- A unique story that steers clear of simple tropes and explores archaic Asian attitudes towards issues such as sexuality and gender roles. To provide some backstory, it is recommended that Analogue: a Hate Story should be played first, though since Mute isn't exactly fleshed out a whole lot in that game, one can probably get away with playing this first.
- Art style is fairly generic, though the sepia-photo visuals do provide some fresh realism and believability to the story.
The enhanced HUD from the next game is pretty nice, though some people have reported issues with it bugging out and failing to display anything. Windowed mode fixes that from memory.
- Good soundtrack that meshes well with the material that it supports.
- Great character development: this ties in with the story, but it's refreshing to see characters who aren't just "I'm tsundere, but really I'm actually really nice, my mum and dad died in a car crash when I was young", or "overly-exuberant moe-blob mk.2000". Both main supporting characters (or protagonists?) are very well developed, and allow NG+ playthroughs.
Cons:
- Game design. The options available to you are so limited compared to the first game. Literally the entirety of the game revolves around decrypting logs, reading through them, and getting your supporting character to interact with them. You get options from a dialogue wheel to choose from, but there's none of the puzzle-solving that was available from the first game.
This flaw was probably the biggest disappointment I had with this game, and what really stopped me from doing a NG+ playthrough.
All in all, a great game especially in the story and visual department. The game mechanics are very bare-bones, though if you haven't played the first game and are familiar with the usual "choose this option" type of VN, you shouldn't find this a problem.

So yeah. This is my first review, but then, this is one of the games I know intimately well. I may only have about 16 hours on record here, but I've logged far more on the 360 version.
The Dead Rising series seems a bit schlocky, and that's not surprising. It's meant to be a tongue-in-cheek take on zombie outbreaks. It remains serious enough to have a cohesive plot, but not so serious that a lot of the bosses and scenarios you encounter seem far-fetched or histrionic.
The fun very much comes from having a whole playground of casinos, mall shops, and an added amusement park to formulate weapons and combat them. In addition to that, you'll encounter a lot of survivors who need to be brought back to the safehouse.
Then there's the sandbox mode. It takes out the merciless clock and timer that often impeded your missions in Dead Rising 2 and the original Dead Rising. That really allows for it to be your playground.
There's a bit of humor, a bit of sexy, a 'reality' TV show that glorifies zombie-killing in a WWE-type format. And what's more: Frank West returns in the Off the Record rendition.
Some of its reviews both here and elsewhere tend to be a bit negatory because DR2:OTR took so very much from DR2... so much that, heck, a lot of it's exactly the same. But what OTR really does is fine-tune, improve, and give a little more freedom. It makes it a lot more fun. It's what kept me coming back. I've probably played through the story twenty to thirty times now... and I expect to keep going. The ride's that fun.
Grab a weapon. Get creative. Explore. You'll find plenty of crazies along the way.

I don't do Steam reviews very often. But Tekken 7 here certainly deserves it. If you haven't picked up Tekken in a long time, or if you're a longtime Tekken fan. If you're a Tekken fan, or a fan of the fighting genre. Please pick this up, and support good games, and ports to the PC. Who knows? If there's a Soul Calibur in the near future, then perhaps we'll get a PC port of that. Trust Namco to deliver a decent product of this calibre.
One thing I'll add, however. Do not pick it up solely for the single player. The content for that is rather lacklustered in comparison to previous titles.

Surgeon Simulator is a first person QWOP game. You take the role of a surgeon named Nigel Burke. Mouse movements control your doctor’s hand, up, down, left, right, and rotating. A, W, E, R and space bar are all used to control individual fingers on the hand, this is used to grasp the utensils, The game play consists of the player trying to complete a number of different operations on your patient, the first being something as simple as a heart transplant.
Once completing the first operations, you then unlock different scenarios, such as ambulance operations, ad space operations, which incorporate bumping round tools and zero gravity,
The graphics are nicely presented and everything looks clean and polished, I don't think photo realism graphics would be something I would be looking for in this type of game anyway. The soundtrack is mainly the general hospital/emergency theme tune the whole time, I had to turn it off after the first hour or two as it just grew very repetitive very fast, all of the sound effects in game of the grinding, sawing and squelching are all very nicely produced.
This game is hard, like, hard as nails hard, I am nowhere near completing it, and I have played for almost eleven hours, your hands start to ache if you play any more than an hour due to the intense holding down of the buttons and thought that goes into picking up a single item, it is unbelievable, I did try out using a controller using Pinnacle Gaming Profile (quick shout out to them while I am at it), and this did make the controls a little easier to use, but it was still stupidly difficult.
I haven't found any technical issues, I would think a potato could run Surgeon Simulator; it's a well optimized game.
A lot of the time I spent on this was playing with friends, just playing around seeing how messed up we could get, and that's what this game is all about, just having a laugh and giggle, it's hard to sit down on your own for hours at a time on this game just because of how strenuous it is on your hand and thought process just to pick something up. But I do recommend that people pick it up, just for the novelty value and for some couch gaming with friends.

A very hard game to review. If you never played it when it first came out. Chances are your going to hate it now. Back then it was seen as a poor first person shooter with clunky controls. The redeeming feature was it possible to play three separate campaigns, each playable as a separate species: Alien, Predator, or human Colonial Marine. The popularity of the films made most players to over look the flaws. Mutiplayer was also impressive at the time with each species having it's own strengths. Fast twitch gameplay required quick reaction times for the players to shoot enemies or to run in and claw enemies.
On the down side it does look worst now and has not aged well. The lighting effects where supposed to be super scary. It just became very annoying instead. Anyone looking for a story will be disappointed. It is just not that kind of game. Basic play involves running through a maze in fastest time whilst trying to get hit. That is it there nothing more here. The game mechanics could also be vomit inducing as species all spend time looking at horrible monochrome special vision views. Whilst running around 3 dimensional mazes.
This is a nostalgic look at the past and nothing more. It will not entertain for long. None the less something worth a buck in a sale. I would recommend is at a reduced price provided you have played before. Otherwise your not going to like it now.
