But I had issues with the UI being hard to play with. I was getting odd bugs like windows sticking, issues with check boxes (if I unchecked a thug in the neighborhood view, I couldn’t check anyone else and had to leave and re-enter the neighborhood). I also had the gamescreen spill over on both sides of my monitor. Though that's likely due to the fact I have two monitors with different resolutions. The UI felt blocky and jerky, like it was made in VB using forms. The jerkiness may just be my laptop as it is 5 years old, though it has 8GB of ram in it.
The UI could also be polished a bit more. I kept moving back and forth between windows to get information. (though that could just be ADD…) For example, when someone's arrested, I'd like to know what job they were doing at the time (or at least their face) because I don’t remember all the names that pass through my organization. Or I’d like to have the thug’s stats on the give orders window. Or I would look at the new recruit’s stats, then go in and look at my crew’s stats, then back out to compare them to the new recruit’s, etc. Having the new recruit in the crew page to begin with would simplify that.
The bit of backstory we are given just didn't feel consistent with the rest of the story during gameplay. The backstory is that you are in a post-apocalyptic city duking it out with another warlord. But, in the game there’s police and courts, meaning there’s a functional government, and you rarely see your rival. So the story during the game felt more like a street gang. Which is fine, it just didn’t jibe with the backstory. The antagonist felt more like it was the police/courts than your rival gang. (Perhaps instead of police and courts, your crew runs into your rival's crew and they have to escape, etc)
There were quite a few pieces I did like; the face generation was amusing, and I liked how there were explanations and tool-tips everywhere, that made diving into the game easy.
Not a bad game, but not quite good enough yet for me to recommend spending money on it. (I got it as a part of a bundle)

Ok, so I've read some of the positive and negative reviews, debated about whether to get this or not, and it dropped to $1.70 or so and I decided, "What the heck, let's give it a spin ..."
The game is basically a 'conquer the city, street by street' game in what plays like a board game format, with some interesting twists.  I'll list here what I feel are some PROS, CONS, and some SUGGESTIONS FOR IMPROVEMENT that I feel might make the game even more interesting / challenging.
PROS
1) Semi-permanent, random events have effects on your gang's success / failure.  Some useful random events are: Police On Strike & Loyal Stand.  Some detrimental random events are: Religious Holiday, Flu Bug, Crime Tariff.  I've only played for a handful of hours so far, so I'm sure I haven't seen all the events yet, but I do like how they add some significant upside / downside to the game, & it's a good idea to keep an eye out for them.
2) You can bribe the police, temporarily ... initially, this is a rather costly thing to do, as it can burn through your available resources fairly quickly.  But it can also help you greatly to get that initial toe-hold you need to get your crime syndicate up & running. You also get an icon that indicates 'bribe in effect' & goes away on the day that your bribes cease to help you out.
3) Even bribed, the police aren't exactly your friends.  So, you have a deal with the police not to arrest any of your gang members this week?  Good for you.  But this week, the police decide to 'clean up' a neighborhood festering with corruption & restore it to the residents.  Nice.  Too bad it was one of YOUR neighborhoods of festering corruption ...
4) Your main opponent finds different ways to pester & annoy you.  From things as simple as " I stole some of your money !" to things a bit more troubling, like "I stole some of your resources !" to things quite a bit more personal, like "I stole one of your best gang members!"  Yeah, like the one I bothered to just equip with a nice shiny new gun & body armor, WTH, lol ...
5) In a pinch, you can convert your resources to cash.  There's a lower $, lower resource liquidation option & a higher $, higher resource liquidation option.  This can be useful early on, but you can get a bit carried away with this ...
6) Occassionally, random help shows up.  Maybe you've got plenty of cash, but resources are tapping out.  Or you need cash & can't burn down resources to get it.  Sometimes an outside source will make an offer to you that involves a swap of some kind.  These don't generally occur often, but they can be helpful from time to time.
7) Pretty Much Bug-Free.  So far the one & only thing that I have noticed has also already been pointed out by others.  Whenever I click the desktop icon to launch the game, it will put up an install window.  Past the point of installing it once, you have to ignore this popup & then the game loads normally each & every time.  But it is a bit of a nuisance b/c it will show this each & every time.  But as far as game mechanics once playing the game itself, I haven't found any bugs at all.
CONS (it appears I ran out of my max allowed words when describing the CONS, so I'll rewrite and be briefer, lol).
There are a number of these, but I'm not without hope that at least some of them might be addressed, as the Dev appears willing to listen to constructive criticism & still appears to be adjusting the game to make it more challenging / interesting.
1) My most serious beef deals with the judge/lawyer/bribe/assassinate/trial system that is set up here.  Quite a few issues with this.
1a) Biggest complaint is that once your gang member is arrested, there is no description indicating which of the 3 judges in the city will be hearing his case.  This is largely baffling - how is it that a crime syndicate entrenched enough to bribe both judges & cops not capable of figuring out which of 3 judges is going to try their gang member the next day?  At least give me an option to 'incentive bribe' someone in a position to know that answer so that I can go from there.  This would help give me an idea if my lawyer (stats prominently displayed when you hire 1 of 3 lawyers) has a snowball's chance in he11 of dealing with that particular judge (those 3 judges stats are also prominently displayed, but don't help much if you can't do anything in light of it that might improve your chances of successfully defending your client).  Of course, if you have the cash, you could just bribe all 3 judges, which leads me to ...
1b) 'Bribed Judges' still find your gang members guilty.  And not just guilty, but often 'bury them under the jail & throw away the key' guilty.  I get that hackers are dangerous, street thugs can be vicious, etc.  The game runs on quite a few turns passing before a full year goes by, so I guess some of these 'life sentences' could, in reality, be 10 - 20 year convictions (which would effectively take them out of any reasonable chance of you seeing them again in the course of your game).  But it'd be cool to see the number of years they got vs. hearing a life in prison sentence for something as simple as being arrested for guard duty at your hideout.  Yes, it does happen.  Also, if a 'bribed judge' is going to get indignant over being offered a bribe & then 'throw the book' at my gang member, I'd like to hear something back after the bribe was offered to that effect.  It might get me to consider sending someone his way ... which leads to another thing ...
1c) Even if you guess correctly & knock off the correct judge, the trial of your gang member will take place first, & then the judge will get waxed.  As near as I can tell, there's no taking out the judge and stalling proceedings until a new (and hopefully more sympathetic) judge comes along.  A couple of other things about the whole lawyer/judge thing ...
1d) You can't get rid of your idiot lawyer to hire a better one.  Your stuck with him or her until the 2 year contract runs its course.  Presumably, you get the one with the best stats from the get go, but one nice thing is that occassionaly, old lawyers & judges go out (in the judge case, often feet first) and new ones come in, sometimes presenting you with new lawyers with better stats.  This system could really hum if you could drop one lawyer for another from trial to trial, depending on you knowing which judge your member would be up against.  This would give you some feeling of say in the final outcome, even if it meant that you shelled out some more $ to rip up contract with one lawyer to pick up a new one.  At the moment, that feels like an area that needs some improvement.
1e) Bribe all 3 judges, shoot the ones that don't toe the line, the new ones come in listing as bribed as well.  This seems like it's likely just a slight oversight.  I wouldn't think the judge would include in his or her last will & testament that their bribes be passed on for the good of the next judge to take their place.  It does kinda make me laugh a bit though whenever I see the new judge listed with 'bribed' already under their heading ...
Okay enough with the judicial system, onto a few other cons ...
2) Guns & armor dry up after you buy the initially offered items at the store.  While these do eventually get replaced, it can sometimes take many, many turns before any new weaponry or armor comes down the line to be offered to your gang.
3) Can't swap guns & armor from member to member.  Argghh ...
4) Resources to cash but no cash to resources, unless you get really, really lucky with an outside offer. So keep your resources up. Or else.
5) Only hacking & searching for your rival seem to grant resources. Chaos only seems to ever add money. Eh. Doesn't make Chaos a particularly useful tactic, then ...
6) No base bonus pts for successfully defending the base. You can lose 'em but can't gain 'em.

While there's potential here for an interesting simulation game, there's absolutely no reason you should purchase it at this time.
When important information is cut off from the end user in a game critical on feedback, there's a major problem. There are no resolution settings, or even ability to change that up, so you'll be guessing half the time what it says. That makes interaction fail on so many levels, and really hurt the user in terms of what's going on.
A lack of tutorial hurts this game immensly. There's help buttons, but they only give you a piece of the overall picture, and interaction is what games should thrive on.
The enemy opponent seems too random. Randomness is good in a game like this, but to a point. Sometimes, within the first 10 turns, I could be attacked and be majorly hurt. Other times, the enemy doesn't want to do anything at all, even though my base is really open to attack.
That also leads to not really having a lot of information about your opponents well being to make an informed decision. Is he gaining power? Should I search for him? What is my best option here?
Again, there seems to be an interesting mechanic buried in here, but it's hard to get past those major points. Like really major. Games work with interactivity. Here, you're along for the ride more then anything else. While yes, you can see feedback at times and maybe keep track of things, it's really hard to get into the "story' aspect of being a gang leader when I'm not really sure what my gang just did. I see values changing. Great, wonderful, I have no idea what they actually did to do that.
The tooltips are nice I suppose, once figuring out they were present, that made information a lot easier to look at. Lack of resolution settings hurts immensly. While a game can be at one resolution, you can see the problem when I still can't see the text. Sorry, I'm going to hit that one over and over again: if I can't read what's going on: there's a problem.
Can't recommend at  this time.

This is a hard game to review.   It's a game with a strong storyline and some genuinely funny dialogue.  The puzzles occasionally lack much logic and can sometimes only be solved through guesswork (or by referring to a walkthrough) but this is a common problem with point-and-click adventure games and I would say that it's no worse than its peers in that regard.
However, it's not a game that everyone will enjoy.    Whereas other adventure game characters like Guybrush Threepwood are hapless and inept, the protagonist of this game, Rufus, is rude, selfish, callous, sexist and egocentric.   This is a protagonist who you should probably not identify with or even sympathise with (although you probably will as you get drawn into the narrative)
The humour is mostly derived from Rufus creating plans that go wrong and behaving in such a way as to cause misery and misfortune to those around them.   This is of course a well-established form of black comedy and I think that most people will be able to take it as it was intended.
However, there are a number of jokes that contain elements that are as likely to cause offence and upset rather than amusement.   There are three main instances of this (from the entire trilogy):
- One character is depicted in a very transphobic light
- One character suffers through a racially demeaning situation (due to the protagonist)
- One character is a paedophile
These are all intended as jokes and the author of the game has clarified that racially charged scene was not meant to convey a positive message about racism (the humour is derived from how awful the situation is) but it may still limit the ability of some people to enjoy the game.
If you particularly enjoy point-and-click games and can tolerate the occasionally moment of humour in bad taste then you will enjoy this game.   If you are sensitive about racism, transphobia or sex crime then you may find that some jokes spoil your ability to enjoy the rest of the game.

~SERIOUS REVIEW~
Dead Rising 2: Off the Record is a great game, with only a few flaws that keep it from being the best game ever.
NOTE: this review is for the Xbox 360 version since my pc is incredibly laggy while playing, and I have put many, many hours into the Xbox port. So, i'm just going to assume that both versions are identical.
-PLOT-
You are Frank West, hero and survivor of the infamous Willamette zombie outbrreak.  Having written a book about it, and  getting YOUR OWN FUC**** TV SHOW, just about you, you are very famous. But one day, that fame is lost, your show has had the plug pulled. You are watching TV, when you see a show called ''Terror Is Reality'' in which contestants earn money for killing thousands of zombies. You think to yourself ''This is my chance to get back in the game!''.
So, for the very beginning of the game, you are pitted against zombies in a wrestling ring and have to kill as many as you can. Once you have won and collected ''THA BIG MONAYYY'', you decide to grab some Zombrex (a drug that stops you from becoming a zombie, spoilers) and head home. However, when you take the elevator, there is a nasty tumble and you pass out. When you awake from your sleep , there are alarms and sirens going off ,screams, and groans. You attempt to wedge open the lift door with all your strength. You can see... *sarcastic gasp* Zombies! To which Frank replies, ''Oh no.'' Just as a certain zombie comes towards you, a running man fortunately runs in front of the zombie, and dies, saving your life. You run out of the arena, into a shelter, along with other survivors. A woman, Stacey, tells you that there is some Zombrex in a nearby plaza. After teaching some looters a lesson, you find a pharmacist (which you take back to the shelter) and some Zombrex. At about 8pm, you go back to the shelter and watch a news report about the incident. Feeling inspired, you must uncover the truth about the outbreak (while brutally murdering thousands upon thousands of zombies), escort innocent survivors, find Zombrex (or buy it for 25 grand) and (hopefully) get back in the game!
-PRESENTATION-
The game looks relatively good. Survivors look like survivors, and Frank looks like, well, Frank West at the age of fourty-one. Where the graphics are mixed, though are the zombies. They look okay at first, but when you play the game more and more, it seems like you've killed a zombie's 119th COMPLETELY IDENTICAL twin. But where the zombies shine, though, are the amount there are. I mean, JESUS, if you have a powerful pc, you can have a thousand zombies on screen before it even drops 1 frame. Even the console ports look good, but i'm saying ''good'' becuz #pcmasterrace :B1: .
-GAMEPLAY-
There are two modes: Story Mode, the mode where♥♥♥♥♥♥actually happens, and Sandbox Mode, which has no plot (kinda), complete freedom,and NO ♥♥♥♥ING DRAINING HEALTH BAR FROM INFINITY MODE MY GOD THAT WAS COMPLETE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥T IN THE FIRST GAM- *cough* and no draining health bar.
New to the mix, are combo weapons. Rather simple, but COMPLETELY NECCESSARY. Examples: Baseball bat+ box o' nails = Spikey bat, Torch + Gems= HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥A LIGHTSABER.
Simple. Other than that, it's the same run of the mill as the first game: escort idiotic (but slightly better in this game) survivors to a safehouse, get PP, woohoo, do a case mission, get progression in the capcom-tier story, woohoo.
Like the first game, there are Psychopaths, which are the game's bosses. Some are easy, some are hard, some are required, some are optional, some are disgusting, some you want a statue of, lar lar lar, lar.
There's one thing that bugs me though. The same as the first game. THE DIFFICULTY. While it's the complete opposite of  the first game, it's still a problem. Dead Rising 1: OH MY GOODNESS THIS IS THE 2006 VERSION OF SUPER MEAT BOY ON STEROIDS. Dead Rising 2: Off the Record: *grooooooooooooooooooooooooooooan* tooooooooooo easyyyyyyyy. psychopaths are ok though.
-CONCLUSION-
Look past the incredibly easy difficulty, and you have a great game. Don't like plots and time limits like me? There's Sandbox Mode, the godsend from Capcom's usually faulty brain. Want something to do?  There's challenges and the normal story mode. I'll also note that I wouldn't buy this if you have the original DR2.
On a scale of one to ten, this gets a well deserved eight out of ten.  Get it if you have a great PC, it'll be worth the money. Don't have a powerful pc? Get the console port for PS3 and Xbox 360.
I hope you enjoyed my review, and it  made you make up your mind about purchasing the game or not.

Overview: First Person Shooter
Note: I used the complete mod to play the game.
The Good:
+ Once again atmosphere is the main selling point of the game. The setting, locations and realistic art style really showcase the destruction of the Chernobyl incident.  The developers really nailed being in a destroyed post apocalyptic nuclear death zone. Buildings are crumbling and dilapidated, broken vehicles litter the roads, small settlements of makeshift homes and building house some of the other inhabitants on the 'zone'. Every aspect of the game facilitates you feeling like you need to survive. With the updated engine, the game looks even better than before
+ lighting effects
+ A new addition is factions. You can join a faction to gain unique quests or help them out in general. Joining one faction usually puts you at odds with another. You can choose not to join anybody.
+ Another new addition is the upgrade system. Different armors/weapons have different upgrades that you can choose to buy making them more powerful/effective in combat. In order to unlock certain upgrades you first have to find the blueprints, usually found in stashes or given as quests rewards.
+ Side Quests have been improved somewhat over the first game. Money and quest rewards are more valuable than before and the quests are a bit more varied. Completing quests feels more meaningful.
+ Game play is nearly identical to the first game. Gameplay consists of killing enemies as you traverse 'the zone', scavenging dead bodies and loot to find weapons, armor, ammo, health etc. Survival is a main underlying component with the game. Weapons and armor degrade over time making them less effective and need to be fixed or replaced, radiation levels have to be checked, getting shot or attacked by mutant animals require you to use bandages to stop bleeding, eating is required every so often and you also need to watch your weight limit. Carry too much and your stamina runs out very quickly forcing you to stop or walk until you regain it back.
+ Gun battles are fun, fast and furious. Certain main missions puts you in unique situations which makes gun fights more fun and satisfying. Certain battles reminded me heavily of Half Life 2. For example one mission has you making your way across a deserted town as you clear the road of enemies. Unlike the first game where gun fights usually took place as you traverse the open environment to your next objective, Clear Sky has more focused concise battles tailored to the specific level.
+Variety of different weapons that feel unique
+Sound Effects
The Average:
With the addition of Factions also comes brain dead AI companions. Like most games, when you go into battle with your teammates, you will do the majority of killing while your 'teammates' sit back and relax. Teammates can also push you aside with ease - a big problem if your aiming down sights ready to make the crucial head shot only to have one of your squad member run into you pushing you aside messing up your aim.
The game features most of the same location as the first game with a few new additions. It doesn't hurt the game by any means as the locations and level design is fantastic however I also find it a bit lazy when developers heavily reuse assets from the previous game.
Long load times.
Minor bugs and glitches.
The Bad:
- (Minor spoiler Alert) There is a part near the middle of the game where you lose all your money without warning. From a story perspective it makes sense, this is a hostile environment and anything can go bad at any minute. From a gameplay perspective this is awful. All the work that went into saving your money so that you can eventually buy your favorite piece of armor or weapon is now gone. Not only was I frustrated but my desire to accomplish any more side quests was also diminished.
-Locating artifacts is a chore and almost unnecessary in this game. Artifacts are items that you can equip that grant you specific bonuses to your stats. In order to actually find these artifacts, you have to first equip your detector, than walk around the level in the hopes it will detect something for you to find. I found the process to be  time consuming and boring. This was a big downgrade from the previous game.
- This game is hard even on the medium setting. Right from the start enemies can kill you with relative ease leading to some very frustrating moments causing me to abuse quick save/load.
Conclusion
Although the game certainly retains a lot of good things from the first game while improving on certain aspects, the overall package is not as good. The pacing and difficulty being the biggest culprits. The addition of factions is a really good idea but not implemented as well as it should have been.  I enjoyed my time with the game but I was glad it was over.

Hate Plus is the sequel to Christine Love's Analogue: A Hate Story, and if you didn't already know that, I personally wouldn't recommend Hate Plus. While the events you're reading about don't require direct knowledge from the first game to understand, its impacts are significantly lessened without first experiencing Analogue.
If you did play Analogue however, you'll know more or less exactly what to expect, at least in term of its mechanics. Hate Plus, like its predecessor, is a visual novel. Long story short, you're going to spend the majority of your time reading and one shouldn't expect much else in term of traditional gameplay (and if you're going to stop reading here because of this then fair enough. Visual novels aren't going to be everyone's thing, though I urge you to at least give one or two a try if you haven't already). You assume the role of a space investigator sent to discover what has happened to a missing Derelict Generation Ship by reading numerous logs with the help of a female companion AI of your choice (or both of them, if you happen to have achieved a particular ending with Analogue). Unlike in Analogue however, your companion is also in unknown territory here, and as the result, is investigating these logs together with you, allowing her to provide interjections as you read. Once in a while, your AI will ask for a break, giving you her thoughts thus far and asking you for your take on the situation, which is one of the few instances where you're granted "agencies". It should be noted, however, that your influence is minimal, and I'm fairly certain the story will proceed to the same end regardless of your choices. While the story does provide a reasonable excuse, the linearity of the plot is likely to disappoint many people. However, I believe the helplessness that comes with the inability to communicate properly with your AI companion is intended, especially concerning a certain event that you may or may not run into depending on your choice of AI companion. The big addition, however, is that you can only beat the game in no less than 3 days. After reading a certain amount of logs, you will be unable to move on until a certain amount of time has passed. This is to provide breathing room and time to digest what you've read, which I do think is important. Many people will no doubt find this annoying, especially between day 2 and 3. You can very easily bypass this by changing your time, though I still recommend you play the game the way the developer wanted you to play it and just sit down and have a think before moving on.
Less important, but still worth mentioning, are the numerous little improvements to the UI. The visual has definitely been improved, the UI looks better than ever and there are somewhat more animation. More importantly, you can actually see portraits of characters if you click on their names, not only did it create more personality for these characters, it also helped me greatly in keeping track since I'm terrible with names (one of my personal quibbles with the first game).
Hate Plus's plot, while taking place directly after Analogue, deals with the events that happened long before the events depicted in first game. In Analogue: A Hate Story, through reading through logs, you discover a society, despite being in a spaceship, that has degraded far from the world we know. The Mugunghwa is filled with stifling gender roles, politically backward ideals and  ignorance. In Hate Plus, you get to see the Mugunghwa before it has gotten to that point and discover how it all happened. Hate Plus centers around the security chief of the ship, Old *Mute, a much older version of one of your AI companion that she has no memory of, and the political games she played as well as her inevitable demise (this is not a spoiler, you discover a log called "The Death of Old *Mute very early on).
For a character you never actually get to see (beside one or two portraits), Old *Mute is, at least to me, a surprisingly strong character. She doesn't take♥♥♥♥♥♥ has a sense of humor and occasionally oozes an incredibly corny air of coolness that nevertheless made me do a mental fist pump. Moreover, she is neither a villain nor hero. While she is manipulative and borderline amoral when it comes to doing her job, she shows an incredibly human side at times. This makes her eventual death all the more bitter, and *Mute's birth all the more tragic. This is why I personally recommend you play through the game the first time as *Mute, the understandably much less popular character. *Hyun-ae was the cute sidekick that is much more affable and relatable to the majority of the audience. *Mute was the chatty yet dutiful security chief of the ship that while I don't think anyone would deem evil, is nevertheless very much a product of an oppressive and dehumanizing society that she very much believes in. Analogue was *Hyun-ae's story, and Hate Plus is very much *Mute's. Her inability to comprehend a more "modern" and "liberal" way as well as her inability to accept her old self fits perfectly with the narrative and her character development. Thus, I very much believe if you're going to play through the game with *Hyun-ae, let it be your second playthrough.
Because one is assumed to have already known that the Mugunghwa will inevitably turn into what most of us perceive as an incredibly morally wrong and disturbing society, it gives the game, especially the latter parts, a sense of impending disaster and hopelessness. Whether your AI companion will end the game on a bitter or hopeful note, you know that Old *Mute and the society she lived in isn't heading toward anywhere pretty. This create many depressing moments that are genuinely hard to sit through, especially if you've chosen a certain AI companion. Personally, I believe Hate Plus to be even darker than Analogue, especially if you play through the game with *Mute. Reading through the logs depicting the lives of the Mugunghwa's citizens, the hatred, paranoia and moral degradation is present around every corner and you know it will be present at the end. Yet, thinking back on the game, I also remember moments of lighthearted romance, brief hopes, and Old *Mute's overwhelming coolness. I think that's important. Too many times, depressing stories make the mistake of staying depressing the whole way through that one eventually learn to get used to and cope with it. Hate Plus provides both moments of hopefulness and despair, and as such, when the time comes, the lighthearted moments feel so much brighter and the inevitable tragedies feel so much more tragic.
Since opinions are quite polarizing when comparing the two games (I personally prefer Hate Plus), I can only offer my own take: Don't play this game if you haven't played the first, you're going to miss out on so much of the character development and the impacts of the events. Moreover, there isn't enough direct improvements to justify skipping the first game. Don't play this game if you don't care about *Mute whatsoever, she is the center of the story this time and you'd rather be involved than detached.  Don't play this game if your experience of Analogue is complete and you do not want some questions answered. Hate Plus isn't needed to complete Analogue. It builds off its predecessor into its own story, but Analogue on its own is a complete experience. That said, if you're interested in the slightest in *Mute, the Mugunghwa's backstory, or just simply some more Analogue-style visual novel about moral degradation, hatred and dehumanization, I can't recommend Hate Plus enough.
(Just to be clear: A) This is my first review. B) I played through the game once with *Mute. C) I've played Analogue: A Hate Story and various of other visual novels. D) Bloody hell that's much longer than I thought it'd be.)

Oh, *Hyun-ae, let's solve mysteries together forever~
Hate Plus is a fantastic... something between a visual novel and a kinetic novel. Both this game and it's predecessor, Analogue, aren't a tangled spiderweb mess of routes, choices, decisions, Good and Bad Ends. There aren't many branching decision points in these games (Hate Plus doesn't even really have any), which kind of removes a lot of their "gaminess." That's okay with me; the visual/kinetic novel genre exists somewhere in the digital melting pot between traditional literature, comic books and video games. That's pretty great, in my opinion.
I won't go into the story because it would be rife with spoilers, but I'll talk some about the game itself. Hate Plus is even more linear than Analogue, which is okay. The bulk of the "gameplay" is spent reading over recovered logs from the derelict generation ship
. You've got the assistance of whichever AI you either choose or carry over from your Analogue clear data. Depending on the choices made in Analogue or when starting a new game, you may have a different relationship with either *Hyun-ae or *Mute.
The meat of the game's story is told through the logs and the AI's commentary on the logs. Because your ship was damaged somehow, you have a limited amount of data you can sift through every 12 hours, which forces the game to be played over a period of at least 39-ish real-time hours (though you can circumvent this, but the author will call you a "jerkface"). Every time you read through six logs or read a log that's very significant to the plot, your AI partner will want to discuss something with you. Depending on your progress, this could either be a discussion about your relationship or about the mystery of the
's reversion to a primitive Neo-Joseon culture. Occasionally you'll receive a message from your employer or other people, usually while you are extracting new data from the encrypted logs.
And that's pretty much the extent of the gameplay. There really isn't much "game" here; it's entirely about the narrative. And that's okay. The narrative is excellent; Christine Love is a fantastic writer. As a writer myself, she makes me jealous. The logs and your progress through them are carefully metered so you're slowly drip-fed the main story while seemingly being distracted by random bits and pieces that don't seem relevant. They become very relevant later.
The plot itself, like its predecessor, is
interspersed with little rejuvenating isles of humor and heartwarming. While I was going through the game (I was playing *Hyun-ae's route; I intend to finish *Mute's route eventually) there were many points where I desperately welcomed *Hyun-ae's insistence that we stop and chat. Some of the stories you read in the logs are soul-crushingly sad. Spending time "talking" with *Hyun-ae and her generally ridiculous levels of adorable sweetness balanced out the intense tragedy of the story from the past. I haven't completely finished *Mute's route, but her "breather episodes" seem to largely be composed of humor (and that's great, too). As the plot progressed further and further, the hopelessness of many past characters' situations started to press heavily upon me, drawing me deeper and deeper into the self-contained world and its terrible drama.
That isn't to say Hate Plus doesn't have problems. It has problems. The "real-life" time limit is my biggest personal gripe, even though you
circumvent it. As a general rule I hate it when games try to control the rate at which I play them. I can't stand turn limits, limited numbers of saves, save points, diminishing returns on experience points gain (I especially hate daily quests in MMOs, but that's a rant for another day). My second-biggest problem was the UI seemed to be very sluggish in responding to my mouse commands. Scrolling through the logs seemed to take far more "spins" of my mouse wheel than I would need to execute to scroll a web page in Chrome, for example. I was spinning the mouse wheel so much my index finger started to get a little numb! I tried lots of keyboard keys in an attempt to find some other way to scroll, but nothing seemed to work. Trying to grab the slider didn't work, either. Occasionally clicks on UI elements wouldn't register. I don't think these issues were part of the "interface screw" from the ship's low power and damage.
A lot of people seem to have another major gripe: the infamous "cake" sequence in *Hyun-ae's route. To be honest, I actually loved this part. Partly because I really did find it completely, adorably cute, and partly because it gave me a brief respite from the
. I happened to be playing at 3AM, but I still went in the kitchen and made a cake (it was pretty tasty, so it worked out). I understand why the developer chose to add this, and I can understand and appreciate why people would be annoyed by it, but I really loved the fact that it was in the game.
Hate Plus is a fantastic visual novel and I'd recommend it to almost anyone, especially fans of science fiction. The plot will make very little sense if you haven't played Analogue, however, so I recommend buying them both and playing them both. Don't let the poor "hours of play per dollar" ratio scare you off; there's some really great story here!
I will warn you though that if you suffer from massive testosterone poisoning, you will probably find both games to be very uncomfortable. Both can be
, especially on *Hyun-ae's routes. For me, that's a big win. The gaming industry as a whole is completely dominated by titles that are aggressively hypermasculine. It's nice to have something that more caters to my side of things.

MKX is everything I expected and more. I would recommend this game to anyone interested in the MK series.  Steam achievements are also supported, which is an additional bonus, as are cards towards a Steam Badge.  Absolutely satisfied.  A must have for any MK fan.

EDIT #2: MKXL announced for Oct 4th 2016

Note that this review is only positive because I mainly play the ofline mode for MKX, there are some very bad parts of the game I will go over.
MKX is the next installment in the Mortal Kombat series, it is a HUGE improvement in many aspects of the previous game, MK9, but in some ways, it does not add up.
tl;dr: Looks good compared to MK9, environment interaction, easier kombo inputs, multiple variations per karacter, brutalities, X-rays and fatalities rock. ♥♥♥♥♥♥ netcode, will abuse your hardware, stutter fps for some, constant lag for others, solid 60 fps for few. I lag a bit, changing settings does nothing. Offline modes however, are good in my opinion, no tag team. Needs a lot of work before it can call itself the game we have all waited for.
Pros:
+Good Graphics compared to that of MK9, very refreshing, might not compare to other current gen games but it's all about opinion.
+Environment Interaction is new in the series, can be very useful and give you the upper hand in a fight if used wisely
+Easier kombos, for example Kano ball is just (Back Forward, A), much simpler than it's MK9 predecessor
+3 variations per Karacter, each providing new cosmetic looks, kombos, and special moves. This helps to add diversity to the game and allows players to tinker with what kombos deal the most % with which variation.
+Very cinematic story, a step up from MK9's O.K. story.
+Good amount of stages, each with somewhat unique interactions with the environment, also has alternate skins for stages.
+Towers and faction wars add new multiplayer interactions.
+Nice selection of offline modes, single fight, test your luck, New towers appearing daily, weekly, etc. and of course practice modes for Kombos and fatalities.\
+The Krypt, if you've ever played legends of grimrock, that's basically what the Krypt is, I don't think I can talk about it objectively. Some people may find it clunky and annoying, others might find it fun and immersive.
Cons:
-The online, online in MK games is mostly♥♥♥♥♥♥ in this installment, High Voltage really left♥♥♥♥♥prints on the port. Unless you play with friends, you will constantly drop matches and lag your brains out, even after trying rooms with people in my area of the US, I still drop matches, randomly disconnect, and watch as my fps is dragged into the netherrealm.
-Story is weak near the end, plot isn't tied up fully, of course this is leaving room for a sequel but it was dissapointing.
-Kombos can be hard to pull off, this depends on your settings, and controller type. However some people report not being able to correctly pull of combos, with videos showing them doing the correct inputs, this is something solveable though through fiddling with some settings in the controllers menu.
-Optimization, wrote this review in a haste so I can't believe I forgot this, the game has some really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ optimization, I am well over the reccomended requirements and I can reach a solid 60 fps in training, however the second I play on a map with any heavy particle effects or a brutality happens my game starts to dip to sub-30 fps. Menus, X-rays, and Fatalities are locked to 30 fps, which is a bit dissapointing, considering developers going for that "cinematic feel" often forget that not everyone enjoys it. Changing video settings has done nothing for me other than make the game look worse. My drivers are up to date and I am well over the req's.
In conclusion, as a new installment into the MK franchise, MKX is promising, new, and quite fun. However until the various technical problems including optimization and online are somewhat patched. HOLD OFF ON BUYING. fps is a huge issue in fighting games because if I lag more than my online opponent, then he has the upper hand, this is the kind of game where good optimization and steady fps are absolutely necessary. VERY MEDIOCRE PC PORT.
IF YOU ARE STILL CONSIDERING BUYING THE GAME, WATCH VIDEOS, READ MORE REVIEWS, WEIGH PROS AND CONS AND BE CAREFUL IN YOUR PURCHASE. Buyer's remorse sucks

Before I start the review, let me get one thing across: Spelunky is a rouge-like. Sure there are shortcuts, but to beat the game you have to do it in one go, without the shortcuts. The joy of this game isn't in beating it, its in playing it. You don't need to win to be satisfied. If you don't like dying, then go buy another game.
Some History: Spelunky used to be a HTML5 game that was extremely pixelated. The old game wasn't necessaraly bad, it's just this verson is alot better. The graphics, controls, and gameplay experience are very refined. The game maintains a slightly cartoony style, but still good graphics.
In Spelunky, you start out with an optional tutorial that teaches through experience. It says: this is how you do it, now go try it out. Afterwards, you are flung into the mines level and are surround by familiar things. Much of the game, including the enemies, the items, traps, and ares you will have to learn on your own. All of these are recorded in a journal for future reference. If you can make it through four levels of the mines, you enter the jungle. If you have what the tunnel man asks for, he will build you a tunnel. Now, instead of starting in the mines, you can start in the jungle. Keep in mind, this is only to practice different stages; you still have to beat the game from the start. You will meet a (seemingly) friendly shopkeeper who sells you a variety of items. If you anger him, he will run at you with a shot-gun. You also can save the damsel (male, female, dog, and if you click the dog option 100 times sloth) in order to regenerate a single heart. If the damsel dies, you can use the carcass as a projectile weapon.
The gameplay itself is smooth and responsive, so when you die (mostly) it is your own fault. There might be a few cheap deaths when an enemy corners you, but these happen rarely and it is a randomely generated game. That said, the generation looks natural and you have ropes and bombs to get out of tough spots. There is also a daily challenge mode, and a deathmatch mode which can be very fun for LAN partys.
Now for the Cons. The game can be hard. I can also be easy. There is a large luck element to winning, but you will most likely still have fun on the failed runs. Also, levels have a time limit that when reached a fog will roll in and a ghost will come across the screen to one hit you. He can be dodged, and this is more of a limitation than a con. A couple easter eggs, a slew of achievements, and everything else make me give this game 9/10

I think it’s easy enough to skim through the other reviews and know that Brothers is a fresh, innovative, beautiful game with very few elements capable of being considered a flaw so instead I want to do my best to explain how it feels to play this game. Additionally, all of my game time was with a 360 pad and I cannot recommend enough that you use a controller when playing Brothers.
The controls are about as straight forward as controls can be; left stick and left trigger move and interact respectively for one brother, right stick and right trigger controls the other brother. That’s it. Yet with only 4 controls this game pulls you in and makes you feel like a part of the world in a way I have not seen in a game before. I think because of the simplicity of the controls, your mind has more attention to invest in the story, the emotions and the world stretching out before you. I wish I could explain one of the most impacting moments of the story without giving any spoilers, but there comes a point late in the game where the controls change in a very deliberate way and there are not enough words on this earth to explain how heavy of an emotional impact that change made.
Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is one of the finest adventures in gaming that I’ve been on, but when you combine the game with the absolute masterpiece of a control scheme it’s no longer an adventure I played.. it’s a memory that I lived.

i'm very torn about this game.  i wanted to love it and in the end i only kinda liked it.
in terms of raw game mechanics, it's better than Stick of Truth.  the placement-based combat is (in theory) more engaging than Stick's timing-based combat, you have a massive variety of powers to choose from and while a lot of the combat buddies end upfeeling *real real samey*, there are quite a few to choose from.
in terms of writing, story, dialogue, personal investment, an overall sensation of being engaged in what is happening and basically everything else, it is a huge step back from Stick of Truth.
in a nutshell, this game just feels like it's trying way too hard.
where Stick's references and in-jokes felt like a celebration of a now-legendary show, Fractured doing the exact same thing feels forced and almost joyless.  there are a few moments where the writing is legitimately funny, but those moments are few and far between and spaced out with jokes that fall flat or just keep ♥♥♥♥ing going on and on and on and will not. ♥♥♥♥ing. end.
the storyline doesn't seem to coalesce until the last two hours which feel frantically paced and cluttered with boss fight after boss fight after boss fight that *should* be exciting, thrilling, and just ends up being exhausting.
what was definitely a good idea on paper - the new Buddy Utility system, in which various characters assist you with simple puzzles - also swiftly becomes extremely tiresome.  the map is cluttered with way too many iterations of each, which force you to stop the game cold, rummage for the right buddy, call him in, complete a simple quicktime event and then sit and wait for the animation to end.
it's okay at first but it gets old *real* fast and once its old, it gets *real real irritating*.
and by the time you get to the end, the game is throwing multiples of these every single screen.
and that's a problem, especially because without the rock-solid storyline of the original, it is just really hard to care about what you're doing.
and that's the biggest problem with this game - it never manages to engage, leaving you with a challenging time just trying to care about what you're doing and a script that seems like it's absolutely desperate to feel like South Park while never feeling like anything more than a video game *based* on South Park.
the appearance of the 'Member Berries as one of *way too many* item hunt sidequests struck me as deeply ironic, because this entire game seems to be saying "MEMBER STICK OF TRUTH? MEMBER WHAT A GREAT GAME THAT WAS?"
sure.  i 'member.
if Stick of Truth was "The Tale of Scrotie McBoogerballs," Fractured But Whole is "The Poop that Took a Pee."
and that is a goddamned shame.

Rewriting my review to reflect more accurate gameplay.
I absolutely cannot recommend this game at full price. Several problems:
1. Bugs, bugs, bugs. If you time a fart pause poorly during a boss it will freeze your game. If the music quits during a battle, you will get kicked out, lots of stupid little bugs that shouldn't be in a full price game like this.
2. Short story. For $60, a 15-20 hour main story line is short. I get that it is South Park and if you like the show you won't be disappointed with the game's story. But, it is short for the price (compared to other AAA $60 RPGs)
3. Several UI issues. Text is small and disappears quickly. I miss most of the joke items (compared to Stick of Truth, I don't get to see what I'm picking up easily, and that makes me miss the jokes).
4. Boss battles are boring. There's a bit of strategy, but the game is mostly walking from one boss to another, it lacks any real depth. I don't feel like I'm really doing much other than equipping new things and moving onto the next boss. There's no real customization other than equipping whatever will give you the most might. Kind of lame.
5. For a role playing game, there's not much role playing. I get you are the "new kid" but there's no real customization other than picking your class abilities and then always equipping the highest level artifacts. Pretty boring. Gear that has no stats, only looks? C'mon
6. Finally, always requires an internet connection to Uplay. Why can't I just play my game offline? Also, DLC on day one is annoying for a full price game. Great for FTP games, but not on a AAA $60 game. Pretty annoying and this business model sucks. Not the biggest gripe with the game, but certainly something worth mentioning.
The only real good thing about it is that it is basically a 15-20 hour episode of South Park based in the "Superheroes" universe. Fun for that alone, but certainly not worth $60. Wait a year and get the GOTY edition with all the DLC for $20-30 and maybe it will be worth it. Get it on sale. But right now, I can't recommend it.

My recommendation comes with a lot of caveats:
- First, if you enjoyed Analogue, you'll probably like this one. However, this will not change your mind if you didn't care for the first game.
- Second, like some other reviewers, I didn't find the overall story quite as engrossing, but I felt more drive to go back and replay to pick up new character reactions/interactions.
- Third, be prepared to be upset about *Mute. A lot.
- Fourth, and the main thing that keeps me from recommending this game whole-heartedly: WOW the narrative's treatment of *Mute's romantic preferences is really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ at times. It basically feels like she's being bullied into liking women in certain situations, and while I appreciate how there's a lot of good commentary about how one's preferences are often shaped by the society in which one lives, I still feel like it could've been handled better. If you're a queer person who's ever felt pressured to feel romantic attraction to someone you're not attracted to, you're probably going to spend a lot of time wincing during *Mute's playthrough(s) if you play as a woman. Especially in the harem route.
- And finally, once again, I recommend picking up the soundtrack. The song "Not Ero" is really cute and catchy, and I've been listening to the other tracks while writing lately.

This is a pretty good little conspiracy and if followed sequentially you get a taste of what's coming in day 1, get a glimpse of the end in day 2, and in day 3 you see it from the conspiracy side. It's a sad little tale where really, no one is happy and the "heroes" lose. I liked that there's not really a big event that's the cause; wheels were in motion before the logs you start reading, and you feel those wheel get a little oiling during the course of events, then turn some more. There's no magic gas or anything behind it all.
The problem is it's less of a game than Analogue. You have enough power over the three days for every log, every single one. So why make me pick? It's completely pointless, you may as well just have fed them to me in a set order. In the original you had a log percentage and you felt like you were investigating, unlocking new avenues as you passed logs to your AI companion. There's none of that there, you unlock the next six logs, read them, then repeat with the next six and so on until you run out of power. There's no reason not to read them in sequential order.
There's also a lack of variety. You had the terminal in Analogue to mix things up a little, plus the bit with the reactor added a little drama to the proceedings. Here it's just so... bland. You read logs, then shut down. Repeat for three days.
There isn't a climax to the story either. You just run out of logs. Contrast that to Analogue where you find out why the Pale Bride doesn't speak, or why everyone on the ship is dead.
It isn't helped that Hyun-ae's route is so unchallenging. There's no conflict, no drama, no tension. How can a relationship survive between someone in a screen and someone in the physical world? Won't the investigator eventually leave her? ♥♥♥♥ that, here's a message about AI bodies to completely dissolve any potential for dramatic tension. The opportunity is also completely missed to draw parallels between your relationship and that of Mute and her security lieutenants, the way she had seen them come and go. What happened when you died and Hyun-ae lived on? Nope, nothing. What about charges against her for her actions on the ship? Nope, answered, no tension. What about her being part of the contract and thus taken from you? Ignored.
Hyun-ae and the story are just completely disconnected from one another, and the new log format doesn't help. She doesn't make any substantive contributions to the narrative, just little one liners here and there, generally along the lines of "harsh" or some such.
I even felt the music wasn't as good this time around.
I hope and pray that when I do it with Mute further down the line that it will be better, because there's someone with a more personal investment in events. There's also that achievement for reading all the logs again on day 3 with her, which would suggest she reviews them in a new light.
I should be interested in the replay, but I can't get enthused. In Analogue I didn't need to re-read logs I still remembered, I could pass them straight to the AI to get the new content. You can't do that here, and I'm not sure I can face the idea of slowly... scrolling... through... every... log... again. It's a game designed to be replayed which isn't designed to be replayed. Or played at all really.
The game really only does one thing better and that's that it ties the side characters more tightly into the story. In Analogue you could know nothing about the Smiths and it wouldn't change a thing, but here all those people provide a window into how society was changing, and the impact it had on people.
I come out the end of this really disappointed. There's a good story underneath it all, but it misses every opportunity to be more.

So, like, I was just about to write this review when, at that very moment, my doorbell rang. It was my sister. So I interrupted my review, got up, and greeted her with a calm "hello". She was just back from the shops, and had bought me a sandwich, so I stopped to eat and have a chat. Her boyfriend was getting on fine, she was enjoying her job, the usual.
After lunch, I wasn't particularly in the mood for writing, so I decided to do something else for a while. I ended up spending most of it on YouTube, where I learned great deals about Blinking and Slamming. It was quite the entertainment, and I felt a lot better afterwards. So I got back to writing this review.
...
If you thought that was a whole load of completely unnecessary prose, then this game is not for you.
Seriously, I knew going in that it wasn't as well-liked as the first one, but I absolutely wasn't expecting it to be so long and drawn out. It's not that there's unnecessary logs - although some are - it's that they're all way, way longer than they actually should be. Condensed by 50% and not lose anything.
The other big issue was that the story simply wasn't very interesting. The A-plot, the politics stuff, is fairly well written, although somewhat let down by that it's very predictable. As for the B-plots, they just don't go anywhere. While the B-plots were important in the first game for setting the tone and getting an idea of what life was like, here they're just mediocre relationship stories.
There's a lot of smaller but important issues too. The time mechanic that does absolutely nothing, that you can read entries out of order basically spoils earlier entries (and sequence breaks dialogue a little bit), there's a lot less AI chat this time, Mute route's badly written plot twist that's just there for the sake of a plot twist, and the goddam awful one-line-at-a-time scrolling.
Overall though, it's simply not a good enough story that I can recommend to anyone. I loved the first game, but this ain't it.

Ladies and Gentlemen, this is the sequel to Christine Love's previous title, "Analogue: a Hate Story" so if you are thinking about looking into this, I suggest you take a look at Analogue first before taking Hate Plus into consideration. The setting now takes place on your spaceship on it's way back to Earth along with whomever you brought along from the Mugunghwa: either *Hyun-ae or *Mute (or both) and you are stuck with them for the next 3 days. The entries you will be reading will take place before the events in Analogue so your save files from Analogue can be transfered over to Hate Plus if you choose to do so. Although the story feels a bit weaker than Analogue, it's still a good story nonetheless and it's themes shift from traditional society into a more democratic society with political instability, including once again sexual themes with some LGBT thrown into the mix. Unfortunately, this is pretty much a linear novel despite having choices, but sadly it is only an illusion and so the only thing that changes is the dialogue so you can be a complete jerk and their opinion of you will remain the same. Scrolling down log files have been fairly annoying due to the fact that it does pause a couple of times for unexplained reasons and with the AI's commentating while you read can be a bit more bad than good because you can accidentally miss a bit of dialogue and there is no way to go back and read what you missed, but as long as you pay attention, it will only be a minor complaint. Once you run out of power for the day and finish reading all of the entries you downloaded, you will have to wait for 12 hours in order to get back into reading again and it can be a bit irritating if you really want to keep reading, but it can be beneficial if you want to take a break, but can't find a good place to stop (there is a way to bypass the 12 hour wait time, but personally I never did that). Overall, I think this is a nice expansion to an already great novel the industry has to offer us, but again I highly recommend that you check out Analogue before jumping into Hate Plus.

I loved MK1-3 as a kid, was disappointed with the next titles and impressed with the nostalgic MK9 reboot. I had high hopes for MKX and they were delivered. The story takes the right turn, the mechanics are deeper, the variations add a new layer of strategy to the genre, the old characters feel fresh, the new ones are a welcome addition and the graphics are definetly next gen (including the Fatalities). And content... LOTS of content! If you are a MK fan, like fighting games or want to start playing them, I highly recommend MKX.
EDIT: no PC support or KP2 as annonced on Jan 20th 2016
EDIT #2: MKXL announced for Oct 4th 2016

Note that this review is only positive because I mainly play the ofline mode for MKX, there are some very bad parts of the game I will go over.
MKX is the next installment in the Mortal Kombat series, it is a HUGE improvement in many aspects of the previous game, MK9, but in some ways, it does not add up.
tl;dr: Looks good compared to MK9, environment interaction, easier kombo inputs, multiple variations per karacter, brutalities, X-rays and fatalities rock. ♥♥♥♥♥♥ netcode, will abuse your hardware, stutter fps for some, constant lag for others, solid 60 fps for few. I lag a bit, changing settings does nothing. Offline modes however, are good in my opinion, no tag team. Needs a lot of work before it can call itself the game we have all waited for.
Pros:
+Good Graphics compared to that of MK9, very refreshing, might not compare to other current gen games but it's all about opinion.
+Environment Interaction is new in the series, can be very useful and give you the upper hand in a fight if used wisely
+Easier kombos, for example Kano ball is just (Back Forward, A), much simpler than it's MK9 predecessor
+3 variations per Karacter, each providing new cosmetic looks, kombos, and special moves. This helps to add diversity to the game and allows players to tinker with what kombos deal the most % with which variation.
+Very cinematic story, a step up from MK9's O.K. story.
+Good amount of stages, each with somewhat unique interactions with the environment, also has alternate skins for stages.
+Towers and faction wars add new multiplayer interactions.
+Nice selection of offline modes, single fight, test your luck, New towers appearing daily, weekly, etc. and of course practice modes for Kombos and fatalities.\
+The Krypt, if you've ever played legends of grimrock, that's basically what the Krypt is, I don't think I can talk about it objectively. Some people may find it clunky and annoying, others might find it fun and immersive.
Cons:
-The online, online in MK games is mostly♥♥♥♥♥♥ in this installment, High Voltage really left♥♥♥♥♥prints on the port. Unless you play with friends, you will constantly drop matches and lag your brains out, even after trying rooms with people in my area of the US, I still drop matches, randomly disconnect, and watch as my fps is dragged into the netherrealm.
-Story is weak near the end, plot isn't tied up fully, of course this is leaving room for a sequel but it was dissapointing.
-Kombos can be hard to pull off, this depends on your settings, and controller type. However some people report not being able to correctly pull of combos, with videos showing them doing the correct inputs, this is something solveable though through fiddling with some settings in the controllers menu.
-Optimization, wrote this review in a haste so I can't believe I forgot this, the game has some really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ optimization, I am well over the reccomended requirements and I can reach a solid 60 fps in training, however the second I play on a map with any heavy particle effects or a brutality happens my game starts to dip to sub-30 fps. Menus, X-rays, and Fatalities are locked to 30 fps, which is a bit dissapointing, considering developers going for that "cinematic feel" often forget that not everyone enjoys it. Changing video settings has done nothing for me other than make the game look worse. My drivers are up to date and I am well over the req's.
In conclusion, as a new installment into the MK franchise, MKX is promising, new, and quite fun. However until the various technical problems including optimization and online are somewhat patched. HOLD OFF ON BUYING. fps is a huge issue in fighting games because if I lag more than my online opponent, then he has the upper hand, this is the kind of game where good optimization and steady fps are absolutely necessary. VERY MEDIOCRE PC PORT.
IF YOU ARE STILL CONSIDERING BUYING THE GAME, WATCH VIDEOS, READ MORE REVIEWS, WEIGH PROS AND CONS AND BE CAREFUL IN YOUR PURCHASE. Buyer's remorse sucks

"Clear Sky" is brutal, uncompromising, and definitely worth a try.
I remember becoming pretty decent at "Shadow Of Chernobyl." Maybe I had the difficulty pulled back a bit for that game. I can't quite remember.
Even so, I don't remember "Shadow" being as downright mean as "Clear Sky" feels.
You will die. A lot. Continuously. I'm not really exaggerating when I say you should consider saving after anything whatsoever goes in your favor. Clear a group of attackers? Save. Take down a single hostile? Save. Walk forward for 30 seconds without getting irradiated, falling into an anomaly, chewed up by dogs, or shot? Save. Stand still for a few moments without anything bad happening? Save. Hear anything even mildly "story-based" in a conversation? Save. Just successfully saved a game? Save again.
Seriously, I was more adept at hitting F5 than the default run-toggle key after only a short time.
And be aware that it's possible (though unlikely) to save a game that won't completely reload. The engine will get to the "Synchronizing" stage and then hang.
Save multiple saves at multiple times.
Oh, and you think you're pretty good with guns in videogames? Yeah - about that. In Clear Sky, here's how it works: Your enemies, even the dirt-poor bandits, fire munitions that can apparently home in on you in the dark from across the map. This behavior extends to individual shotgun pellets. Also, their grenades are seemingly possessed of a malevolent intelligence that WILL find you. Through walls. In the dark.
Now, for your part, any weapon that is not a sniper rifle fired from the prone position has about an 80% chance of MISSING whatever it is you're trying to kill. You will fire entire magazines - and I'm talking about one shot at a time, not full-auto - and every bullet but one will guide itself to a point that is not the thing in your crosshairs. If you do hit something by micraculous happenstance, you will have to hit it many MANY times before it drops. This applies to the aforementioned bandits, and the well-equipped military. (It's just that the military kills you faster and takes twice the lead before they drop.) With the notable exception of the Bloodsuckers, any hostile you encounter can be expected to behave as though they were made of solid steel and wearing armor of similarly solid steel.
You, of course, are made of wet tissue-paper. Some decent armor will upgrade you to dry cardboard. The thin kind, I mean. Not the cool stuff that they make shipping boxes with.
Oh, and ammunition is pretty scarce. Also expensive. And the stuff you scrounge and sell to the traders? They buy it cheap. Some things they won't even pay you for. What they sell to you, naturally, carries a hefty premium. You can eventually build a stockpile of essentials, but it will take a while. It will also take a while because the fast-travel system (the guides) costs money to use, and you need to save that money for bullets. A trip to a trader that has anything worth buying often requires walking across nearly the whole world.
Getting rewards for completed missions also follows that formula. That squad-leader you just risked life and limb for? No, he doesn't have the money with him. You have to walk all the way back to The Cordon for that measly 750 RU. No, he doesn't want to buy anything you have on you, except food and vodka. Have a nice trip! Hope you don't get ambushed on the way!
And you should definitely build that ammo stockpile. As soon as you commit to a certain kind of weapon, you will go up against a horde of enemies that are carrying weapons chambered for whatever you DON'T prefer. It's almost uncanny.
Also, before getting rolled up into the endgame, make sure you have all the best gear that exists in the world. Otherwise, you will be like me. You'll get all the way to Chernobyl, and then the game will become effectively unwinnable because you're up against nearly invincible enemies that warp in and can magically shoot around cover. You will need lots of bandages - as in, every single one you can find, and probably ten more. Plus every medkit you can get your hands on, and the best armor in the game. All that, and 1000 rounds of AR ammo. And every bullet you can possibly get for two different sniper rifles. You might have a chance.
All of the above sounds terrifying and awful, but I also have to say something else: "Clear Sky" is oddly compelling. It took me almost 27 hours of getting abused by the game before I finally decided that I didn't care. Up to that point, I was thoroughly engrossed. The bleak, strange, and unsettling environment is intriguing, and the overall challenge somehow manages to make you want to try again (most of the time). Oh, and when the game decides to mess with your mind, it REALLY succeeds.
So, give "Clear Sky" a shot. Several shots, actually. Like I said, good luck with actually HITTING anything.

Deponia is a great point-and-click adventure game. It has a fantastic art direction, interesting and well fleshed-out characters, a compelling storyline, and many hours worth of gameplay. It's a great series and you won't be disappointed.
That being said, let's consider a few of the cons. Deponia suffers from the curse that haunts most point-and-click adventures: puzzle design. Progress in the game fan often consist not in figuring something out, but on clicking on everything, everyone, in every order imaginable. However, this is mostly a fault of the genre as a whole, true of even great masterpieces like Monkey Island, so you probably know if you can handle this kind of thing or not.
Another con is the occasional villainous nature of the protagonist. While Rufus is certainly an anti-hero with plenty of personal faults that people will readily point out to him and which he will readily ignore, a few of his actions are simply mean-spirited. People being harmed by his carelessness is fun and good, but on more than one occassion he sets out to deliberately cause serious harms to his friends. This clashes with the rest of his character, and these moments really do stand out.
The jokes can occasionally be crude as well. Nothing vulgar, and always humorous in my opinion, but I can also understand if others disapprove.
And lastly, as spoiler free as I can say this, the end of the trilogy leaves several major loose ends.
That all being said, Deponia was a fantastic experience and one I will readily share with my friends. The humor is clever, the dialogue is well written, the plot well constructed, and the game only improves as it goes on. Buy this game, support the developers, and demand a sequel trilogy, because this series deserves and demands one!

I loved South Park: The Stick of Truth, so as soon as this game released I knew that I had to pick it up. What I looked forward to was a similar experience as the first game, and that, in theory, is what I got. However, as of right now I cannot recommed  spending your money on this game in its current state.  It is simply to full of bugs to spend $60 on it.
Within the first hour, I had to Alt+F4 and restart the game due to my character getting stuck in place after exiting a cutscene.  I have had to use Alt+Enter in order to fix a black screen problem on start up, or after cutscenes. There have been multiple times that I thought that I had to restart the game as a field cutscene simply stopped in its progress, characters just standing around and blinking for 20-30 seconds, in what I can only assume is a poorly designed loading period. The final straw that caused me to finally write a review and want to warn others was after in the middle of a story fight, the game got stuck in an animation loop, not allowing me to click out, and simply holding it there where I could only hope that the autosave is not far behind where it froze.
As for the combat which is definitely the thing most changed from Stick of Truth, it has grown on me considerably. Instead of the traditional teams-lined-up style that SoT had, you fight on a grid, manuvering to where you and your party will get the most damage done with AoE, knockback combos, and position swaps.
Though I have not beaten the game yet, what you can expect from this game is more of the stick of truth, just with a bit more of an ingruiting battle system.  I'm sure that it will be a great game as soon as the problems are fixed, but I would recommend waiting for that to happen instead of trying to power through the many techincal problems the game has.

Following up on Analogue: A Hate Story, Hate Plus is a game about reading the records of a dead spaceship society alongside your female AI companion(s) in order to piece together just what screwed it all up. In Analogue, we learned about why the entire population of the ship died following a stint as a weird emperor-and-male-superiority-centric culture (I am told that this is reminiscent of Korea's Joseon Dynasty; as I don't know Korean history, I will take the Internet's word on this). In Hate Plus, we seek to dig deeper into the ship's history and find out what caused this cultural regression in the first place.
Hate Plus was initially conceived as a DLC for Analogue, but quickly grew too large to be contained in an add-on. Thus, Hate Plus became its own game, though still very much connected to the original. If you have a save from a completed game of Analogue, you can continue from it in Hate Plus, with the same AI(s) you ended with, viewing you in the same light that you left them viewing you in. If you haven't played Analogue, or didn't keep an ending save, never fear! Hate Plus will ask you a series of questions to get you going so you can pretend like you've been here, all along.
Which gets us to the gameplay. Just like Analogue, 95% of the game is spent reading document after document after document. But where Analogue had a cool command line puzzle bit towards the end, Hate Plus is pretty much just reading. When you're not reading documents, you'll be reading what your AI pal has to say, and occasionally picking responses from a dialogue wheel.
Effort has been made to make the AIs seem more natural, this time around. When you hover over a choice, their facial expression changes as they anticipate which answer you'll give. And instead of clicking a button to hear their thoughts after each document, they're ever-present through the full read. This is... kind of good, kind of bad.
When the AI has something interesting to say, it's nice to see it pop up on the side. Although it does carry the problem that they react to what's just scrolled onto the bottom of the screen, while I prefer to keep the text I'm reading at the top of the screen. Plus I did accidentally scroll too far and cause the AI's observations to permanently disappear on a couple occasions. But the big problem I have with it is that the AIs just often have nothing important to say. This is especially true of *Hyun-ae, whose observations seem to consist mainly of "oh"s, sentences that trail off before the important bit, and telling me how cute different relationships are.
In the first game, *Hyun-ae was a major player in the historical plot. She had a lot to say and was sad and hopeful and fascinating and informative. *Mute, on the other hand, had a strong connection to the society and culture that we were reading about, and offered an equally-fascinating antithesis to *Hyun-ae coupled with insight into how everybody who wasn't *Hyun-ae thought and acted at the time. In this game, *Mute is the major player in the plot, more or less, while *Hyun-ae is just kind of... there.
*Hyun-ae's purpose (beyond pointing at things that swear and screeching, proper Invasion of the Body Snatchers style) is to play the waifu, but if anything she makes me realize what a mistake that right-guy-in-the-right-place relationship built over the course of the first game probably was. Despite managing to convince me to bake an IRL cake for a video game character, *Hyun-ae bores me. In Analogue, she was in a position of weakness, and the player was given the opportunity to play the heroic shoulder to cry on. You were given the chance to make a connection and bond with this character. But now it's a year and a half later, and the connection needs to be reestablished, and in my opinion, it's not. Though, I can't help but feel like Christine Love maybe wrote it that way on purpose, to instill all of that doubt about the basis of the AI-player waifu relationship experienced above.
And, I mean, if so, I admit I have to respect that.
Now, *Mute, on the other hand, has a much better showing during the frame story. During the course of Hate Plus, you'll read about what *Mute could be, and what she's capable of. You develop an appreciation for her personality, and she becomes a much more endearing character, despite her current misogynistic ideals. For Hate Plus, I definitely recommend taking the ride with *Mute.
Actually, no, that's a lie, I just lied to your face. I regret nothing.
If I have to make a recommendation about which AI to read old documents with, I'm going to recommend
. Since you could get a special ending in Analogue by beating the odds and finishing the game with both AIs, it's possible to play through Hate Plus with both. And I honestly feel like this is the playthrough that Hate Plus was built for. It's the best of both worlds. It improves on both characters' frame stories. Dull comments are largely replaced by conversations between the two. All of the interesting twists and turns from *Mute's path are available, with the bonus that you can still read Block 3 (which is never unlocked when going through with *Mute only) AS WELL AS Block 13 (which is never unlocked when going through with *Hyun-ae only). It also fixes the problem presented by *Hyun-ae being a boring waifu, as *Mute and *Hyun-ae's interactions are about as adorably tsundere as it gets. And as an added bonus, you're presented with a few fun segments reminiscent of Deus Ex: Human Revolution's social battles that are essentially the game's only puzzles.
So that's the frame story, but what about the meat of the game? What about the documents that you'll be spending most of your time reading?
Well, they range from cute to interesting to pret-ty dang boring. I'd say on the whole, the story presented in Hate Plus's documents does not reach nearly the same "holy♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; level of intrigue that Analogue pulled off so well. It does answer the question of what happened to cause the Mugunghwa's people to regress to a far outdated way of thinking, but I feel that the answer just isn't as astounding as I was hoping.
There are some twists and turns, relationships of all sorts, and political intrigue. One block is entirely comprised of logged conversations between important political figures that the AIs find boring. On the other hand, I think it's one of the more interesting bits to read, though that may just be because the format is easier to plow through.
The logs you'll be reading are definitely longer than in Analogue. The more boring ones can be a bit of a trudge. Block 3 is generally the last one unlocked in any route with *Hyun-ae. As such, it should be the final end-all be-all wow factor ending, but it's honestly the most boring block in the game, to me. On the other hand, *Mute gets Block 13 from the beginning. This block covers the early days of the re-Joseoned age, and I find it to be one of the more interesting blocks available.
The game does focus on some things for a bit too long. I'm no stranger to writing far too much (I mean, wow, are you actually still reading this review?), but sometimes the documents just go and go and go. Most of Blocks 1 and 2 are dedicated to young people falling in and out of love, and I'd go so far as to say that, while the actual personalities of the people differ, the main relationships of Block 1 and Block 2 are similar enough to be a little redundant (though still cute to read about).
Please don't let any of that dissuade you, though. Hate Plus may not be quite up to Analogue's standards, but the tales presented are certainly worth reading. Just, you know, they're
worth reading if you're reading them alongside *Mute. And they're the
worth reading if you're reading them alongside both *Mute and *Hyun-ae at once.
