A sequel to Analogue: A Hate Story. Like that "game," this one is essentially a semi-interactive epistolary novella (even less interactivity than the first game, actually). Adjust expectations accordingly.
Hate Plus satisfyingly concludes the plot threads left hanging at the end of Analogue, but I think it falls short compared to its predecessor in many key areas:
1. A questionable game pacing decision forces the player to wait 12 hours before progressing in the brief story--twice. Luckily, this can be skipped easily by pressing "S" on the save screen.
2. The altered UI attempts to focus more on the AI characters by putting them onscreen beside story content, but ends up slowing down faster readers with some choppy scrolling issues (even on a very powerful rig).
3. The original soundtrack is still high-quality but is somehow less memorable than Analogue's. The funny non-canon "bonus" ending song is an exception, however.
4. The game's plot focuses more on the personal lives of various characters than the socioeconomic ramifications of their actions--something of a change from Analogue. Much less mystery, much less suspense. Not really a surprise given Hate Plus's premise, though.
If you really enjoyed Analogue and want to see some proper closure for the AI characters, Hate Plus is worth the time and money. If not, feel free to skip.

Warband is quietly one of the best games you will ever come across. Seriously. It doesn't look like much, but in actual fact its a deep low-fantasy simulation of a medieval world. It lets you recruit armies, train individuals, marry, interact with lords, become a vassal, start a rebellion, create your own kingdom, start businesses, attack traders etc. What is particularly important however, is the fact this is a third-person game; you are doing this from the front lines; scaling the siege ladders, chasing down the merchants, sneaking into town dungeons, battling on the plains. Its all there for you.
In addition to this, the wealth of mods that can be seamlessly turned on and off for Warband is immense. Want to leave the pseudo-history of the base game and go do the same in Middle-Earth? The Old World? Well you can.
Don't be put off by the way it looks; buy it and lose your life to it.

Mount & Blade isn't really comparable to any games, save for the ones that are DIRECTLY (and blatantly) inspired by it.
It's a flawless mix of strategy, RPG and action. You create your character, set your stats and attributes by a classic skills sheet and then you are thrust into the realm of Calradia.
You move around, via top-down-ish view, the world map, going to villages, towns, forts and bandit encampments. You will spend your time tracking and fighting parties of enemies with your own custom party or running from them. Attack merchant caravans for plunder or battle Nobles of other kingdoms for either glory or strategy.
The combat system is awesome and feels 'right'.
The graphics are very dated but this is the only problem with the game, due to its age and scope. The graphics will improve drastically with the sequel in 2017/18, but until then the mod support will keep you going.
You don't just play M&B, you experience it.

One thing you should know immediately: dying is not a shameful event in Spelunky. If anything, it's equally a moment for learning and for laughing.
Spelunky is a game where you traverse 15 levels and fight a boss at the end. But it is so much more than that. I've played the Xbox arcade version for over 500 hours, so take my word on this: your experience will differ every single time. The levels are completely randomized, with the exception that the standard exit is always somewhere at the bottom of the level. But along the way, you'll encounter enemies and some friends as well. Well, the shopkeeper is your friend until some enemy angers him. But that's what makes this game so fun: it is a dynamic, ever-changing experience and I promise, if you make the same mistake enough times, you'll learn something, and be better for it.
This is without a doubt my favorite game of all time.

So when I hear that the next Stalker game was on the horizon (instead of waiting for seven years), I couldn’t wait to see what GSC Game World have in store. Well, just a year later, along arrives Stalker, Clear Sky (CS) – a prequel to SoC and sadly, also a lessor game in most areas as the new features like Faction Wars just didn’t pan out effectively.
Like most open world games, it’s hard to say how long to beat it. For me, as I like to do literally everything and explore every nook and cranny, took me about 65 hours to complete, so I can safely assume average will be around 20 or so. Pretty decent with a good array of missions / side quests and diversions, CS is unfortunately a step down from SoC. The new features like Faction Wars and able to customise your weapons did not pan out well enough as actually, they are more of a hindrance or simply, not worth investing your time. However the emission blowout was pretty awesome due to its sudden nature. So if you are coming from SoC, expect to be disappointed however if this is your first Stalker game, it’s an enjoyable ride but expect spoilers. I guess you can view CS as a rock and a hard place.

Performance:
Well optimized game, likely thanks to using the Unreal Engine. Manages to stay at 60 FPS even on lower performance machines. A few minor bugs are in but they don't hinder gameplay in any way (e.g. alt-tabbing is a bit iffy sometimes).
Netcode:
Works really well. Probably the best netcode of any fighting game out there right now. Of course you gonna have some lags with people that have internet issues, but if you experience a lot of lag issues, it's probably you.
Content:
The Story mode is only 2~3 hours. Some fights can feel really unfair, especially for newer players or players unfamiliar with the story-relevant characters.
There is only one side mission fight for each character; a bit lackluster.
Some features from previous game iterations are no longer present, like team vs team or survival, but honestly, I think they weren't that popular anyway.
There is a huge assortment of customization options making your main fighter individual. It's pretty neat.
The online features are satisfying, the lobby system works and the tournament mode is a really nice addition.
Graphics:
Eh, isn't like Skyrim with Mods, and there is obviously priority on performance rather than overdone fancy graphic details, but it still looks great.
Gamepad support:
XInput and DirectInput are both supported, therefore nearly every controller should work. Keybindings can be freely re-assigned and even keyboard bindings can be fully customized to suit your needs.
Gameplay:
A well balanced fighter, definitely slower than games like SFV, but way more tactical depth. I personally enjoyed every round so far even if I got beaten hard. The roster is colorful and offers something for every kind of playstyle preference.
Summary:
I enjoy the game a lot. In the 20 hours since release I played 17 hours and wrote that review. Lost some rounds, won some rounds, but definitely a enjoyable experience.

Forewarning: Do not play Hate Plus if you have not played Analouge: Hate Story. You won't understand a thing.
While I am recommending this, I am recommending it with a hint of caution. The story, much like the first, is well-written and decent. However, Hate Story is the superior version in my eyes, and while I prefer to judge a game on it's own merits, it's impossible to do so for Hate Plus since it boldly and transparently rides on Hate Story's plot and method to it's madness.
To get the negatives out of the way, this game focuses on shedding some light on *Mute's backstory, Pre-Year 0. And this is essentially the biggest negative on the game. One out of the three possible playthrough is rendered unfulfilling due to the lack of *Mute being available. Meaning *Hyun-ae and the player are spending three days just reading backstory to kill time (and making cake). This is unlike Hate Story where both *Hyun-ae and *Mute were focused on and had relevance to the story at hand. Granted, *Hyun-ae had the stronger focus, but up until the reactor meltdown happened, you had the ability to learn a lot about *Mute.
That leads to my next negative: The lack of interactivity with the GUI in this game. Honestly, my favorite part of Hate Story was stopping that reactor meltdown, trying to read and understand the numbers and trying to switch batteries while trying to not accidentally mispell or shut off communications. Hate Plus doesn't have any of that at all, and I found that to be quite disappointing.
The ability to show logs to your AI has also been taken out, and instead allows your AI(s) read alongside with you, and they openly react to what you're reading and keep track of any key figures. I actually like this part, however scrolling was a bit of a pain because the GUI wasn't very smooth. Beyond that, I largely prefer flipping pages because I am a fast reader.
And take this as more of a personal negative rather than an objective one, but I feel *Hyun-ae and *Mute's personalities were simplified in this game. They both felt more flat this time, and it may be because they've become saturated in my mind. However I feel it's worth noting because I do believe there is a noticable lack of wholeness. I'll refrain from going into detail about it though.
Lastly, the most controversial part of this game has to be the time barriers that were meant to increase immersion for the player. It... doesn't work for me. Sorry, I know others agree with it, but I don't enjoy it. There is a reason why other games refrain from doing this, and it's because it doesn't work. If the game locks you out from continuing on, chances are your players will be turned off and they will just stop playing the game completely. Furthermore, it doesn't even matter. Changing the clock on your computer bypasses the 12 hour lockout, so there's no point to it in the first place. I believe making a cake for *Hyun-ae is an ingenius idea, but that is because you are interacting with the game. Locking a player out is the complete opposite of that, and I find it to be a horrible idea.
With negatives out of the way, I can move on to the positives, which isn't much in quantity but very strong in quality. First, the story is very impactful. I am an incredibly tolerant and open-minded person (Which is why even though I prefer *Mute's straightforwardness, I can't get behind her closed mind), so things hardly phase me. But even I had a frown reading through Hate Plus' log entries about *Mute. Again, I feel Hate Story is the superior version, but I enjoyed the plot very much, and I believe since you can bypass the lockout, it makes up for all the other issues in the game.
Another thing I enjoyed was the Harem route. I feel the banter made the story much more colorful, and the minor fourth-wall breaks were hillarious. I wish the author decided to make this route canon, but I understand the unlikeliness of this happen due to what you have to do in Hate Story (in fact according to *Mute it's outright impossible).
Overall I feel the plot is good enough to warrant a buy, especially at it's incredibly cheap price. It's a steal, even.

First off let's get some things out of the way.
Don't buy this if you haven't played Analogue: A Hate Story or have no intentions of buying it.
Hate Plus is a sequel or, as some people in the reviews call it, an add on to Analogue. And besides you can't play the Harem route without Analogue.
There is a real life 12 hour "lock out" period between days. I say "Lockout" with pretend air quotes here as you can skip this time by hovering over the save file while it's on countdown and pressing the "S" key. This does however ruin one single achievement.
Anyhow with that out of the way let's talk Hate. (Possible SPOILERS ahead. I'm not gonna say since I really don't know what some people may consider spoilers. If anything I'm just gonna be spoiling the first VN/game.)
Like the previous Analogue you will yet again be playing the role of Space Investigator reading documents with your cute AI companion(s) who you convinced to come aboard your ship's computer by either accepting their virtual love, friendzoning their hopes and dreams or even possibly unlawfully kidnapping an AI. Either way they're back to make comments while you read documents, but In real time document scrolling action.
What's that? You left alone?
Well too bad that's not a route. You'll be scientifically provided with your choice of *Hyun-ae or *Mute if you start a new game instead of starting off a save file from Analogue. The Loner end to Analogue is locked as a grey file that you can not start from.
Once you do start a game from either a save file or the new game button you well be met with a new interface which will be colored depending on the current route you are on.
*Hyun-ae is Blue.
*Mute is Yellow-Male Space Investigator.
*Mute is Red-Female Space Investigator.
*Harem Route is Pink.
Besides this the command screen isn't in this game so no more comman shenanigans.
Document acquisition greatly differs from Analogue as you have access to (mostly) all of the documents straight from the get go. However the catch to this is you have to extract them at a rate of 6 documents per go which you can do until you run out of power. Essentially you get around 15 documents on day 1 21 ish on day 2 and day three varies a bit.
This means you're free to read what catchs your eye first, then either expand on the topic or try something else.
I personally like this system. Replayability is questionable because of it due to the fact that the documents never change no matter what AI you've got. If you're playing different routes you're doing it for that AI's reactions and comments on the documents.
And for their break chat events.
That isn't to say you shouldn't play all the routes. Each route has different AI specific events which are related to the story for the most part. I personally enjoyed the Harem route because it's hilarious with the AI's bantering between each other even while you're reading a document.
The story is on par if not better than Analogue's. It's the backstory of how the Mugunghwa became what it was.
The focus of this VN/Game seems to be more player immersion as the real time comments by the AI's while you scroll through the document and read it give it a more realistic feeling as if you were actually reading documents on a computer with AI's on it. The 12 hour wait periods are supposed to help with the immersion but if they do is questionable as reading all the documents for a day can take maybe 30 minutes to one hourish. Other things are that (MINOR SPOILER) in *Hyun-ae's route she asks you to bake her a cake. if you agree to there are times dialogue options that won't let you use them properly unless you wait about 2 minutes for on and around 20 minutes for the part where you should be baking the cake. You can then take an image with your phone or camera of the cake you baked on a certain screen and then send that to the developer for an achievement. To my eternal shame I did indeed make the 5 minute microwave cake and sent in an image.
As a side not if you're rushing through routes you may want to turn on "Minimal Animations" in option. For some reason even on a fairly powerful computer the game lags whenever your AI companion has a facial expression change or says something while you're scrolling a document. Which can get very annoying. It's mainly noticable on the Harem route as you have 2 AI's making faces and saying things.
The music is good although after going through the OST I realized I never really noticed the music changing half the time. Harem Route ending theme is fantastic though.
Overall yes I would recommend this VN/Game/Document Reading Simulator if you're a fan of the author, the series, or just want more cute AI waifus.

It's very easy to accidentally play Hate Plus in a way that will rob you of your enjoyment. If you have not played Analogue yet, stop reading this review right now and go play that game instead. Without the background of that story, Hate Plus has very little to offer you. If you have played through Analogue already, and earned the super-secret harem ending, I implore you to NOT choose the Harem route for your first play through of Hate Plus! Instead, play through *Mute and *Hyun-Ae's stories first. In many ways the Harem route is the most interesting (because you can see the interplay of the two heroines), but tackling that route first is like eating your dessert before your dinner...you'll lose your apetite to go back and miss out on the real meat of the story as a result.
Recommended route order: *Mute, *Hyun-ae, harem.
With that public service message out of the way, on to my real review. Hate Plus is a surprising follow-up to Analogue: A Hate Story. There's a lot to dislike about this follow-up. For as little gameplay as the original had, Hate Plus has even less. You won't find any command line puzzles to work through, and unlocking and reading logs doesn't feel nearly as interactive or satisfying. Instead of having a dialogue with your AI companion, you merely select the article you want to read from a list, and dig through the records at your leisure. As a result, the experience is less curated and directed, and doesn't have the same air of mystery that the original game seemed to embody.
Despite that, there's still a lot to recommend this game. Hate Plus answers all the questions that the first Visual Novel raised, and adds in the very interesting character of "Old *Mute" who plays a prominent role in the history of the Mugunghwa. And while the flow of the game isn't as tightly curated as a traditional Christine Love game, the story is incredibly fascinating when approached appropriately. (Pro-tip, Try your best to read the logs chronologically.) Moreover, the interactions with the AI really shine, and are really what make the game worthwhile. *Hyun-Ae will make you question the nature of fictional characters and artificial love, while *Mute will open her own can of worms.
Ultimately, if you liked Analogue and find yourself thirsting for more info about the Mugunghwa's slide into Neo-Confucianism, Hate Plus will certainly scratch that itch.

Clear Sky is considered the red headed step child of the STALKER franchise, but in all honesty it's my favorite of the 3 STALKER games and I will explain why to you.
Clear Sky (CS) revamped a lot of the clunky design that was present in Shadow of Chernobyl (SoC), and paved the way for a lot of the useful features that were present in Call of Pripyat (CoP).  First off, CS overhauled your PDA immensely, cutting out a lot of the unnecessary features and streamlining your available options.
Artifacts also received a major makeover in the game in how you acquire them, and their overall functionality.  Thanks to CS, artifact hunting means you have to actually "hunt".  In STALKER's predecessor, artifacts could be found just laying on the ground and were in a huge abundance.  In CS, you actually have to jump into anomalies with a special detector to find the goodies inside.  And the goodies are actually worth it as well.  An artifact that increases your endurance (recovery speed from jumping, running etc.) has a more limited value than in SoC, prompting you to equip more than one if you're going out on a long raid.  On the up side, health restoring artifacts have a major impact on keeping you alive and actually heal you faster than they do in CoP.  If I had to take a guess, I'd say that little feature has a lot to do with your character's "gift", but you'll figure out what that means when you play it.
The world feels more alive, with many of the NPCs getting unique voice actors, as well as a lot of them also interacting with each other.  You can really get a feel for this when you get to Freedom's base and meet the two stalkers that keep hijacking the outpost's loudspeaker to talk smack to each other.  Plus the NPCs are more reactive, they will tell you to buzz off if you're trying to talk to them with a gun in their face, or they'll smack your gun out of your hands if you keep trying to talk to them with it out.  They're also liable to smack you in the face if you keep trying to talk to them while they're in the middle of a firefight or on their way to complete their own objectives.
The ALife in this game can be buggy at times, but that's because of the extra features added to the system since SoC.  Enemies can, and will use grenades on you.  And they've all got their own pre-programmed cycles and tactical combat styles.  Some enemies will try to flank you, while others will box you into a tight space with no escape.  Some may charge at you blindly, while others will retreat to call in reinforcements.  A hungry mutant that spots you may follow you throughout the Zone until you either dispatch it, or it dispatches you...while a less hungry mutant may just be protecting its territory and will leave you be once you leave its area.
But my favorite thing about the game is how it sets up the story for the STALKER universe.  This game is prequel to Shadow of Chernobyl, and as such it tries to paint a picture of a more beautiful Zone; one that's still bustling with human interaction and chipper attitudes despite the hellish landscape they live in.  SoC is the opposite of this, by the time it takes place the Zone is nearly lifeless and it really makes you feel empty and alone inside.  What makes Clear Sky so great though, is the tragic ending of the game.  SoC has multiple endings, but only two "true" endings...and of those two only one is cannon to the story.  But it's a happy ending overall.  In Clear Sky you don't get such a happy ending because it has to show you why the Zone is such a nightmare in the future to come.
In closing, Clear Sky gets a lot of flak for being the weakest of the 3 games.  But it is not a weak game, not by a long shot.  GSC Gameworld took some risks when they introduced Clear Sky because it changed the mold that Shadow of Chernobyl had set after so many years of being in development.  Overall, I personally feel like it paid off.  I prefer the way NPCs interact with one another and the game world, I love the rebalancing of artifacts and the methods of hunting them down, and if you can get past the occasional hiccup or two due to shoddy programming...the experience is worth it.

First I want to say that this game is extremely difficult, even on "Stalker" (Normal). Near the end of the game you will not be able to purchase bandages or medkits, and trust me you will need them. If you run out of medkits you will have to turtle your way through massive and very cheap spawning enemies. Now I don't think this is a bad game, if it was intended to be hard then they nailed it. The problems I have with it are such:
-Enemies have a hitbox inefficiency, some enemies take massive amounts of ammo (1-2 clips) and others take a few shots even if they are the same. Don't bother aiming for the head it works on the lesser enemies.
-The game goes from a really decent RPG to a linear shooting gallery where you hind behind numerous walls and crates with a "hold" crouch which does not fit well.
-The ending of the game is something that unless you find out ahead of time you will never beat it. Unless you see that you need ungodly amounts of medkits and bandages "YOU WILL NOT WIN".
-There are bugs yes but sometimes freaking out and hitting the move keys enough you can get out. If not you better have saved recently.
-Autosaves are only when you go to new areas, other than that if you don't save you will be playing this game a very long time.
-Gun upgrading is expensive for the lack of money you normally have. Plus the weapon will lower in condition very quickly so money in this game is your best friend.
-Finally, the money, if you don't farm and chore through the swamps and all the anomalies to find artifaces or pick up every gun you see, you will have "NO" money.
Other than these things I find that it is weirdly addicting and quite fun and funny sometimes. If you like really hard games well this game is great.

A blast from the past, AVP will forever be that game that made you s*** yourself everytime you heard something creeping up behind you followed by that distinctive hiss...
Atmosphere plays a big part in the drama, visuals, music, as well as the varied playing style offered by the three distinctive and different species; colonial marine, predator and of course the alien. This game is of course very dark and the lighting (or the lack of it) plays a big part in the single player campaigns as well as survival modes, and of course the multiplayer aspect.
Each species deals with this in its own way, as well as how it traverses the environment whether it be footslogging it, giant leaps, or climbing up walls etc. The arsenal of weapons at each species disposal reflects the inherent influences of the movies associated in this tie-up. Just don't ask where the Predators' plasma pistol came from though...
AvP Gold Edition was a subsequent release which added more maps, skins and content, and generally polished the game up a bit. This release appears to have all the content, a bit like an anniversary edition.
Though dated by today's standards (2017), this low polygon, Pentium2, dialup era classic offers a fond reminder of great and distinctive games of the past; and was definitely an early contender amongst is genre for multiplayer replayability.

Played the first level of the Alien campaign to start my first playthrough, but I've had as much as I can stand from this game. Mission objectives can be hard to spot, enemies are diverse but indistinguishable in appearance, and there are a finite amount of saves you can use.
Textures in this game are low-quality by today's standards. This wouldn't be a problem if it weren't for the fact that every mission objective for the Alien is a physical entity in the world. A destructible computer, a destructible barricade, or a destructible wire conduit looks the same as the ambient textures in the game, which complicates player progression. With each new objective a line of text appears on the screen briefly, but only once, and you cannot look up the objective after the message disappears. I didn't want to spend twenty minutes clawing at every texture in the game, so I looked up what my objective was online. I don't like being forced to interrupt my game for something as ridiculous as looking up the next objective.
The first enemies you face are humans armed with different weapons - automatic rifles, shotguns, handguns, or firebombs. All the enemies look like generic grunts or armored marines, with no way to tell what kind of weapon they're holding. You could take a few rifle or handgun rounds and go on swinging, but a shotgun at close range is an instant death. Some humans would rather commit suicide than fight the Alien, so they kill themselves with a firebomb if you get too close. Fire cannot be put out, and the only way to regain health is to eat a non-burned corpse. Bodies despawn quickly, so the chances to acquire health are few and far between, more so if you approach a human and can't tell if they're holding a pistol or a molotov.
The last issue speaks for itself, though I should expand on it: limited number of saves. There were no checkpoints from what I could see, so the saves you get are the only ones you'll have. If you waste one, you cannot delete a save to regain another one. Save files cannot be deleted, but they can be overwritten. I don't know what determines the number of saves, whether it's a set amount for the entire game, each level, or each character, but any limitation is disappointing nonetheless.

In a world where survival horror games try to ramp up the fear factor with scripted spring loaded cats, limited ammo, and sometimes even penalize you just for looking at the monsters, here's Aliens vs. Predator. It's a game where you slide through the scenery as nimbly as the Doom marine, your default weapon is an assault rifle with underslung grenade launcher that pulverizes enemies in seconds, and otherwise does nothing to handicap the player to ramp up the fear factor. AND IT'S TERRIFYING.
Why? Simply because Weyland Yutani skimps on lightbulbs, you can have only 4 flares burning at any one time, and Xenomorphs are FAST! The monsters are coming for you, and if you don't spot them fast enough it's over. That's all it takes, and it never gets old.
The Colonial Marine levels are the meat of the game, and I'm not gonig to penalize it for the weaknesses of the other two modes. The main thing I'll dock it for is occasionally obscure level requirements. There's one level in particular I was stuck on for weeks before I realized some strips in front of a locked door were actually shootable objects keeping it shut.
The predator levels are amusing at first, playing with all the vision modes and other toys, but you're so indestructible it gets boring fast.
The Alien levels were great in the original release, and they're still lots of fun, but they seem to be a little bugged, if you'll pardon the expression, in this release. You sometimes get stuck on geometry when crawling over polygon edges, human "auras" constantly change color, and the stealth mechanics seem to be completely broken. Even if you break every light in the room, the marines always spot you instantly.
But I re-emphasize, this game is all about playing the colonial marine, and in that part of the game it's an absolute classic. Too bad the sequels didn't capitalize on this game's strengths and used the scripted Half-Life-wannabe funhouse ride approach.

I don't often comment on games and especially not early access games but I'd really like to say that this game is fantastic for the price. This is everything an early access game should be! It's playable, engrossing, relatively stable and complete in that no content needed to play the game is missing.
The most common gripe I've been seeing is that there is a lack of purpose and I think those people are confusing progression with purpose. Unlike Minecraft, you don't start the game with the ability to collect and use various materials. The purpose, however, is exactly the same - do whatever you want. The progression determines what you can do and how long you have to play before you can do it but the purpose is the same. The system of progression keeps things fresh! You collect new materials to build new weapons and armor to fight new enemies and bosses to find new materials. Please just keep in mind that the progession is to keep the things that are normally very mundane about Minecraft new and exciting but that the progression is not the purpose!
Anyways, I just thought I'd say my piece on the matter and really hope that the developers keep at it!

While I don't hate this game, I find that it's much weaker than the first game. There's a three day gimmick while interesting the first time around, is just a weird barrier that ultimately doesn't mean anything, since you can just skip through it by holding space down in the main menu. On the one route I've played, I played along with the gimmick, and it just felt bizarre having to wait, though I will admit that there was quite a bit of anticipation between the second and third day, so if that was the objective, then I suppose it was done well enough.
There are a few quirks that are quite annoying - for instance, for some reason you're unable to just smoothly scroll down a page, it has to pause every few seconds. I'm unsure if this was an intentional design decision or not, but relative to the first game where everything felt a lot more smooth and responsive, it's quite annoying. Another thing I disliked is how you obtain the data this time around. Instead of talking with your AI companions and having them slowly reveal the story to you, you instead just select and choose which entries you want to read. Furthermore, the AI companions aren't essential to the plot of this game, and feel more like side kicks than anything else.
That being said, the AI sidekicks in this game aren't bad, and in fact, it's interesting to hear their thoughts on the going-ons of what occurred on the ship a few hundred years ago. They inject a bit of light heartedness into what is ultimately a tragic story, though *Mute's route definitely has some even darker themes on the third day. I can't speak for Hyun-ae's route, since I never did get around to doing her route, but I'm positive the third day with her won't have nearly the same impact that Mute's did.
And that is one of my big problems - this is subjective of course, others may loved it - but the ending to Mute's route is quite dark, as mentioned before. It deals with some really serious issues, and while it was quite effective, and it hit me like a bus, I didn't particularly care for it.
Overall, only buy this if you're a HUGE fan of the original like I was, but make sure to avoid Mute's route until you finished Hyun-ae's, otherwise it'll probably sour your experience.

A worthy sequel for those, who enjoyed this game's predecessor, Analogue: A Hate Story and/or admire Christine Love's storytelling in general. Following a while after the events of Analogue, you are tasked into another starship known as the White Princess to uncover the mysteries behind the rise of the New Joseon Dynasty that plagued Mugunghwa for centuries. You will go through all of the message logs left by the former crew and population of Mugunghwa, arraging from business meetings to just normal-day cuddling, working and everyday stuff.
This game should be played AFTER completing Analogue: A Hate Story at least ONCE, since you can transfer your Analogue data (providing you've completed the game within that save data) into the game to stay up to date and have a better understanding of the game's lore.
Of course, should you choose to start differently as opposed to how you finished Analogue, you can start a new walkthrough with different settings, from choosing between *Hyun-ae or *Mute and adjusting their behaviour towards you.
The only flaw (if it should be considered as such) is the time delay between each "game day": after consuming the White Princess' emergency power by copying logs and reading them, you will have to wait for 12h of IRL time to advance to the next day, and thus be able to extract more messages. This method breaks the flow and pace of the game, and it really, REALLY sucks, even before the final day.
That being mentioned, the game's soundtrack fits really well with the atmosphere, let it be reading a whole dark, novel-sized text log or conversations between you and your AI companion. Plus, if you're an otaku, like me, you will feel yourself even more connected to your partner, should it be either the sympathetic, platonic *Hyun-ae or the wise-cracking, stoic *Mute.
Overall, Hate Plus should be recommended to those who have played Analogue: A Hate Story and want to further expand the storyline, who love Christine Love's handiwork of the story or those that just like visual novels.

Without even thinking about it, Warband is the best value for money game I have ever purchased.  Having clocked around 300 hours or so now, and having managed, finally, to rule all of calradia on normal difficulty, I'm taking a break. I may play a little more before the release bannerlord which if warband is anything to go by should be incredible. If it isn't I will be immensely disappointed.
A few things:
Sieges do not work especially well owing to the limitations of the AI. In order to stop your troops getting glitched out behind staircases or running facefirst into castle walls whilst being shot to death by archers, you do need to utilise the commands, which are far too basic to suit complex situations in which you find yourself. Avoid frustration by expecting them to be a bit crap from the offset. Your soldiers are prone to doing stupid chit and sometimes they're going to do it, which make some battles turn into monty python skits.
Don't give your followers lands and titles early in the game, if at all.  If they defect from your faction, you cannot get them back unless you wind up conquering all of Calradia.Moreoever if you defeat them in a battle, you cannot even incarcerate them in a dungeon. This is a big problem as their party skills are extremely helpful and beneficial to your overall gameplay.
Swadian knights are on balance the best troops for field battles  followed by sarranid mamlukes. However, slaver chiefs are vastly superiror to both if you're trying to capture enemies for recruitment purposes. These are the leveled version of manhunters.
For sieges: You want Nord huscarls, and rhodok sharpshooters ( failing this, swadian sharpshooters or vaegir marksman).
Tip: Do NOT loot and plunder villages, as low and hostile standings with villages will mean you are unable to recruit from them. It's very easy to tank your standing with a village, and much harder to win it back--doing this involves boring, annoying quests ( like herding cattle, which is a royal PITA.
DO NOT USE THE AUTOSAVE OPTION! This is known to cause a 'no string error' that effectively ruins your entire saved progress as it resets all your skill points back to zero without giving you the option to re-spend them. It basically wipes your character back to the starting level. I lost about 40 hours this way during my initial playthrough. Always, always manually save.
The reputation system which works well for the most part does become virtually impossible to balance as you accrue more lords to fight for you over time, apportion territories and try to to balance interpersonal disputes. Again, this is an old game, and the sophistication of AI relfects Its vintage. It's a problem, but a forgivable one, all said and done.
Hit detection in this game is perfect, and you're not. Expect to find yourself saying 'how the ♥♥♥♥ did that possibly ♥♥♥♥ing miss' quite a lot at first. I recoomend turning the battle speed up to highest as, for whatever reason, the game just seems to prefer it this way mechanically. It's just better.
Make sure you turn the number of troops per battle up to maximum also; failure to do this will, when facing a large enemy army, result in you spawning on the field with 10 troops and the enemy with over a hundred, and you will get roflstomped. The game will always fill to max capacity with AI troops, not yours.
For all its imperfections, bugs and general datedness Warband really is an immensely satisfying and enjoyable game that is well worth purchasing--especially given that you can pick it up for about the price of a happy meal most of the time. Nothing to lose here.

This is a game you will try for 15 minutes and then immediately put away, never to look at again. Yes, it's free. Yes, it's only 23 MB. But this game is boring, repetitive, tedious, un-customizable, frustrating, unintelligent, and unrewarding.
In Super Crate Box, you're a short, pixely character who seems to move way too loosely given his size. You start off with a basic gun and you have to shoot enemies who drop down from the top and inevitably come at you from the left and right sides. If they make it to the bottom, they fall into a pit of fire and drop back down from the top of the screen in a frenzied state where they move much faster. It's easy to get swarmed and some enemies take more than one shot to kill. You're going to die quickly and frequently. Your objective is collect boxes (crates) that each contain a different weapon and which instantly replaces your previous one. You can't change back to the one you just had, and you MUST use the new one (sometimes down-grading you). You can unlock better weapons, but the one you get with each new box is random. Now, gameplay-wise the control is all right (I find the jumping to be somewhat awkward) but my main issue gameplay-wise is that you can't customize the controls. Come on, this is 2014, players deserve better (and before anyone rushes to assumptions, let me just say that some people are left-handed and prefer using WASD for movement over the arrow keys; thanks).
Let's be honest here, this is one of THOSE games, the kind whose sole purpose is to be more frustrating and challenging than interesting, involving, or innovative. I honestly don't know what others see in this game. It's more like a game you'd use to play a trick on your friends than one you'd actually take seriously. At its core, it's simply an arcade game where you see how long you can last. That's it. The "official" reviews make it sound like it blew the reviewers out of the water: "Slightly less addictive than crack cocaine"? Hm, speaking from experience? "...[C]ondensed milk...only with fun instead of milk"? Is that really a review? "Elegant, explosive, and truly unmissable"? Huh? Were they playing the same game as me? Now, I realize that I'm complaining about something that's free, but after playing Super Crate Box I had to write this review. I frankly don't see any features that would keep me coming back to it, and so I can't recommend it.

15 hours in and my impressions/feedback:
Impression:  Game is not mindblowing but has solid potential.  It's not as fast paced as your typical modern day shooter.  It has much more strategy due to scale of maps.  There's a lot of foliage which is very fun--though graphically far from impressive-- but it brings in an aspect of fear from not knowing entirely where the enemy could be at, thus bringing a little more realism from that aspect of WW2.  BUT there is a lot of downtime from running around especially if you die a lot in a match.  Also, there is nearly no zoom when using iron sights (the sights themselves are quite small), so targeting enemies from medium to long distance is incredibly difficult--including with rifles-- especially on a smaller monitor.  I finally got my first scope for the Gewehr and it made the game a lot better imo.  New players may find this irritating (especially coming from other major shooter games) and the grind for a better scope is overwhelming especially since the scope comes at the end.  If it was made so the first sight attachment improved zoom on the iron sights alone (made them bigger on screen) then this would be much better.
Feedback:
- improve zoom on iron sights, even if it's only to rifles.  Rifles should fit more of a medium range weapon.  From my experience, smg's dominated simply because it was very difficult to view things from a reasonable range thus usually fighting an smg close range with a rifle which you usually lose.  I have gotten better but still, very difficult and a lot of squinting lol.
- Downtime between spawn locations and fighting needs vastly improved.  There's a lot of downtime for Infantry men that makes it a bit annoying and overly punishing when you die.  If there was a way to maybe spawn on a Squad mate once then goes on cooldown for a certain time, maybe that could help?  I understand that you cannot allow spawning on top of capture points, but the distance for the spawn locations to capture points (or even enemy's capture points) seems a bit extreme.
- Placeable defenses like barbed wire or sand bags.  I feel like this is a semi-missed opportunity.  Currently, barbed wire is only aesthetic minus you are able to jump on them to get over obstactles like fences.  Would be nice to be able to have these destructable and also hurt infantry.  Because these maybe unecessary on Encounter, maybe make an Engineer class where a soldier gets 4 barbed wire that's 5 meters in length to place in various locations.  Same could be done with sand bags and even caltrops to impede vehicles from certain locations.  It doesn't have to be something major and game breaking but I think it would be a nice touch for strategic purposes and gameplay variety.
- Spawn rate of rocket launchers is ridiculous.  Rocket launchers spawn in crates in set locations around the map.  But they respawn so quickly, you literally can non-stop raining rockets with one of these crates.  These need to be more strategic when you use them.  Significantly lower the spawn rate, or force a cooldown timer per use for each player.
- Too many grenades per player.  If I recall, you're equipped with 4 grenades when using them.  This needs to be 2.  Got grenade happy people all over the place (myself included).  Force people to use ammo supplies if need be.  Also, visibility of thrown grenades needs improved.  Of course, you can hear the sound and maybe see it leave a persons hands, but it's difficult from there--could possibly be I'm playing on lower specs too.  Not saying to add an indicator like other games, but just make it graphically a little easier to see.  Maybe add a perk (or medal, cannot remember what it's called) that gives us an indicator of it's location.  On top of it, anti-tank grenades are unbelievably op against tanks.  Enemy just strolls up in a jeep behind you and there's nothing you can do unless you have teammates protecting you constantly.
- Matchmaking....over 1000 people currently in chat yet it takes over a couple minutes to get into a game.  Not only that but I've played many more games where there's less than 8 people per team on these massive maps.  Hell, I don't even know what the max player count is because I rarely get above 10/team.  This needs dramatically improved.
The game is not bad.  Can even be very fun but needs a lot of work from my perspective.  I do recommend especially since it's f2p.

I've been eyeing Spelunky for a while now and finally took the plunge during the holiday sale. I saw lots of positive reviews and thought the game would scratch an itch for me but alas it was not to be.
Yes, the game is hard. I was expecting as much from the reviews and tags, no biggie. I grew up on the NES, I can do hard, but this game is straight unfair as well. There are so many deaths awaiting you from off-screen that it leaves a bad taste in the mouth to die cheaply after skillfully completing a difficult section. That's not difficult, it's just annoying. There are other minor things that artificially increase the difficulty, such as the platforming being a little slidey, magnetic ledges, the UI blocking up a corner of the screen, or messy level generation. Glitching into a wall within the first hour of play didn't help either. When I want to play a difficult game, I want to control my own destiny.
The combat in the game is pretty bland. You start with a basic slow whip and can pickup or purchase better/different weapons as you progress but you can tell combat was never the focus of the game and that's fine. It's a means to an end.
Spelunky isn't even really a rogue-like. It's more like a NES platformer that sends you back to the start when you die. It reminds me more of Bubble Bobble or the Ducktales game than most modern rogue-likes.
Most unfortunate, however, was my realization that Spelunky was not an adventure game either. I was hoping for a game where I could explore to my heart's content. I wanted to root and dig and have grand adventure, bomb through walls to discover cool areas. The game does not deliver this experience. Sadly the game is on something of a timer, after spending about 2 or 3 minutes in a level a ghost chases you around to make you hurry up and get out (oh yea, the game is based on smallish levels, not open exploration, FYI).
Yes, Spelunky is not an adventure game, it is a speedrun game. That's a fun genre, Super House of Dead Ninjas is one of my favorites! My issue is that they give you tools to adventure and ask you to speedrun. Combine this with my previously mentioned issues, and it just seems like a game that threw a bunch of concepts together without really shining in any unique way.
I don't have much time in the game so far but I do plan on trying it further. If my opinion changes I will update the review accordingly. However, with so many games available that immediately grab my attention and are exciting from the start, I can't guarantee I'll play this again.
PROS:
Fun graphics
Interesting concept
CONS:
Nothing new
Doesn't excel in any specific area
Random and cheap deaths
Not a true adventure game or rogue-like
MEH:
Music ranges from bland to weird
Controls a little soft/slippery for my taste
Procedural level generation is all over the board in terms of difficulty/fairness
What I was hoping for: Rogue Legacy meets Terreria
What I got: Digdug meets Bubble Bobble

My review is written as a presentation / review cause it was for a school assignment back in the day about writing for game magazines.
INTRO:
Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a beautiful and sometimes darkly mature echo of the fairytales that thought us about the world as children.
Through out the journey of two brothers trying to save their dying father, i experienced a theme of death and depression that hit me at a personal level.
Through out the game you'll encounter dream-like locations, interact with the world in unique ways. Despite the game being set with twinsticks on an xbox controller were confusing, I quickly managed to get used to it, the story was just as effective and attractive.
PRESENTATION:
The game presents you that you've lost your mother, and now your father is dying. It's up to you, controlling the brothers to save your father.
A lot of Brothers charm lies within the non verbal story telling, where the characters speak in a imaginary and fantasy language, so it's up to the player to get information through exploring and interacting with the enviorment.
One of the most succesfull aspects of brothers is that it is built up for each players style. If you want to charge through an area, you can do so to solved the puzzles, instead of doing it step by step, and rush through the game, but be warned that your gonna miss out on side stories and moments of charactisations that helps making this story even more special.
Though you start your adventure out in a nordic-like village, you will eventually end up in an ancient battlefield, where the rives flow with blood, frozen lakes that contains mysterious creatures and prisons placed at the peak of a mountain.
The settings never failed to impress me, and the way Brothers continusly kept providing me with the more beautifull scenery was just amazing.
The characters are created with a different style than the scenery, and despite them being set in their own design, i was still impressed and found them just as charming as the world itself.
GAMEPLAY:
While the world and themes of Brothers are fantastic, prepear for a new setup of controls. It's an interesting setup, where you use the right side of the controller to control the younger brother, and the left side to control the other brother, and cooperate with them together. A great example is that if you place one brother at the base of a wall, and interact with it, he will prepear to throw his younger brother up the wall.
While a lot of players is frustrated over the controllers, and not being able to learn them quick enough over the 3 hour long campaign, the world is full of interesting things to see and interact with.
For example; along the way you will find a man trying to hang himself. You can walk right past him and let him die, or you can save him with getting nothing in reward. Despite not being encouraged to save him, you'll only be rewarded with the fact that he lives because of you.
The thing i also love about Brothers is the interactions. Each brother interact in their own way. While the little brother would potentially play, the older brother would work, and show that he is more mature and responsible than the younger brother.
The unique silence of story telling and expressing the character through out interactions, where fear and skill is shown, while they present a story based up on a silenced story, proves the unique level of story telling that only games can accomplish.
VERDICT:
Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a unique experience, and a game full of imaginations. It's just waiting for you to pick it up and play.
The story in itself, along with the game play and scenery makes this one of the most memorable games I've ever played.
RATING:
+ BEAUTIFUL SCENERY
+ OUTSTANDING THEMES
+ FANTASTIC STORY
- FRUSTRATING CONTROLS

It's evident from the reviews of Train Simulator that there is a lot of negativity towards it, some of it is justified, some of it is not, personally I am a big fan and it has become the source of hours passing the time.
So first common complaint - "it's boring!"
simple answer to that is that driving a train is essentially using a limited number of controls in order to make the train move backwards and forwards, stopping and starting, paying attention to signals, opening and closing doors at platforms and/or emptying payload at freight depots.
On Train Simulator most of the trains handle in a completely unique manner and this handling changes dependant on the routes you are driving and the weather conditions, so with regards to being a Simulator which accurately depicts driving a train it is probably as close as you can come to the real thing.  If you want added realism you can always purchase one of the third party "train controllers", beyond this the only further improvement to realism would be to have Virtual Reality to allow hands free cockpit navigation, though with the complexity of the graphics at present you would likely need a super computer if that kind of enhancement were ever to be made.
Onto the next common complaint - "graphic quality"
My personal computer is based on an AMD FX6300 3.5GHz 6 core CPU, 16gb RAM with a 2GB GeForce GT 610 graphics card, it has taken a while for me to tweak the graphic settings in game to an optimal setting, though on the most part have settled with disabling FXAA filtering and 8 x Anisotropic Filtering running at my monitors maximum resolution of 1366 x 768.
With those settings I find that most routes work at a very smooth rate, however you have to bear in mind that different production teams have created the routes so the graphic quality does vary significantly across the different routes, and is also impacted by different weather conditions in game and also by some of the individual train models, I personally tend to find that the German routes in particular are extremely heavy on the graphics and often end up with the frame rate dropping significantly, and with that also comes the appearance that time in the game is slowing down (the real time clock does not advance in real time).
Next common complaint - "The DLC's cost too much"
A quick look through the reviews and it comes up time and time again, people complain about the cost of the add-on's and the fact that in their eyes the base game doesn't have enough content.
So first point of note, with the initial game you typically get around 4 routes and circa 8 - 12 locomotives to drive, the routes vary greatly in terms of their length and number of scenarios, though from the base game alone the scenarios will take you in excess of 50 hours to complete should you decide to play all of them, on the scale of things 50 hours of gameplay for a base game is on the higher side of time taken in order to "complete" the base content, so really the criticism there is completely unfounded.
Personally, I first purchased Train Simulator 2015, initially didn't really play it much, most of my time spent playing and expanding the game has been over the last 3 - 4 months, and I'm now at the point where I have over 40 different routes and over 100 different locomotives which has probably cost me a couple of hundred pounds, but I've not paid anything like full price for the DLC's I have purchased.
So if you were to purchase every single DLC for this game at full price it would cost you well over £4000, but the whole idea of the DLC marketplace element of this game is to allow you to pick and choose the expansions you want, also added to which, if you look at the time it would take to complete every scenario it would stretch into many thousands of hours so realistically for most people if you did actually own every single DLC it would take you YEARS of regular play to even come close to completing all the scenarios.
I have expanded my route and locomotive collection by using 3 different methods with the end result being a tiny fraction of the normal cost of purchasing them, and with all the content I have, the surface has barely been scratched with the time I have already spent playing Train Simulator.
So first self explanatory money saving method with the DLC's is to purchase them when they are on sale, at present there are Flash Sales regularly occurring on steam for Train Simulator DLC's, and  most weeks even if there is not a major sale there are usually a handful of them available with significant discounts, so it pays to regularly check on the Steam marketplace for the bargains.
Next money saving method is to purchase the various collections and/or premium editions of the game, for example, if you have purchased the base Train Simulator 2017 Standard Edition game, you can purchase the First Class Editions of the game to get the 3 additional routes that come with them, just because they have the TS2017 base game included doesn't stop you from taking advantage of the massive savings to be made on the routes, such are the savings to be had on the First Class versions they are cheaper for the 4 additional routes than the individual cost of 1 of the routes included with them, there are also a number of route collections available for Train Simulator which have a "complete your collection" feature where you get a significant discount purchasing compared to the individual cost of each item in the collection.
And then what for me has been the most significant savings on Routes, using marketplaces such as♥♥♥♥♥to purchase the Steam code for older versions of the game, yes it can be done, as I mentioned before, even if you already have the Train Simulator base game, you can purchase different versions and Steam will recognise this and give you the Route's and locomotives from the different versions of the game, so I have personally purchased every Train Simulator 13, 14, 15, 16 & 17, in most instances paying only £2.50 - £5 for each version and getting all the routes that come with them including many of the more expensive routes like London Faversham High Speed, Donner Pass, Munich - Augsburg, Sherman Hill and many others, the savings made equate to in excess of a 95% saving on every one of the routes.
And the final common complaint - "there are too many bugs"
It can't be denied that there is a massive amount of inconsistency across the DLC's, and the bugs can be extremely frustrating, you will no doubt have already read about the most common of them, many of the routes have sudden changes in the speed limit which have no signposting on the rails or indication on the HUD to let you know about them, in some instances the HUD and signposting are telling you the speed limit is changing to one speed when in reality it is changing to a much lower speed so you get hammered with point deductions when attempting to complete career scenarios.  Other common bugs include locomotives that simply won't go anywhere, and if you do eventually get them moving the first time you stop they have an inexplicable emergency stop which you are seemingly unable to reset.
With regards to these bugs, every single game you will buy EVER is ALWAYS going to have some kind of bug, most of the time the developers do absolutely nothing to fix them, there are a lot of the bugged routes which have not been fixed, but the fault with this does not necessarily lay with Dovetail Games, but often lays with the third party developers that created the routes in the first place.
If you have looked in detail you will have seen that there are many different organisations involved in the creation of routes and locomotive add-on's for Train Simulator, it is evident that many of the developers are quick to fix bugs, where some others don't ever seem to fix anything, so it's not really fair to blame Dovetail for all the bugs.
I could go on, but will conclude, Great Simulator and Highly Recommended

My only gripe is that the DOS style interface is gone for system commands, but that's just me.

If you didn't like Analogue: A Hate Story then you aren't going to like Hate Plus.  If you did like Analogue you will almost certainly like Hate Plus.  And if you haven't played Analogue, you really shouldn't play Hate Plus until you do.  The differences between the two with respect to game design are fairly minor but I personally found the story in Hate Plus to be much more riveting, which is no small feat.  Whereas a few story arcs in Analogue fell a bit flat for me, Hate Plus had no such weakness.  I would also say the plot is more intricate, warranting an entire second read just to pick up on details you couldn't have possibly seen before.
Fair warning: this is a tragedy.  In fact it is multiple intertwined tragedies.  While there are certainly cute and heartwarming moments, this game hurts, but only because it makes you care.

You thought it was all over. You thought you knew it all. How silly could you be?
I played Analogue and fell completely in love with Hyun-ae. To this day, her story haunts me as one of the most striking, poignant works of fiction I've ever read. Yet at the end of Analogue, I felt like I was missing something ... Mute. I knew she had her own ending (as a completionist I achieved all three), but her character had always seemed so... new, and childish, and born of her society as opposed to being older than it.
If you felt the same way, then Plus is the answer to all your questions, and more. How on earth (sorry, how on Mugungwe) could a society degenerate from the one Hyun-ae fell asleep in to the one the Pale Bride woke up in. How quickly did it happen? Didn't Mute notice it?
While you can choose to have either, or both, of the most darling AIs ever watching over you as you read (depending on your save files, or choice pre-game), the historical documents in Plus are to Mute what Analogue was to the Pale Bride. Curiosity about her life as ship's AI will finally be sated - and since we know how the story ends, you can guess that Mute's has a couple of rough moments. Emotional and full of feeling, Plus tells us everything we did, and didn't, want to know, along with a few day-in-the-life stories of some cute couples that'll show you how events effected far more than just Mute and the Pale Bride. Come for the cuties, stay for the feels.
And any time you're lonely, boot up the program and have cake with your new waifu, Hyun-ae. :D

First off, there's only one other game I've ever played which had an experience similar to that of Mount & Blade: Warband. That was Sid Meier's: Pirates! Though much less cartoony than Pirates! and more a gruff and rough experience closer to that of a Medieval Western European experience over the sunny tropics of the Caribbean. Anyways.
Mount and Blade: Warband has a rough feel to it at first with a bit of a high learning curve that the uninitiated had better learn quickly. This game is unforgiving if you decide to bite off more than you can chew. Starting off by yourself, handling the smallest of the small in terms of bandits and the petty deeds of local lords. You can recruit volunteers from villages and become a small company of mercenaries working for lords, become nothing more than bandits raiding villages for wares and loot, serve as a vassal or declare allegiance to a kingdom. In terms of freedom, your waist deep in it.
However in terms of learning the world, your first play may very well be a failure depending on the difficulties you've set for yourself. But the game is fairly organic intuitive enough to figure out after a few hours of wandering around. Combat can feel janky at first, but once you begin to understand how to engage your foes and the combat system, things will become easier. But to those with little patience or are looking for more action, this may not be the game for you. Plus some small but consistant bugs here and there haunt the game, but in my experience so far none are game breaking; though some may force a retreat or reload, such as siege towers locking. But most bugs will go by unnoticed.
Pros:
-Simplistic over world view for travelling
-Great amount of freedom in this open world
-Fairly decent representation of medieval politics and society
-Fun combat, but difficult combat
-Decent leveling system
-Game runs great
-Fairly simple intuitive user interface
-You can make for a considerably different experience based on the backstory you pick for your character and their sex
Cons:
-Graphics are a little dated
-Steep learning curve
-Repetition can bore some
-Gaining honor and reputation can be an extreme grind
-AI doesn't feel very smart
-Needs more variation in sieges and battles to avoid repetition
Overall, this is a solid game worth it's price. I haven't played any of the other Mount & Blade titles, but I'm sure they reflect similar gameplay. As for pc performance, I'm certain any pc as far back as the games release date can easily run this game.

I spent a decent amount of time in this game and I would say, for the most part, I was happy however I'm not recommending this game due to the following:
1)The game was FAARR too easy and I can't stress this enough.
At level 17 with Iron level gear, pretty much all quality 8 (and it goes up to 30 I think) I defeated the level 30 boss without any issues. His whirlwind was hitting me for like 80 each assuming it even touched me as it was slow and easily avoided.
You might ask, how did you get to the final level 30 boss at level 17? Well, you simply need to equip a bow and you can kill any normal mob in the entire game. The pathing literally has the units running directly at you and if there is a gap in the middle or you are above them they just stop. "If I keep going I will fall off the cliff, Guess I should stop and not find a way around this hole"
If the game never gave you experience I am 100% confident you could do the entire game at level 1 with a starting bow, with ease.
2) There is basically no difference in classes.
Once you hit level 15 or 20 you can be 5% worse (in the same gear) than any of the other classes. (Warrior 5% worse than a Wizard for instance). Every level you increase all 3 of your stats.. there is no picking and choosing what to get better at to actually bridge the gap between your class and any other class.
Honestly, based on one of the talents that reduces magic damage taken by Wizards I consider them the BETTER TANK than a warrior. What?!
There is no gear or weapon lock outs. So while I'm not totally opposed to this it makes the lack of talent / class differences mean that a mage wearing plate + a melee weapon is the exact same thing as a warrior (and based on my previous point, probably better).
3) The game has no challenges and/or different experiences **Not to be confused with #1**
To progress through the worlds you just need to collect 'Shards' which combine to unlock the doorway to the next area. How do you get these shards? Just kill stuff or mine... So for 20 something different worlds you just grind mobs basically.
If you grind mobs for long enough on world 1 you can progress right on through to world ~6 until you hit the next 'Shard color'. (Blue -> Yellow -> Green -> Red(Only 1 door) )
This is something I accidently did... just happened to collect 12 blue portal cubes and after porting through the first world I just walked over to the next portal and dumped in another 6... so yeah you can just skip entire 'worlds'.
tl;dr This game isn't what you might think it is... they want you to just mine like crazy and the classes / bosses / enemies were a total afterthought while making the game.

I've been eyeing Spelunky for a while now and finally took the plunge during the holiday sale. I saw lots of positive reviews and thought the game would scratch an itch for me but alas it was not to be.
Yes, the game is hard. I was expecting as much from the reviews and tags, no biggie. I grew up on the NES, I can do hard, but this game is straight unfair as well. There are so many deaths awaiting you from off-screen that it leaves a bad taste in the mouth to die cheaply after skillfully completing a difficult section. That's not difficult, it's just annoying. There are other minor things that artificially increase the difficulty, such as the platforming being a little slidey, magnetic ledges, the UI blocking up a corner of the screen, or messy level generation. Glitching into a wall within the first hour of play didn't help either. When I want to play a difficult game, I want to control my own destiny.
The combat in the game is pretty bland. You start with a basic slow whip and can pickup or purchase better/different weapons as you progress but you can tell combat was never the focus of the game and that's fine. It's a means to an end.
Spelunky isn't even really a rogue-like. It's more like a NES platformer that sends you back to the start when you die. It reminds me more of Bubble Bobble or the Ducktales game than most modern rogue-likes.
Most unfortunate, however, was my realization that Spelunky was not an adventure game either. I was hoping for a game where I could explore to my heart's content. I wanted to root and dig and have grand adventure, bomb through walls to discover cool areas. The game does not deliver this experience. Sadly the game is on something of a timer, after spending about 2 or 3 minutes in a level a ghost chases you around to make you hurry up and get out (oh yea, the game is based on smallish levels, not open exploration, FYI).
Yes, Spelunky is not an adventure game, it is a speedrun game. That's a fun genre, Super House of Dead Ninjas is one of my favorites! My issue is that they give you tools to adventure and ask you to speedrun. Combine this with my previously mentioned issues, and it just seems like a game that threw a bunch of concepts together without really shining in any unique way.
I don't have much time in the game so far but I do plan on trying it further. If my opinion changes I will update the review accordingly. However, with so many games available that immediately grab my attention and are exciting from the start, I can't guarantee I'll play this again.
PROS:
Fun graphics
Interesting concept
CONS:
Nothing new
Doesn't excel in any specific area
Random and cheap deaths
Not a true adventure game or rogue-like
MEH:
Music ranges from bland to weird
Controls a little soft/slippery for my taste
Procedural level generation is all over the board in terms of difficulty/fairness
What I was hoping for: Rogue Legacy meets Terreria
What I got: Digdug meets Bubble Bobble

Alien versus Predator is one of the many, many Alien versus/vs Predator games, and the second one to be an FPS. In it, you can play as either an Alien, a Colonial Marine, or a Predator, each with different gameplay and story. Accordingly, I'll review each campaign separately, then offer some general thoughts.
The Alien campaign is probably the worst, although I wouldn't say it's bad—it's just kinda janky and overly ambitious. Like in the films, the Alien is ridiculously mobile and deadly. You can climb on walls and ceilings effortlessly (which is a bit disorienting but really fun), and pressing attack will kill and dismember just about anything in a 6-foot radius in front of you. Additionally, biological enemies emit a glow, making it easy to keep track of them and maintain the element of surprise. However, it's also pretty fragile—one or two shotgun blasts will take it down at full health, and a single Molotov cocktail can bring it to the brink of death. You're supposed to use stealth to get rid of enemies (most of which are humans or androids, with two Predators making up a final boss), but the Alien moves so quickly that caution is almost a lost cause. Just running up to things and killing them before they kill you, then biting their heads to get some health back is more or less your only option, which can get pretty trial-and-error. As a result, the Alien campaign is kinda hard to get into, and might put off some newcomers.
The Colonial Marine campaign is probably the best of the three. You're well-armed, with a healthy selection of weapons including dual pistols, the Marine assault rifle, an auto-aiming Smartgun, a flamethrower, and at least one rocket launcher. However, the Marine is probably the most vulnerable of the three protagonists, despite having plenty of health and armor. As the Marine, you're constantly unaware, with enemies being able to sneak up on you at any time and kill you in a few hits. Every shadow (and there are many) could contain another Alien waiting to jump out and claw you to pieces, and the night vision can only do so much to alleviate that. It's probably the most atmospheric and viscerally frightening of the campaigns, and it's a lot of fun.
The Predator is almost a reward for completing the other two. True to the films, the thing is absurdly overpowered, with plenty of lethal weapons and lots of health. My strategy was to move through each level, waiting for my helmet to auto-target enemies and then pressing one button to instantly cut them in half with my shoulder-mounted blaster (for humans, anyway—Aliens require a whole two shots). The only real threat is when your slowly-recharging energy gets low and more than one Alien is attacking at once, but that only happens a few times and you've still got your spear gun for those situations. It's a lot of fun, but without the same tension of the other campaigns.
Gameplay for each campaign is fairly similar: you travel through a series of semilinear and poorly-lit levels, kill enemies, break machinery, and press buttons. It's a bit easy to get lost, but that's what Internet walkthroughs are for. The atmosphere is very good, offering lots of claustrophobic tension (at least for two campaigns) and fear of what might be around the corner. Enemies respawn infinitely, but ammunition is either unnecessary, infinite, or so common that it's rarely an issue; additionally, it adds to the unrelenting feel that the game so accurately replicates from its source films.
Saves are limited to four per level on the normal difficulty, which is really goddamn annoying. I eventually set them to infinite using the console midway through the Alien campaign; I was a little conflicted about doing so, but then I learned that there originally weren't any, so if I'm already sort of cheating I might as well go all the way. You might think this is a minor issue and I'm just bad at games, and you might be right, but the game has enough random elements and surprise challenges that I feel more saves are worthwhile.
I really like the execution of the androids. They don't glow for the Alien, which is a nice touch, and they're not at all bothered by loss of limbs. If you cut off an android's arm, it'll drop its shotgun, pull out a pistol, and continue shooting you, just like an android would. I just think they're neat.
Overall, Alien versus Predator is good. It's atmospheric, varied in gameplay, challening, and fairly creative. It has its share of frustrating elements, and sometimes it'll do something ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tty, but most of the time you feel like you're actually playing an Alien or Predator film, which is the mark of a good adaptation. I recommend it.

There are enough of these ARPGs out there now that everyone should be able to find the one that suits them best.  TL2 seems to capture the hearts and minds of those that prefer the traditional skill tree, like to distribute points and don't want an "always online" experience.
I personally think the traditional skill tree combined with an ability to only respec the last 3 levels makes for a rather boring experience in Torchlight 2.  It ensures that you need to invest long hours to get any kind of meaningful payoff.  I tend to prefer the Diablo 3 mechanic where every level-up is something new to play around with.  That kind of thing makes even a limited time investment worthwhile.
While the TL2 gameplay mechanics seem tedious to me, much of the rest of the game is fairly pleasing.  I enjoy the art style.  The animation is and special effects are excellent.  I like the map designs and varied environments.  The music is great.  And the game even offers some unique and clever features.  It's overall a very decent game that provides a rich and more traditional ARPG experience over something like Diablo 3.  Still, I tend to prefer D3.
