Without even thinking about it, Warband is the best value for money game I have ever purchased.  Having clocked around 300 hours or so now, and having managed, finally, to rule all of calradia on normal difficulty, I'm taking a break. I may play a little more before the release bannerlord which if warband is anything to go by should be incredible. If it isn't I will be immensely disappointed.
A few things:
Sieges do not work especially well owing to the limitations of the AI. In order to stop your troops getting glitched out behind staircases or running facefirst into castle walls whilst being shot to death by archers, you do need to utilise the commands, which are far too basic to suit complex situations in which you find yourself. Avoid frustration by expecting them to be a bit crap from the offset. Your soldiers are prone to doing stupid chit and sometimes they're going to do it, which make some battles turn into monty python skits.
Don't give your followers lands and titles early in the game, if at all.  If they defect from your faction, you cannot get them back unless you wind up conquering all of Calradia.Moreoever if you defeat them in a battle, you cannot even incarcerate them in a dungeon. This is a big problem as their party skills are extremely helpful and beneficial to your overall gameplay.
Swadian knights are on balance the best troops for field battles  followed by sarranid mamlukes. However, slaver chiefs are vastly superiror to both if you're trying to capture enemies for recruitment purposes. These are the leveled version of manhunters.
For sieges: You want Nord huscarls, and rhodok sharpshooters ( failing this, swadian sharpshooters or vaegir marksman).
Tip: Do NOT loot and plunder villages, as low and hostile standings with villages will mean you are unable to recruit from them. It's very easy to tank your standing with a village, and much harder to win it back--doing this involves boring, annoying quests ( like herding cattle, which is a royal PITA.
DO NOT USE THE AUTOSAVE OPTION! This is known to cause a 'no string error' that effectively ruins your entire saved progress as it resets all your skill points back to zero without giving you the option to re-spend them. It basically wipes your character back to the starting level. I lost about 40 hours this way during my initial playthrough. Always, always manually save.
The reputation system which works well for the most part does become virtually impossible to balance as you accrue more lords to fight for you over time, apportion territories and try to to balance interpersonal disputes. Again, this is an old game, and the sophistication of AI relfects Its vintage. It's a problem, but a forgivable one, all said and done.
Hit detection in this game is perfect, and you're not. Expect to find yourself saying 'how the ♥♥♥♥ did that possibly ♥♥♥♥ing miss' quite a lot at first. I recoomend turning the battle speed up to highest as, for whatever reason, the game just seems to prefer it this way mechanically. It's just better.
Make sure you turn the number of troops per battle up to maximum also; failure to do this will, when facing a large enemy army, result in you spawning on the field with 10 troops and the enemy with over a hundred, and you will get roflstomped. The game will always fill to max capacity with AI troops, not yours.
For all its imperfections, bugs and general datedness Warband really is an immensely satisfying and enjoyable game that is well worth purchasing--especially given that you can pick it up for about the price of a happy meal most of the time. Nothing to lose here.

This game is more complete than most fully released titles in its current state, and very fun if you're the type of person who enjoy Sandbox RPGS. Its fairly basic in its current iteration but there's still plenty of content to keep you busy. I still haven't reached the endgame and I'm still having quite a bit of fun, especially with friends.
Combat is a little strange since you can't jump during a fight (makes flying enemies really annoying for a melee class); but it is still quite fun. Much like in Terraria, you can choose to forego your classes traditional weapons and armor to use another class, if the stats just speak to you more, which is always a plus. Enemies have a good diversity of attacks and abilities that should keep you entertained throughout your engagements.
The class structures are on the low end in terms of diversity; abilities you get from leveling up are fairly linear and they don't change up combat too much besides giving you a bit more powerful towards your default archiatype. That's the point though, since every weapon, armor and even ability in the game can be crafted by any of the classes; its designed for you to more pick how you want to play, instead of just being chicken-holed into a certian style.
Well worth the 15 dollars; especially considering the amount of content is just going to quadruple as the game goes along.
Also Its being published by the publishers of Terraria; I imagine those publishers have good taste.

Brothers, A Tale of Two Sons - A Commentary
Controllers are the nexus of the the game experience, they stand at the intersection of gamer and game.  Countless innovations on the controller’s design and implementation have been applied to gaming over the years.  One of the most common questions game developers are confronted with is, “How do we map our controller?”  In a small Danish game studio a new improvisation has emerged, providing a new paradigm for the conventional controller.  In “Brothers, A Tale of Two Sons,” the controller is used in ways that exceed the standard user/avatar UI of typical role playing games.  The controller functions as an inherently deep gameplay element and a powerful story metaphor for an experience of cinemagraphic emphasis.
The narrative itself is simplistic, but effective, it’s minimalist approach is reminiscent of Danish 30s cinema.  Ironically the game was made by the Danish Starbreeze Studios.  Nothing is used unintentionally within the game’s design, this is true for all the elements from props to plot devices.  The logical progression behind behind the game is clear cut, the desires, ambitions and fears of it’s characters all have causes, achieving a flawless parallel between plot and theme.  One of the unique strengths of a minimalist narrative with no intelligible dialogue is that it takes away the premonition that the player can control the dialogue.  This let’s an aspect of the narrative that cannot be influenced fade into the background.
In “Brothers a Tale of Two Sons” by Starbreeze studios the controller is not only used for its typical interface between player and avatar, it is a story metaphor.  The story itself clearly illustrates the dynamic features behind the relationship of the brother.  It reinforces the story’s base narrative and operates seamlessly within the metaphors of the story.  It demonstrates the reliance of the two brothers on each other during navigation and puzzles, the player being a single essence provides the uniting features of these notions, this is hammered in through the steep learning curve of controlling both characters simultaneously.  The artifacts of this design choice are seen in simple plot devices where the player must give up control of the younger brother so the older can carry him through the water, and in the more sophisticated puzzles where communication between the brothers is paramount.
It is always difficult to quantify emotional impact.  In this case however most of the story’s weight branches from its basic narrative and the functional weight of the gameplay system.  This may seem obvious, but within interactive media the term “basic narrative” is rarely seen.  This particular game thoroughly engages the player through all the senses it has at it’s disposal.  Visually it bares a system that places an emphasis on story elements and lets all else fade into the background.  It’s soundtrack is both compelling and beautiful.  The controller provides excellent tactile feedback.  The metaphorical system on the controller is not only symbolically correct it provides a brilliant area where the affection of the characters can be betrayed.  The controller splits vertically down it’s middle, the left side corresponds to the older brother the right side corresponds to the younger.  This creates a geographic expression for the two brothers’ relationship which is not only fantastically metaphorical, the player comes to love being the means to the brother’s relationship.  We see the organism of the game as an extension of ourselves.
This is all an elaborate setup for the butchery of this organism, when the older brother dies the player's connection to the story is cut off.  The player feels the loss and seeks comfort with the only individual that can relate to her/his plight, the younger brother.  This leaves the player as an engraved element in the story’s structure when it ends, the end of the narrative leaves the player unfulfilled.  The death of the older brother brings out some of our darkest fears as humans, it reminds us that even in an interactive game, just as in life, we have no control over death.   The player realizes that in spite of his/her governing power over the brother’s relationship, they can only implement the choices the characters made for themselves.  When the voice of the older brother returns at the resolution of the story, the player watches as their control disperses further as death, an element totally out of their control as humans, once again takes the wheel.
In Brothers, A Tale of Two Sons, a fixed narrative is presented, using emergence strictly as an utility for enhancing the experience of the game.  The most unique element of the game is it’s use of the controller as a story metaphor and tactile plot device, reaching beyond the utilitarian design scheme of the conventional game.  This mechanic fits flawlessly into it’s minimalist visuals and compelling soundtrack taking the gaming community on an emotional rollercoaster they won’t soon forget.

Do I recommend it? Yes but not at the full price. Because I paid full price this review is based off of that. If it were $20 or even $30 it would be different.
No longer are there weapons and armor to collect and customize (you do get costumes which have no benefit).
Artifacts replace the perks system from SoT.
A lot of the missions feel very much the same, the map feels tedious (especially if you did a SoT run through in anticipation of FBW) and it lacks a lot of the grandure SoT had.
Even the other developing game mechanics feel like they were pulled nearly directly from SoT. *See a particular out of place item with a chest nearby* "Looks like I have to wait to get *that* powerup"
SoT had a solid story between the two parties, leading up to a mutual enemy and so forth.
FbW has a fairly weak story thusfar and fetch side missions barely or not at all connected to the main story.
The fight mechanics and boss battles are a nice touch, albeit take some time to get used to. The group fighting does add to some more complex stategy potential.
Lastly are the crashes and glitches. More than a handful of times now have I had text boxes that are blank and missing information, 1 bluescreen crash, a few of the toilet games glitch and 3 soft locks on the start of a fight (enemy gets knocked out by first attack and microaggression then the fight is locked waiting on the knocked out enemy's move).
In short if you're a huge South Park or SoT fan go for it but dont expect to get blown away. If not, wait for it to drop to the sub ~$30 price point.

This game, if only for a moment, had me sharing a piece of cake with a fictional character as if she were really there. For all intents and purposes, I completely forgot that I was in fact, playing a video game. If that isn't a testament to how good this game's writing is, I don't know what is.
This game is also a sequel to Analogue: A Hate Story, so as such, my reccomendation is simple:
If you enjoyed the first game, play this without question. If you haven't played the first one, either play that game right now or tell me why you are reading this.
A few thoughts on the differences from the first game:
I'd actually argue that the writing in Hate Plus is even better than Analogue: A Hate Story. It's certainly better paced thanks to the three day system. No doubt that mechanic was inspired by Majora's Mask, but I think it actually works better here than it did in Zelda... save for the fact that there's no time travel. The game actually locks you out of playing after progressing a certain amount. You are literally meant to play this game over the course of three real world days.
Forcing you to stop playing after a certain amount of time causes you to think more about what little plot you know so far, and considering gameplay mostly consists of reading paragaphs upon paragraphs of writing, taking a break is helpful. Also the breaks help immerse you more in the experience. You're not just reading a novel here. This game has so much more to offer beyond just that.
Also the addition of more art is a major improvement over the original. Nearly all of the characters you're reading about over the course of the game each have a portrait you can view, which again, adds more to the experience of this being more than just a book.
And the soundtrack is even better than the original's IMO. Although the lack of a simulated terminal interface this time around makes me a little sad, that would also have to be the only complaint I have.
I love this game. I love this series. I really hope one day we'll be able to see a third installment.

Hate Plus feels a bit like an add-on rather than standalone game. It's predecessor Analogue: A Hate Story was really good. Great atmosphere from the start ( story is on a abandoned ship and you have to investigate what happened, music was great and one time you had to hack a console to prevent core meltdown while developing relationship with the AI. ). It brought new things to the table of Visual Novels and it was fresh...
Hate Plus feels like a downgrade. Music is not memorable and there is no feeling of supspence and exploration unlike in Analogue: A Hate Story. There are at least two design decisions that I hate in Hate Plus :D. First when you run out of power which can be pretty fast if you aren't intrested in some lousy stories ( of what it appears to be homosexual relationships ) you have to wait ONE REAL LIFE day to progress the game... well thanks a fricking lot.
What if you have kids to pick up from kindergarden? You have work tomorrow and then you won't have time in the afternoon? Well this game doesn't give a flying fart. You have to adjust or start New game and try different route and pick different logs.
Imagine that you are playing Call of Duty you have finished first chapter and then game tell you : Your soldier is tired he needs to rest ONE REAL LIFE DAY in order to progress to the next battlefield... ARE YOU FRICKING KIDDING ME??!
Next bad decision is the graphics. They have been slightly enlarged compared to Analogue. In my opinion it looks a bit itimidating and too close ( maybe they wanted players to feel closer to the AI... ). Whatever they thought It doesn't work for me...
On top of that navigating through the menues is cumbersome because of the speed that windows appear ( unfold ). On top of that scrolling speed is slow...
Apart from that for those who have played first game this will feel a bit like a downgrade but as a curious person I need to see it to the end. That might be the only thing that drives me... see the ending. Because I can't enjoy the ride this time around....
Thanks for reading. Have a nice day.

EDIT - I've rewritten this review, because my first one was just too rambling.
Hate Plus is a fascinating visual novel that attempt to follow up the first game with a somewhat forced extension of the original story. It's... mostly successful in what it sets out to do, but there's no denying that it's not nearly as gripping as Analogue: A Hate Story. But it's hardly the first sequel that didn't live up to the original - and that said, it's certainly still good.
First up, I should mention that this is NOT a game where you should skip the previous installments and jump right in. You'll want to play Analogue: A Hate Story first. Although you could theoretically skip the first game entirely and still make some sense of the story, it would be... difficult. The story is already complex enough without deliberately hacking major chunks out of it.
Now then, we'll start with the good. Hate Plus is very well written - although this should come as no surprise, since Christina Love (the developer) is a fantastic writer. I loved the writing in the first game, and that hasn't changed with the second. Granted, the story is a bit more... rambling and disconnected, but it's still fascinating to piece together. The sound track is also exceptional, if not revolutionary. The music is generally simple and repetitive, but there are several tracks that really do help set the mood as you wade through dozens of old computer logs that range from innocent to scandalous to horrifying. The interface is also subtly improved, reducing the amount of backtracking and note-taking that you had to do in the first game - most notably by providing a collection of 'Character Files' on all of the major characters that are updated as you discover new information.
And now the bad. As with the first game, Hate Plus suffers from the usual limitations of the Visual Novel genre - it's rather short, fairly linear, and only grants you the illusion of choice. Unlike in the first game, there's no muddling your way to five or six different endings. This time, you make your choices right at the beginning of the game (or load your save file from the first game) and THAT more or less determines how things will play out as you progress. There are still four or five different endings, but those endings all require you to start a completely fresh file since they're absolutely mutually exclusive of each other. And, sadly, while each of those play throughs is distinctly different in some key aspects, it doesn't change the fact that you'll end up wading through dozens of the SAME files over and over again (and reading the same plot twists over and over again) if you want to try for the different endings.
But of special note is the subtle nods to immersion. I appreciated the little touches in the first game (typing into the "ship console" for example), but Hate Plus takes it a step further. This time around you don't just read a file and then ask your AI companion what she thinks of it - she actually "reads" it alongside you, commenting on new twists and reveals as you scroll through the files. She'll regularly interject between files (usually every three to six files), to share her thoughts or concerns about what you've found out so far. And heck, there's even a fake little "spacemail" button that occasionally updates with new letters that are largely unrelated to the game, giving you insight into the world of the far-flung future (the intergalactic variant of the Nigerian Bank Scam is particularly entertaining).
Then again, not all of the attempts at immersion are entirely fun, though. Hate Plus makes heavy use of a "time-lock" feature that essentially locks up your progress between each "game day" (and sometimes during certain special events). The game takes place over a period of three "in-game" days, and apparently the creator wanted that to be represented by having the player actually spend three days on it - so each time you finish an in-game day, your save file actually locks until your computer timeclock reaches the next day in real life. It's simple enough to circumvent, but still more annoying than cute - especially once you've already beaten the game once or twice.
But for me, jumping through the hurdles (minor as they are) was worth it. For those who enjoyed the first game and want to find out more about the Hate universe, then Hate Plus is a must. It's a good bit heavier on political intrigue and NSFW computer logs, but the story is still fascinating if a bit disjointed. If you're like me, then you'll love to Hate.

My first waifu will always be there to tease, to play with, to share her wit and insight. Kind, sweet, and only a little murderous, she'll always have a place in my heart. For her, I'd eat a cake every day.
The other one, well, I'll never get tired of looking into those vivid blue eyes, appreciating that cat like grin that creeps up on her face, her elegant way of dress or how in a moment she can deal out a harsh and shunning attitude that whips my heart full of passion. The beauty of it all is that no matter how many times she may wish to die, we shall always be in the perpetual spring of marriage, for there will always be a reset, and day three, will never come again. Not now, not ever.

This is the kind of game I had been needing for a long time. Not because of its genre. Because of its charm. Its passion and attention to detail. Its... OK, you get the point.
You play as Rufus, a despicable inhabitant of the massive wasteland that is Deponia, and a damn cool character all around. No matter how many messes he has and is still getting into, you will definitely take his side in every confront of the game - because, well, it's him who you're rooting for since the beginning! This, blended with the game's very lively sense of humour and the intelligent puzzles that come along the way, make for an outstanding experience in Rufus' egotistical point of view.
It's difficult not to love Goal. She is adorable even while in her unfortunate damaged status, and becomes even more lovable after waking up and realising what is going on. On a more personal side, perhaps I may have connected her far too much to someone I love - but let's not get that in the way, shall we? At least for now.
Overall, this... game? Wait, scratch that. To classify Deponia as a simple "game" is to insult this masterpiece of humour, storytelling and cringe-inducing moments.
So, if you're not even remotely interested in getting it for you and giving it a go, I'd recommend checking your brain activity and blood pressure. I'm serious.

The game starts out simple enough: spiders drop from the ceiling when you walk underneath, bats fly at you when you get close to them, snakes slither back and forth. Fine. You can run and jump, use a rope to climb to places you wouldn't otherwise reach, drop a bomb to bring down a wall or make a hole and get to otherwise unreachable areas. Cool. I don't normally review games, but I decided to write this review since I think this game is underappreciated.
Eon Altar is a great couch co-op roleplaying game, designed to emulate the experience of playing traditional tabletop RPGs, like Dungeons & Dragons.
One of the most original (and judging by the review, somewhat controversial) features of the game is that the players interact with the game via a smartphone app (free). The game requires only one PC to host the game, and a wireless connection; a session can accomodate up to 4 players, that will be controlling their characters on their smartphones. The smartphones and the PC need to be connected to the same wireless network. In other words, up to 4 people can play with the same copy of the game.
There are 5 characters, which are quite different in terms of playstyle and personality.
The characters gain levels and can use a number of resources to upgrade their special abilities and equipment. There are two main game modes - campaign and combat arena. The campaign at the moment has 3 episodes/chapter and get the characters through a number of  dungeons, with a (mostly linear) storyline on the background. There are occasional choices, and interestingly the characters may have different or even opposing personal goals (e.g. one character might want to destroy a particular magic item for personal reasons, while another character might want to use it). Having played tabletop RPGs for the past 20 years or so, I have to say that the developers were quite successful in recreating the experience of the typical D&D campaign (including the classical careless fireball that hits your companions). The combat arena challenges the players with increasingly difficult fights.
I played Eon Altar with my non-gamer wife and we really really enjoyed it. It is a relatively simple game with a low entry barrier. Controlling the characters via the smartphone app is sometimes a bit clunky but I really liked how innovative the concept is, and I really appreciate that the developers released the App for free. The game has a few annoying features (eg. the lack of a minimap, or the fact that some of the mechanics are not explained very well) but overall these are minor hiccups.
Pros:
Cons
At the moment three episodes are released for the main campaign as DLCs; the story is not finished, and I really hope that the developers will release more stuff. I wouldn't mind extra characters as DLCs.
This game is probably not for you if you are an hardcore RPG gamer, if you like to delve into complex storylines or if you like to spend hours customizing/optimizing your character or trying different builds. I would encourage you to try it if you want a relatively simple, light RPG to play in co-op with friends, family or with your partner. Personally I really liked it and I hope more content is released.

I desperately wanted this game to be good.
Sadly after several hours of playing i have to say it has very little to offer.
the further you go in this game the bigger the grind becomes to make stuff. from these portals to even basic items like a iron pickaxe.
At first crafting seems like the standard thing. 4 copper here and 2 coal for an iron ingot. but then the next step already is 10 iron ore and 4 coal and then 20 gold ore and 6 coal!
This would not be a problem if it was not already a pain in the arsh to collect some of it. but because its so spread out and the supply is so very limited. it can take you hours to gather enough for maybe a weapon or some armor.
its so padded out that it tries to make it look like it has plenty to offer. but its so slugish and slow that before you know it your done with this already. since every isle you come across looks like a Swis cheese you dont really feel like fixing them up. are there any liquids in this game? i have only seen the acid that the first boss bathes in but besides that there has been no water to speak off.
My simple question remains. what is this game trying to be?
A minecraft clone that looks better? it sure looks better but it thats a subjective oppinion. but building a house can be done in minecraft, in every buildy buildy game and they do it better.
An adventure game? there is so much grinding to do that the only adventure there is are the boss fights.
The "dungeons" are simply another cave with nothing at the end of it to reward you or make it worth the effort. a simple chest perhaps with material drops from enemies you already beated the crap out of.
Speaking of a load of crap.
The inventory gets clogged up with every random bits you encounter. like 20 diferent seeds for tree's and plants and veggies and whatnot. it would not be a problem if the inventory had more then just 32 slots. this includes the 8 hotkey action bar. in which you must have a weapon, some wetstones, pickaxe and healing atleast. thankfully armor equiped does not take inventory space but there is still so little room to work with. the first chests you can make only hold 12 items. For some reason the UI and item images are FAR to freaking large. having them even a half the size would be more pleasant to look at then these "cutsie" items.
Overall i would seriouslly wait to see what this game will become. maybe its the second minecraft? but for that it would require so much more. maybe its the next Windborne and gets canceled because it has nothing to offer at the moment.
I seriously hope it is the first of the two but that remains to be seen.

I usually don't write review, but I thought this was necessary because of the way this game is being handled, I will try to be objective but I also wish to give some personal thoughts at the end.
I am one of the people who have purchased the game before the release in order to play it right away, when the game released it was not available right away, which was a big disappointment but this problem was caused by a new download method that Valve decided to use on Steam and this caused the game to not succesfully load for those who pre-ordered the game, in this matter the developer studio is not responsible for the problem.
About the game, it is fun, the single player experience will present most of the things that were already available in MK9 but in addition to what was already there, the game now comes with additional tower mods that include ones such as "Klassic" and Endless. The story mod itself unfrotunately is short and doesn't seem like it has much thought given to it, however it gives a nice exposion over the new characters that were added to the game such as Cassie Cage, who appears to be the daughter of Johnny Cage and Sonya Blade.
Mostly based on their relation to other characters, every new combatant seems to be some sort of combination a pair of older combatants, this does not include D'vorah and Ferra/Tor, who are unique in their fighting style.
Unlike what most people might think and what NR might say, the fighting styles are not a new feature added to the franchise at this point, they were present in Mortal Kombat Deception, and players back then were even able to change their styles during combat instead of during character select. In any case it's a nice feature and presents more about the characters to be explored by the players. However in some cases, mainly Raiden the styles appear to have taken what was already there in the characters fighting style and than split it in half and present it as two distinct fighting styles, which is unpleasent.
To be more precise, Raiden in all the earlier games was able to teleport at will, but in Mortal Kombat X, he is only able to do so in his Displacer fighting style, which makes the overall character look like he's lost more than he has gained. This is only a minor concern however and does not represent the entire batch of characters. The feature is as welcome as ever and adds a good learning curve to the game.
Multiplayer wise the game is quiet rich. You may challenge other players to fight you based on various statistics that are presented to you that include your chances of winning as well as the option to be part of a faction. Factions in this game represent the ones that were already in the story of the game, such as the White Lotus and every victory you have, will benefit your faction in a way. There are timed faction battles that invite you to take part in Kombat against players from other factions in order to represent their group. This however isn't all that is presented because there are also other mods that are present such as the King of the Hill. Overall the online experience has been very pleasent while not being too concerned about the minimal amount of lag that I have faced.
All of these aside, if I have to be honest, the game does feel like a bad port. Considering my setup, which I will provide at the bottom, the game has some technical issues that feel like they should not be there. Random frame rate drops that is caused by memory leak and stuttering that is caused because of the use the bad use of CPU has made the game unplayable at some points even at the lowest settings available. I was able to slightly stabilize how the game worked by tinkering around the Nvidia Control Panel, however overall it was still feeling very choppy which leads to be say that the port developer did not know what they were doing with the PC port. Aside from tachnical issues, there are also some other issues concerning bugs that the game faces right now that need to be fixed immediately, which as missing animations in the character select screen and the unavailability of the configurations at the startup of the game, on top of this the graphics options given to the player are very limited and the screen resolution options are pathetic.
Overall I thought this game was very fun, but plagued by issues that start from graphical setting variety to menu bugs and outright unplayable choppy framerates. This makes me want to make a distiction as there are other versions of the game that seem to be playable, the game itself is good and very fun to play with rich options of gameplay and replay value, but this PC port does not feel to have good stability so I do not wish to recommend the game for PC, but I will, because there are some fixes going around the community that help stabilize the game a bit, but I expect some effort from the developer too.

Pre-ordered this the moment it was available on Steam. It doesn't disappoint and it's well worth the wait.
Pros:
-Really optimized for PC. You can run it 60fps consistently with no problems even if your rig isn't the toppest of the line. Keyboard mapping/binding is possible, and it natively supports different controls
-Stunning visuals, especially at 4k. The game is a wonder to look at.
-Very rich and jam-packed Training mode. Lots of options for you to set whenever you want to practice a new combo or mixup.
-Gallery Mode contains all the past CGI movies in previous Tekkens for your viewing pleasure.
-Fresh additions to the meta such as:
>Rage Arts - these correspond to supers in other games
>Rage Drives - they work similarly to EX moves in other games
>Power Crush - an armored attack that lets you absorb up to 3 hits of any high or mid attack while being vulnerable to low attacks or throws
-The slow-down when two incoming attacks collide upon nearing KO is mad hype. I found myself enjoying each of these epic slow-mos.
-Customization is packed with options for you to personalize and customize not just your character, but even stuff like your health bar, information panels, and so on.
-Fantastic story mode that really takes advantage of the stunning visuals and immersive soundtrack.
-Arcade Mode and Treasure Battle are really fun and engaging offline modes for people who like to play offline Single Player.
-In the settings, there's an option for "Tournament Mode". This is a really big help for tournament organizers as this reworks the Offline VS Battle into a more tournament-friendly configuration with stuff like disabling pausing mid-battle via the start button or even controllers being disconnected. Every fighting game that doesn't already have this should follow suit.
-The addition of Akuma and Eliza allows people coming from 2D fighting games such as Street Fighter to get into the action while easing themselves into Tekken-style of play since Akuma and Eliza function like 2D characters with sidestepping. They even have a super meter and jump attacks.
Cons, there aren't much but here's some of them below:
-No proper tutorial. Some newcomers might find this a turn off, but to compensate you can just head straight into Practice/Training mode and look at the sample combos near the bottom of the command list of your character. To be fair though, this isn't a real substitute for a proper tutorial.
-No crossplay. The dev team has stated their reasons for this, but it's definitely a con.
-This port doesn't have Tekken Jukebox, a mode on the PS4 version where you can listen and use tracks from all the previous Tekkens(Tekken 1 to Tekken Revolution) except for Tekken 3D Prime.
Overall: 9/10.
T7 is by no means perfect, but it's getting there. I recommend getting this game for all fighting game afficionados out there on Steam, even those who don't play 3D fighting games, because Tekken is that awesome.

Train Simulator is - at least to me - the most realistic train simulator out there. The variety of the DLC's that you can buy allows you to play in the most known railways in the world. The controls are, for me pretty nice and realistic. But this game has flaws. Way too many flaws...
- Realistic train controls
- Nicely modeled trains and environments
- Huge variety of content
- The base game brings only a few scenarios and trains to drive
- The DLC's, where you can bring more scenarios and trains, are often expensive
- There's a huge flaw that makes the game crawl when it needs to load the scenario - not on the loading screen, but while you're driving
- While loading the scenario, the games becomes almost inresponsive, so if you try to brake there's a huge chance that that's not going to happen
- Some scenarios are almost impossible to achieve the 1000 points mark, the max you can get. For instance, with the
DLC you have a scenario where you need to wait on a red signal before stopping in the last station, making you get a penalty due to arriving at the station late
-
There's a probability where after resuming a scenario, the save corrupts
- When, for any reason, the game crashes, it can lock your computer. In my case I have to disconnect the HDMI cable, connect it again, press CTRL + ALT + DELETE and open the Task Manager, press WINDOWS + TAB and set the Train Simulator window in another Desktop - otherwise I can't click on anything -, go to the Task Manager and close the Train Simulator there.
If you like trains, and like simulators, then this might be the game for you - I don't know other train sims out there that can beat this one, to be honest -, but keep in mind that you'll probably need to spend a lot of money in DLC's, deal with freezes and crashes that the workaround is not acceptable - or play in windowed mode.

Hate Plus starts off directly where Analogue: A  Hate Story ends. Depending on which ending you achieved in the first game will depend on how your experience begins in Hate Plus, which I love. It will also dictate which AI will be accompanying you; either Hyun-ae, Mute or if you are lucky enough (like I was)...both!  I feel like the design of this game had really improved since Analogue. It's smoother and much easier to navigate through the log files. Even the writing has improved, along with rapport between yourself and your AI. The way the game is setup is interesting: you can only read a set number of logs per day, before you run out of energy. The AI bid you goodnight, and the game shuts itself off for 12 hours. I don't think I've ever played a game like that, but it really adds to the realism of the entire experience. This game explores more of the backstory, deepening it. At the same time you must tend to your relationship with your AI, which can be tenuous at times. I found this game incredibly entertaining on many levels. The humor is spot-on, but so is the drama. It really makes you question things when it comes to gender, politics, tradition and the notion of free will. I can't wait to see more from Christine Love!!

A well-made RPG with the uncommon control method of a phone app, which serves as both movement and a menu to upgrade stats and equipment. While there's not a way of making a unique character, the characters that are able to be selected from have significantly different playstyles and personalities. What's made easier by the phone controller is allowing characters to have competing/secret objectives or conversations with NPC's, which has led to a few amusing interactions between myself and my friends. Combat is turn-based, with all the enemies going, and then your side acting, no initiative rolls from what I can tell. Friendly fire is on, both for melee and spells, which encourages tactical discussion...and allows for tactical blunders when your mage fireballs both the warrior and paladin because they forgot to check the range on the AoE. While there is a method for solo play, I would *highly* reccomend finding two or three other people to play with, both for the storytelling and the combat, as most fights seem to be balanced around having multiple party members. But if you've got a group of friends able to come over to a house and play, I highly recommend this one for co-op.

Racing shooters are dime a dozen, as it's relatively easy to make... but hard to make well. Either you have too many weapons (little variation among them), or you end up too much like Mario Kart. MadOut is a surprisingly decent entry from an indie developer who did not went for fancy (no hover, no crazy weapons...), but instead concentrated on the decent parts: physics (which affects handling and weapons), as well as huge variety of tracks, as it seems to have over 100 different tracks (albeit, many of them are just combinations of the assets from previous races, while others are "no shooting" races.
The handling in the game is excellent as the car behave realistically in corners, and you can even handbrake slide around corners. if you run up side of a hill you will fly... Though you probably won't have time to admire your handling as you'd be too busy dodging shots, mines, terrain, and each other.
There are only three weapons: mines, machine gun (auto-aimming) and seeking missiles (they don't turn that well though). Your fourth button is nitro boost.
Your opponents, AI, are probably not that good drivers... as they slide all over the place, run into each other and you, understeer and slide to the outside (thus allowing you to cut inside), bouncing off walls... probably just like you are. And they will shoot you, and shoot you a lot.
If you are killed, you are respawn with no weapons or boost a few seconds behind. But that just means all the other guys are in front of your weapons, right?
There are a lot of variations on cars, and each have up to a dozen paint jobs. Weapons have a few variations and some upgrades cost $$$. You earn money by kills and wins, and you lose money if you got killed. The idea is to get into top three to open up the next race, and as I said, there are dozens and dozens (over 100?) races available, day or night, various terrains from icy tundras to city to desert to ruins and railyards and much more.
The game is surprisingly agile and on max graphics 1680x1050 on my rig of several years old it's running at max frame rates and works really well. My main complaint is the viewpoint is too close to one's own vehicle from behind, and on some courses you get killed X times in a row with no chance to get ahead as enemies just keep killing you again and again.
Don't pay $20 for it. But $5? Sure.

More MadOut!
There is another MadOut on Steam already and this is sort of it's sequel.  For some reason, this one has a lower retail value ($5.59 US) versus it's predecessor ($14.99) and this one is actually better.  If you are curious if you want to try out these games, this is the one to get.
The car types seem to be the same between the two games, there may be some differences but at first glance they appear to be the same, although there are new paint schemes and skins.
MadOut is a combat racing game and it has fantastic physics, graphics, and handling.  My favorite part about the series is just how perfect the weapons operate.  The guns are actually rotating around on top of your car and focusing on the guy in front of you so you don't have to actually aim the whole car just to shoot someone.  They just need to be in range.  Same with rockets, it's nice to be able to focus on the racing!  As I mentioned earlier, the graphics are amazing.  Sure it's not cutting-edge stuff here, but for such a small game studio, they sure are able to push their limits.
What's the difference between this one and the old one?  MadOut Ice Storm has 80 levels,  MadOut has 56 levels.   I haven't actually played all the way through them to tell if the levels are all new or if they are the the same 56 with 24 new ones but they appear to be all new.  Looking at the level selection screen, they are at minimum in a different order, and one can only hope that there are changes to them.  I will try to see if I can do a comparison of the two games in depth.  Regardless, here we have MORE MADOUT for 1/3 of the price!!  For newcomers, you will get a much, much more value here.
What's bad?
The UI is functional but it's not the showpiece here.  If they could create a new, 3D, or animated UI some day it would really look more professional.  But for now, it's a bit ordinary and serviceable.  Also, it would sure be nice to have a bit more on offer than just a series of races.  There's really nothing missing, but it just seems a bit odd not to have Arcade, Career, Time Trials, and so on.  Definitely come into this knowing that this game is just a whole bunch of races you need to win.  You can upgrade your car and earn money in between races, and that's the story of MadOut.

I usually don't write review, but I thought this was necessary because of the way this game is being handled, I will try to be objective but I also wish to give some personal thoughts at the end.
I am one of the people who have purchased the game before the release in order to play it right away, when the game released it was not available right away, which was a big disappointment but this problem was caused by a new download method that Valve decided to use on Steam and this caused the game to not succesfully load for those who pre-ordered the game, in this matter the developer studio is not responsible for the problem.
About the game, it is fun, the single player experience will present most of the things that were already available in MK9 but in addition to what was already there, the game now comes with additional tower mods that include ones such as "Klassic" and Endless. The story mod itself unfrotunately is short and doesn't seem like it has much thought given to it, however it gives a nice exposion over the new characters that were added to the game such as Cassie Cage, who appears to be the daughter of Johnny Cage and Sonya Blade.
Mostly based on their relation to other characters, every new combatant seems to be some sort of combination a pair of older combatants, this does not include D'vorah and Ferra/Tor, who are unique in their fighting style.
Unlike what most people might think and what NR might say, the fighting styles are not a new feature added to the franchise at this point, they were present in Mortal Kombat Deception, and players back then were even able to change their styles during combat instead of during character select. In any case it's a nice feature and presents more about the characters to be explored by the players. However in some cases, mainly Raiden the styles appear to have taken what was already there in the characters fighting style and than split it in half and present it as two distinct fighting styles, which is unpleasent.
To be more precise, Raiden in all the earlier games was able to teleport at will, but in Mortal Kombat X, he is only able to do so in his Displacer fighting style, which makes the overall character look like he's lost more than he has gained. This is only a minor concern however and does not represent the entire batch of characters. The feature is as welcome as ever and adds a good learning curve to the game.
Multiplayer wise the game is quiet rich. You may challenge other players to fight you based on various statistics that are presented to you that include your chances of winning as well as the option to be part of a faction. Factions in this game represent the ones that were already in the story of the game, such as the White Lotus and every victory you have, will benefit your faction in a way. There are timed faction battles that invite you to take part in Kombat against players from other factions in order to represent their group. This however isn't all that is presented because there are also other mods that are present such as the King of the Hill. Overall the online experience has been very pleasent while not being too concerned about the minimal amount of lag that I have faced.
All of these aside, if I have to be honest, the game does feel like a bad port. Considering my setup, which I will provide at the bottom, the game has some technical issues that feel like they should not be there. Random frame rate drops that is caused by memory leak and stuttering that is caused because of the use the bad use of CPU has made the game unplayable at some points even at the lowest settings available. I was able to slightly stabilize how the game worked by tinkering around the Nvidia Control Panel, however overall it was still feeling very choppy which leads to be say that the port developer did not know what they were doing with the PC port. Aside from tachnical issues, there are also some other issues concerning bugs that the game faces right now that need to be fixed immediately, which as missing animations in the character select screen and the unavailability of the configurations at the startup of the game, on top of this the graphics options given to the player are very limited and the screen resolution options are pathetic.
Overall I thought this game was very fun, but plagued by issues that start from graphical setting variety to menu bugs and outright unplayable choppy framerates. This makes me want to make a distiction as there are other versions of the game that seem to be playable, the game itself is good and very fun to play with rich options of gameplay and replay value, but this PC port does not feel to have good stability so I do not wish to recommend the game for PC, but I will, because there are some fixes going around the community that help stabilize the game a bit, but I expect some effort from the developer too.

I first picked this up for myself and a friend so we could play it together. It's not too expensive, and it looks kinda fun.
Well, in a nutshell, it IS.
Don't go expecting this to be like all those minecraft clones out there, this is more of an action game with the building blocks play tacked on than the reverse. The action works quite well too. It's *mostly* smooth when playing, aside from the few times where it decides to lock your target onto something entirely different than what you were pointing at (pretty simple to fix that though), and the dodge mechanic could use a little more polish.
When attacking your character will automatically lock on to what you're aiming at, which is handy for lazy ranged players as it then will try to automatically adjust your shots to hit the target. It's basically an aim-bot. This could be a downside for those players looking for a more challenging play, as it turns into more or less a simple "DPS them down and dodge when they attack" -fest.
I'd love to see an option to turn off auto aim, just to make it more challenging for more veteran players.
Graphically the game is great, everything looks vivid and colorful, the animations are decent, as are the baddies, though the characters themselves are little more than glorified lego men (and women), and the variety of enemies right now isn't amazing. Given that it's early access though, there's hope to see more in the future.
I picked this game up specifically to play multiplayer, and for the most part it was smooth sailing. My friend and I had no trouble connecting up and playing the game together, and we had very few problems while playing. It's all coop, as far as I can tell, so you won't be hurting your friends. The only thing that annoys about the MP is that you and your friends are trapped playing on the same islands. If one player warps to another island, so does everyone else. Given that we were working together this didn't turn out to be too much trouble, just an ocassional irritation.
The levels are a bit crazy at the moment. It's like someone tried to scale a whole chunk of world and cram it onto a tiny island. You'll end up with incredibly tall moutains right next to mini forests, caves, pitfalls... all within a stone's throw of each other. This is probably the weakest part of the game. This is NOT what you can truly call an open world game. Yes you can move between islands via portals, and they seem to be mostly procedural, but they're not very big. (I'd say less than a square km, roughly.) They're also not entirely random, as the portals are all pre-planned and follow a level curve. The crowding of all those land features into a small space also soon wears out it's welcome, as "exploring" to find the next portal is less about actually exploring and more about navigating a tedious landscape. Again though, early access, hopefully in the future there will be more randomness and much, much larger areas. THEN maybe we can actually explore.
The amount of things on the tiny islands are an issue as well, as there's random ruins and huts etc. all over the place. This kind of robs me of the desire to make my own place, as it would just be yet another building on a tiny island full of ruins. So instead I felt it would be better to just move into some ruins.
Overall the game is a lot of fun to play, and is quite well polished for an early access title. For the low price of $15, it's an easy one to recommend.

+Polished
+Simple without being stupid.
+Quite a bit of fun for only $15

Maybe the game just isn't for me but here are some of the reasons why I dislike it.
Weapons and ammo are named for people who like guns in real life rather than being named so that gamers can easily identify what is what at a seconds glance.
The bleeding mechanic is annoying. You get bleeding for pretty much any hit so you better scavenge any and all healing items (apart from food which is just going to weigh you down) you come across.
Your weapons rarely feel like they have an "impact" on enemies. You can hit an enemy 8 times with a weapon and they barely look like they are harmed by it. There is no limping, no slowing down of movements, no trying to escape when their life is too low, no stumble when hit by a heavy impact weapon like a shotgun. The only times it feels like your weapons have an impact is when you hit an enemy in the head at which point they're instakilled.
Combat in general is tedious. You have to attack multiple enemies and they all take so many bullets (unless you manage to get good headshots (which isn't easy with how inaccurate weapons are)) to go down while you only need to take a handful to die. You end up playing pop a mole from cover most of the time and there is rarely any other tactic to use since if you kill an enemy pretty much all other enemies are alerted to your presence so sneaking is out of the question. And maybe it is just because I never found a good long range weapon but sniping wasn't viable for me. Neither was storming the place either. It's pretty much just pop a mole from cover for the most part.
The dialogue in the game is "topic dialogue". Meaning that your character asks questions and the NPC's spew out paragraphs of exposition. I don't care for this kind of dialogue as characters just end up being meat shield/walking lore pamphlets.
I'm not well versed with this regions names, culture and dialects so for me every character blended together with one another. Pretty much no one stood out so I ended up not caring about any of them.
On that note, I don't even care about the main character. From what I saw during my playtime you are some random ♥♥♥♥ with amnesia or whatever who can survive strange emissions but they will gradually harm you until you die so you need to go to the center of the zone in order to find answers. However, since the character you play as has pretty much no personality or backstory or even motive to go into the zone (from what I understand the outside world isn't completely ♥♥♥♥ed up so why couldn't "Scar" just leave if the emissions are so harmful in the zone?) I don't care about him. I don't care about wanting to solve this mystery because the game gives me ♥♥♥♥ all of an incentive to solve it. I just don't care.
Anyway, whenever I play a game for a while to get a good feel for it I sit down and think about the game as to why I'm playing it and why I should continue.
So is the game challenging? Well, no. It is at first, but once you figure out how the mechanics work it stops being challenging and just grows frustrating or tedious.
Does the game have an amazing story? Not really, as I explained above.
Is the game at least a fun time consumer to just waste time in? Not really. The gameworld is pretty barren for the most part and all you find is anomolies and enemies which quickly get repetitive and boring.
Does it at least have an amazing atmosphere to immerse into? Not really. It doesn't feel dark or dreary or anything really. It feels cartoonish if anything.
Like I said, it might just not be the kind of game for me but I can't see any reason to keep playing it. The story never grabbed me, the characters blend together, the world is barren (apart from enemies), the combat gets repetitive and tedious and the atmosphere is lacking.

I still feel this game is one of those rare ones that actually made me truly really care and hate characters in a game. I have felt the same in books (Recently redThe Last WereWolf by Glenn Duncan, and found the romance in it to be very captivating and heartwrenching), in films (Watched the Original Old Dog, and loved it), but games...not that much that I can remember.
And yet, this game actually made me grit my teeth and strain my hands and just wish that this kind of pain and misery portrayed in the game didn't actually exist, and yet has and might always will. I have not played the original, but this game...well, I should do the summary.
You are a investigator for a company in the far off future, and explore a derlict space vessel that once held thousands of people from Korea. But when all are found dead under mysterious circumstances, you interrogate/investigate the AI's of the ship (Either the ships security Mute* or/and Hyun-ae) and find out what happened and why.
One keypoint in the game that I noticed early on is how the AI is protrayed as cartoon characters (an anime cute girl), but all the pictures are of very realistic people. This suggests a very clear design choice by not only the programmer of the game, but the programmers of the ship as well to create a world within the vessel. There are many suggestions that are like that which create a interesting but very strange and discomforting world of lies, politics, and failed romances.
This game does not try to sugarcoat anything from you, as it goes into the lifes of the occupants of the vessel who range from scientists who are trying to work for the betterment of their generation to a pop idol who falls in love with a poor girl. They all branch into other paths and such, but they all come down to one piece of data that is so visible and yet so mysterious that even the character's themselves comment on it.
Another thing that is incredibly refreshing is that the characters themselves comment on the data you read, and show disgust, anger, frustration, enjoyment, embarrasement, and all types of emotions that make them incredibly relatable.
And one thing that makes it so fascinating is that the game actually progresses through three real days; you work one one huge batch of data, and then you are forced to rest for twelve hours before continuing. This creates a incredible plot point in the second day that is so gut punchingly awful to the senses that I actually struggled to not bash the next man's face in due to how it made me feel. But the third day...the third day made the pain smooth over, made me calm down as the AI expresses their own feelings about it as well, creating a rare moment when I actually really cared about what the game told me to do. And no, I bought a pound cake...but I was honest :I.
Do I recommend this game: YES

Perhaps work on a sequel to this where the AI's continue on working with the player character? Just a thought. Even if this is the end, I still highly trust your judgement and writing abilities, and will wait for your next release.

I felt that this game was banking off of the success of the first game because it proves that weird observation where the sequel is always worse than the original.  That said, there are many things in this game that were skimped on when you compare it to the first game.
For instance, no Extras menu.  Not only that, you get the feeling that there should be an alternate route for Mute*.  And the story just felt limited in general.  Like it created loose ends that were never tied together.  It barely explains how the colony ship ends up how it did, with how much pointless filler we had in between obscuring the view.  Hell, and I know this is taking it out of context, but even the AI's were commenting how they failed to see the point of some of the messages.
That said, I suppose you could say that this game is a step up in terms of content + work.  Personally though, I preferred the simplicity from the first because with this new "HD Interactive" edition, you ended up having to scroll one line at a time just to see the character's reactions to the text.  Since I read way faster than that, I can't tell you how many times I wanted to jump paragraph by paragraph instead.
Personally, I'm not a fan of the real-life character portraits.  They clash horribly with the colorful sprites.  Despite that, I do admit that I was somewhat interested in seeing the source material for Hyun-ae and Mute's portraits when they eventually popped up.  Or is it the reverse.
Mm...but, I do have one positive things to say.  Mute is my favorite character.  So I had to get this anyway.
I'd recommend the original, Analogue: a Hate Story.  As for Hate Plus, go in with low expectations.  Appreciate the new layouts and marvel at the decryption animation.  Don't go in hoping for a shocking reveal like in Analogue.  Do that and you should come out without disappointment.

This game is not for everyone. Understand that before you buy. There are some games that might not look all that appealing or interesting to you, let's say Civilization V for example. But play it and you are almost certain to grow to love it. Warband is not one of those games.
Warband is the sort of game where f you don't like it within the first hour of play, you probably won't ever like it. It's a tough game to get into. Do I recommend it? Of course. I just don't think it's for everyone.
It's got some interesting roleplaying elements in it, but because there is no "real" story to it that I have discovered in my 35+ hours (as of writing this), I completely ignore most of the roleplaying and just play the mechanics. I love the army building, I love how the tactics work. It takes time to learn how to properly use tactics, but once you figure it out, it's awesome. With proper execution, you can siege a castle that has a garrison of 200 men with just 40 mid-tier soldiers. You can have a 30 man army hold off a 150 man army in the field, with minimal casualties. That's the sort of gameplay I like.
Characters are one-dimensional at best, simply pawns of the various monarchs. Thankfully the game isn't about people, it's just about you building your warband, so I'll let it slide.
Gameplay is a bit clunky. Menus are a little weird, combat is a bit clunky. This is no Chivalry. Thankfully, the majority of combat outside of tournaments is mostly you giving orders to your troops, so it gets a somewhat of a pass there.
Graphics were never used as a selling point, so I will not be criticizing them. They're not terrible, but they're not beautiful either. What they are good at, however, is making things easily identifiable. You can easily see how terrain is shaped, armors are easy to distinguish from each other, and you can see the arrows coming at you very easily.
So overall, it's a good game. It's just not for everyone. If you are unsure about purchasing this over the sometimes clunky feeling combat and meh appearance, then I would recommend waiting until Mount & Blade II: Bannerlords is released next year. I look forward to conquering that one.

Deponia is a classic point-and-click adventure game in the style of the classic LucasArts adventure games of time long past.  It's a futuristic-type tale that takes place on, you guessed it, Deponia, a toxic world of trash that the upper crust left behind a long time ago to live on the floating city of Elysium.  Rufus, the protagonist, has had enough of living on Deponia, and is actively trying to reach Elysium by any means necessary.  There have already been a few failed attempts by the time the game starts, but this new one is entirely different.
THE GOOD:
THE BAD:
TL;DR If you like a good, classic adventure game and don't mind a little bit of jank, it's a good example of one and is decently funny to boot.  If a lot of minor issues with language, character, and writing will get in the way of you enjoying this game, I can't really recommend it that much.  Personally, I would think that I would be in the second camp, and I spend a lot of time kind of tearing at it for its myriad faults, but I'm ultimately not sorry I played this game.  If you can pick it up for like $5, I'd say go for it.  It's really pretty.
If you want to read more of my thoughts on it, I'll go into some more detail.
The game was developed by Daedalic Entertainment, based out of Germany, and it is immediately obvious that this game wasn't originally written in English.  The lyrics of the singing interludes by the chorus-type character have been cruelly shoved into some kind of rough rhyming scheme, one that I am sure plays a lot better in German.  The subtitles of the translation are also littered with grammatical errors (at one point the subtitles read "motive" where the spoken text correctly reads the line as "motif"), which is a real shame to see because I don't think that hiring a decent editor - one that has a firm grasp of the English language - would be that difficult.  Some of the lines don't play exactly correctly, either, as the voice actors place the wrong emphasis on the wrong word at points.  These are lines which could be read differently in context and it would be a producer or director's job to ensure that they read correctly according to the situation.  In short, the dialogue is a little janky.  Not enough to ruin the experience, but it's there, and if you're as annoying about grammar as I am then it'll bother you too.
Which isn't to say that the VO in the game is bad.  They actually get some decent actors, including Alix Wilton Regan of Mass Effect 3, and more recently Dragon Age: Inquisition fame, and they turn out a great performance.  With what they're given.
There isn't a lot to like about the main characters in Deponia.  Rufus, your protagonist, is kind of a dirtbag.  He gleefully smashes his way through everything in sight trying to reach his goal (and his Goal; the Elysian girl he accidentally knocks out of the sky at the beginning of the game is
this game is not subtle at all) and he just runs roughshod over everyone while proclaiming how brilliant and compassionate he is.  I'll admit, some of his lines are genuinely funny, but over the course of the game I just felt like I was getting hit over the head by how much of a real jerk this guy was.  Even when you, the player, try to choose a dialogue option that's not completely terrible, the person you're talking to basically disregards it and you get railroaded into something awful happening.  And I can understand why it's written that way, because Rufus has some big ol' glaring flaws that he needs to work through for redemption, but in the end I just felt like it was a little much.
The game also has some weird attitudes regarding women.  The receptionist at Town Hall is obviously a man in drag, complete with the transition between super deep voice and high squeaky girl voice that's played for laughs.  In one scene the men of the town all bid to be the one to take the beautiful girl home and "care for her."  Goal herself spends most of the game passed out and is only an object that Rufus has to carry from point A to point B and call his girlfriend without even talking to her.    I don't like the story as much as I could have, for sure.
Deponia is a classically styled adventure game.  Which means you have a gigantic inventory, you pick up everything that isn't nailed down, combine every item with everything else trying to get it to work, and then use every item on every interactable object to try and make the game go.  In an effort to make the game challenging it also has a bad case of adventure game logic, where you have to put things together in a way that doesn't necessarily make sense just to solve the puzzle.  Not only that, in the second major portion of the game you get about four or five different distinct objectives, with no way to track them and no idea where to start.  My advice: walk around, pick everything up, talk to everybody, click on everything.  A lot of progress is gated behind dialogue options too.
If there's one thing I don't have a complaint about, though, it's the graphics.  Everything is fully rendered in a gorgeous hand-drawn art style and there are a lot of little details worked into everything that make it a joy to look at.  They even drew idle animations for Rufus that are pretty fun.  Of course, in the rare instance where an animation doesn't have enough frames it can look a little weird, but that's a pretty minor issue.  The cutscenes are all that and then some, as they incorporate CGI for some of the set pieces to really make them pop out of the screen, to wonderful effect.  You can watch any of these in the Bonus section at any time and they were well worth it.
Ultimately, I would say that the game is worth it, especially if you enjoyed games like The Secret of Monkey Island, Loom, Full Throttle, Grim Fandango... I'd name others than purely LucasArts games but they are just not coming to me right now.  Maybe get it on sale if you're on the fence about it.  I don't know if it's worth full price, honestly.

Basics:
-Essentially a 3D Terraria, with elements from Zelda and Super Mario 64
-More RPG and less pure sandbox
-Very easy to pick up with a built in tutorial
-Quite streamlined
-Quick to get into the action
-Decent amount of content for Early Access
-Core mechanics are all present
-Excellent UI
-Night and Day mechanic
-Plays smoothly once you get used to it
Pros:
-Already very polished with attention to detail
-Very good looking with great particle effects
-Grinding is an enjoyable (not too boring) experience
-Great mix of questing/adventuring and sandbox crafting/building
-Good variety of worlds with corresponding minerals, creatures, etc.
-Boss levels
-Death isn’t so bad, you merely respawn on each island with lower health
-Well done procedurally generated island worlds
Cons:
-Game crashes every once in a while, especially in multiplayer (although it’s quick and painless to jump back into the game)
-Islands could afford to be bigger at times
-No player scripting
-No mechanics for creating items and/or furniture which interacts automatically with the world (no in-game programming of any kind, or player controlled scripting)
-Unable to move while attacking or mining (could be an explicit decision for balance issues)
-VERY basic talent tree (with little to no options to choose from)
-Lack of real item customization
-No weather (as of yet)
-Unable to hold anything on one hand while equipping a weapon on the other (such as a torch in dark places)
-Only 3 classes to choose from: Ranger, Warrior and Wizard
To sum up:
A very delightful experience and well-worth the money, especially if you’re a Terraria fan. Quite impressive for an early access game with all mechanics present and a good amount of content for dozens and dozens of hours of gameplay. Multiplayer (4 co-op max) is very fun, although the group has to constantly stick together and stay in the same world. Would recommend it, because it’s already very fun to play and doesn’t take itself too seriously.
P.S. Not hardcore sandbox enough for serious fans of the genre, and not RPG heavy for those looking for easy adventuring without taking the time to actually mine and harvest materials followed by crafting.

I have played all 3 Sniper Elite's in the series and was excited to learn they are working on a 4th. I have also played the Zombie versions of the game (which I didn't like NEAR as much).
Overall, this is my favorite in the series and it seems as each release gets more and more polished than the last. While I play single player 99% of the time, I have dabbled in the co-op multiplayer and it is fun but I do wish it allowed multiple snipers instead of the sniper/spotter setup currently. I realize this is technically more correct, we, as players, want to play as the sniper and when we are playing as spotter it feels we are just playing nice until our turn.
I really only have a few gripes with the game that I can think of right now.
First: (And this is a big one) you can't set your elevation on your scope. Every person that shoots firearms knows you can set your "zero" on your scope so that it is "dead-on" at a certain distance. Then, you can hold over or under depending on whether the target it closer or further.
Second: This whole series has suffered from what I refer to as the "trigger effect" where enemies don't appear, or certain things happen until you hit a certain trigger. Usually the trigger is reaching a certain place on the map, or killing a certain person, or percentage of enemies. While not as pronounced as it was on the 2nd in the series, nothing like carefully scouting your approach, then moving forward and hitting a trigger point, and have enemies all around you. Often, once I figured out where that trigger point was, I moved forward until I triggered it, then ran back to my sniper nest and clear a path.
Third: Enemies in vehicles see WAY to well. If you have ever been in an armored vehicle or tank, you will know that visibility is NOT their strong point. They should have excellent defense and firepower like they do in real life and do in the game but shouldn't be able to see you near as well unless near an enemy patrol.
Fourth: Inconsistant mechanics regarding long range shooting alarming enemies. I have played the game 250+ hours, and still can't determine whether an enemy will hear my shots at a given place or distance except around broken generators and such. Incidentally, it seems logical that if backfiring generators at your location mask your sounds, you should be able to shoot a generator near the enemy and make it back firing then you could shoot towards him even if you are not by a generator any longer. (does that make sense?)
A few more "mentions" of other things about the game I wish were different.
Why can't we jump in the game?
I wish you could turn off the wind, without turning off elevation. It is harder to "feel" the wind in a game.
I had some occasional issues with the game doing a red flicker when SLI was enabled. This was the only game that ever did that. Normally, just changing the resolution and restarting it fixed it. Ironically, I could alternate between two resolutions and they both worked; AFTER the other one messed up.
Every time you reload your side arm, it goes through the "chambering" animation. Just because you drop the magazine, and put in a full one, doesn't mean the chamber will be empty. Yes, there are a FEW firearms that the magazine is loaded from the top, usually with a "stripper clip" where you would potentially cycle it like that, but aside from the M1 Garand rifle and the Mauser C96 (which I don't remember any in the game), nothing should load like that. For a game that obviously desires for accuracy and realism, it seems like an odd oversight.
Snipers don't fall for thrown rocks, no way to get them to move short of killing them.

With a name like 'Super Crate Box', it can only be expected that the average player is going to start asking questions like 'What is this game about?' 'What do you do in this game?' 'And what exactly is a Super Crate Box?' The answer to the last question there is really quite a simple one: it's the name of one highly enjoyable and highly addictive game.
Super Crate Box is; simply put; a game of survival in the form of a 2D platformer. Confined to a small area consisting of numerous platforms and a fire pit, the player assumes control over what is best described as a gun-wielding, walking box as they traverse the stage collecting boxes that spawn at random locations, all the while avoiding the deadly green walking boxes that drop down from the top of the screen, gradually working their way to the bottom of the stage. Collecting a box earns you a new weapon, which you can then use to blow up, slice in half or otherwise utterly decimate your square-shaped assailants before they get too close. Killing a box often results in the appearance of a ghost, which slowly chases the player around the stage until it is dispatched. In the event that one of the green boxes reaches a fire pit, it will respawn at the top of the stage as a red box and proceed to move through the level in the same manner as before, albeit much faster. Every so often, giant boxes will appear to make the player's life more difficult. These characters move slower, but can withstand a much greater degree of punishment before going down. As with their regular counterparts, the giant boxes are also capable of returning from the grave as red variants of themselves.
As time passes in a level and more and more enemies are allowed to go running about unchecked, the number of red boxes running amok can increase quickly. It's quite something to watch half a dozen giant red boxes cascade down each platform and follow each other to their demise, especially when you're caught in the middle of a stage with the said boxes pouring down on either side of your character.
Should you happen to die (and you
die), the number of boxes you've collected up to that point is reset to zero and you start again. Collecting a certain number of boxes across all your playthroughs will unlock new stages, weapons and characters, though it's worth taking into account that the last of those three is purely for cosmetic purposes.
It's a simple premise, and one that works extremely well. Super Crate Box is the perfect example of a game for the player with little time to spare who's looking to get some hardcore action into their day. The joy of playing a stage over and over again and setting a new record never seems to dissipate, even after dying for the twentieth time. The concept of making the player take 'one last go' has clearly been well-applied here.
Super Crate Box goes for the tried and true retro art style that many indie developers have opted for. While the art style does its job and gives the game the desired feel, it's nothing new. It's been done before countless times, even in cases where the theme of the game doesn't actually mesh well with the chosen art style. Each stage has its own unique BGM track, although it's worth mentioning that almost all of these tracks are monotonous and annoying.
Super Crate Box may not be the deepest platformer around, but its charm is undeniable. Its sheer simplicity and accessibility are what make the game so enjoyable. Ultimately Super Crate Box is a great platformer for anyone looking to spice up their day with a little hardcore platforming action.
