Dead Rising 2 was one of my favorite games back on the Xbox 360, and I spent weeks exploring it with my best friend and enjoying all of the hidden content and sillyness the game could provide.
If I could, I'd take it all away and never have played Dead Rising 2.
Off the Record is just that much better.
Bringing back the old Picture-Taking system from the first Dead Rising but allowing for PP (The in game Experience points) gains through the same means as the original second game really helped to keep me speeding along and brought leveling to a very comfortable pace. As you level up your character becomes stronger and gains more health, but most importantly more inventory slots.
Why is that important? Because there are just so many fun ways to take out a horde of Zombies in Dead Rising 2: Off the Record.  The story falls a bit flat of being something remarkable but the gameplay makes up for it in the sheer joy you can experience when driving a dirt bike with chainsaws duct taped onto it through a street of zombies.
Where this game really shines is in it's cooperative gameplay. A friend can drop in and out at a moment's notice and continue playing the story alongside you. The fun of destroying hordes of zombies and battling pyschopaths was only amplified by having a friend running around alongside you.
For $29.99, it's a hard offer to pass up. But Dead Rising 2: Off the Record should be experienced with a friend.

I don't normally play early access releases for what are probably common reasons many people don't.  I enjoy being able to bite into a finished product with relaxed escapism for hours. After being introduced to Minecraft years ago by a lifelong friend, I've played that sandbox until my eyes bled and have been looking for a refreshing spin on that idea for almost as long. I can't even touch Minecraft anymore in the same way I can't touch Skyrim, it's a want of nostalgia that remains as a crater in my gaming soul. Then came along an ad for Portal Knights on a mainstream gaming site and in spite of my better judgement, because I hate ads, I clicked it and was immediately impressed by the charming visuals, the potential in its combat, and the simplicity of its cubic world and crafting system that too many "Minecraft" clones often convolute.
Now that I have the game I can't recommend it enough. It is an extremely polished opening act for a game that is literally just gettting started. Portal Knights nails its first set of features with a surprising level of polish. The game sets out to deliver to its audience accessible gameplay concepts along with a very handy, but not intrusive tutorial. As opposed to many games of this genre that drop players into its realm with no information, Portal Knights begins with a non-mandatory tutorial. So if you'd like to take a moment to know the basics, it lays out everything for you, while if you prefer to set out and learn along the way you can do that as well.
Crafting is simple with a unique, RPG styled user interface. The music is reminiscent of the original entry of Fable, and the art is just as nostalgic to my eyes. Portal Knight's combat feels like a return to the "Z-Targeting" era of the Legend of Zelda franchise and the interface for this combat system pays direct tribute to that legacy with an HP system managed by "hearts" and a magic system by a mana bar. It expands on its RPG inspired concepts also by allowing players to level up, incease their stats, and develope their characters along a skill tree as they so choose.
Exploring happens by traveling through, well, portals as opposed to wandering through an endless wilderness - but with good reasons. By creating a world of islands, the developers of Portal Knights have created a world that they can easily expand upon without forcing players to explore obscenely long distances through "old version" terrain before they experience new content in coming updates.
In short, by using islands players will sooner encounter new content than by using one massive, solid landmass for exploration - which is a fantastic approach.
As of this writing, I am extremely excited for Portal Knights future. The game is extremely polished, but be warned - it is a proof of concept. It has all it needs to be a functional, enjoyable game but its limited in its current roster of things that players can do before they have done everything. If you're like me and want an early start on what could be the next crafting phenomenon, then jump in to a portal near you.

tl;dr:
if you want your money's worth. Keep an eye out for it, it might be great later.
That is the best assessment that I can with good conscience give this game after playing through all the available content in the few days after early access started.
Portal Knights looks great, sounds pleasant, and the concept had me hooked from the start since I'm a lover of RPGs and Minecraft-like crafting & exploration games.  I'm pleased with the fact that character creation allows for a surprising amount of freedom - even the ability to give female characters facial hair, something I've personally only encountered in one other game so far. The characters are expressive, well animated, and the classically styled armors give them a charming old-timey RPG look but with snazzy up-to-date graphics.
Unfortunately, at this point in development the game doesn't really stand up to scrutiny or prolonged play. There's no story to speak of. Combat isn't quite as fluid yet as it should be. Dodging is very unresponsive, and the disparities between classes are quite stark. Warrior is nigh useless and liable to die more often than kill; sorcerer is the most fun and varied class, but suffers a bit when fighting enemies that are resistant to the type of magic you currently use; and ranger is safe, easy, and incredibly boring since all you do is press one button and dodge sometimes. My biggest gripe with the game at the moment though is the sheer amount of rewardless grind in it. The further you progress, the more apparent it becomes that the new area you found may look a little different - and don't get me wrong, very lovely! - and may have a new resource in it... But the mobs are all the same. Dungeons are always castles with skeletons inside - even in
. Just about every biome has a slime enemy corresponding to the element of the area. This combined with the utterly atrocious grind at high levels - 200 titanium ore just for one bow? - makes the game feel very unrewarding after a while. There's no point in finding the next area if the monsters are going to be exactly the same except maybe with a new skin color and a different spell in their arsenal. The boss fights are a splash of colour in the piling grey sludge of strip mining islands to open up new islands to strip mine. They're mostly fun and I genuinely loved the looks of some of the monsters (that dragon is cute as ♥♥♥♥ okay?), but they, too, suffer from the curse of sameyness as the tactic for winning seems to always be the same: target one of the small things, slap it a bit, and then take some free hits on the boss while it's stunned. The final boss was underwhelming, to say the least: I felt like I had fought regular mobs more difficult than what was supposed to be the climactic encounter.
All in all, if the developers pump a serious amount of content into the game - different monsters and dungeon types, bigger islands, an actual story and a responsive dodge mechanic to start with - this could be an
experience. The game as it is now, on Leap Day 2016, is more like a very compelling sales pitch, a good-looking but empty demo with a baffling amount of "content" that is ultimately just artificial difficulty in the form of grind for materials. I played through it mostly to be able to form an objective opinion of the entire early access game, not necessarily because I found it fun to spend half an hour just looking for some gatdamn titanium. Keep an eye out for this one though, it could end up being a gem once it's finished.

What a game. It's not often I download a game and sit and play through it in one sitting but Brothers, was one of them. It's not a long game by any stretch (2-4 hrs) but, the mechanics and journey it takes you on is well worth the price.
Basically the game is about two brothers who have to journey across the land overcoming obstacles to reach a far off place to find elixir for their father. However, this is where the game breaks from the norm as you have to control both brothers together - at the same time. It sounds incredibly complex and convoluted but is quite possibly, the greatest and most creatively innovative mechanic I have seen employed in a game. It works wonderfully well and the puzzles and obstacles you must overcome whilst controlling both brothers, require both thought and dexterity. None of the puzzles are overly taxing and all require a modicum of brainpower to overcome.
Ultimately, this game is about the journey shared by the brothers and the highs and lows (both euphoric and sad) that they experience throughout. It's different, thought provoking, innovative and affects you on every level due to the genuine emotion generated and shared by the two protagonists. It's simply an incredible game that every gamer should buy and play and I cannot give it any higher praise than that.

I bought this when it was on offer a few years back. It had, like it does now, various DLC included (Hitachi high speed train, test track etc in my case) whch was fun. Imagine my surprise when it upgraded to next release and all the extra bits that came with the game disappeared from the choices available.
Yup! When it upgrades to the new version (which it will automatically unless you tell it not to), you lose access to those extra trains/tracks your version came with. They're still installed (you can see them in the "DLC" section of your library) but you can't use them. And, of course, you can't install the old version to get your content back either.
Similarly, you don't get the new DLC which are listed on the store page for the new version (e.g. the SNCF train in the 2017 version). After the first year, you're left with nothing but the base game and content, and no alternative but to buy DLC again if you want to have the same trains/tracks that you purchased the game with.
Another niggle is that you can only use specific trains on each route so if you want to drive a diesel on the Dorset line, or a freight train on the West Coast line from Paddington to Oxford, you're out of luck. Same track guage, no go on the driving.
The interface isn't great when choosing a train/route combo either. When I was doing a free drive, I managed to confuse the system so much that I couldn't get the list to show all the trains again so I had to restart the game completely.
Other bugs I've found include (but are not limited to):
- Showing trains that, by all accounts are installed, but choosing one of them selects a different train (Big Boy 2-10-0 selected a German train)
- Being able to choose a train and route which you haven't actually purchased but still allowing you to drive the route in the train, but with no scenery (Chatham to Victoria with the HST give you invisible tracks, no grass/bridges/signals etc)
The only improvement I've found in the 2017 release is a major improvement in loading times. I don't now have a chance to make a cup of coffee
This game is listed in the 2017 Guinness Book of Gaming Records as having the most expensive DLC (if you buy all of it). It's already out of date - it's listed as only having about £1300 worth. It's over £3000 now!
To sum up, if you want to simulate driving a train, visit your local model store and start splashing the cash there. At least that way you won't lose stuff that you've paid for when you buy a new train. Alternatively, become a member of your local heritage train line and go down that route - you'll get more satisfaction from it

95% of the bad reviews on here are because of crybabies salty over the fact that they did not get to play the game 10 hours before official release.
Now that the game has been released and patched, it is very playable and is easily the most fun I've had with any fighter, ever, and I am a tournament veteran of MK9 and SF4. It's very easy to get into and yet also very rewarding with fun and smooth combos. The variations system is absolutely excellent, there is certain to be something for everyone to enjoy and it keeps things very fresh. The fatalities and gore are detailed and fun and are joined by the return of brutalities, which are varied and many. The new characters are interesting and most people will like them with the exception of one or two. The game's plethora of online features add quite a lot of replayability and depth to MKX. First are the living challenge towers which change hourly, daily, and weekly. These are excellent for a quick play, and they will even allow you to try out future DLC characters before you buy them. The towers award you koins, which you can use to unlock content such as alt costumes, brutalities, fatalities, concept arts, developer notes, and more in MKX's Krypt - the best Krypt yet in the entire MK series. This particular one is very large and the atmosphere in it is superb. Be warned, though, you will be attacked by creatures while wandering the Krypt. It takes the form of a first-person pseudo-RPG with grid-based exploration; think Legend of Grimrock. When you first start MKX, you will be asked to join one of 5 factions. From this point, everything you do in the game will earn you faction experience, unlocking cool rewards such as faction fatalities, of which there are 5 for each faction. Each of these faction fatalities can be done by all characters in addition to their normal fatalities, provided you are a member of that faction. Online, players can participate in 3v3 and 5v5 faction battles, in which the teams battle each other in an attempt to defeat all 3 or 5 of their team's players first to claim victory for their faction. Netcode-wise the online is very much improved over MK9 or Injustice. I have noticed far less input delay and no dropping thus far.
Overall, I would say that this is easily the best MK ever, and if you are even remotely interested in the series you would be doing yourself a great disservice were you to miss it.

If you played Analogue: A Hate Story and liked it, you'll probably like Hate Plus, as it's largely more of the same, though with greater emphasis on politics (being the story of how the Mugunghwa got to be the way it was), and it's mostly *Mute's story instead of *Hyun-ae's (though she still has plenty to do on her route). If you haven't played Analogue, then I don't know what you're waiting for, go do that. You might still like Hate Plus though, if you're into feminism, political thrillers, and visual novels, since Hate Plus can stand on its own decently. Either way, it's an excellent game and I highly recommend it to anyone looking for something different and thought-provoking, though do be advised that, due to the subject matter, a big slew of trigger warnings apply. If you can stomach it, it's worth a look.

Like it's predecessor Analogue, and Digital before it, this game aims to tell a compelling story while conveying a powerful message about society, and it succeeds on all accounts. Hate Plus delves more into the socio-economic side of the story than it's predecessor, and as a result it reads much like a political drama.
This game not only tells the story leading up to Analogue, but it puts that story in a broad and powerful socio-political environment that is as thought-provoking as it is entertaining.

Hate Plus picks up where Analogue: A Hate Story left off and continues expanding on the backstories and society of AIs *Hyun-ae and *Mute that may not have been so clear in the original game.
First and foremost, Christine Love's writing has improved leaps and bounds from the original game. There's a much sharper focus on fleshing out both characters and how the changes in the world directly and indirectly impacted their existences. Navigating through logs and the myriad of often confusing Korean names is made much easier thanks to a cleaner interface that features cross-linked profiles and portraits of the key players in the story.
There's no reason not to grab Hate Plus if you enjoyed Analogue. It's a much richer and fulfilling experience, and all the loose ends come together as they should.
If you don't buy it you obviously hate cute AI girls and want them all to die.

If you played Analogue and enjoyed it, there is no need to explain why you should get Hate Plus - the ultimate answers of what happened on the Mugunghwa spaceship are to be discovered here, especially about *Mute's past. And don't forget to get ready for some cakes or other things with your waifus. Soundtrack is as excellent as the one of Analogue.

Played for a few hours during a free weekend.
The game plays well from a controls point of view. The quick menu is smooth, you have shortcuts for switching weapons, covering and vaulting are responsive. The only part that seems off is sprinting where you can't easily change direction.
There's an element of customization where you can choose your loadout before every mission. Weapons and items unlock as you progress through the campaign, or by gathering collectibles and doing optional quests. You can even upgrade your rifle, though the stock rifle with the stock parts seems the most balanced.
The graphics are good, although I find the sunlight overly white. There's also some weird pixelation when light shines through the leaves of a tree.
Killing any enemy will probably result in a kill cam that traces the path of the bullet all the way to the enemy and through them. They're gory, fun, but repetitive. Fortunately you can skip them. Sometimes they look a bit blurry, especially the bone fragments and the blood.
The game feels very easy. With the enemy difficulty set to the highest level, you can't help but feel overpowered. The AI is simply dumb. You can pick enemies one by one as long as you relocate between shots. They'll instantly forget that you wiped half their base if they can't see you anymore. Even exploding oil barrels next to them won't hold their attention for long. At many times I had enemies look right at me and have them take a good 3-4 seconds before they even start thinking of shooting me. In that time you can easily switch weapons, miss a shot or two and take your time to line up a headshot.
In the end, I recommend the game because it's fun. You can choose to go stealthy and take enemies from behind without getting noticed, or you can shoot everything in sight with little to no consequences due to poor AI. It's a good way to spend a lazy weekend, but it's not a game to commit yourself too. Compared to Ghost Warrior (the first one), this game feels polished.

9.5/10 Wow, what a great game.  Do yourself a favor and get this.  Finally, something that drew me in and took me somewhere.
I get tired of uninspired level design in overly dreary locations, uninspired characters, weak stories, and shallow endings.  This game has none of that!  It starts off simple and innocent (at first I was concerned this would be too much the case), but as you progress everything just gets deeper and more interesting.
Level design: Truly beautiful and inspiring.  Locations are meaningful and contribute to the development and exposition of the characters.  The graphics engine runs silky smooth and the emphasis is on artistry over hardware specs. For me, I also saw amazing (but subtle) symbolism in the locations and experiences the brothers go through that really adds to the depth of the story concept and characters.
Story: Brilliant, not just because of the plot itself, but because of it's method  of delivery.  I was hooked from the start, and half way in or so it really takes off and gets you invested in the characters and their mysterious world.  And just like a good story, it continues to build all the way to a climactic end.  The characters grow and evolve in response to their environment.  You really experience this world with the same sense of intrigue and wonder that the 2 young boys do.  I would LOVE a full-blown action-RPG in this setting.
Gameplay: It kind of reminds me of older games in that the controls are simple in terms of what they literally are, but they get used in various ways throughout.  Controlling 2 characters at once is an interesting idea, but the true genius is the way that the gameplay mechanics are actually used to help tell the story and develop the characters.
Puzzles: They are not hard, but they are enjoyable and more importantly -- meaningful.
Game Length: Fairly short.  I don't like to rush it, so I've got about 9.7 hours into it the first run through (although I think it counts all the time I paused it and stepped away).  Totally worth it, and I will definitely do another replay.
Conclusion:   A wonderful little masterpiece.  Buy it.  Now.  And even if it seems too "young" for you at the beginning, trust me, it won't by the end (in a good way).  Be sure to interact with everything if you want to get the full story, and have fun!

Everyone should play this at least one time through. This short, yet powerful tale, is truly a masterpiece.

Hate Plus is a direct continuation of Analogue:  A Hate Story, both in story and feeling of the game.  I was a bit worried that the wait between days would be a little... gimmicky, for lack of better word, but it honestly works, as trying to power through this much powerful but depressing storytelling would most likely be extraordinarily difficult to do.
While it's not as if it takes a great deal to impress me, I found the writing and characters to be well done, along with their interactions with either you or each other.  There's a great deal of both comedy and tragedy put into this game; I found it to be a good experience to play through.
If you enjoyed Analogue, you'll want to pick this game up.  If you've never played Analogue, I'd really recommend to start with that, as it will really help you enjoy this one.  Overall, it's a good game and excellent continuation of the last.

If you are a Fan of visual novels this one is a must. Continuing only a few days after the first game this installment tells you about the *Mute, the other ships security AI as well as what exactly happened to cause the downfall of the ship

The sequel to Analogue: A Hate Story, Hate Plus attempts to answer the question everybody in the world has been asking for their entire lives:  "HOW did the generation ship Mugunghwa degenerate into a restrictive patriarchal society reminiscent of Korea's Joseon Dynasty?"
And it delivers.
Picking up right where Analogue left off, you play as an investigator  drifting through space with your AI companions, reading through recently uncovered logs written by those living on the Mugunghwa during its early days. As the story unravels motivations that originally were assumed to be pure evil are are revealed to be almost anything but.
With Christine Love's typical wit and about double the length of the original, it's well worth a purchase if you have finished the original.
Now I've got to go bake a real-life cake for *Hyun-ae because that's an actual achievement and I am a weak, weak man.

(Note: Hate Plus is a game that encourages at least three playthroughs, due to three separate starting conditions that will determine dialogue throughout the game. I have only played through once as of now.)
I enjoyed Hate Plus. This isn't really a surprise as I love Digital: A Love Story and Analogue: A Hate Story. -- Hate Plus is a direct sequel to Analogue: A Hate Story and it's HIGHLY HIGHLY recommended that if this game interests you, that you play Analogue first. To highlight the connection - the game does have an option to start a fresh new game, and it will ask you some questions to determine how the game starts. OR,  you can simply load one of your Analogue cleared game save files (as in, the save file created when you beat the game) and depending on the ending of that save game, it will "start" (continue your Analogue game) with the information from your Analogue game.
So, Hate Plus is not too different from Analogue as far as game play. You're still researching the Mugh...spelling...the history of the ship via reading log files and interacting with either/boith of the AI from the ship, as you read through the logs. It is a visual novel, so reading reading reading! If you dislike reading, then don't bother. If you dislike themes of sexuality, don't bother - they're more highlighted in this than they are in Analogue. "Hate" being in the title - and hopefully having played Analogue - you'll continue to read logs dealing with mature themes that can be rather dark. The overall story may not (or may??) be dark and unhappy, but the history of the ship and the lives you read about are filled with tragedy. But not without a reason. Christine (I've incorrectly wrote her name as Christina in the past  >.>) Love is not simply writing dark ficttion or - at times - semi-erotic fiction just because. It all ties into larger issues and themes that deal with real world issues and problems. Whether it's sexism, classism, homo or transphobia, socio-political and cultural issues, and the list goes on. It's a rather serious examination of quite a lot of things, so don't let it being a visual novel trick you into thinking it's fluff, or that the more sexual/erotiic parts are simply to add sex to the story.
Hate Plus adds one gameplay feature that is both interesting and frustsrating - depending on how you decide to handle it and .. how much per sitting you want to play it in the first playthrough. There is a game mechanic added that ties into something in the story that forces you to "shut down" the computer of your ship after reading so many logs (has to do with the power supply of your ship.) At that point, you will see a screen with a 12 hour, real time, countdown and you will be unable to play that save file until 12 hours have passed. This is neat to me in that I find the concept rather intersting - you're on a 3 day journey and you can only read so many logs a day due to your ships power supply. Both you (the character) and the AI are anxious to read more but cannot. So this concept not only makes the game more "real time" but it also creates - for the person enjoying the game - that same feeling of "I want more now!" ---- the downside,  of course, is .. wanting more now. Hate Plus is like. really good. Analogue was a well written cool little game, and Hate Plus is a good companion, and the 4th wall breaking stuff in the game to try and align you more with the character you're playing is interesting and surprisingly well done, even if the wait between days is a tiny bit irritating. Also the trailer song is pretty funny and some of the achievements are amazing. Send in that cake picture. Do it.

This is the sequel to Analogue: A Hate Story which was a politically charged tale wrapped in the framework of a science fiction visual novel complete with cute Anime companions.
You don't need to have played Analogue to play Hate Plus but I would strongly recommend doing so as it gives you context for what happened to the world the AI came from and in particular really goes into depth about the character Hyun-ae.
Where the first game was Hyun-ae's story, this game is Mute's story. It's just as politically charged, probably even more so, and deals with the biggest mystery from Analogue, which was how a modern society reverted to conservative Neo-Confucianism ideals. If you're not familiar with Asian culture at all the nearest Western equivalent I can think of would probably be The Handmaid's Tale. This game deals with the events that lead up to that big change.
If it sounds serious, it is. And it isn't. It's all told through the personal journals and political council meeting minutes. In particular there several different people whose stories you follow over a series of years and get to see how the subtle and not so subtle changes to their society affect them.
There are also some really fun, light hearted moments with the AI companions including one where you are asked to bake a cake. In real life with a real recipe and then further are encouraged to take a picture of your cake with your companion and send it to the developer to get an achievement. It's all real and I have the achievement to prove it. It was a refreshingly fun meta moment to the game and there are a few others as well like a when the AI cheekily break the fourth wall at rare moments.
There are three main paths which in turn lead to multiple different endings depending on the choices you made. While the texts you read through are the same, the tone and the events that happen with your AI companion(s) are completely different so it really is worth playing through each of the 3 paths at least once.
The game takes place what's supposed to be a small spaceship that you, the space investigator, are on with your AI companion on a 3 day trip back to Earth where you both try to piece together the mystery of the Mugunghwa (the ship that Analogue took place on).
Each path is divided into 3 days where on each day you can only extract a certain number of logs before the ships battery is drained and needs to be recharged requiring you to wait 12 hours. So yes the game does ask you to play the game in installments over the course of 3 days. However there is a way out where once you power down and save you can hover your mouse over that save file, hit the 'S' key and then continue. Note if you do this you cannot get one of the achievements though.
Another alternative is to play day 1 of one path, then day 1 of the other, then day 1 of the 3rd, then 12 hours+ later do day 2 path 1, day 2 path 2 etc. This is what I ended up doing. I think it works well and gives a nice immediate contrast between the differing paths.
One of the changes in Hate Plus is you now get hyper links when people's names are mentioned that gives an image (in realistic art style) of the person with a commentary description from the AI. This made a big difference for me personally as I not only was able to keep track of the names better but also felt like I connected with them more.
Another change is that the AI are reading the logs in Hate Plus for the first time along with you and you get their reactions and commentary that really run the gamut. Even when going back through the documents you already read for the other paths you'll want to scroll through all of it to get the AI reactions because they do differ for each path.
If you do all the paths the game should take somewhere between 9-12 hours, which may vary depending upon how slow/fast of a reader you are, how much time you spend to stop and bake a cake, etc.
Overall I would highly recommend Hate Plus to anyone who enjoyed Analogue, has in interest in visual novels or is just looking for a strongly story oriented game.

Review Time: I've got about 48 hours of game play logged and I have to say the game is pretty good. I got into PC gaming around era of the first Call of Duty and Battlefield 1942. If your Battlefield 1942 or Vietnam fan this game is right up your alley, I myself have been waiting a long pretty log time for another game to come out with that general type of game platy. Massive Online Multiple player game, with top notch graphic. I'm running dual GTX 770, and Asus 32 inch Gaming Monitor and the HD detail from guns, uniforms, maps, and vehicles are super impressive, topped off by effects of explosions and fire. WHooooo! HOWEVER, you don't need a massive gaming rig to play this game, I actually find the game more enjoyable with moderate to low graphics depending on the map. The reason for this the graphics are so detailed its a lot for your eyes to take in at one time. Dumbing down the graphic as I call it, makes it easier to see everything going on. Trust me at times it can be a lot. The game has around 20 maps, city, factory, airfield, to open country with farm type housing. The maps can be played at the break of dawn with hazy fog rolling across the battlefield, mid-day or at night. On the larger assault maps, the three factions are divided up across the map, each holding points. Majority of the battles are with two factions pairing off and last 15 to 30 minutes, with one faction defending to main spawn locations with the other factions assault the map from one or two locations. The offensive team, has a main deployment area and has to take multiple spawn points, defend and push on to the next point. The game is one when one team or the other defends or holds all spawn points, or occurs enough team points, or completely kills off the other team.
If your looking to jump into driving tanks or flying right away, you'll have to hold your horses. There is a small progression in the game you will have to endure. Everyone starts out as infantry, as you make rank with your character and award ribbons you unlock upgrades for your character. I learned early on, to pay attention to the ribbons awarded, understand what you have to accomplish to unlock your next upgrade.
Progressing forward with your infantry character you will unlock the other type of soldiers in the game. You will have to purchase these characters for each factions with in game credits or using real money to purchase Gold. The other class are as followed: Paratrooper, basically is infantry guy that spawns in a transport aircraft flying over the battlefield. Your able to select your drop zone by the third person you view, and jump out of the plane when your ready by pressing "E". The next unlock I believe is Recon, these guys are your typical snipers, and defenders, also can be used to assault depending on how your progress you character. You start out Recon with bolt action rifle with a scope. After Recon comes your Tankers, so far this has been one of my favorite classes. I spent several years playing World of Tanks, so I know the tanks very well and super excited to see which tanks they put into the game. So far each iconic tanks like the Sherman Easy 8, Hellcat, Persian the German Leo, Panther, Tiger and Hetzer live up to the legends they were on the battlefield for you WWII buffs. I've personally have run through the German class and the American Tank lines from private up to LT on both characters. I love cruising around, and setting up ambush for enemy tanks with my squad mates. Assault spawn points, with the mounted machine guns and shredding through troops. Careful though, every class in the game can wreck your world from anti tank mines, bazookas, sticky bombs, and those OG pilots who set up strafing and bombing runs. You can guess what the next class to unlock is Pilots. I have yet to play a pilot, they are pretty prices with in game credits, and I've been having way to much fun in tanks to even attempt to move on. I have made a few friends who are pilots in the game and they say it takes a minute to get use to flying. However once you get half way descent at it, you make tons of in game credits, and is loads of fun. I've also seen on the forums a few people complain that they spent Gold on buying pilot, only to get sick playing the character and begging for a refund. Don't know if that's good or bad. However the dog fighting over the battle and seeing a plane go down in flames is amazing. Specially in dusk or night battles and seeing all the AA going off and planes trying dual it out, while dodge enemy fire all at the same time. The next class or rank is the Generals. Which is a whole other aspect of the game that have yet to dive into. Basically how Generals works is once you either grind a character up to the rank General or purchase a General using gold. (Buy Gold with Real Money!) You can go on the EU map and range war with your faction and try to take over Europe. Wars typically last 5 to 7 days until one of the factions either take over the map, or time runs out and the map is reset. To my understanding the way war works is, you as player select your factions you wish to enter the war with. You as General choose your troops to assault the the town or the map with. Depending on the troops you select, players will queue for that match and fight the battle. Those battles are pretty much the same as assault maps, depending on what troops a general has at his disposal, is what's enter in the battle. Some battles can be extremely lopsided or pretty even. Again I haven't made it to rank of General yet, however I have fought in several "War Elite" battles. It is very cool concept... although I feel if you jump straight into Generals with out doing a little research on how to run a battle and have idea of what works and doesn't work. You could cause a lot of heartache for your faction, loosing a lot of ground or even the war. If you ever played the game MAG for PS3, they had similar concept with Squad leaders, Platoon leaders, Company Commanders, and Battle Commanders, except on a much larger scale.
Pros: Graphics, Wide Variety of guns and vehicles for every class. Large Maps. A lot of fun to be had with friends working together to take spawn point. Game play is smooth, and has a very classic, old school feel to it. Once you get the hang of the game, is a loads of fun.
Cons: Players not use to these type of games may feel over whelmed. Players who play the newer style first person shooters may feel that the game does not progress fast enough at first. Large Maps, if your on foot, or select the wrong spawn point, you could be on foot for a while. Playing the game at max graphics can make the screen very busy and hard to see enemy troops. In game directions for starting out and learning the game are non existent. You will have to refer to website. Due to graphics and the old school play of the game most player will struggle at the start of the game, due the game play is similar but not the same as the new era shooting games. Queue for games on average is around 2 minutes and up to 10 minutes for War Elite depending on what class character your trying to queue.

If you are new to fighting games or have simply enjoyed recent ports to PC, Tekken 7 may seem much ado.   If you've been playing fighting games for a long time, it's much ado about nothing.  That said, I would rather give a neutral opinion than dislike.  Between dislike and like, I gotta go with dislike.
Compared to Injustice 2 (on PS4 Pro @ 4k w HDR), Tekken 7 pales in comparison, lacking features included on day one with I2.   Visually Injustice 2 looked superior on my PS4 Pro to Tekken 7 on my  PC @ 4k/60 fps/ultra.   Lots of low-res and muddy textures pollute the graphics of Tekken 7.
Arcade mode can be finished in a few minutes, probably even fewer if you play it on easy.    Story mode is meh with no VO localization.   As with most fighting game, developers cheap out on animations.  It gets so old so fast hearing the same lines at start/finish.
Online is decent, but Injustice 2 is so much better with far more to do.
The SP is a joke.   Harada says they need the money to continue support--rubbish.  Be honest or say nothing.  Don't lie.  Most of the costumes, for example, are already done.  They were in the original arcade game, but have been removed for DLC/SP.
Call me jaded, but other fighting games at launch (such as T5, T6, SC4, DOA 4, etc.) seemed so superior to Tekken 7.
Different experience bring different expectations.   For PC gamers starved for day one releases, I can see the appeal of Tekken 7.   For those of us with less shallow experiences, Tekken 7 is meh.   It ain't awful by any means, but it's lacking a lot of meat on its bones.

I first played DR2 as a free game though the Xbox 360's Games with Gold program. I would end up getting over 30 million PP. Unfortunately, the PC versions of DR2 and OTR use Games For Window Live, but I won't take points off for that. The Arkham games had used them for so long and just recently have been released with clean versions.
Dead Rising 2 improves on all fronts where Dead Rising 1 left off. It introduces combo weapons, which are a more efficient way to get PP to level up than saving survivors alone. The AI of the survivors is no longer frustrating, they can defend themselves better than ever and follow directions. Granted they're not quite AS smart in Off The Record on PC compared to DR2 vanilla on PC, but OTR has check points. There are a few psychopath bosses, they adjusted the survivor roster, there's more combo cards and a whole new section of the map called Uranus Zone. That whole part of the map was under construction in DR2 vanilla.... so lead it to Capcom to make you buy the game twice to play the full game just like Street Fighter IV. There's a lot to hate about Capcom since Resident Evil 5 came out, but I love DR2 and Off The Record in the definitive version here on PC. I love the time management, the frantic decisions and scheduling you have to do to rescue as many people as possible. The PP (Prestige Point) gives it arcade fun and I find myself still playing DR2 after reaching the max level of 50. I can't get bored of this game. If I start playing I gotta keep going until I reach a point where after I save it'll be a book marked time in the story of a playthrough.
Dead Rising gets my vote for the most improved series since 2005. DR1 was a frustrating game, a 360 exclusive with an antiquated save system. DR2 improved everything and added so much more, then Off The Record raised it as if the Chuck Greene game was incomplete. I really wish DR3 wasn't an XB1 exclusive. I'm done with consoles, love live Steam! You should've have to buy extra hardware for segregated limited platforms. Resident Evil series get's worst fall from grace since Resident Evil 4 topped off the series in 2005.

You gotta play the game like a speed run as much as you can and take every advantage with you including combo weapons, skill books and mixed drinks. Don't play it dumb and you'll be alright.
After playing the hell out of DR2 on 360, I completed OTR on PC within 3 days without having to restart the story. I went from level 1-42 in my first playthrough.

I picked this up with a Humble Bundle recently, and was excited to try it out.  My wife and I had played Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance together pretty extensively, and had a lot of fun.  Since Dark Alliance, I've not had a lot of luck finding co-op fantasy RPGs in a similar vein (and we were too late to get DA2, unfortunately).  More recently, we've been playing D&D together with some friends, but scheduling has been a pain (being grown-up sucks..), and Eon Altar synergizes nicely with that, too.
We're only an hour in, but this game is scratching both itches marvelously, and we can't wait to log another hour tonight.
The RPG components are inspired, in my opinion.  The game will deliver secret knowledge to certain players in certain situations, and allow them to make private decisions, without the other players necessarily knowing what is going on.  In addition, the players get to voice their character's dialogue, which is nice practice for D&D, and adds an element of "party game" fun.
Overall, I can't recommend this game enough, particularly at the price-point.  Now I am wondering how I can go about getting a scenario/game editor, so I can start creating my own stories in this engine...

Bought Episode one on release, and played through it with 3 friends shortly thereafter. Found it to be great fun, but a bit rough around the edges.
Just played through episode 2 and 3 with those same friends. We have all really enjoyed the experience together and it feels quite a bit nicer than on release.
The stats are minorly confusing, as a lot of them aren't directly explained in game, but can be figured out pretty easily through play or a quick google if you're into min maxing your characters, but you can play perfectly fine without specifically learning about them.
The story is fine, interesting enough if you want to follow it, for a single player experience is probably lacking a little compared to other titles. The real fun comes from playing with your friends, having personal quests/motives that you can either share with each other to try to complete, or not tell them and just do your option (some party members have conflicting quests).
Performance could be better, it plays fine, but considering my system I would expect higher fps, its not an issue at all though as it doesnt require high fps and animations etc still look smooth.
It could not be played locally without using phones for controllers, and after an inital "how the hell does this work" it feels perfectly fine and works pretty well. Giving you your personal trackers, thoughts and motivations, as well as dialogue to interact with NPC's or each other. We have all upgraded our phones since our first stint on the game, so have used it across 6 android and 2 iOS devices with no issues.
For a full party which includes a healer/tank and two dps, the game could be harder. We played on standard difficulty, and the majority of fights were cake, no strategy or co operation beyond just vaguely knowing what your class is meant to be doing.  But then there were certain fights, and boss fights, that required actually using teamwork and buffs etc. Just would prefer more of the standard fights to be a bit tougher so as to still require teamwork. Although due to how easy a lot of fights can be, and everyone wanting to murder everyone, it does create some fun "dont charge in im going to AOE them...oh, you're dead...But I GOT 8 KILLS!!!" moments :D
If playing through again, we will probably up the difficulty to maximum for more challenge, but it obviously depends on how you want to play.

Sequel to "Analogue: A Hate Story." Continues where the previous game left off (you can even import your save data from it.) The gameplay has been reworked, being more streamlined than the previous game. The AI characters will give their thoughts as you read through each message, rather than having to switch to them. There's also portraits and summaries of characters that you'll read about, which is a great addition. The story focuses heavily on character relationships and political struggles. You can theoretically play this without having played the first, but you will miss out on a lot (especially if you want to get all of the different endings.) Took me ~6 hours to get through the story once (although the game is split in 3 segments and each segment is supposed to be played with 12 REAL-TIME hours in-between.) Highly recommend playing both games if you're into interactive visual novels.

I'm going to help squash some of the negativity that wanders the reviews.
First off, for those who think it's boring, you don't get the point of a simulator. This is to SIMULATE running a full size train over many miles, taking in to account weather, tonnage, horsepower, braking power, grade percantage, speed, and timing. If that isn't your thing, don't buy it. You want to just run trains? Go buy TANE.
Yes I'm aware there are many DLC, you have to take into account that some of these have been around since the beginning of the simulator when it was still Railworks, so as time moves on, the content has improved over the years. Plus there is a variety of locomotives and routes, the object isn't to buy them all, just buy what interests you. For me, it's US railroading, 40's to 50's. Plus there are many free engines and cars, just have to look depending on what you are looking for.
Of course there are bugs, I don't know of a single game or simulator that doesn't have any bugs. Just report what you find.
People report having FPS issues: Simple, upgrade your computer. Before you whine about "shouldn't need to upgrade a computer to run a program," tell me then what the definition of "progress" and "technology advancement." My computer runs the game on highest settings with no issues.
I've been running train simulators since 2001 with the release of MSTS, then spent many years with the Trainz franchise from 03 to 12, then went to Railworks from there to now. During that time I've seen many advancements in the train sim world, I work on a real railroad and nothing else can compare overall like Train Simulator 2017*
*Yes I know TSW will be released this year, however with no backwards compatability, I doubt I'll make the change anytime soon.

If you are new to fighting games or have simply enjoyed recent ports to PC, Tekken 7 may seem much ado.   If you've been playing fighting games for a long time, it's much ado about nothing.  That said, I would rather give a neutral opinion than dislike.  Between dislike and like, I gotta go with dislike.
Compared to Injustice 2 (on PS4 Pro @ 4k w HDR), Tekken 7 pales in comparison, lacking features included on day one with I2.   Visually Injustice 2 looked superior on my PS4 Pro to Tekken 7 on my  PC @ 4k/60 fps/ultra.   Lots of low-res and muddy textures pollute the graphics of Tekken 7.
Arcade mode can be finished in a few minutes, probably even fewer if you play it on easy.    Story mode is meh with no VO localization.   As with most fighting game, developers cheap out on animations.  It gets so old so fast hearing the same lines at start/finish.
Online is decent, but Injustice 2 is so much better with far more to do.
The SP is a joke.   Harada says they need the money to continue support--rubbish.  Be honest or say nothing.  Don't lie.  Most of the costumes, for example, are already done.  They were in the original arcade game, but have been removed for DLC/SP.
Call me jaded, but other fighting games at launch (such as T5, T6, SC4, DOA 4, etc.) seemed so superior to Tekken 7.
Different experience bring different expectations.   For PC gamers starved for day one releases, I can see the appeal of Tekken 7.   For those of us with less shallow experiences, Tekken 7 is meh.   It ain't awful by any means, but it's lacking a lot of meat on its bones.

Dead Rising 2: Off the Record is basically an updated and better version of Dead Rising 2.  As a game on it's own, it is very fun and engaging as it allows you to unravel the story in the game or simply mess around with anything that surrounds you.  During your time in the game you encounter bosses known as psychopathes every now and then.  While the world you play in is plauged by zombies, the real threat is the people, and battling these psychos prove to be very difficult when you are not prepared to take them on.
Compared to Dead Rising 2, the main difference is the story; instead of playing as Chuck Greene, who needs to find zombrex for his daughter and trying to clear his name from being framed during the outbreak, you play as Frank West who tries to uncover the incident behind the outbreak.  Gameplay wise, the two games are mostly the same, but OTR pulls it off somewhat better, as it has a sandbox mode that replaces DR2's TIR (Terror is Reality) Contests, fine-tuned game mechanics and a photography mode that originates from the first Dead Rising game.  If you've already played Dead Rising 2 you won't find yourself playing a completely new game.  If you haven't though, then this version is the better version.  Both versions support co-op, but the two games cannot intercommunicate with eachother, so if you're planning to play with a friend, make sure he owns the same version as you do or plan to get.  The only reasons you would own both DR2 and OTR is that you are interested in the changed game mechanics and story, manage to pick up DR2 complete for a great price, or simply because you know Frank West has covered wars, you know.

In
you simultaneously control two brothers on a quest to acquire some magical medicine to heal their ailing father. Their journey is visually stunning with detailed environments and well-executed set pieces. It is also rather brief, taking about 3-4 hours to complete.
The gameplay is unique; you use two separate analog sticks to control the two brothers from a roughly overhead perspective. The games’ puzzles generally involve the brothers needing to use their individual strengths in a complementary way and cooperating to overcome an obstacle. For instance, the bigger brother will hoist the little brother up a ledge, and the little brother will then lower a rope.
Despite its originality, the gameplay leaves something to be desired. The difficulty of both the puzzles and the controls plateaus early on, and instead of pushing the boundaries of controlling two characters,
is content to just scratch the surface.
The plot is very simple, even for such a sort game. The characters speak in a fictional language with no subtitles, so the content of in-game dialogues are left for you to extrapolate based on the characters’ gestures and tone of voice. I found myself growing a little weary of the gibberish words after a while, but it was a good stylistic choice for this game.
’ achievement is storytelling. Every aspect of the game (the art, gameplay, music, pacing, etc.) is in support of a central theme to which it is very committed. The plot may simple and the puzzles are same-y, but in a way
uses those flaws as a strength; it leaves more of your attention open to play around, to observe the character development and the brothers’ personality differences, and to admire the scenery.
Overall a truly wonderful experience which I keep thinking about even weeks after completion. Highly recommended for those interested in storytelling through video games!

As ARPG's go, the great contenders, as in the games in this category people usually talk about are, as of date, Diablo 3, Path of Exile and Torchlight 2. They all serve their respective niches and some people are unhappy about one or two (or three) of them that other people just go crazy for. That's fine, that's the internet, that's life, that's opinion.
I'm the guy that goes crazy for Torchlight 2.
Like all great ARPG's, the story is there for flavor purposes, it not something you pay close attention to and, lets be honest, it plays out like Diablo 2 to a fault (no suprises there, considering the makers). All that stuff about the Dark
Alchemist, roaming the world, looking and finding power for some goal plays exactly like you'd expect it to. It's a vehicle, a decent, middle range, reliable one. Used.
But what it provides you with it's a way to stomp, bash, explode, [insert prefered method of destruction here], your way through hordes of enemies without making you feel you're a crazy person on a homicidial rampage through the native flora, fauna and other the bits. And you get loot for it. Lots of it. Gives you loot like it's Christmas (or any other  holiday you're into, nothing wrong with that).
It offers 4 distinct classes that never feel samey or that you're gonna play one like the other. Even in those classes there are multiple ways you can play them. This is pretty much standard in ARPG's (or it should be / feels like it is), but it should be said regardless.
The game also allows you to go for the hardcore experience right off the bat too, a major plus for me, but if you're into the casual side of games, it lets you do that too, no questions, no issues with you playing like that. Example: it doesn't give you less loot or lesser loot for it.
Mod support is, for some, the cherry on the cake, plucked from the cherry tree of the gods (or something). It's not something I'm into but I acknowledge that it improves the expiration date immensely, giving you new tools, stuff, enemies, even classes or a whole new game.
Graphically speaking, we're talking about a cel-shaded affair, it doesn't look half bad all things considering but some people might be put off. It does the job well enough. Me? I love it. Soundwise? Diablo 2. Period. Love it too.

I don't know why steam users are becoming bigger and bigger crybabies about things that couldn't matter less. I remember when you read these reviews and got funny jokes about gameplay or insightful information about the actual game you're buying. On this title in particular I see a lot of, "has dlc so it's bad" reviews, what the hell honestly is the point of that? How are you helping, really?
TL;DR - I'd say the game is a firm 7 or 8/10 with a little over 6 hours played I feel like I'm a decent chunk of the way into the game. The sound and music is excellent, the inside-jokes you expect from a title like this are great and the combat is surprisingly enjoyable.
Actual Review:
I was hesitant to buy the game at first because I was shocked it had mixed reviews, a lot of the primers and preview info I saw pointed to this game being a great followup to the Stick of Truth. It's a good thing I checked out some Youtube reviews so I could see some legitimate information about the actual game because that's what caused me to buy it (and subsequently enjoy the hell out of it, shout out to ACG's channel). In the beginning there's a mild full-screen snafu that you work around by hitting alt+enter (something PC veterans should know by now, it's pretty damn common) and it'll bring you into windowed mode, once you set up all your visual options though it fixes itself and the issue hasn't come back. As far as bugs go, I haven't run into a single one yet past the first launch's intro being blank.
Day 1 DLC - I know this is a recent development in gaming and a real point of contention to some, but I don't really understand it in most cases. This whopping five dollars is an optional addon to the game that in no way makes or breaks the experience, you don't like it - don't buy it, it literally effects you in no way past that. I think people see DLC and their blinders go on immediately, god forbid a content developer wants to push out some extra content. I feel like a lot of people don't understand development cycles and how game releases work, you got the full game when you bought it, this stuff is extra - and not even necessary.
Microtransactions - I've seen this brought up in a ton of reviews on Steam, there are no microtransactions in this title. I realize a lot of you hate Ubisoft for 'insert bandwagon hate reason here' but the "currency" that Ubisoft's launcher utilizes is given to you based on your achievements in games that you play that uses the Ubisoft launcher. Getting a reward and a little something extra for playing a game, I remember this concept from long, long ago but maybe some of you are too young to remember playing a game to unlock secrets / extra stuff, etc. You can look like an iron man ripoff for taking a couple dumps in toilets in about 20 minutes and have nearly every unlockable paid for with the in-game currency. If anything this is how achievements should be handled, it gives you a legitimate reason to go and do something extra you might not normally do in lieu of a little steam popup that gives you nothing.
Graphics - Honestly it's true to form, if you're looking for a major update to Stick of Truth you aren't really going to get it. I feel like they did go above and beyond in a lot of ways that fell short in the previous edition, there's some pretty slick animated summons and the character creation is pretty in depth. You spend a lot of time crafting new costumes and finding eyewear, masks, makeup etc so if customization is your thing you're pretty open. Summons look pretty great as well.
Gameplay - It's pretty solid, the puzzles range from mind-numbingly easy to pretty intuitive and the rewards don't feel like hot garbage as you're going through the game. Combat is pretty fluid and mildly tactical, enough to keep you engaged to pay attention to the combat as a feature but not so much that it takes away from playing the game in the first place. A lot of it you can outright avoid just by walking past Agents of Chaos or the 6th graders that challenge you in the beginning parts of the game. Leveling up is a bit of a slow process but every level gives you a significant payoff, it gives you a slot to place an artifact that gives your characters boosts in specialty areas as well as stats making you better in combat all around. Artifacts can be found or crafted and allow you to manipulate in-combat focuses like increases knock back combo damage or increasing your health regeneration, basic attack damage etc. Quests are pretty straight forward, you have to pay attention to the quest-givers when they tell you what to do because they don't usually repeat it. You'll get handy Coonstagram messages when you're close to a more vague quest giver's goal however, an example for this is at the police station you have to put up a sketchy detective's comedy flier at a couple places throughout town. He'll routine send you messages letting you know where a good place is to set them up, it's a little bit on the hand holding side but otherwise you'd be running around the entire map spamming the use button trying to figure out where it's supposed to go - honestly I'd prefer this method.
Audio / Soundtrack - This is the best part of the game if you ask me, we get the same basic South Park soundtrack that you'd typically experience watching the show. When school lets out and you're on for day two it actually plays the same music that happens, this is pretty obvious and to be expected but the payoff of it is still awesome. There's some custom tracks as well that play during specific encounters or my personal favorite the Booger n'♥♥♥♥♥jingle that plays every time you pick up a Yelp container. You'll also notice that when you go into some businesses you'll be met with old songs from the show like Kany's "Gay Fish", I heard the Hamster song as well and a few other oldies on the TV or Radio. Combat sounds like you think it would, they've added a ton of samples from the show from their own scuffle scenes as well as new and pretty great ones for the summons, I don't want to spoil anything but if you're a long-time fan of the show the audio easter eggs and jokes you'll get are constantly coming at you in typical South Park fashion - it's really a treat.
Overall - I played it for about 6 hours straight when I knew I had things to do the next day and regret about 0 minutes of it. It's really unfortunate how steam is playing out this title because it really, really doesn't deserve it. The game is well rounded and definitely put together by a team of passionate people who really cared about the project and it's paid off incredibly by what you experience when you get over DRM that literally doesn't effect you or a Ubisoft launcher that pops up only when you launch South Park and closes when you close the game. If people actually reviewed the game they played I'm pretty sure more folks would really enjoy it, long-time fans of the series will get a serious kick out of the game and all the references and new fans of the series will be able to experience some of it for the first time and that's just plain what I'd expect from a South Park game after Stick of Truth.

It may look like it on the surface, though Aliens versus Predator is a game that simply cannot be dismissed as anything else. It is one of the few games that can completely capture the intensity, and the nervousness of it's source material. It offers three separate campaigns, each playing as a different species; an Alien, Colonial Marine, or a Predator. Right from the beginning, it understands that whoever is going to play this game understands what Aliens and Predators are, and doesn't bother to waste your time with the trivia. In each campaign, from start to finish, all you have to worry about is completing the objectives, and staying alive. But the problem is that it's not as easy as it sounds. Not one bit. You spend your time worrying about what might be waiting around that dark corner. The corner with bloodstains and bullet holes on the wall. You know very well that whatever is around the corner may very well be a whole lot deadlier than you are. This cancels your will to move forward, and makes you want to find a nice tight corner and sit in it for the rest of your life. But if you do that, you feel like you're being watched. That's what this game does. It completely retracts your rational side. This was also how it stays completely true to the movies as well. You know that if the characters do nothing but hide in an attempt to save their own skin, nothing will be accomplished but fatality, but at the same time, they shouldn't be opening that door. This was how it matched, and sometimes even superseded, the horror of the original films, and is why this is one of the few games that have ever truly frightened me.

Three of us played the first episode of Eon Altar and the experience sits somewhere between a classic hack-sand-slash dungeon crawler and a game of good old tabletop D&D.
Each player must download an app, join the same wifi network and then join a game instance started on a PC. This process worked without issue for us on a variety of devices (Pixel XL, iPhone 6 and Samsung Galaxy S6). We chose our characters and we were on our way.
At various points, your character will have internal thoughts, that you can share with the party at your discretion, and there will be spoken passages which you must read out loud to the other players, much in the same way you may speak to your players in a game of D&D, although there is much less freedom as you are reading from a script.
Movement can be controlled by either dragging and dropping an icon on your phone, or using the phone as a joystick. This worked well for the most part, but there were some minor latency issues likely related to using a mobile app as a controller.
Combat is turn based and works well for the most part, choosing from basic attacks that charge energy which you can then spend later on your heavier hitting attacks.
Progression is fairly linear with the most part, with levels offering some exploration but ultimately funnelling you in one direction. Leveling up characters and gear is also fairly linear, and is done by spending a variety of different currencies you pick up during your adventure. Each class is limited to only a couple of archetypical roles. For example, I played Silent Thorn, and I could progress in either Archery or Assassination, but little else.
Having only played the first episode so far, I cannot comment on the story overall, but it will be familiar to anyone who has played a video game in the RPG genre in the last 5 years.
While this game may not be the best RPG to come out recently, it is certainly unique, and the social aspect of actually playing your character with your friends is the closest a video game has come (for me) to feeling like one of our D&D games. For the price, if you are looking for something to fill in a night when not everyone turns up to play your favourite tabletop RPG then this could well fill the hole for a couple of nights.

This game is a GREAT idea, executed VERY well.
The IDEA:
All players have group objectives, and personal objectives. Your personal objectives and information is displayed on YOUR phone only, you choose what to share. In conversations with other player characters you voice your own toon (as in character or flat as you like) and you choose to be friendly or secretive to other players. It works PERFECTLY with the phone (I HATE phone-based games, but I fell in love with this after a few minutes).
Gameplay:
Fairly simplistic rpg-lite. It is a "turn-based" system when the fighting happens, and real time out of combat. There are 2 turns. The enemys turn, and the heroes turn. When the heroes have their turn, all heroes can execute their commands at the same time, which creates a perfect pace. The game slows down so you dont have to stress about clicking your phone faster, but at the same time you dont have to wait for the other players to do their thing. It might be tactically smarter to wait since there is friendly fire on AOE, but you dont have to. It is for a lack of a better word, a perfect idea. The player have the choice how to play and the game does not suffer from it at all.
Story:
Fairly standard fantasy stuff so far, but where the game really shines is in the storytelling between characters, regarding their past, what they choose to share and their personal beliefs/objectives.
Final thoughts:
Its been a long, LONG time since I've played a good couch coop. I play all kinds of games, and I run/play table-top RP. This game scratches ALL the right itches for me. The tactics is not very deep, but its interesting enough to keep you playing. The story is decent, but the character stuff is just great. This is NOT a single player game. Grab a friend, or rather 2-3 friends and have a GREAT time. Preferably friends that can be bothered to voice their characters in an interesting/fun way.
One would think the phone thing is just a gimmick, but its not. Imo its next generation stuff. A truly original and smart way to use smart phones. Smart.
Also, its CHEAP. And FOUR players can play with ONE copy. Why arent you playing yet?

Spoiler free review:
Gameplay was so tedious and the co-op is unplayable; there was even more co-op between prisoners and captors in a concentration camp. Characters were completely flat and void of any depth, soundtrack was subpar and at times misplaced, and the art design was so poorly done it could only have been the work of an individual suffering late stages of glaucoma. Each puzzle was so simplistic it essentially boiled down to a game of walking around holding down the interact button, but, the platforming was revolutionary; it combined the best platforming aspects of Deadly Premonition, Osu! Tatakae! Ouendan, and Typing of the Dead (Dreamcast 2001 Edition). The stories depth was written so well to the view of a child that it makes the entire game irrelevant.
It would appear that the writer took too much creative freedom in developing the story of two childhood friends travelling through a world in which the writer could not settle on a genre. The story begins in a beautifully set middle earth world as we follow the tale of two roommates whose landlord suddenly falls ill. To the great guidance of the town drunk, these work colleagues set out on a journey through a village of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, to a steampunk cathedral where we meet a cage dancer and rescue her from her pimp. The game then takes a grisly turn when it delves into animal cruelty as these two civil partners kidnap, abuse, mutilate, and mount a majestic griffon to death. It soon becomes clear that these two felons are completely void of any human decency; corpse mutilation, limb ripping, decapitation, blood bathing, these are all of a few of the satanic rituals they conduct.
When the two scholars save a poor woman from being sacrificed to the giant gods with seemingly no ulterior motives, she offers them a place to rest, and even shows them her vulnurable motherly form; creating a nice web of love to keep them warm in the night. To repay in kindness, they quickly remove each of her eight limbs and leave her to die. In her dying throes she attempts to hug the two tenants one last time as an act of love. The most sadistic of the two proceeds to impale himself on one of her limbs to let her know that she's nothing but a monster in her last moments alive. She then dies in anguish as the two revel in her death.
The kouhai (TN Note: kouhai is korean for junior) shows no signs of remorse as he digs a hole and throws his senpai's newly mutilated body into a ditch on the side of the path. He fills the hole with various scat that he can find. He then finds the elixir of life and selfishly pours it onto his senpai's body; mocking him that he is void of life.
The story ends when he returns to his landlord with the rent (the elixir).
This tale was truly an enthralling adventure that teaches us the dangers of technology abuse. It's commentary on social media is a clear cut warning to us all.
10/10, would not recommend.

Disclaimer: This is a review I wrote when the game was new, copied from another site. It was based off my time with the Xbox 360 version and I've only put in a short time on the PC version. So issues with GFWL or it's removal are NOT taken into account. From 2011.
*****************************************************************************************************************
OK let me preface this by saying that I am a Dead Rising fanboy. A major one. I am well aware of all the games flaws and issues and I couldn't care less. I enjoyed the first Dead Rising like no game before it. As a huge fan of Romero films and zombie fiction of all kinds, Dead Rising was the first game I felt truly captured the feeling of an oppressive "Zombie Event". And of course the parallels to Dawn of the Dead didn't hurt it either. The original Dawn is a timeless classic that has been a high water mark for decades and it's remake holds the unique position of being just as good as the film that it's based on.
Fast Forward from 2006 to 2010 and Dead Rising 2. I was initially shocked that Frank was not planned for the sequel of Dead Rising. But with time and some gameplay I warmed up to Chuck Green. The Combo Weapon system was great and the irreverant humor from the original was well intact. For my money, it was another success. But I never did stop missing Frank despite putting upwards of 30 hours into DR2 and even more into Case Zero and Case West.
Now on to the reason for this write up, Off the Record (hereafter; 'OtR'). OtR is a curious title, even for me. Being the big fan of zombie games, of Dead Rising 1, and of Frank West, I was on board with this one from the word GO. The problem though, is who other than me would even consider this game a valid purchase? And releasing in one of the most cluttered fall release schedules since 2007? This game just doesn't seem to have an audience outside of the insane DR fans like myself, and even for us it's starting to feel like Capcom is pulling another Street FIghter 2 here with constant reiterations instead of moving on. And all in the span of 13 months.
The game itself is pretty great. The same formula that made the other Dead Rising products enjoyable is still here with some nice new additions. Serious fans will enjoy the subtle changes to make the protagonist swap fit and there have been adjustments to the looters and the zombies seem more aggressive than in the other DR games. New combo weapons and the return of the camera mechanic round out a pretty impressive list of "Pros" for this game.
The issue at hand though, is the list of "Cons". No matter how fun it may be, if you played DR2 proper, this is just not enough of an upgrade for the casual fan to embrace. The hardcore DR nut will love OtR but I wonder just how many of us there are and if we number high enough to make this game profitable?
I've been a big supporter of this series. And I've always done my best to try and steer people to playing it. Forum posts asking "What 360 games should I play?" always see me trumpetting Dead Rising and Dead Rising 2's greatness. This game though, I just don't think I can be it's emmisary. I cannot "sell" this game to people. If you're on board, you were already on board and if you're on the fence, I'm not going to be trying to push you over. It is a good game. And on paper it's probably the best Dead Rising to date. But even with all the good stuff it has to offer (not the least of which is finally adding the checkpoint system fans have been wanting since 2006!), I just can't push a game like this. While it's a 5 star for me personally, I can't even imagine that anyone else would share that view of this one.
To Bottom Line it, it's a great fun romp though a zombie outbreak with a charasmatic protagonist. It's just that the romp is basically the same one you took last year with DR2 proper. OtR can only truly be recommended to either those who never played DR2, or who are major Frank West fans who are willing to overlook the fact that they already played this game a year ago. It's definately a curious animal, but I doubt most people will feel the need to have it on their mantle.
