Dead Rising 2: Off the Record is the remake of the earlier Dead Rising 2 game, changing the protagonist from Chuck Greene to Frank West from the original Dead Rising, changing the missions and dialogue to accommodate the new protagonist.
This game is incredibly fun and it is incredibly over the top, allowing you to combine weapons, learn silly moves and do pretty much what you want in an endless zombie horde sandbox based in a fictional spoof of Las Vegas. Do you want to drive around on a bike with chainsaws strapped to the handlebars? You can! Do you want to do bad cosplay as a "superhero" and suplex zombies? You can!
The missions are entertaining, the story is pretty far fetched for the most part and it does have multiple endings with lots of side missions, some of which require special steps to even activate. This gives the game a higher amount of replay value if you want to discover more of what the game has to offer. In addition to this it has boss battles in some missions, which are incredibly entertaining. (Look for some of them if you aren't convinced)
One of the major downsides of the game is that if you played Dead Rising 2, this game doesn't have much to offer besides an alternate take on the story. Unless you are a fan or a newcomer, this may not be worth investing in, as it doesn't do enough differently to make it a completely new experience compared to Dead Rising 2.
Overall, I would reccommend the title because of how fun it is, and the co-op mode makes it an even greater experience with friends. The game also contains a sandbox mode similar to Dead Rising, and gives some challenges to make the game last longer. I loved spending time just doing silly things or completing missions, as it never really felt dull or repetitive compared to some other zombie games. It also has a fairly unique sense of humour compared to other zombie titles these days.
SIDE NOTE: At the time of writing this review, the title is still using Games for Windows Live, this may be something to consider when purchasing due to the service being fairly close to shutting down. As far as I know there has been no word on Capcom removing/changing the system in place within Dead Rising 2: Off the Record.

Brothers is one of those games you get from a *Humble Bundle* or during
*Steam Sales* even though you have absolutely no idea what to expect. The short
version: **ABSOLUTELY BEAUTIFUL**.
Yes, it had to be in CAPS.
First things first, the music is perfect, as is the art style of the game, both
go really well together.
The controls are not really intuitive at first, even though they're quite
minimalistic (basically just both analog sticks and bumpers when playing with a
controller) but because you're controlling both brothers individually, even
late-game it can get confusing but after you get used to it, it simply
feels as the right way to play the game.
There is much love to details in the game, every single piece of the game (
environment and NPCs) are hand-crafted (or at least it seems so) and not
much duplication (if any) is found, in short a beatutiful landscape
throughout the game.
The puzzles in the game are somewhat too easy in my opinion, but the atmosphere
of the game actually totally makes up for that.
The story is actually pretty difficult to review without saying too much about
it. I only have to say that at first it seemed like a classic adventure, two
kids going on an adventure to save their dad, but it actually got darker by the
minute and the were actually some surprises in there.
There are many symbolics in the game (guilt, loss, death, reunion,
freedom, ...) which range from the actual stuff you see on your monitor to the
controls of the game.
The level design is pretty amazing and I'm not only talking about the graphics,
environment or the art style but also how the game is introducing the player to
new game concepts he needs to use in order to progress in the game, completely
intuitive and cleverly integrated into the game itself without the need of
those damn popup tutorials (**cough** Sims4 **cough**).
In short, even though there is a lack of challenge: I can only recommend this
game.

Dead Rising 2: OTR (SP Only) *** Combining DR2 and DR2:OTR ***
Story (5/10):
DR2: OTR's story is largely the same as the other two DR installments. A somewhat bland story, sometimes perked by Capcom's characteristically silly character interactions. Overall, not a strong point of the game.
Gameplay (7/10):
DR2: OTR delivers the same Dead Rising experience that fans of the series have come to know, and sometimes love. Hordes of zombies flood the screen, and as usual, your job is to smite them using a variety of crazy weapons, ranging from laser shooting masks to chainsaw-tipped kayak paddles. DR2 and DR2:OTR really picked up from DR in the sense that they added a LOT of new weapons, which helps the game keep fresh throughout its duration. It personally never got old to smash through piles of enemies using an ever-expanding arsenal of ridiculous armaments. The added infinite mode is worth looking into, since you are unbound by the time constraints of the normal game, and given challenges to complete for money and xp, which carries over into the main game. This can be helpful if you are stuck in the main storyline.
Unfortunately, this is where the fun ends. As with previous DR installments, boss fights are tedious and cheap, escorts are constant and frustrating, and many parts of the game feel drawn out and devoid of content or direction. If you are not satisfied with killing zombies, you will find little else of value in this game.
Mechanics (6/10):
DR2/DR2:OTR's new mechanic is the weapon combination mechanic, which allows you to combine weapons into new devastating combinations. This system is unfortunately limited by your need to find/unlock blueprints to use combo weapons to their full potentional, as well as the need to find specific "maintenance rooms" where the combos can be made. A more on-the-fly system may have been easier. Otherwise, mechanics remain somewhat unchanged from DR1, and are as usual, buggy and unforgiving.
Visuals (7/10): DR2:OTR looks decent, probably mediocre, by today's standards. Edges are clean, textures are not obviously stretched out or degraded, and lighting effects are present to some degree. The technical prowess of the game comes from its ability to maintain hundreds of enemies on-screen at the same time, which still remains impressive, and a trademark of the series.
Sound (7/10):
The only comment I have about the sound is the game's tendency to have the constant moan of zombies drown out all other noise. It gets tiresome. Otherwise, the game does not have any noticeable sound achievements or problems.
Replayability (9/10):
DR2:OTR are both strong contenders in the "Replayability" category. There are a lot of weapons to unlock, skills to upgrade, and powerful costumes to unlock (especially the famous Zero armor, from Megaman). After beating the main game, I went through a second time, in order to beat down my opponents using a souped-up Frank West, complete with overpowered weapon combinations. Very satisfying.
OVERALL:
DR2:OTR is a fun, satisfying game, held back by poorly implemented mechanics, a buggy nature (see: Capcom games), and perhaps a lack of foresight.
Do you like zombies? Do you like killing them? Tons of them? PILES of them? Yes? Then you'll love this game.

This is a fantastic point-n-click adventure game. If you've played any of the old LucasArts or Sierra adventure games from the 90's, you'll feel right at home with Deponia. It's art style and sense of humor is reminiscient of Monkey Island or Day of the Tentacle, and its puzzles are definitely challenging without being outlandishly obscure. It's a perfect balance of logic and wackiness.
The story and characters are also well done, though it took a little bit for the main character, Rufus, to grow on me (he's obnoxious and grating at first). Since this is part 1 of a trilogy, the ending will leave you hanging and wanting more. However, don't let that fool you into thinking it cuts short. I finished this in 12 hours, which is unheard of for point-n-click games in this day and age.
If you loved the adventure games in the 90's from LucasArts or Sierra, this is definitely worth your time and money, and I can't wait to play the sequels.

As fan of adventure games, and one who has grown up on Monkey Island series and later games like Full throttle and Sanitarium, I was excited about playing this game... until 5 minutes in, when I got stuck first time. Ok, I google-it, found solution and continue on... for next 5 min, until I got stuck AGAIN! And after looking up on google for solution once more, I figured out system how this game works; enter area, play pixel hunting to find all clickable items so that you can collect them, then try out all items from inventory on all noncollectable items in that room, and if that doesn't work, then try to combine all items in your inventory one with another till you get new item. When you craft new item, try him out with everything in room, and then with everything in your inventory (because sometimes you have to combine more items to get something useful)... And if after all of that, you didn't do anything that will progress story further on, go to next area and repeat procedure. And you have to do all of that due to twisted and borderline insane logic behind all puzzles in this game, so there is very little things that will be logical at first (or ever).
So, does that sound like fun? For me it didn't... So I grabbed first walk-trough I found online, and finished game with it, and that makes me sad because characters (except main character), visuals, humor, animation and atmosphere are wonderful... Shame.
And I really can't say that I liked main character in this game (he is borderline sociopath); maybe they intended to do that, but It just make me dislike him in general, and If I don't like main character, I tend to like game less (this is personal preference, so take that that in consideration). And there are some questionable moral agendas in this game regarding females....
Overall, I don't recommend this game, due to insane puzzles that barely make any sense, and they reduce game to tedious clicking and trying out everything on everything until you make something new.

Quick overall:
Play this game as what it is: an action/adventure FPS. This is NOT A RPG and this is NOT A SURVIVAL game. You just shoot things that appear in your way (and loot their corpses) in order to advance in the linear plot.
There's no moral decisions to be made, no different paths to follow, no interesting characters to know, no customization of the abilities of your character, no basic needs that you need to fulfill from time to time. It seems the developers kinda started shaping it into a RPG (big maps, side-missions, inventory system), but aborted the idea. If you deal with it as an action/adventure FPS, it's an OK game. Another thing: I played it with the "Road to Limansk" mod, which corrects some bugs of the vanilla game and I recommend.
THE GOOD
- Solid gameplay, weapons fire nicely and each one feels different from another. You can have readily equipped a main gun, a side weapon and grenades, besides a Geiger-counter stuff to locate artifacts (stones that give you some bonuses). There are many upgrades that can be made in your weapons and armor. You can walk/run/crouch/jump effectively, running and jumping use stamina.
- The density of individuals in the map is good: there are few NPCs wandering around (Ukraine Exclusion Zone, after all), but not few enough to the point that it would make the game boring. BTW, the map of the game is divided in separate regions; in order to go from one to another, there's a loading screen.
- There's a "faction system" that, albeit simple, works. If two enemy factions meet randomly on the map, there will be gunfight. A faction's outpost may be overrun by another faction's guys from time to time. Also, you can belong to some faction of your choice if you want to.
- Interesting setting: Ukraine Exclusion Zone.
- Good diversity of items to loot, and the inventory is somewhat realistic regarding weight.
- Nice graphics without stressing your pc. Some landscapes and building are quite impressive for a 2008 game.
- Some interesting mods available with which you can customize your game.
THE BAD
- Generic characters. With the exception of some few key characters that have a bigger array of dialogue lines, are partially voiced and have a visible face (things that just diminish their blandness), the random guy has some 3 whatever dialogue lines, is not voiced and doesn't even have a visible face (ALL of them use some cloth or helmet to hide it). All of them use the same body model and move exactly the same. Besides, in my 28 hours of game I didn't see a single woman, NPCs are all male so far.
- The side-missions are not only bland, but too quick. It's the same old "go there/get that" style of mission, but instead of going through immense caves or labyrinthical forgotten vaults to "get that", you just walk some 200m, open a crate, walk back and collect your reward.
- Lack of lore-elements to enrich the Exclusion Zone setting. There are no pieces of lore to be found/seen, like diaries, newspapers, radio stations, books, texts or things like that regarding the context of the game. I know, we can read about the real Exclusion Zone in Wikipedia, but the game's one is different and we can't go deep on it.
- Soundtrack as generic as the characters. Generic techno beat during the action and generic ambient music outside of action moments. Play the game with music off.
- Corrupt save-files. Sometimes your saves don't load. I heard that it happens after some scripted event in the game. I had this issue with 2 saves, after that I started quick-saving and hard-saving in 2 different slots before transitioning from one region to another. Haven't had problems after that.

The second game in the series, but the first chronologically (being a prequel), this game is by far the most underrated of the series. 9/10, if you ask a S.T.A.L.K.E.R's least favorite game in the series... it's this one, it gets a lot of hate for the fact that on release it was very unoptimized and buggy and there really wasn't any workaround for it. But now, of course, like any other game in the series, a ton of mods are available for us to choose from and almost all of them include bug fixes and optimization features. Some of them stop there, upgrading the graphics a little, optimizing the game for you, and fixing common bugs and issues. Others, however, expand on the open faction system that this prequel provides. Unlike in Shadow of Chernobyl, this game allows you to interact openly and work with the factions outside of their main quest lines, going as far as joining them after reaching a certain status; and that's not just Duty and Freedom, that's almost any faction in the game.
The story, while not expanding too much on the events its predecessor, provide a little insight into what was going on in Shadow of Chernobyl and why it was happening, as well as revealing to you (Scar) information that Strelok did not know at the time. Don't get me wrong, Strelok is a cool guy, but Scar is probably my favorite character of the series. Either way, don't ignore this game because of earlier setbacks and whatnot, with the mods you have available now you can experience the game in almost a completely vanilla state (if you so wish) with all of the bugs and unoptimized mess fixed and cleaned up.
Again, an excellent series; the story, atmosphere, characters, and mod variety all make it worth its price. Tons of replayability to be had.

Spelunky is a must-have for any PC Gamer. It should be one of the essentials in any PC. It has an insane replay value, with an unique balance between simplicity in principle and mechanics, and complexity in the adaptability necessary for surpassing its many hardships and obstacles.
You have a SNES-like command config: the main ones being the four directionals (climb, walk and crouch), jump, run, and pickup/throw/use, along with buttons for using ropes and bombs, that work with the directionals: up+rope throws the rope up, while down+rope on a ledge drops the rope instead of a fall that would hurt you; pressing the bomb button throws it in front of you, up+bomb throws it high, down+bomb drops in your feet. The throw button functions similarly with things picked up in the levels, like stones and skulls.
You start on the top of a stage, and have to get to the bottom, where a door leads to the next stage. Each four stages, you get to a next level. You start in the mines, then you get to the caves, then to the icy depths. The obstacles are many, besides a set of enemies and traps specific to the level (e.g., mines have snakes, spiders, and arrow spitters, while the caves have toads, carnivorous plants and spike totems), some stages have an overall theme, like the dark stage, that give you a torch in the start and you can light other torches on the way to the end, or the stages occupied with some type of enemy (snakes, spiders, undead, yeti, etc.).
You find treasure along the level, and with it you can buy things from shopkeepers that appear now-and-then. These can be the basic ropes and bombs, or a variety of tools, with usefulness (and proportional price) that goes from small, like glasses that show hidden treasure, to game-changing, like a jetpack.
In every level, there is a "being in distress" (originally a blonde lady, but with the option of including a guy in... interesting clothes and a dog) which if taken to the exit door of the level, is saved and gets you an extra hit-point.
The most appealing characteristic of the game is perhaps that, despite the skill, tools, and extra hit-points you get, you can be far into the game, with everything in favor of your ultimate success, and then you make one simple mistake, that leads to a horrible death. It doesn't matter: the game is so much fun that even dying is fun. You'll be restarting and trying again, with new tactics, perhaps next time you'll focus on gold, or this time I'll see what happens if I blow the altar, or I'll try shooting the shopkeeper, or buying this camera to see what it does.
At "spelunkyworld", the official site, you can get the original, pixelated and freeware version, which I played A LOT before getting this release. Before (inevitably) buying this game, try it and be hooked.

This game puts emphasis on sandbox construction; it's clear they want you to be building a base through the addition of many decoration blocks, farming and the crafting being focused around placed, upgradable workbenches. Conflictingly, at the same time the game forces you to jump worlds frequently due to the fact that each one is incredibly tiny and spawn only a very small fraction of the resources you need, so to progress craftwise you need to visit many worlds. In addition to this, the RPG character development is tied to jumping through progressively harder worlds. In multiplayer, everyone has to jump a world together, nobody can be left behind, which makes this the first game of its type to actually downgrade with multiplayer.
What does this game want you to do? You can't progress without building a base, but you can't build a base because you need to progress. Why include base mechanics if you are supposed to be constantly adventuring? Why is the crafting based around placed crafting benches??? You have to carry the benches around to craft on the move, but why have them like that in the first place? Why is there farming when you don't stay in one place?!
Basically the devs couldn't choose between two types of games, so they decided to do both and made no effort to allow them to compliment each other (unlike Terraria), so they end up destroying each other instead.
I suggest either;
A: increase each world size by about a factor of 100 and significantly reduce the prevelance/need of world jumping.
B: Remove all mechanics that are based on staying in one place; remove farming, forget decoration/furniture/building and allow you to craft everything without benches, instead focus on adventure, character progression and combat.
Don't tell players to constantly move around *and* stay in the same place at the same time, this is a paradox that makes the game unplayable.

A super cool, cute, and fun game drawing inspiration from popular games (Terraria, Minecraft, and Zelda). There are three classes so far, a bunch of customization options (for the game being in Early Access so far) and more. The only disappointment I have with the game, rather than being an open world (like Terraria, or Minecraft) it's more based on stages (or levels).

I realize this is early access, but at this point the game is not close to ready yet; and the fact that devs feel that it is ready/near complete is scary. It's scary because it would be a shame to see a game with this much potential amount to nothing more than what Portal Knights currently is.
What Portal Knights currently is: a beautiful, but sadly very simple, linear storyline game with sandboxlike elements, but not a true sandbox game.
So yes, I obviously cannot recomend this as of now. Portal Knights has so much potential, but it could easily just be a moneyrun from the develeopers. Read my conclusion statement (bottom of the review) for a further explaination.
PROS:
Combat is done well in my opinion, but could be harder; rolling to dodge attacks, timing is key
Feels very polished in terms of gameplay mechanics
Clean; Portal Knights isn't glitchy or buggy, just very flat and lifeless
Looks amazing
CONS:
Game progression is extremely linear; does not feel like a sandbox game
World(s) are very small; only one biome per world
Abysmally small worlds take away all feelings of exploration
Random generation algorithms are bad; floating blocks, nothing for caves/islands/towers/castles
Barely any unique armor or weapons
Tier amror/weapon progression; copper->iron->gold is boring, not to mention gold armor makes no sense
Character creation needs more options
3 Simple classes doesnt feel like enough
Classes almost don't matter; the game allocates all your stat points for you; can't truly customize
Classes aren't balanced; playing as a warrior is a handicap
Worlds feel like a conglomerance of randomly generated blocks, there's no developed strctures and all in all it just feels empty
In depth:
Game Progression is too lienar - "Randomly generated" worlds need to be a little more "random" in regards to their generation. It feels like I am playing a campaign for a storyline almost, except with no plot whatsoever... (the intro was nice backstory was nice, but there is nothing in the game) not a sandbox game. Don't get me wrong, I had fun playing the game up to this point - but it is simply ailed with too many flaws in its current state, which (I hope) are mostly from the game being underdeveloped.
It does not feel like a sandbox game, this is because progression is too linear. This right now is a "tiers" game, where you just go copper -> iron -> gold with little to no varation, except the levels you explore feel like missions, which make exploring for resources not even really feel like exploring. They need randomly generated armor/weapons or much more variety within the tiers instead of just 1 amror/weaponset per tier for each class.
Because the levels/portals you play are so small, you really don't end up doing any exploring or feel like you are exploring. As I've said, it just feels like I am playing a campgain and not really a sandbox game. There is no algoritims to randomly generate caves, islands, towers/castles - its really all just congomerated terrain. And when you combine this with how small the levels are, its not a pretty picture.
This game is fun but unless the update it with some major fixes, the game itself, just like the levels/portals is very fleeting and far too linear. They need to update it to fix some the things I've said above to get a recomendation from me. I want to like this game, I really do. It has so much potential, but it just isn't developed fully enough right now.
If the devs don't update the game to make it feel more like a sandbox game and less like a campaign/storymode, I'd say to stay clear of it. I will have to say this game isn't worth $10. In it's current state right now, it's worth maybe $5. Let's hope this game isn't a simple attempt at a moneyrun from the devs, because it has so much potential. Lack of a developer response as to where they are going with the game at this point is scary to me.
Conclusion statement:
Game progression is too linear, and it doesn't feel like a sandbox game - but rather a storyline game with no plotline. This game could become something great, I would keep an eye on it. It is maybe worth $5 in its current state, but not $10, and sure as hell not $20.
But, the sad part about it all is that Portal Knights feels like it could be a finished game, just a very, very flat and lifeless one. If the devs did nothing more to it as of now, it could be considered complete; which they seem to be suggesting in what little statements they chose to divulge in regards to the game's development.
Again, let's hope that the above isn't the case. In it's current state the game is fun, but doesn't last very long and just feels like it is missing a lot to me. Gameplay is very solid though and there is very little bugs or glitches.
I would love to be able to recomend this game, but I can't as of now.

I thought the Stick of Truth was a phenomenal game and The Fractured But Whole improves on that formula. The combat is a lot more involved with different artifacts to strenghthen and change your character's build focus. Your character also has their main class and subclass which allows you access to many more movesets for both up close and ranged combat. You can assign allies to fight with so if you want you'll be able to switch it up as frequently as you want to change how the fights go. Each character, including your own, has an ultimate ability so it was fun to change allies just to see everyone's ulti. Plenty of hidden secrets and little side quests that you can accomplish as well as having a feature where you'll have to unlock new allies in order to traverse certain parts of the map that are blocked by lava or the height of an item. Most of the notable characters homes are also available for you to be able to explore and loot which can be really helpful for crafting and finding more things to do. Lots of good in here and I'm having an absolute blast. Bottom line is if you like the show I'll have a really hard time believing that you won't like the game.

tldr; 5/10 Save your money.
It's a lot of... little things. Some areas of the game are absolute steps forward. Others are huge leaps backwards. Overall the game just doesn't standup for me as being better than Stick of Truth, but if you're just here for a new south park story you'll likely enjoy it.
Cons:
Definitely a weaker RPG than Stick of Truth on the mechanics side. Item progression and worth are pretty terrible. The story is good and there are plenty of laughs to be found in it but overall it feels less... epic and rediculous than the previous game. Terrible DRM and uplay is mandatory; it's listed on the store page but worth repeating. Meaningless DLC on day 1.
PC keyboard/mouse controls are almost famously bad. This was not a good port.
It's glitchy enough to have some story-line breaking bugs that require a new character.
Pros:
Better combat overall. South Park looks and feels a lot more fleshed out. The more linear and gated approach to progression in the town really help sell the experience and you find yourself walking around more than just fast traveling everywhere. The expanded party system is nice, even if it feels under utilised.

If you enjoy South Park you will enjoy the game. Plain and simple. The story is very much a South Park story, and will have you laughing at times and going WTF at others, as much as you expect. I've completed the game and a majority of the achievements, and will most likely start a second play through to complete the few I am missing.
The only negatives might be the combat, which can get a tad long winded at times, but as long as you keep up with gearing, set ups and make changes where appropriate for encounters, combat can be handled quickly. It's a bit more strategic now than Stick of Truth was, but still will result in your eventual set up finding the winning combo that will make combat go quickly.
If you are an SJW or Snowflake, you might take offense with the games many blunt and to the point commentary on many ridiculous social issues as well as pointing out actual injustices (such as making fun of SJWs and their attempt to make every little comment out to be hate speech).
Majority of the review bombs are just that, bombing for nit picky things; rebels without a clue arguments basically that just want something to be outraged over. UPlay is not a concern, and neither is a day one DLC costume pack. Very simple solution to that; don't buy the pack it isn't required. This is my first time bothering to review something but I liked this game enough that I want it to succeed. Bought this game through Humble Bundle. Thoroughly enjoying it.
Pros:
a classic D&D style quest/crawling game.
COUCH CO-OP! I'll say it again: COUCH CO-OP! There's not enough couch co-op in the modern gaming area, but this executes it nicely.
Phone controller (more later).
Decent Graphics.
Nice music.
Pretty good voice acting.
Ingenuity in personal objectives.
Lots of dialogue options between characters.
Cons:
The space between checkpoints can be a little punishing.
No save feature beyond checkpointing.
No map.
Limited (albeit relatively diverse) character options.
Inability to backtrack to beaten sub-episodes (as far as I can tell).
Typical minor glitches with a phone app. Cross-platofrm integration is hard.
The phone controller is more than just a controller gimmick. You get to have your entire character management suite is there. Because every player has access to a second, hidden, screen, the game can display personal thoughts and hidden objectives to you. This is an excellent first implementation for an idea like this, and lends a lot of credibility to what coudl have just been a clunky controller. The main downside is the movement mechanics can be a bit troublesome, but the game uses a turn-based combat system to sort of remedy the problem. I have controller integration list as a con, but only because it's not perfect. It's a little unfair because it seems like a very difficult thing to perfect. All in all, it does not detract from the play expereince in a notable enough way for me to not enjoy the game.
If you can find the money (or the whopping $1 in Humble Bundle) for this game, and don't hate your friends, get it. Play with them.

This game...this game is simplistic, yet beautiful. It is unsettling, yet fulfilling. It is casual and yet breathtaking.
Do not read anything about this game's story before you play it, and play it through in one sitting. The entire game will only take you about 3 hours, but it is a journey that will lead to a wonderful new place. The environments are absolutely incredible and will remind you a fairy tale. The gameplay is puzzle/adventure based, and although the puzzles are clever, you will not find anything to be difficult. This game is more of an atmospheric experience than anything, an interactive story, if you will, everything down to the control scheme is used to convey aspects of story to player.
However, I would reccomend this game to anyone, it is absolutely beautiful and it is a story that needs to be witnessed. Pick this game up on sale if you can, but don't hesitate. This is a must play!

Take your time to dwell on the marvellous art and fantastical landscapes; these are what the game really are, at bottom. But the landscapes are great - the more surreal and otherwordly they became as you progressed.

Let me start of this review by saying, I had high hope for the game. A squad based World War 2 shooter, where players would be able to command the war effort. Sign me up, sounds cool. But then you get into the game, and you slowly start to realize that, while the trailers and promos showed off one thing, the actual game play is really different.
Team issues: You could be put on a skirmish map, fighting over three objectives, and skirmish maps are small to get more action out of the games, which is a good concept, until you have Panthers and Tigers going up against M2A2 light tanks, armed with a .50 cal and a .30 cal, or Hetzers and Panzer IV's against M3 Lee's.
Weapon issues: Most teams will consist of people using MP-34's (if german) or PPD's and PPSH's (if russian) and the base damage on rifles such as the M1 Garand, SVT-40, and G43 are bad, which means you have to try and get headshots on guys who are using weapons that will outclass you in amout of ammo thrown out, making your progression hard because you can't get kills to unlock new weapons or weapon parts to increase your damage. OHK weapons like high damage modified Kar98, Mosin-Nagants, and M1903 Springfields are used alot as well, thus your semi-automatic rifle doesn't do you any good as, unless you are very luck to get the drop and first shot off (and hit) you will be one hit killed by a torso or leg shot, while the 2 to 3 rounds you put into your opponent are worthless.
Progression: Progression had a good idea attached to it, do actions in game, such as trying to unlock tanks and jeeps or get kills with a Semiauto rifle to unlock things like the BAR, which lead to unlocking Machine Guns, or using a Pz II to unlock your Pz III and then on to the Pz IV and Tiger. But this is where the issue comes in, most of the time, trying to do things such as unlock vehicles takes too long, because you don't have the badge that you need to increase your unlock speed, which leads to you getting killed before you can do anything, or if you manange to kill your attacker, you get to start the whole unlock process over. So it comes down to things like this, where you need to use a BAR to unlock your MG's, but you can't use a BAR, unless you pick it up off the ground and can get kills with it, or you can use your Semiauto rifle and try to get kills with it (see: Weapons issues)
Pay to Win: This game is pay to win, as you can instantly finish any badge progession, unlock any weapon mod, any weapon, any soldier type, camos for your player and his weapons, with cash. You can only get the full amount of XP that you rightfully earned in a match, by paying for Veteran status, aka Subscribe, aka Premium. If you don't have veteran status, you can lose out on 100's of exp points in your rank progression, which puts a limit on the amount of credits you can earn, as a rank 7 player makes 12,000 credits for an hour of play. So if you can't rank up, you can't get access to the higher credits for game time spent. Your badge exp is almost similarly limited, meaning your progression towards ribbions, which are used to unlock badges, weapons, and weapons mods (like ammo, springs, sights, triggers) is slowed, making it hard for you to get to say Tank thief, which lets you unlock tanks faster.
So take this review with a grain of salt, as I am speaking from my personal time spent in this game, that while it can be fun, if you have a group and can get the squad points need to bring things like Tanks, Aircraft and Recon along with your plain infantry squad, there are too many issues, such as hackers who go unpunished by the Developers and the un-noticable "anti-cheat" system, the pay to win nature of the game, that limits the amout of exp you can get out of a match, the number of badages you can wear (FtP: 1 badge, Veteran/PtW: 2) and things like extra weapon slots which could be the difference between having 5 AT grenades and having 10 because you can bring a second AT grenade type.

Cons:
Definitely a weaker RPG than Stick of Truth on the mechanics side. Item progression and worth are pretty terrible. The story is good and there are plenty of laughs to be found in it but overall it feels less... epic and rediculous than the previous game. Terrible DRM and uplay is mandatory; it's listed on the store page but worth repeating. Meaningless DLC on day 1.
PC keyboard/mouse controls are almost famously bad. This was not a good port.
It's glitchy enough to have some story-line breaking bugs that require a new character.
Pros:
Better combat overall. South Park looks and feels a lot more fleshed out. The more linear and gated approach to progression in the town really help sell the experience and you find yourself walking around more than just fast traveling everywhere. The expanded party system is nice, even if it feels under utilised.

If you enjoy South Park you will enjoy the game. Plain and simple. The story is very much a South Park story, and will have you laughing at times and going WTF at others, as much as you expect. The only negatives might be the combat, which can get a tad long winded at times, but as long as you keep up with gearing, set ups and make changes where appropriate for encounters, combat can be handled quickly. It's a bit more strategic now than Stick of Truth was, but still will result in your eventual set up finding the winning combo that will make combat go quickly.

A great classic that is actually scarrier then many other horror games today.

Updated review: (origianl review is below)
finished Episode 1 twice, and just started Ep2.
i'll start with the bad: you need to buy all episode to finish the story. but they are all cheap.
Good: nice gameplay, simple to learn. only has couch co-op. using phone app. turn based combat (which i love), but live gameplay.
as for the Turnbased combat, you don't zoom in to a combat like HoMM or something, the game pause and give turns based on speed etc. you can start attacking before the enemy see's you, and have a first strike. if he see's you, his turn is first...
as for live gameplay. the camera follows everyone. so that means, that you can't advance to other areas and live your friends behind like in most MMORPG i played (WoW, TL2, KoToR, etc).
as for loot, it is divided into resources. and free for all loot system. it works well, because if a friend needs some loot you got, you can trade. don't want to trade? fine, that quest you wanted to do, nope, not doing.
oh, there are group quests (kill the bad guy, duh). and personal quests. those are harder. you can either share them with your friends, or not. you can be nice, or not.
you need to have real people over (friends, spouse, kids, etc) my advice? make some popcorn or something with some wine, each episode is about ~4 hours.
best part? good interaction between characters in game, and as such, interaction between players. you voice your own characters, there are no actors for your characters, only for the npc :).
9/10 (cause no one gets a perfect 10...)

In all honesty, probably the best interpretation of an Aliens game that I've played. While the multiplayer is pretty much obsolete if not dead, the 3 campaigns the game offers are well worth the price. The Aliens' campaign is by far the most fun and unique, and if youre a fan of the series, you'll be especially happy because every level feels like it came right out of the franchise. The movement and pase of the game are perfect and combat between the species is tense and frightening. The Marine campaign which i assumed was just going to be a glorified space shooter, actually was brilliantly written. The Marine campaign became extremely difficult and scary fighting the fast moving aliens, and it felt more like a horror game then i expected. The Predator's campaign was the weakest in my opinion, but the gadgets that you get to play around make up for it, and the campaign follows the small movie details of the predators arsenal to the book. Overall, a very fun game for a fan of the franchise, serves as a benchmark for all other games in the Aliens franchise.

While I didn't like this game, I don't think it is a terrible game. I was dissatisfied with the following:
1) The game is in swedish. The only thing they did was changed the interface to english. The voice is in swedish and there is no subtitle which makes following the story a bit difficult. The story is fairly simple but not having subtitles makes you guess a lot.
2)  The gameplay and controls. In this game you basically have to control 2 characters to solve puzzles. While the game does well at making you coordinate 2 characters to play the game, A LOT of basic game mechanics is flawed.
For example, I was stuck at triggering a lever with 2 characters for 5+ mins multiple times. You can't do anything besides from pressing space and ctrl and wait. This really put me off because it so basic and the game got it wrong.
The game was also overly simple. The should've implemented certain things like a timed challenge or penalty. The boss fights is very easy. This game is more geared towards casual players.
3) The storyline. While a lot of characters in the game is creative, the plot is not. It is basically fantasy adventure that meets a realistic ending. I wasn't impress and I don't understand about the hype of the story.
Overall, it is still a solid game for $5.

I really enjoyed this game. It's a visual treat, with puzzles that are fun and challenging without being frustrating and repetitive. What the developers have done exceptionally well is develop the characters in such a short space of time (you could easily get through this game in three or four hours) even though there's not a word of English anywhere in the game! The sheer amount of emotion this game is able to conjure makes the length of it far more appropriate; there's simply no way to keep up the barrage of darkness, desperation, depression alongside happiness, achievement and celebration over the course of a 20+ hour game and this makes it short and sweet, rather than abrupt and unfulfilling.
Although I wholeheartedly recommend this beautiful game, I will say one thing against it (and many, many people will disagree with me)...
****POSSIBLE TEENY-TINY HALF-SPOILERISH LIKE PARAGRAPH****
They got the ending wrong. To me, it felt like an unnecessary last gasp, desperate grab for some cheap feels which lessened the sense of achievement I got upon completion, but without really adding anything from a storyline perspective. Many people have enquired as to an alternate ending and I think it might be good for them to add one, maybe as a reward for completing a second play through and thus also improve replayability. Regardless, it was effective, and I still greatly enjoyed the game overall.

Note: Writing this review with 15.3 hours into the game. Some of it was spent with me AFK making food or tending my kids lol.
So far, the game is fun and enjoyable considering it's an Early Access game there are some flaws and bugs here and there obviously. You have 3 classes to choose from: Warrior, Mage, and Ranger / Archer. As of right now, I feel the Warrior got the short end of the stick from the 3. Since he's CQC and with the current combat system, the whole not being to move while swinging your weapon doesn't work too great. Now, going forward... The game starts you off on a small island with barely any monsters to fight so it's an introduction to the game.  Get some wood, make a workbench, kill a skeleton, grab some blue crystal shards and then form blue crystal cubes and rebuild the portal. That is practically what you will do to progress further into the other islands. For accessing the boss islands from what I've seen, instead of blue shards, they're yellow shards. The shards are relatively easy to farm but, I try not to rush through each island considering each island has it's unique resources to farm. The game is not difficult for me, for others I don't know but, I enjoy it because I play it to enjoy the scenary and explore each island and find the hidden treasure chests that they have. So for those who have been rushing through, you probably missed a few. I won't say it's a mandatory thing or the reward from the chests is something amazing but, it's something to do instead of just rushing through to reach the final boss and say... oh well, now what?
I just had my first co-op experience today with a buddy of mine. So far, I feel there should be a trade function or a drop item button, because as of right now... the only way you can give an item to a friend is by placing it in a chest and having your friend get it from the chest. That can be really annoying especially if you pick up some loot that he or she was getting from a loot chest and you happened to be close by and it goes to you instead.
First boss was nothing too special but, I will say I died the first encounter because I wasn't sure what to expect lol.
Cons:
Auto-lock camera combat needs work.
Progression to other islands are too simple (reduce the drop rate on shards to where it's not so easy or... add a mini-boss spawn when you are opening a new portal to the new zone... something along the lines).
Warrior needs some work, seems slighty weak for the current combat style.

I won't lie, this game has its problems, its glitches, and general dissapointments at times, such as not being able to make full use of my 144hz monitor as the game will have rubberbanding issues when running at 144fps. The combat isn't the most in depth and yes, I made a warrior character and I realize that they are practically useless when compared to the mage and archer class, but that adds a challenge right? A lot of people point out these among many other things you can complain about the game saying the game is bad, or it doesn't have enough content, as far as I'm concerned the only thing that they really do have to do something about is the lack of it really being a sandbox game. What makes a sandbox game a sandbox game is when you have the freedom to build whatever you want however you want, and while it does have this, the fact that you don't have a hub world that you can travel back to, and the inability to travel back to previous worlds, does kind of reuin that experience for me. However, what I think most people are overlooking is the price, at the time of writing this review and when I bought this game, the game is $13.59 CAD which is pretty damn cheap for me, I don't expect much out of games fairly inexpensive and still in Early Access, which means they'll improve it, so far I've been having a lot of fun and have had a seemless experience in Co-op.
If you are someone who feels like they need a perfect game no matter what the price is, you shouldn't be looking into early access, and to everyone who has already bought the game and is upset, it will  improve, look at Ark, it has undergone massive changes and is one of my favorite games on steam *despite the horrible optimizations* so just wait it out if you think you might not enjoy it.

Although I do not like writing reviews for games that I have not finished, I felt that it was warrented for this game. It has a lot of negative reviews that I do not think are justified. I'm going to explain to you why you shouldn't just listen to the negative reviews. Most of the negative reviews are not about the actual game itself, so I feel that I can chime in on this issues.
-One major complaint is the fact that it uses Uplay. Personally, I do not understand what is the big deal with Uplay. The only thing that I notice is that it takes a little bit longer to start up, not much else. Even with Uplay, the game still has achievements and trading cards. Also, I do not think Uplay should be reason enough to hate a game.
-Another big complaint is the fact that there is day one dlc. While there is dlc, it is entirely for cosmetic character items. It does not add anything special to the game, just a bunch of cosmetics. They have not taken anything major away from the game for this dlc, just cosmetics.
-This one goes with the one above, but their were complaints that some items were only available for people with Uplay Club. All of these items are again entirely cosmetic and do not change the game.
-I've also seen some complaints about the preorder bonus, which I find amusing. I preordered, and the bonus is literally just a towel. Every once in a while, as long as you have the towel, Towlie will come up and give you a minor tip, but these tips have all been mostly useless. This item is entirely useless, and I do not think it should warrent anger against it.
-In terms of "glitches," I have only experienced one that it seems everyone has been experiencing. When you first start up the game, it is at a black screen. It can easily be fixed by pressing ALT + Enter. I agree that this definetely should have been fixed before release, it does not draw away from the gameplay.
Most of the criticisms towards the game are petty and have little to do with the game itself. From what I've played so far, the game is awesome and hilarious. Just from playing the early game, I am already enjoying the game more than the Stick of Truth. If you want the game for its gameplay and comedy and don't mind a couple of minor annoyances, I recommend that you buy this game.

I give the developers credit for experimenting. Before Dead Space or FEAR, this was a somewhat novel idea, and had never been tried on quite this scale. Truth is it almost feels refreshing compared to today's games. Based on the 2016 remake's success, fans wanted an arena shooter with QTEs and two hours of cutscenes, not a claustrophobic horror game that tried to deliver exposition in a subtle, streamlined way. The ironic thing is that the old Doom games constantly utilized abruptly-spawning enemies, and hidden monsters behind doors, guarding ammo caches and even in dark coridors. Which makes me think some of the people who criticized this game for departing too much from the original may not have ever actually played Doom. The real difference is that the original was so forgiving. Doom games in the '90s had overpowered weapons and AI on par with Pac-Man.
Sure, there's problems--the shotgun is trash and they insist on the old clown-car gimmick in a few spots (endlessly spawning enemies simply to chew up ammo & health or artificially speed up your pace)--but at least there's no color-specific card collecting.

This is a slightly worse Metal Gear. The levels that I saw don't have the long open areas that are good for sniping, and they mostly look like a 1940's African reimagining of the less-good Halo 4 sections. Lots of tight spaces and close-quarters fighting. I spent 70% of my time crawling around like Solid Snake, 25% hiding behind whatever cover is available because some pisshat saw my ankle for a quarter of a second and alerted every ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ within a mile radius, and the last 5% being proud of a shot I made despite it only being about a third of the range most shots in V2 were.
The pre-mission briefing is gone, so you have no idea what kind of loadout you should take, though to be fair there are a bunch of weapon choices and being able to fine-tune your rifle is a nice touch.
The levels aren't as linear as V2 was, which is nice in some spots. But it feels more like a sequence of tiny sandboxes separated by narrow doors and just doesn't feel as tight as V2.
Never tried the multiplayer, but this just doesn't seem like the kind of game where that would work. (though to be fair I thought the same of MGSV and it turned out to be pretty cool)
The tweaks and additions to the killcam are neat, especially the vehicular kills, but it just didn't seem as satisfying as V2 for some reason I just can't put my finger on.
You remember that one level from V2 towards the end in that industrial sector with the Russians and Nazis duking it out? Imagine that, but everything's made of beige stone and the godrays block your vision half the time. That is the entirety of SE3 that I experienced.
TL;DR : just play MGSV with a sniper rifle.

Simply put, this is a beautiful game that I recommend to any gamer, especially those who favored PlayStation's Ico many years ago. The visuals, music, story, and gameplay are amazing. Yes, it's a short game with no "real" replay value, but I believe it makes up for that in other aspects, such as the story and how beautifully crafted the landscapes are. It was a great 3 hours of gameplay that I'd gladly play again in the future because I enjoyed it so much the first time around. I've already replayed a few of the chapters to get some achievements that I missed. It's a shame that the game/story did not go on longer, but at the same time, the brief gameplay experience also makes it somewhat magestic in its own way. All in all, this game is something everyone should at least try.

Instead of our usual tabletop RPG sessions, one of my players invited our DnD group over to play Eon Altar at his place.
It was SO. COOL.
As soon as we saw the screen that said "You are your characters voice," we were sold. The character banter/interactions are awesome and present an interesting frame to learn eachother's "secret" thoughts. The crusader's loud and long winded speeches are the perfect counterpoint to the assassin's withdrawn and calculated jabs.
The combat takes a fight or two to get used to, but it's usually easy enough for everyone to just do their own thing. During more difficult battles, communication and cooperation are crucial. For instance, the sellsword gets extra attacks after a kill, so the assassin can weaken a group of enemies to give him a path for his carnage. Or that moment when the mage's player puts his arm out in front of the crusader and says, "Wait! Dont rush in you idiot! I'm gonna use a fireball!" Brilliant.
It took us almost 4 hours to get through the first episode, including a break for pizza. It was a great experience, and an awesome substitue for our regular RPG session. We'll be getting together again in two weeks to knock out chapter 2!

First off, do not go into Clear Sky if you haven't at least played Shadow of Chernobyl first.
I'll begin with my overall opinion of CS. It's inferior compared to SoC, and especially inferior compared to CoP. The Faction Wars system, one of the main selling points to CS, is confusing at best. You can side with three different factions in each area of the game (though you automatically side with one by default at the beginning), and then certain factions become hostile towards you. In return, you get the chance to earn extra jobs and top-tier equipment earlier than normal. The only problem is when you have to actually fight the opposing factions. You need to travel to certain areas of the map, take out any resistance you encounter there, and wait for backup to arrive. In addition, if any of those areas come under attack, you're expected to show up and help out. Thus, you sometimes wind up with scenarios where you're halfway across the map, and get a call from a lone survivor armed with a shotgun to high-tail it over to their position and kindly take out the group of seven guys all armed with military-grade automatic rifles, please. The worst part is that your opposing factions don't stay dead. I've captured every single point including the main base, and killed everyone I possibly could, and they just respawn the second you leave. The good news is, while you will still have to help your allies out, you still get paid a substantial amount of cash for taking out the main base, so it's not all bad, I suppose.
Without a doubt, the worst part of CS is the enemy AI. For the most part, it's the same as SoC, except for the fact that these enemies can use grenades. Even on lower difficulties, you'll be tapping the quicksave button every few kills just in case they decide to spontaneously send an entire squads' worth of grenades next to your feet. Even worse is the fact that the AI is ungodly accurate with those grenades. Wherever they throw them, they end up directly at your feet with a one-second fuse. It's not at all uncommon to watch an enemy throw a grenade in the wrong direction (as in, they're facing away from you), only to see it reverse directions in mid-air and teleport right next to you. This is especially bad on the final mission, where enemies literally spawn from nowhere armed with automatics loaded with armor-piercing rounds and grenades primed and ready. The most common thing I found myself looking for in CS was not ammo, or artifacts, or even money, as opposed to SoC. No, it was bandages and medkits to replenish any health I was losing from unfair grenades. If you're playing through on higher difficulties, your first priority is to find some armor that isn't completely terrible, and then stock up on as many healing items as you can. Otherwise, you most likely won't stand a chance.
If you're coming from SoC, you should know that the system for picking up artifacts is radically different than how it used to be. Where they used to be waiting on the ground in plain sight for you to just grab, they're now hidden in the centers of anomalies. You won't be able to grab an artifact unless you have your detector out (press the O button to pull the detector out, and press 2 to dual-weild it with your pistol), and unless the anomaly you're looking at happens to contain one. Most anomalies don't. Personally, I held off on artifact hunting until I got a better detector, but if you can deal with lots of trial-and-error and quicksaving, you're welcome to try.
Speaking of artifacts, not every piece of armor you find can actually equip them. For some, you need to take it to a person who can upgrade weapons and armor, and pray that they're capable of adding an artifact container or two. Thankfully, most armors can, although it will cost you a good amount of money, even more than upgrading a top-tier assault rifle. Speaking of upgrades, if you couldn't already tell, you can do that now. The same people who offer upgrades also repair your damaged weapons and armor (for a nominal fee, of course), sell you locations of stashes (which can also be found on dead bodies, although sometimes the person selling you a location will tell you what you can find before you open it), and offer you jobs which usually consist of "find information on a particular upgrade in a stash somewhere and bring it back to me". Keep in mind that you still need to find the stash first, as it's not marked on your map.
CS has a much different atmosphere compared to SoC and even CoP. While the other two are generally dark and dreary, Clear Sky is actually rather nice. By comparison, I mean. It's still the Zone, after all. It feels a bit out-of-place compared to the other two, but given that this is a prequel and things aren't as bad yet, it's to be expected. The mutants are still there, so it's not too different, but it is certainly noticeable.
All that being said, I still think Clear Sky is a fun game. If you can deal with the grenades, the different atmosphere, and the gameplay changes from SoC, you shouldn't have any problems at all with it. Be warned that it is a STALKER game, and is prone to bugs and crashes. I got lucky and only had two with this one, as opposed to CoP which wouldn't launch for the longest time, and SoC which crashed several times and wouldn't let me begin a new game without freezing until I messed with the options. If these happen to you, the very first things you should try are running Steam as administrator, disabling the Steam overlay while in-game, and switching the lighting options to Static. Those will solve a large amount of the issues you'll encounter.

This review is for people who have played Shadow of Chernobyl.  It's about the single-player campaign, with the Complete mod.
I hope you liked the previous game, because you're essentially about to play it again.  Given that this one is a prequel, there are so many similarities in the environment (which is about 80% the same as the first) that you get a kind of wistful echo of adventures past (or rather, future).  It's a bit interesting to see what various parts of the zone were like before SoC.
You play as Scar, a merc who has survived emissions from the Zone for some unknown reason.  Once again you're chasing Strelok (really!?!).  The first time he entered the heart of the zone it set off an emission which was similar to a small cataclysm, setting all the factions against each other.  Your objective is to prevent him from doing it again, which would possibly produce a lethal emission killing everyone.
The new wrinkle this time is the faction system.  It's really just an extension of the old system, with some capture the flag type elements.  You can even take part in the initial war between Duty and Freedom this time around if you like.  Although the rewards are meager for this type of activity, it nonetheless makes the zone a far more dynamic place than it used to be, with NPC's shifting around constantly depending on who wins what fights.  Inconsequential, but you do get this vague sense that you have a hand in shaping the zone.
The combat system is still bull****.  I hope you weren't expecting any serious improvements.  Bullets still go wherever the **** they want, even with the Dragunov on occasion.  Enemy AI is just as bad, possibly a little worse (and that's with a patch to improve it!).  Even so, it is definitely satisfying getting the headshots with a scoped weapon.
This time around you can actually upgrade your weapons at various smiths, and find schematics to deliver to the appropriate npcs in order to get specific upgrades.  Kinda neat, and meant to extend the life of the game, but wholly unnecessary.  Same goes for your typical stash drops, which are now a part of NPC dialogues.  Fork over some dough for the information, and most of the time they'll tell you what's in it before you even leave camp.
You'll still reload frequently, but nowhere near as much or nearly as rage-inducing as the first game.
I can't testify as to how bad the final mission is (remember the last one on SoC?).  My game permanently crashed on all saves about two areas before the end, so I had to watch the ending on Youtube.  It was moderately unsatisfactory, and frankly I'm glad that I didn't have to worry about however bad the last mission was probably going to be.
A lot of other stuff is recycled.  The game looks a little better, but you can tell they didn't particularly try.  If you look at my play-time, I'm guessing it's about the same length as the first, maybe even a little shorter.  The shelf life was no doubt meant to be extended via multiplayer and dynamic zone faction wars.  This is Shadow of Chernobyl 1.5, essentially.  How much you liked the first game will directly determine if you like the second.

You're trying to save your ailing father, after all!
Nevertheless, this game has something that I'll call artistic value, not to mention something to say. It's about growing up and the acceptance of death, and learning that life can be difficult at too young of an age, but finding the strength to go on. The gameplay is fun and a bit out of the ordinary, the scenery is gorgeous and the game has no understandable dialogue but manages still to have one; humans say a lot with body language, after all.
All in all it was quite an enjoyable experience, and seeing as I picked it up for under five dollars with a sale and some money in my steam wallet from trading cards, I'd say it was worth much more than I paid, despite its short length.

For this review, I'm going to ignore the fact that the launch was inexcusably bad. I'm going to ignore the fact that the game was unplayable until the afternoon of the next day. All I will focus on in this review is the gameplay itself.
It is not good. MK9 was one of my favorite fighting games because it blended 2 certain things really well: It is graphically appealing, and its mechanics are fluid and enjoyable. Now let's look at MKX. It does indeed look attractive, but graphics do not make a game. Some of my favorite games are indie games that aren't fancy in the graphics department (Risk of Rain, Terraria, etc). And when it comes to a fighting game of all game genres, graphics should not be the priority. Unfortunately, it seems Netherrealms was too preoccupied with making a pretty game than a good one.
I am not a fan of these "Variations". Look at Melty Blood; Varations are not a good system. In theory, character variations give players different ways to play the same character, each variation having different strengths and weaknesses. In practice, however, you get poop. Some variations just suck. period. Some characters have variations that are just flat out better than the other ones they have. I think I speak for most people when I say I would MUCH rather have a character that is polished than have 3 half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥versions of the same character to pick from.
The combat does NOT feel good. In MK9 and MKX, you can jump over your opponent and hit them with a punch to start off a combo. in MK9, it looks and feels smoother than it does in MKX. In MKX, sometimes it doesnt connect. other times you land before the punch connects. Also, sometimes your character is facing the complete opposite direction when he tries punching his opponent... it feels sloppy. in MK9, dashing was infinitely better than it is in this game. There are about... 100X more frames in a MKX dash than in a MK9 dash. it does not feel good to combo with a dash in this game. The best thing to do is slowly walk towards your airborne opponent.
If you are like me, you loved your kombos. In MK9, your basic combos involved using a kombo string and linking in a special to end the combo (or keep it going). 1. MK9's kombos did more damage and felt better to perform. Not only that, but in MKX, a lot of the special moves have 0 combo potential unless you throw in a bar of your meter. What is this nonsense? Some character variations can barely combo, if at all, unless you use meter. which is awful.
and lastly, there seems to be some mechanical issues with MKX's combos. This may be just my controller, but I doubt it. Pick johnny cage using his normal variation. try doing inputting this combo like you would any other combo: 1 2 down back 3. What is supposed to happen is Johnny Cage will punch twice and then perform a backflip kick. But what actually happens is Johnny with throw 2 punches and then throw an energy ball. I input 1 2 down back 3, but it THINKS I'm doing 1 2 down back 2. I'm clearly pressing 3, but it thinks I'm pressing 2 a second time. Which I'm not. Again, this could just be a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ controller problem, and I hope it is, but it might not be.
Overall this game feels like a downgrade in every category save the graphics, and in the end, graphics are the least important quality of any game. Unfortunately, spoiled rotten gamers have convinced AAA names that graphics are all that matters, and anything else is secondary. This game is not a COMPLETE mess (anymore), but it's not a very good fighting game. On top of everything that I've stated, the PC port is BAD. Even after the fixes, there are still many players (including me) suffering from inconsistent FPS issues and random crashes. If you MUST buy this game, then buy it on the PS4 (or the Xbone if you make poor life decisions). But if you have neither and feel like you must buy this game on the PC, then... good luck.

Fun little survival on alien world/s early access game. Collect resources, build your base up, perform research and explore the surface and underground caverns (and then other planets/moons). Game is very much in alpha, but able to be enjoyed in single player currently, recognising that you will have some crashes and glitches. If you expect your games to be optimised, with polished controls and relatively bug free, then wait until release.
Multiplayer is enabled but I wouldn't recommend doing more than just taking a look. Sync issues are rampant and there appears to be no mechanism to routinely resync. When driving, lag can result in the non-host players getting ahead of landscape detail being rendered, causing physics issues when things pop in underneath or inside you. Falling through the terrain is a regular occurrence. Some messages e.g. research outcomes are only displayed to the host. Basically, the multiplayer allows others to jump into the hosts game and help them out. They don't have separate bases of their own and can't save their own progress - it simply saves to the host and non-host players rejoin from scratch, hoping to locate and raid their previous backpack (corpse). Potential to be an enjoyable co-op experience once the dev's get around to working on the multiplayer. They've apparently published a roadmap on their site/forum, but I've not taken a look at it yet to see where mp sits in their priority list.
As at the date of this review, only recommended if you plan on playing single player. Not recommended in its current state if you primarily want to play multiplayer - wait for some multiplayer specific patching to occur.
Reviewed based on 20 December 2016 version (four days day after release into early access and with a couple of patches).

A quick notice before you read:
I decided to post this because the System Requirements look scary, but the game doesn't really need half of them to play Single-Player. Low spec fans of the franchise shouldn't feel intimidated because of some miscalculated requirements.
I will give Tekken 7 a proper review next month once I get back on my desktop.
Hi, I'm that guy who dares to play your favourite fighting games on really low specs online.
CPU: Intel Core i5-5400U
GPU: NVIDIA GeForce 920M
All graphical settings turned down to their bare minimum. All of them. It still looked good enough to know what the heck was happening.
This game runs at a constant 60fps on this computer.
Multiplayer didn't desync ONCE in two seperate matches with my friend who's on an actual gaming computer. In fact, he didn't feel any lag at all. Not only that, I'm on Wi-Fi with a crap signal. I had a tiny bit of input lag, though.
Matchmaking works somewhat well. I have a lot of "connection with the opponent has failed" or some other similar prompt appear sometimes when I find a new match, but I think that's the game's way to softly tell me that the adversary just doesn't want to play against a guy named "meme magic" who is playing Lili.
Take that as you will. In my opinion, for the first online Tekken on PC, this is perfect.
Beautifully optimized and no controller needed. After buying Injustice 2 on PS4 and Tekken on PC, in my opinion, Tekken wins without a doubt. Highly recommend this game.

The characters are all diverse visually and from a gameplay-wise, while also being (seemingly balanced). It took a while before I settled on Lili as my main, but I’ve been able to enjoy my time with any character I pick up. However, I trust the avid Tekken community to find imbalances in characters I may have missed in my relatively short review period.
Moving on, the game is visually interesting. While Tekken 7 doesn’t feel like it is bringing much new to the table in terms of visuals for fighting games as a whole, every scene in the (bizarre) story was fun to watch… as long as I didn’t care about the plot. It did come at the expense of some longer-than-usual load times on my PC, but nothing too long that wasn’t forgivable.
Tekken 7 delivers true fighting game experience. It has solid online multiplayer, pretty up to date graphic, nice soundtracks, big initial roster, unique character and in game UI customization, sharp input controls, and challenging combo. What it lacks is single player/offline content. It has a story mode but it's very shallow or should I say rushed. If you are looking for a great, fun, and challenging fighting game, look no further. If you're looking for story/offline content, better rent or wait for sales
PROS
+Massive roster of varied fighters
+Satisfying combat with loads of depth
+Robust online mode with decent netcode
Cons
-Doesn’t do enough to teach newcomers
-Not Much Of Single Player Content( I do not care much.....i am in for online play only)
Conclusion and verdict:Tekken 7 is one of the best games in the series gameplay-wise, but it's a little short in terms of single-player modes. 4/5 (will get my♥♥♥♥♥♥beaten by Gouki Again)

Clear Sky, in it's untouched state was unplayable for me until I installed the COMPLETE mod. At that point the game opened itself up to me, and I'm loving it nearly as much as SoC.
Like the original, it's initally unforgiving, with an excellent soundtrack and a seriously ominous and unnerving world. The map is improved to give the player more detail as to who is around them and what their function and intentions are, and the interactions between the different factions are a lot easier to interpret, which makes intervening and helping people out a lot easier.
You spend a bit of time re-treading old locations, which can be a bit disappointing. However, the areas are occupied by different factions with different goals and it's kind of nice to see how the area changed over time between this game and the SoC, to which Clear Sky is a prequel.
It also has some new graphical features, particularly when it comes to lighting, that really brings out some more polish in the game's visuals, and makes any action performed during nightime a terrifying affair.
This is not my favourite of the Stalker series - that remains SoC - but the world is still compelling and oppressive as balls, and the core mechanics are more refined than those of its predecessor, so it certainly is worthy of the player's attention after finishing SoC.

Pros: The missions are very long and involved and you generally have an unlimited way to approach them within the bounds of the game. A single mission can last a couple of hours. The sniper kill graphics are pretty cool but tire after the first 10 times or so. You can easily skip the slowmo by hitting space bar to get back in the game. The player AI is pretty good and the NPCs generally work to seek you out if they are aware of your presence.
Cons: There are still significant bugs and restrictions in the game. Clipping errors and bounding regions that are too restrictive are a big issue. Areas that you should be able to fit through in the game are often frustratingly blocked. Also, the 'open world' is not as open as it could be. This really limits the immersiveness of the game by forcing you to stick within the walled bounds of the playfield and restricts your ability to move around. Areas where you should be able to climb or walk or crawl are restricted which makes the game play frustrating at times.
It's a decent game but not worth the $54.99 regular price. Even at the sale price of $10.99 I'm not sure it's worth it.

You guys may have released your game, but it needs a lot of work to be up to par. In September 2013 Rockstar released GTA V. It was impressive in some ways, disappointing in others. The open world was satisfyingly detailed, and the main characters were entertaining to spend time with. On the other hand we were never given much incentive to explore the world; the structure was all a bit sloppy (the flying school, for example, is never brought to your attention, unlike in San Andreas); the main story never really went anywhere; and there are only two talk radio stations (the fewest in any GTA I can remember). None of the characters learned anything or changed in any way. On the whole, worth £30, but it never could hope to reach the heights of the Ballad of Gay Tony. All a bit slapdash, and carried the air of a product with a few too many people working on it and which consequently lost its focus.
The PC release added some novelties, and it's a good port, but nothing fundamental has changed. I've played a lot more BoGT than GTA V on any platform.
All in all GTA V was a solid effort, and great grounds for future expansions. Unfortunately we're never going to get those expansions. Two or even three single-player DLCs were planned which would have fitted into the game beautifully and given us a reason to go back. Alien invasions and zombies - check out the Mount Chillad mystery reddit for details. Unfortunately Take Two cancelled these in order to focus on the microtransaction cash cow that is GTA Online.
Plenty of other reviews detail the problems with GTA Online. I played it for a while with friends when it was first available on the 360. We rapidly lost interest though, as there wasn't really anything to do that other, more focused games couldn't do better. And that was before T2 started focusing all their efforts on more microtransactions in lieu of doing anything about the omnipresent cheaters and hackers.
So: no single-player DLC to give after-sales support, and multiplayer isn't worth a damn. So why would you buy the PC version? Mods was the obvious answer. However, T2 have now decided to oppose modding. That thing which the fans were doing better than them: adding value to the GTA V product. By shutting down OpenIV T2 have made it much harder to get the majority of mods running, and they won't stop here. They don't want you to have fun with mad stuff that the community makes up. They want to engage you in constant psychological warfare in order to drain your wallet with microtransactions. Apparently being the fourth or fifth bestselling videogame OF ALL TIME, not including the HUNDREDS OF MILLIONS OF DOLLARS they make from microtransactions ever year simply isn't enough money.
I feel bad for the devs at Rockstar. Once upon a time they made videogames, new story campaigns, worlds and characters for us to explore. All creatively fulfilling work. Now they're expected to feed the microtransaction machine by adding the occasional new gun and new vehicle. I understand that Rockstar's already started to lose staff, and I wouldn't be surprised if some of them were simply bored out of their skulls making this crap and decided to go and do more interesting work. And when T2 finally get bored of making all the money in the world and want a new GTA game...well the talent base, passion and experience has already started to leave.
