I have only played about an hour and a half of the game, but from what I can tell, there isn't much too it.
You start out on an abysmally small floating island, and are presented three quests to complete in order to teach you the basics of the game. Make a pick axe, kill some mobs, create a portal.
The point of the game is to go to all the worlds and then kill the boss at the end, I guess. The systems in the game are very clunky and strange. Anyway, to the nitty gritty.

1. The game is very pretty and is visually impressive, for what it's worth.
2. The crafting holds promise for the future, but there is really no point to it other than upgrade your equipment and forget about it.
3. You can customize your character differently, so there's that.
4. There are 3 different classes, I'll touch on this later.
5. Can play first person or in third person mode, which is really nice option.

--
--
1. Auto Targeting is awful. It is a Tab-Targeting oriented combat, which doesn't really work out very well.
2. Can't move while attacking. You swing your sword/axe/mace and it moves you toward your targeted enemy a small distance, hopefully so you stay within hit radius.
3. Camera Locks in combat, and it's very bad. It zooms in and goes into a letterbox mode.
4. Automatic. You just right click and wait for the enemies lifebar to go away.
5. Clunky mechanics. You can't Evade attacks midswing, and must be standing stationary in order to execute an Evade.
6. You cannot attack a mob on a block higher or lower than you in melee.
Now, the combat could be worse, but it's also nothing special. It's extremely basic and feels very automated to the extent where you literally just hold Left Click and drink a potion once in a while.
--
--
1. Nonexistant. The "Worlds" you go to are nothing more than tiny floating islands. By tiny, I mean depressingly tiny. Small enough to where you can explore the entire thing in 3 minutes.
2. Uninspired. The worlds are all disconnected and isntanced chunks of land. There is no reason at all to ever stop and build, because you will leave the island in 7 minutes and be on your way.
3. Linear. There is no need explore anything, you kill some mobs, get your portal made and then leave the island. There is nothing noteworthy to find and it leaves the adventure feeling dead and bland.
4. The entire world is made the same every time. Same mob spawns, same layout, everything.
5. This game feels like the sandbox was an afterthought. You could play the entire game without ever crafting or building anything other than a crafting table.
--
--
1. You cannot allocate your stat points when you level up manually, they are automatically allocated, and the Skill Talents are boring and very dry.
2. The inventory/menu is tragic.
3. You cannot drop items or trade items. The only way to give another player an item is to put it in a chest for them to pick it up.
4. No Sprint/Run ability. Can't jump in combat, can't look around in combat.
This game leaves much to be desired.
In order to progress to the next world, require you to perform a task or defeat a mob, complete a puzzle, something in order for you to feel you are progressing towards something, not just killing some mobs to get your portal crystals and leave.


No portals. At all. The system is dumb and doesn't make sense in a sandbox game. Sandbox games are supposed to be an open world, not a series of instanced islands (extremely small islands, at that). Give a reason to build a base and crafting station. Perhaps create a "Peace Zone," that instead of "Portal Crystals" you get "Purity Crystals" that you can create a beacon of sorts to cause mobs not to spawn in X radius, and allows you to build Peace Zone only items, such as beds to spawn in or teleport to, crafting stations to upgrade armor and weapons, things of that nature.
The game desperately needs a large seemless environment, it's the biggest hinderance to the game in my opinion. I had little to know satisfaction running from island to island mindlessly killing mobs for portal crystals. It's a shame, because the game could be great.

Allow custom stat allocation. Let me put my points where I want them. There needs to be many more Skill Traits, and better ones too. Seriously, 30% increased mining speed? 15% Reduced Mining Durability damage? What the actual hell? Where is the "build your own story" part of the game at? You aren't given
tools to do this with. There are no quests other than the first 3 on the first world that is more of a .readme file.

Remove the Tab Targeting system entirely. You should not be tab targeting in an action combat game, it should be hitbox swing radius based. You should be able to cancel attacks with dodge roll, and be able to RUN ffs. Enemies are only dangerous in large packs, and melee is horrifically imbalanced and bad. Warriors are useless.
There is a lot of things I could suggest, but it's 6am and I need to go to bed.
All in all I feel very ripped off. This game should not have the Sandbox, Survival, Crafting, or Building tags. There is literally not a single Survival based element in the entire game, other than "don't take too much damage because you'll die."
It is in early access, but I feel that if they don't change a vast majority of the games systems, it won't do well. In its current state it is barely enjoyable. It was good for the first 40 minutes until I realized that there is no point in the game and nothing felt rewarding or exciting.
Do I recommend this game? No. Absolutely not. There are many other great voxel sandbox games out there to play.

Doom 3... the odd one out in the Doom series. Unlike its predecessors this game is slow paced and focuses more on the atmosphere rather than the fast paced, arcade styled shooter people have come to expect from Doom. This is why it is deemed to be "the controversial entry", because this game tries to be something different than the other games, and for some people they enjoy it however some are dissapointed by not playing with the style of Doom they have come to love. Does this game do what it's trying to do well (make a good survival-horror game)? Yes it does, at least in my opinion. But whether or not you will like this survival-horror stylized game is up to your own taste.
The absolute highlight of this game that makes it a memorable experience is definitely its atmosphere. You are a marine who has been assigned a job as part of the UAC (a mars research facility) until things go wrong and demons start teleporting into the facility and  wreak havoc. Machines are malfunctioning, alarms are blaring, scientists are being possessed and a menacing, demonic cackle echoes through the intercom. It feels intense. Even though it isn't fast paced it is still adrenalin inducing due to the exciting circumstances. Although exploring the dark, underground science facility of mars was a great time it was a bit dissapointing that nearly the entire game was spent in this setting. Fairly late in the game you teleport to hell and it is absolutely incredible and was by far my favourite segment of the game. However the segment was unfortunately very brief and after going through hell a little bit and having a boss battle Doomguy returns indoors where he spends the remainder of the game in.
Story-wise this game is admittely basic. The story is fairly cliché and feels like a bit of a clone of Half-Life 1. I think it's cool how Half-Life was inspired by the original Doom and now this game is making a full circle and getting inspiration from Half-life but it's a shame the story is made so similar and didn't attempt to be more unique. If you want the backstory of this game fully explained to you you have the option to listen to audio logs that are scattered throughout the journey which means
the story isn't forced and it is an option as to whether or not you want to know about the story. I personally don't like learning the story in this format and couldn't be bothered listening to all the audio logs but for all those who do like it you can if you want to and for all those who only want to play the game for the gameplay you can simply ignore them.
In terms of the horror aspect it isn't scary since there is no fear of jumpscares nor is there the fear of being chased down by terrifying enemies unarmed, however all the satanic elements are pretty disturbing and f*cked up which is the style of horror this game strives for. If you are easily frightened by horror games and want to venture into the survival-horror genre this game is a good place to start, however if you judge the quality of a horror game by the amount it scares you this game will leave you unimpressed.
At the beginning of this game you will start with a pistol and as you progress you will find more and more weapons until you have an option of choosing between 12 different weapons. Most of which are the iconic weapons returning from the previous Doom games, with the addition of a few new weapons that are fun to play with. These weaopons will be used to kill enemies that have also returned from the classic Doom games. Enemies look different in this game and have been designed to look more scary. Some enemies are easily recognisable and same aren't. They all function in the same way as the classic doom games with the exception of the Arch-vile whose projectiles are now avoidable which is a great tweak seeing as how a pain in the @$$ Arch-viles were in Doom II. Gameplay is something that is pretty typical for a first-person shooter and doesn't really attempt to do much out of the ordinary but it is definitely a solid shooter and not something to be scornful about. Boss battles are dissapointingly easy to defeat and the scaricity was bosses was a shame.
There is a bit of a dispute between the Doom 3 community as to which edition is the superior version. Graphics are more customizable in Doom 3 and through mods it can be made to look quite impressive whereas the BFG edition has a set graphical setting to it that cannot be tweaked through the menu. Some PC buffs perceive the limited customizable options for the BFG edition as too "casual" but for most people it won't bother them at all. The BFG edition is the optimal version in my opinion and the game looks nice... apart from the character models. For some reason the character models still look a bit outdated even though everything else looks nice. Another notable change is how in vanilla Doom 3 you can't have the flashlight activated while using a weapon but rather you have to manually switch between weapons and the flashlight. It makes things feel more frantic and it makes the lab look a hell of a lot darker for the duration of the game. In the BFG edition the flashlight can be turned on or off while having a weapon equipped. Whether you think Doom 3 is best experienced without the constant dependcy of the flashlight or whether switching between the flashlight and the weapon just adds a tedious, unnecessary difficulty is up to you.

Absolute best game ever. Especially if you enjoy a realistic medieval war game. After 489 hours of gameplay and all the recent hype for this game's successor, I feel compelled to write a review for it. Typically my reviews are long and arduous, but I'm going to really condense this one because I simply feel like there's not much you need to hear about this game.
M&B is packing on the years now, but it has aged like a fine wine from Southern France. This game is everything you want an open-world RPG to be, create your character's backstory, put some points into some attributes and then you ready to enter the chaotic world of Calradia, where your character can be just about anything from the commander of massive army to a wealthy travelling merchant, you can even be a ruthless bandit who plunders villages in the countryside if you want to.
M&B is a game that focuses on episodic combat where the player fights alongside their party, typically this leads to some highly entertaining scenarios where you end up beating the odds (my personal favorite, a player-controlled army of 200 soldiers defending a city under siege by an enemy war party of approx. 1000 soldiers. By the end of the battle, my characters entire body was coated in the blood of enemy and ally and alike, truely one of my favorite moments with this game).
If you ever get tired of vanilla gameplay, there's mods, I highly suggest getting Gekokujo, a mod that changes the game's entire setting to feudal Japan where you can slice and dice (and even shoot) your way to the top, it changes just about everything and adds a whole new level of gameplay.
I also recommend the Napoleonic Wars DLC, you can really tell that the dev team really poured their heart and soul into it. Unfortunately, NW is multiplayer only, but there's something incredible about playing as a footsoldier in a massive line battle as smoke obscures your sight and musket shots roll like thunder all around you or when you lead a calvary charge and your fellow comrades let out a rallying war cry as they prepare to cut down an enemy regiment with their sabers. Most of my playtime was spent in NW, I used to play it just about every day.
M&B Wardband is without a doubt, one of the best games I have ever had the privilege of playing. It's criminal how cheap this game and its DLC are, if this thing goes on sale, do not hesitate to buy it immediately.

It wasn't until the latest Steam Summer Sale that I have heard about this game. I bought it for mere 2 euros then, but after playing the game I can assure you that it is even worth the full price.
Throughout my gaming years I have encountered many different games with many different stories, gameplay mechanics, etc. But this game stands out as a unique example of a gaming masterpiece. Why, might you ask yourself?
First, the game tells a story that maybe isn't the most original story ever told before, but the way it presents itself is simply amazing. You will almost instantly develop emotional connection with both of the brothers and it will last till the very last moment of the game. I can count with one hand the number of games that had such an emotional impact on me as this game did.
Second, the mechanics and gameplay are something I've never seen before. The reason Steam warns you that you need a controller to play is because you control both brothers at the same time. It seems tricky, but in reality is very natural and fluid. You will get a hold of it in minutes. I liked the concept.
All things being said, this game is short, but will take you on such emotional rollercoaster in it's 3-4 hours of story that you will never forget.
Must play.

Deponia is a comedic point & click adventure game very similar to the Lucas Arts classics Monkey Island and Day of the Tentacle.
I'm assuming that you are already familiar with the genre, so I'll keep this short and sweet.
Pros:  Fluid animation, high resolution graphics, good soundtrack, interesting plot, funny dialog.
Cons:  Puzzles are thrown in with arbitrary handicaps and do not contribute to the plot or integrate well.  The writers got lazy a few times and used the item descriptions from looking at an object as the narration when using the item as well.  It gets annoying hearing the same line multiple times when exploring or experimenting.
Recommendation: If you like this sort of game, get it.  You can always look up a walkthrough to deal with the puzzles.
Warning: This comedy in a later episode gets quite dark.  If you cannot stomach Southpark type humor, then you're better off skipping this trilogy.

Remember the classic animated point-and-click adventures?  Well here it is again with updated mechanics and even more off-color humor.  Great story and lots of DLC to you laughing for months (assuming you're a really slow player).

Germany. Elegant cars, cold winter, awesome beer. Ok, I'm definitely relying too much on stereotypes, but from now on we could surely add "very nice point and click adventure games" to that list. Interesting enough, german developers released a lot of good adventure games in the last few years, becoming probably the main contributor to this little "renaissance" of the point and click genre. And Deponia is one the best examples.
Someone described Daedalic as "the European Lucasarts" and I'm not entirely sure I can agree to that, but their games are solid. Very good story, challenging puzzles, polished graphics, everything is surely above average, Deponia is definitely a nice game. Characters are crazy enough to make you often laugh, A LOT of location to explore, non linear puzzle solving, and Daedalic recently added new languages, which is always kind. As a first chapter of a trilogy Deponia works just fine, the player is always pushed to play more to see how the plot will evolve. I got stuck two or three times, which is great in my opinion, 'cause it means they focused a lot on the intellectual challenge of the game and not only on the narrative side.
Definitely worth a shot, I don't think you'll be disappointed.

Portal Knights
If you like mining for materials, building structures, fighting mobs and falling off islands placed precariously in the sky then Portal Knights might be the game for you.
Character creation gives you a choice of 3 classes: Fighter, Mage or Archer and is pretty minimal. It's interface feels like you're creating a Nintendo Mii rather than creating anything complex and the characters have a rounded Lego look to them. Each class has abilities that they learn as they level up although some choices are somewhat confusing: the warrior uses STR as his primary stat so at level 15 he can increase his agility or int which are both pointless for him. The archer can increase STR (melee damage) or Int - again, both pointless?
Once you've created your character you're dropped on the starter world and given a series of quests to handhold you through the learning process of how things work. Once those have been completed the quests vanish and you're on your own from there to do what you want.
Once on an island defeating monsters (and, to a lesser degree, mining) gives you portal shards and these are used in the creation of portal stones via the crafting system and six of these special stones placed in one of the defunct portals around the island will power it up and permanently re-enable it for use. This gives you your gateway to another island and is Portal Knights method of progression.
There are 4 types of Portal stone that you can create and each colour stone takes a differing number of shards - the early starter worlds are accessed using blue portals and blue portal stones only take two blue shards to create each stone. Yellow portals start to appear around level 10 and yellow portal stones take 3 yellow shards so higher level portal stones take more materials to make. A portal will need 6 stones to activate it.
Travelling to another island opens up new blocks, ores, plants and mobs and each island can have multiple portals dotted around it. There's usually a dungeon too and these start off quite small but grow to a decent size on the later levels and are wonderfully lit. Mob variation within the dungeons seems a bit restricted though as far as I've seen - there's flying eyeballs, skeletons and..well, thats about it really.
Once you get to a certain point progression-wise you'll find one of the portals will take you to a special island. This only has a single mob on it and is a good, old fashioned boss fight. No spoilers here but its an interesting mechanic to drop in between the island exploring and isnt just a straight forward hold-fire-until-its-dead fight.
Crafting could probably do with a mention too. It reminds me somewhat of Starbounds crafting system in that you need specific machines to make different bits and those bits are used in other machines to make items (ie use a furnace to smelt ore > bars then use the workbench to fashion the bars into weapons).
When you craft something though it stays in the machine until you click it rather than going directly into your inventory. This is somewhat annoying but Im guessing this is so you can set up large batches of things that take a while and then go do something else while its crafting.
Overall its a very pretty game thats quite polished considering its just come into early access but obviously it still has its bugs. Quite a few people have had crashes/startup errors although the only ones I've personally seen have been a placement graphic bug (it was showing a doorway instead of the correct graphic when trying to place a chest) and a crash to desktop when I used a grenade to blow up a wall because I was too idle to mine it manually.
Tips:
-  Press M to get the map up. On the map screen clicking on a world will let you set that world as your home world or travel to it allowing quick travel to any world you've opened up. Clicking the tabs at the top of that screen will show you what mobs, plants and ores that world has. Useful if you're looking for something specific.
- On the map screen pressing the icon at the bottom right will port you to the entrance zone in point. Useful if you're stuck down a mine/on a cliffside and cant get back to the surface. Clicking the icon on the bottom left ports you to your home world (home world can be set from the map screen too).
- Things like doors/windows/furniture/statues in dungeons can be destroyed and picked up for use in your home. I found it particularly useful to rob the nearest dungeon of its doors to keep the drafts out of my new house.
- The level of the crafting machines define the number of recipes it has access to. Get the materials and upgrade them (up arrow icon at the far right of its interface) to get access to new, higher level stuff.
- Armour isnt class dependant. Any class can equip any armour/use any weapon.
- If you're a Warrior and having problems with flying things, carry a bow around as well as your main weapon.
Pros
+ Graphics engine is very pretty especially its lighting.
+ Music is also very good.
+ Crafting is in, working and already quite evolved.
+ Boss fights!
+ Leveling up and selectable skills for your character.
Cons
- Islands are miniscule and need to be considerably larger. This is my one major gripe about this game - there's hardly any exploration as you can pretty much see from one side of the zone to the other and cross it in about 60 seconds.
- Islands are also somewhat samey. So far I've seen 1 desert biome, 1 snow biome, 1 swamp biome and 11 green/leafy biomes. Hoping that gets a bit more varied in the terms of ratios of different types.
- The combat lock-on is annoying. I *know* I can hit tab to retarget. I dont need to be told every single fight.
- Cant rebind any of the keys.
- No real graphics options other than resolution,Window/Fullscreen and AA. There's also a Screen border x/y slider but I couldnt see that do anything?
- No run button. It feels odd to get attacked by something and then just nonchalantly wander away from it.
TLDR;
Very pretty game in the Cubeworld/Trove/Minecraft family. A few aspects of it are still buggy but overall its quite slick. Worth picking up if you're into those types of games (especially with the 20% off this week).
Its buggy (which is to be expected in an early access title) but its building a solid foundation for a great game.

You ever come across something once in your life where you feel you need to play, watch, listen to, or read but find something along those same lines which is absolutely better than what you found in the first place? This has happened to me several times. Meshuggah with their Obzen album and then finding their Destroy Erase Improve album, deep and engrossing anime with Neon Genesis Evangelion and then Serial Experiments Lain, the Rainbow Six series with Lockdown & Critical Hour and then Rogue Spear and Raven Shield, things like that.
The biggest example would be the Alien Vs. Predator movie, and then exploring both series' previous movies because I loved the creature design so much. As a kid in 5th grade, I watched the original Predator movie (GET TO THE CHOPPAH!!!!) and it absolutely blew me away. I had never seen anything like it and it really blew AVP out of the water. Then I watched the original Alien movie on VHS (It was at a yard sale for god's sake!) and again I was blown away. It was a good thrill and I found out why people hated AVP and AVPR so much.
But alas, AVP would soon get a second chance. I found out that there was a video game coming out called Aliens Vs. Predator and that it would be coming out on a bunch of platforms. Xbox 360, PS3, and this new thing called OnLive. I tried it out for the first time at my sister's house, my nephews owned the game, and I was blown away again (Okay I'm easy to please when it comes to Sci-Fi. :P)! I finally got to play as these deadly creatures, and a human soldier, and I would be playing through a story which is played out through three separate campaigns. I had to own this game immediately!
Then...time passed. I never got to own the game. Hell, I still don't own it. What I DID stumble upon though was that there were already quite a few AVP games that were released throughout the years. Knowing I had already stumbled upon a bunch of awesome classic shooters before, I decided to try this AVP game out. Holy...f***ing...sh*t. This game right here makes the 2010 AVP look like Call Of Duty. This game is a freaking blast. I'm not even joking when I say that this game needs to be in everyone's collection. It's THAT good. Now I know what you're asking, why do you think this game is so good when the other AVP game you checked out before was more recent. Well, let me tell you why.
Alright so story...uh...well...I'm not really sure what the story is. It does have three campaigns though, so I will tell you all I really know. As the Colonial Marine, I guess there's a Xenomorph embryo inside you, so I guess you're looking for some way to get it out of you I never really beat the game, which I will get to in a moment, but guessing by the whole embryo thing, Weyland-Yutani is probably going to use it for research. With the Alien, I guess your location has been violated by the Marines, not really surprising, and you gotta get them out. Predator...I'm not sure what he's doing there. Okay sure I'll be honest. The story is garbage, but whatever. Who plays these kinds of games for the story, anyway?
Okay so as I've said, the game contains three separate campaigns, one for each creature, so how do they play? Exactly how they do in the movies. With the Colonial Marine, you pretty much go around shooting the crap out of the Xenomorphs, which literally come out of the god damn walls, and also shooting up Predators, which have no time to bleed. With the Xenos, it's all about causing as much mayhem as possible. You not only have his claws, but also the signature tail. Not only that, but you can use the infamous bite when sneaking up on foes. With the Predator, it's just like in the movies. You HAVE to use stealth. Luckily, you have all of the Predator's weapons at your disposal. From the shoulder cannons to the wrist blades, you are sure to have a good time.
There are a few problems I have with the game though. One of my biggest complaints is...it's a little too dark. Like yeah, I can understand going for suspense, but because the game is supposed to be a classic shooter like Quake or Doom, this really doesn't fit. I know there are vision modes for both the Xenos and the Marines, but, at least in the Marine's case, there are moments where in the dark the lights are pretty dim, but they are blinding in night-vision mode. Another problem I have is the difficulty. There are some REALLY cheap deaths on the higher difficulties. I can barely get through a level without swearing at least once. Luckily, however, there is an unlimited save feature exclusive to Classic 2000, albiet via command, that makes this game a bit easier. If you are a fan of a challenge like this, buy it.
My other problem with this is the multiplayer. Well it's not really the game's fault, but it's really...empty. There's no excuse for it being this empty either. Rebellion made sure that in this re-release that this game would be compatible with not only Steam players, but GOG players! Why is nobody playing? Come on! This game is amazing! I know it's a nearly 20-year-old game, but it's no excuse. Quake III and Unreal Tournament still have people playing, so there's no reason as to why this game doesn't!
But overall, the reason you should get this game, even with its small annoyances, is how well this game really emulates the feeling the movies have with the three species you play as. With the marine, you really do need to kill or you will be killed. With the Xenomorph, you need to stay in the shadows while at the same time making humans your prey. With the Predator, you need to stay invisible and kill the humans stealthily or you will be shot. This game is amazing. If you are a fan of either the Alien franchise, the Predator franchise, or even both, you need to add this game to your collection.
And please, play some multiplayer. This game needs some love.

again, except Frank West returns along with his own original move set and attack animations, the story is shuffled around a little and there's a whole new area in the city - a space-themed amusement park. There's also a couple of new weapons (including combo weapons), a couple of new bosses, and a handful of gameplay changes, the things I remember the most being:
- Frank is infected and needs Zombrex every 24 hours, but he can inject himself no matter where he is, which removes the element of rushing back to the safehouse every day for Katey
- Frank's picture-taking mechanic returns
- If you're lightly damaged while holding a weapon you can't store in your inventory (say, a Gem Blower), you won't always drop it. You'll still drop it if you get knocked down, though.
The co-op is even better than before, because Player 2 still plays as Chuck Greene (still using his own move set and attack animations) and him and Frank have a fair amount of dialogue for shouting at one another. They're really rude to each other for no reason at all, which is really funny.
"Hey, zombie boy! I've got your drug!" -Chuck
(the actual reason being the dialogue was recorded for
- an X360-exclusive expansion (thanks capcom) - where the two of them start off on the wrong foot)
Oh, and let's not forget about the Sandbox mode! In this mode, you're free to just goof off with no time limits to worry about. You're free to carry over levels, PP and money you earn in Sandbox to the 72-hour mode and vice versa. Most of the bosses will spawn in their usual places at certain times, but the friendly survivors are now hostile and will spawn in set places and attack you. There's also challenges around the map, with objectives like earning large numbers of PP, luring zombies to a specific area, racing to a finish point, or just plain killing zombies, so that gives you something to do besides just mucking around and exploring, which is still always fun.
It's not as good of a port as the original
, which in itself was only an
port, but it's still not too bad. The most notable thing is that you can't turn depth of field off without hex editing, but it runs a little better after you disable that.
+ It's still DR2 - Still fun and funny, music's still good, the city still looks nice, co-op is still incredibly fun
+ The new additions and subtractions are generally welcome, most notably Sandbox mode
- It's still DR2 - Still kind of buggy and rickety and immature, having to earn speed upgrades by leveling up is still a huge pain
- It really didn't need to be a seperate, full-priced game

English(Deutsch weiter unten):
Train Simulator aka Railworks - the name doesn´t matter, the program is out for some years and still hasn´t become better, but even worse.
Where to begin with?
At first there would be the power hunger for just average graphics. My PC is not the issue - with i7 6700K, 16GB RAM, R390X and SSD drive it is strong enough to handle newer games.
However Railworks makes it necessary to reduce the graphics by a large amount so that it even looks more mediocre than before. And it is still plagued by ugly aliasing.
Maybe the game works better on Nvidia GPUs - but then it is just impudence as AMD is an equal competitor to Nvidia.
But graphics is not everything.
No, the program is also a joke in other aspects. Some versions ago they added this ridiculous shaking of the cab which you can´t turn off - this is NOT realistic and would make any real train derail. Guys, it is a train on rails, not a plane!
Then there is the steering of the program. Using the keyboard feels unresponsive and mouse steering is just mere moving of the cursor. Yawn.
Also the scenarios aren´t good. You only get a very basic set of them and they aren´t exciting. And especially the german routes are the same old stuff already released years ago for the MSTS, but then much better.
The activities are also nonsense and badly scripted, so not enjoyable at all.
The carrier mode is just a joke, who cares about a score for driving a train?
The rolling stock is also of bad quality. We got diesel locomotives that sound like a lawn mower and the class 143 sounds even worse than the oldest one for MSTS - like some air conditioning.
Railworks wants to follow in the steps of the Microsoft Train Simulator, but it will never reach that goal.
It will never have this large base of routes and rolling stock as the classic.
Also because of the outrageous pricing. 13,99 € for a single locomotive(!) or nearly 30 bucks for a route with small size are rip-off.
In MSTS times you paid 19,99 € for a route and it was much bigger than these for Railworks.
No wonder that there aren´t any good developing companies like German Railroads interested in making content for this.
You can buy a TGV route with 30 minutes of riding time - laughable. There is another TGV route with nearly 3 hours travel time available for free(!) for MSTS/Open Rails.
Overall this game and it´s content aren´t even worth buying it when on sale.
I rather recommend(especially for people interested in german routes): Get some addons for the MSTS and Open Rails(freeware) as modern MSTS version, then you have better graphics, performance and much more fun as this half-hearted collection of mediocre undersized routes and lackluster rolling stock with it´s bad controls and performance including the noddy-shaky cab view. And if you want more realism get the freeware Loksim 3D or the more expensive but even more detailed Zusi.

Deutsch:
Train Simulator aka Railworks - egal welcher Name, das Programm dümpelt schon seit Jahren vor sich dahin und wird nicht besser, eher schlechter.
Womit fange ich an?
Da wäre erstmal der enorme Leistungsbedarf für allenfalls mittelmäßige Grafik. An meinem PC liegt es nicht - der ist mit i7 6700K, 16GB RAM und einer R390X nebst SSDs durchaus stark genug für anspruchsvollere Titel, die ansonsten ja auch gut laufen.
Nur Railworks erfordert die Reduzierung der Details um ein beträchtliches Maß, damit es überhaupt erträglich läuft. Dennoch ist die Grafik von häßlichen Aliasing-Artefakten geplagt.
Ob es eventuell daran liegt, daß das Programm eher Nvidia-affin ist? Wenn ja, ist das eine unfaire Benachteiligung von Käufern von AMD-Grafikkarten, schließlich ja ein gleichberechtigter Wettbewerber.
Aber Grafik ist nicht alles.
Nein, das Programm ist im Großen und Ganzen auch so unbrauchbar und macht keinen Spaß.
Vor einigen Versionen hat man z.B. das lächerliche Führerstandsruckeln eingefügt - wir sitzen hier aber nicht in einem Flugzeug! Das Ganze ist unrealistisch und unpassend. Bei dem Gewackel würde ja jedes Fahrzeug entgleisen.
Dann wäre da noch die Steuerung. Tastatur ist viel zu schwammig, Maussteuerung reduziert das Ganze auf Hin- und Hergeschiebe von den immer gleichen Schaltflächen. Gähn.
Auch die Szenarien überzeugen nicht. Standardmäßig enthalten sind nur wenige Strecken, davon sowieso einige der Marke Asbach uralt, die schon zu MSTS-Zeiten umgesetzt wurden - und schon damals deutlich besser.
Die vorhandenen Aufgaben sind ebenso Quarks - schlecht geskriptet und alles andere als vergnüglich.
Der Karrieremodus ist derbe unnötig, wozu sollte man Punkte für das Fahren eines Zuges bekommen?
Das Rollmaterial ist ein Witz, die Dieselloks hören sich an wie ein Rasenmähertraktor und wann es endlich mal eine 143 mit anständigem Sound in der virtuellen Eisenbahnwelt unabhängig vom Programm gibt, steht wohl auch in den Sternen. Die von Railworks hört sich auch nur an wie eine Klimaanlage auf mittlerer Stufe.
Railworks möchte quasi in die Fußstapfen des MSTS treten, was jedoch nicht mal im Ansatz gelingt.
Das Programm wird nie den Umfang und die Spielbarkeit des Klassikers erreichen.
Dazu trägt auch die dreiste Preispolitik bei. Man läßt sich ja jeden Kleinkram vergolden, eine einzelne Lok für 13,99 € ist echt unverschämt und daß Addons in der Regel sowieso knapp 30 Tacken kosten, ebenso. Das kann man nur als pure Abzocke bezeichnen.
Früher für den MSTS waren eher 19,99 € pro Addon die Regel, und dafür bekam man in der Regel auch wirklich was geboten.
Es wundert nicht, daß sich z.B. Qualitätshersteller wie German Railroads bislang gar nicht für Railworks haben blicken lassen.
Wenn ich sehe, daß man hier eine TGV-Strecke vom Umfang von einer halben Stunde kaufen kann - lachhaft. Für den MSTS gibt es eine andere und sehr gut gemachte TGV-Strecke mit ca. 3 Stunden Fahrzeug als Freeware(!).
Der ganze angebotene Krempel ist es nicht mal im Sale wert, gekauft zu werden.
Es gibt jedenfalls deutlich bessere Alternativen zu Railworks. Holt euch lieber die MSTS-Addons für wenig Geld und Open Rails(kostenlos) als moderne MSTS-Alternative, das ist grafisch dann auch im moderneren Look und macht deutlich mehr Spaß als diese halbgare Ansammlung von mageren Strecken, schlechtem Rollmaterial mitsamt miserabler Steuerung und Wackeldackel-Führerstand. Und wer realistische Zugsicherungssysteme will, findet mit Loksim 3D(kostenlos) und Zusi(anspruchsvoller und kostet auch was) auch bessere Alternativen.

If I were to rate this game, I would give it a 6/10. I do like running trains around, and some of the simulations in this game are really, REALLY good. (FEF-3 is my pick for best DLC.) But if you think this game is without fault, you are seriously mistaken. This game has several large setbacks: 1) If you have a lower end computer, DON'T get this game. Even if your computer belongs in NASA, you will still experience large lag spikes due to the chunk based system this game uses for routes. The engine (the game engine, not the ones you operate) is really old and outdated. Thank god they're making a simulator that uses a better engine for this. 2) The DLC model is terrible. $40 for a route, $20 for a locomotive is the standard price for DLC in this game. Don't adjust your monitor; $40 a route, $20 a loco. Seriously. If you want to actually get your money's worth, WAIT FOR THE SALES. And 3) The simulations themselves. The quality in the DLC fluctuates more than Donald Trump's ideologies. THAT is an accomplishment in itself. As a rule of thumb, if DTG made it, don't expect a large amount of quality. If you want an actual simulation and not a toy, look to the Pro range thing they have. There are some good pieces in there. "SMEAGOL!!", you may ask. "Why are you giving this thing a thumbs up if you wrote a huge paragraph explaining everything wrong with it??" The answer is simple: because you CAN find enjoyment in this game. Even with its glaring flaws, there are times when you enjoy yourself playing this game. I have never been happier than I've been letting the UP 844 pound its way up Sherman Hill, listening to some classic rock, and towing a rather large train.  And I'm sure you can find yourself some ways to enjoy the game yourself. Just make sure to keep the downsides of this game in mind and you'll be in good shape.

Looking at some of the other reviews, I almost wonder if somehow a totally different game downloaded for me. The concept of this game is amazing, but it's just plagued by terrible execution in literally every aspect of the game.
I'll start with the technical aspects. The controls are OK I suppose, the movement controls are very touchey, the UI on the phone isn't organized very well either. The graphics are terrible, and the art style is generic and boring. It's also very poorly optimized. It wasn't playable on my laptop with it's integrated graphics card, so I figured no biggie I'll play it on my desktop (i5, 16 gig ram, ssd, and a GTX 1070). Needless to say it runs anything out now at rock solid 60 FPS at 1080p. Well anything until Eon Altar, where during the only "large" battle I fought my franerate dropped to an absurd 18 FPS.
The characters, world, story, and dialog are bland as plain cream of wheat. All the generic fantasy characters are here, spouting cliches left an right. Talking to the other characters is a nice touch I guess, but even that is all standard and predictable.
The gameplay is equally sleep inducing. It's not a traditional turn based, grid movement style, kind of system. The heroes all have a turn, where they move and perform an action simultaneously, and the enemies then have their turn doing the same. Positioning seems extremely unimportant sadly, as enemies can just rush right through melee characters to get to ranged or injured heroes, and rear attacks didn't seem to make make any difference. I could be wrong on that, as the "tutorial" provides scant information well after you'd first need it.
Overall its like almost anything, if you're playing it 3 friends who are fun, you can still have some fun. The problem is literally every other couch co op game, card game, board game, role playing game, movie, etc would be more fun. It's entirely possible I'm being overly negative because I expected greatness, or at least playability, based on the glowing reviews, and maybe players who have less experience with table top, card, board, or other couch Co op games would enjoy it. It's a great concept, and one I hope is attempted again, but this game failed at almost every single step of the way.
Nice bonus, I can't refund it because I waited 3 weeks until I could get 3 buddies together to play it. If you do buy it, at the very least try it out right away so you don't get screwed like me.

Mortal Kombat X brings everything from the Mortal Kombat universe together in a perfect upgraded-package. The visuals are great, the way every single character has 3 different movesets allows for amazing variety between the cast, and the game runs perfectly.

This game really feels like the culmination of all the other games come together. The game handles the same as ever, controls haven't changed much at all over the years which means it is very easy to pick up and play. Of course there is more depth to it than mere button bashing and the range of combos that can be carried out is better than ever. Each character now has 3 variants which are significantly different to each other and will encourage a huge amount of replay value learning all their intricacies.
Of course the fatalities, brutalities are back and as gruesome as ever plus the X-Ray moves from MK9 return but beefed up and feel far more rewarding. There is a huge roster of characters with 8 entirely new characters, plus most of the favourites in there all looking better than ever it must said, the graphics really are excellent.
New to this game is the introduction of factions when starting the game for the first time you will be prompted to join one of these factions, every person in this faction whether playing multi-player or not contributes xp to that faction and levels up. When finished maxing out in that faction you can then switch to one of the others and start again; admittedly this isn't all that exciting as levelling up is nothing more than playing the game but it does add extra replay value to the completionists out there who will want to max out every faction.
As far as single player goes the story is fairly short and I have knocked it out in just under 4 hours, far more substantial is the Tower which contains a number of challenges (not sure how many yet) that get progressively harder, completing these unlocks additional content and Koins which can be used to purchase various items in the in game shop similar to MK9.
Multiplayer is the usual fare of 1v1 local or online and King of the Hill winner stays on battles and will doubtless be where the majority of time is spent having battles with friends and is great fun as ever.
Overall this is a superb Mortal Kombat game, may yet prove to be the best to date but will need more time with it before taking that decision.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky is the prequel to S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl. I recently delved into this game again, and I figure I should review it. S.T.A.L.K.E.R. has always had a focus on factions, but Clear Sky soups up the faction system like crazy. You can join any of the not-immediately-hostile major factions (i.e. Military and Monolith), which include, off the top of my head, Duty, Freedom, Bandits, Loners, and Clear Sky. You get special gear for joining specific factions. I prefer Duty, personally.
The gameplay is solid, although it's essentially the same as Shadow of Chernobyl but touched up a little bit. The accuracy is dictated by whether or not you are crouching, or if you are using iron sights. You bleed if you are shoot in a non-vital spot, so do enemies. Enemies, if hit in a location that bleeds a lot, will eventually keel over and die or curl up on the ground dying. If you hit an enemy in the head, it's an instant kill, unless they are armored up with some of the more powerful gear, or unless they are a zombie. I think it takes 2 or 3 shots to the head to drop a zombie or a guy wearing an exoskeleton.
A big perk of this game that they added in Clear Sky is the upgrade system. You can attach/detach silencers and scopes, as you could in SoC, but now you can go to NPCs who can upgrade your weapons and armor. You can upgrade gear with composite plates, extra carry weight, artifact slots, etc., and improve accuracy, fire rate, recoil, and even reduce bullet drop and change ammunition type on some weapons.
For those who played SoC, artifacts are significantly harder to find in this game. Rather than being able to see artifacts, you need to find them with an anomalous activity tracker, which will track them with beeps. I strongly suggest getting to Yantar ASAP and upgrading that puppy to one that has a map attached to it.
I feel like there is more to do in this game than SoC, with the faction wars and such. But it does seem like there are less side-missions. That's kind of a con I suppose. Anyway:
This game has a lot of pros: The combat is interestingly difficult and forces you to think out your combat encounters, or have your entire carry weight taken up by medkits (Don't do that, that's a terrible idea). The faction system and faction wars are awesome. The upgrades are neat, the game is gorgeous, and blah blah blah.
On cons: This game suffers from pretty much the same issues that Shadow of Chernobyl did. Those are bugs, lots of bugs, the game tends to crash every so often (Quicksave! F5 is your friend. Do it often!), and... An issue I had with SoC that I still have with this game, is that it has an ABSURD difficulty spike in the last act of the game. I can't help but find it irritating. You have a set-up and souped up gear that has allowed you to breeze through everthing else, and then come the last act, you feel like you're wearing the leather hoodie you start off with, equipped with a... I don't know... BB gun.
Anyway, this game is an excellent game, it should be played.

I've never been a fan of point-and-click games, I picked up Deponia since "uh-it's-cheap-I*ll-give-it-a-go" and then kind of forgot about it for months. Until recently, when I decided to sit down and actually see what it's all about. I instantly fell inlove with the atmosphere, I love the graphic scenery and the dump that is Kuvaq, the little village on Deponia. Rufus is the kind of guy that himself claims to be master of everything, but as far as others are concerned, he's master of disaster. Still, he manages to assemble the most peculiar things in his inventory - the very first struggle I had was "how the heck do I get a hold of that TOOTHBRUSH????" - it takes a good amount of thinking before getting used to the whole "pick up everything you can and if you can't use it instantly, try to combine it with something else in the inventory". Needless to say, I don't play puzzle games on a daily basis but I do have a tendency to explore everything in one area before proceeding to the next - which is basically what you want to do in this game too. Otherwise, it's easy to miss picking up something or miss an important clue given from some of the characters while speaking to them.
The minigame puzzles aren't obvious on how they should be solved, and even if patiently listening through a whole conversation with clues both once and twice, I had my fair share of problems when trying to solve them. Nonetheless, they are amusing and once succeeded, you'll probably feel a bit "ha-HA! There ya go!" - until you encounter the next one..
As for the story, it's pretty straightforward. Rufus desperatly wants to leave Deponia and will do anything in order for that to happen - when encountering the beautiful Elysian girl Goal he sees his new opportunity rising - he manages to get her into trouble but from his point of view that's excellent news, now he can help her and claim a reward for doing so - to get off Deponia! The road to success isn't all straight and narrow though, but bumpy and grindy - with loads of obstacles along the way.
I like the characters, Rufus especially - his well-meaning intentions aren't always apparent, though. I like the story, it has all elements in it - a bit of action, love, humor, betrayal, villains and of course the old conscience acting up - "what's best for not me alone, but for everybody?". To me, the game is exactly as long as it has to be, in the end it actually feels like "Oh, come on already, aren't we through yet?" *but* it also left me with a feeling of "Now I want to play the next part of this trilogy, I want to know what happens next!". I understand those who thinks the game is quite short, but to me it was sufficent.
What I don't like about this game is the tedious multiple choices you have to go through in order to obtain certain items. It's okay when playing on normal mode but when unlocking Droggeljug mode (after finishing the game) they don't make sense anymore. Even if I instantly replayed the game in Droggeljug mode, I couldn't remember how to obtain a certain item from Hannek and it left me extremely frustrated.
I didn't play through the whole game in Droggeljug mode to get the achievement for doing so, I had a saving quite close to the end and played from there on (even then, it was a bit tedious as it's quite much conversations happening near the end) - when every option in multiple choices is replaced with DROGGELJUG, you need to remember which number of the options is the right one - and if the question is branched into several pieces, you can easily lose your temper. I had to mute the game because I got tired of hearing "Droggeljug" constantly :P
I recommend the game if you like humorous point-and-click games with catchy soundtrack, clever puzzles, wacky characters and a good story. To each their own, if you don't like those things, don't buy the game.
An enjoyable point-and-click adventure with interesting characters and setting. Puzzles make sense and are possible to figure out even if, like me, you are not an expert at the genre. Well worth it.

Alien versus Predator Classic 2000 is a first-person "shooter" made by Rebellion. As being both an Alien fan and a Predator fan, I bought this game having little to no knowledge about the game. My results... well let's take a look shall we:
Pros:
+Amazing Gameplay - Each character (Alien / Xenomorph, Colonial Marine, and Predator) has a different play style. Example: Xeno. = Stealth & Speed, Predator = Michael Bay everything, and Marine = Survival. This variety of gameplay makes the game more diverse gameplay-wise.
+The Campaigns - The Campaigns are done very well. None of the Campaigns feel the same. It's almost like playing three games in one. Alien campaign = Alien: Isolation Xenomorph's point of view, 2. Marine campaign = What Aliens: Colonial Marines should've been, 3. Predator campaign = The perfect Predator game (Come on Terminator wheres your game)
+Respect for the source material - The entire game respects the source material from both the Alien and Predator franchises. Locations like Fury 161 and LV-426 and weapons like the smart gun and the shoulder canon are faithfully recreated.
+Facehuggers - Thats all I'm going to say...
+Not made by Gearbox or Paul W.S. Anderson
Cons:
- While playing as the Alien, the Alien's fast speed does cause the camera to go all over the place. This may cause motion sickness.
-Level design may cause some confusion since there are no maps and some parts of some levels may look the same as other parts.
-Objectives can be tedious as sometimes you may or may not know what to do / where to go. Objectives are given by messages that pop up on the top of the screen, but they can easily be missed.
-Graphics have not aged that well, but their decent for the time. The graphics kind of look like Half-Life 1's graphics.
Overall, (8.5/10) AVP Classic 2000 is a really good game. However, this game does have some flaws and is a bit challenging at times (but it can be completed if you have a lot of paitence). If your fine with the cons and are an Alien / Predator fan, then this game is for you.

The "Academy" is quite poor - repetitive short scenarios which fail to properly explain controls, etc.  The Academy contains only the most basic of instruction, no info that I saw on how to access various in-game menus etc., which I found later by pressing buttons to see what did what.   The 4 included routes seem to conatin no tutorial missions.  Nothing in the Academy, for example, explains how to properly use the dyamnic braking system.  This is just one example; there are many things not explained.  I've had several other rail sims in the past and even done some training as a fireman on real setam locos, so I'm not exactly a complete novice where it comes to trains - even so, finding it hard to control the trains reliably.  There may be scope to adjust the control sensitivty, for example, which would no doubt help.
Career missions rated "easy" are, notwithstanding the rating, annoyingly easy to fail completely.  Examples include tight timing which has to be achieved or the mission fails - if you don't travel at or very near the maximum allowed speed you will be late and get penalties.  No doubt that will improve with practice.  It is possible to set up a "quick drive" in which you have no goals, so one can learn to drive the trains like that, but better tutorial missions or a better "Academy" which teaches more, rather being so reptitive, would give the novice player a better chance fo succeeding.
So far the game is tolerably reliable.  The career screen, where you select route and scenario can be infuriating - I have yet to really determine how to reliably select the add-on package I want, it seems to reset them more or less at random.  I've no doubt there's some logic to it, but like the operation of the trains, it's not really explained.  Nor did I find the "manual" button did anything.  I don't know if Steam installed manuals, but if it did the game doesn't open them.
I have experienced one crash to desktop, which I don't expect from such supposedly high end software - this was during a tutorial from the "Sherman Hill" add-on; which does at least HAVE two tutorials, unlike the add-ons included in the "premium" package.  Of course, that add-on costs additional money, which doesn't bother me too much, but kind of makes me wish I'd gone for the basic game and then chosen add-ons I wanted.
With all that said, the actual graphics and simulation are pretty good.  I have no real beef on that score, although the frame rate suffers a bit on my fairly high-end (Nvidia GTX960 4GB graphics, 8-core Athlon, 16GB main ram ) machine, when there is a lot of detail to draw, such as on the NJ lines with overhead wires and many tracks.  I did have the graphics quality set to "high", though.  It is possible to set custom graphics parameters.  The graphics are starting to show the age of the underlying engine, though.
Altogether, although the graphics and simulation seem decent, the game doesn't feel as good as I hoped it would, and in all honesty doesn't really feel like a polished, finished product.  There's considerable variation in the quality of DLC, too - some of the older locos, especially, could do with better textures - although with TrainSimWorld in the pipeline that is probably wishful thinking.
As others point out there is much DLC - some of it very good - but much of it too expensive, in my view.  Routes are typically tolerable, but some individual loco add-ons are too expensive, espeically as it would appear to be pot luck what you get:  by buying some add-on locos you unlock additional scenarios in routes you already have - but especially the in-game store system is very poor at telling exactly you what you'll get.  In some cases there is more info in Steam, but the in-game store is much better for finding what you want, making purchasing unnecessarily complicated.
One final gripe:  How hard would it be to build in an auto-save?  Almost every other game I've had for years has such a feature.  Without it, it's possible to play 95% of a 2-hour scenario and lose all the progress due to a fault, crash, or mistake, so you have to do the whole thing again.  Realistic, maybe - but very annoying.
This review thing won't let me be non-committal on whether I recommend it.  I suppose, if you like rail sims, I do: at least some of the issues go away with further practice and more fiddlin' to see what does what.   That said, if I were a complete novice at driving trains, I suspect I would by now be abandoning it.  It would be better, rather than yes/no (or in addition to, maybe) if we could rate out of 5 or 10.

Just an hour or so into the game at the moment of this review.
I was NOT a fan of Minecraft.
I AM a fan of Portal Knights.
I think it's just a level of polish when I played the games. Aside from a bug with the resolution, this game has been very smooth. This seems to be an EA title done right. There are quests and purpose but there is also sandbox exploration. I spend a good 45 min in the first level tinkering and exploring. What you don't see in the First Look lets play videos is that there's a whole cave system under the first level with chests and few loot stashes to be found.
Enemies seem to be changing in the first level as well as I level up. I started out with just the slimes, then they threw in "Parrots" that look more like mutant little dragon things than birds... And what looks like undead knights at lvl 3.
I got the game on sale for 20% off but I think what I've seen so far justifies the 14.99. If it keeps up this pacing it could probably get away with 19.99 or more and still be a good value.
Now, It IS an EA title so there are issues. As I said, there is currently a bug with changing the resolution where you have to edit a .cfg file manually. (Search the steam forums for 'Resolution' and you'll find the fix instructions easily.) It's not difficult just annoying.
Attacking locks you in place. There is a dodge mechanic but if you're attacking, dodging does not take priority. While this is annoying, it could be by design to add some skill to combat. I could go either way on this one but I'll post it in the negatives as I think most would not be happy with it.
The game explains a good deal of your purpose in the world but there are still some areas which need a little attention. For example, your house. A little over an hour into the game and bags are full. I need to start thinking about building storage but the game hasn't introduced your home at all. You have to muddle through the menues and happen to see a house icon on the world map. It just doesn't match the level of introduction the rest of the features have atm. I expect it will get better as development continues.
I definitely recomend the game while it's on sale and after as well. Seems like it will be a good time eater.

Basically think of it as a lite version of minecraft + trove. The combat is simplistic but more tactical than minecraft, with a simple dodge mechanic. Note that attacking freezes you in place, so you have to time your dodges and attacks, no spamming. But once you get the hang of it, it's easier to play than most games.
The building functionality is very light weight as well. Basic array of materials, with very little variety at the start. It's not Terraria, Minecraft, Starforge where you have a lot of variety of blocks early on.
Everything is strictly tiered. Not a lot of alternatives with give or take. Just straight improvement over improvement.
My recommendation is to use this as a cheap or relaxing way to get into voxel based games, but if you're looking for an advanced builder or combat game, all the other options are better in some regard.

This is just to summarize as whatever I typed below is more like a Journal:
Portal Knights is like Minecraft with much, MUCH more fun Boss Fights. Mostly focussed on co-op play though so bring a friend.
Journal:
This game is good. There is a bit of lag on mine, where the character either move too fast or can't keep up with the mouse movement. I think that might be my own computer problem though.
On gameplay, good luck to those who choose warrior. It's my job and i'm drinking those hp potions like crazy! Dodging is hard on warrior, as I keep holding the attack key which spams attack and can't dodge in time. Have not tried the other 2 classes yet, but it should be easier than the warrior class since they are ranged.
This is more focus on being a multi-player game though, as the moment I went to the 2nd world and tried fighting during the night, I was mobbed like crazy. Good thing the mine was nearby so I could easily escape. Death has no penalties in the game so far which I like.
Overall, besides the mouse sensitivity and lag problems which i think might be due to my computer not the game, I enjoyed this game alot.
Update after playing awhile more:
Ok so warrior is not that weak. After I upgraded my wooden sword to copper battle axe, killing things got much, MUCH easier. With the spells added in I can survive now.
Walking around feels a bit awkward though, with the 3rd person view sometimes going wonky and the first person view not showing much at all. And during combat the first person view does not auto-aim the monsters unlike 3rd person view, and yet you can't move freely as well, always walking around the monster you have targetted.
2nd (and probably the last) Update :
I've fix my lag issues, thanks to helpful reviews in the store page. All is fine now, except that gameplay gets a bit tedious after awhile. Once you have found a trick to melee gameplay, as long as you don't get mob you'll definitely win. For flying enemies, it's a good thing we are allowed to use other weapons like the bow, because the electric bats you encounter in the early dungeons just never, ever, goes to the ground! Died to them 2x before remembering a review saying that we can use other weapons beside those for our jobs as well.
I've not fought the boss yet, but it should probably be around the same like Minecraft ones, with more action probably.
3rd Update:
I've done the first boss fight. Victory in the first try. Maybe the boss needs to be stronger? I went in there thinking it would be much harder than that. Even prepared a few regular healing potions, and made sure I got full viking armour set too. The first boss definitely can be harder than that.
4th Update:
I've found the range weapon for the warrior. And now that I've advanced further in, there's seriously a lot of weapons and armour set, and each have it's pros and cons too. Combat gets much harder the deeper you go into the game, and that heal spell saved my life plenty of times.
It would be nice if we could have multiple buffs on at the same time though, but each buff for the warrior currently only last 10seconds at most. Currently the warrior +Att Spell and +Def Spell are seperate, and since both only last for 10seconds and you can't use it together, having to choose between which to bring along makes things difficult. Maybe late game spells have a option of joining those 2 together so I can have the best of both worlds? I'm only at tier 2 upgrades after all, on iron equip so I have no idea about the late game spells.
5th Update:
I finally reach the 2nd boss fight, and damn what an adventure it was! This is not minecraft or terraria or any other game that previously came out that is similar to it. THIS IS PORTAL KNIGHTS! And the 2nd boss fight showed it. Damn it was good. And I thought it was going to be as easy as the 1st boss too! It wasn't though, the balance was just nice.
Conclusion:
This is a great game, and I would recommend you to play it. Just try to play it with a friend since it can get a bit tedious after awhile, as being alone makes it very tiring collecting items and grinding.
Currently everything in this game is about encouraging co-op play, with the heal spell upgrading to healing a partner as well, and the warrior spells being split into +Att and +Def, which means having 1 person tank while another attack is the recommended gameplay. Mobs also get much hugher HP further in, so having more people together means faster completion of the level. Finding the portals also gets harder too, so having more people helps.
I've only at most reach mid-game status though, so I hope it improves later on for those that prefer playing solo. But this game is definitely different from any other blocky game out there!

*WARNING: This review is based on the vanilla version. Modders discretion is advised.*
Doom 3 is certainly a great reimagining of Doom 1 with a heavy emphasis on atmosphere and subtle narrative, the only downside being the shooting.
POSITIVES
+ The Half-Life feel in the beginning, setting up the events that will unravel
+ The Half-Life feel throughout the game (meeting survivors & scripted events)
+ Terribly scary
+ Hellish imagery/iconography
+ Great use of lighting and shadow
+ Complex and coherent level design
+ Video files, audio logs and emails adding to the background story
+ Pinky Demon, Archvile, Hellknight, Mancubus, Cyberdemon redesign
+ Memorable boss fights
+ Simple and clever puzzles
+ The Soul Cube
+ Great length for a single player FPS (between 9-12 hours)
NEGATIVES
- Shotgun is ridiculously inaccurate
- Machine gun, chain gun and plasma gun feel underpowered (rate of fire and damage output)
- Shotgunner zombies shoot at you with pinpoint accuracy and double rate of fire
- Enemies never flinch when getting shot by automatic weapons (bullet sponge syndrome)
- Over reliance on trapping the player in unavoidable situation (cheap ambush & monster closet tactics)
- We only get the BFG at the very end of the game
- Only one level set in Hell
- Engine uncapable of generating gibs or dismemberments, making the rocket launcher kills unimpressive
- Low polygon count models
Verdict: Doom 3 definitely stoods the test of time, although not a masterpiece. It is an audacious take on the franchise as it trades the straightforward action for a more slow paced experience.
Rating:
8.5 / 10

To all the people who refunded this game and called it the biggest scam of the year: Thank you for doing so, we don't need that kind of impatience and stupidity in the MK community. For those of you who did and will download the whole thing before calling it a waste of money and ♥♥♥♥♥ing about every little thing that they never got to experience because they're mentally challenged, congratulations! Welcome to the beautiful world of MKX, full of everything that's good in the fighting game genre. I can't say I got too far in the story, as I was downloading it for most of the night and then had to stop shortly after I started due to work in the morning, but what I did play was phenomenal. The fighting in the single fight games I played were fantastic, the fatalities even more brutal than the last game, the combos and specials were fun and easy enough to use, and looked beautiful (Much like the rest of the game, I might add). The Krypt was also a very pleasant surprise. Where as before, it was just a scrolling area to unlock concept art and costumes and such with Koins, now it's a grid based mini-adventure game with statues and other things littered around to purchase costumes and concept art and brutalities and such. It still has the functionality of the old Krypt, with the added bonus of being a little mini-game in and of itself. I spent a good portion of my download time here just playing around and unlocking stuff (Seeing as you get a ton of koins for just doing things there, I managed to buy a good chunk of the unlockables, despite entering the krypt with only 1500 somethign koins). The new characters in the game are also incredibly interesting, and fantastically designed. This game is quite possibly one of the best games I've played in the fighting game genre to date, and it's going to take quite a bit to top it.
Overall, do I recommend this game? Yes, if you like fighting games. I'd even recommend this to those that don't like fighting games, just because of how good the final product is. I feel bad for those who refunded the game, as they're missing out. But hey, maybe the whole slow download process was Nether Realms way of weeding out the idiots from the community. I can only hope they don't come back.

In September 2013 Rockstar released GTA V. It was impressive in some ways, disappointing in others. The open world was satisfyingly detailed, and the main characters were entertaining to spend time with. On the other hand we were never given much incentive to explore the world; the structure was all a bit sloppy (the flying school, for example, is never brought to your attention, unlike in San Andreas); the main story never really went anywhere; and there are only two talk radio stations (the fewest in any GTA I can remember). None of the characters learned anything or changed in any way. On the whole, worth £30, but it never could hope to reach the heights of the Ballad of Gay Tony. All a bit slapdash, and carried the air of a product with a few too many people working on it and which consequently lost its focus.
The PC release added some novelties, and it's a good port, but nothing fundamental has changed. I've played a lot more BoGT than GTA V on any platform.
All in all GTA V was a solid effort, and great grounds for future expansions. Unfortunately we're never going to get those expansions. Two or even three single-player DLCs were planned which would have fitted into the game beautifully and given us a reason to go back. Alien invasions and zombies - check out the Mount Chillad mystery reddit for details. Unfortunately Take Two cancelled these in order to focus on the microtransaction cash cow that is GTA Online.
Plenty of other reviews detail the problems with GTA Online. I played it for a while with friends when it was first available on the 360. We rapidly lost interest though, as there wasn't really anything to do that other, more focused games couldn't do better. And that was before T2 started focusing all their efforts on more microtransactions in lieu of doing anything about the omnipresent cheaters and hackers.
So: no single-player DLC to give after-sales support, and multiplayer isn't worth a damn. So why would you buy the PC version? Mods was the obvious answer. However, T2 have now decided to oppose modding. That thing which the fans were doing better than them: adding value to the GTA V product. By shutting down OpenIV T2 have made it much harder to get the majority of mods running, and they won't stop here. They don't want you to have fun with mad stuff that the community makes up. They want to engage you in constant psychological warfare in order to drain your wallet with microtransactions. Apparently being the fourth or fifth bestselling videogame OF ALL TIME, not including the HUNDREDS OF MILLIONS OF DOLLARS they make from microtransactions ever year simply isn't enough money.
I feel bad for the devs at Rockstar. Once upon a time they made videogames, new story campaigns, worlds and characters for us to explore. All creatively fulfilling work. Now they're expected to feed the microtransaction machine by adding the occasional new gun and new vehicle. I understand that Rockstar's already started to lose staff, and I wouldn't be surprised if some of them were simply bored out of their skulls making this crap and decided to go and do more interesting work. And when T2 finally get bored of making all the money in the world and want a new GTA game...well the talent base, passion and experience has already started to leave.

Brothers:  A Tale of Two Sons is absolutely beautiful!  Every scene is a work of art, but that's not even the high point - the storyline is definitely what this game is about.  Actually, I think I would call it a story, not a game, maybe an interactive fiction.
Mechanics:  I played this game with a keyboard when it first came out (yes, it does work just fine with a keyboard) and although it is a bit difficult to learn to control two characters, it only serves to keep you from rushing through and missing the beauty of the story.  My second play, several months later, was with an XBox 360 controller, and it was even better that time, even if I already knew what was about to happen next.
Puzzles:  Well...some are more difficult than others, but none are fiendishly difficult, as in games like the Myst series.  They're clever, but not difficult.
The one low point is a slight cheesiness to the little brother.  But then again, he is a little boy and the cheesiness fits.
I would recommend this game especially for children, but people of all ages will enjoy it if they're NOT looking for battle or hack/slash.

A simple, yet extremely annoying bug. Given the game isn't new, how this bug still exists in the game is a mystery.
What bug is this? Well - you line up a shot, you fire... nothing happens. The enemy is still alive. You think "well, OK, perhaps I twitched at the last moment and missed?". You line up a second shot, fire... another miss. What gives? Well, you're shooting the small wall / barrier / plank in front if you rather than the target. The scope suggests you're well above it, but nope, you're not shooting where you think you are. The "hold breath" also shows the bullet should hit the target (not obstructed).
This bug appeared so many times during my relatively short game, than I really don't wish to bother with it any more. Which is a damn shame, because the game otherwise seems great.

While this is 99% true, there will be times when an orange frog sets off a shopkeeper and then bam! you're fighting shopkeepers on every floor. This game is a rogue-like filled with a ton of secrets and two different endings for different skill levels. If you can get all the achievements on this game I commend you. Be prepared to play patiently, making every action deliberate with thought put into it. That's not to say you can play slowly, as the ghost will be bearing down on you if you move too slow. On a good run, your heart will be pounding through your chest as you make your way past Anubis (being mindful not to use his rod to accidentally melt your own brains) down to Olmec-- and if you're good enough through Hell to Yama. I recommend this game for those who are prepared to die, a lot. The only way to win is to get better. Good luck!

This is a *very* hesitant "no".
AVP(1) is an old game, about half of which totally holds up, while the other half doesn't and in both cases it's for the same reason; it's designed based on somewhat antiquated principles. So, you have three campaigns; Alien/Xenomorph, Colonial Marine and Predator. The visuals were subpar even when the game came out in '99 and they're even worse now, but the atmosphere is top-notch. The game does a great job putting you into the shoes of each of its characters and properly making you feel like them. The marine is standard claustrophobic horror shooter where darkness is prevalent, the Predator is a proper killing machine pit against lesser species and the Xenomorph is rightly fast and stealthy and, well, alien.
That's the half that works. The half that doesn't is that difficulty isn't balanced. There are handicaps against the player in all three campaigns; the Xenomorph may as well have the campaign renamed to "Motion Sickness: The Game", the Predator is a powerhouse, but its weapons suck (except for the shoulder-cannon; respect the shoulder cannon) and the Marine is a weaklink whose weapons feel like nerf pistols. The level design is often a confusing mess and the save system is a pain. When the game launched, there was no save system; they later implemented one, but it offers limited saves based on difficulty (8 for easy, 3 for normal, none for hard). On top of that, because of its age the game is prone to glitches, bugs and crashes. Let me tell you; there are few things more frustrating in this world than spending fifteen minutes gunning down Xenomorphs, only to be sent back to the last save (or the beginning of the level), because a sliding door accidentally killed you.
See, despite all that, the game is still very enjoyable so many years later, but what tips the scale toward a moderate "no" is that the multiplayer is dead. The game doesn't support dedicated servers and unless you already know of people that play the game, you're out of luck. Ironically, considering this was launched with a campaign and the multiplayer was added later, it actually feels like a multiplayer game with a campaign tacked on as an afterthought. Part of this is that the campaigns are actually short (just hard to beat), but also simply the system that pits three different species with different strengths and weaknesses against one another. It's the Starcraft principle; it makes for balanced online play.
So, here's the thing; if you have played the game before and you're a fan, this is still recommended. It's so cheap (especially during sales) that the nostalgia alone will keep you entertained. But if you're a newcomer looking for rich content, spend your money elsewhere, be it in its most recent sequel or the thematically-similar (but mechanically completely different) Natural Selection 2. Alternatively, get 5 copies on sale and share with friends for parties. That should work.
Either way, do yourselves two favours: 1) Download mods for the thing. There are at least a couple that do wonders for the visuals and are worth your time. 2) If you do tackle the campaign(s), go to Launch Options and add "-unlimitedsaves" (without the brackets). You can imagine what that does.
