You can choose from 3 campaigns: Marine, Xenomorph and Predator and each one is very very different. And what's more, it's challenging, which is great. With each character you play as you must adopt different strategies based on their strengths and weaknesses to successfully hunt each character you fight based on THEIR strengths and weaknesses. For example, as Predator, while you can tear through Marines, they can easily overwhelm you so you adopt stealth. But then, stealth won't work on a Xenomorph because they always know where you are. So you end up having to deploy about seven or eight different strategies across the game to beat your opponents. This is much more in-depth than I expected this game to be.
Having said that, it still holds that arcade feel to it, you can pick it up and put it down whenever because the game knows what it is. Gruesome, stabby, shooty, sneaky, face-munching action. For a bit of meaningless fun for you movie-lovers, look no further.

Eon Altar, a game where your smartphone IS your character, seriously. You have lines to deliver, thoughts to remember, and entities to discover. You download the free app of the same name, and connect it to a local network, such as a simple hotspot tethering, with NO INTERNET CONNECTION REQUIRED. Definitely a huge plus for me, being a peron with no internet access. The game supports 4 players, meaning one copy of Eon Altar can serve as a game for 4 separate people using their own smartphones.
The game runs smoothly, and has no input lag whatsoever. The story line of the game is superb, one of the best story-rich titles I have ever encountered. The game offers free-roaming, but switches to a turn-based action scheme during battles, which enables an exciting and calm game at the same time.
Eon Altar offers a genuine and unique, local co-op experience that brings families, friends, and loved ones together.

I've always heard about Doom 3 being known as not a good Doom game, just a slow-paced horror version of Doom. I think this isn't entirely true, recently I've gone through Doom, II, and 64 and just got done playing 3. The first 3 games are much more fast paced, and about running around in big open areas shooting the crap out of hoards of demons
Now for Doom 3, the gameplay is slower, the enviroment is tighter, and it tries to be more tense with a story. I didn't care much for the story,  the games not forcing you to read the files you pick up or listen to charaters talk. You can just ignore everything for the most part and run through the levels to get to the action. However since the game tries to be more scary it puts enemies in cheap spawns where they can get free hits on you to "jumpscare" you, also the running hardly differs compared to your normal walk speed. But despite all this, the gunplay is still there. You still have alot of weapons to cycle through, the weapons pack a solid punch like older Doom games, after getting abit into the game you get the kind of gameplay with enemies constantly running at you and blasting through them all. Less eneimes compared to the earlier versions, but it feels pretty tight for the kind of space you have to work with. I guess you can see it as a journey where you start out not knowing how to handle the situation, into becoming used to everything happening and just blasting through hoards of demons, turning into a badass space marine that isn't afraid of anything.
I think the game is good, older Doom games are more fun to play but it doesn't mean this one isn't worth playing. I'd say to give it a try, pretty much once you get a shotgun you can go nuts. The game might have been more loved if it was marked as a spin-off instead of a mainline series, no one really posts complaints about Doom RPG being too slow paced.

I can recommend the singleplayer, if that's your thing.
The multiplayer has lots of potential, but is only being abused by the developers and publishers to lure players into spending real money for overpriced ingame stuff that is mostly there to show off or troll other players. Of course, you can earn it all ingame after hours of repetitive grinding. It takes some time until it gets repetitive, but eventually it does.
Then there are lots of hackers, who apparently can do anything they want. Sometimes you will just die, other times you will suddenly have insane amounts of ammunition for a weapon unobtainable in multiplayer (so you actually look like a hacker), if you're unlucky you will just lose money or RP.
There is some freeroam stuff to do, which is not bad, but gets repetitive quickly. Also you need a good amount of money until you are able to start with it. Everything else is locked behind an atrocious lobby system, which will eat up your time. You will spend much time searching for a lobby or have the game search one for you, whereas there are way too few filter options or a *just take me to a lobby that is about to start* feature. You will spend loads of time waiting in lobbies, watching how two players leave out of boredom right in the second the last player to fill the lobby joins. You will spend motherloads of time looking at a faded out top down view on the city, which acts as the loading screen, because each time you enter a lobby or the game decides to kick you out of one or move you to another or when you're about to enter an actual game session this screen turns up. Sometimes it won't even go away. It will just stay there and after five or ten minutes you need to decide whether to restart the game or keep waiting. I've seen loading screens disappear as if nothing was wrong after fifteen minutes of waiting and no indication or whatsoever what it was doing. It is interesting to see that the vanilla version of Doom 3 is still available on Steam despite the fact that a bundle version titled BFG Edition has already been released. That particular pack includes all Doom episodes released so far (with the exception of Doom 4) and Doom 3 is present in a more enhanced, HD version.
Since the game is rather "old" (release date was back in 2004) if you pick this version over the BFG Edition you'll miss out on the achievements and in order to play it in widescreen resolution you need a little workaround (thank god for the community and their useful guides).
It could be argued which version is better; the HD version has a bit too much light and perhaps the shadows are not as crispier as here. The main decision factor is probably the flashlight which is conveniently mounted on the protagonist's shoulder whilst here you need to press a separate button to equip it. You heard it right: using your flashlight and shooting cannot happen at the same time. Some say this adds an unnecessary difficulty factor while others say this increases the terror we got so accustomed to in Doom.
In either case, I am happy to recommend Doom 3; it was certainly an interesting experience back then due to its slow pace and more focus on the story - something a lot of people hated and for them Doom 4 was a godsend. For me it is a classic and while at the time Half Life 2 was better and I believe it successfully dethroned id in the genre Doom 3 was still a major player.
If you don't mind missing out on the achievements and the rest of the classic Doom games you can pick this one instead of the BFG Edition (which also includes 2 expansions to this game).

Tekken is one of those francises that has followed me since childhood. I still have fond memories of playing Tekken 2 way back in the old PSX days. It's been a long road, and not an entirely smooth one. But we're here. Tekken 7. And finally, available on our master race boxes!
I know decent graphics are expected at this point, but they're still worth mentioning. The game is exceptionally beautiful. I would even go so far as to say it's likely the best looking fighting game of year. Yes. Even better than Injustice 2. I'm not sure if it's because I'm still running a 1080p monitor, but I can run the game on ultra with no drop in framerate whatsoever. I'm thinking that maybe Namco might have overestimated the required specs?
In game action feels better than ever too. Unlike most other fighters which seek to reinvent themselves constantly, Tekken adheres to the old notion, 'if it isn't broken, don't fix it. But maybe tweak it here and there'. And tweak they did. You now have things such as rage arts, super armor, and various other things here and there. Also, Akuma from Street Fighter has jumped ship to join the fray. His presence here is important. For years now, almost all fighers have stayed within the realms of 2.5D, with only Dead or Alive 5 being the other fully 3D figher being actively played right now. Akuma, despite mostly staying rigid to his Street Fighter style of gameplay, is a surprisingly fun addition to the roster. Perhaps his presence here could be a turning point for fighting games, where full 3D systems become more common again.
You'll also find that there's just as much to do offine as there is online. That being said, I have a few gripes here. As well as the main story, characters have their own individual stories. That's great, but these chapters are severely lacking in length and depth. Unlike certain other games*coughSTREETFIGHTERFIVEcough*, we have a proper arcade mode to play. My opinion, it would've been better to tack on character endings in arcade mode. Separating them into two separate modes seems kind of pointless. Also, no 8 man team battle! What kind of heresy is this?!
But character customization is where I take the biggest issue with the game. Tekken 6 had the best customization of the series. There, you could mix and match 5 separate bodygroups full of unique clothing items for each character to truly make something your own. Sadly, Tekken 7 seems to be a step further in decline from TTT2's dissapointing offer. There's not much in the way of unique items for each character, and you can't really do much with what little you're given. It's a shame, really. The fight money you earn is intended to be used for the customization suite. But when there isn't much worth buying, fight money seems to lose it's worth.....
....Oh, but on that note, LET'S TALK ABOUT THOSE SWIMSUITS THAT GOT CUT FROM THE WESTERN RELEASE! Roughly a year ago, Katsuhiro Harada announced that our version would not be getting the swimsuit pack, blaming SJW culture for the decision. I'm sorry, but I'm calling bullsh#t. Katrina still has a swimsuit in game you can unlock, and if you pre-ordered and got Eliza, SHE gets a swimsuit too. Add this inconsistency with the fact that Harada hinted that MAYBE we might get them as paid DLC. I am entirely convinced that this decision was NOT influenced by SJW politics, rather they're using it as a boogeyman to mask a bit of nickel and diming of the western audience. Everyone gives Capcom for shady business practices, but seriously. Keep your eyes on these guys. But what's the diff? They were all just retextures of Lili's TTT2 bikini anyways. Give it a few months, and it's likely modders will figure out a way to get them in the game eventually.
Issues aside, I still think that if you're a fan of both Tekken, and fighting games in general, this is definitely worth your purchase.

Aliens versus Predator Classic 2000 is one of my all-time favorite first person shooters. It does tremendous justice to the source material upon which it is based and is one of the finest examples of an excellent game based around movie licenses.
The alien, predator, and marne campaigns all play very differently from one another. The strengths and weaknesses peculiar to each species really make the online multiplayer experience something special, although predators and marines do move absurdly fast during deathmatches. It seems like the developer was trying to balance movement between the species, but doing this by artificially speeding up marines and predators to move as quickly as aliens just seems wrong. Movement speeds are normal in skirmish matches, which I prefer to deathmatches.
Although AVP's online netcode is peer-to-peer based, it is easily the best impementation of P2P netcode I have ever experienced. In fact, it consistently outperforms dedicated servers for other games - even when I play AVP with players from across the world while stationed in mainland China (which has some of the worst internet anywhere).
There is still an online community for this game, and the regular players tend to be very down to earth and friendly. Unfortunately, you may encounter the odd cheater from time to time, but the Steam port allows you to set up private games with your friends. It would have been better if players were given tools to kick and ban cheaters from their games by way of vote, but considering how well native netcode was incorporated into a game this old, it's hard to complain about that (or the lack of native voicechat.)
As great as the online experience is, it's hard for me to say enough positive things about the single player campaigns. While there is a very minimal sense of plot, you do feel like you have purpose to your actions and that all the carnage the unfolds does so for good reason.
The atmosphere and tension in the game are incredible. When ambushed by aliens, you can easily die a sudden death. Aliens pose a very real threat to the player and do not strike exclusively during scripted sequences (like in the game's sequels). What that means is that you'll need to be on your toes at all times while playing this game. Its hard but fair, and that's the way I like it. AVP has treated me to some of the most startling moments I've ever experienced, and it's nice knowing that I can experience those kinds of moments again and again despite how much time I've spent enjoying the game.
If you're going to play the alien campaign, be aware that the very first stage is probably the most difficult one you'll encounter. That's because is so easy to be nearly burned to death from the moment you encounter the first human carrying a molotov cocktail, and there are many of them throughout the stage. Not only are you very likely to be slowly incinerated by their concoctions if they are thrown anywhere in your general vacinity, but also if you kill a human who happens to be carrying one.
As an alien, it's also very easy to get mowed down by stage 1's automated machine gun turrents unless you can find a way to sneak around them. A viable - but also very challenging - alternative to overcoming those obstacles is to crawl on ceilings and dart past the turrents at a 60 degree angle.
It took me many, many replays before I was finally able to develop a good sense of how to overcome stage 1's cocktail-wielding humans and automated machine gun turrents. Had I known that you can enable unlimited saves by saving a command line in the game's launch options, I could have saved myself a lot of frustrating but strangely fun chalenge while trying to beat the first alien stage.
While doing business abroad, I was able to play AVP perfectly with full settings on a friggin' netbook. Not even the original Doom or Heretic can run on that kind of hardware without occasional slowdown when launched with Zandronum or zDoom.
In conclusion, AVP Classic 2000 is one of the very best puchases I have ever made, even though I owned the retail version of the game prior to buying the Steam port for convenient online multiplayer access. Get this game now, even if there is no discount at the time you are reading this review. The game is worth it, and then some. I tip my hat to Rebellion software for this great game.
MY RATING FOR AVP CLASSIC 2000 (ACROSS VARIOUS KEY FACTORS):
Graphics: 7.5 / 10. They were pretty good at the time of the game's release, and there are moments when the game's visuals still inspire awe, like the waterfall at the end of the predator's first stage.
Sound: 10 / 10.
Single-player content: 10 / 10.
Online experience: 9.5 / 10. The native matchmaking system that was incorporated into the 'Classic 2000' port of the game is very good, and the game's netcode is - in my experience - unparalleled. Even though the netcode is P2P-based, it consistently outperformes many dedicated servers supporting other games. The main reason why the game doesn't get a perfect score in this category is because the absence of dedicated servers means that sometimes you have to wait a while until someone joins an online game that you host for lack of being able to find an online match to connect to. Other than incorporating native voice chat and giving players a voting system for banning cheaters / jerks / etc., there isn't much more that I could ask for from the game's excellent multiplayer component.
Plot: 6 / 10. This is the game's weakest link. There really isn't much of a plot to the game, but there are videos that play on monitors as you progress through the single-player modes. You can ignore the videos if you like, but Rebellion deserves credit for incorporating these clips into the game without slowing it down for those who want to focus on action. To be fair, the game intended to showcase atmosphere over plot and really did a fine job in that regard. (It's like the original Quake, albeit with scripted FMV playback that gives purpose to new challenges you experience.)
Gameplay: 10 / 10. Incredible! Play the game and experience the terror, the suspense, and the frantic action for yourself!
Overall: 88 / 100

The game itself isn't terrible in the least. It's got good controls and an almost QUAKE style of movement where you can almost outrun the aliens without any serious impact on accuracy. This is very much an early 2000's shooter, and still retains the charm of games of the era while still being appreciable for the modern times.
The problems come about when it comes to the story mode, primarily. The Marine is probably the best character with a wide array of weapons to choose from, very little platforming necessary, and with probably the minimal amount of save scumming required. The predator come second, because again, diverse weapons and limited platforming, but with the bonus of being able to cloak and use genuine stealth tactics appropriate for the early 2000s. But then comes the Alien. The xenomorph is undoubtedly one of the most unplayable characters, and this seems to be a trend among games featuring the Alien because platforming is a huge deal, which can be a problem. When you're a marine or a predator, you can find your way around because you're only limited to the floor. The alien, meanwhile, can go everywhere there's a surface, which means you'll spend a bunch of time crawling on walls and ceilings and ultimately end up lost without a walkthrough. While all the characters necessitate a walkthrough, because this did come from the age when video games hated telling the player things, it gets even worse when you can literally end up lost in the vents for a good thirty minutes going in circles at about 100 miles per hour.
The combat is pretty solid for all characters. Enemies become easily detatched from their limbs, flames and explosions are catastrophic, and when you hit some dude with lazer forged wristblades he's not gonna have a good time. The marine is exclusively ranged, the alien is exclusively melee, and the predator contains a mix of the two.
The graphics are actually pretty nice for a game made in 2000. Imagine Oblivion or Fallout 3 but with super primitive articulation. The textures can be a bit of a problem, as they never seem to mask when a wall or a floor is outright flat, making it especially hard to find a switch that just blends into the graphic.
All in all, I'd recommend checking a playthrough of the game played in Skirmish mode before actually buying it. It'd be good to get on sale to try out, as it stands on the combat alone, but if you're going to do any of the stories make sure to have a walkthrough available because one can not be faulted for getting stuck in the story.

This is my first review, but will be quite in-depth as I've a lot to say about this game.
I've owned Train Simulator since the days of Railworks, and I've seen how it has changed and progressed over the years. A lot of people have posted in their reviews that there is a lot of DLC, and crucially that it's too expensive. Whilst it is true that there is a lot of DLC, you have to bear in mind that this is only loosely a game in the conventional form, where there may be two or three story-related DLCs. Train Simulator to me, in recent times at least, has become a platform that you buy with a couple of starter routes and then add to based on what you personally enjoy. I agree that trying to collect all of the DLC isn't really the point of TS, and it's also far too much of a financial outlay.
Unfortunately, as has been mentioned previously, not all of the DLC is to the same standard. Some locomotives (routes too, but Locos in particular) appear to have been rushed; whether it's the lack of a passenger view, or the re-use of sounds from another pack (a particularly common theme in the German traction, which often shares a motor whine or other sound), or whether it's just bugs that shouldn't be appearing. Having said that, there is some seriously good stock out there. 3rd party developers play a particularly large role in this - one to mention is Railright's class 40, which is just stunning. I have poured a lot of money into this game, buying countless DLC packs, but I don't actually regret any of them. If I'm being honest, I do think my £17.99 from the 'Return to Maerdy' pack could have been better used elsewhere, but not because it's a poor DLC; more because it's just not my thing and I'm not entirely sure why I bought it.
I do appreciate the free upgrades to the next edition of the game, but not when only the name has changed and I've actually recieved a reduced version of the game, which I'll need to buy year after year to recieve the full benefits of. I think DTG's bug fixing could do with a bit of bug fixing itself, as there seem to be updates every couple of weeks that are mostly just an inconvenience - they never seem to actually fix anything, even if it's an issue that makes a piece of Rolling stock unusable. I highly regard the community support available; someone else will have already had the problem you're experiencing and will have found a solution to it (or if they haven't, at least there's someone else to rant about it with).
My advice to a newcomer to the game is this: Think about what you want to drive, and focus on those only. If you have a particular interest in Germany, why not try the German 1st Class Edition, for example? I also can't stress enough that looking at the ratings for a DLC is not enough! READ the reviews to find out why people did/didn't like it. I read one the other day where somebody had not recommended a 'Pro range' product because it was too complicated? Isn't that what it's designed to do? Also, look around the web a bit if you're not happy with a piece of DLC. Armstrong Powerhouse's sound packs have re-ignited a passion for me for some of the stock purely because it now sounds correct! The class 37 from their Wherry Lines sounds just like it should and NOT like the flatulent splutter from the Kuju model.
Whether you like the sheer tractive effort from UP's Gas Turbine, the precision of the modern Deutsche Bahn, tearing along the East Coast of England above 100mph in a class 91, or weaving your way through the alps on the Glacier express there is something here for every Railway enthusiast. Bugs are tedious, but you can always refund stuff you don't like!
Still don't understand why most simulator-type games have to be so resource hungry. Is a pretty fun game, but I think it could be engineered a lot more efficiently.
If you buy the standard version (ideally when on sale) then it's not a bad game. Just avoid the dlc.

Gameplay:
Portal Knights is an action game with click-heavy auto targeting combat that allows you to roll away from enemy attacks. When you kill enemies, there is a chance that the enemy will drop a portal shard - when you have enough portal shards, you can finish crafting a portal, placing the portal pieces in a Minecraft, block-placing fasion, you can teleport to the next small arena for harvesting portal shards. Eventually, there is a boss.
That's pretty much it. There is a whole system of materials, a workbench and furnace to craft more advanced items, and a whole host of decorative items from knight statues to different types of doors. Players barely ever need to touch any of it. Mechanically, combat feels clumsy. The movement and dodge roll on your character never seems to cooperate with the environment, like sometimes I'd end up on top of a bush or fall down a one block deep hole and get stuck for a second, but it didn't matter much since the enemies are nearly brain dead. The only ones you have to watch out for are the ones with quick lightning attacks in close quarters. Sometimes there are dungeons that go deep within the floating island that is each area, but the movement isn't tuned for indoors, so to fight enemies I just ate the damage and healed up when necessary.
I picked a wizard and used a magic wand to fight enemies. I think there are spells but after a handful of levels, and realizing the crafting/building portion of the game is completely unnecessary, I didn't acquire any before quitting. I actually think the minecraft part of the game hinders the game overall, as the block-based nature of the environments make them frustrating to navigate, and placing blocks is glitchy, as sometimes when building a dirt pole to ascend cliffs, I would occasionally place a dirt block directly above me, rather than below. The level generator did not produce anything inspiring during my play time.
Aesthetics
The game looks good for a block-based game. I appreciated the variety of enemies and how well-animated they were, but the enemies looked dumb standing there humping a wall or bumping up against me. My favorite was probably the turtle who would shell up and roll toward you, as video game turtles do. The foliage sometimes made the areas hard to navigate, and I'm just talking about the grass on top of dirt tiles, not to mention the various cotton shrubs, berry bushes, and agave plants that adorn the different grassy and desert environments. The whimsical look and tunes often reminded me of Fable.
Early-Access Verdict
No. I don't think it's Early Access that hurts this game. Portal Knights is one of the most polished Early Access games I've played, but the end goal of Keen seems to be adding MORE stuff, and I just don't think that's going to do the game any favors. The crafting is unnecessary, and without it you just have a barebones, tedious action game that wouldn't be any better with or without friends.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky starts off with a terrible first impression. The main menu not only looks almost exactly like the first game's, but even the main menu music is the same. This isn't necessarily bad, but it's like a sick foreshadowing to the travesty that is this game.
GRAPHICS
Visually, this game is fairly good. However, it's nothing impressive. The first game allowed great immersion, even if you were only playing at the medium graphical settings. This game, however, fails to draw you into the setting, and I just groaned in contempt when I reached the end, where even the legendary and infamous Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant failed to stimulate my visual senses.
GAMEPLAY
The game in terms of gameplay is definitely superior to the first entry. With more accurate weaponry and less shooting-through-walls glitches, I found myself not getting nearly as infuriated with the game as I did with the first. However, the survival/horror was absent entirely. The mutants were nearly nonexistent, whereas in the first game I was constantly on edge with the terror of the fantastic and varied enemies. But in this game, I found myself bored with fighting too many human enemies. Still, the mechanics are far superior than the first game, and I can give this props for that.
MULTIPLAYER
Don't play this mode. Please, for the love of all that is good and sane in this world, NEVER PLAY THIS MODE. Weapon balance is nearly nonexistent, maps and game modes are recycled from the first game. On top of that, you'll be hard pressed to find anyone playing this game's multiplayer. Stay clear of it.
STORY
The game's story takes a massive hit. It is nothing more than a pale shadow in comparison to Shadow of Chernobyl. This game takes place one year before the events of the first game and tells the story of the zone and how Strelok came to be where he was in the first game. Sounds great on paper, but is overall disappointing. The game says multiple times that there are new areas to explore in the game because emissions have changed the radiation levels around the zone. This is complete and utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥T. There are a total of two new places to explore in the game. Otherwise, you visit literally EVERY SINGLE LOCATION FROM THE FIRST GAME. Actually, even less than that! The fact that I completed this game's story, while completing a few of the dull, uninspiring optional missions along the way, in a whopping 6 hours, proves that the developers were simply lazy with the game. You will shoot hundreds of humans all around the same places you've been to in the first game, and then sometimes shoot a mutant, repeat. Strelok is barely in the game at all, very little of the first game's supposed background history is given in this game, and it fails to inspire and enthrall like the first game. There was no mystery, horror, or intrigue throughout the course of this painfully short campaign, and it felt like a chore to go through.
VERDICT
This game is $10 U.S. dollars not worth spending. This was a money-grabber after the success that was S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl. There was so much potential in this game that was simply wasted, and I was painfully reminded throughout the course of the game that I wasted money on a game that I will probably never play again. Make no mistake, this is one of the worst video games that I have ever played, a copy-and-paste of the original with less content and a worthless story.

Nowhere near ready yet.  However I see it's been in development since Oct 2013, so I have little hope.
- Physics are terrible.  For a snow game, this is imperative to get right, but they're weird as hell.  Keep mashing the button that makes your character boost himself forward, and
.  Then you have the issue where you don't seem to accelerate correctly going downhill, but can carry that momentum indefininitely over flat or rough terrain.  You can test this by skiing/boarding to the bottom of the mountain, through a village, then just keep going through the rolling hills between the mountains.
- Multiplayer doesn't work.  Period.  If you're in the Eastern US, don't bother.  You can try to join US East servers and the connection icon will spin indefinitely with no way to quit other than alt+F4.  Or you can join a European server with ~160 ping and stutter every two seconds, to the point where it's unplayable.  This is a major flaw since it's advertised as multiplayer.
- no map or compass.  The freeroam portion hinges on being able to find new areas, but you have literally no way of telling where you are or where you've been.  From my research this has been a known demand to the devs since at least Oct 21st 2013, but in a news post on their site they say they have no idea how to implement an interactive map.  That's a very bad sign.
- instead of letting you take off your gear and walking if you want to explore something uphill,
To go up a hill.  Assuming, of course, you can't trick the physics engine to send you uphill anyway.
- Solo mode is utterly empty.  No life at all, no AI skiiers or boarders, you're the only one in a massive mountain range.  Very eery and ties into why having a broken multiplayer mode is a bad thing.
- No snow physics and your equipment is always clipping.  Minor annoyance more than anything; it constantly looks like your character is riding across the snow in just their boots.  Your trail is just a 2D mask placed over the surface that also clips into the terrain.  This is a practice used since the 90s, by 2017 the devs should at least introduce some terrain deformation and be able to keep your character high enough above the terrain to not clip.  I only bring this up because literally every snowboarding/skiing game I can think of in the past decade has done this...
In conclusion:  Very rough, very empty, very broken, from what I understand the devs are taking the money and running with it.
Good concept, bad outcome.

AVP Classic is quite a primitive game, even for FPS' of its time - you have some weapons and some poorly-lit hallways, and you must traverse said hallways using said weapons to kill your attackers, completing some minor objectives to open the path to the end. Simple as that. Half-Life came out a year or so before this, and unlike many games that then followed, AVP aschews almost all pretence of a narrative. In this way it feels like a darker, scarier Doom. It is a literal run-and-gun game, and incomparible to almost anything contemporary, even to it's own sequel, which is a vastly different experience.
AVP is also brutally difficult, and requires the player to have fast reflexes while also keep their wits about them as the blaze through the corridors. Kill anything that moves, and kill it quick. This makes for a tense and frenetic game, and facehuggers whipping out of no-where to one-hit-kill me always makes me jump.
This won't be everyone's cup of tea, especially if you're migrating backwards from AVP2, hoping for more of the same. But with the few tools at its disposal, playing AVP is a uniquely exhilirating experience and rewards a skillful (and lucky) player with the few minutes of well-earned rest at the end of each level before the next one begins.
I recommend this if you have a few bucks to spare and you're after a fast, simple, challenging FPS.

Mount & Blade: Warband, in my opinion, is the most innovative medieval fighting game released in this last 6 years. This game uses mouse movement to control your players' attacks and defenses (unless otherwise toggled), unlike any other game in this genre (with the exception of the War Of Roses). The singleplayer and the multiplayer are two different experiences using the same combat system. Singleplayer is the more complete RPG exerience, with customizable armies, companions, nations, entirely open map, and an unforgiving, uncaring world. (Quite realistic.) Multiplayer is mostly combat, with the exception of a customizable avatar and what you bring into combat (essentially your loadout). This game almost reaches it's full potential if you're willing to modify it (singleplayer, anyways).
PROS: Extensive RPG experience, Original combat system, Singleplayer/Multiplayer, Large & active playerbase, realistic, Globally played, Difficulty is easily adjusted, Entirely Open Word, Decent price, Almost 2 games in 1.
CONS: O.K. graphics (This isn't Skyrim, folks), Tendancy to house Bugs, Glitches, and other Parasites, , Difficult to learn, Addictive ; )
In CONCLUSION, this game is worth picking up if you're a true RPG/Fighting fan.

After a few hours in, I really like the game and how the story plays out. It's very similar to its prequel "The Stick of Truth" with some new and improved mechanics. If you know what South Park is, then you know what kind of absurd humor to expect from this series.
While the game is good, basically everything surrounding it is utter trash. My "Not recommended" rating is based on:
- The game not starting properly. You need to hit ALT + ENTER to disable full screen and set it to "Windowed Fullscreen" once you manage to get to the game options menu. As far as I've read community discussions, it seems like literally everyone is affected by that bug. For 60 bucks, you should be able to expect a basic minimum of quality control!
- Forces UPlay on your PC. I don't want that, I don't need that, just get lost Ubisoft.
- Extremely annoying self-advertisement for some Ubisoft Creation Club IN THE GAME. There are items in your inventory that are marked with some "Ubisoft exclusive"-label that fill your inventory space but can only be used if you join the Ubisoft club.
- In the same vein, paying 60 bucks and feeling like not getting the full game.
Overall, it's just an extremely hamfisted attempt from Ubisoft to get more money and branding out of South Park.
Edit after completing the game:
I took about 17 hours to complete the game. A large part of that was spent on walking between locations since the fast travel points are somehow placed in a way that they barely save time when moving between commonly visited places.
While the humor and plot was in typical South Park style, some of it just felt flat and just didn't hit the mark in my opinion. Where "The Stick of Truth" had some hilarious moments that I still remember today, there wasn't really anything that stood out in this game. The ending was also very unsatisfying and just felt rushed.
Overall, I'd not recommend this game. If, at one point, this game drops below 20 bucks, it might be worth the price. For the time being, not so much.

Do note that this re-bundle DOES include the Gold maps. So there's that. If you're looking for a fast-paced, classic and inexpensive game to have a taste of what it was like back in 1999, this is for you.
Pros:
-Many levels over three campaigns, short, straight forward but tough
-Unadulterated challenge
-Multiplayer can still hold up with friends, play it over GOG and/or Steam's network
Cons:
-Frustrating xeno AI and movement
-I found a game breaking bug (save related)
-Weak if any story
You'll end up blasting through each mission but thankfully they're numerous and challenging to beat even on the Medium difficulty setting, and you might get irritatedat how the xenos apparently fly around rather than lunge towards you. Still, you can die pretty quickly as any species and so can they, so make your shots count. Thankfully, the game is somewhat generous when it comes to giving you items, with each playthrough being inherently different as spawns and numbers change each time.
I've to say that even for 1999's standard, it wasn't the best looking game, so it hasn't aged particularily well, but it's not the worst either. The music is great as is expected for any game in this franchise, and multiplayer seems optimized well enough. It's actually one of the better games in the Aliens and/or Predator series simply because it's unadulterated and simple fun. The three campaigns seem to be cleverly set up from annoying, to hard to satisfying (as the predator), so I'd suggest playing it in that order.

The only good thing about this game is the bulletcam. Watching your enemies testicles explode or faces get just destroyed is extremely amusing. You'd think it'd get old fast but I enjoyed it through the entire campaign. Which brings us to the first issue.
The campaign is way too short. I completed it in a night.
The weapon selection and customization options are lacking, and some rifles that are unlocked at the very start of the game are just better than others in every possible way. It's pointless to have a bunch of unlocked rifles where some of them are just♥♥♥♥♥♥
The detection system for enemies is glitchy, especially vehichles and muffled sounds from planes.
Any time you damage a vehichle, even if its with a landmine and you are on the other side of the map, it knows exactly where you are instantly and you suddenly get "attacking" status and all enemies know where you are. Plus any time it loses sight of you and you come back into it's field of vision it sees you within a fraction of a second, turns the cannon absurdly fast (think like one of those weird garrysmod videos) and fires a shot. All within about one second.
Planes fly overhead on most missions periodically providing sound cover for your shots, but while you can hear the plane flying by with the same noise and volume every time, you only get sound cover from it some of the time. Also on at least one of the levels the planes don't seem to fly overhead if you're stationary. Only when moving around the map making them useless to help you snipe which is their entire purpose.
The game is full of invisible walls, cliffs that should be easily scalable but are instead impassable AND the terrain is unrealistic. So like, the worst of both worlds.
Many of the good sniping points, hell even most of them, are inaccessible by stealth until you've taken out half or more of the enemies that you'd want to be in the sniping point to take out. I don't feel so much like a sniper in this game as a grunt.
There are an unrealistic number of explosives EVERYWHERE. EVERYTHING EXPLODES. And yet somehow the explosives are almost never in a useful spot.
In the difficulty screen they try to boast that there's a difficulty level for sniping purists. Enemies that work together to root you out and hunt you down, and gravity affecting bullet trajectories. First of all, what about wind? you're gonna put gravity in but not wind? But the real problem is the enemies on the highest difficulty are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The AI is average at best. They don't work together to hunt you down, they occassionally walk in a straight line towards your position, always hitting traps and almost always by themselves.
I've never been flanked by enemies trying to trap me, I've never had enemies avoid or disarm my traps after they saw their buddy get blown up by the first one, or despite the fact that the trap is an anti tank mine sitting in plain sight. And much of the time I can sit in one position, pick off two enemies, wait for the detection bar to go down, pick of two more, and repeat till all enemies are dead, even though they heard where my shot came from, they never come to investigate.
Overall the game was fun but very disappointing for something that supposedly was aiming to be difficult and realistic. If you're going to buy it, buy it for the gimmick, the bulletcam. It's so ♥♥♥♥ing funny.

I like the sound and music design - it's low key enough to not get grating as you try the same areas over and over again. I also thing the visuals make it way easier to tell what is going on then the previous version of Spelunky. Unfortunately, if you're someone who value their enjoyment/hour, I just can't recommend this game.
It's too frustrating. Games like Super Meat Boy are fun because you make a mistake, die, and get to try again. In this game, you don't get to do that. Furthermore, when you make mistakes, the punishment varies wildly due to the stupid hitstun mechanic that causes you to bounce around and inevitably go into some spikes or something that instantly kills you. Furthermore, the actions you take just don't feel precise enough compared to other platformers. Frequently, I found myself dying because of a throw not going where I wanted or slighlty over or under shooting a jump or things like that, which are all due to the really odd physics of the movement and throwing and other interactions. It feels difficult to get comfortable with the physics and, though I've played a lot of the older version, I still don't feel like I can get the game to consistently do what I want.
If you play games because you want to have fun and feel a sense of accomplishment, this game is just too frustrating and doesn't have enough fun per minute to justify itself over the myriad other platformers.
Oh, and co-op sucks. The game seems like it was designed around single player and co-op was just tacked on. Honestly, I'm sure it's fun to mess around with, but if you want a solid co-op experience this is not the game for that.

Good game, needs more work but that is what early access is.
Pros:
-Graphics are wonderful
-Music is nice (granted repetitive, ended up just turning it off)
-Animations are well designed (although if you use an item then switch to a weapon fast enough it will continue that animation but do the weapon's ability)
-Hardly any bugs (or I'm that lucky)
-Progression is obvious
Neutral:
-Combat locks your ability to jump by replacing your jump button with a dodge, which sometimes refuses to go up 1 block (the heigh you can walk up). One can, however, exit combat mode by right clicking, giving the ability to jump freely. Annoying that dodge isnt another button, but atleast they made a workaround.
-Combat can become bland at times. It is just like Pokemon or any game with a 'weak to ___' feature. Once you learn how to exploit a creature's weakness it makes combat predictable and fast. Good for grinding, but I like a challenge.
-World isn't exactly "randomly generated." Not sure if it is suppose to be but there are plenty of islands to explore.
-Multiple islands almost discourage sandbox building. Because there are so many islands to discover you almost don't want to build until you search them all, but you can freely change your Home Island at any time so no restrictions on that.
-Classes in a creative sandbox game. This isn't so big of an issue as I am making it sound but character classes are rather linier with you being able to choose a 'this-or-that' every other 5 levels for a skill. Stats are also automatically placed so one can't experiment. And everyone can equip anything, so classes only restrict stats and skills.
-Boss battles are dull and predictable. When I faced the first boss I felt a sense of excitement and fear thinking 'what if I can't defeat it' the entire time. It however played like any classic game where it has a weakness and almost presents it on a silver platter. Oh man are they pretty to look at, great colors and animation to boot.
Cons:
-Lack of content (obvious early access con so don't take it at face value, just letting you know whats up.)
-No server list or Steamworks.
-Up to 4 player co-op. (maybe obvious set up for a console release so I get afraid of them abandoning PC once tested)
-Game is set up for quests but so far nothing past tutorial short of 'take on all the bosses and discover all the islands.'
-No penalty for dying (yet). Not a big deal but I like to know there will be consequences for failing.
-All Item's share the same cooldown. (Hp Potions, Mana Potions, Sharpening Stone [repairs a weapon's durability btw])
-No cosmetic slot. Again not a big deal but I love the looks of certain items while I hate the ones with good stats.
-Creative character customization, but looks like choosing male or female doesn't matter when they share the same cosmetic appearances and voices. (Maybe armor looks different on them, I don't know. I try to stay as true to myself as possible to make it an extension of me [ego])
-No point in crafting any tools other than copper, they all mine at the same rate. Havn't tested any other tool since there is no restriction for mining the highest tier with a copper pickaxe.
When it all boils down this game is really great, but I feel before moving on the game needs to figure the rest of its core mechanics first. I can see a great game deep down, and maybe it'll be my alltime favorite sandbox. Until then I hope the developers do things right and with the community at large.

Easy to obtian loot and resource gathering at the beginning leaves you annoyed later when the mining becomes more grind orientated. By the end you relize that just farming the final boss is faster than mining ore nodes.
The game has a ton of great features but most are just the beginning of what I would like to see. This game is also in some need of more backers or work, it has the potential to be as big as terraria. I hope 505 and keen bring this game into its full potential.

Mount & Blade: Warband, in my opinion, is the most innovative medieval fighting game released in this last 6 years. This game uses mouse movement to control your players' attacks and defenses (unless otherwise toggled), unlike any other game in this genre (with the exception of the War Of Roses). The singleplayer and the multiplayer are two different experiences using the same combat system. Singleplayer is the more complete RPG exerience, with customizable armies, companions, nations, entirely open map, and an unforgiving, uncaring world. (Quite realistic.) Multiplayer is mostly combat, with the exception of a customizable avatar and what you bring into combat (essentially your loadout). This game almost reaches it's full potential if you're willing to modify it (singleplayer, anyways).
PROS: Extensive RPG experience, Original combat system, Singleplayer/Multiplayer, Large & active playerbase, realistic, Globally played, Difficulty is easily adjusted, Entirely Open Word, Decent price, Almost 2 games in 1.
CONS: O.K. graphics (This isn't Skyrim, folks), Tendancy to house Bugs, Glitches, and other Parasites, , Difficult to learn, Addictive ; )
In CONCLUSION, this game is worth picking up if you're a true RPG/Fighting fan.

Essential things to make the game playable:
-Accuracy mod: remove RNG accuracy.
-Antialiasing on DX10 and above set to 2x or downsample on your own; use SGSSAA on DX9 or an injection--SMAA (SweetFX) forces the game to DX9. So use eFX if you want DX10.
-God rays mod: it makes the game look awesome (and it didn't affect performance in my case).
Also, don't install Shaders max mod; it has a lot of compatiblity issues and it affects the performance negatively instead (as the mod author states that it affected half of the users).

Summary: Don't waste your time with this outdated, dysfunctional piece of crap. If you want to play it, install mods BEFOREHAND and WASTE a large amount of time. I really liked it at first and liked its aesthetics; I am simply disgusted at the fact that I wasted over 5 hours trying to get the damn game to work after installing a couple of mods, and trying to deal with the shooting mechanics. I am 10+ hours into the game and I will not restart just to install a mod that is essential to play the weakest entry in the series.
I will start with the most important thing in  video games: gameplay and how functional it is. Clear Sky is not only the weakest entry in the series (supposedly lacking in atmosphere but it is my first Stalker game), but it is utterly unplayable (once you start fighting things and shotguns miss at point blank range) and makes you wonder if the developers/game designers have been exposed to an excessive amount of radiation to even THINK of such game mechanics--the stupid RNG accuracy.
First and foremost, shots are based on RNG, which means you will miss 30ft shots and have to waste a magazine at least to land a SHOT; enemies have a huge amount of HP and they have absurd accuracy and aggro mechanics. I am obviously talking about the hardest difficulty in the game, but shooting is dysfunctional either way; the game is simply boring on lower difficulties. Also weapon jamming (RNGesus), bad maps/no cover when you attack a base, stealth doesn't work properly, FRIGGIN SWAY THAT LASTS HALF A SECOND WHEN YOU MOVE AND AIM, slow aim, slow weapon switching, slow reload...etc. The combat is ****.
With that said, you HAVE to install mods in order to have fun on normal difficulties or something functional on the highest difficulties, which brings us to how crappy is the game when it comes to modding. You will spend hours just troubleshooting and figuring out in the end that there is some shader incompatibilty or some crappy dll file missing. And the worst of all is having to restart a new game when you install an overhaul or other types of mods.
Another point is the optimization and lack of a proper Antialiasing. The latter completely destroys the performance when you max out the game on DX10.1. I ended up with a much better game that runs on high frame rate and looks good with godrays  mod, but jaggies and transparent object edges are there; 2x is the most subtle option. Trying to use SMAA or FXAA injections means you have to use DX9, so good luck making a decision there.
The good point is that the game does feel and look atmospheric, but the combat is an utter piece of crap. The best course of action is to play CoP or SoC (if you can bear with wasting time trying to mod that crap).

A very fluid and engrossing top-down turn-based coop game. After getting past the tutorial and the lore lesson the gameplay speed picks up quite nicely. As players become more familiar with the controls and their character playstyle the adventure actually gains real traction. The only obstacle for the speed and story comprehension lies with the player participation with dialogue.
The biggest gameplay obstacle I can imagine is the coop dialogue. Players actually need to speak their dialogue to the group because player characters are not voiced and the script is displayed on only that player's phone/tablet. If you are familiar with roleplaying and speaking aloud for your character this a non-issue however if you're not into reading and speaking then the adventure is going to be rough. Speaking character dialogue is required as it holds important plot information and character development of each player. Character dialogue is where Eon Altar can shine.
Each player character has their own story, some of which is displayed secretly on the respective player's phone. Inevitably each player will be questing for their own reasons and keeping their motives to themselves thus creating some humorous divisions amongst players. Some players may want to venture West while another player may want venture East because they secretly know that is where the plunder lies. The division creates unscripted roleplaying dialogue between the players which makes for a hilarious battle of wit.
After a playthrough or two the secrets between characters disappear. Eon Altar still holds strong with combat, level design, and leveling up.
Pros:
+Level Design is clean and fresh. Maps are not too cluttered or too empty. The atmosphere really comes together as players reach farther into the game.
+Combat is super fluid and seamless when players know what they are doing
+Ability to trade resources between players helps the group level up if they are willing to share the wealth
+Spells and attacks are appealing
+Players can drop in and out
+Gear does not exist; instead players upgrade their skills and attributes. This removes the tediousness seen in other games involving picking up gear and trying them all on
+Buying and upgrading new skills and attributes is easy. Having to decide how to spend resources effectively adds to the sense value of each for the character as a whole
Cons:
-The beginning of the game is so full of lore it feels suffocating
-Dialogue can be a bit of a snooze, cheesy, or even long-winded. Everything can be skipped but on a first playthrough skipping dialogue really kills the adventure comprehension. Fortunately the dialogue does thin out after awhile
-Leveling up is at first is difficult because stats are not well explained. Each tree uses different stats and it's difficult to remember which are which. For example Agility can provide Accuracy on one tree but the other tree Agility is used for Defense. Switching characters or playing a new campaign can be confusing.
-Text is small especially for personal quests.
-Being secret about personal quests can make completing them impossible. Personal quests grant level up points and it can be frustrating trying to open 7/7 large treasure chests when the other 3 players just want the chests for the loot.
Other thoughts:
-Characters can't be chosen twice. Players need to pick different characters
-I don't feel like I connect with any of the character playstyles. They are all fine but I personally don't feel the connection

Eon Altar is something amazing.
Up to four player co-op? NICE! Reading up on your skills and abilities and upgrading your equipment without slowing the rest of the party down? YES, THANK YOU. Local Co-op without the need for multiple controllers or PC's? HELL YEAH! Secret goals and motives for your player characters? AWESOME.
Eon Altar, from techonological point of view, is truly marvelous.
The game itself is pretty basic old-school dungeon crawling arpg with solid design:
The loot you find will either be resources, which you use to upgrade your equipment (or craft potions), or consumables. While I normally enjoy comparing weapons and armour and pondering, which one I should equip, the fact that Eon Altar has basically none of that is refreshing, and makes the gameplay a lot friendlier to a casual player. There's no real inventory management either, which further makes the game and interface simplier to learn and navigate.
Calling Eon Gate "simple" or "dumbed down", though, would be insulting. Each character has three skill trees and two equipment trees which unlock various abilities and bonuses, and unlocking different paths can make the same character perform in a very different manner.  The combat is semi-turn based: First you and your allies act, then the enemies, and this system gives surprising flexibility to tactics when acting as a team.
I wholeheartedly recommend Eon Altar. The voice acting is good, the atmosphere is nice, and the game offers, by itself, a solid dungeon crawling experience. Add in the fact that you can play it with our friends, with just one game, one PC, and a couch (and your mobile phones, obviously) - this is probably one of the best games I've bought this year.
Based on playing through the prologue, the implementation and writing are light and fun, the tactics are intriguing, and my entire group was excited to play again!

After a few hours in, I really like the game and how the story plays out. It's very similar to its prequel "The Stick of Truth" with some new and improved mechanics. If you know what South Park is, then you know what kind of absurd humor to expect from this series.
While the game is good, basically everything surrounding it is utter trash. My "Not recommended" rating is based on:
- The game not starting properly. You need to hit ALT + ENTER to disable full screen and set it to "Windowed Fullscreen" once you manage to get to the game options menu. As far as I've read community discussions, it seems like literally everyone is affected by that bug. For 60 bucks, you should be able to expect a basic minimum of quality control!
- Forces UPlay on your PC. I don't want that, I don't need that, just get lost Ubisoft.
- Extremely annoying self-advertisement for some Ubisoft Creation Club IN THE GAME. There are items in your inventory that are marked with some "Ubisoft exclusive"-label that fill your inventory space but can only be used if you join the Ubisoft club.
- In the same vein, paying 60 bucks and feeling like not getting the full game.
Overall, it's just an extremely hamfisted attempt from Ubisoft to get more money and branding out of South Park.
Edit after completing the game:
I took about 17 hours to complete the game. A large part of that was spent on walking between locations since the fast travel points are somehow placed in a way that they barely save time when moving between commonly visited places.
While the humor and plot was in typical South Park style, some of it just felt flat and just didn't hit the mark in my opinion. Where "The Stick of Truth" had some hilarious moments that I still remember today, there wasn't really anything that stood out in this game. The ending was also very unsatisfying and just felt rushed.
Overall, I'd not recommend this game. If, at one point, this game drops below 20 bucks, it might be worth the price. For the time being, not so much.

First a word of caution for all those who don't plan on buying a 360 controller:
This game is indeed at parts unplayable without a proper two-stick joypad.
I found in my drawer, an old Mega Drive-fashioned joypad that came with a 3.5" floppy and after installing the x360ce wrapper , mapping as many as keys as possible to it, I started doing thumb, pinky and elbow acrobatics trying to achieve simple things. It was long, repetitive, and challenging. Lots of falling off cliffs why trying to keep all my 12 fingers working but towards the end (and it took me many days to reach that - much more than the 3 hours that steam reports)) I realized that most of the time it's much easier NOT to use a joypad (unless you have a 360 one in which case the game is indeed short). There are 2-3 points where you have to use a pad, but for the most part it's more playble with the keyboard. So key that in mind.
Having said all that, the game was a beauty! Crazy graphics, crazy world. A sad story, but a nice one nonetheless and not too cliche. The game is short (unless you handicap yourself with the abovementioned tricks) but the whole world is so rewarding that you could think it as a beatiful interactive movie (and much longer one). With that in mind, it's worth any price (let's say below 20euro)!

I'd never encoutered a rougelike before. Never knew what the term meant till Spelunky. And now I totally get the appeal.
Spelunky plays like a great side scrolling platformer. Maps randomly generate everytime you play through and the options to get to the end of each map are expansive. Having limited health and resources adds to the tension of the game and players have to balance the urge to speed run and resource management.
The controls are sharp. I played on both the keyboard and 360 controller and highly recommend the latter, but it's not required.
The graphics have a nice clean animation sytle to them and I love the fact I'm given the choice of whom to rescue (woman, man, dog). And while the alternate unlockable playable characters are nothing more than new skins, unlocking them all does take some effort.
My biggest complaint/recommdation: don't play this right after Super Meat Boy or any other speed runner. This is not that type of game. You will die. Alot. And it'll take a long time to beat the game if that's your mentality.

With endless replayability Spelunky is consistently challenging but rarely unfair, and shames current AAA titles with their endless focus on hyper realistic graphics and multiple game mode by being simple, focussed and brilliant at what it does.
The Daily Challenge is just the icing on the cake. It forces you to get better at the game and you can feel that progress. It's completely satisfying and completely frustrating at the same time. Potentially my favorite game on Steam (at least in the top 3), Spelunky exudes polish from every angle.  The initial road is punishing and extreme, and there is some trial-and-error involved with learning the game's levels and traps, but once they are ingrained in your mind, you'll find yourself breezing through much of the game. An absolute must-play!

What could be said about Spelunky that hasn't been said yet? Yes, it's very hard. But yes, it's one of the most enjoyable games I've ever played. Thanks to its randomly generated levels, the replayability is almost infinite. What's absolutely delightful about Spelunky is that it's one of those "perfect" games. That means that you'll always know why you lost a game, and how you could improve. There are hundreds of tiny tips and tricks to know and discover, and the "secret" levels are always a joy to go through.
Spelunky can please the most hardcore players, but it also allows a more casual gameplay. People will either want to complete the game as fast as possible, or with the biggest amount of gold, or simply try and beat the final boss. In the end, what's the most amazing thing about this game is that you won't necessarily play it for its entended purpose (beat the game, deliver damsels, get treasures..), but rather for the journey you'll embark whenever you press Start.
Absolutely amazing game, I couldn't recommend it enough.

Similar to Cube World and Minecraft in playability (minus the combat system) and has a certain appeal to it graphically that Dungeon Defenders had. For the price I can safely say it's worth every penny.
Pros:
The game runs flawlessly from what I've experienced
Enough content to satisfy the pricetag, even if it is somewhat linear
Beautiful graphics
Little to no bugs so far
Easy to understand UI and progression
Cons:
Combat system (Only because you have to finish/wait for an existing action to to start/finish before dodging or anything else. This could easily be remedied with instant casting and existing action cancellation when another is triggered.)
44 islands so far and it is a little misleading on the sandbox tagging/advertising (the game generates randomly upon a new world but the islands are very small and linear to a degree, don't expect open world or the more normal sandbox titles out there)
Fps is locked at 60 and no higher (not a major issue since it's 60 fps after all and the game runs smoothly anyways)
NO key rebinding currently (though controller support is coming at least)
All in all it's the worth money and even at its current state you could easily get 50+ hours out of this.

Verdict (tl;dr): 9/10 The game is awesome. In fact, I think it might just be the best fighting game I have ever played. Not 10 out of 10, because it has some things missing. Do not let the low user review rating decieve you: most of the negative reviews don't review the game, but only its launch.
Gameplay and combat: Gameplay is the most important aspect of a fighting game. And in this field Mortal Kombat X truly shines. The movesets are interesting and fluid, and the fights have a really nice pace. The combat mechanisms are a little bit more complex than in MK9, which in my opinion is a good thing, but then again, kombos are pretty easy to learn, so something for everyone here. As a downside some of the moves allow some very cheesy tactics, but this is common in fighting games in general.
All the characters have three different stances from which you pick one before the fight. The stances change some special moves and the way the character is played. Its impact differs from character to character.
Story: No spoilers here, but the story is good for a fighting game. It's not a novel by G.R.R. Martin, but it kept me interested. I was actually surprised how well some of the characters were written.
Roster: The roster is missing out some characters I would have loved to play (for example Baraka), but it's not a huge issue. The game and story has to move forward, right? All in all the roster is full of interesting characters, and some of the new ones really shine.
Performance: Some people have had big performance issues, but I for one get a solid 60fps and everything has been smooth on high settings after I updated to amd's newest beta CCC (Rig: i5 3570k, HD7950 3gb, 8gb ram). There should be more options, for example more AA options. Now there's only FXAA which some people find bad.
Multiplayer: Sometimes it takes a long, long time to find a ranked match online, which sucks. Other than that the online matches have been good. Local multiplayer feels very limited. Tag teams are missing. I would also want to be able to form a local multiplayer team and fight online against other teams. But no.
